| Must call sites annotate it?                     | No, it is inferred   | Often, when ambiguous          |
| Typical role                                     | Output (`Item`, `Output`, `Target`) | Input (`Rhs`, `From<T>`) |

> Key Takeaways
> - An associated type is a type placeholder that each implementation fills in
>   exactly once.
> - Use it when the related type is determined by the implementor (an output);
>   use a generic parameter when the caller should choose (an input).
> - Refer to it as `Self::Item` or `T::Item`, and constrain it with
>   `Trait<Item = X>` or `where T::Item: Bound`.
> - Bounds on the declaration (`type Item: Display;`) let default methods rely on
>   those capabilities.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `Iterator` for a `Fibonacci` struct with `type Item = u64` and print
>    the first ten values with `.take(10)`.
> 2. Write `fn longest<I>(it: I) -> Option<String> where I: Iterator<Item =
>    String>` that returns the longest string.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Iterator` defined with `type Item` instead of as
>    `Iterator<T>`? (Hint: how many different item types should one iterator be
>    able to produce, and what would type inference have to do at every
>    `.next()` call?)

#### Associated Constants

Sometimes what varies between implementors is not behavior but a *value*: the
number of sides of a shape, the symbol of a unit, the maximum size of a buffer. You
could expose it through a method, `fn sides() -> u32 { 4 }`, but a method is not a
compile-time constant and cannot be used where the compiler needs one.

Associated constants solve this. A trait declares `const NAME: Type;`, optionally
with a default value, and each impl provides the value. They are accessed through
the type, `T::NAME` or `Self::NAME`, never through an instance, and they are
evaluated at compile time like any `const`.

They pair especially well with the marker types from Chapter 4.4: a zero-sized
`Feet` type has no fields, but it can still carry `NAME = "ft"` and a conversion
factor as constants.

There are limits. A generic constant cannot yet be used as an array length
(`[u8; T::SIZE]` inside a generic function does not compile on stable Rust), and a
trait with associated constants cannot be used as a trait object (Section 5.3).

```rust
trait Unit {
    const NAME: &'static str;               // required constant
    const PER_METER: f64;
    const PRECISION: usize = 2;             // constant with a default
}

struct Meters;
struct Feet;

impl Unit for Meters {
    const NAME: &'static str = "m";
    const PER_METER: f64 = 1.0;
}

impl Unit for Feet {
    const NAME: &'static str = "ft";
    const PER_METER: f64 = 3.28084;
    const PRECISION: usize = 1;             // override the default
}

// No instance of U is ever created; only its constants are used
fn format_length<U: Unit>(meters: f64) -> String {
    format!("{:.*} {}", U::PRECISION, meters * U::PER_METER, U::NAME)
}

// Inherent associated constants exist too (no trait needed)
struct Packet;
impl Packet {
    const MAX_LEN: usize = 1500;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", format_length::<Meters>(2.5));  // 2.50 m
    println!("{}", format_length::<Feet>(2.5));    // 8.2 ft

    let buf = [0u8; Packet::MAX_LEN];              // fine: concrete, not generic
    println!("{} {}", buf.len(), i32::MAX);        // 1500 2147483647
}
```

| Kind of item       | Varies per type? | Needs an instance? | Usable in const context? |
| ------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------ |
| Method `&self`     | Yes              | Yes                | No                       |
| Associated fn      | Yes              | No                 | Only if `const fn` (not in traits) |
| Associated const   | Yes              | No                 | Yes                      |
| Associated type    | Yes              | No                 | N/A (a type, not a value)|

> Key Takeaways
> - Associated constants attach compile-time values to a trait implementation.
> - They are accessed through the type (`T::NAME`), not an instance.
> - Defaults are allowed and can be overridden per impl.
> - Generic associated constants cannot yet size arrays, and they make a trait
>   unusable as `dyn Trait`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Yards` unit to the example and print `format_length::<Yards>(10.0)`.
> 2. Define `trait Polygon { const SIDES: u32; }` and write a generic function
>    `fn interior_angle_sum<P: Polygon>() -> u32` that returns `(SIDES - 2) * 180`.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose an associated constant over a method that
>    returns a fixed value? (Hint: think about compile-time evaluation and whether
>    an instance exists.)

#### Supertraits

Some behaviors only make sense on top of others. You cannot print an outlined box
around a value unless you can print the value; you cannot claim a total order
(`Ord`) unless you have equality (`Eq`). A *supertrait* expresses that dependency:
`trait OutlinePrint: Display` means "to implement `OutlinePrint`, a type must
also implement `Display`".

Think of licences: a truck licence requires a car licence first. Holding the truck
licence does not mean the truck school taught you to drive a car; it only checks
that you already can.

That analogy captures the key point: a supertrait is a **requirement**, not
inheritance of implementation. The subtrait does not get the supertrait's code; it
gets the *guarantee* that the methods exist, so its default methods may call them.
Each trait is still implemented in its own `impl` block. Multiple supertraits are
combined with `+`.

The standard library relies on this constantly:

| Trait              | Supertraits                 | Reason                                  |
| ------------------ | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Copy`             | `Clone`                     | A copy is a special, trivial clone      |
| `Eq`               | `PartialEq`                 | Total equality refines partial equality |
| `Ord`              | `Eq + PartialOrd`           | Total order refines partial order       |
| `std::error::Error`| `Debug + Display`           | Errors must be printable both ways      |
| `DerefMut`         | `Deref`                     | Mutable access implies shared access    |

Since Rust 1.86, a `&dyn Sub` can also be *upcast* to `&dyn Super`, so a trait
object of the subtrait can be passed where the supertrait object is expected.

```rust
use std::fmt;

trait OutlinePrint: fmt::Display {          // Display is a supertrait
    fn outline_print(&self) {
        let text = self.to_string();        // available because Display is required
        let border = "*".repeat(text.len() + 4);
        println!("{border}");
        println!("* {text} *");
        println!("{border}");
    }
}

struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

impl fmt::Display for Point {               // the requirement...
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y)
    }
}

impl OutlinePrint for Point {}              // ...then the subtrait (all defaults)

struct Hidden;
// impl OutlinePrint for Hidden {}          // error[E0277]: `Hidden` doesn't
                                            // implement `std::fmt::Display`

// Generic code can rely on both traits with a single bound
fn show_both<T: OutlinePrint>(v: &T) {
    println!("plain: {v}");                 // Display used through OutlinePrint
    v.outline_print();
}

fn main() {
    show_both(&Point { x: 1, y: -3 });
    // plain: (1, -3)
    // ***********
    // * (1, -3) *
    // ***********
    let _ = Hidden;
}
```

```text
     fmt::Display          supertrait: "you must already be able to..."
          ^
          | requires
     OutlinePrint          subtrait: may call Display methods in defaults

     impl Display for Point       <-- written separately
     impl OutlinePrint for Point  <-- compiles only because the first exists
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `trait Sub: Super` requires every implementor of `Sub` to also implement
>   `Super`.
> - It is a requirement, not code inheritance: each trait has its own `impl`.
> - A `T: Sub` bound implies `T: Super`, so generic code gets both for free.
> - Upcasting `&dyn Sub` to `&dyn Super` works in Rust 1.86 and later.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define `trait Animal { fn name(&self) -> String; }` and `trait Pet: Animal`
>    with a default `fn greet(&self) -> String` that uses `name`.
> 2. Write a trait `Entity: Debug + Clone` and a provided method that returns a
>    cloned, debug-printed copy of `self`.
> 3. Interview: Is a Rust supertrait the same thing as class inheritance? (Hint:
>    consider which code is reused, and whether a `Pet` value "is" stored as an
>    `Animal` in memory.)

#### The Orphan Rule

Suppose crate A implements `Display` for `Vec<i32>` one way and crate B implements
it another way. A program depending on both now has two answers to the question
"how do I print a `Vec<i32>`?", and nothing can resolve it. Rust prevents this by
guaranteeing *coherence*: for any trait and type, there is at most one
implementation in the whole program.

The rule that enforces it is the *orphan rule*: you may write `impl Trait for
Type` only if **the trait or the type is defined in your crate**. An impl where
both are foreign would be an "orphan" belonging to neither owner. Because
`Display` belongs to `std` and `Vec` belongs to `std`, only `std` may connect them.

The full rule is slightly more generous for generic traits: an impl is also allowed
when a *local type appears as a type argument* of the foreign trait, provided no
uncovered generic parameter comes before it. That is why `impl From<MyType> for
String` compiles. A few "fundamental" wrappers, notably `&T`, `&mut T`, and
`Box<T>`, count as local when `T` is local.

When the rule blocks you, there are two standard workarounds:

- **Extension trait**: define your own trait and implement it for the foreign type
  (local trait, foreign type).
- **Newtype**: wrap the foreign type in a local struct and implement the foreign
  trait on the wrapper (Section 5.4).

| Impl                                   | Allowed? | Why                                      |
| -------------------------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `impl Display for MyType`              | Yes      | Local type                               |
| `impl MyTrait for Vec<i32>`            | Yes      | Local trait                              |
| `impl From<MyType> for String`         | Yes      | Local type as the trait's type argument  |
| `impl Display for Box<MyType>`         | Yes      | `Box` is fundamental; `MyType` is local  |
| `impl Display for Vec<i32>`            | No       | `error[E0117]`: both are foreign         |
| `impl Display for Vec<MyType>`         | No       | `Vec` is not fundamental, so still foreign |
| `impl<T> Display for T`                | No       | `error[E0210]`: uncovered type parameter |

```rust
use std::fmt;

// --- Workaround 1: extension trait (local trait on a foreign type) ----------
trait Shout {
    fn shout(&self) -> String;
}

impl Shout for str {                        // `str` is foreign, `Shout` is local
    fn shout(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}!", self.to_uppercase())
    }
}

// --- Workaround 2: newtype (foreign trait on a local wrapper) ---------------
// impl fmt::Display for Vec<String> { ... }   // error[E0117]: only traits
                                               // defined in the current crate
                                               // can be implemented for types
                                               // defined outside of the crate
struct List(Vec<String>);

impl fmt::Display for List {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "[{}]", self.0.join(", "))
    }
}

// --- Local type as a type argument of a foreign trait -----------------------
struct Celsius(f64);

impl From<Celsius> for String {             // allowed: `Celsius` is local
    fn from(c: Celsius) -> String {
        format!("{:.1} C", c.0)
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", "hello".shout());                        // HELLO!
    println!("{}", List(vec!["a".into(), "b".into()]));     // [a, b]
    let s: String = Celsius(21.456).into();                 // Into comes free
    println!("{s}");                                        // 21.5 C
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Coherence guarantees at most one implementation of a trait for a type across
>   the whole program.
> - The orphan rule: implement a trait only if the trait or the type is local
>   (with extra allowances for local type arguments and fundamental wrappers).
> - Use an extension trait to add methods to foreign types.
> - Use a newtype to implement a foreign trait for a foreign type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Try to implement `std::fmt::Display` for `Option<u8>` and read the full
>    compiler error. Then fix it with a newtype.
> 2. Write an extension trait `IsEven` for `i64` with `fn is_even(&self) -> bool`.
> 3. Interview: Two popular crates each want to provide a `Serialize`
>    implementation for the other crate's main type. Why can neither do it
>    directly, and how does the ecosystem usually solve it? (Hint: think about
>    where the trait lives and optional Cargo features.)

<a id="52-standard-library-traits"></a>
### 5.2 Standard Library Traits

The standard library defines a vocabulary of traits that the language, the
formatting machinery, and the collections all build on. Implementing the right
ones makes a custom type feel built-in. Most can be derived with
`#[derive(...)]`, and knowing when to derive and when to implement by hand is the
core skill of this section.

#### Debug and Display

Every type that a human might want to see needs a text form, but there are two
different audiences. A developer debugging a program wants every field, with
structure, exactly as stored. An end user wants a clean, deliberate presentation.
Rust separates these into two traits so neither has to compromise.

- **`Debug`** powers `{:?}` (compact) and `{:#?}` (pretty, multi-line). It is for
  programmers, should show internal structure, and can almost always be derived.
  `assert_eq!`, `unwrap`, and `dbg!` all require it to print failing values.
- **`Display`** powers `{}`. It is for users, has no single correct form, and so
  **cannot be derived**: you must write it. Implementing `Display` also gives you
  `.to_string()` for free, through a blanket implementation of `ToString`.

Both traits have one method, `fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter) -> fmt::Result`.
Inside it you usually call `write!(f, ...)`. The `Formatter` also exposes the
caller's flags (`f.alternate()` for `#`, `f.precision()`, width and fill) and
helpers such as `f.debug_struct(...)` for building `Debug` output by hand, which
is the standard way to hide a sensitive field.

```rust
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug)]                            // derived: shows every field
struct Point {
    x: f64,
    y: f64,
}

impl fmt::Display for Point {               // hand-written: the user-facing form
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        if let Some(p) = f.precision() {    // honour {:.N} from the caller
            write!(f, "({:.*}, {:.*})", p, self.x, p, self.y)
        } else {
            write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y)
        }
    }
}

struct Credentials {
    user: String,
    password: String,
}

impl fmt::Debug for Credentials {           // manual Debug that redacts a field
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("Credentials")
            .field("user", &self.user)
            .field("password", &"<redacted>")
            .finish()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.5 };
    println!("{p:?}");          // Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.5 }
    println!("{p:#?}");         // Point {
                                //     x: 1.0,
                                //     y: 2.5,
                                // }
    println!("{p}");            // (1, 2.5)
    println!("{p:.2}");         // (1.00, 2.50)
    let s: String = p.to_string();          // from the ToString blanket impl
    println!("{}", s.len());    // 8

    let c = Credentials { user: "ana".into(), password: "hunter2".into() };
    println!("{c:?}");          // Credentials { user: "ana", password: "<redacted>" }
    let _ = c.password;
}
```

| Aspect               | `Debug`                         | `Display`                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Format specifier     | `{:?}`, `{:#?}`                 | `{}`                         |
| Audience             | Developers                      | End users                    |
| Derivable            | Yes                             | No                           |
| Gives `to_string()`  | No                              | Yes (via `ToString`)         |
| Required by          | `assert_eq!`, `unwrap`, `dbg!`  | `std::error::Error`, `to_string` |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Debug` is the developer view (`{:?}`), almost always derived.
> - `Display` is the user view (`{}`), always written by hand, and provides
>   `to_string()`.
> - Use `f.debug_struct` and friends to customize `Debug`, for example to redact
>   secrets.
> - Respect formatter flags such as precision when your `Display` prints numbers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive `Debug` for an enum `Status { Active, Suspended { days: u32 } }` and
>    print it with both `{:?}` and `{:#?}`.
> 2. Implement `Display` for a `Money { cents: i64 }` type so that `Money { cents:
>    1234 }` prints `$12.34`.
> 3. Interview: Why can `Debug` be derived but `Display` cannot? (Hint: is there a
>    single correct way to show a value to a user?)

#### Clone and Copy

Chapter 3 introduced the ownership consequences of these two traits: `Copy` types
are duplicated implicitly on assignment, everything else is moved, and `Clone` is
the explicit way to duplicate. This topic looks at them as traits: what they
promise, how they are implemented, and how to decide which to provide.

`Clone` has one required method, `fn clone(&self) -> Self`, plus a provided
`clone_from` that can reuse an existing allocation. A clone can do arbitrary work:
copying a `Vec` allocates and copies every element, while cloning an `Rc` just
bumps a counter. The trait makes the cost visible by forcing an explicit call.

`Copy` has **no methods**. It is a marker telling the compiler that a plain bitwise
copy is a complete, valid duplicate, so the original stays usable after
assignment. That has hard requirements:

- `Copy` requires `Clone` (it is a supertrait), and the two must agree.
- Every field must itself be `Copy`. A `String` or `Vec` field rules it out
  (`error[E0204]`).
- A type that implements `Drop` cannot be `Copy` (`error[E0184]`), since a type
  that needs cleanup cannot be safely duplicated bit for bit.

Deriving on a generic type adds the bound to every parameter: `#[derive(Clone)]`
on `Wrapper<T>` produces `impl<T: Clone> Clone for Wrapper<T>`. Usually that is
what you want, but it is overly strict for wrappers like `Rc<T>`-holders, where a
manual impl without the bound is the fix.

Making a public type `Copy` is a long-term commitment: removing it later breaks
every caller that relied on implicit copies.

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]    // small, plain data: Copy is ideal
struct Pixel {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]                     // owns heap data: Clone only
struct Image {
    pixels: Vec<Pixel>,
}

// #[derive(Clone, Copy)]                   // error[E0204]: the trait `Copy`
// struct Bad { name: String }              // cannot be implemented for this type

// Manual Clone without a `T: Clone` bound: cloning only bumps the refcount
struct Shared<T> {
    inner: Rc<T>,
}

impl<T> Clone for Shared<T> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        Shared { inner: Rc::clone(&self.inner) }
    }
}

struct NotClone;                            // implements nothing at all

fn main() {
    let a = Pixel { r: 255, g: 0, b: 0 };
    let b = a;                              // bitwise copy; `a` still valid
    println!("{:?} {}", a, a == b);         // Pixel { r: 255, g: 0, b: 0 } true

    let img = Image { pixels: vec![a; 3] };
    let mut copy = img.clone();             // explicit, allocates a new Vec
    copy.pixels[0].g = 255;
    println!("{} {}", img.pixels[0].g, copy.pixels[0].g);   // 0 255

    let s = Shared { inner: Rc::new(NotClone) };
    let s2 = s.clone();                     // works although NotClone isn't Clone
    println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&s2.inner));            // 2
}
```

| Question                      | `Clone`                    | `Copy`                           |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| How is duplication triggered? | Explicit `.clone()`        | Implicitly, on assignment/pass   |
| Can it run custom code?       | Yes                        | No, always a bitwise copy        |
| Cost                          | Anything                   | Cheap (size of the value)        |
| Allowed with `Drop`?          | Yes                        | No                               |
| Allowed with heap-owning fields? | Yes                     | No                               |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Clone` is explicit, possibly expensive duplication; `Copy` is an implicit
>   bitwise copy with no methods.
> - `Copy` requires `Clone`, all-`Copy` fields, and no `Drop` implementation.
> - Derives on generic types add `T: Clone` / `T: Copy` bounds; write the impl by
>   hand when those bounds are unnecessary.
> - Adding `Copy` to a public type is easy; removing it later is a breaking change.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive `Clone` and `Copy` on a `Vec2 { x: f32, y: f32 }` and show that the
>    original remains usable after passing it to a function by value.
> 2. Add a `name: String` field to `Pixel` and read the resulting error. Which
>    derive must be dropped?
> 3. Interview: Why can a type not be both `Copy` and `Drop`? (Hint: after an
>    implicit copy, how many times would the cleanup code run?)

#### PartialEq, Eq, and Hash

To compare values with `==`, a type needs `PartialEq`. Why "partial"? Because
mathematics demands that equality be *reflexive* (`a == a` for every `a`), and
floating point breaks that: `NaN != NaN`. Rust therefore splits equality in two:

- **`PartialEq`** provides `eq` (and a default `ne`). It must be symmetric and
  transitive, but not necessarily reflexive. `f32` and `f64` stop here.
- **`Eq`** is a marker with no methods that adds the reflexive promise. It is
  required wherever equality must be fully trustworthy, such as `HashMap` keys.

`Hash` turns a value into a stream of bytes fed to a `Hasher`. Hash tables rely
on one invariant: **if `a == b` then `hash(a) == hash(b)`**. Derived `PartialEq`
and `Hash` both use every field, so they agree automatically. The danger is a
*manual* `PartialEq` that ignores some fields while `Hash` still includes them;
equal keys then land in different buckets and lookups silently fail.

`PartialEq` is also generic, `PartialEq<Rhs = Self>`, so a type can be compared
with a different type. This is how `String == &str` works.

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::hash::{Hash, Hasher};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]  // all fields, consistent by construction
struct Tag(String);

// Identity is the `id`; `cached_name` is a cache and must not affect equality
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    id: u64,
    cached_name: String,
}

impl PartialEq for User {
    fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
        self.id == other.id
    }
}
impl Eq for User {}                         // marker: no body

impl Hash for User {
    fn hash<H: Hasher>(&self, state: &mut H) {
        self.id.hash(state);                // MUST use the same fields as eq
    }
}

// Comparing with a different type
impl PartialEq<u64> for User {
    fn eq(&self, other: &u64) -> bool {
        self.id == *other
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = User { id: 7, cached_name: "Ana".into() };
    let b = User { id: 7, cached_name: "ANA (stale)".into() };
    println!("{}", a == b);                 // true
    println!("{}", a == 7u64);              // true: PartialEq<u64>

    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    seen.insert(a);
    println!("{}", seen.contains(&b));      // true: same id, same hash

    let nan = f64::NAN;
    println!("{}", nan == nan);             // false: why f64 is not Eq
    // let s: HashSet<f64> = HashSet::new(); // compiles, but insert() needs
                                             // f64: Eq + Hash -> error[E0599]
    let t: HashSet<Tag> = [Tag("x".into())].into();
    println!("{} {}", t.len(), b.cached_name);  // 1 ANA (stale)
}
```

| Type              | `PartialEq` | `Eq` | `Hash` | Usable as `HashMap` key |
| ----------------- | ----------- | ---- | ------ | ----------------------- |
| `i32`, `char`     | Yes         | Yes  | Yes    | Yes                     |
| `String`, `&str`  | Yes         | Yes  | Yes    | Yes                     |
| `f64`             | Yes         | No   | No     | No                      |
| `Vec<T>`          | If `T` is   | If `T` is | If `T` is | If `T` is         |
| Derived struct    | If all fields are | If all fields are | If all fields are | If all fields are |

> Key Takeaways
> - `PartialEq` gives `==`; `Eq` adds the reflexivity promise that floats cannot
>   make.
> - Hash maps and sets require `Eq + Hash` on their keys.
> - Invariant: equal values must hash equally. Derive both, or hand-write both
>   using the same fields.
> - `PartialEq<Rhs>` allows comparisons between different types.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive `PartialEq, Eq, Hash` for `struct Coord { x: i32, y: i32 }` and use it
>    as a `HashMap<Coord, &str>` key.
> 2. Write a `CaseInsensitive(String)` type whose `PartialEq` ignores case, and
>    write a matching `Hash` impl (hash the lowercased string).
> 3. Interview: A colleague implements `PartialEq` by hand to compare only an `id`
>    field but keeps `#[derive(Hash)]`. What goes wrong at runtime, and why does
>    the compiler not catch it? (Hint: the invariant connecting the two traits is
>    a convention, not a type-level check.)

#### PartialOrd and Ord

Ordering mirrors equality. Comparing `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` needs `PartialOrd`,
whose core method is `partial_cmp(&self, other) -> Option<Ordering>`. It returns
`None` when two values are incomparable, which again is the floating-point story:
`NaN` is neither less than, equal to, nor greater than `1.0`.

`Ord` is the total version: `cmp(&self, other) -> Ordering`, always an answer.
Anything that must put values in a definite order requires it: `slice::sort`,
`BTreeMap` keys, `BinaryHeap`, `Iterator::max`. `Ord` has supertraits `Eq +
PartialOrd`, and all four traits must agree with each other.

Derived ordering is **lexicographic by field declaration order** for structs and
**by variant declaration order** for enums. Reordering fields therefore changes
the ordering, which matters for version numbers, priorities, and similar types.

When you implement `Ord` by hand, write `cmp` and then make `partial_cmp` delegate
to it (`Some(self.cmp(other))`) so the two can never disagree. Useful helpers:

- `Ordering::then` / `then_with` to chain tie-breakers.
- `std::cmp::Reverse(x)` to invert an order, for example to turn the max-heap
  `BinaryHeap` into a min-heap.
- `f64::total_cmp` to sort floats using a defined total order.

```rust
use std::cmp::{Ordering, Reverse};
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

// Derived: compares major, then minor, then patch (field order matters)
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Version {
    major: u32,
    minor: u32,
    patch: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Employee {
    dept: String,
    salary: u32,
}

impl Ord for Employee {
    fn cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> Ordering {
        self.dept
            .cmp(&other.dept)                           // dept ascending...
            .then_with(|| other.salary.cmp(&self.salary)) // ...salary descending
    }
}

impl PartialOrd for Employee {
    fn partial_cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> Option<Ordering> {
        Some(self.cmp(other))               // delegate: guaranteed consistent
    }
}

fn main() {
    let v1 = Version { major: 1, minor: 10, patch: 0 };
    let v2 = Version { major: 1, minor: 9, patch: 7 };
    println!("{}", v1 > v2);                // true (10 > 9 at the 2nd field)

    let mut staff = vec![
        Employee { dept: "ops".into(), salary: 50 },
        Employee { dept: "dev".into(), salary: 60 },
        Employee { dept: "dev".into(), salary: 90 },
    ];
    staff.sort();                           // needs Ord
    for e in &staff {
        print!("{}:{} ", e.dept, e.salary); // dev:90 dev:60 ops:50
    }
    println!();

    let mut xs: Vec<f64> = vec![2.5, -1.0, 9.0];
    // xs.sort();                           // error[E0277]: `f64: Ord` not satisfied
    xs.sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b));
    println!("{xs:?}");                     // [-1.0, 2.5, 9.0]

    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new();       // max-heap by default
    for n in [5, 1, 8] {
        heap.push(Reverse(n));              // Reverse turns it into a min-heap
    }
    println!("{:?}", heap.pop());           // Some(Reverse(1))
}
```

| Trait        | Method                              | Total? | Required by                    |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ |
| `PartialOrd` | `partial_cmp -> Option<Ordering>`   | No     | `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`           |
| `Ord`        | `cmp -> Ordering`                   | Yes    | `sort`, `BTreeMap`, `BinaryHeap`, `max` |

> Key Takeaways
> - `PartialOrd` may say "incomparable" (`None`); `Ord` always gives an answer.
> - Derived ordering follows field order (structs) or variant order (enums).
> - When writing `Ord` manually, implement `cmp` and have `partial_cmp` return
>   `Some(self.cmp(other))`.
> - Use `then_with`, `Reverse`, and `total_cmp` for multi-key, reversed, and
>   floating-point orderings.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive ordering for `enum Priority { Low, Medium, High }` and sort a vector
>    of them in descending order.
> 2. Sort a `Vec<(String, f64)>` by score descending, breaking ties by name
>    ascending.
> 3. Interview: Why does `vec_of_f64.sort()` fail to compile while
>    `vec_of_f64.sort_by(...)` works? (Hint: what would `sort` do when it meets a
>    `NaN`?)

#### Default

Many types have an obvious "starting" value: zero for numbers, empty for strings
and collections, `None` for options, `false` for booleans. The `Default` trait
names that value through one associated function, `fn default() -> Self`.

Having a common name unlocks generic code that needs to create a value from
nothing:

- `..Default::default()` in struct update syntax fills every field you did not
  list, which makes configuration structs pleasant to build.
- `Option::unwrap_or_default()` and `HashMap::entry(k).or_default()` produce a
  fallback without you naming it.
- `std::mem::take(&mut x)` moves a value out and leaves `Default::default()` in
  its place, a common trick for moving out of a `&mut`.

Deriving works when every field implements `Default`. For enums, mark one unit
variant with `#[default]`. When the natural default is not "all zero", for
example a port of 8080, implement it by hand.

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, Default)]                   // all fields are Default
struct Stats {
    count: u64,                             // 0
    label: String,                          // ""
    tags: Vec<String>,                      // []
}

#[derive(Debug, Default, PartialEq)]
enum Mode {
    #[default]                              // the chosen default variant
    Normal,
    Verbose,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Config {
    host: String,
    port: u16,
    mode: Mode,
    retries: u8,
}

impl Default for Config {                   // hand-written: non-zero defaults
    fn default() -> Self {
        Config {
            host: "localhost".into(),
            port: 8080,
            mode: Mode::default(),
            retries: 3,
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", Stats::default());     // Stats { count: 0, label: "", tags: [] }

    let cfg = Config { port: 9000, ..Default::default() };   // override one field
    println!("{} {} {:?} {}", cfg.host, cfg.port, cfg.mode, cfg.retries);
    // localhost 9000 Normal 3

    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    for w in ["a", "b", "a"] {
        *counts.entry(w).or_default() += 1; // inserts 0 the first time
    }
    println!("{}", counts["a"]);            // 2

    let mut name = String::from("temp");
    let taken = std::mem::take(&mut name);  // leaves String::default() behind
    println!("{taken:?} {name:?}");         // "temp" ""
    println!("{}", Mode::Verbose != Mode::default());   // true
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Default::default()` produces a type's natural starting value.
> - Derive it when every field has a sensible default; implement it by hand when
>   the defaults are domain-specific.
> - Enums choose their default variant with `#[default]`.
> - `..Default::default()`, `or_default()`, `unwrap_or_default()`, and
>   `mem::take` all build on this trait.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Derive `Default` for a `Score { points: u32, player: String }` and print it.
> 2. Write a `ServerConfig` with a manual `Default` and build three variations
>    using struct update syntax.
> 3. Interview: How does `std::mem::take` let you move a `String` out of a struct
>    you only hold `&mut` to, when moving out of a reference is normally
>    forbidden? (Hint: what is left behind?)

#### From, Into, and TryFrom

Conversions between types are everywhere: a `&str` to a `String`, a `u8` to a
`u32`, a low-level error into an application error. Rust standardizes them in a
small family of traits so that conversions look the same everywhere and generic
code can ask for "anything that converts into X".

- **`From<T> for U`**: an infallible conversion, `U::from(t)`. This is the one you
  implement.
- **`Into<U> for T`**: the same conversion seen from the source side, `t.into()`.
  You almost never implement it, because a blanket impl provides `Into` for every
  `From`. Implementing `From` gets you both.
- **`TryFrom<T>` / `TryInto<U>`**: fallible conversions returning
  `Result<U, Self::Error>`, for example `u8::try_from(300_i32)`. Again, implement
  `TryFrom` and receive `TryInto` for free.

Two integrations make `From` especially valuable. First, the `?` operator calls
`From::from` on the error, so `impl From<io::Error> for MyError` lets `?` convert
errors automatically (Chapter 7). Second, `impl Into<String>` in a parameter lets
callers pass a `&str` or a `String` without ceremony.

A `From` impl should be lossless and unsurprising. If the conversion can fail or
lose information, use `TryFrom` or a named method instead.

```rust
// TryFrom and TryInto are in the prelude since edition 2021: no import needed

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);

impl From<(u8, u8, u8)> for Rgb {           // infallible: any tuple is a color
    fn from((r, g, b): (u8, u8, u8)) -> Self {
        Rgb(r, g, b)
    }
}

impl TryFrom<&str> for Rgb {                // fallible: a string may be malformed
    type Error = String;

    fn try_from(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        let hex = s.strip_prefix('#').ok_or("missing '#'")?;
        if hex.len() != 6 {
            return Err(format!("expected 6 hex digits, got {}", hex.len()));
        }
        let part = |i: usize| {
            u8::from_str_radix(&hex[i..i + 2], 16).map_err(|e| e.to_string())
        };
        Ok(Rgb(part(0)?, part(2)?, part(4)?))
    }
}

struct Person {
    name: String,
}

impl Person {
    fn new(name: impl Into<String>) -> Self {   // accepts &str, String, ...
        Person { name: name.into() }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Rgb::from((255, 136, 0));
    let b: Rgb = (255, 136, 0).into();          // Into, provided by the blanket impl
    println!("{}", a == b);                      // true

    println!("{:?}", Rgb::try_from("#ff8800")); // Ok(Rgb(255, 136, 0))
    println!("{:?}", Rgb::try_from("ff8800"));  // Err("missing '#'")
    let c: Result<Rgb, _> = "#12".try_into();   // TryInto, also free
    println!("{c:?}");                           // Err("expected 6 hex digits, got 2")

    let small: Result<u8, _> = u8::try_from(300_i32);
    println!("{}", small.is_err());              // true: 300 does not fit
    let wide: u64 = u64::from(42_u32);           // lossless widening
    println!("{wide}");                          // 42

    let p1 = Person::new("Ana");
    let p2 = Person::new(String::from("Bo"));
    println!("{} {}", p1.name, p2.name);         // Ana Bo
}
```

| Trait         | Direction          | Can fail? | Implement it? | Typical use                     |
| ------------- | ------------------ | --------- | ------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `From<T>`     | `T -> Self`        | No        | Yes           | Constructors, error conversion  |
| `Into<U>`     | `Self -> U`        | No        | No (blanket)  | Generic parameters              |
| `TryFrom<T>`  | `T -> Self`        | Yes       | Yes           | Validated parsing, narrowing    |
| `TryInto<U>`  | `Self -> U`        | Yes       | No (blanket)  | Call-site convenience           |

> Key Takeaways
> - Implement `From` (or `TryFrom`); the blanket impls give you `Into` (or
>   `TryInto`) automatically.
> - `From` must be infallible; anything that can fail belongs in `TryFrom`.
> - `?` uses `From` to convert error types, which is why error enums implement it.
> - `impl Into<String>` parameters make APIs accept both `&str` and `String`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `From<Rgb> for u32` that packs the three bytes as `0xRRGGBB`.
> 2. Write `struct Percent(u8)` with a `TryFrom<i32>` that rejects values outside
>    0 to 100.
> 3. Interview: Why does the standard library tell you to implement `From` rather
>    than `Into`? (Hint: look at which direction the blanket implementation goes.)

#### Deref and DerefMut

Smart pointers such as `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>`, and `String` are structs that own or
point to some inner data. To be convenient, they should *feel* like that data:
`*boxed` should give the value, and a `&String` should work where a `&str` is
expected. `Deref` is the trait that makes this happen.

`Deref` has an associated type `Target` and one method, `fn deref(&self) ->
&Self::Target`. It drives three behaviors:

1. **The `*` operator**: `*x` on a non-reference type becomes `*Deref::deref(&x)`.
2. **Auto-deref in method calls**: `x.method()` searches `x`, then `*x`, then
   `**x`, and so on, until it finds the method.
3. **Deref coercion**: a `&A` is silently converted to `&B` when `A: Deref<Target
   = B>`, following the chain as many steps as needed.

`DerefMut` (with supertrait `Deref`) does the same for `&mut`. Implementing only
`Deref` gives read-only transparency, which is exactly right when the wrapper must
protect an invariant: a sorted vector can expose all of `[T]`'s read methods but
must not hand out `&mut [T]`, or callers could unsort it.

A word of caution: `Deref` is meant for pointer-like and wrapper types. Using it to
fake inheritance ("my `Manager` derefs to `Employee`") produces confusing method
resolution and is widely considered an anti-pattern.

```rust
use std::ops::Deref;

// A minimal smart pointer
struct MyBox<T>(T);

impl<T> Deref for MyBox<T> {
    type Target = T;
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        &self.0
    }
}

// Read-only transparency: Deref but deliberately NO DerefMut
struct SortedVec<T: Ord>(Vec<T>);

impl<T: Ord> SortedVec<T> {
    fn from_vec(mut v: Vec<T>) -> Self {
        v.sort();
        SortedVec(v)
    }
    fn insert(&mut self, x: T) {            // the only way to mutate
        let pos = self.0.binary_search(&x).unwrap_or_else(|p| p);
        self.0.insert(pos, x);
    }
}

impl<T: Ord> Deref for SortedVec<T> {
    type Target = [T];                      // expose every read-only slice method
    fn deref(&self) -> &[T] {
        &self.0
    }
}

fn greet(name: &str) {
    println!("hello, {name}");
}

fn main() {
    let b = MyBox(String::from("Ana"));
    println!("{}", *b);                     // Ana: `*b` is `*Deref::deref(&b)`
    greet(&b);                              // hello, Ana
    // deref coercion: &MyBox<String> -> &String -> &str
    println!("{}", b.len());                // 3: auto-deref finds String::len

    let mut s = SortedVec::from_vec(vec![5, 1, 4]);
    s.insert(3);
    println!("{:?} {} {:?}", &*s, s.len(), s.first());   // [1, 3, 4, 5] 4 Some(1)
    println!("{:?}", s.binary_search(&4));               // Ok(2)
    // s.reverse();                         // error[E0596]: cannot borrow data in
                                            // dereference of `SortedVec<i32>` as
                                            // mutable (no DerefMut)
}
```

```text
   Deref coercion chain for greet(&b):

   &MyBox<String> --deref--> &String --deref--> &str
        (yours)                (std: String: Deref<Target = str>)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Deref` makes a wrapper behave like a reference to its `Target` via `*`,
>   auto-deref, and deref coercion.
> - Coercions chain: `&Box<String>` can become `&str` automatically.
> - Implement `Deref` without `DerefMut` to expose read access while protecting an
>   invariant.
> - Reserve `Deref` for pointer-like and wrapper types; do not use it to emulate
>   inheritance.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `DerefMut` impl to `MyBox<T>` and mutate the inner `String` through it
>    with `push_str`.
> 2. Write `struct NonEmpty(Vec<i32>)` that derefs to `[i32]` and whose
>    constructor rejects empty vectors.
> 3. Interview: Why is using `Deref` to make `Manager` behave like `Employee`
>    considered an anti-pattern? (Hint: consider trait implementations, generic
>    bounds, and what happens when both types have a method with the same name.)

#### Drop

Chapter 3 introduced RAII: a value's resources are released automatically when it
goes out of scope. `Drop` is the trait that lets a type hook into that moment. It
has one method, `fn drop(&mut self)`, which the compiler calls exactly once,
right before the memory is reclaimed. Files close, locks release, and buffers
flush this way.

The rules around it are strict, because the compiler owns the timing:

- **You cannot call `x.drop()` yourself** (`error[E0040]`). To drop early, call
  `std::mem::drop(x)`, which simply takes ownership and lets the value fall out of
  scope.
- **Order is deterministic**: local variables are dropped in *reverse* order of
  declaration; struct fields are dropped in *declaration* order, after the
  struct's own `drop` runs.
- **`Drop` and `Copy` are mutually exclusive**, as covered above.
- **You cannot move a field out of a `Drop` type** (`error[E0509]`), since `drop`
  would later see a half-empty value. `Option::take` or `mem::take` on the field
  is the usual escape hatch.
- **Not running a destructor is safe.** `std::mem::forget` and reference cycles
  can leak values. Unsafe code must never rely on `drop` running for soundness.

```rust
struct Noisy(&'static str);

impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.0);
    }
}

struct Pair {
    first: Noisy,
    second: Noisy,
}

impl Drop for Pair {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop Pair (fields follow)");
    }
}

fn main() {
    let _a = Noisy("a");
    let _b = Noisy("b");
    let c = Noisy("c");

    // c.drop();                            // error[E0040]: explicit use of
                                            // destructor method
    drop(c);                                // drop c   (early, by moving it)

    {
        let _p = Pair { first: Noisy("p1"), second: Noisy("p2") };
    }                                       // drop Pair (fields follow)
                                            // drop p1
                                            // drop p2  (fields: declaration order)

    let leaked = Noisy("leaked");
    std::mem::forget(leaked);               // destructor never runs: safe, not UB

    println!("end of main");
}                                           // drop b
                                            // drop a   (locals: reverse order)
```

```text
   Output order:
   drop c
   drop Pair (fields follow)
   drop p1
   drop p2
   end of main
   drop b
   drop a
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Drop::drop` runs automatically, exactly once, when a value goes out of scope.
> - Call `std::mem::drop(x)` to drop early; calling `x.drop()` directly is an
>   error.
> - Locals drop in reverse declaration order; fields drop in declaration order
>   after the parent.
> - Leaking is safe in Rust, so correctness must never depend on a destructor
>   running.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Timer` struct that records `Instant::now()` on creation and prints
>    the elapsed time in `drop`. Use it to time a loop.
> 2. Predict, then verify, the drop order of a `Vec<Noisy>` containing three
>    elements.
> 3. Interview: Why can you not move a `String` field out of a struct that
>    implements `Drop`? (Hint: what would `drop(&mut self)` see afterwards?)

#### Index and Operator Overloading

Mathematical types such as vectors, matrices, and money read best with ordinary
operators: `a + b`, `-v`, `m[(1, 2)]`. Rust supports this, but in a disciplined
way: each operator corresponds to a trait in `std::ops`, and `a + b` is literally
sugar for `Add::add(a, b)`. You cannot invent new operators or change precedence;
you can only give existing operators meaning for your types.

Most binary operator traits are generic over the right-hand side, with a default
of `Self`, and have an associated `Output` type:

```rust
trait Add<Rhs = Self> {
    type Output;
    fn add(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output;
}
```

That design allows mixed-type operations such as `Vec2 * f64`. Note that `add`
takes `self` **by value**: for non-`Copy` types, `a + b` moves both operands.
Implementing the trait for references (`impl Add for &Matrix`) avoids that.
Compound assignment (`+=`) has its own traits (`AddAssign`) taking `&mut self`.

Indexing works differently: `Index::index` returns a **reference**, `&Self::Output`,
and `container[i]` is sugar for `*container.index(i)`. `IndexMut` provides the
mutable version used by `container[i] = x`. The index type is generic, so a matrix
can be indexed by a `(row, col)` tuple.

```rust
use std::ops::{Add, AddAssign, Index, IndexMut, Mul, Neg};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct Vec2 {
    x: f64,
    y: f64,
}

impl Add for Vec2 {                         // Vec2 + Vec2
    type Output = Vec2;
    fn add(self, o: Vec2) -> Vec2 {
        Vec2 { x: self.x + o.x, y: self.y + o.y }
    }
}

impl Mul<f64> for Vec2 {                    // Vec2 * f64 (mixed types)
    type Output = Vec2;
    fn mul(self, k: f64) -> Vec2 {
        Vec2 { x: self.x * k, y: self.y * k }
    }
}

impl Neg for Vec2 {                         // -Vec2 (unary)
    type Output = Vec2;
    fn neg(self) -> Vec2 {
        Vec2 { x: -self.x, y: -self.y }
    }
}

impl AddAssign for Vec2 {                   // v += w
    fn add_assign(&mut self, o: Vec2) {
        self.x += o.x;
        self.y += o.y;
    }
}

struct Matrix {
    cols: usize,
    data: Vec<f64>,
}

impl Index<(usize, usize)> for Matrix {     // m[(row, col)]
    type Output = f64;
    fn index(&self, (r, c): (usize, usize)) -> &f64 {
        &self.data[r * self.cols + c]       // returns a reference, not a value
    }
}

impl IndexMut<(usize, usize)> for Matrix {  // m[(row, col)] = value
    fn index_mut(&mut self, (r, c): (usize, usize)) -> &mut f64 {
        &mut self.data[r * self.cols + c]
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 };
    let b = Vec2 { x: 0.5, y: -1.0 };
    let mut c = a + b * 2.0;                // precedence unchanged: * before +
    println!("{c:?}");                      // Vec2 { x: 2.0, y: 0.0 }
    c += -a;
    println!("{c:?}");                      // Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: -2.0 }

    let mut m = Matrix { cols: 2, data: vec![0.0; 4] };
    m[(1, 0)] = 7.5;                        // IndexMut
    println!("{} {}", m[(1, 0)], m[(0, 1)]);  // 7.5 0
}
```

| Operator      | Trait            | Method signature (simplified)          |
| ------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `a + b`       | `Add<Rhs>`       | `fn add(self, rhs) -> Output`          |
| `a - b`       | `Sub<Rhs>`       | `fn sub(self, rhs) -> Output`          |
| `a * b`       | `Mul<Rhs>`       | `fn mul(self, rhs) -> Output`          |
| `-a`          | `Neg`            | `fn neg(self) -> Output`               |
| `!a`          | `Not`            | `fn not(self) -> Output`               |
| `a += b`      | `AddAssign<Rhs>` | `fn add_assign(&mut self, rhs)`        |
| `a[i]`        | `Index<Idx>`     | `fn index(&self, i) -> &Output`        |
| `a[i] = v`    | `IndexMut<Idx>`  | `fn index_mut(&mut self, i) -> &mut Output` |
| `a == b`      | `PartialEq`      | `fn eq(&self, other) -> bool`          |
| `a < b`       | `PartialOrd`     | `fn partial_cmp(&self, other) -> Option<Ordering>` |

> Key Takeaways
> - Each operator is sugar for a trait method in `std::ops` (or `cmp` for
>   comparisons); only existing operators can be overloaded.
> - Binary operator traits are generic over the right-hand side and declare an
>   `Output` type, enabling mixed-type arithmetic.
> - Arithmetic traits take operands by value; implement them for references to
>   avoid moving non-`Copy` values.
> - `Index` returns a reference; `IndexMut` enables assignment through `[]`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `Sub` and `Mul<Vec2> for f64` (so that `2.0 * v` works) for
>    `Vec2`.
> 2. Implement `Add` for `&Matrix` so that `&m1 + &m2` returns a new `Matrix`
>    without consuming either operand.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Index::index` return `&Self::Output` instead of
>    `Self::Output`? (Hint: think about `v[0] = x` and about indexing into a
>    `Vec<String>` without moving the element out.)

<a id="53-static-and-dynamic-dispatch"></a>
### 5.3 Static and Dynamic Dispatch

A call through a trait has to be routed to the right implementation, either at
compile time (static dispatch) or at runtime (dynamic dispatch). This section
covers the syntax for each, the rules that decide when dynamic dispatch is
possible, what it looks like in memory, and how to choose.

#### impl Trait in Argument Position

Writing `fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T)` is precise but noisy when the type
parameter is used exactly once. `impl Trait` in argument position is shorthand
for it: `fn notify(item: &impl Summary)` reads as "any type that implements
`Summary`", and the compiler turns it into an anonymous generic parameter.

Because it *is* a generic, everything from Chapter 4.4 still applies: the
function is monomorphized per concrete type, dispatch is static, and there is no
runtime cost. The differences are only in what you can express:

- Each `impl Trait` is a **separate** anonymous parameter. `fn f(a: impl Display,
  b: impl Display)` allows `a` and `b` to be different types. To force them to be
  the same type, you need a named `T`.
- The parameter has no name, so callers **cannot use turbofish** to specify it,
  and you cannot refer to it elsewhere in the signature.
- Combined bounds use `+`: `impl Display + Clone`.

Use `impl Trait` for simple, single-use parameters, especially closures (`impl
Fn(i32) -> i32`) and iterators (`impl IntoIterator<Item = u32>`); switch to named
generics when the type must be referenced twice or specified by the caller.

```rust
use std::fmt::Display;

// These two are equivalent after desugaring
fn shout(x: impl Display) -> String {
    format!("{x}!")
}
fn shout_generic<T: Display>(x: T) -> String {
    format!("{x}!")
}

// Two impl Trait params = two independent type parameters
fn pair(a: impl Display, b: impl Display) -> String {
    format!("{a} & {b}")
}

// A named T forces both arguments to share a type
fn same<T: Display + PartialEq>(a: T, b: T) -> bool {
    a == b
}

// The most common real-world uses: closures and iterables
fn apply(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 {
    f(x)
}

fn total(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = u32>) -> u32 {
    items.into_iter().sum()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", shout("hi"));                // hi!
    println!("{}", shout_generic::<i32>(7));    // 7!   (turbofish possible)
    // shout::<i32>(7);                         // error[E0107]: function takes 0
                                                // generic arguments (the impl Trait
                                                // parameter cannot be named)
    println!("{}", pair(1, "one"));             // 1 & one   (different types)
    println!("{}", same(3, 3));                 // true
    // same(3, "3");                            // error[E0308]: mismatched types

    println!("{}", apply(|n| n * 10, 4));       // 40
    println!("{}", total(vec![1, 2, 3]));       // 6
    println!("{}", total([4, 5]));              // 9: arrays work too
}
```

| Feature                          | `impl Trait` argument | Named generic `<T: Trait>` |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Dispatch                         | Static                | Static                     |
| Turbofish at call site           | No                    | Yes                        |
| Reuse the type elsewhere         | No                    | Yes (`-> T`, other params) |
| Force two params to share a type | No                    | Yes                        |
| Readability for one-off bounds   | Better                | Noisier                    |

> Key Takeaways
> - `impl Trait` in argument position is syntactic sugar for an anonymous generic
>   parameter.
> - It is statically dispatched and monomorphized, exactly like a named generic.
> - Each occurrence is an independent type; use a named `T` to tie types together
>   or to allow turbofish.
> - It shines for closures and iterator parameters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite `fn print_all<T: Debug>(items: &[T])` as `fn print_all(items: &[impl
>    Debug])` and confirm both versions accept the same calls.
> 2. Write `fn compose(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, g: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) ->
>    i32` returning `g(f(x))`.
> 3. Interview: Is `fn f(x: impl Trait)` statically or dynamically dispatched, and
>    how does it differ from `fn f(x: &dyn Trait)`? (Hint: how many copies of `f`
>    end up in the binary?)

#### impl Trait in Return Position

In argument position, the **caller** picks the concrete type. In return position,
the meaning flips: the **function** picks one concrete type, and the caller only
learns that it implements the trait. This is sometimes called an *opaque* or
*existential* type.

It exists because some types cannot be written down at all. Every closure has a
unique, unnameable type, and an iterator chain such as
`v.iter().filter(..).map(..)` has a type like `Map<Filter<Iter<'_, u32>,
{closure}>, {closure}>`. Without `-> impl Iterator<Item = u32>` you would have to
spell that out (impossible for closures) or box it and pay for dynamic dispatch.

The essential rule: **all return paths must produce the same concrete type.** The
opaque type is one fixed type chosen at compile time; it is not "any type that
implements the trait". Returning a `Vec` iterator in one branch and a `Range` in
another is `error[E0308]`. When you genuinely need different types, return
`Box<dyn Trait>` or an enum that implements the trait.

Two modern details:

- **Lifetime capture.** In edition 2024, a return-position `impl Trait` captures
  all generic parameters and lifetimes in scope. If the hidden type does not
  actually borrow from an argument, you can opt out with precise capturing,
  `-> impl Iterator<Item = u32> + use<>` (Rust 1.82+).
- **In traits.** Since Rust 1.75, trait methods may return `impl Trait`, and
  `async fn` in traits builds on the same mechanism.

```rust
// Iterator chains have long, unwritable types: hide them
fn evens(limit: u32) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> {
    (0..limit).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0)
}

// Closures have unique, unnameable types: impl Fn is the only static option
fn make_adder(n: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    move |x| x + n                          // `move` copies n into the closure
}

// Borrowing from an argument: the returned iterator captures the lifetime of `words`
fn long_words<'a>(words: &'a [&'a str], min: usize) -> impl Iterator<Item = &'a str> {
    words.iter().copied().filter(move |w| w.len() >= min)
}

// Different concrete types per branch: impl Trait cannot express this
// fn numbers(rev: bool) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> {
//     if rev { (0..3).rev() } else { 0..3 }  // error[E0308]: `if` and `else`
// }                                          // have incompatible types

// Fix: box the iterator (dynamic dispatch)
fn numbers(rev: bool) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = u32>> {
    if rev { Box::new((0..3).rev()) } else { Box::new(0..3) }
}

// Return-position impl Trait in a trait (Rust 1.75+)
trait Container {
    fn items(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &i32>;
}

struct Bag(Vec<i32>);

impl Container for Bag {
    fn items(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &i32> {
        self.0.iter()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let v: Vec<u32> = evens(10).collect();
    println!("{v:?}");                                  // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

    let add5 = make_adder(5);
    println!("{}", add5(10));                           // 15

    let words = ["a", "rust", "trait", "is"];
    let long: Vec<_> = long_words(&words, 4).collect();
    println!("{long:?}");                               // ["rust", "trait"]

    let r: Vec<_> = numbers(true).collect();
    println!("{r:?}");                                  // [2, 1, 0]

    let sum: i32 = Bag(vec![1, 2, 3]).items().sum();
    println!("{sum}");                                  // 6
}
```

| Position | Who chooses the concrete type | Can vary per call?           | Dispatch |
| -------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------- |
| Argument | The caller                    | Yes, one instance per type   | Static   |
| Return   | The function body             | No, exactly one hidden type  | Static   |

> Key Takeaways
> - Return-position `impl Trait` hides one concrete type chosen by the function;
>   the caller sees only the trait.
> - It is how you return closures and iterator chains without boxing.
> - Every return path must produce the same type; otherwise use `Box<dyn Trait>`
>   or an enum.
> - Trait methods can return `impl Trait` since Rust 1.75, and edition 2024
>   captures in-scope lifetimes by default (`use<..>` narrows it).

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn squares() -> impl Iterator<Item = u64>` that yields an infinite
>    sequence of squares, and print the first five with `.take(5)`.
> 2. Write `fn make_counter() -> impl FnMut() -> u32` that returns 1, 2, 3, ...
>    on successive calls.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `fn f() -> impl Display` and `fn
>    f() -> Box<dyn Display>`? (Hint: consider how many concrete types each can
>    return, where the value lives, and how calls are dispatched.)

#### Trait Objects with dyn

Generics and `impl Trait` require the concrete type to be known at compile time.
Sometimes it is not. A drawing program keeps a list of shapes that the user adds
at runtime: circles, rectangles, text. A `Vec<T>` holds one type only, and a
`Vec<impl Shape>` would still be a single hidden type. You need a value that says
"some type implementing `Shape`, decided at runtime".

That is a *trait object*, written `dyn Shape`. Its concrete type is erased, and
method calls are resolved at runtime through a table of function pointers (the
next topics cover how). Because different implementors have different sizes,
`dyn Shape` is **unsized** and must always sit behind a pointer:

| Pointer form          | Ownership                 | Typical use                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `&dyn Trait`          | Borrowed                  | Parameters, temporary views          |
| `&mut dyn Trait`      | Mutably borrowed          | Writers, visitors (`&mut dyn Write`) |
| `Box<dyn Trait>`      | Owned, single owner       | Heterogeneous collections, return types |
| `Rc<dyn Trait>` / `Arc<dyn Trait>` | Shared ownership | Plugins or handlers shared across code |

Additional details you will meet in real code:

- **Auto traits can be added**: `Box<dyn Trait + Send + Sync>` is required to send
  a trait object across threads.
- **Default lifetimes**: `Box<dyn Trait>` means `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`, so it
  cannot hold a type that borrows short-lived data unless you write `Box<dyn Trait
  + 'a>`. `&'a dyn Trait` defaults to `+ 'a`.
- **Downcasting**: recovering the concrete type requires the `Any` trait
  (`downcast_ref::<T>()`), which should be the exception, not the design.

Analogy: a generic is a specialist hired for one specific machine; a trait object
is a universal remote that sends "power" to whatever device happens to be in
front of it, looking up the right signal at the moment you press the button.

```rust
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
}

struct Circle(f64);
struct Square(f64);

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.14159 * self.0 * self.0 }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "circle" }
}

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 }
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "square" }
}

// Accepts any Shape behind a reference; ONE copy of this function exists
fn report(s: &dyn Shape) {
    println!("{:>6}: {:.2}", s.name(), s.area());
}

// Concrete type decided at runtime
fn parse(kind: &str, size: f64) -> Option<Box<dyn Shape>> {
    match kind {
        "circle" => Some(Box::new(Circle(size))),
        "square" => Some(Box::new(Square(size))),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn main() {
    // A heterogeneous collection: impossible with a plain Vec<T>
    let mut shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![Box::new(Circle(1.0)), Box::new(Square(2.0))];

    if let Some(s) = parse("square", 3.0) {
        shapes.push(s);
    }

    for s in &shapes {
        report(s.as_ref());     // Box<dyn Shape> -> &dyn Shape
    }
    // circle: 3.14
    // square: 4.00
    // square: 9.00

    let total: f64 = shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum();
    println!("total = {total:.2}");     // total = 16.14

    // Thread-safe trait object: requires the concrete type to be Send
    let job: Box<dyn Fn() -> u32 + Send> = Box::new(|| 42);
    let handle = std::thread::spawn(move || job());
    println!("{}", handle.join().unwrap());  // 42
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `dyn Trait` is a value whose concrete type is erased and whose method calls
>   are resolved at runtime.
> - It is unsized, so it always lives behind `&`, `&mut`, `Box`, `Rc`, or `Arc`.
> - Trait objects enable heterogeneous collections and runtime-chosen
>   implementations.
> - `Box<dyn Trait>` implies `'static`; add `+ Send + Sync` for cross-thread use.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Triangle` to the example and build the collection from a list of
>    `(&str, f64)` pairs using `parse`.
> 2. Write a `Logger` trait with `fn log(&self, msg: &str)` and store a
>    `Vec<Box<dyn Logger>>` that fans out each message to a console logger and a
>    prefixing logger.
> 3. Interview: Why can you write `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` but not `Vec<dyn Shape>`?
>    (Hint: what does a `Vec` need to know about each element to lay them out
>    contiguously?)

#### Object Safety Rules

Not every trait can become a trait object. The official term is now **dyn
compatibility** (formerly *object safety*), and both names appear in error
messages and documentation. The rules follow from one fact: a trait object
dispatches through a fixed table with one function pointer per method, built for
a concrete type the caller no longer knows.

Anything that cannot be represented by a single, fixed function pointer that takes
a pointer to the erased value is ruled out:

| Rule                                                     | Why                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| No generic methods (`fn f<T>(&self, t: T)`)              | Would need infinitely many table entries, one per `T`        |
| No returning `Self` by value (`fn dup(&self) -> Self`)   | The caller cannot know the size of the erased type           |
| Every method needs a receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&mut self`, `Box<Self>`, `Rc<Self>`, `Arc<Self>`, `Pin<P>`) | Without a value there is nothing to dispatch on |
| No associated constants                                  | Constants are looked up by type, which is erased             |
| No generic associated types                              | Not supported in the vtable model                            |
| No `impl Trait` returns or `async fn` in the trait       | Each impl returns a different hidden type                    |
| The trait must not require `Self: Sized`                 | `dyn Trait` itself is unsized                                |

There is an escape hatch: a method annotated with `where Self: Sized` is excluded
from the vtable. The trait stays dyn compatible, the method remains callable on
concrete types, and it is simply unavailable through `dyn Trait`. This is how
`Iterator` keeps `map`, `filter`, and friends (all generic) while still allowing
`Box<dyn Iterator>`.

The classic casualty is `Clone`, since `clone` returns `Self`. A `Box<dyn Shape>`
cannot be cloned directly; the standard workaround is a `clone_box` method that
returns `Box<dyn Shape>` instead.

```rust
// NOT dyn compatible
trait Duplicate {
    fn dup(&self) -> Self;                  // returns Self by value
}
// fn bad(x: &dyn Duplicate) {}             // error[E0038]: the trait `Duplicate`
                                            // is not dyn compatible

// Dyn compatible thanks to `where Self: Sized` opt-outs
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;                  // in the vtable

    fn scaled<T: Into<f64>>(&self, k: T) -> f64   // generic: opted out
    where
        Self: Sized,
    {
        self.area() * k.into()
    }

    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>;  // the clone workaround
}

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Square(f64);

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        self.0 * self.0
    }
    fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape> {
        Box::new(self.clone())              // concrete Self is known here
    }
}

impl Clone for Box<dyn Shape> {             // allowed: Box<dyn Shape> is local
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        self.clone_box()
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sq = Square(2.0);
    println!("{}", sq.scaled(3));           // 12: fine on a concrete type

    let obj: Box<dyn Shape> = Box::new(sq);
    println!("{}", obj.area());             // 4: dispatched through the vtable
    // obj.scaled(3);                        // error: the `scaled` method cannot be
                                             // invoked on a trait object

    let copy = obj.clone();                 // works via clone_box
    println!("{}", copy.area());            // 4
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Only dyn-compatible (object-safe) traits can be used as `dyn Trait`.
> - Generic methods, returning `Self`, receiver-less functions, and associated
>   constants break dyn compatibility because a fixed vtable cannot express them.
> - `where Self: Sized` removes a method from the vtable while keeping the trait
>   usable as an object.
> - Use a `clone_box` method to clone trait objects.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a trait with `fn new() -> Self` and try to use it as `&dyn Trait`. Fix
>    it with `where Self: Sized`.
> 2. Implement the `clone_box` pattern for a `Plugin` trait and clone a
>    `Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>`.
> 3. Interview: Why can `Iterator` be used as `dyn Iterator` even though it has
>    dozens of generic methods like `map`? (Hint: look at the `where` clauses on
>    those methods in the documentation.)

#### Vtables and Fat Pointers

How does `s.area()` find the right function when the type of `s` is erased? The
answer is in the pointer itself. A `&dyn Shape` is a **fat pointer**: two
machine words instead of one.

1. A **data pointer** to the concrete value (the `Circle` or `Square`).
2. A **vtable pointer** to a static, read-only table generated by the compiler for
   that specific `(concrete type, trait)` pair.

The vtable holds the information needed to use and destroy the value without
knowing its type: a pointer to its destructor (`drop_in_place`), its size and
alignment (needed by `Box` to deallocate), and one function pointer per trait
method, including methods inherited from supertraits.

A call `s.area()` compiles to: load the vtable pointer, load the `area` slot at a
fixed offset, and make an indirect call passing the data pointer as `self`. There
is one vtable per type, shared by every trait object of that type, so the cost
per object is just the extra pointer word.

Slices use the same idea with different metadata: `&[T]` and `&str` are fat
pointers carrying a **length** instead of a vtable. This differs from C++, where
the vtable pointer lives *inside* every object; in Rust the object stays plain
data, and the pointer carries the type information only when you ask for a trait
object.

```text
   let c = Circle(1.0);
   let s: &dyn Shape = &c;

   s (fat pointer, 16 bytes)        stack                    static memory
   +------------------+          +-------------+
   | data ptr         | -------> | Circle(1.0) |
   +------------------+          +-------------+          vtable <Circle as Shape>
   | vtable ptr       | ------------------------------->  +------------------------+
   +------------------+                                   | drop_in_place::<Circle>|
                                                          | size  = 8              |
                                                          | align = 8              |
                                                          | area  -> Circle::area  |
                                                          | name  -> Circle::name  |
                                                          +------------------------+

   s.area()  ==>  (vtable.area)(data ptr)      one indirect call
```

```rust
use std::fmt::Display;
use std::mem::size_of;

trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
}

struct Circle(f64);
impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        3.14159 * self.0 * self.0
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Sizes on a 64-bit target (one word = 8 bytes)
    println!("{}", size_of::<&Circle>());           // 8   thin pointer
    println!("{}", size_of::<&dyn Shape>());        // 16  data + vtable
    println!("{}", size_of::<Box<dyn Shape>>());    // 16  same layout, owned
    println!("{}", size_of::<&[u8]>());             // 16  data + length
    println!("{}", size_of::<&str>());              // 16  data + length
    println!("{}", size_of::<Box<dyn Display>>());  // 16
    println!("{}", size_of::<Circle>());            // 8   no hidden vptr inside

    // Two trait objects of the same type share one vtable
    let a = Circle(1.0);
    let b = Circle(2.0);
    // (different data pointers, identical vtable pointers)
    let (ra, rb): (&dyn Shape, &dyn Shape) = (&a, &b);
    println!("{:.2} {:.2}", ra.area(), rb.area());  // 3.14 12.57
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `&dyn Trait` and `Box<dyn Trait>` are fat pointers: a data pointer plus a
>   vtable pointer.
> - Each `(type, trait)` pair gets one static vtable holding drop glue, size,
>   alignment, and method pointers.
> - A dynamic call is one load plus one indirect call through the vtable.
> - Unlike C++, Rust objects carry no hidden vtable pointer; the type information
>   lives in the pointer, and only when you create a trait object.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `size_of` for `&dyn Shape`, `&mut dyn Shape`, `Rc<dyn Shape>`, and
>    `Option<Box<dyn Shape>>`. Explain why the last one is still 16 bytes.
> 2. Draw the vtable for a `Square` that implements a trait with three methods and
>    a supertrait with one method.
> 3. Interview: Where does Rust store the vtable pointer, and how does that differ
>    from C++? What does that difference cost or save for a `Vec` of a million
>    small structs that are never used as trait objects? (Hint: count bytes per
>    element.)

#### Performance Trade-offs

With generics, `impl Trait`, and `dyn Trait` all available, which one should you
use? The choice is a trade-off between runtime speed, binary size, compile time,
and flexibility, and the right answer depends on which of those matters in a given
place.

**Static dispatch** (generics, `impl Trait`) resolves every call at compile time.
The optimizer sees the concrete function and can inline it, which in turn enables
constant folding, vectorization, and dead-code elimination across the call. The
cost is one copy of the generic code per concrete type: larger binaries and longer
compiles.

**Dynamic dispatch** (`dyn Trait`) compiles the calling code once. Each call is an
indirect jump through the vtable, which is cheap by itself (a few nanoseconds),
but it usually **blocks inlining**, so the optimizations above are lost. Trait
objects often come with a heap allocation (`Box`) and a pointer chase. In
exchange you get heterogeneous collections, smaller binaries, faster compiles, and
types chosen at runtime.

A third option is often overlooked: **enum dispatch**. When the set of types is
closed and known (all the shapes your program supports), an `enum` with one
variant per type and a `match` in each method gives static, inlinable dispatch,
values stored inline with no `Box`, and a heterogeneous `Vec`. The price is that
adding a new type means editing the enum.

| Criterion                  | Generics / `impl Trait` | `dyn Trait`               | Enum                       |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Call cost                  | Direct, inlinable       | Indirect, rarely inlined  | Branch on tag, inlinable   |
| Heterogeneous collection   | No                      | Yes                       | Yes                        |
| Heap allocation            | No                      | Usually (`Box`)           | No                         |
| Binary size                | Grows per type          | One copy                  | One copy                   |
| Compile time               | Higher                  | Lower                     | Lower                      |
| Open to new types          | Yes                     | Yes, even from other crates | No, closed set           |
| Type chosen at runtime     | No                      | Yes                       | Yes, among known variants  |

A practical rule: default to generics in hot paths and library APIs, reach for
`dyn Trait` for plugin points, callbacks stored in structs, and heterogeneous
collections of an open set of types, and use an enum when the set is closed.
Measure before optimizing: in most programs the indirect call is not the
bottleneck.

```rust
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
}

struct Circle(f64);
struct Square(f64);
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) -> f64 { 3.14159 * self.0 * self.0 } }
impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.0 * self.0 } }

// 1. Static: one specialized copy per T; but a Vec<T> holds a single type
fn total_static<T: Shape>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()   // area() can be inlined
}

// 2. Dynamic: one copy; mixed types; each call goes through a vtable
fn total_dyn(shapes: &[Box<dyn Shape>]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()   // indirect call per element
}

// 3. Enum: closed set; mixed types; no Box; match is static and inlinable
enum AnyShape {
    Circle(Circle),
    Square(Square),
}

impl AnyShape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            AnyShape::Circle(c) => c.area(),
            AnyShape::Square(s) => s.area(),
        }
    }
}

fn total_enum(shapes: &[AnyShape]) -> f64 {
    shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let squares = [Square(1.0), Square(2.0)];
    println!("{:.2}", total_static(&squares));      // 5.00

    let mixed: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![Box::new(Circle(1.0)), Box::new(Square(2.0))];
    println!("{:.2}", total_dyn(&mixed));           // 7.14

    let mixed_enum = [AnyShape::Circle(Circle(1.0)), AnyShape::Square(Square(2.0))];
    println!("{:.2}", total_enum(&mixed_enum));     // 7.14
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Static dispatch is fastest because it enables inlining, at the cost of binary
>   size and compile time.
> - Dynamic dispatch costs an indirect call and lost inlining, often plus an
>   allocation, but gives runtime flexibility and heterogeneous collections.
> - Enum dispatch combines heterogeneous storage with static calls when the set of
>   types is closed.
> - Choose by context and measure; the indirect call is rarely the real
>   bottleneck.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Triangle` to all three versions of the example. Which version required
>    changes in the most places?
> 2. Benchmark `total_static`, `total_dyn`, and `total_enum` over a million
>    elements with `std::time::Instant` in `--release` mode and compare.
> 3. Interview: You are designing a plugin system where third-party crates add new
>    handlers. Would you use generics, trait objects, or an enum, and why? (Hint:
>    which options let code you have never seen add new types after your crate is
>    compiled?)

<a id="54-advanced-trait-techniques"></a>
### 5.4 Advanced Trait Techniques

With the fundamentals in place, this section turns to the techniques that shape
real library APIs: traits parameterized by types, implementations that cover
whole families of types, traits that carry no methods, wrappers that work around
coherence, explicit disambiguation, and traits that outsiders may use but not
implement.

#### Generic Traits and Type Parameters

Associated types (Section 5.1) let each implementor fix a related type once. Some
relationships are not one-to-one, though. A `Meters` value can be built *from* an
`f64`, *from* a `Feet`, *and from* a `Centimeters`. Each of those is a separate
capability, so the trait must be implementable several times for the same type.

A trait with a **type parameter**, `trait From<T>`, does exactly that. `From<f64>`
and `From<Feet>` are, as far as the compiler is concerned, two different traits,
and `Meters` can implement both. The parameter is an *input*: the user of the
trait chooses it, and the compiler selects the matching implementation, often by
inference from the argument type.

Type parameters on traits may have **defaults**. `Add<Rhs = Self>` means `impl Add
for Vec2` is shorthand for `impl Add<Vec2> for Vec2`, while `impl Add<f64> for
Vec2` remains possible. Defaults keep the common case short without closing off
the general one.

The flexibility has a cost: with several implementations available, inference can
become ambiguous, and you sometimes need a type annotation to pick one.

```rust
use std::ops::Add;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Meters(f64);
```
