```rust
struct Feet(f64);

// A generic trait: one impl per source type
trait Convert<T> {
    fn convert(value: T) -> Self;
}

impl Convert<f64> for Meters {
    fn convert(v: f64) -> Self {
        Meters(v)
    }
}

impl Convert<Feet> for Meters {
    fn convert(v: Feet) -> Self {
        Meters(v.0 * 0.3048)
    }
}

// Default type parameter in action: Add<Rhs = Self>
impl Add for Meters {                       // means Add<Meters>
    type Output = Meters;
    fn add(self, o: Meters) -> Meters {
        Meters(self.0 + o.0)
    }
}

impl Add<Feet> for Meters {                 // a second, mixed-type impl
    type Output = Meters;
    fn add(self, o: Feet) -> Meters {
        self + Meters::convert(o)
    }
}

// A generic trait used as a bound: "anything convertible to Meters"
fn total<T>(items: Vec<T>) -> Meters
where
    Meters: Convert<T>,                     // bound on the TARGET, not on T
{
    items.into_iter().map(Meters::convert).fold(Meters(0.0), |a, b| a + b)
}

trait Describe<Lang> {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}
struct English;
struct Italian;

impl Describe<English> for Meters {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("{} meters", self.0) }
}
impl Describe<Italian> for Meters {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("{} metri", self.0) }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Meters::convert(2.0);           // picks Convert<f64> from the argument
    let b = Meters::convert(Feet(10.0));    // picks Convert<Feet>
    println!("{:.4}", (a + b).0);           // 5.0480
    println!("{:.4}", (a + Feet(1.0)).0);   // 2.3048

    println!("{:?}", total(vec![1.0, 2.5])); // Meters(3.5)

    // println!("{}", a.describe());        // error[E0283]: type annotations
                                            // needed (two impls apply)
    println!("{}", Describe::<Italian>::describe(&a));  // 2 metri
    println!("{}", <Meters as Describe<English>>::describe(&a));  // 2 meters
}
```

| Aspect                         | Generic trait `Trait<T>`         | Associated type `type T`         |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Impls per implementing type    | Many, one per `T`                | Exactly one                      |
| Who picks `T`                  | The caller (input)               | The implementor (output)         |
| Inference                      | May need annotations             | Always determined                |
| Standard library examples      | `From<T>`, `Add<Rhs>`, `PartialEq<Rhs>` | `Iterator::Item`, `Deref::Target`, `Add::Output` |

> Key Takeaways
> - A type parameter on a trait turns it into a family of traits; a type can
>   implement each member separately.
> - Use type parameters for inputs the caller chooses, associated types for
>   outputs the implementor determines; `Add` uses both.
> - Default type parameters (`Rhs = Self`) keep the common case concise.
> - Multiple applicable impls can make inference ambiguous; disambiguate with
>   turbofish or fully qualified syntax.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `impl Convert<Centimeters> for Meters` and call `total` with a
>    `Vec<Centimeters>`.
> 2. Implement `PartialEq<Feet> for Meters` so that `Meters(0.3048) == Feet(1.0)`
>    holds (compare with a small tolerance).
> 3. Interview: `Add` has both a type parameter (`Rhs`) and an associated type
>    (`Output`). Why is each one the right tool for its role? (Hint: ask who
>    decides each type, and how many answers there should be for a given pair of
>    operands.)

#### Blanket Implementations

Implementing a trait type by type works until you notice that the implementation
is the same for every type with some property. Every type that implements
`Display` can be turned into a `String` the same way. Writing that impl for each
type would be endless, and it would never cover types that do not exist yet.

A **blanket implementation** implements a trait for *every* type that satisfies a
bound, in a single `impl`:

```rust
impl<T: Display + ?Sized> ToString for T { /* ... */ }
```

That one line in the standard library is why any `Display` type has
`.to_string()`. Other famous blanket impls: `impl<T, U: From<T>> Into<U> for T`
(which is why you implement `From` and get `Into`), `impl<T> From<T> for T`, and
`impl<I: Iterator> IntoIterator for I`.

Two common patterns:

- **Extension traits for families of types**: define a trait with default methods
  and blanket-implement it for every type with a bound (`impl<I: Iterator>
  MyIterExt for I {}`). This adds methods to all iterators at once, the way the
  `itertools` crate does.
- **Forwarding impls**: `impl<T: Shape + ?Sized> Shape for &T` or `for Box<T>`
  so that references and boxes satisfy the same bound as the values they point
  to.

Blanket impls interact with coherence. Two impls that could apply to the same type
conflict (`error[E0119]`), and the compiler must assume a foreign type *might*
gain an implementation in the future. Adding a blanket impl to an already
published trait is therefore a breaking change: it can collide with impls users
already wrote. Overlapping impls with a "more specific wins" rule
(*specialization*) are still unstable.

```rust
use std::fmt::Debug;

// 1. A behavior for every Debug type, written once
trait Inspect {
    fn inspect(&self) -> String;
}

impl<T: Debug + ?Sized> Inspect for T {     // covers i32, Vec<_>, str, user types...
    fn inspect(&self) -> String {
        format!("<{:?}>", self)
    }
}

// impl Inspect for i32 { ... }             // error[E0119]: conflicting
                                            // implementations: i32 is already
                                            // covered by the blanket impl

// 2. Extension trait: new methods on every iterator of i32
trait SumSquares: Iterator<Item = i32> + Sized {
    fn sum_squares(self) -> i32 {
        self.map(|x| x * x).sum()
    }
}

impl<I: Iterator<Item = i32>> SumSquares for I {}   // empty body: all defaults

// 3. Forwarding impl: &T satisfies the bound whenever T does
trait Area {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
}
struct Square(f64);
impl Area for Square {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        self.0 * self.0
    }
}
impl<T: Area + ?Sized> Area for &T {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        (**self).area()                     // delegate to the pointee
    }
}

fn sum_areas<A: Area>(items: &[A]) -> f64 {
    items.iter().map(|a| a.area()).sum()
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Token(u8);

fn main() {
    println!("{}", 42_i32.inspect());       // <42>
    println!("{}", "hi".inspect());         // <"hi">
    println!("{}", Token(7).inspect());     // <Token(7)>: user type, no extra impl

    println!("{}", vec![1_i32, 2, 3].into_iter().sum_squares());   // 14
    println!("{}", (1..=3_i32).sum_squares());                      // 14: a Range too

    let a = Square(1.0);
    let b = Square(2.0);
    let refs = [&a, &b];                    // a slice of &Square
    println!("{}", sum_areas(&refs));       // 5: works thanks to the forwarding impl
}
```

```text
   impl<T: Debug + ?Sized> Inspect for T

        all types
   +-------------------------------------+
   |   types that implement Debug        |
   |  +-------------------------------+  |
   |  | i32  str  Vec<u8>  Token  ... |  |  <- all get Inspect from ONE impl
   |  +-------------------------------+  |
   |   NotDebug, closures, ...           |  <- no Inspect
   +-------------------------------------+
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A blanket impl, `impl<T: Bound> Trait for T`, implements a trait for every
>   type satisfying the bound.
> - It powers `ToString`, `Into`, and extension traits such as `itertools`.
> - Forwarding impls for `&T` and `Box<T>` let wrappers satisfy the same bounds as
>   their contents.
> - Blanket impls block overlapping impls, and adding one to a published trait is
>   a breaking change.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a trait `Doubled` with `fn doubled(&self) -> Self` and blanket-implement
>    it for every `T: Clone + std::ops::Add<Output = T>`. Test it on `i32` and
>    `f64`.
> 2. Add an `Area` forwarding impl for `Box<T>` and pass a `Vec<Box<Square>>` to
>    `sum_areas`.
> 3. Interview: Why is adding `impl<T: Display> MyTrait for T` to an existing,
>    published library a semver-breaking change? (Hint: what happens to a user who
>    already wrote `impl MyTrait for TheirType` and `TheirType` implements
>    `Display`?)

#### Marker Traits

Some properties are not behaviors. "This type can be copied bit for bit." "This
type can be sent to another thread." "This type has a size known at compile time."
There is nothing to *call*, only something to *guarantee*. Rust expresses such
guarantees as **marker traits**: traits with no methods at all, used purely as
bounds.

The standard library's marker traits fall into groups:

| Trait   | Meaning                                       | Implemented how                         |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Copy`  | Bitwise copy is a valid duplicate             | Derived or written explicitly           |
| `Eq`    | Equality is reflexive                         | Derived or written explicitly           |
| `Sized` | Size is known at compile time                 | Automatically by the compiler           |
| `Send`  | Ownership can move to another thread          | Auto trait                              |
| `Sync`  | `&T` can be shared between threads            | Auto trait                              |
| `Unpin` | Safe to move after being pinned               | Auto trait                              |

**Auto traits** are implemented automatically for a type when all of its fields
implement them. A struct of `i32` and `String` is `Send` with no code from you; a
struct containing an `Rc` is not, because `Rc` is not `Send`. Opting out of an
auto trait is done by containing a type that lacks it (for example
`PhantomData<*const ()>`); opting in for a type the compiler rejects requires
`unsafe impl Send for T {}`, because you are now vouching for a guarantee the
compiler could not verify. Chapter 10 covers `Send` and `Sync` in depth.

**`Sized`** is special: every generic parameter has an implicit `T: Sized` bound.
Writing `T: ?Sized` ("maybe sized") relaxes it so the function also accepts
unsized types such as `str`, `[T]`, and `dyn Trait`, provided they are behind a
pointer.

You can also define your own marker traits to classify types at compile time, for
example to mark which message types are safe to log, or which units are lengths.

```rust
use std::fmt::Debug;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

// A custom marker trait: no methods, used purely as a compile-time tag
trait Loggable {}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Login { user: String }
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Password { secret: String }

impl Loggable for Login {}                  // explicitly approved for logging
// Password is deliberately NOT Loggable

fn log<T: Loggable + Debug>(event: &T) {
    println!("[log] {event:?}");
}

// ?Sized lets the function accept str, slices, and trait objects by reference
fn show<T: Debug + ?Sized>(value: &T) {
    println!("{value:?}");
}

fn main() {
    log(&Login { user: "ana".into() });     // [log] Login { user: "ana" }
    let p = Password { secret: "x".into() };
    // log(&p);                             // error[E0277]: `Password` is not Loggable
    let _ = p.secret;

    show("a str");                          // "a str"   (str is unsized)
    show(&[1, 2, 3][..]);                   // [1, 2, 3] ([i32] is unsized)

    // Send is inferred from the fields
    let shared = Arc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);   // Arc<Vec<i32>>: Send + Sync
    let h = thread::spawn(move || shared.len());
    println!("{}", h.join().unwrap());      // 3

    let local = Rc::new(5);
    // thread::spawn(move || *local);       // error[E0277]: `Rc<i32>` cannot be
                                            // sent between threads safely
    println!("{local}");                    // 5
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Marker traits carry no methods; they encode a guarantee checked at compile
>   time.
> - Auto traits (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`) are implemented automatically when all
>   fields qualify; manual opt-in requires `unsafe impl`.
> - Every generic parameter is implicitly `Sized`; `?Sized` relaxes that to accept
>   `str`, slices, and trait objects behind pointers.
> - Custom marker traits are a cheap way to whitelist types for an operation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}` and call it as `assert_send::<String>()`
>    and `assert_send::<Rc<u8>>()`. Read the second error.
> 2. Remove the `?Sized` from `show` and observe which calls stop compiling.
> 3. Interview: Why does implementing `Send` manually require `unsafe`, when
>    implementing `Display` does not? (Hint: what can go wrong if the promise is
>    false, and who can detect it?)

#### Newtype Pattern

A *newtype* is a tuple struct with exactly one field: `struct Meters(f64);`. It
looks trivial, yet it solves several unrelated problems, because it creates a
brand-new **local** type with the same runtime representation as the wrapped one.

1. **Bypassing the orphan rule.** You cannot `impl Display for Vec<String>`
   (both foreign), but you can `impl Display for Names` where `struct
   Names(Vec<String>)`.
2. **Type safety.** `UserId(u64)` and `OrderId(u64)` are both a `u64` at runtime,
   but the compiler rejects passing one where the other is expected. This turns a
   whole class of mix-ups into compile errors.
3. **Invariants by construction.** If the field is private and the only
   constructor validates the input (`Email::parse`), every `Email` value in the
   program is valid. This is often summarized as "parse, don't validate".
4. **Different trait behavior.** A `Reverse<T>` or a case-insensitive string
   wrapper can implement `Ord` or `PartialEq` differently from the inner type.

Newtypes are zero-cost: the wrapper has the same size and layout as its content
(guaranteed with `#[repr(transparent)]`). The cost is ergonomic: the wrapper hides
all of the inner type's methods. Solutions, from most to least controlled, are to
forward the methods you need, expose an `as_inner()` / `into_inner()` accessor,
or implement `Deref`, which exposes everything and therefore weakens point 3.

```rust
use std::fmt;

// 1. Orphan-rule workaround
struct Names(Vec<String>);

impl fmt::Display for Names {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{}", self.0.join(" | "))
    }
}

// 2. Type safety: same representation, different types
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct UserId(u64);
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct OrderId(u64);

fn cancel(order: OrderId, by: UserId) {
    println!("order {} cancelled by user {}", order.0, by.0);
}

// 3. Invariant by construction: private field + validating constructor
mod email {
    #[derive(Debug)]
    pub struct Email(String);               // field is private to this module

    impl Email {
        pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Email, String> {
            if s.contains('@') && !s.starts_with('@') && !s.ends_with('@') {
                Ok(Email(s.to_lowercase()))
            } else {
                Err(format!("invalid email: {s}"))
            }
        }
        pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {      // controlled, read-only access
            &self.0
        }
    }
}

use email::Email;

fn send_welcome(to: &Email) {               // no re-validation needed here
    println!("welcome sent to {}", to.as_str());
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", Names(vec!["Ana".into(), "Bo".into()]));    // Ana | Bo

    let user = UserId(7);
    let order = OrderId(1001);
    cancel(order, user);                    // order 1001 cancelled by user 7
    // cancel(user, order);                 // error[E0308]: expected `OrderId`,
                                            // found `UserId`

    match Email::parse("Ana@Example.com") {
        Ok(e) => send_welcome(&e),          // welcome sent to ana@example.com
        Err(msg) => println!("{msg}"),
    }
    println!("{:?}", Email::parse("nope").is_err());   // true
    // let fake = email::Email(String::new());          // error[E0603]: tuple
                                                        // struct constructor is private

    println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<UserId>());     // 8: same as u64
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A newtype wraps one value in a new local type with identical runtime layout.
> - It bypasses the orphan rule, prevents mixing up values that share a
>   representation, and enforces invariants through private fields.
> - It is zero-cost at runtime; `#[repr(transparent)]` guarantees the layout.
> - The downside is that inner methods are hidden; forward them selectively
>   rather than reaching for `Deref` by default.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create `struct Celsius(f64)` and `struct Fahrenheit(f64)` with `From`
>    conversions both ways, and confirm a function taking `Celsius` rejects a
>    `Fahrenheit`.
> 2. Write `struct NonZeroCount(u32)` with a constructor returning `Option<Self>`
>    and a `get()` accessor.
> 3. Interview: When would you implement `Deref` on a newtype, and when would that
>    defeat its purpose? (Hint: compare a transparent wrapper used only for the
>    orphan rule with a wrapper that guarantees an invariant.)

#### Fully Qualified Syntax

Nothing stops two traits from defining methods with the same name, and nothing
stops a type from implementing both, plus an inherent method of the same name.
When you write `x.fly()`, the compiler needs a rule to pick one:

1. **Inherent methods win** over trait methods.
2. If only trait methods match and more than one trait in scope provides one,
   the call is **ambiguous** (`error[E0034]`).

To pick explicitly, Rust offers increasingly specific forms:

| Syntax                             | Use when                                                   |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `x.method()`                       | No ambiguity                                               |
| `Trait::method(&x)`                | A method with a `self` receiver; the receiver identifies the type |
| `<Type as Trait>::function()`      | An associated function without `self`, or to name the exact impl |
| `<T as Trait>::Assoc`              | An associated type, when `T::Assoc` would be ambiguous     |

The last two forms are the *fully qualified syntax*. Without a `self` argument
there is nothing to infer the type from, so `Animal::baby_name()` alone cannot
know whether you mean the `Dog` or the `Cat` implementation; `<Dog as
Animal>::baby_name()` says both.

Analogy: calling out "Alex!" in a crowded room works until there are two people
named Alex; then you have to say "Alex from accounting".

```rust
trait Pilot {
    fn fly(&self) -> String;
}
trait Wizard {
    fn fly(&self) -> String;
}

struct Human;

impl Pilot for Human {
    fn fly(&self) -> String { "This is your captain speaking.".into() }
}
impl Wizard for Human {
    fn fly(&self) -> String { "Up!".into() }
}
impl Human {
    fn fly(&self) -> String { "*waving arms furiously*".into() }   // inherent
}

trait Animal {
    fn baby_name() -> String;               // no `self`: associated function
}

struct Dog;

impl Dog {
    fn baby_name() -> String { "Spot".into() }          // inherent
}
impl Animal for Dog {
    fn baby_name() -> String { "puppy".into() }
}

// Disambiguating an associated type in generic code
fn first_item<I: Iterator>(mut it: I) -> Option<<I as Iterator>::Item> {
    it.next()                               // `I::Item` works too; the full form
}                                           // is needed when several traits
                                            // define `Item`

fn main() {
    let p = Human;
    println!("{}", p.fly());                // *waving arms furiously*  (inherent wins)
    println!("{}", Pilot::fly(&p));         // This is your captain speaking.
    println!("{}", Wizard::fly(&p));        // Up!
    println!("{}", <Human as Wizard>::fly(&p));  // Up!  (fully qualified)

    println!("{}", Dog::baby_name());       // Spot  (inherent)
    // println!("{}", Animal::baby_name()); // error[E0790]: cannot call associated
                                            // function on trait without
                                            // specifying the corresponding `impl` type
    println!("{}", <Dog as Animal>::baby_name());   // puppy

    println!("{:?}", first_item("ab".chars()));     // Some('a')
    let zero = <i32 as Default>::default();         // explicit trait + type
    println!("{zero}");                              // 0
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Inherent methods take precedence over trait methods with the same name.
> - `Trait::method(&x)` selects a trait when the receiver identifies the type.
> - `<Type as Trait>::item` (fully qualified syntax) is required for associated
>   functions without `self` and for ambiguous associated types.
> - Ambiguous calls are compile errors (`E0034`, `E0790`), never silent guesses.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement both `std::fmt::Display` and a custom trait `Render` with a method
>    `fmt` for one type, and call each explicitly.
> 2. Give a struct an inherent `new()` and a trait `Factory` with `fn new() ->
>    Self`, then call both.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Animal::baby_name()` fail to compile while
>    `Pilot::fly(&p)` succeeds, even though both name only the trait? (Hint: where
>    can the compiler find the implementing type in each call?)

#### Sealed Traits

When you publish a trait, you usually make two promises at once: "you may use
this trait" and "you may implement this trait". Sometimes you want only the
first. Perhaps your code relies on a closed set of implementations (every
`Encoding` is one of three you wrote), or you want freedom to add required
methods later without breaking anyone, which is only possible if nobody outside
your crate has written an implementation.

A **sealed trait** is public to use but impossible to implement outside its
crate. Rust has no keyword for it; it is a pattern built on the privacy rules:

1. Create a **private** module containing a **public** trait, conventionally
   `Sealed`.
2. Make your public trait require it as a supertrait: `pub trait Format:
   private::Sealed`.
3. Implement `Sealed` only for your own types.

Downstream code can name `Format`, use it as a bound, and call its methods. But to
implement `Format` it would also have to implement `private::Sealed`, and it
cannot even *name* that trait, because the module is private. The standard library
uses this, for example, for `SliceIndex`, which is why you can index slices with
ranges but cannot add your own index types.

Sealing is a deliberate API commitment in the other direction: users lose the
ability to extend the trait. Document it, so they understand why their impl does
not compile. A related variant seals individual *methods* by giving them a
parameter of a private type, which lets outsiders implement the trait but not
call or override that method.

```rust
// --- In the library crate (simulated by a module) ---------------------------
mod formats {
    mod private {
        pub trait Sealed {}                 // public trait in a PRIVATE module
    }

    pub trait Format: private::Sealed {     // usable everywhere, implementable here only
        fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
        fn encode(&self, data: &[u8]) -> String;
    }

    pub struct Hex;
    pub struct Binary;

    impl private::Sealed for Hex {}
    impl private::Sealed for Binary {}

    impl Format for Hex {
        fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "hex" }
        fn encode(&self, data: &[u8]) -> String {
            data.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect()
        }
    }

    impl Format for Binary {
        fn name(&self) -> &'static str { "bin" }
        fn encode(&self, data: &[u8]) -> String {
            data.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:08b}")).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ")
        }
    }
}

// --- In a downstream crate (simulated by the parent module) -----------------
use formats::{Binary, Format, Hex};

fn dump(f: &impl Format, data: &[u8]) {     // using the trait as a bound: allowed
    println!("{}: {}", f.name(), f.encode(data));
}

struct Base64;
// impl Format for Base64 { ... }           // error[E0277]: the trait bound
                                            // `Base64: formats::private::Sealed`
                                            // is not satisfied
// impl formats::private::Sealed for Base64 {}  // error[E0603]: module `private`
                                                // is private

fn main() {
    dump(&Hex, b"Hi");                      // hex: 4869
    dump(&Binary, &[5, 255]);               // bin: 00000101 11111111
    let _ = Base64;
}
```

```text
   crate `formats` (library)                    downstream crate
   +---------------------------------+          +------------------------------+
   | mod private (not pub)           |          |                              |
   |   pub trait Sealed   <-- hidden ---- X --- | cannot name Sealed           |
   |                                 |          |                              |
   | pub trait Format: Sealed  --------------->  | can use Format as a bound    |
   | impl Format for Hex, Binary     |          | can call name(), encode()    |
   +---------------------------------+          | cannot impl Format           |
                                                +------------------------------+
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A sealed trait can be used and called by anyone but implemented only inside
>   its defining crate.
> - The pattern: a public `Sealed` trait inside a private module, required as a
>   supertrait of the public trait.
> - Sealing lets a library add methods freely and rely on a closed set of
>   implementations.
> - It removes users' ability to extend the trait, so document the decision.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a third format, `Octal`, inside the `formats` module and confirm it can
>    be passed to `dump`.
> 2. Move the "downstream" code into a separate module `app` and verify that the
>    sealing still holds there.
> 3. Interview: You maintain a library trait and want to add a required method in
>    a minor release. Under what conditions is that not a breaking change, and how
>    can you guarantee those conditions in advance? (Hint: who else could have
>    implemented the trait?)

## 6. Collections, Strings, and Iterators

Almost every program spends most of its time storing groups of values, handling
text, and walking through sequences. This chapter covers the standard library's
collection types and how to choose between them, Rust's UTF-8 string model and
why it refuses to let you index a string by position, and the iterator and
closure machinery that lets you process data in expressive pipelines that
compile down to plain loops.

<a id="61-standard-collections"></a>
### 6.1 Standard Collections

The `std::collections` module provides a small, carefully chosen set of data
structures. This section covers each of them, what it costs, and when to reach
for it.

#### Vec and Capacity

Arrays (`[T; N]`) have a size fixed at compile time. Most real data does not:
lines read from a file, users connected to a server, results of a search. `Vec<T>`
is Rust's growable array and by far the most used collection. It stores its
elements contiguously on the heap, so indexing is a single address computation
and iteration is as cache-friendly as it gets.

A `Vec` is a small struct of three words on the stack: a **pointer** to the heap
buffer, a **capacity** (how many elements the buffer can hold), and a **length**
(how many it currently holds). Pushing into spare capacity is just a write. When
the buffer is full, `push` allocates a larger buffer (roughly double), moves the
elements over, and frees the old one. Because the size grows geometrically,
`push` is *amortized* O(1): the expensive copies happen rarely enough that their
average cost per push is constant.

Think of a bookshelf. Length is how many books you own; capacity is how much shelf
you have. When the shelf is full you buy one twice as big and move everything,
which is slow, but you do it rarely.

Capacity management tools:

- `Vec::with_capacity(n)` allocates room for `n` elements up front when you know
  the size, avoiding every intermediate reallocation.
- `reserve(n)` ensures room for `n` *more* elements.
- `shrink_to_fit()` releases unused capacity after a large vector has shrunk.
- `clear()` sets the length to zero but **keeps** the capacity for reuse.

Reallocation moves the elements, so any reference into the old buffer would
dangle. This is exactly the bug the borrow checker prevents: you cannot `push`
while holding a reference to an element (`error[E0502]`).

```text
   let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(4); v.push(10); v.push(20); v.push(30);

   stack (Vec<i32>)            heap buffer
   +----------+               +----+----+----+----+
   | ptr      | ------------> | 10 | 20 | 30 |  ? |
   | cap = 4  |               +----+----+----+----+
   | len = 3  |                 initialized    spare
   +----------+
```

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();         // no allocation yet: capacity 0
    let mut last_cap = v.capacity();
    for i in 0..20 {
        v.push(i);
        if v.capacity() != last_cap {         // report each reallocation
            println!("len {:>2} -> capacity {}", v.len(), v.capacity());
            last_cap = v.capacity();
        }
    }
    // Typical output (growth policy is an implementation detail):
    // len  1 -> capacity 4
    // len  5 -> capacity 8
    // len  9 -> capacity 16
    // len 17 -> capacity 32

    let mut w = Vec::with_capacity(100);      // one allocation, up front
    w.extend(0..100);
    println!("{} {}", w.len(), w.capacity()); // 100 100

    w.truncate(10);
    w.shrink_to_fit();                        // give memory back
    println!("{} {}", w.len(), w.capacity()); // 10 10

    // Core operations
    let mut names = vec!["ana", "bo", "cy", "di"];
    names.insert(1, "ed");                    // O(n): shifts the tail right
    let removed = names.remove(0);            // O(n): shifts the tail left
    let swapped = names.swap_remove(0);       // O(1): moves the last into the hole
    println!("{removed} {swapped} {names:?}");    // ana ed ["di", "bo", "cy"]

    println!("{:?} {:?}", names.get(1), names.get(99));  // Some("bo") None
    // names[99];                             // panics: index out of bounds

    let first = &names[0];
    // names.push("zed");                     // error[E0502]: cannot borrow `names`
                                              // as mutable because it is also
                                              // borrowed as immutable
    println!("{first}");                      // di
}
```

| Operation                 | Cost            | Notes                                |
| ------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `push`, `pop`             | Amortized O(1)  | At the end                           |
| `v[i]`, `get(i)`          | O(1)            | `[]` panics, `get` returns `Option`  |
| `insert(i, x)`, `remove(i)` | O(n)          | Shift every later element            |
| `swap_remove(i)`          | O(1)            | Does not preserve order              |
| `contains(&x)`            | O(n)            | Linear scan; sort + `binary_search` for O(log n) |

> Key Takeaways
> - A `Vec` is a pointer, a capacity, and a length; elements live contiguously on
>   the heap.
> - Geometric growth makes `push` amortized O(1); `with_capacity` and `reserve`
>   avoid reallocations when the size is known.
> - Reallocation moves elements, which is why you cannot push while holding a
>   reference into the vector.
> - Prefer `get` over `[]` when an index might be out of range.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a `Vec<String>` of 1,000 entries twice, once with `Vec::new()` and once
>    with `Vec::with_capacity(1000)`, counting reallocations in each case.
> 2. Write a function that removes all even numbers from a `Vec<i32>` in place
>    using `retain`, and compare it with collecting into a new vector.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Vec::push` described as "amortized O(1)" rather than
>    O(1)? What would happen to its complexity if the vector grew by a fixed 10
>    elements each time? (Hint: sum the cost of all copies over `n` pushes.)

#### VecDeque

A `Vec` is fast at one end only. Removing the *first* element shifts every other
element left, which is O(n). That makes it a poor queue: a task scheduler,
breadth-first search, or a sliding window over a stream all add at one end and
remove at the other.

`VecDeque<T>` ("vector double-ended queue") solves this with a **ring buffer**. It
keeps a contiguous buffer plus a `head` index; the elements may wrap around the
end of the buffer back to the start. Pushing or popping at either end only moves
the head or the length, so all four operations (`push_front`, `push_back`,
`pop_front`, `pop_back`) are O(1) (amortized for pushes).

The price is that the elements are not always contiguous in memory. You can still
index with `dq[i]` in O(1), but you cannot take a single `&[T]` slice without
first calling `make_contiguous()`; `as_slices()` returns the two pieces instead.

```text
   capacity 8, head = 6, len = 4      logical order: A B C D

   index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
          +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
          | C | D |   |   |   |   | A | B |
          +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
                    ^ back            ^ head (front)

   push_front(Z) writes at index 5;  push_back(E) writes at index 2
```

```rust
use std::collections::VecDeque;

fn main() {
    // A FIFO queue: push at the back, pop from the front, both O(1)
    let mut queue: VecDeque<&str> = VecDeque::new();
    queue.push_back("job1");
    queue.push_back("job2");
    queue.push_front("urgent");               // jumps the line
    while let Some(job) = queue.pop_front() {
        print!("{job} ");                     // urgent job1 job2
    }
    println!();

    // Round-robin scheduling: rotate the front element to the back
    let mut players: VecDeque<_> = ["ana", "bo", "cy"].into();
    for _ in 0..4 {
        let p = players.pop_front().unwrap();
        print!("{p} ");                       // ana bo cy ana
        players.push_back(p);
    }
    println!();

    // Sliding window: keep only the last 3 readings
    let mut window = VecDeque::with_capacity(3);
    for reading in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] {
        if window.len() == 3 {
            window.pop_front();               // drop the oldest
        }
        window.push_back(reading);
        let avg: i32 = window.iter().sum::<i32>() / window.len() as i32;
        print!("{avg} ");                     // 10 15 20 30 40
    }
    println!();

    // Indexing works; slices need care because the data may wrap
    let mut dq: VecDeque<i32> = (1..=5).collect();
    dq.rotate_left(2);                        // [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
    println!("{} {:?}", dq[0], dq);           // 3 [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
    let slice: &[i32] = dq.make_contiguous(); // rearranges into one block
    println!("{slice:?}");                    // [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
}
```

| Operation                | `Vec<T>`        | `VecDeque<T>`  |
| ------------------------ | --------------- | -------------- |
| Push/pop at the back     | O(1)            | O(1)           |
| Push/pop at the front    | O(n)            | O(1)           |
| Index `x[i]`             | O(1)            | O(1)           |
| Contiguous `&[T]`        | Always          | Only after `make_contiguous` |
| Typical use              | Lists, stacks   | Queues, windows, BFS |

> Key Takeaways
> - `VecDeque` is a growable ring buffer with O(1) operations at both ends.
> - Use it for queues, round-robin rotation, sliding windows, and breadth-first
>   search.
> - Indexing is still O(1), but elements may wrap, so slices need
>   `make_contiguous` or `as_slices`.
> - If you only ever touch the back, a plain `Vec` is simpler and slightly faster.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a breadth-first traversal of a small graph stored as `Vec<Vec<usize>>`
>    using a `VecDeque<usize>` as the frontier.
> 2. Write a function that checks whether a string is a palindrome by pushing its
>    characters into a `VecDeque<char>` and popping from both ends.
> 3. Interview: How does a ring buffer achieve O(1) removal from the front without
>    shifting elements? (Hint: what changes, the data or an index?)

#### HashMap and Entry API

Looking a value up by position is easy with a `Vec`; looking it up by *name* is
not. A phone book, a cache, a word counter, or a configuration table needs to go
from a key to a value without scanning everything. `HashMap<K, V>` does this in
O(1) on average by hashing the key to find a bucket directly.

Requirements and properties:

- **Keys must implement `Eq + Hash`** (Chapter 5.2). Floats therefore cannot be
  keys directly.
- **Iteration order is unspecified** and changes between runs. The default hasher
  (SipHash 1-3) is randomly seeded to resist hash-flooding denial-of-service
  attacks. If you need ordering, sort the output or use a `BTreeMap`.
- **Ownership**: `insert` takes the key and value by value. Inserting a `String`
  key moves it into the map. Lookups take a borrowed form (`&str` for `String`
  keys) thanks to the `Borrow` trait, so you do not need to allocate to search.
- `insert` returns the **previous** value as `Option<V>`; `get` returns
  `Option<&V>`; `remove` returns `Option<V>`.

The **Entry API** solves a pattern that is awkward in most languages: "if the key
exists, update it; otherwise insert a default". A naive version looks the key up
twice (and fights the borrow checker). `map.entry(key)` does one lookup and
returns an `Entry` that is either `Occupied` or `Vacant`, with helpers to finish
the job:

| Method                         | Effect                                                 |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `.or_insert(v)`                | Insert `v` if vacant; return `&mut V` either way       |
| `.or_insert_with(\|\| make())` | Same, but compute the default lazily                   |
| `.or_default()`                | Insert `V::default()` if vacant                        |
| `.and_modify(\|v\| ...)`       | Modify if occupied; chain with an `or_*` for vacant    |
| `match entry { Occupied(..), Vacant(..) }` | Full control over both cases           |

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::collections::hash_map::Entry;

fn main() {
    // Basic operations
    let mut stock: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
    stock.insert("apple".to_string(), 3);
    let old = stock.insert("apple".to_string(), 5);    // replaces
    println!("{old:?}");                                // Some(3)
    println!("{:?}", stock.get("apple"));               // Some(5)  (&str lookup)
    println!("{:?}", stock.get("pear"));                // None
    println!("{}", stock.contains_key("apple"));        // true

    // Entry API: word frequency with a single lookup per word
    let text = "the cat saw the other cat the end";
    let mut freq: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for word in text.split_whitespace() {
        *freq.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;            // &mut usize returned
    }

    // HashMap order is random: sort before printing for stable output
    let mut pairs: Vec<_> = freq.iter().collect();
    pairs.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));
    println!("{:?}", &pairs[..2]);                      // [("the", 3), ("cat", 2)]

    // Grouping: or_default creates the Vec on first sight of a key
    let mut by_len: HashMap<usize, Vec<&str>> = HashMap::new();
    for w in ["hi", "cat", "yo", "dog", "a"] {
        by_len.entry(w.len()).or_default().push(w);
    }
    println!("{:?}", by_len[&3]);                       // ["cat", "dog"]

    // and_modify + or_insert: update or initialize
    let mut scores: HashMap<&str, i32> = HashMap::new();
    for (name, pts) in [("ana", 10), ("bo", 5), ("ana", 7)] {
        scores.entry(name).and_modify(|s| *s += pts).or_insert(pts);
    }
    println!("{}", scores["ana"]);                      // 17

    // Matching on Entry for full control
    match stock.entry("kiwi".to_string()) {
        Entry::Occupied(e) => println!("already {}", e.get()),
        Entry::Vacant(e) => {
            e.insert(12);
            println!("added kiwi");                     // added kiwi
        }
    }
    println!("{}", stock.len());                        // 2
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `HashMap` gives average O(1) insert, lookup, and removal; keys need `Eq +
>   Hash`.
> - Iteration order is unspecified and randomized; never rely on it.
> - Owned keys move into the map, but lookups accept borrowed forms such as `&str`.
> - The Entry API performs "update or insert" with a single lookup and no borrow
>   checker friction.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Count the occurrences of each character in a sentence with
>    `HashMap<char, usize>` and print them sorted by character.
> 2. Build an index `HashMap<String, Vec<usize>>` mapping each word to the line
>    numbers where it appears.
> 3. Interview: Why does Rust's `HashMap` use a randomly seeded hash function by
>    default, and when might you swap it for a faster one? (Hint: think about who
>    controls the keys.)

#### BTreeMap and Ordering

A `HashMap` scatters keys deliberately, so it cannot answer questions about
*order*: "what is the smallest key?", "list all events between 9:00 and 12:00",
"give me the entries in sorted order". `BTreeMap<K, V>` keeps its keys sorted at
all times, making those questions cheap.

It is a **B-tree**: a balanced search tree where each node holds several keys
(rather than one, as in a binary tree). Packing keys into nodes means fewer
pointer hops and better cache behavior. Operations are O(log n), and keys need
`Ord` instead of `Hash`.

What you gain over `HashMap`:

- **Sorted iteration**, deterministic between runs, which also makes output and
  tests reproducible.
- **Range queries** with `range(a..b)`, in O(log n + k) for `k` results.
- **Min and max** via `first_key_value()`, `last_key_value()`, and `pop_first()`.

What you pay: each lookup is O(log n) and involves comparisons, so for pure
key-value lookup with no ordering needs, `HashMap` is usually faster.

```rust
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    // Events keyed by minute of the day
    let mut timeline: BTreeMap<u32, &str> = BTreeMap::new();
    timeline.insert(13 * 60, "lunch review");
    timeline.insert(9 * 60, "standup");
    timeline.insert(17 * 60 + 30, "deploy");
    timeline.insert(10 * 60 + 15, "design sync");

    // Iteration is always in key order
    for (minute, event) in &timeline {
        println!("{:02}:{:02} {event}", minute / 60, minute % 60);
    }
    // 09:00 standup
    // 10:15 design sync
    // 13:00 lunch review
    // 17:30 deploy

    // Range query: everything from 10:00 up to (not including) 14:00
    let morning: Vec<_> = timeline.range(10 * 60..14 * 60).map(|(_, e)| *e).collect();
    println!("{morning:?}");                    // ["design sync", "lunch review"]

    // Smallest and largest keys
    println!("{:?}", timeline.first_key_value());   // Some((540, "standup"))
    println!("{:?}", timeline.last_key_value());    // Some((1050, "deploy"))

    // "Next event at or after 12:00"
    let next = timeline.range(12 * 60..).next();
    println!("{next:?}");                       // Some((780, "lunch review"))

    // Entry API works the same as HashMap
    let mut letters: BTreeMap<char, u32> = BTreeMap::new();
    for c in "mississippi".chars() {
        *letters.entry(c).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    println!("{letters:?}");                    // {'i': 4, 'm': 1, 'p': 2, 's': 4}
}
```

| Property               | `HashMap<K, V>`             | `BTreeMap<K, V>`              |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Key requirement        | `Eq + Hash`                 | `Ord`                         |
| Lookup / insert        | O(1) average                | O(log n)                      |
| Iteration order        | Unspecified, random         | Sorted by key                 |
| Range queries, min/max | No                          | Yes                           |
| Deterministic output   | No                          | Yes                           |
| Best for               | Fast lookup by key          | Ordered data, ranges, reports |

> Key Takeaways
> - `BTreeMap` keeps keys sorted; it needs `Ord` keys and gives O(log n)
>   operations.
> - It supports range queries, min/max access, and deterministic iteration.
> - Choose `HashMap` for raw lookup speed and `BTreeMap` when order matters.
> - B-trees store many keys per node, which keeps them cache-friendly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Store student grades in a `BTreeMap<String, u32>` and print them
>    alphabetically, then print only names from "c" up to (not including) "m".
> 2. Given a `BTreeMap<u32, f64>` of price changes by timestamp, find the most
>    recent price at or before a given timestamp using `range(..=t).next_back()`.
> 3. Interview: Why does Rust's ordered map use a B-tree rather than a red-black
>    tree like C++'s `std::map`? (Hint: think about memory layout and cache
>    misses per lookup.)

#### HashSet and BTreeSet

Often you care only whether something is present, not about an associated value:
"have I visited this node?", "which tags does this post have?", "remove the
duplicates from this list". A set answers membership questions efficiently and
guarantees each element appears at most once.

Rust's sets are thin wrappers over its maps: `HashSet<T>` is essentially
`HashMap<T, ()>`, and `BTreeSet<T>` is `BTreeMap<T, ()>`. They inherit the same
trade-offs: `HashSet` is O(1) average and unordered (needs `Eq + Hash`), while
`BTreeSet` is O(log n), sorted, and supports ranges (needs `Ord`).

Sets also support mathematical **set operations**, each returning a lazy iterator:

| Operation              | Method                     | Operator (on references) |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Union (in either)      | `a.union(&b)`              | `&a \| &b`               |
| Intersection (in both) | `a.intersection(&b)`       | `&a & &b`                |
| Difference (in a only) | `a.difference(&b)`         | `&a - &b`                |
| Symmetric difference   | `a.symmetric_difference(&b)` | `&a ^ &b`              |

`insert` returns a `bool` telling you whether the value was new, which is handy for
"first time seen" logic.

```rust
use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashSet};

fn main() {
    // Deduplicate while preserving first-seen order: insert() returns false on repeats
    let visits = ["home", "about", "home", "blog", "about", "shop"];
    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    let unique: Vec<_> = visits.iter().filter(|p| seen.insert(**p)).collect();
    println!("{unique:?}");                     // ["home", "about", "blog", "shop"]

    // Set algebra with sorted sets (sorted output is deterministic)
    let rust: BTreeSet<&str> = ["ana", "bo", "cy", "di"].into();
    let go: BTreeSet<&str> = ["cy", "di", "ed"].into();

    let both: Vec<_> = rust.intersection(&go).collect();
    println!("{both:?}");                       // ["cy", "di"]
    let only_rust: BTreeSet<_> = &rust - &go;   // operator form builds a new set
    println!("{only_rust:?}");                  // {"ana", "bo"}
    let either: BTreeSet<_> = &rust | &go;
    println!("{either:?}");                     // {"ana", "bo", "cy", "di", "ed"}
    let one_side: Vec<_> = rust.symmetric_difference(&go).collect();
    println!("{one_side:?}");                   // ["ana", "bo", "ed"]

    // Relations
    let core: BTreeSet<&str> = ["cy"].into();
    println!("{} {}", core.is_subset(&go), rust.is_disjoint(&go));  // true false

    // BTreeSet ranges and extremes
    let nums: BTreeSet<i32> = [7, 1, 9, 4, 4, 12].into_iter().collect();
    println!("{nums:?}");                       // {1, 4, 7, 9, 12}
    println!("{:?}", nums.range(5..).next());  // Some(7): smallest >= 5
    println!("{:?}", nums.last());              // Some(12)
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Sets store unique values and answer membership in O(1) (`HashSet`) or
>   O(log n) (`BTreeSet`).
> - They are maps with `()` values and share the same key requirements.
> - Union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference are available as
>   methods (lazy) and operators on references (new set).
> - `insert` returning `bool` makes "first occurrence" checks one line.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Given two `Vec<u32>` of user IDs, print the IDs present in both, using
>    `HashSet`.
> 2. Write `fn has_duplicates<T: Eq + Hash>(items: &[T]) -> bool` that stops at the
>    first duplicate.
> 3. Interview: You need to deduplicate a 10-million-element `Vec<u64>`. Compare
>    `sort` + `dedup` against collecting into a `HashSet`. (Hint: consider memory
>    usage, whether order matters, and constant factors.)

#### BinaryHeap

Some problems need "the most important item next", over and over, while new items
keep arriving: a job scheduler, an event simulation, Dijkstra's shortest path, or
"the top 10 scores in a stream". Sorting after every insertion would be O(n log n)
each time. A **priority queue** does better.

`BinaryHeap<T>` is a max-heap stored in a `Vec`: a complete binary tree in which
every parent is greater than or equal to its children. The maximum is always at
the root, so `peek` is O(1), while `push` and `pop` are O(log n) because they only
repair one root-to-leaf path. Elements need `Ord`.

For a **min-heap**, wrap elements in `std::cmp::Reverse` (Chapter 5.2). For custom
priorities, implement `Ord` on your type, or push tuples like `(priority, item)`,
which compare by their first field first.

Iterating over a heap (`iter()`) visits elements in internal array order, **not**
priority order. To get sorted output, pop repeatedly or call `into_sorted_vec()`.

```text
   BinaryHeap after pushing 3, 9, 4, 1, 7          array layout
                 9                                 [9, 7, 4, 1, 3]
               /   \                                children of i: 2i+1, 2i+2
              7     4
             / \
            1   3          pop() removes 9, moves 3 to the root, sifts it down
```

```rust
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Task {
    priority: u8,                             // compared first (field order)
    name: &'static str,                       // tie-breaker
}

fn main() {
    // Max-heap: the largest comes out first
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from(vec![3, 9, 4, 1, 7]);
    println!("{:?}", heap.peek());            // Some(9)
    heap.push(8);
    let order: Vec<_> = std::iter::from_fn(|| heap.pop()).collect();
    println!("{order:?}");                    // [9, 8, 7, 4, 3, 1]

    // Scheduler with derived Ord on a struct
    let mut tasks = BinaryHeap::new();
    tasks.push(Task { priority: 2, name: "email" });
    tasks.push(Task { priority: 9, name: "outage" });
    tasks.push(Task { priority: 5, name: "review" });
    while let Some(t) = tasks.pop() {
        print!("{}({}) ", t.name, t.priority); // outage(9) review(5) email(2)
    }
    println!();

    // Min-heap with Reverse: earliest deadline first
    let mut deadlines = BinaryHeap::new();
    for (day, job) in [(14, "taxes"), (3, "rent"), (7, "report")] {
        deadlines.push(Reverse((day, job)));
    }
    if let Some(Reverse((day, job))) = deadlines.pop() {
        println!("next: {job} on day {day}"); // next: rent on day 3
    }

    // Top-k largest of a stream in O(n log k): keep a min-heap of size k
    let stream = [5, 1, 22, 9, 14, 3, 30, 7];
    let k = 3;
    let mut top = BinaryHeap::with_capacity(k + 1);
    for x in stream {
        top.push(Reverse(x));
        if top.len() > k {
            top.pop();                        // evict the smallest of the k+1
        }
    }
    let mut best: Vec<_> = top.into_iter().map(|Reverse(x)| x).collect();
    best.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));
    println!("{best:?}");                     // [30, 22, 14]
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `BinaryHeap` is a max-heap priority queue: O(1) `peek`, O(log n) `push`/`pop`.
> - Use `Reverse` for a min-heap and `Ord` (derived or manual) for custom
>   priorities.
> - Iteration order is not priority order; pop or use `into_sorted_vec` for sorted
>   output.
> - A size-k min-heap finds the top k elements of a stream in O(n log k).

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Merge three sorted `Vec<i32>` into one sorted vector using a min-heap of
>    `Reverse((value, source_index, position))`.
> 2. Implement a `Job` type whose `Ord` puts higher priority first and, among
>    equal priorities, the smaller `id` first.
> 3. Interview: Why is building a heap from an existing vector with
>    `BinaryHeap::from(vec)` O(n) and not O(n log n)? (Hint: most nodes in a
>    complete binary tree are near the bottom.)

#### Choosing the Right Collection

Every collection is a set of trade-offs, and choosing the wrong one usually shows
up as code that is either slow or awkward. A good rule from the standard library
documentation itself: **use `Vec` unless you have a specific reason not to**.
Contiguous memory is so fast on modern CPUs that a linear scan over a small `Vec`
often beats a hash lookup.

Ask three questions, in order:

1. **How will I find elements?** By position (`Vec`, `VecDeque`), by key
   (`HashMap`, `BTreeMap`), by membership (`HashSet`, `BTreeSet`), or always the
   largest/smallest (`BinaryHeap`)?
2. **Does order matter?** Insertion order (`Vec`, `VecDeque`), sorted order
   (`BTree*`, or sort a `Vec`), or not at all (`Hash*`)?
3. **Where do insertions and removals happen?** Only at the end (`Vec`), at both
   ends (`VecDeque`), anywhere by key (maps and sets)?

`LinkedList` also exists in `std::collections`, but it is rarely the right choice:
poor cache locality and per-node allocation make `Vec` or `VecDeque` faster for
almost every workload.

```text
   Need key -> value?
     yes -> Need sorted keys or range queries?  yes -> BTreeMap
                                                no  -> HashMap
     no  -> Only need "is it present?" / uniqueness?
              yes -> Need sorted order?  yes -> BTreeSet
                                         no  -> HashSet
              no  -> Always take the max/min next?  yes -> BinaryHeap
                     no  -> Add/remove at the front?  yes -> VecDeque
                                                      no  -> Vec
```

| Collection      | Access by       | Order            | Insert / remove           | Lookup            |
| --------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `Vec`           | Index           | Insertion        | O(1) end, O(n) elsewhere  | O(n), O(log n) if sorted |
| `VecDeque`      | Index           | Insertion        | O(1) both ends            | O(n)              |
| `HashMap`       | Key             | None             | O(1) average              | O(1) average      |
| `BTreeMap`      | Key             | Sorted by key    | O(log n)                  | O(log n)          |
| `HashSet`       | Value           | None             | O(1) average              | O(1) average      |
| `BTreeSet`      | Value           | Sorted           | O(log n)                  | O(log n)          |
| `BinaryHeap`    | Max only        | Heap order       | O(log n)                  | O(1) max only     |

Because all collections implement `FromIterator`, switching between them is often a
one-word change to the target type of `collect` (Section 6.3).

```rust
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, BTreeSet, HashSet, VecDeque};

fn main() {
    let words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "fig", "kiwi", "apple"];

    // Same input, different collections: only the target type changes
    let list: Vec<&str> = words.iter().copied().collect();        // keeps duplicates
    let unique: HashSet<&str> = words.iter().copied().collect();  // unordered, unique
    let sorted: BTreeSet<&str> = words.iter().copied().collect(); // sorted, unique
    let queue: VecDeque<&str> = words.iter().copied().collect();  // ready for pop_front
    let lengths: BTreeMap<&str, usize> =
        words.iter().map(|w| (*w, w.len())).collect();            // key -> value

    println!("{} {} {}", list.len(), unique.len(), queue.len());  // 6 4 6
    println!("{sorted:?}");          // {"apple", "fig", "kiwi", "pear"}
    println!("{lengths:?}");         // {"apple": 5, "fig": 3, "kiwi": 4, "pear": 4}

    // Small data: a linear scan over a Vec is perfectly fine (and often fastest)
    let small = vec![("red", 0xff0000), ("green", 0x00ff00), ("blue", 0x0000ff)];
    let green = small.iter().find(|(name, _)| *name == "green").map(|(_, v)| v);
    println!("{:06x}", green.unwrap());   // 00ff00
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Default to `Vec`; switch only for a concrete reason such as key lookup, front
>   removal, uniqueness, ordering, or priority.
> - Pick between `Hash*` and `BTree*` by whether you need order and range queries.
> - `LinkedList` is almost never the best choice in Rust.
> - `collect` makes changing the collection type cheap, so it is easy to measure
>   alternatives.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For each scenario, pick a collection and justify it: an LRU cache's recency
>    list, a spell-checker dictionary, a leaderboard printed in rank order, and an
>    undo stack.
> 2. Rewrite a function that uses `Vec::contains` inside a loop over 100,000 items
>    to use a `HashSet`, and measure the difference in `--release` mode.
> 3. Interview: When can a linear search over a `Vec` outperform a `HashMap`
>    lookup? (Hint: consider the cost of hashing and cache misses for small `n`.)

<a id="62-strings-and-text"></a>
### 6.2 Strings and Text

Text handling is where Rust feels most different from other languages, because
it refuses to hide the fact that text is encoded. This section explains the
owned/borrowed split, the UTF-8 model and its consequences, and the specialized
string types used at operating-system and C boundaries.

#### String vs &str

Rust has two main string types, and the split mirrors `Vec<T>` versus `&[T]`
(Chapter 3.2):

- **`String`** is an **owned**, growable, heap-allocated buffer of UTF-8 bytes.
  Internally it is a `Vec<u8>` with the guarantee that the bytes are valid UTF-8.
  It owns its data, can be modified, and frees its buffer when dropped.
- **`&str`** ("string slice") is a **borrowed view** into UTF-8 bytes that live
  somewhere else: inside a `String`, in the program binary, or in any buffer. It
  is a fat pointer (address + length) and cannot grow.

String literals such as `"hello"` have type `&'static str`: the bytes are baked
into the executable and live for the whole program.

Analogy: a `String` is a notebook you own and can write in; a `&str` is a
photocopy of a few pages that you can read but not change, and it is only valid
as long as the notebook exists.

The practical API rule follows from this: **functions that only read text should
take `&str`**. A `&String` coerces to `&str` automatically (deref coercion,
Chapter 5.2), so a `&str` parameter accepts literals, `String`s, and slices of
either. Take a `String` only when the function needs to keep or modify it.

```text
   let s = String::from("hello world");
   let w: &str = &s[6..];

   s (String: ptr, cap, len)        heap
   +-----------+                   +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
   | ptr       | ----------------> | h | e | l | l | o |   | w | o | r | l | d |
   | cap = 11  |                   +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
   | len = 11  |                                             ^
   +-----------+                                             |
   w (&str: ptr, len)                                        |
   +-----------+                                             |
   | ptr       | --------------------------------------------+
   | len = 5   |
   +-----------+
```

```rust
// Takes &str: works with literals, String, and slices
fn count_vowels(s: &str) -> usize {
    s.chars().filter(|c| "aeiouAEIOU".contains(*c)).count()
}

// Takes String: needs ownership because it stores the value
struct User {
    name: String,
}

impl User {
    fn new(name: impl Into<String>) -> Self {     // accept &str or String
        User { name: name.into() }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let literal: &'static str = "hello";          // lives in the binary
    let owned: String = String::from("world");    // heap-allocated, growable
    let also_owned = literal.to_string();         // &str -> String (allocates)
    let borrowed: &str = &owned;                  // String -> &str (free)
    let explicit: &str = owned.as_str();          // same, spelled out

    println!("{}", count_vowels(literal));        // 2
    println!("{}", count_vowels(&owned));         // 1  (&String coerces to &str)
    println!("{}", count_vowels(&owned[1..3]));   // 1  ("or")

    let mut greeting = also_owned;                // only String can grow
    greeting.push_str(", ");
    greeting += borrowed;
    println!("{greeting}");                       // hello, world

    let u = User::new("Ana");
    let v = User::new(String::from("Bo"));
    println!("{} {} {}", u.name, v.name, explicit);   // Ana Bo world

    println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<String>()); // 24: ptr + cap + len
    println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<&str>());   // 16: ptr + len
}
```

| Aspect           | `String`                         | `&str`                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Ownership        | Owns its buffer                  | Borrows someone else's bytes        |
| Mutable / growable | Yes                            | No                                  |
| Size on stack    | 3 words (ptr, cap, len)          | 2 words (ptr, len)                  |
| Created by       | `String::from`, `to_string`, `format!` | Literals, `&s[..]`, `as_str`   |
| Use for          | Struct fields, building text     | Function parameters, read-only views |

> Key Takeaways
> - `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer; `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8
>   bytes.
> - String literals are `&'static str`.
> - Accept `&str` in functions that only read text; `&String` coerces to it.
> - Converting `String -> &str` is free; `&str -> String` allocates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` and call it with a literal, a `String`,
>    and a slice of a `String`.
> 2. Change a struct field from `&'a str` to `String` and explain which lifetime
>    problems disappear.
> 3. Interview: Why is `fn f(s: &str)` preferred over `fn f(s: &String)`? (Hint:
>    list every kind of string value each signature can accept.)

#### UTF-8 Encoding and Indexing

In many languages `s[3]` returns the fourth character. In Rust, it does not
compile. The reason is the encoding. Rust strings are **UTF-8**, a
variable-width encoding in which a single character takes between **1 and 4
bytes**:

| Character | Code point | UTF-8 bytes          | Byte count |
| --------- | ---------- | -------------------- | ---------- |
| `a`       | U+0061     | `61`                 | 1          |
| `é`       | U+00E9     | `C3 A9`              | 2          |
| `€`       | U+20AC     | `E2 82 AC`           | 3          |
| `𝄞`       | U+1D11E    | `F0 9D 84 9E`        | 4          |

Because widths vary, "the fourth character" cannot be found without scanning from
the start, which would make `s[i]` secretly O(n). Worse, returning "the byte at
position i" would hand back meaningless fragments of characters. Rather than pick
a surprising answer, Rust refuses: `s[i]` is a compile error (`error[E0277]: the
type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}``).

Consequences to internalize:

- **`len()` returns bytes, not characters.** `"héllo".len()` is 6.
- **Slicing uses byte ranges** (`&s[0..3]`) and **panics** if a boundary falls
  inside a multi-byte character. `is_char_boundary(i)` and `get(a..b)` (which
  returns `Option`) let you check safely.
- **You choose the unit explicitly**: `.bytes()`, `.chars()`, or grapheme
  clusters (next topic).

UTF-8's benefits explain why Rust accepts this friction: ASCII text is stored
unchanged at one byte per character, it is the dominant encoding on the web and in
files, and it needs no conversion at I/O boundaries.

```rust
fn main() {
    let s = "héllo€";

    println!("{}", s.len());                // 9 bytes: h(1) é(2) l l o(3) €(3)
    println!("{}", s.chars().count());      // 6 characters (O(n) to compute)

    // let c = s[1];                        // error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot
                                            // be indexed by `{integer}`

    // The n-th character must be found by scanning
    println!("{:?}", s.chars().nth(1));     // Some('é')

    // Byte-range slicing must respect character boundaries
    println!("{}", &s[0..3]);               // hé   (bytes 0..3 = 'h' + 2 bytes of 'é')
    println!("{}", s.is_char_boundary(2));  // false: byte 2 is inside 'é'
    println!("{:?}", s.get(0..2));          // None: safe alternative to panicking
    // let bad = &s[0..2];                  // panics at runtime: byte index 2 is
                                            // not a char boundary

    // Looking at the raw encoding
    for c in ['a', 'é', '€', '𝄞'] {
        let mut buf = [0u8; 4];
        let encoded = c.encode_utf8(&mut buf);
        println!("{c} U+{:04X} {} byte(s) {:02X?}",
                 c as u32, c.len_utf8(), encoded.as_bytes());
    }
    // a U+0061 1 byte(s) [61]
    // é U+00E9 2 byte(s) [C3, A9]
    // € U+20AC 3 byte(s) [E2, 82, AC]
    // 𝄞 U+1D11E 4 byte(s) [F0, 9D, 84, 9E]

    // Invalid UTF-8 is rejected at construction
    let bytes = vec![0x66, 0x6F, 0xFF];     // 0xFF never appears in UTF-8
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8(bytes).is_err());           // true
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&[0x66, 0x6F, 0xFF])); // fo� (U+FFFD)
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Rust strings are UTF-8; a character occupies 1 to 4 bytes.
> - `s[i]` does not compile because "the i-th character" is ambiguous and O(n).
> - `len()` counts bytes; slicing uses byte ranges and panics off a character
>   boundary; `get` returns `Option` instead.
> - Every `String` and `&str` is guaranteed valid UTF-8; invalid bytes are rejected
>   when the string is created.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print the byte length and character count of `"naïve café"` and explain the
>    difference.
> 2. Write `fn safe_prefix(s: &str, max_bytes: usize) -> &str` that returns the
>    longest prefix of at most `max_bytes` bytes that ends on a character boundary.
> 3. Interview: Why does Rust not allow `s[i]` on strings, while Python does?
>    (Hint: compare how each language stores text internally and what the
>    operation would cost.)

#### Chars, Bytes, and Grapheme Clusters

"How many characters are in this string?" has more than one correct answer, and
Rust makes you pick. There are three levels:

1. **Bytes** (`.bytes()`, `as_bytes()`): the raw UTF-8 code units, `u8`. Right for
   binary protocols, hashing, ASCII-only parsing, and performance-critical scans.
2. **Chars** (`.chars()`): Unicode *scalar values*, `char` (always 4 bytes in
   memory). Right for most text processing that is not displayed character by
   character.
3. **Grapheme clusters**: what a human perceives as one character. `é` can be one
   `char` (U+00E9) or two: `e` followed by the combining accent U+0301. Flags,
   family emoji, and many Indic syllables are also multi-`char` graphemes.

The standard library stops at `char`. For grapheme clusters, use the
`unicode-segmentation` crate. That matters for anything user-visible: cursor
movement, truncating names for display, reversing text, or counting "letters".

`.char_indices()` pairs each `char` with its **byte** offset, which is how you
safely compute slice boundaries from character positions.

```text
   "ne\u{301}e"   displayed as "née"

   graphemes:   [ n ]  [ e + ◌́ ]  [ e ]           3 user-perceived characters
   chars:       'n'    'e' 'U+0301'  'e'          4 chars
   bytes:       6E     65  CC 81     65           5 bytes
```

```rust
fn main() {
    let decomposed = "ne\u{301}e";          // n, e, combining acute, e -> "née"

    println!("{}", decomposed.len());               // 5 bytes
    println!("{}", decomposed.chars().count());     // 4 chars
    // Graphemes: 3, but only with the unicode-segmentation crate (see below)

    // Bytes: raw u8 values
    let bytes: Vec<u8> = decomposed.bytes().collect();
    println!("{bytes:X?}");                 // [6E, 65, CC, 81, 65]

    // char_indices: char plus its BYTE offset
    for (i, c) in "aé€".char_indices() {
        print!("{i}:{c} ");                 // 0:a 1:é 3:€
    }
    println!();

    // Reversing by chars breaks combining marks: the accent moves to the wrong letter
    let reversed: String = decomposed.chars().rev().collect();
    println!("{:?}", reversed);             // "e\u{301}en": accent now on the first e

    // ASCII fast paths operate on bytes and are always safe
    let id = "user_42";
    println!("{}", id.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'_')); // true
    println!("{}", "Hello".to_ascii_uppercase());   // HELLO

    // char methods understand Unicode
    println!("{} {} {}", 'é'.is_alphabetic(), '7'.to_digit(10).unwrap(), 'ß'.is_lowercase());
    // true 7 true
}
```

With the `unicode-segmentation` crate (`cargo add unicode-segmentation`):

```rust
use unicode_segmentation::UnicodeSegmentation;

fn grapheme_demo() {
    let s = "ne\u{301}e";
    let g: Vec<&str> = s.graphemes(true).collect();   // `true` = extended clusters
    println!("{}", g.len());                          // 3
    let reversed: String = s.graphemes(true).rev().collect();
    println!("{reversed}");                           // "eén": accent stays with its e
}
```

| Unit              | API                        | Type   | Use for                                      |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| Byte              | `.bytes()`, `.as_bytes()`  | `u8`   | Protocols, ASCII parsing, hashing            |
| Unicode scalar    | `.chars()`, `.char_indices()` | `char` | General text processing                   |
| Grapheme cluster  | `unicode-segmentation`     | `&str` | Anything a user sees: cursors, truncation, reversal |

> Key Takeaways
> - Text can be viewed as bytes, `char`s (Unicode scalar values), or grapheme
>   clusters, and each gives a different "length".
> - A `char` is not a user-perceived character; combining marks and many symbols
>   span several `char`s.
> - `char_indices` yields byte offsets, the safe bridge between characters and
>   slicing.
> - Use `unicode-segmentation` for user-visible operations on graphemes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Count the ASCII digits in a string using `.bytes()` and then using `.chars()`.
>    Do the results ever differ?
> 2. Write `fn truncate_chars(s: &str, n: usize) -> &str` that returns the first
>    `n` chars using `char_indices` to find the byte cut point.
> 3. Interview: A user reports that your app shows broken accents after
>    truncating their name to 10 characters. What went wrong, and how do you fix
>    it? (Hint: which unit did the truncation count?)

#### String Slicing and Concatenation

Once you can read strings, you need to cut them apart and stick them together.
Rust offers several ways to do each, and the differences are mostly about
**ownership** and **allocation**.

**Slicing** produces a `&str` borrowing from the original, with no copying:
`&s[start..end]` uses byte offsets (and panics off a character boundary), while
`s.get(start..end)` returns `Option<&str>`. Higher-level methods usually avoid
manual offsets entirely: `split`, `split_once`, `strip_prefix`, `trim`, `find`.

**Concatenation** options:

| Method                         | Allocates?                     | Notes                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| `s.push_str("x")`, `s.push('x')` | Only if capacity runs out    | Mutates `s` in place                        |
| `s1 + &s2`                     | Reuses `s1`'s buffer           | **Consumes** `s1`; right side must be `&str` |
| `s += "x"`                     | Reuses `s`'s buffer            | `AddAssign`; same as `push_str`             |
| `format!("{a}-{b}")`           | Always a new `String`          | Most readable, borrows all inputs           |
| `[a, b].concat()`, `.join(sep)` | One new `String`, sized exactly | Best for many pieces                     |

The `+` operator surprises newcomers. Its signature is effectively `fn add(self,
other: &str) -> String`: it takes the left `String` **by value**, appends to its
buffer, and returns it. That is efficient (no copy of the left side), but the
left operand is moved. And because there is no `impl Add for &str`, `"a" + "b"`
does not compile: two borrowed slices have no buffer to grow.

```rust
fn main() {
    // --- Slicing ---------------------------------------------------------------
    let line = "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1";
    let method = &line[..3];                        // "GET": bytes 0..3
    let (verb, rest) = line.split_once(' ').unwrap();   // no manual indices
    let path = rest.split(' ').next().unwrap();
    println!("{method} {verb} {path}");             // GET GET /index.html

    let file = "report.final.pdf";
    let ext = file.rsplit_once('.').map(|(_, e)| e);
    println!("{ext:?}");                            // Some("pdf")
    println!("{:?}", "v1.2".strip_prefix('v'));     // Some("1.2")
    println!("[{}]", "  padded  ".trim());          // [padded]
    println!("{:?}", line.find("HTTP"));            // Some(16): a byte offset

    // --- Concatenation ---------------------------------------------------------
    let mut s = String::with_capacity(32);
    s.push_str("hello");
    s.push(',');
    s += " world";                                  // AddAssign<&str>
    println!("{s}");                                // hello, world

    let a = String::from("tic");
    let b = String::from("tac");
    let c = a + "-" + &b + "-toe";                  // `a` is MOVED into the result
    // println!("{a}");                             // error[E0382]: borrow of
                                                    // moved value: `a`
    println!("{c} {b}");                            // tic-tac-toe tac  (b only borrowed)

    // let bad = "a" + "b";                         // error[E0369]: cannot add
                                                    // `&str` to `&str`
    let good = "a".to_owned() + "b";
    println!("{good}");                             // ab

    let x = 3;
    let msg = format!("{b} has {x} letters");       // borrows; nothing moved
    println!("{msg}");                              // tac has 3 letters

    let parts = ["usr", "local", "bin"];
    println!("/{}", parts.join("/"));               // /usr/local/bin
    println!("{}", ["ab", "cd", "ef"].concat());    // abcdef

    // Building from an iterator
    let csv: String = (1..=4).map(|n| n.to_string()).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(",");
    println!("{csv}");                              // 1,2,3,4

    // Removing and replacing
    let mut t = String::from("one two three");
    t.replace_range(4..7, "2");                     // byte range, in place
    println!("{t}");                                // one 2 three
    println!("{}", t.replace("three", "3"));        // one 2 3   (new String)
    t.truncate(3);
    println!("{t}");                                // one
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Slices borrow without copying; prefer `split_once`, `strip_prefix`, `trim`,
>   and `find` over hand-computed byte offsets.
> - `push_str`, `push`, and `+=` grow a `String` in place.
> - `String + &str` consumes the left operand and reuses its buffer; `&str + &str`
>   does not compile.
> - Use `format!` for readability and `join`/`concat` for many pieces.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Parse `"key=value"` pairs separated by `;` into a `Vec<(&str, &str)>` using
>    `split` and `split_once`, without allocating.
> 2. Build the string `"1, 2, 3, ..., 10"` three ways: with `push_str` in a loop,
>    with `format!`, and with `join`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `let s3 = s1 + &s2;` move `s1` but only borrow `s2`?
>    (Hint: look at the signature of `Add for String` and think about whose buffer
>    the result lives in.)

#### Parsing and Formatting

Text is how programs exchange data with people and other programs, so converting
between text and typed values is constant work. Rust handles each direction with
a trait.

**Parsing (text to value)** goes through `FromStr`, exposed as `str::parse`. Parsing
can fail, so `parse` returns `Result<T, T::Err>`, and the target type must be known:
annotate the variable or use turbofish, `"42".parse::<u32>()`. Implementing
`FromStr` for your own types lets them be parsed the same way. Parsing usually
pairs with splitting helpers: `split`, `split_whitespace`, `lines`, `split_once`,
and `trim`.

**Formatting (value to text)** goes through `Display`/`Debug` (Chapter 5.2) and the
`format!` family: `println!`, `write!`, `eprintln!`, `format_args!`. The format
specification mini-language controls layout:

| Spec          | Meaning                         | Example                         | Output       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------ |
| `{:>8}`       | Right-align in width 8          | `format!("{:>8}", "hi")`        | `      hi`   |
| `{:<8}` `{:^8}` | Left / center align           | `format!("{:^6}", "hi")`        | `  hi  `     |
| `{:*^7}`      | Fill with `*`, centered         | `format!("{:*^7}", "hi")`       | `**hi***`    |
| `{:.3}`       | Precision                       | `format!("{:.3}", 3.14159)`     | `3.142`      |
| `{:08.2}`     | Zero-pad width 8, precision 2   | `format!("{:08.2}", -3.5)`      | `-0003.50`   |
| `{:+}`        | Always show sign                | `format!("{:+}", 5)`            | `+5`         |
| `{:x}` `{:#x}` | Hex, with `0x` prefix          | `format!("{:#x}", 255)`         | `0xff`       |
| `{:b}` `{:#010b}` | Binary, prefixed and padded | `format!("{:#010b}", 5)`        | `0b00000101` |
| `{:e}`        | Scientific notation             | `format!("{:e}", 1234.5)`       | `1.2345e3`   |
| `{name}`, `{0}` | Named / positional argument   | `format!("{0}-{0}", "a")`       | `a-a`        |
| `{:>w$}`      | Width from a variable           | `format!("{:>w$}", 1, w = 3)`   | `  1`        |

To build a `String` incrementally without allocating a temporary for every piece,
use `write!` with the `std::fmt::Write` trait in scope.

```rust
use std::fmt::Write as _;                    // brings write! for String into scope
use std::num::ParseIntError;
use std::str::FromStr;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

// Parse "x,y" such as "3,-4"
impl FromStr for Point {
    type Err = String;

    fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
        let (x, y) = s
            .trim()
            .split_once(',')
```
