```rust
            .ok_or_else(|| format!("missing comma in {s:?}"))?;
        let parse = |t: &str| t.trim().parse::<i32>().map_err(|e| e.to_string());
        Ok(Point { x: parse(x)?, y: parse(y)? })
    }
}

fn sum_numbers(text: &str) -> Result<i64, ParseIntError> {
    text.split_whitespace().map(|w| w.parse::<i64>()).sum()   // stops at first error
}

fn main() {
    // Parsing built-in types
    let n: u32 = "42".parse().unwrap();                 // type from annotation
    let f = "2.5".parse::<f64>().unwrap();              // type from turbofish
    println!("{n} {f}");                                // 42 2.5
    println!("{:?}", "4x2".parse::<u8>());              // Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })
    println!("{:?}", "300".parse::<u8>().is_err());     // true: out of range
    println!("{:?}", "true".parse::<bool>());           // Ok(true)

    // Parsing a custom type
    let p: Point = " 3, -4 ".parse().unwrap();
    println!("{p:?}");                                  // Point { x: 3, y: -4 }
    println!("{:?}", "3;4".parse::<Point>());           // Err("missing comma in \"3;4\"")

    println!("{:?}", sum_numbers("10 20 12"));          // Ok(42)
    println!("{}", sum_numbers("10 x 12").is_err());    // true

    // Parsing lines of structured text
    let input = "ana 31\nbo 27\ncy 45";
    let ages: Vec<(&str, u8)> = input
        .lines()
        .filter_map(|l| {
            let (name, age) = l.split_once(' ')?;
            Some((name, age.parse().ok()?))
        })
        .collect();
    println!("{ages:?}");                               // [("ana", 31), ("bo", 27), ("cy", 45)]

    // Formatting a table
    let mut report = String::new();
    writeln!(report, "{:<6}|{:>5}", "name", "age").unwrap();
    for (name, age) in &ages {
        writeln!(report, "{name:<6}|{age:>5}").unwrap(); // inline args with specs
    }
    print!("{report}");
    // name  |  age
    // ana   |   31
    // bo    |   27
    // cy    |   45

    let width = 10;
    println!("[{:^width$}]", "mid");                    // [   mid    ]
    println!("{:#x} {:#010b} {:+.2} {:e}", 255, 5, 1.0, 1234.5);
    // 0xff 0b00000101 +1.00 1.2345e3
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `str::parse::<T>()` uses `FromStr`, returns a `Result`, and needs the target
>   type from an annotation or turbofish.
> - Implement `FromStr` to make custom types parseable with the same API.
> - The format mini-language controls alignment, width, fill, precision, sign, and
>   radix; widths and precisions can come from variables.
> - Use `write!`/`writeln!` with `std::fmt::Write` to build strings incrementally.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `FromStr` for `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)` that accepts `"10,20,30"`.
> 2. Read lines of `"name,score"` from a string, parse them, and print a table
>    with names left-aligned in 10 columns and scores right-aligned with one
>    decimal place.
> 3. Interview: Why does `"5".parse()` alone often fail to compile? (Hint: how
>    many types implement `FromStr`, and where does the compiler learn which one
>    you want?)

#### OsString and CString

`String` guarantees valid UTF-8, but the outside world does not. File names on
Linux are arbitrary byte sequences (anything except `/` and NUL). Windows paths
are sequences of 16-bit units that may contain unpaired surrogates. C functions
expect a pointer to bytes terminated by a NUL byte, with no length stored at all.
Forcing any of these into a `String` would either fail or lose data.

Rust therefore provides additional string pairs, each owned plus borrowed, like
`String`/`&str`:

| Owned       | Borrowed | Guarantees                                   | Used for                          |
| ----------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `String`    | `&str`   | Valid UTF-8                                  | Ordinary text                     |
| `OsString`  | `&OsStr` | Whatever the platform considers a string     | Environment vars, OS APIs         |
| `PathBuf`   | `&Path`  | An `OsString` with path-manipulation methods | File system paths                 |
| `CString`   | `&CStr`  | NUL-terminated, no interior NUL bytes        | Passing strings to and from C (FFI) |
| `Vec<u8>`   | `&[u8]`  | Nothing                                      | Raw binary data                   |

**`OsString` / `OsStr`** come from APIs like `std::env::args_os()`,
`std::env::var_os()`, and file names in directory listings. Converting to `&str`
is fallible: `to_str()` returns `Option<&str>`, and `to_string_lossy()` replaces
invalid sequences with U+FFFD. `Path` and `PathBuf` are built on `OsStr` and add
`join`, `extension`, `file_name`, and `parent`. Prefer them over manual string
handling of paths.

**`CString` / `CStr`** bridge to C. `CString::new` appends the terminating NUL and
returns an error if the input contains an interior NUL (C would silently truncate
there). `as_ptr()` gives the `*const c_char` that C expects; the `CString` must
outlive every use of that pointer. In the other direction, `CStr::from_ptr` wraps a
pointer received from C (an `unsafe` operation, since Rust cannot verify it). Since
Rust 1.77, C-string literals `c"hello"` produce a `&'static CStr` directly.

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, CStr, CString, OsStr, OsString};
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

// Declaration of the C library's strlen (Rust 2024 requires `unsafe extern`)
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize;
}

fn main() {
    // --- OsString / OsStr ------------------------------------------------------
    let os: OsString = OsString::from("report.txt");
    let as_str: Option<&str> = os.to_str();          // fallible in general
    println!("{as_str:?}");                          // Some("report.txt")

    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt;
        // A valid Unix file name that is NOT valid UTF-8
        let raw = OsStr::from_bytes(&[b'f', 0xFF, b'.', b'l', b'o', b'g']);
        println!("{:?}", raw.to_str());              // None
        println!("{}", raw.to_string_lossy());       // f�.log (U+FFFD substituted)
    }

    // Paths are OsStr with path semantics
    let mut p = PathBuf::from("/var/log");
    p.push("app");
    p.set_extension("log");
    println!("{}", p.display());                     // /var/log/app.log
    println!("{:?}", p.extension());                 // Some("log")
    println!("{:?}", Path::new("a/b/c.tar.gz").file_stem());   // Some("c.tar")

    // Environment variables may not be UTF-8: var_os never fails on encoding
    match std::env::var_os("HOME") {
        Some(home) => println!("home is {} bytes", home.len()),
        None => println!("HOME not set"),
    }

    // --- CString / CStr --------------------------------------------------------
    let c = CString::new("hello").unwrap();          // adds the trailing NUL
    println!("{:?}", c.as_bytes_with_nul());         // [104, 101, 108, 108, 111, 0]

    let len = unsafe { strlen(c.as_ptr()) };         // C reads up to the NUL
    println!("{len}");                               // 5

    let err = CString::new("bad\0string");           // interior NUL is rejected
    println!("{}", err.is_err());                    // true

    let lit: &CStr = c"literal";                     // C-string literal (1.77+)
    let back: &str = lit.to_str().unwrap();          // CStr -> &str checks UTF-8
    println!("{back} {}", lit.count_bytes());        // literal 7
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `OsString`/`OsStr` hold platform strings that may not be UTF-8; convert with
>   `to_str()` (fallible) or `to_string_lossy()`.
> - Use `Path`/`PathBuf` for file paths instead of `String`.
> - `CString`/`CStr` are NUL-terminated strings for C interop; interior NUL bytes
>   are rejected.
> - Keep a `CString` alive for as long as C uses the pointer from `as_ptr()`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Iterate over `std::env::args_os()` and print each argument with
>    `to_string_lossy()`.
> 2. Write `fn change_ext(p: &Path, ext: &str) -> PathBuf` and test it on paths
>    with zero, one, and two extensions.
> 3. Interview: What is wrong with `let ptr = CString::new("hi").unwrap().as_ptr();`
>    followed by passing `ptr` to C? (Hint: when is the temporary `CString`
>    dropped?)

<a id="63-iterators"></a>
### 6.3 Iterators

Iterators are Rust's universal interface for sequences: collections, ranges,
lines of a file, characters of a string, and values generated on the fly. This
section covers the trait itself, the three ways to iterate a collection, the
adapter and consumer methods that build pipelines, and how to plug your own types
into the system.

#### The Iterator Trait

Every language needs a way to visit the elements of a sequence one at a time. The
classic approach, a counter and an index (`for (i = 0; i < n; i++) v[i]`), ties
the loop to one particular data layout, risks off-by-one errors, and needs a
bounds check on every access. Rust instead uses **iterators**: objects that hand
out the next element when asked, and say clearly when there are no more.

The entire abstraction is one trait with one required method:

```rust
pub trait Iterator {
    type Item;                                       // what each step yields
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;        // Some(item), or None at the end
    // ...plus about 75 provided methods built on `next`
}
```

`next` takes `&mut self` because advancing changes the iterator's internal
position. Returning `Option` makes the end of the sequence an ordinary value
instead of a sentinel or an exception. Once `next` returns `None`, a well-behaved
iterator keeps returning `None` (iterators that guarantee this implement the
marker trait `FusedIterator`).

Think of a ticket dispenser: each pull gives you the next ticket, and when the
roll is empty it says so. You never need to know how the roll is wound.

The `for` loop is just syntax over this trait. `for x in collection { body }`
calls `IntoIterator::into_iter(collection)` once, then calls `next()` repeatedly
until it returns `None`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let v = vec![10, 20, 30];

    // Driving an iterator by hand
    let mut it = v.iter();                  // the iterator must be `mut`: next() advances it
    println!("{:?}", it.next());            // Some(10)
    println!("{:?}", it.next());            // Some(20)
    println!("{:?}", it.next());            // Some(30)
    println!("{:?}", it.next());            // None
    println!("{:?}", it.next());            // None (stays exhausted)

    // What `for x in &v { ... }` desugars to
    let mut iter = IntoIterator::into_iter(&v);
    while let Some(x) = iter.next() {
        print!("{x} ");                     // 10 20 30
    }
    println!();

    // Same sequence, three iterator sources, one interface
    let from_range: i32 = (1..=3).sum();
    let from_str = "a-b-c".split('-').count();
    let from_vec = v.iter().max();
    println!("{from_range} {from_str} {from_vec:?}");   // 6 3 Some(30)
}
```

| Approach            | Bounds checks          | Works on non-indexable sources | Off-by-one risk |
| ------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------- |
| Index loop `v[i]`   | Every access (usually) | No                             | Yes             |
| Iterator / `for`    | None needed            | Yes (files, trees, generators) | No              |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Iterator` has one required method, `next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>`,
>   and dozens of provided methods built on it.
> - `None` marks the end of the sequence; exhausted iterators normally keep
>   returning `None`.
> - `for` loops desugar to `IntoIterator::into_iter` plus repeated `next` calls.
> - Iterators avoid index bookkeeping and per-element bounds checks.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Call `next()` manually on `"hi there".split(' ')` until it returns `None`,
>    printing each result.
> 2. Rewrite `for i in 0..v.len() { println!("{}", v[i]); }` as an iterator-based
>    loop, then as a loop that also needs the index (`enumerate`).
> 3. Interview: Why does `Iterator::next` take `&mut self` rather than `&self`?
>    (Hint: where is the "current position" stored?)

#### iter, iter_mut, and into_iter

A collection can be iterated in three ways, and the difference is exactly the
ownership distinction from Chapter 3: do you want to **look** at the elements,
**change** them, or **take** them?

| Method          | `for` shorthand  | Item type | Collection afterwards |
| --------------- | ---------------- | --------- | --------------------- |
| `v.iter()`      | `for x in &v`    | `&T`      | Unchanged, still usable |
| `v.iter_mut()`  | `for x in &mut v`| `&mut T`  | Possibly modified, still usable |
| `v.into_iter()` | `for x in v`     | `T`       | Consumed (moved), no longer usable |

The trap is the bare `for x in v`: it calls `into_iter()` on the vector by value,
so the vector is moved and cannot be used after the loop. If you only meant to
read, write `for x in &v`.

`into_iter` is also context-dependent: it is a method of the `IntoIterator` trait,
which is implemented for `Vec<T>` (yielding `T`), for `&Vec<T>` (yielding `&T`),
and for `&mut Vec<T>` (yielding `&mut T`). So `(&v).into_iter()` is the same as
`v.iter()`. Since edition 2021, arrays also implement `IntoIterator` by value.

Maps follow the same pattern, yielding pairs: `iter()` gives `(&K, &V)`,
`iter_mut()` gives `(&K, &mut V)` (keys are never mutable, since that would break
the hashing or ordering), and `into_iter()` gives `(K, V)`. They also offer
`keys()`, `values()`, and `values_mut()`.

```rust
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    let mut scores = vec![70, 85, 92];

    // iter(): shared references; vector untouched
    let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum();
    for s in &scores {                      // same as scores.iter()
        print!("{s} ");                     // 70 85 92
    }
    println!("total {total}");              // total 247

    // iter_mut(): mutable references; modify in place
    for s in scores.iter_mut() {            // same as `for s in &mut scores`
        *s += 5;                            // deref to write through &mut i32
    }
    println!("{scores:?}");                 // [75, 90, 97]

    // into_iter(): takes ownership of the elements
    let names = vec![String::from("ana"), String::from("bo")];
    let upper: Vec<String> = names
        .into_iter()                        // yields String, not &String
        .map(|mut n| { n.make_ascii_uppercase(); n })   // reuse each buffer
        .collect();
    // println!("{names:?}");               // error[E0382]: borrow of moved
                                            // value: `names`
    println!("{upper:?}");                  // ["ANA", "BO"]

    // Arrays iterate by value in edition 2021+
    for x in [1, 2, 3] {
        let _: i32 = x;                     // x is i32, not &i32
    }

    // Maps: keys are always shared, values can be &mut
    let mut stock: BTreeMap<&str, u32> = BTreeMap::from([("apple", 3), ("pear", 0)]);
    for (_, qty) in stock.iter_mut() {
        *qty += 10;
    }
    for (fruit, qty) in &stock {
        print!("{fruit}={qty} ");           // apple=13 pear=10
    }
    println!();
    let owned: Vec<(&str, u32)> = stock.into_iter().collect();
    println!("{owned:?}");                  // [("apple", 13), ("pear", 10)]
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `iter()` borrows (`&T`), `iter_mut()` borrows mutably (`&mut T`), and
>   `into_iter()` consumes (`T`).
> - `for x in v` moves `v`; use `for x in &v` or `for x in &mut v` to keep it.
> - `into_iter` behaves according to what it is called on: a value, `&`, or `&mut`.
> - Map iterators yield pairs, and keys are never mutable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Given `let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];`, double every element in place with
>    `iter_mut`, then print the sum with `iter`.
> 2. Move every `String` out of a `Vec<String>` into a `HashSet<String>` without
>    cloning.
> 3. Interview: Why can `HashMap::iter_mut` give mutable access to values but not
>    to keys? (Hint: what would happen to the map's internal layout if a key
>    changed?)

#### Adapters: map, filter, take, skip

The power of iterators comes from **adapters**: methods that take an iterator and
return a new iterator that transforms the stream. Chaining them builds a pipeline,
like an assembly line where each station does one job and passes items along.

The four essential adapters:

- **`map(f)`** transforms each item: `x` becomes `f(x)`.
- **`filter(p)`** keeps only items where the predicate `p(&x)` is `true`.
- **`take(n)`** yields at most the first `n` items, then stops.
- **`skip(n)`** discards the first `n` items and yields the rest.

They compose with many others:

| Adapter                    | Effect                                                    |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enumerate()`              | Pairs each item with its index: `(i, x)`                  |
| `zip(other)`               | Pairs items from two iterators; stops at the shorter one  |
| `chain(other)`             | Yields all of one iterator, then all of another           |
| `filter_map(f)`            | `map` + `filter` in one: keep the `Some` results          |
| `flat_map(f)` / `flatten()`| Expand each item into an iterator and concatenate them    |
| `take_while(p)` / `skip_while(p)` | Take or skip while a predicate holds               |
| `step_by(n)`               | Every `n`-th item                                         |
| `rev()`                    | Reverse order (needs a double-ended iterator)             |
| `peekable()`               | Look at the next item without consuming it                |
| `inspect(f)`               | Run `f` on each item for debugging; passes items through  |
| `cloned()` / `copied()`    | Turn `&T` items into `T`                                  |

Adapters take closures (Section 6.4). Note the reference levels: `filter` passes a
**reference** to each item, so filtering a `.iter()` over `i32`s gives the closure
`&&i32`. Patterns such as `|&&x|` or `|x| **x > 2` handle that, as does calling
`.copied()` before filtering.

```rust
fn main() {
    let nums = [3, 8, 1, 12, 7, 6, 15, 4];

    // map + filter + take: the first three even numbers, squared
    let evens_sq: Vec<i32> = nums
        .iter()
        .filter(|&&x| x % 2 == 0)           // closure receives &&i32
        .map(|&x| x * x)                    // map receives &i32
        .take(3)
        .collect();
    println!("{evens_sq:?}");               // [64, 144, 36]

    // skip + step_by: every second element after the first two
    let picked: Vec<_> = nums.iter().copied().skip(2).step_by(2).collect();
    println!("{picked:?}");                 // [1, 7, 15]

    // enumerate + filter_map: indices of numbers greater than 10
    let big: Vec<usize> = nums
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter_map(|(i, &x)| if x > 10 { Some(i) } else { None })
        .collect();
    println!("{big:?}");                    // [3, 6]

    // zip: combine two sequences element-wise
    let names = ["ana", "bo", "cy"];
    let ages = [31, 27];
    let pairs: Vec<String> = names.iter().zip(ages).map(|(n, a)| format!("{n}:{a}")).collect();
    println!("{pairs:?}");                  // ["ana:31", "bo:27"]  (shorter wins)

    // chain + rev
    let both: Vec<_> = (1..=3).chain(7..=8).rev().collect();
    println!("{both:?}");                   // [8, 7, 3, 2, 1]

    // flat_map: split sentences into words
    let words: Vec<&str> = ["a b", "c", "d e f"].iter().flat_map(|s| s.split(' ')).collect();
    println!("{words:?}");                  // ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]

    // take_while / skip_while: stop or start at a condition
    let head: Vec<_> = nums.iter().take_while(|&&x| x != 12).collect();
    println!("{head:?}");                   // [3, 8, 1]

    // filter_map with parsing: keep only successful parses
    let parsed: Vec<i32> = ["1", "two", "3"].iter().filter_map(|s| s.parse().ok()).collect();
    println!("{parsed:?}");                 // [1, 3]

    // peekable: group consecutive equal items
    let mut it = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3].into_iter().peekable();
    while let Some(x) = it.next() {
        let mut count = 1;
        while it.peek() == Some(&x) {       // look ahead without consuming
            it.next();
            count += 1;
        }
        print!("{x}x{count} ");             // 1x2 2x3 3x1
    }
    println!();
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Adapters transform one iterator into another; chaining them builds a pipeline.
> - `map` transforms, `filter` selects, `take` limits, `skip` offsets.
> - `enumerate`, `zip`, `chain`, `filter_map`, `flat_map`, and `peekable` cover
>   most remaining needs.
> - Watch the reference level in closures: `filter` adds one `&` on top of the
>   item type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. From `1..=50`, produce the squares of the numbers divisible by 3, skipping
>    the first two results and taking the next four.
> 2. Given `Vec<&str>` of lines, produce `Vec<(usize, &str)>` of 1-based line
>    numbers and lines that are not empty.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `map(...).flatten()`,
>    `flat_map(...)`, and `filter_map(...)`, and when would you use each? (Hint:
>    look at the return type of the closure in each case.)

#### Consumers: collect, fold, sum

Adapters only describe a pipeline; something must pull items through it and
produce a result. Methods that do this are **consumers** (or terminal
operations). They take the iterator by value (or `&mut`), drive it by calling
`next`, and return a final value.

**`collect()`** gathers items into any type implementing `FromIterator`: a `Vec`,
`String`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `BTreeMap`, and more. Since many targets are
possible, the compiler needs to know which one, through an annotation
(`let v: Vec<_> = ...`) or turbofish (`.collect::<Vec<_>>()`). It has a powerful
special case: collecting an iterator of `Result<T, E>` into `Result<Vec<T>, E>`
stops at the first error and returns it, and the same works for `Option`.

**`fold(init, f)`** is the general-purpose accumulator: start with `init`, combine
it with each item using `f`, return the final accumulator. Most other consumers
could be written with `fold`. `reduce(f)` is the variant that uses the first item
as the initial value and returns `Option` (empty input gives `None`).

**`sum()`** and **`product()`** add or multiply all items. Like `collect`, their
result type must be known, so you often see `.sum::<i32>()`.

Other common consumers:

| Consumer                       | Returns            | Short-circuits? |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------ | --------------- |
| `count()`                      | `usize`            | No              |
| `min()`, `max()`               | `Option<T>`        | No              |
| `min_by_key(f)`, `max_by(f)`   | `Option<T>`        | No              |
| `find(p)`                      | `Option<T>`        | Yes             |
| `position(p)`                  | `Option<usize>`    | Yes             |
| `any(p)`, `all(p)`             | `bool`             | Yes             |
| `last()`, `nth(n)`             | `Option<T>`        | `nth` stops early |
| `for_each(f)`                  | `()`               | No              |
| `partition(p)`                 | `(B, B)`           | No              |
| `try_fold(init, f)`            | `R` (e.g. `Option`/`Result`) | Yes, on failure |

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Order {
    customer: &'static str,
    amount: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let orders = vec![
        Order { customer: "ana", amount: 120 },
        Order { customer: "bo", amount: 40 },
        Order { customer: "ana", amount: 60 },
        Order { customer: "cy", amount: 300 },
    ];

    // sum / count / max_by_key
    let revenue: u32 = orders.iter().map(|o| o.amount).sum();
    let big = orders.iter().filter(|o| o.amount >= 100).count();
    let top = orders.iter().max_by_key(|o| o.amount).unwrap();
    println!("{revenue} {big} {}", top.customer);          // 520 2 cy

    // fold: total per customer in one pass
    let per_customer = orders.iter().fold(HashMap::new(), |mut acc, o| {
        *acc.entry(o.customer).or_insert(0) += o.amount;
        acc                                                // return the accumulator
    });
    println!("{}", per_customer["ana"]);                   // 180

    // collect into different targets
    let names: Vec<&str> = orders.iter().map(|o| o.customer).collect();
    let initials: String = names.iter().map(|n| n.chars().next().unwrap()).collect();
    let lookup: HashMap<&str, u32> = orders.iter().map(|o| (o.customer, o.amount)).collect();
    println!("{names:?} {initials} {}", lookup.len());     // ["ana", "bo", "ana", "cy"] abac 3

    // collect Result<Vec<_>, _>: all-or-nothing parsing
    let good: Result<Vec<u32>, _> = ["1", "2", "3"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<u32>()).collect();
    let bad: Result<Vec<u32>, _> = ["1", "x", "3"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<u32>()).collect();
    println!("{good:?} {}", bad.is_err());                 // Ok([1, 2, 3]) true

    // find / position / any / all short-circuit
    println!("{:?}", orders.iter().find(|o| o.customer == "bo").map(|o| o.amount)); // Some(40)
    println!("{:?}", orders.iter().position(|o| o.amount > 200));                   // Some(3)
    println!("{} {}", orders.iter().any(|o| o.amount == 0),
                      orders.iter().all(|o| o.amount > 10));                        // false true

    // partition: split into two collections
    let (small, large): (Vec<&Order>, Vec<&Order>) = orders.iter().partition(|o| o.amount < 100);
    println!("{} {}", small.len(), large.len());           // 2 2

    // reduce and product
    let longest = names.iter().copied().reduce(|a, b| if b.len() > a.len() { b } else { a });
    let factorial: u64 = (1..=10).product();
    println!("{longest:?} {factorial}");                   // Some("ana") 3628800

    // try_fold: stop as soon as the sum would overflow a u8
    let r = [100u8, 100, 100].iter().try_fold(0u8, |acc, &x| acc.checked_add(x));
    println!("{r:?}");                                     // None
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Consumers drive the pipeline and produce a final value; without one, nothing
>   happens.
> - `collect` builds any `FromIterator` type and needs the target type spelled out;
>   it can turn `Iterator<Item = Result<T, E>>` into `Result<Vec<T>, E>`.
> - `fold` is the general accumulator; `sum`, `count`, `max`, and others are
>   specialized forms.
> - `find`, `any`, `all`, `position`, and `try_fold` stop as soon as the answer is
>   known.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the average of a `Vec<f64>` with a single `fold` that tracks both sum
>    and count.
> 2. Parse a comma-separated string of integers into `Result<Vec<i32>, _>` and
>    print either the vector or the error.
> 3. Interview: How would you implement `sum`, `count`, and `max` using only
>    `fold`? Which consumers cannot be written efficiently with `fold`, and why?
>    (Hint: think about short-circuiting.)

#### Lazy Evaluation

Calling `.map(...)` on an iterator does not run anything. It returns a new iterator
struct (`Map<I, F>`) that stores the original iterator and the closure, and does
nothing until someone calls `next` on it. Every adapter works this way. Work
happens only when a consumer pulls items, and only for the items actually pulled.

This **laziness** has important consequences:

- **A pipeline without a consumer does nothing.** The compiler warns: "unused
  `Map` that must be used: iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed". A
  common mistake is using `map` purely for side effects; use a `for` loop or
  `for_each` instead.
- **Items flow one at a time through the whole chain.** Item 1 goes through every
  stage before item 2 starts. No intermediate collections are built between
  stages.
- **Infinite iterators are fine.** `(1..)`, `iter::repeat`, and `cycle()` never
  end, but `take`, `find`, or `take_while` stop pulling once they have enough.
- **Short-circuiting saves work.** `find` on a lazy `map` computes `map` only up
  to the first match.

Laziness is also why iterator chains are a *zero-cost abstraction*. After
inlining, the compiler typically fuses the chain into a single loop equivalent to
hand-written code, often with bounds checks removed and sometimes vectorized.

```text
   (1..).map(square).filter(is_odd).take(2)

   Pull-based, one item at a time:

   take asks filter -> filter asks map -> map asks range -> 1 -> map 1 -> filter keeps 1 -> take yields 1
   take asks filter -> ... range 2 -> map 4 -> filter rejects -> asks again
                       ... range 3 -> map 9 -> filter keeps 9 -> take yields 9
   take has 2 items: stops. Range values 4, 5, 6, ... are never produced.
```

```rust
fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];

    // Nothing printed here: the adapter chain is only a description
    let pipeline = v.iter().map(|x| {
        println!("  map {x}");
        x * 10
    });
    println!("pipeline built, nothing ran yet");

    // Consuming it pulls items through, one at a time
    let firsts: Vec<i32> = pipeline.take(2).collect();
    println!("{firsts:?}");
    // pipeline built, nothing ran yet
    //   map 1
    //   map 2
    // [10, 20]          (items 3..6 were never mapped)

    // Vertical, item-by-item order across stages
    let found = v
        .iter()
        .inspect(|x| println!("  saw {x}"))
        .map(|x| x * x)
        .find(|sq| *sq > 10);
    println!("{found:?}");
    //   saw 1
    //   saw 2
    //   saw 3
    //   saw 4
    // Some(16)          (find stops at the first match)

    // Infinite source, finite result
    let first_powers: Vec<u64> = (0..).map(|n| 2u64.pow(n)).take_while(|&p| p < 100).collect();
    println!("{first_powers:?}");           // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]

    // Mistake: map for side effects without a consumer
    v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));      // warning: unused `Map` that must be used
                                            // prints NOTHING
    v.iter().for_each(|x| print!("{x} "));  // correct: 1 2 3 4 5 6
    println!();
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Adapters are lazy: they build a description of work, and nothing runs until a
>   consumer pulls items.
> - Items flow one at a time through every stage; no intermediate collections are
>   created.
> - Laziness makes infinite iterators and early termination natural.
> - Do not use `map` for side effects; the compiler warns that unconsumed iterators
>   do nothing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `inspect` calls between each stage of a `filter().map().take()` chain and
>    predict the printed order before running it.
> 2. Find the first number above 1,000 whose square ends in `21`, using an infinite
>    range.
> 3. Interview: Compare `v.iter().map(f).filter(p).collect()` in Rust with the
>    equivalent eager JavaScript `v.map(f).filter(p)`. How many intermediate arrays
>    does each create? (Hint: trace when each stage actually runs.)

#### Implementing Custom Iterators

The standard library provides iterators for its own types, but your types and
algorithms can join the system too. Implementing `Iterator` takes two steps: a
struct that holds the iteration **state**, and an `impl Iterator` with `type Item`
and `next`. The payoff is large: every adapter and consumer (`map`, `filter`,
`sum`, `collect`, `zip`, ...) then works on your iterator for free.

Typical shapes of state:

- **A counter or generator**: the current value of a sequence (Fibonacci,
  Collatz, IDs).
- **A cursor into borrowed data**: a slice reference plus a position. The struct
  needs a lifetime (`struct Windows<'a>`), and the items can borrow from the
  underlying data.
- **A stack or queue**: for tree and graph traversals, holding nodes still to
  visit.

For one-off cases, you can skip the struct:

- **`std::iter::from_fn(closure)`** turns a closure returning `Option<T>` into an
  iterator; the closure's captured variables are the state.
- **`std::iter::successors(first, f)`** yields `first`, then `f(&prev)` repeatedly
  until `f` returns `None`.

Combined with `-> impl Iterator<Item = T>` (Chapter 5.3), these let a function
return a custom sequence without exposing its type.

```rust
// 1. A generator: Fibonacci numbers, stopping before overflow
struct Fib {
    curr: u64,
    next: u64,
}

impl Iterator for Fib {
    type Item = u64;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> {
        let out = self.curr;
        let new_next = self.curr.checked_add(self.next)?;   // None on overflow ends it
        self.curr = self.next;
        self.next = new_next;
        Some(out)
    }
}

fn fib() -> Fib {
    Fib { curr: 0, next: 1 }
}

// 2. A cursor over borrowed data: consecutive pairs of a slice
struct Pairs<'a, T> {
    slice: &'a [T],
    pos: usize,
}

impl<'a, T> Iterator for Pairs<'a, T> {
    type Item = (&'a T, &'a T);             // items borrow from the slice, not the iterator
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let a = self.slice.get(self.pos)?;
        let b = self.slice.get(self.pos + 1)?;
        self.pos += 1;
        Some((a, b))
    }
}

fn pairs<T>(slice: &[T]) -> Pairs<'_, T> {
    Pairs { slice, pos: 0 }
}

// 3. A tree traversal with an explicit stack
struct Node {
    val: i32,
    children: Vec<Node>,
}

fn depth_first(root: &Node) -> impl Iterator<Item = i32> + '_ {
    let mut stack = vec![root];
    std::iter::from_fn(move || {            // the closure's captures are the state
        let node = stack.pop()?;
        stack.extend(node.children.iter().rev());   // visit children left to right
        Some(node.val)
    })
}

fn main() {
    // Adapters and consumers work automatically
    let even_fibs: Vec<u64> = fib().filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).take(5).collect();
    println!("{even_fibs:?}");                      // [0, 2, 8, 34, 144]
    println!("{}", fib().count());                  // 92: stops before u64 overflow

    let temps = [18, 21, 19, 25];
    let rises = pairs(&temps).filter(|(a, b)| b > a).count();
    println!("{rises}");                            // 2

    let tree = Node {
        val: 1,
        children: vec![
            Node { val: 2, children: vec![Node { val: 4, children: vec![] }] },
            Node { val: 3, children: vec![] },
        ],
    };
    let order: Vec<_> = depth_first(&tree).collect();
    println!("{order:?}");                          // [1, 2, 4, 3]

    // successors: Collatz sequence from 6
    let collatz: Vec<u64> = std::iter::successors(Some(6u64), |&n| match n {
        1 => None,
        n if n % 2 == 0 => Some(n / 2),
        n => Some(3 * n + 1),
    })
    .collect();
    println!("{collatz:?}");                        // [6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1]
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A custom iterator is a state struct plus `impl Iterator` with `type Item` and
>   `next`.
> - Implementing `next` unlocks every adapter and consumer for free.
> - Iterators over borrowed data carry a lifetime so their items can borrow from
>   the source.
> - `iter::from_fn` and `iter::successors` create iterators from closures without
>   a named struct.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement an iterator `Primes` that yields prime numbers indefinitely, and
>    print the first ten with `take(10)`.
> 2. Write `fn chunks_of<T>(v: &[T], n: usize) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[T]>` using
>    `from_fn` (do not use the built-in `chunks`).
> 3. Interview: In `Pairs<'a, T>`, why is the item type `(&'a T, &'a T)` and not tied
>    to the lifetime of `&mut self` in `next`? What kind of iterator would need the
>    latter? (Hint: search for "lending iterator" and consider whether two items
>    can be alive at the same time.)

#### IntoIterator and FromIterator

`Iterator` describes a sequence in progress. Two companion traits describe how
values enter and leave the iterator world:

- **`IntoIterator`** means "can be turned into an iterator". It is what `for` loops
  call, and what generic functions should accept when they want "anything
  iterable". Every `Iterator` implements it trivially, and collections implement it
  three times (for `T`, `&T`, and `&mut T`), which is how `for x in &v` works.
- **`FromIterator`** means "can be built from an iterator". It is what `collect`
  calls. If your type implements it, `.collect::<YourType>()` works.

`Extend` is the third member of the family: it appends items from an iterator to
an existing collection (`v.extend(other)`).

Implementing these for your own collection types makes them first-class: they work
in `for` loops, can be produced by `collect`, and can be passed to any function
taking `impl IntoIterator`. When implementing `IntoIterator` for a wrapper, the
simplest approach is to delegate to the inner collection's iterator type, as the
example does with `std::vec::IntoIter` and `std::slice::Iter`.

```rust
// FromIterator is in the prelude since edition 2021: no import needed

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Playlist {
    songs: Vec<String>,
}

// `for song in playlist` (consumes)
impl IntoIterator for Playlist {
    type Item = String;
    type IntoIter = std::vec::IntoIter<String>;     // reuse Vec's iterator
    fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter {
        self.songs.into_iter()
    }
}

// `for song in &playlist` (borrows)
impl<'a> IntoIterator for &'a Playlist {
    type Item = &'a String;
    type IntoIter = std::slice::Iter<'a, String>;
    fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter {
        self.songs.iter()
    }
}

// `.collect::<Playlist>()`
impl FromIterator<String> for Playlist {
    fn from_iter<I: IntoIterator<Item = String>>(iter: I) -> Self {
        Playlist { songs: iter.into_iter().collect() }
    }
}

// `playlist.extend(...)`
impl Extend<String> for Playlist {
    fn extend<I: IntoIterator<Item = String>>(&mut self, iter: I) {
        self.songs.extend(iter);
    }
}

// Generic over anything iterable: Vec, array, &Playlist, ranges, ...
fn total_len<I>(items: I) -> usize
where
    I: IntoIterator,
    I::Item: AsRef<str>,
{
    items.into_iter().map(|s| s.as_ref().len()).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let mut list: Playlist = ["intro", "verse"].iter().map(|s| s.to_string()).collect();
    list.extend(vec!["outro".to_string()]);

    for song in &list {                     // uses IntoIterator for &Playlist
        print!("{song} ");                  // intro verse outro
    }
    println!();

    println!("{}", total_len(&list));       // 15
    println!("{}", total_len(["ab", "c"])); // 3
    println!("{}", total_len(vec![String::from("xyz")]));   // 3

    let upper: Playlist = list.into_iter().map(|s| s.to_uppercase()).collect();
    println!("{:?}", upper.songs);          // ["INTRO", "VERSE", "OUTRO"]
}
```

| Trait          | Meaning                          | Called by                  | Std examples                 |
| -------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `Iterator`     | A sequence in progress           | Adapters, consumers        | `std::slice::Iter`, `Map`    |
| `IntoIterator` | Can become an iterator           | `for` loops, generic APIs  | `Vec<T>`, `&Vec<T>`, arrays  |
| `FromIterator` | Can be built from an iterator    | `collect`                  | `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap`   |
| `Extend`       | Can absorb an iterator's items   | `extend`                   | `Vec`, `String`, `HashSet`   |

> Key Takeaways
> - `IntoIterator` powers `for` loops; implement it for `T`, `&T`, and optionally
>   `&mut T` on your collections.
> - `FromIterator` powers `collect`; `Extend` powers `extend`.
> - Generic functions should accept `impl IntoIterator<Item = X>` rather than a
>   specific collection.
> - Delegating to the inner collection's iterator types keeps implementations
>   short.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `impl<'a> IntoIterator for &'a mut Playlist` so that `for s in &mut list`
>    can modify each song.
> 2. Implement `FromIterator<(String, u32)>` for a `Scoreboard` type that keeps
>    only the highest score per name.
> 3. Interview: Why does a `for` loop call `IntoIterator::into_iter` instead of
>    requiring an `Iterator`? (Hint: what would `for x in &v` and `for x in v`
>    look like otherwise?)

#### DoubleEnded and ExactSize Iterators

A plain `Iterator` only promises "give me the next item". Some sequences can do
more, and two extra traits let them advertise it so that adapters and consumers can
take advantage.

**`DoubleEndedIterator`** adds `next_back()`, yielding items from the **end**.
Slices, ranges, `Vec` iterators, `chars()`, and `BTreeMap` iterators all support
it. It unlocks `rev()`, `rfind()`, `rposition()`, `nth_back()`, and `rfold()`.
Front and back meet in the middle: once they cross, both return `None`.

**`ExactSizeIterator`** promises that the iterator knows **exactly** how many items
remain, exposed as `len()`. Slice iterators and ranges qualify; `chars()` does not
(counting characters requires decoding UTF-8), and neither does `filter` (it cannot
know how many items will pass).

Underneath both is `size_hint()`, available on every iterator, returning `(lower,
Option<upper>)`. `collect` uses it to allocate the right capacity up front, so
iterators that report accurate hints make collection faster. An
`ExactSizeIterator` must report `(n, Some(n))`.

Adapters preserve these traits only when they can: `map` and `rev` keep both;
`filter` drops `ExactSizeIterator` (but keeps double-endedness); `chain` drops
exact size because the total could overflow `usize`.

```rust
// A range-like iterator that supports both ends and knows its length
struct Span {
    front: u32,
    back: u32,                              // exclusive end
}

impl Iterator for Span {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.front < self.back {
            self.front += 1;
            Some(self.front - 1)
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        let n = (self.back - self.front) as usize;
        (n, Some(n))                        // exact: lower == upper
    }
}

impl DoubleEndedIterator for Span {
    fn next_back(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.front < self.back {
            self.back -= 1;                 // move the back cursor toward the front
            Some(self.back)
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

impl ExactSizeIterator for Span {}          // len() comes from size_hint

fn main() {
    let span = || Span { front: 1, back: 6 };          // 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

    println!("{}", span().len());                        // 5
    println!("{:?}", span().rev().collect::<Vec<_>>());  // [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    println!("{:?}", span().rfind(|x| x % 2 == 0));      // Some(4)

    // Front and back cursors meet in the middle
    let mut s = span();
    println!("{:?} {:?}", s.next(), s.next_back());      // Some(1) Some(5)
    println!("{:?}", s.collect::<Vec<_>>());             // [2, 3, 4]

    // Size hints through adapters
    let v = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];
    println!("{:?}", v.iter().size_hint());                       // (4, Some(4))
    println!("{:?}", v.iter().map(|x| x + 1).size_hint());        // (4, Some(4))
    println!("{:?}", v.iter().filter(|&&x| x > 15).size_hint());  // (0, Some(4))
    println!("{:?}", "héllo".chars().size_hint());                // (2, Some(6)): bytes bound it
    println!("{}", v.iter().map(|x| x * 2).len());                // 4: map keeps ExactSize
    // v.iter().filter(|_| true).len();     // error[E0599]: the method `len` exists
                                            // but its trait bounds were not satisfied

    // chars() is double-ended even though it is not exact-size
    println!("{:?}", "abc".chars().rev().collect::<String>());    // "cba"
}
```

| Iterator                        | `DoubleEnded` | `ExactSize` |
| ------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
| `slice.iter()`, `vec.iter()`    | Yes           | Yes         |
| `0..n` (integer ranges)         | Yes           | Yes (for most integer types) |
| `str.chars()`                   | Yes           | No          |
| `str.bytes()`                   | Yes           | Yes         |
| `.map(f)` over X                | If X is       | If X is     |
| `.filter(p)` over X             | If X is       | No          |
| `.chain(other)`                 | If both are   | No          |
| `HashMap::iter()`               | No            | Yes         |
| `BTreeMap::iter()`              | Yes           | Yes         |

> Key Takeaways
> - `DoubleEndedIterator` adds `next_back`, enabling `rev`, `rfind`, and other
>   operations from the end.
> - `ExactSizeIterator` guarantees an exact remaining count, exposed as `len()`.
> - `size_hint` exists on every iterator; accurate hints let `collect` allocate
>   once.
> - Adapters keep these traits only when the guarantee still holds.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `DoubleEndedIterator` for the `Fib` iterator from the previous topic.
>    Why is it impossible without changing its design?
> 2. Write a function that accepts `impl DoubleEndedIterator<Item = char>` and
>    checks whether the sequence is a palindrome by comparing `next` and
>    `next_back`.
> 3. Interview: Why is `str::chars()` double-ended but not exact-size? (Hint:
>    what can you learn about a UTF-8 string by looking only at its last few bytes,
>    and what do you need for an exact count?)

<a id="64-closures"></a>
### 6.4 Closures

Closures are anonymous functions that can capture variables from the scope where
they are created. They are the glue of iterator pipelines, callbacks, sorting
keys, and thread bodies. This section covers their syntax, how they capture,
the three traits that classify them, and how to store, return, and replace them
with plain function pointers.

#### Closure Syntax and Inference

Many APIs need a small piece of behavior from the caller: how to sort, which items
to keep, what to do when a value is missing. Writing a named function for each of
these is verbose, and a named function cannot see the local variables around the
call. Closures solve both problems: they are written inline, and they can use
variables from their surroundings.

Syntax: parameters between pipes, then a body expression.

```text
   fn  add_one(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }      // function
   let add_one = |x: i32| -> i32 { x + 1 };  // fully annotated closure
   let add_one = |x| x + 1;                  // types inferred, braces optional
   let say_hi = || println!("hi");           // no parameters
```

Unlike functions, closures **usually need no type annotations**. The compiler
infers parameter and return types from the body and from how the closure is used,
for example from the signature of `map` or `sort_by_key`. Inference happens
**once**: the first use fixes the types, and calling the same closure with a
different type afterwards is an error (`error[E0308]`). Closures are not generic.

Every closure has its own **unique, anonymous type**, generated by the compiler.
Two closures with identical code still have different types, so they cannot be
stored in the same `Vec` without boxing (Section 6.4, Returning Closures). That
unique type is also why closures are cheap: the compiler knows exactly which code
to call and can inline it.

```rust
fn main() {
    // Same behavior, four spellings
    fn add_one_fn(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }
    let add_one_full = |x: i32| -> i32 { x + 1 };
    let add_one = |x| x + 1;                    // type of x inferred from first use
    println!("{} {} {}", add_one_fn(1), add_one_full(1), add_one(1));   // 2 2 2

    // Multi-statement body: use braces; the last expression is the return value
    let classify = |n: i32| {
        let sign = if n < 0 { "negative" } else { "non-negative" };
        format!("{n} is {sign}")
    };
    println!("{}", classify(-4));               // -4 is negative

    // Capturing a local variable: impossible for a nested fn
    let threshold = 10;
    let above = |x: &i32| *x > threshold;       // reads `threshold` from the scope
    let v = vec![4, 12, 9, 30];
    println!("{:?}", v.iter().filter(|x| above(x)).collect::<Vec<_>>());  // [12, 30]
    // fn above_fn(x: i32) -> bool { x > threshold }  // error[E0434]: can't capture
                                                      // dynamic environment in a fn item

    // Types fixed by the first call
    let echo = |x| x;
    let s = echo(String::from("hi"));           // echo is now String -> String
    // let n = echo(5);                         // error[E0308]: mismatched types
    println!("{s}");                            // hi

    // Inference from the API: sort_by_key knows the closure gets &(&str, u32)
    let mut people = vec![("ana", 31), ("bo", 27), ("cy", 45)];
    people.sort_by_key(|&(_, age)| age);        // destructuring pattern in parameters
    println!("{people:?}");                     // [("bo", 27), ("ana", 31), ("cy", 45)]

    // Each closure has a unique type, even with identical bodies
    let k = 2;
    let f = move |x: i32| x * k;
    let g = move |x: i32| x * k;
    // let fs = vec![f, g];                     // error[E0308]: no two closures,
                                                // even if identical, have the same type
    println!("{} {}", f(2), g(3));              // 4 6
    // (Closures that capture nothing are the exception: they coerce to a common
    //  `fn` pointer type, covered under Function Pointers.)
}
```

| Aspect                     | `fn` item                 | Closure                            |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Type annotations           | Required                  | Usually inferred                   |
| Can use local variables    | No                        | Yes (captures them)                |
| Generic                    | Can be                    | No: types fixed at first use       |
| Type                       | Unique per function       | Unique, anonymous per closure      |
| Defined                    | As an item                | As an expression, anywhere         |

> Key Takeaways
> - Closures are written `|params| body`, can appear anywhere an expression can,
>   and can use variables from their environment.
> - Parameter and return types are inferred, usually from the API receiving the
>   closure, and are fixed after first use.
> - Each closure has a unique anonymous type, which enables inlining but prevents
>   storing different closures together without boxing.
> - Nested `fn` items cannot capture local variables; closures can.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Sort a `Vec<String>` by length, then by reverse alphabetical order, using
>    `sort_by` with a closure.
> 2. Write a closure that captures a `prefix: &str` and formats any `&str` as
>    `"{prefix}: {msg}"`. Use it inside `map`.
> 3. Interview: Why can a closure's parameter types be inferred while a function's
>    cannot? (Hint: consider where each is visible and whether it is part of a
>    public API.)

#### Capture Modes

When a closure uses a variable from its environment, it must keep access to it
somehow. Rust chooses among three **capture modes**, picking the **least
restrictive** one that the closure body needs:

1. **By shared reference (`&T`)** when the body only reads the variable.
2. **By mutable reference (`&mut T`)** when the body modifies it.
3. **By value (`T`, a move)** when the body consumes it, for example by returning
   it, passing it to a function that takes ownership, or dropping it.

A closure is effectively a compiler-generated struct whose fields are these
captures, plus a method containing the body. While the closure exists, its
captures follow the normal borrowing rules: a closure holding `&mut count`
prevents any other use of `count` until the closure's last use. Non-lexical
lifetimes (Chapter 3.3) mean the borrow ends at the closure's last use, not at the
end of the scope.

Since edition 2021, closures capture **disjoint fields**: a closure that uses
`self.name` captures only that field, not the whole struct, so other fields
remain available. Before 2021, the entire variable was captured.

```text
   let mut count = 0;
   let name = String::from("ana");
   let mut c = || { count += 1; println!("{name}"); };

   compiler-generated, roughly:
   struct Closure<'a> {
       count: &'a mut i32,       // modified        -> captured by &mut
       name:  &'a String,        // only read       -> captured by &
   }
```

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Player {
    name: String,
    score: u32,
}

fn main() {
    // 1. By shared reference: reading only
    let greeting = String::from("hello");
    let greet = || println!("{greeting}, world");
    greet();                                    // hello, world
    println!("{greeting}");                     // still usable: only borrowed

    // 2. By mutable reference: modifying
    let mut count = 0;
    let mut inc = || count += 1;                // closure must be `mut` to call
    inc();
    inc();
    // println!("{count}"); inc();              // error[E0502]: cannot borrow `count`
                                                // as immutable because it is also
                                                // borrowed as mutable (by `inc`)
    println!("{count}");                        // 2: inc's borrow ended at its last use

    // 3. By value: the body consumes the variable
    let ticket = String::from("T-42");
    let redeem = || {
        let owned: String = ticket;             // moves `ticket` into the body
        owned.len()
    };
    // println!("{ticket}");                    // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value
    println!("{}", redeem());                   // 4

    // Disjoint field capture (edition 2021+)
    let mut p = Player { name: "ana".into(), score: 10 };
    let mut bump = || p.score += 5;             // captures only `p.score` mutably
    println!("{}", p.name);                     // ana: `p.name` is still accessible
    bump();
    println!("{p:?}");                          // Player { name: "ana", score: 15 }
}
```

| Body does                          | Captured as | Effect on the variable while the closure lives |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Reads                              | `&T`        | Others may also read                           |
| Modifies                           | `&mut T`    | No other access                                |
| Moves / consumes                   | `T`         | Variable is moved into the closure             |

> Key Takeaways
> - Closures capture each variable by `&`, `&mut`, or value, choosing the least
>   restrictive mode the body needs.
> - A closure behaves like a struct holding its captures, and those captures obey
>   the normal borrowing rules.
> - A closure that mutates a capture must itself be declared `mut`.
> - Edition 2021 captures individual fields, not whole structs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a closure that appends to a captured `Vec<String>`, call it three times,
>    and print the vector afterwards.
> 2. Trigger the `E0502` error from the example on purpose, then fix it by
>    reordering statements.
> 3. Interview: How does a closure capture `self.items` when used inside a method
>    on `&mut self`, and why did this change in edition 2021? (Hint: compare
>    capturing the whole `self` with capturing one field path.)

#### Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce

Functions that accept closures need to say what they will do with them. Will the
closure be called once or many times? Might two calls overlap? The answers depend
on how the closure treats its captures, and Rust encodes them in three traits that
every closure implements automatically:

- **`FnOnce`**: can be called **at least once**. Calling it may consume its
  captures, so it may not be callable again. *Every* closure implements `FnOnce`.
- **`FnMut`**: can be called repeatedly and may **mutate** its captures. Calling
  it needs `&mut` access to the closure.
- **`Fn`**: can be called repeatedly, even concurrently, and only **reads** its
  captures. Calling it needs only `&` access.

They form a hierarchy: every `Fn` is also `FnMut`, and every `FnMut` is also
`FnOnce` (`Fn: FnMut: FnOnce`). Which traits a closure implements depends on what
its body does with captures, **not** on how it captured them. A `move` closure that
only reads its captured data is still `Fn`.

The choice of bound in an API is a trade-off between caller and callee:

| Bound in your API | Callers may pass                          | Your function may          |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `F: FnOnce()`     | Any closure                               | Call it once               |
| `F: FnMut()`      | Closures that read or mutate              | Call it many times, sequentially |
| `F: Fn()`         | Only closures that read                   | Call it many times, even from several threads |

Pick the **most permissive bound that still lets your function work**. The
standard library follows this: `Option::unwrap_or_else` calls its closure at most
once, so it takes `FnOnce`; `Iterator::for_each` calls it per item, so `FnMut`;
`thread::spawn` runs it once, so `FnOnce`.

```rust
// Accepts anything callable once
fn run_once<F: FnOnce() -> String>(f: F) -> String {
    f()
    // f()                                   // error[E0382]: use of moved value: `f`
}

// Calls repeatedly; closure may mutate its state
fn repeat<F: FnMut()>(n: usize, mut f: F) {  // parameter must be `mut` to call
    for _ in 0..n {
        f();
    }
}

// Calls repeatedly through a shared reference only
fn apply_twice<F: Fn(i32) -> i32>(f: F, x: i32) -> i32 {
    f(f(x))
}

fn main() {
    // FnOnce: consumes a captured String by returning it
    let name = String::from("ana");
    let give_away = move || name;            // returns the capture: FnOnce only
    println!("{}", run_once(give_away));     // ana

    let token = String::from("t-1");
    // repeat(2, move || drop(token));       // error[E0525]: expected a closure that
                                             // implements `FnMut`, but this closure
                                             // only implements `FnOnce`
    drop(token);

    // FnMut: mutates a captured counter
    let mut calls = 0;
    repeat(3, || calls += 1);
    println!("{calls}");                     // 3
    // apply_twice(|x| { calls += 1; x }, 1);   // error[E0594]: cannot assign to
                                                // `calls`, as it is a captured
                                                // variable in a `Fn` closure

    // Fn: reads only
    let offset = 10;
    println!("{}", apply_twice(|x| x + offset, 1));  // 21

    // An Fn closure is also FnMut and FnOnce: accepted by all three
    let shout = || String::from("hey");
    repeat(1, || { shout(); });
    println!("{}", run_once(shout));         // hey

    // Standard library examples
    let missing: Option<String> = None;
    let fallback = String::from("default");
    println!("{}", missing.unwrap_or_else(move || fallback));  // FnOnce: default
    let mut log = Vec::new();
    [1, 2, 3].iter().for_each(|x| log.push(x * 2));            // FnMut
    println!("{log:?}");                     // [2, 4, 6]
}
```

```text
        FnOnce        every closure                 call(self)
          ^
          |
        FnMut         does not move captures out    call_mut(&mut self)
          ^
          |
         Fn           does not mutate captures      call(&self)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `FnOnce` closures may consume captures; `FnMut` may mutate them; `Fn` only
>   reads them.
> - The hierarchy is `Fn: FnMut: FnOnce`; a closure implements every trait its body
>   allows.
> - The traits depend on what the body *does* with captures, not on `move`.
> - In APIs, choose the most permissive bound that works: `FnOnce` if called once,
>   `FnMut` if called sequentially, `Fn` if shared or concurrent.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn call_n<F: FnMut() -> u32>(n: usize, f: F) -> Vec<u32>` and test it
>    with a closure that returns an increasing counter.
> 2. For each of these closures, list which of `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce` it
>    implements: `|| x + 1`, `|| v.push(1)`, `move || drop(s)`, `move || s.len()`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `thread::spawn` require `FnOnce` instead of `Fn`, and
>    `Iterator::map` require `FnMut` instead of `Fn`? (Hint: for each, how many
>    times is the closure called, and what would a stricter bound forbid?)

#### move Closures

By default a closure borrows what it can. That is ideal when the closure is used
within the current scope, but breaks down when the closure must **outlive** that
scope: a thread that keeps running after the function returns, a closure returned
from a function, or a callback stored in a long-lived struct. A borrow of a local
variable cannot outlive the variable, so the compiler rejects it
(`error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function`).

The **`move`** keyword forces every captured variable to be captured **by value**.
The closure then owns its data and can live as long as it needs. For `Copy` types
such as integers, "by value" means a copy, so the original remains usable. For
owned types such as `String` or `Vec`, the original is moved and no longer usable
outside the closure.

Two clarifications prevent common confusion:

- **`move` changes how variables are captured, not which `Fn*` traits the closure
  implements.** A `move` closure that only reads its data is still `Fn`.
- **To move some captures and borrow others**, create references beforehand and
  move those (`let r = &data; move || r.len()`): the reference is moved, the data
  stays put.

When several closures or threads each need their own handle to shared data, the
standard idiom is **clone before move**: clone an `Arc` (or a `String`) into a new
variable, then move the clone.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

fn make_greeter(name: String) -> impl Fn() -> String {
    // Without `move`: error[E0373] — `name` would be borrowed past the function's end
    move || format!("hello, {name}")
}

fn main() {
    // Threads require 'static closures: move ownership in
    let data = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let handle = thread::spawn(move || data.iter().sum::<i32>());
    // println!("{data:?}");                // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value
    println!("{}", handle.join().unwrap()); // 6

    // Copy types are copied, so the original remains usable
    let factor = 3;
    let triple = move |x: i32| x * factor;
    println!("{} {factor}", triple(5));     // 15 3

    // Returned closures must own their captures
    let g = make_greeter(String::from("ana"));
    println!("{}", g());                    // hello, ana
    println!("{}", g());                    // hello, ana  (still Fn: only reads)

    // Clone before move: each thread gets its own Arc handle to shared data
    let shared = Arc::new(vec!["a", "b", "c"]);
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..3 {
        let shared = Arc::clone(&shared);   // new handle, same data
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || shared[i].to_uppercase()));
    }
    let results: Vec<String> = handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect();
    println!("{results:?} {}", shared.len());   // ["A", "B", "C"] 3

    // Moving a reference: borrow the data, move only the reference
    let big = String::from("large buffer");
    let r = &big;
    let peek = move || r.len();             // moves `r` (a &String), not `big`
    println!("{} {big}", peek());           // 12 large buffer
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `move` forces all captures to be by value, giving the closure ownership.
> - It is required when a closure outlives its scope: threads, returned closures,
>   stored callbacks.
> - `Copy` captures are copied; non-`Copy` captures are moved and unusable
>   afterwards.
> - `move` does not change which `Fn*` traits apply; use clone-before-move to give
>   each closure its own handle.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Remove `move` from the `thread::spawn` call in the example and read the error
>    message's suggested fix.
> 2. Spawn five threads that each print their index and a shared `Arc<String>`
>    label, using the clone-before-move pattern.
> 3. Interview: A `move` closure captures a `Vec` but only calls `.len()` on it.
>    Is the closure `FnOnce`, `FnMut`, or `Fn`? (Hint: separate how the data got
>    into the closure from what the body does with it.)

#### Returning Closures

Functions that build behavior, such as a multiplier for a given factor, a
validator for a given rule, or a handler for a given route, need to return
closures. Because each closure has a unique, unnameable type, you cannot write the
return type directly. There are two ways around this, mirroring static versus
dynamic dispatch (Chapter 5.3):

- **`impl Fn(...) -> R`** returns one concrete closure type, hidden from the
  caller. It is zero-cost (no allocation, calls can be inlined), but every return
  path must produce the **same** closure.
- **`Box<dyn Fn(...) -> R>`** returns a heap-allocated trait object. It costs an
  allocation and an indirect call, but different branches can return different
  closures, and boxed closures can be stored together in collections.

Returned closures almost always need `move`, since any local they borrowed would
be gone once the function returns.

The same choice applies to **storing** closures in structs: a generic parameter
`F: Fn(...)` (static, one closure type per struct instance) or a
`Box<dyn Fn(...)>` field (dynamic, any closure, and many of them in a `Vec`).

```rust
// Static: one concrete hidden type
fn multiplier(k: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    move |x| x * k
}

// Dynamic: different closures depending on runtime input
fn operation(name: &str) -> Option<Box<dyn Fn(i32, i32) -> i32>> {
    match name {
        "add" => Some(Box::new(|a, b| a + b)),
        "sub" => Some(Box::new(|a, b| a - b)),
        "pow" => Some(Box::new(|a, b| a.pow(b as u32))),
        _ => None,
    }
}
// fn bad(add: bool) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
//     if add { |x| x + 1 } else { |x| x - 1 }    // error[E0308]: `if` and `else`
// }                                              // have incompatible types

// Composition: a closure built from two others
fn compose<A, B, C>(f: impl Fn(A) -> B, g: impl Fn(B) -> C) -> impl Fn(A) -> C {
    move |x| g(f(x))
}

// Storing closures: generic field vs boxed field
struct Validator<F: Fn(&str) -> bool> {
    rule: F,                                     // static: one closure type
}

struct EventBus {
    handlers: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&str)>>,            // dynamic: many different closures
}

impl EventBus {
    fn on(&mut self, h: impl Fn(&str) + 'static) {
        self.handlers.push(Box::new(h));
    }
    fn emit(&self, event: &str) {
        for h in &self.handlers {
            h(event);
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let double = multiplier(2);
    let triple = multiplier(3);
    println!("{} {}", double(5), triple(5));     // 10 15

    for name in ["add", "pow", "mod"] {
        match operation(name) {
            Some(op) => println!("{name}: {}", op(2, 5)),   // add: 7 / pow: 32
            None => println!("{name}: unknown"),            // mod: unknown
        }
    }

    let parse_then_double = compose(|s: &str| s.len(), |n: usize| n * 2);
    println!("{}", parse_then_double("abcd"));   // 8

    let min_len = 3;
    let v = Validator { rule: move |s: &str| s.len() >= min_len };
    println!("{} {}", (v.rule)("ab"), (v.rule)("abc"));   // false true
                                                          // (parentheses call the field)
    let mut bus = EventBus { handlers: Vec::new() };
    let prefix = String::from("[log]");
    bus.on(move |e| println!("{prefix} {e}"));
    bus.on(|e| println!("event length {}", e.len()));
    bus.emit("saved");
    // [log] saved
    // event length 5
}
```

| Approach                     | Allocation | Dispatch | Different closures per branch | Store many together |
| ---------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `-> impl Fn(..)`             | No         | Static   | No                            | No                  |
| `-> Box<dyn Fn(..)>`         | Yes        | Dynamic  | Yes                           | Yes                 |
| Struct field `F: Fn(..)`     | No         | Static   | N/A                           | No (one type)       |
| Struct field `Box<dyn Fn(..)>` | Yes      | Dynamic  | N/A                           | Yes (`Vec<Box<..>>`) |

> Key Takeaways
> - Return `impl Fn` for a single closure type at zero cost; return `Box<dyn Fn>`
>   when the closure varies at runtime.
> - Returned closures need `move` so they own what they capture.
> - Store closures as generic fields for speed or as boxed trait objects for
>   flexibility and collections.
> - Call a closure stored in a field with `(self.field)(args)`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn make_counter() -> impl FnMut() -> u32` returning 1, 2, 3, ... on
>    successive calls.
> 2. Build a `HashMap<&str, Box<dyn Fn(f64) -> f64>>` of unit conversions ("km_to_mi",
>    "c_to_f") and apply them by name.
> 3. Interview: Why can a function not return `Fn(i32) -> i32` directly, and what do
>    `impl Fn` and `Box<dyn Fn>` each do to solve that? (Hint: what size does the
>    caller need to reserve for the return value?)

#### Function Pointers

Closures are not the only callable values. A plain, named function can be passed
around as a value too, and its type is the **function pointer type**, written with
a lowercase `fn`: `fn(i32) -> i32`. Unlike the `Fn` traits, `fn` is a concrete type:
a single pointer to code, with no captured environment.

Key facts:

- **Named functions coerce to `fn` pointers**: `let f: fn(i32) -> i32 = add_one;`.
  Each function item has its own zero-sized type, which coerces to the pointer type
  when needed.
- **Non-capturing closures coerce to `fn` pointers** as well, because they have no
  state to carry. Capturing closures cannot (`error[E0308]`).
- **`fn` pointers implement `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce`**, so they can be passed to
  any API that takes closures. This is why `.map(str::len)`, `.map(Some)`, and
  `.map(String::from)` work: method paths, enum variant constructors, and tuple
  struct constructors are all functions.
- **One type for all**: unlike closures, all functions with the same signature
  share the type `fn(A) -> B`, so a table of operations can be a plain array or
  `HashMap` of function pointers, with no boxing.
- **C interop**: callbacks passed to C must be `extern "C" fn` pointers, since C
  understands code addresses but not Rust closures.

Prefer accepting closures through generics (`impl Fn`) in APIs; that accepts both
closures and function pointers. Use `fn` types when you specifically need a
uniform, non-capturing, storable callable.

```rust
fn add_one(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x + 1
}

fn double(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x * 2
}

// Takes a function pointer explicitly: only non-capturing callables fit
fn apply_ptr(f: fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 {
    f(x)
}

// Takes any closure or function: the more flexible signature
fn apply_any(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 {
    f(x)
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Meters(f64);

fn main() {
    // Named functions and non-capturing closures become fn pointers
    let f: fn(i32) -> i32 = add_one;
    let g: fn(i32) -> i32 = |x| x - 1;          // no captures: coerces fine
    println!("{} {}", f(1), g(1));              // 2 0

    let offset = 10;
    println!("{}", apply_any(|x| x + offset, 1));   // 11
    // apply_ptr(|x| x + offset, 1);            // error[E0308]: expected fn pointer,
                                                // found closure (it captures `offset`)
    println!("{}", apply_ptr(double, 4));       // 8
    println!("{}", apply_any(double, 4));       // 8: fn pointers implement Fn

    // A table of operations with one shared type: no boxing needed
    let ops: [(&str, fn(i32) -> i32); 3] = [("inc", add_one), ("dbl", double), ("neg", |x| -x)];
    for (name, op) in ops {
        print!("{name}={} ", op(5));            // inc=6 dbl=10 neg=-5
    }
    println!();

    // Functions, methods, and constructors passed directly to adapters
    let words = ["hi", "there"];
    let lens: Vec<usize> = words.iter().copied().map(str::len).collect();
    let owned: Vec<String> = words.iter().copied().map(String::from).collect();
    let wrapped: Vec<Option<i32>> = vec![1, 2].into_iter().map(Some).collect();
    let dists: Vec<Meters> = vec![1.5, 2.0].into_iter().map(Meters).collect();
    println!("{lens:?} {owned:?} {wrapped:?} {dists:?}");
    // [2, 5] ["hi", "there"] [Some(1), Some(2)] [Meters(1.5), Meters(2.0)]

    // Sizes: function items and non-capturing closures are zero-sized;
    // fn pointers are one machine word; closures are as big as their captures
    let c = move |x: i32| x + offset;
    println!("{} {} {}",
             std::mem::size_of_val(&add_one),   // 0: the function item type
             std::mem::size_of::<fn(i32) -> i32>(),   // 8: a code pointer
             std::mem::size_of_val(&c));        // 4: one captured i32
}
```

| Aspect                      | `fn(A) -> B` pointer         | Closure / `impl Fn(A) -> B`        |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Captures environment        | No                           | Yes                                |
| Type                        | One shared concrete type     | Unique per closure                 |
| Size                        | One pointer                  | Size of its captures (may be 0)    |
| Storable in arrays/maps     | Directly                     | Needs `Box<dyn Fn>`                |
| Inlining                    | Only if the target is known  | Yes, via monomorphization          |
| C callbacks                 | Yes (`extern "C" fn`)        | No                                 |

> Key Takeaways
> - `fn(A) -> B` is a concrete function pointer type with no captured state.
> - Named functions, methods, constructors, and non-capturing closures all coerce
>   to function pointers.
> - Function pointers implement all three `Fn*` traits, so they work anywhere a
>   closure is accepted.
> - Accept `impl Fn` in APIs for flexibility; use `fn` types for uniform tables
>   and C callbacks.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a calculator that maps operator symbols to `fn(f64, f64) -> f64` in a
>    `HashMap<char, fn(f64, f64) -> f64>` and evaluates `"3 * 4"`.
> 2. Convert a `Vec<&str>` into a `Vec<String>` and a `Vec<usize>` using only
>    function paths in `map` (no closures).
> 3. Interview: Why can a closure that captures nothing be converted to a `fn`
>    pointer, while one that captures a variable cannot? (Hint: where would the
>    captured value live, and how would the caller pass it?)

---

## 7. Error Handling

Every non-trivial program meets failure: files go missing, input is malformed,
networks drop, and code has bugs. Rust separates failure into two kinds:
recoverable errors, carried as ordinary `Result` values that the type system
forces you to handle, and unrecoverable errors, signalled with `panic!` when a bug
has left the program in a state it cannot reason about. This chapter covers the
mechanics of both, how to design error types that other code can work with, and
the conventions that separate a library's errors from an application's.

<a id="71-recoverable-errors"></a>
### 7.1 Recoverable Errors

A recoverable error is one the caller can sensibly respond to: retry, fall back to
a default, ask the user again, or report it and carry on. This section covers the
tools for working with `Result` values without drowning in `match` statements.

#### Result Combinators

Chapter 4 handled a `Result` with `match`. That works, but a pipeline of several
fallible steps turns into a staircase of nested matches in which the actual logic
is hard to find. Most of those matches do the same thing: transform the value if
it is `Ok`, and pass the `Err` through untouched (or the reverse).

**Combinators** are methods on `Result` that capture these recurring shapes. Each
takes a closure and applies it to *one side only*. A useful picture is a railway
with two parallel tracks: an `Ok` track and an `Err` track. Every combinator is a
piece of track that acts on one of them:

- `map` transforms the value travelling on the `Ok` track.
- `map_err` transforms the value travelling on the `Err` track.
- `and_then` runs a step that can itself fail, so it may switch the train from
  the `Ok` track to the `Err` track.
- `or_else` gives an error a chance to recover, switching back to `Ok`.

```text
              map(f)          and_then(g)             map_err(h)
   Ok(v)  ----- f(v) --------- g(..) ---+-------------------------------> Ok(..)
                                        | g returned Err
   Err(e) ------------------------------+------------- h(e) ------------> Err(..)
```

Once a value is on the `Err` track, every `map` and `and_then` after it is skipped;
once it is on the `Ok` track, `map_err` and `or_else` are skipped.

```rust
fn parse_even(s: &str) -> Result<i32, String> {
    s.trim()
        .parse::<i32>()                                   // Result<i32, ParseIntError>
        .map_err(|e| format!("not a number: {e}"))        // Result<i32, String>
        .and_then(|n| {                                   // a second step that can fail
            if n % 2 == 0 { Ok(n) } else { Err(format!("{n} is odd")) }
        })
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", parse_even(" 42 "));    // Ok(42)
    println!("{:?}", parse_even("7"));       // Err("7 is odd")
    println!("{:?}", parse_even("x"));       // Err("not a number: invalid digit found in string")

    // map: transform the success value, leave errors alone
    println!("{:?}", parse_even("10").map(|n| n * 2));          // Ok(20)

    // or_else: try to recover from an error
    println!("{:?}", parse_even("7").or_else(|_| parse_even("8")));  // Ok(8)

    // Combining two results: and_then + map
    let sum = parse_even("2").and_then(|a| parse_even("4").map(|b| a + b));
    println!("{sum:?}");                                        // Ok(6)

    // Leaving the Result world with a fallback value
    println!("{}", parse_even("x").unwrap_or(0));               // 0
    println!("{}", parse_even("x").unwrap_or_default());        // 0
    println!("{}", parse_even("3").map_or(-1, |n| n / 2));      // -1

    // Querying without unwrapping
    println!("{}", parse_even("4").is_ok_and(|n| n > 2));       // true

    // Side effects (logging) without changing the value
    let r = parse_even("3").inspect_err(|e| println!("warning: {e}"));  // warning: 3 is odd
    println!("{}", r.is_err());                                 // true

    // ok() and err() turn one side into an Option and discard the other
    println!("{:?} {:?}", parse_even("3").ok(), parse_even("3").err());
    // None Some("3 is odd")

    // as_ref() lets you use combinators without consuming the Result
    let owned: Result<String, String> = Ok("hello".to_string());
    let len = owned.as_ref().map(|s| s.len());
    println!("{len:?} {owned:?}");                              // Ok(5) Ok("hello")
}
```

| Method                  | Acts on | Closure returns    | Produces          |
| ----------------------- | ------- | ------------------ | ----------------- |
