| `map(f)`                | `Ok`    | `U`                | `Result<U, E>`    |
| `map_err(f)`            | `Err`   | `F`                | `Result<T, F>`    |
| `and_then(f)`           | `Ok`    | `Result<U, E>`     | `Result<U, E>`    |
| `or_else(f)`            | `Err`   | `Result<T, F>`     | `Result<T, F>`    |
| `unwrap_or(v)`          | `Err`   | (value, eager)     | `T`               |
| `unwrap_or_else(f)`     | `Err`   | `T` (lazy)         | `T`               |
| `unwrap_or_default()`   | `Err`   | (uses `Default`)   | `T`               |
| `map_or(d, f)`          | both    | `U`                | `U`               |
| `ok()` / `err()`        | both    | none               | `Option<T>` / `Option<E>` |
| `inspect` / `inspect_err` | `Ok` / `Err` | `()`        | unchanged         |
| `is_ok_and` / `is_err_and` | `Ok` / `Err` | `bool`     | `bool`            |

Arguments to the non-closure variants are evaluated **eagerly**, before the method
is called. `r.unwrap_or(expensive())` calls `expensive()` even when `r` is `Ok`;
`r.unwrap_or_else(|_| expensive())` calls it only when needed. The same applies
to `ok_or` versus `ok_or_else` and `map_or` versus `map_or_else`. Clippy's
`or_fun_call` lint catches the eager form when the argument is a function call.

> Key Takeaways
> - Combinators apply a closure to one side of a `Result` and pass the other side
>   through unchanged.
> - `map`/`map_err` transform values; `and_then`/`or_else` chain steps that can
>   themselves fail or recover.
> - Use the `_else` variants when the fallback is expensive to compute.
> - `as_ref()` lets you inspect a `Result` with combinators without consuming it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn parse_percent(s: &str) -> Result<u8, String>` that rejects values
>    above 100, using only combinators (no `match`, no `?`).
> 2. Write `fn add_strs(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, String>` that parses both
>    inputs and returns their sum, first with nested `match`, then with
>    `and_then` and `map`. Compare readability.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `r.unwrap_or(load_default())` and
>    `r.unwrap_or_else(|_| load_default())`, and when does it matter? (Hint: when
>    is each argument evaluated, and what if `load_default` has side effects?)

#### The ? Operator

Combinators suit linear pipelines, but most functions interleave fallible calls
with ordinary code: `let` bindings, loops, conditionals. Expressing all of that as
closure chains gets awkward quickly. What you usually want is simpler: "give me
the value if this worked; otherwise stop here and hand the error to my caller".

The postfix `?` operator says exactly that. Applied to a `Result`, it evaluates
to the `Ok` value, or returns the `Err` from the *enclosing function* immediately.
Before returning, it passes the error through `From::from`, so the error can be
converted into the function's own error type (Section 7.3 builds on this). Written
by hand, `let n = text.parse::<i32>()?;` is roughly:

```rust
let n = match text.parse::<i32>() {
    Ok(value) => value,
    Err(error) => return Err(From::from(error)),
};
```

`?` also works on `Option`: `Some(v)` evaluates to `v`, and `None` returns `None`
from the enclosing function. The rules about where it can be used are strict:

- The enclosing function (or closure, or `async` block) must return a compatible
  type: `?` on a `Result` needs a function returning `Result`, and `?` on an
  `Option` needs a function returning `Option`. Mixing them requires an explicit
  conversion (see "Option and Result Interop").
- The error type of the expression must convert into the function's error type
  via `From`.
- `main` may return `Result<(), E>` for any `E: Debug`. If it returns `Err`, Rust
  prints `Error: {e:?}` to stderr and exits with status 1.

```rust
use std::num::ParseIntError;

// Without ?: every fallible step needs its own match
fn add_strs_verbose(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError> {
    let x = match a.parse::<i32>() {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(e) => return Err(e),
    };
    let y = match b.parse::<i32>() {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(e) => return Err(e),
    };
    Ok(x + y)
}

// With ?: identical behaviour
fn add_strs(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError> {
    Ok(a.parse::<i32>()? + b.parse::<i32>()?)
}

// ? on Option, in a function returning Option
fn first_char_upper(s: &str) -> Option<char> {
    let c = s.chars().next()?;           // None -> return None
    c.to_uppercase().next()
}

// ? inside a loop: stop at the first bad line
fn sum_lines(text: &str) -> Result<i64, ParseIntError> {
    let mut total = 0;
    for line in text.lines() {
        total += line.trim().parse::<i64>()?;
    }
    Ok(total)
}

fn main() -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {   // main may return a Result
    println!("{:?}", add_strs_verbose("2", "3"));   // Ok(5)
    println!("{:?}", add_strs("2", "x"));           // Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })
    println!("{:?}", first_char_upper("rust"));     // Some('R')
    println!("{:?}", first_char_upper(""));         // None
    println!("{:?}", sum_lines("1\n2\n 3 "));       // Ok(6)

    // In a closure, ? returns from the closure, not from main
    let parse_all = |items: &[&str]| -> Result<Vec<u8>, ParseIntError> {
        let mut out = Vec::new();
        for s in items {
            out.push(s.parse()?);
        }
        Ok(out)
    };
    println!("{:?}", parse_all(&["1", "2"]));       // Ok([1, 2])

    let n: i32 = "40".parse()?;                     // ? works in main too
    println!("{}", n + 2);                          // 42

    // fn no_result() { "1".parse::<i32>()?; }
    // error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that
    //               returns `Result` or `Option`

    let _bad: i32 = "forty".parse()?;               // main returns Err here
    Ok(())
    // stderr: Error: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }   (exit status 1)
}
```

| Expression type   | Enclosing function returns          | On success | On failure                    |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------- |
| `Result<T, E>`    | `Result<U, F>` where `F: From<E>`   | `T`        | `return Err(F::from(e))`      |
| `Option<T>`       | `Option<U>`                         | `T`        | `return None`                 |
| `Result<T, E>`    | `Option<U>`                         | n/a        | Compile error (E0277)         |
| `Result` or `Option` | `()`                             | n/a        | Compile error (E0277)         |

Precedence matters in chains: `?` binds tighter than unary operators, so `-x?`
means `-(x?)`, and method chains read naturally: `file.read_line()?.trim()`.
The predecessor of `?` was the `try!` macro, which you may still see in old code;
`try` is a reserved keyword since the 2018 edition.

> Key Takeaways
> - `expr?` unwraps a success value or returns the failure from the enclosing
>   function.
> - On `Result`, the error passes through `From::from`, enabling automatic
>   conversion to the function's error type.
> - `?` on `Option` requires a function returning `Option`; the two do not mix
>   without an explicit conversion.
> - `main` can return `Result<(), E: Debug>`; an `Err` prints the error and exits
>   with status 1.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a function that parses three strings into `f64` and returns their
>    average, first with explicit `match` and then with `?`.
> 2. Write `fn middle_name(full: &str) -> Option<&str>` that returns the second of
>    three whitespace-separated words, using `?` on `Option`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `?` call `From::from` on the error instead of returning it
>    unchanged? What would error handling look like without that step? (Hint:
>    picture a function that calls one API returning `io::Error` and another
>    returning `ParseIntError`.)

#### Propagation Across Functions

Errors usually arise deep in the call stack, inside a file read, inside a parser,
inside a startup routine, but they can only be handled meaningfully higher up,
where someone knows what to do about them: show a message, use a default, retry.
Every function in between faces the same choice: **handle** the error here, or
**propagate** it to the caller. Because `?` makes propagation a single character,
that choice stays a conscious decision instead of a chore.

Think of a support ticket escalated through an organization. Each desk either
resolves it or forwards it upward, ideally with the original ticket intact. The
desk that can actually make a decision should be the one that does.

```text
   main()                       handles: prints a message, sets exit code
     ^  Err(e)
   load_port(path)              handles NotFound (uses a default),
     ^  Err(e)                  propagates everything else
   read_port(path)              propagates with ?
     ^  Err(e)
   fs::read_to_string(path)     the failure originates here
```

At each boundary, the error types must line up: either the same type flows
through, a `From` conversion exists, or you convert with `map_err`. A function can
also handle *selectively*: match on the error, deal with the kinds it understands,
and propagate the rest.

Propagation also works through iterators. `collect` can build a
`Result<Vec<T>, E>` from an iterator of `Result<T, E>`: it stops at the first
`Err` and returns it. `sum` and `product` short-circuit the same way. When you
want *every* error rather than the first, use `partition` instead.

```rust
use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::path::Path;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum SettingsError {
    Io(io::Error),
    BadPort(String),
}

fn read_port(path: &Path) -> Result<u16, SettingsError> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path).map_err(SettingsError::Io)?;   // convert, propagate
    let text = text.trim();
    text.parse::<u16>().map_err(|_| SettingsError::BadPort(text.to_string()))
}

// Handles one kind of failure, propagates every other
fn load_port(path: &Path) -> Result<u16, SettingsError> {
    match read_port(path) {
        Err(SettingsError::Io(e)) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::NotFound => Ok(8080),
        other => other,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir();
    let good = dir.join("port_good.txt");
    let bad = dir.join("port_bad.txt");
    fs::write(&good, "3000\n").unwrap();
    fs::write(&bad, "http\n").unwrap();

    println!("{:?}", load_port(&good));                       // Ok(3000)
    println!("{:?}", load_port(Path::new("/no/such/file")));  // Ok(8080)
    println!("{:?}", load_port(&bad));                        // Err(BadPort("http"))

    // collect into Result<Vec<_>, _>: stops at the first Err
    let all: Result<Vec<u16>, _> = ["80", "443", "8080"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<u16>()).collect();
    let one_bad: Result<Vec<u16>, _> = ["80", "x", "99999"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<u16>()).collect();
    println!("{all:?}");        // Ok([80, 443, 8080])
    println!("{one_bad:?}");    // Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })

    // sum short-circuits as well
    let total: Result<u32, _> = ["1", "2", "3"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<u32>()).sum();
    println!("{total:?}");      // Ok(6)

    // partition when you want every error, not just the first
    let (oks, errs): (Vec<_>, Vec<_>) =
        ["1", "a", "3", "b"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<i32>()).partition(|r| r.is_ok());
    let oks: Vec<i32> = oks.into_iter().map(Result::unwrap).collect();
    println!("{oks:?}, {} errors", errs.len());   // [1, 3], 2 errors
}
```

| Strategy                 | Code                                   | Use when                                  |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Propagate unchanged      | `call()?`                              | The caller is better placed to decide     |
| Convert and propagate    | `call().map_err(MyErr::from)?` or `From` | Your function has its own error type    |
| Handle and recover       | `match`, `unwrap_or`, `or_else`        | A sensible fallback exists at this level  |
| Handle and report        | `if let Err(e) = call() { eprintln!(..) }` | You are at the top (e.g. `main`)       |

> Key Takeaways
> - Each function chooses between handling an error and propagating it; handle it
>   where a meaningful decision can be made.
> - Error types must line up at every boundary, through the same type, `From`, or
>   `map_err`.
> - Match on the error to handle selectively and propagate the rest.
> - `collect`, `sum`, and `product` over `Result` items stop at the first error;
>   `partition` keeps all of them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a three-layer program: read a file, parse each line as a number,
>    compute the average. Propagate errors to `main` and print a single message.
> 2. Extend `load_port` so that `PermissionDenied` also falls back to the default,
>    but prints a warning first.
> 3. Interview: An iterator of `Result` values has side effects in its `map`
>    closure, and the second item fails. If you call
>    `.collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()`, how many side effects happen, and why?
>    (Hint: iterators are lazy, and `collect` stops pulling at the first `Err`.)

#### Option and Result Interop

Real code mixes the two types constantly. `HashMap::get` returns `Option`, while
`str::parse` returns `Result`. Inside a function returning `Result`, `?` on an
`Option` is a compile error (E0277), because `None` carries no error value to
return. You need a bridge, and choosing it means answering one question: **is
absence an error in this context, and if so, what is the reason?**

- A *required* configuration key that is missing is an error: convert the
  `Option` into a `Result` with `ok_or` or `ok_or_else`, supplying the reason.
- When the reason for a failure does not matter, convert a `Result` into an
  `Option` with `ok()`, discarding the error.
- An *optional* value that must be valid *if present* produces an
  `Option<Result<T, E>>`. `transpose` flips it into `Result<Option<T>, E>`, which
  works with `?`.

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ConfigError {
    Missing(&'static str),
    Invalid(&'static str, String),
}

fn parse_config(map: &HashMap<&str, &str>) -> Result<(String, Option<u64>), ConfigError> {
    // Required key: absence is an error, so convert Option -> Result
    let host = map.get("host").ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("host"))?.to_string();

    // Optional key: absence is fine, but a present value must parse.
    // Option<Result<u64, _>>  --transpose-->  Result<Option<u64>, _>
    let timeout = map
        .get("timeout")
        .map(|s| s.parse::<u64>().map_err(|_| ConfigError::Invalid("timeout", s.to_string())))
        .transpose()?;

    Ok((host, timeout))
}

fn main() {
    let full = HashMap::from([("host", "example.org"), ("timeout", "30")]);
    let minimal = HashMap::from([("host", "localhost")]);
    let broken = HashMap::from([("host", "x"), ("timeout", "soon")]);
    let empty = HashMap::new();

    println!("{:?}", parse_config(&full));      // Ok(("example.org", Some(30)))
    println!("{:?}", parse_config(&minimal));   // Ok(("localhost", None))
    println!("{:?}", parse_config(&broken));    // Err(Invalid("timeout", "soon"))
    println!("{:?}", parse_config(&empty));     // Err(Missing("host"))

    // Result -> Option when the reason does not matter
    let maybe: Option<i32> = "12".parse().ok();
    println!("{maybe:?}");                      // Some(12)

    // Keep the values that parsed, silently dropping failures
    let nums: Vec<i32> = ["1", "two", "3"].iter().filter_map(|s| s.parse().ok()).collect();
    println!("{nums:?}");                       // [1, 3]

    // Lazy error construction: the format! only runs for None
    let key = "port";
    let r: Result<&&str, String> = full.get(key).ok_or_else(|| format!("missing {key}"));
    println!("{r:?}");                          // Err("missing port")

    // Option<Option<T>> -> Option<T>
    let nested: Option<Option<i32>> = Some(None);
    println!("{:?}", nested.flatten());         // None
}
```

| From                    | To                         | Method                      | Notes                            |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `Option<T>`             | `Result<T, E>`             | `ok_or(e)`                  | `e` built eagerly                |
| `Option<T>`             | `Result<T, E>`             | `ok_or_else(\|\| e)`        | `e` built only on `None`         |
| `Result<T, E>`          | `Option<T>`                | `ok()`                      | Discards the error               |
| `Result<T, E>`          | `Option<E>`                | `err()`                     | Discards the success value       |
| `Option<Result<T, E>>`  | `Result<Option<T>, E>`     | `transpose()`               | Optional-but-valid values        |
| `Result<Option<T>, E>`  | `Option<Result<T, E>>`     | `transpose()`               | The reverse direction            |
| `Option<Option<T>>`     | `Option<T>`                | `flatten()`                 | Collapses one level              |
| iterator of `Result<T, E>` | iterator of `T`         | `filter_map(Result::ok)` or `flatten()` | Silently drops errors |

> Key Takeaways
> - `?` cannot mix `Option` and `Result`; convert explicitly.
> - Use `ok_or`/`ok_or_else` when absence is an error with a reason, and `ok()`
>   when the reason is irrelevant.
> - `transpose` handles "optional, but valid if present" values cleanly.
> - Discarding errors with `ok()` or `filter_map` is a decision; make it
>   deliberately, not by reflex.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn get_age(map: &HashMap<String, String>) -> Result<u8, String>` that
>    reports "missing age" and "invalid age: ..." as distinct messages.
> 2. Given a `&[&str]`, return `Result<Option<i32>, ParseIntError>`: `Ok(None)`
>    for an empty slice, otherwise the parsed first element.
> 3. Interview: When is calling `.ok()` on a `Result` a code smell? (Hint: what
>    information is thrown away, and who further up the stack might have needed
>    it?)

#### Early Return Patterns

Readable error handling keeps the **happy path** (the code that runs when nothing
goes wrong) aligned at the left margin and reading top to bottom. The opposite,
sometimes called "arrow code", nests each check inside the previous one until the
real work is buried several levels deep and every `else` is far from its `if`.

The fix is the **guard clause**: reject each bad case as soon as you can detect it
and return early, so that by the time execution reaches the end of the function,
every precondition holds. Rust offers several tools for this:

- `?` for propagating an existing error.
- `if condition { return Err(..); }` for validation checks.
- `let ... else { return ...; }` (Chapter 4) when you need to destructure a value
  or bail out; the `else` branch must diverge.
- `match` arms that `return` when different errors need different treatment.
- An immediately invoked closure or a labeled block when you want early exit
  from *part* of a function. (`try` blocks, which would do this directly, are
  not yet stable.)

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
}

// Nested style: the happy path drifts to the right
fn register_nested(name: &str, age: &str) -> Result<User, String> {
    if !name.is_empty() {
        if name.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric()) {
            match age.parse::<u8>() {
                Ok(age) => {
                    if age >= 13 {
                        Ok(User { name: name.to_string(), age })
                    } else {
                        Err("too young".to_string())
                    }
                }
                Err(_) => Err("age is not a number".to_string()),
            }
        } else {
            Err("name must be alphanumeric".to_string())
        }
    } else {
        Err("name is empty".to_string())
    }
}

// Small helper in the spirit of anyhow's ensure!
fn ensure(condition: bool, msg: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    if condition { Ok(()) } else { Err(msg.to_string()) }
}

// Guard style: reject bad cases first; the happy path reads top to bottom
fn register(name: &str, age: &str) -> Result<User, String> {
    if name.is_empty() {
        return Err("name is empty".to_string());
    }
    ensure(name.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric()), "name must be alphanumeric")?;
    let Ok(age) = age.parse::<u8>() else {          // bind, or diverge
        return Err("age is not a number".to_string());
    };
    ensure(age >= 13, "too young")?;
    Ok(User { name: name.to_string(), age })
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", register("ana", "30"));          // Ok(User { name: "ana", age: 30 })
    println!("{:?}", register("ana!", "30"));         // Err("name must be alphanumeric")
    println!("{:?}", register("bo", "ten"));          // Err("age is not a number")
    println!("{:?}", register_nested("cy", "9"));     // Err("too young")

    // Immediately invoked closure: ? exits the closure, not main
    let product: Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> = (|| {
        let a: i32 = "4".parse()?;
        let b: i32 = "x".parse()?;
        Ok(a * b)
    })();
    println!("{product:?}");                          // Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })

    // Labeled block: break out early with a value
    let input = "12,abc";
    let point = 'parse: {
        let Some((x, y)) = input.split_once(',') else { break 'parse None };
        let (Ok(x), Ok(y)) = (x.parse::<i32>(), y.parse::<i32>()) else { break 'parse None };
        Some((x, y))
    };
    println!("{point:?}");                            // None
}
```

| Pattern                              | Use when                                          |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `expr?`                              | An existing error should propagate as is          |
| `if cond { return Err(..) }`         | Validating a condition                            |
| `let Pat = expr else { return .. };` | You need the binding, or must bail out            |
| `match` with `return` arms           | Different failures need different handling        |
| Closure or labeled block             | Early exit should stay local to part of a function |

> Key Takeaways
> - Guard clauses reject bad cases early, keeping the happy path flat and
>   readable.
> - `let-else` combines destructuring with a mandatory early exit.
> - Small helpers like `ensure` turn conditions into `Result`s that work with `?`.
> - Immediately invoked closures and labeled blocks scope early exits to a block.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Refactor a nested password validator (length, has digit, has uppercase, not
>    equal to username) into guard clauses.
> 2. Write `fn parse_point(s: &str) -> Option<(i32, i32)>` for input like
>    `"3,-4"` using `split_once`, `let-else`, and `?`.
> 3. Interview: `try` blocks are not yet stable. How would you limit the reach of
>    `?` to part of a function today, and what are the trade-offs of each option?
>    (Hint: which constructs define their own return target?)

<a id="72-unrecoverable-errors"></a>
### 7.2 Unrecoverable Errors

Some failures are not the caller's to handle, because they mean the program itself
is wrong. This section covers how Rust stops a thread in a controlled way when
that happens, the tools that trigger such a stop on purpose, and how to diagnose
and contain them.

#### panic! and Abort vs Unwind

A `Result` is for failures that are part of normal operation: a missing file, bad
user input, a dropped connection. Other failures indicate a **bug**: an index past
the end of a vector, an invariant that should be impossible to break, a state the
code was never designed for. Continuing after such a failure would mean computing
with values the program can no longer reason about, which risks corrupting data
or producing wrong answers silently. Returning a `Result` would not help either,
since no caller can meaningfully "handle" a bug in the code it called.

For these cases Rust **panics**. If `Result` is a courier handing back a parcel
marked "could not deliver", a panic is pulling the fire alarm: normal work stops,
and the building is evacuated in an orderly way.

Panics come from explicit `panic!("...")` calls and from many standard operations:
`unwrap`/`expect` on a failure, out-of-bounds indexing, division by zero, integer
overflow in debug builds, a second mutable borrow of a `RefCell`, and failed
assertions.

What happens next depends on the **panic strategy**:

- **Unwind** (the default). The panic message is printed by the *panic hook*.
  Then the runtime walks back up the stack, running `Drop` for every live value
  (closing files, releasing locks, flushing buffers) until it reaches the top of
  the thread. If that thread is `main`, the process exits with status 101. If it
  is a spawned thread, only that thread dies: `JoinHandle::join` returns `Err`, and
  other threads keep running. A `Mutex` held by the dying thread is marked
  *poisoned*, so other threads learn that the data it protects may be
  inconsistent.
- **Abort**. The panic message is printed, then the process terminates
  immediately. No destructors run, and no thread survives.

A panic that starts while another panic is already unwinding (for instance, a
`Drop` implementation that panics during unwinding) always aborts, because two
unwinds cannot proceed through one stack at the same time.

```text
   unwind (default)                          abort
   ----------------                          -----
   main()     drop(locals)  <--+             main()
    parse()   drop(locals)  <--+              parse()
     panic!("bad") --unwinds---+               panic!("bad") --> process ends now
   thread ends; for main, exit 101           no destructors run; SIGABRT on Unix
```

```rust
use std::thread;

struct Guard(&'static str);

impl Drop for Guard {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.0);          // runs during unwinding
    }
}

fn inner() {
    let _g = Guard("inner");
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let i = v.len();
    println!("{}", v[i]);                     // index out of bounds: panics
}

fn main() {
    let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
        let _g = Guard("outer");
        inner();
        println!("never printed");
    });

    let result = handle.join();               // the panic stops at the thread boundary
    println!("worker panicked: {}", result.is_err());
    println!("main continues");
}
// thread '<unnamed>' (2817) panicked at src/main.rs:15:21:
// index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3
// note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
// drop inner
// drop outer
// worker panicked: true
// main continues
```

The strategy is selected per profile in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[profile.release]
panic = "abort"     # smaller binary, no unwinding machinery, no catch_unwind
```

|                                    | Unwind (default)                    | Abort                                      |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Destructors run                    | Yes                                 | No                                         |
| Other threads survive              | Yes                                 | No, the whole process ends                 |
| Can be caught (`join`, `catch_unwind`) | Yes                             | No                                         |
| Binary size                        | Larger (unwind tables, landing pads) | Smaller                                   |
| Exit status (Unix)                 | 101 when `main` panics              | Killed by `SIGABRT` (shell shows 134)      |
| Typical use                        | Most applications and libraries     | Embedded, size-sensitive binaries, services that prefer to crash and restart |

The decision rule between the two mechanisms is short: **return a `Result` when
the failure is something the caller could reasonably expect and handle; panic
when it can only mean a bug**. A library should almost never panic on input it
received from its caller, unless the documentation states a precondition (for
example, `slice::chunks` panics if the chunk size is zero) under a `# Panics`
heading.

> Key Takeaways
> - Panics are for bugs and broken invariants; `Result` is for expected failures.
> - By default a panic unwinds: destructors run, the thread ends, and a panic in
>   `main` exits with status 101.
> - A panicking spawned thread does not take down the process; `join` reports it.
> - `panic = "abort"` skips unwinding entirely: smaller binaries, but no cleanup
>   and no recovery.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Spawn three threads, one of which panics. Join all of them and print which
>    succeeded and which panicked.
> 2. Build the example above with `panic = "abort"` in the profile you run, then
>    compare the output and the exit status (`echo $?`) with the default.
> 3. Interview: Why does a panic that occurs during unwinding (for example, in a
>    `Drop` implementation) abort the process instead of continuing to unwind?
>    (Hint: what would the runtime have to track if two panics were in flight on
>    one stack?)

#### unwrap and expect

`unwrap` and `expect` turn a recoverable error into an unrecoverable one. On `Ok`
or `Some` they return the value; on `Err` or `None` they panic. `unwrap` prints a
generic message plus the error's `Debug` output; `expect(msg)` prints your message
first. Calling either is a *claim*: "if this fails, it is a bug, not a situation
the program should handle".

That claim is legitimately true in several situations:

- **Tests and examples**, where a panic is exactly the failure report you want.
- **Prototypes**, where error handling comes later. Searching for `unwrap` is
  then the to-do list for hardening.
- **Invariants the compiler cannot see**: parsing a string literal that you
  wrote, compiling a constant regular expression, or `Mutex::lock().unwrap()`,
  which only fails if another thread already panicked while holding the lock.
- **Values just checked**, although restructuring the code to avoid the separate
  check (with `if let` or `let-else`) is usually better.

Prefer `expect` over `unwrap` when the reason is not obvious. Write the message
as the *expectation that was violated*, ideally with "should": `expect("PORT
should be set by the launcher")`. The resulting panic then reads as a diagnosis
instead of a shrug.

Both methods are marked `#[track_caller]`, so the panic location reported is the
line in *your* code that called `unwrap`, not a line inside the standard library.
You can put the same attribute on your own helper functions that panic.

```rust
use std::net::IpAddr;

#[track_caller]
fn must_be_positive(n: i32) -> i32 {
    if n <= 0 {
        panic!("expected a positive number, got {n}");   // location reported: the caller
    }
    n
}

fn main() {
    // A hard-coded literal: failure would be a typo in this file, i.e. a bug
    let localhost: IpAddr = "127.0.0.1".parse().expect("hard-coded IP should be valid");
    println!("{localhost}");                                  // 127.0.0.1

    let n: i32 = "42".parse().unwrap();
    println!("{}", must_be_positive(n));                      // 42

    // When failure is expected, do not panic: use a fallback or propagate
    let port: u16 = "http".parse().unwrap_or(80);
    println!("{port}");                                       // 80

    let r = "300".parse::<u8>();
    // r.unwrap() would panic with:
    //   called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: PosOverflow }
    // r.expect("byte value should fit in u8") would panic with:
    //   byte value should fit in u8: ParseIntError { kind: PosOverflow }
    println!("{}", r.is_err());                               // true

    must_be_positive(-1);
    // thread 'main' (2817) panicked at src/main.rs:30:5:   <- this line, not the panic! line
    // expected a positive number, got -1
}
```

| Instead of `unwrap()`      | Use                          | Effect                                   |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| When the caller can handle | `?`                          | Propagate the error                      |
| When a default exists      | `unwrap_or(v)`, `unwrap_or_default()` | Substitute a value              |
| When the default is costly | `unwrap_or_else(f)`          | Compute a value only on failure          |
| When it truly is a bug     | `expect("why it should hold")` | Still panics, with a useful message    |
| To ban it in a codebase    | Clippy `unwrap_used`, `expect_used` | Lint every occurrence             |

There is also `unwrap_unchecked`, an `unsafe` method that skips the check
entirely. Calling it on `None` or `Err` is undefined behavior, so it is reserved
for proven hot paths (Chapter 14).

> Key Takeaways
> - `unwrap` and `expect` convert a failure into a panic, asserting that the
>   failure would be a bug.
> - Appropriate in tests, prototypes, and for invariants the compiler cannot
>   verify; inappropriate for anything that depends on external input.
> - Prefer `expect` with a message describing the violated expectation.
> - `#[track_caller]` makes a panic report the caller's location; use it on your
>   own panicking helpers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a short program with several `unwrap` calls and classify each as a
>    justified invariant or as something to replace with `?` or a fallback. Fix
>    the latter.
> 2. Write a helper `fn env_var(name: &str) -> String` that panics with a helpful
>    message when the variable is missing. Compare the reported location with and
>    without `#[track_caller]`.
> 3. Interview: "`unwrap` should never appear in production code." Argue both for
>    and against this rule. (Hint: consider `Mutex::lock`, string literals, and
>    what the alternative return type would force on every caller.)

#### Assertions

An **invariant** is a condition that must hold whenever the code is correct: a
slice handed to binary search is sorted, a balance is never negative, a computed
index is within bounds. When an invariant silently breaks, the symptom usually
appears much later and far away, as corrupted data or a wrong result. An
**assertion** checks the invariant at the point where it matters and panics
immediately if it does not hold, catching the bug close to its cause. Assertions
also double as executable documentation: they tell the reader what the author
believed to be true.

Rust's assertion macros all panic on failure:

- `assert!(cond, "fmt", args..)` checks a boolean condition.
- `assert_eq!(a, b)` and `assert_ne!(a, b)` compare two values and print both
  (with `Debug`) on failure, which makes them far more informative than
  `assert!(a == b)`.
- `debug_assert!`, `debug_assert_eq!`, and `debug_assert_ne!` are identical but
  compiled only when `debug_assertions` is enabled, which it is in the dev
  profile and not in release. Use them for checks too expensive to run in
  production.
- `unreachable!()` marks a branch that should never execute.
- `todo!()` marks unfinished code; `unimplemented!()` marks functionality that is
  intentionally not provided. Both have type `!`, so they satisfy any return
  type during development.
- `const _: () = assert!(...);` evaluates an assertion at compile time, turning a
  broken invariant into a build failure.

Assertions guard against **programmer** errors, never **user** errors. Input from
a file, a network, or a person must be validated with `Result`, because invalid
input is an expected situation, not a bug.

```rust
use std::cmp::Ordering;

/// Returns the index of `target` in a sorted slice.
fn binary_search(sorted: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<usize> {
    // O(n) precondition check: worth it during development, too slow for release
    debug_assert!(sorted.is_sorted(), "input must be sorted: {sorted:?}");

    let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0, sorted.len());
    while lo < hi {
        let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        match sorted[mid].cmp(&target) {
            Ordering::Less => lo = mid + 1,
            Ordering::Greater => hi = mid,
            Ordering::Equal => return Some(mid),
        }
    }
    None
}

fn percent(part: u32, whole: u32) -> u32 {
    assert!(whole > 0, "whole must be non-zero (part = {part})");   // cheap: always on
    part * 100 / whole
}

fn bucket(n: u8) -> &'static str {
    match n % 3 {
        0 => "zero",
        1 | 2 => "nonzero",
        _ => unreachable!("n % 3 is always below 3"),   // the compiler cannot prove it
    }
}

// Compile-time assertion: a violation fails the build, not the program
const BUFFER_SIZE: usize = 64;
const _: () = assert!(BUFFER_SIZE.is_power_of_two());

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", binary_search(&[1, 3, 5, 7], 5));   // Some(2)
    println!("{}", percent(1, 4));                       // 25
    println!("{}", bucket(4));                           // nonzero
    assert_eq!(percent(1, 2), 50, "half should be 50%");

    assert_eq!(percent(1, 3), 34);
    // thread 'main' (2817) panicked at src/main.rs:43:5:
    // assertion `left == right` failed
    //   left: 33
    //  right: 34
}
```

| Macro                         | Active in release | Purpose                                    |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `assert!`                     | Yes               | Cheap invariants and preconditions         |
| `assert_eq!` / `assert_ne!`   | Yes               | Equality checks that print both values     |
| `debug_assert!` family        | No                | Expensive checks during development        |
| `unreachable!`                | Yes               | Branches that cannot logically execute     |
| `todo!`                       | Yes               | Placeholder for unfinished code            |
| `unimplemented!`              | Yes               | Deliberately unsupported functionality     |
| `const _: () = assert!(..)`   | Compile time      | Invariants over constants and types        |

A related setting is `overflow-checks`: integer overflow panics in debug builds
and wraps silently in release. If the correctness of your program depends on
detecting overflow, use `checked_add` and friends, which return `Option`, rather
than relying on the debug-only panic.

> Key Takeaways
> - Assertions check invariants and panic as close to the bug as possible.
> - `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` print both values; prefer them to `assert!(a == b)`.
> - `debug_assert!` checks are removed from release builds; never rely on them for
>   memory safety.
> - Validate external input with `Result`; reserve assertions for programmer errors.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn merge_sorted(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` with
>    `debug_assert!` checks that both inputs are sorted. Call it with unsorted
>    input in a debug build and in a release build, and compare.
> 2. Add a compile-time assertion that a struct of yours is at most 16 bytes,
>    using `std::mem::size_of`.
> 3. Interview: Why must a check that protects memory safety in `unsafe` code use
>    `assert!` rather than `debug_assert!`? (Hint: what remains of the check in a
>    release build, and what does the `unsafe` code then do with invalid input?)

#### Backtraces

A panic message tells you *where* the panic happened, but not *how execution got
there*. When an `unwrap` inside a helper fails and that helper is called from
thirty places, the location alone is not enough. A **backtrace** is the list of
stack frames that were active at the moment of the panic: the full call chain,
from the panicking function back to `main`.

Rust captures and prints a backtrace on panic when the `RUST_BACKTRACE`
environment variable is set:

- `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` prints a *short* backtrace, trimmed to the frames between
  the runtime's entry point and the panic machinery.
- `RUST_BACKTRACE=full` prints every frame, including runtime internals.

Read a backtrace from the top (innermost frame) downward and look for the first
frame that belongs to your crate. File and line numbers appear only if the binary
has debug information: dev builds include it, release builds do not by default.
Setting `debug = "line-tables-only"` in the release profile adds file and line
information at a modest size cost. Given this program in a crate named `demo`:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn lookup(map: &HashMap<&str, i32>, key: &str) -> i32 {
    *map.get(key).unwrap()                     // line 4: panics on a missing key
}

fn main() {
    lookup(&HashMap::new(), "missing");        // line 8
}
```

```text
$ RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo run
thread 'main' (33491) panicked at src/main.rs:4:19:
called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
stack backtrace:
   0: __rustc::rust_begin_unwind               \
             at .../std/src/panicking.rs:679:5  |
   1: core::panicking::panic_fmt                |  panic machinery
   2: core::panicking::panic                    |  (std and core)
   3: core::option::unwrap_failed               |
   4: <core::option::Option<&i32>>::unwrap     /
   5: demo::lookup                              <- first frame in your code
             at ./src/main.rs:4:19
   6: demo::main                                <- who called it
             at ./src/main.rs:8:5
   7: <fn() as core::ops::function::FnOnce<()>>::call_once
note: Some details are omitted, run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=full` for a verbose backtrace.
```

Backtraces are useful for *errors*, not just panics. `std::backtrace::Backtrace`
lets an error value record where it was created:

- `Backtrace::capture()` respects the environment and is a cheap no-op unless
  backtraces are enabled. `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE` controls it independently of panics
  (for example, `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0` with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` keeps panic
  backtraces but disables error captures); if it is unset, `RUST_BACKTRACE`
  applies.
- `Backtrace::force_capture()` always walks the stack, which is expensive; use it
  sparingly, such as in a panic hook.
- `status()` reports whether a capture actually happened.

```rust
use std::backtrace::{Backtrace, BacktraceStatus};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct TracedError {
    message: String,
    backtrace: Backtrace,                     // where the error was created
}

fn deep_failure() -> Result<(), TracedError> {
    Err(TracedError {
        message: "disk quota exceeded".to_string(),
        backtrace: Backtrace::capture(),      // no-op unless enabled by the environment
    })
}

fn main() {
    // A panic hook that always logs a backtrace, regardless of RUST_BACKTRACE
    std::panic::set_hook(Box::new(|info| {
        let trace = Backtrace::force_capture();
        eprintln!("FATAL: {info}\n{trace}");
    }));

    if let Err(e) = deep_failure() {
        println!("error: {}", e.message);
        match e.backtrace.status() {
            BacktraceStatus::Captured => println!("created at:\n{}", e.backtrace),
            BacktraceStatus::Disabled => println!("(set RUST_BACKTRACE=1 to see where)"),
            _ => println!("(backtraces are not supported on this platform)"),
        }
    }
    // Without the environment variable:
    // error: disk quota exceeded
    // (set RUST_BACKTRACE=1 to see where)
}
```

| Environment                                  | Panic prints backtrace | `Backtrace::capture()` |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Neither variable set                         | No                     | Disabled               |
| `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`                           | Yes, short             | Captured               |
| `RUST_BACKTRACE=full`                        | Yes, every frame       | Captured               |
| `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`, `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`   | Yes, short             | Disabled               |
| `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1` only                  | No                     | Captured               |

> Key Takeaways
> - A backtrace shows the call chain that led to a panic; enable it with
>   `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` or `full`.
> - Look for the first frame in your own crate; file and line numbers need debug
>   information (`debug = "line-tables-only"` in release).
> - `Backtrace::capture()` lets error values record their origin at no cost when
>   disabled.
> - `force_capture()` is expensive; reserve it for rare paths such as panic hooks.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a three-level call chain that ends in `unwrap()` on `None`. Run it with
>    `RUST_BACKTRACE` unset, set to `1`, and set to `full`, and locate your frames.
> 2. Build the same program in release mode with and without
>    `debug = "line-tables-only"` and compare the backtraces.
> 3. Interview: Why would capturing a backtrace in every error value on a hot path
>    be a problem, and how does the standard library let you avoid the cost?
>    (Hint: what does `capture()` do when the environment variables are unset?)

#### catch_unwind

With the unwind strategy, a panic travels up to the boundary of its thread and
stops there. Sometimes you need such a boundary *without* spawning a thread:

- **FFI boundaries.** A panic must never unwind out of a Rust function into C
  code. Since Rust 1.81, a panic escaping an `extern "C"` function aborts the
  process, so the function should catch the panic and return an error code
  instead.
- **Hosts that run untrusted or independent units**, such as a plugin system, a
  thread pool, or a request handler, where a bug in one unit should not take the
  others down.
- **Test harnesses**, which run each test and report a panic as a failure.

`std::panic::catch_unwind(closure)` runs the closure and returns `Ok(value)` if
it finished normally, or `Err(payload)` if it panicked. It is **not** a general
try/catch mechanism, and it is not meant for ordinary error handling:

- It does nothing under `panic = "abort"`; the process ends regardless.
- The payload is a `Box<dyn Any + Send>`, usually holding a `&'static str` (from
  `panic!("literal")`) or a `String` (from a formatted message), so you downcast
  it to read the message.
- The panic hook still runs, so the message is still printed unless you replace
  the hook with `set_hook` (and restore it with `take_hook`).
- `resume_unwind(payload)` re-raises a caught panic.

The closure must be `UnwindSafe`. A panic can interrupt code halfway through an
update, leaving data it was mutating in an inconsistent state. Types through
which such half-finished state could be observed afterwards, such as `&mut T` or
`&RefCell<T>`, are not `UnwindSafe`. Wrapping the closure in `AssertUnwindSafe`
tells the compiler you have considered that risk. This is a guardrail against
*logic* bugs, not a memory-safety guarantee, which is why `AssertUnwindSafe` is a
safe wrapper.

```rust
use std::any::Any;
use std::panic::{self, AssertUnwindSafe};

fn risky(n: i32) -> i32 {
    if n < 0 {
        panic!("negative input: {n}");
    }
    n * 2
}

fn panic_message(payload: &(dyn Any + Send)) -> &str {
    if let Some(s) = payload.downcast_ref::<&'static str>() {
        s                                         // from panic!("literal")
    } else if let Some(s) = payload.downcast_ref::<String>() {
        s                                         // from panic!("formatted {x}")
    } else {
        "unknown panic payload"
    }
}

// An FFI entry point: a panic must not escape into the C caller
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn double_checked(n: i32, out: &mut i32) -> i32 {
    match panic::catch_unwind(|| risky(n)) {
        Ok(v) => {
            *out = v;
            0                                     // success code
        }
        Err(_) => -1,                             // error code instead of unwinding
    }
}

fn main() {
    panic::set_hook(Box::new(|_| {}));           // silence the default panic message

    let ok = panic::catch_unwind(|| risky(21));
    println!("{ok:?}");                           // Ok(42)

    let err = panic::catch_unwind(|| risky(-1));
    if let Err(payload) = &err {
        println!("caught: {}", panic_message(payload.as_ref()));  // caught: negative input: -1
    }

    // A closure capturing &mut is not UnwindSafe; we must assert we accept the risk
    let mut log = Vec::new();
    let r = panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
        log.push("started");
        risky(-5);
        log.push("finished");                     // never runs
    }));
    println!("{} {:?}", r.is_err(), log);         // true ["started"]  (half-updated state)

    let mut out = 0;
    println!("{}", double_checked(-3, &mut out)); // -1

    let _ = panic::take_hook();                   // restore the default hook
}
```

| Appropriate                                     | Not appropriate                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Converting panics into error codes at FFI edges | Ordinary error handling (use `Result`)           |
| Isolating plugins, jobs, or requests in a host  | Recovering from expected failures                |
| Test frameworks and harnesses                   | Code built with `panic = "abort"`                |
| Logging a panic before re-raising it            | Hiding bugs by ignoring the payload              |

A related safety net is **mutex poisoning**: if a thread panics while holding a
`Mutex`, later calls to `lock()` return `Err(PoisonError)`. The data is still
reachable through `PoisonError::into_inner`, but the error forces you to decide
whether a half-finished update is acceptable (Chapter 10).

> Key Takeaways
> - `catch_unwind` stops an unwinding panic at a boundary you choose and returns
>   it as `Err(payload)`.
> - Use it at FFI boundaries and in hosts that isolate independent units, not as
>   a substitute for `Result`.
> - It cannot catch anything under `panic = "abort"`, and the panic hook still
>   runs.
> - `UnwindSafe` warns about observing half-updated state; `AssertUnwindSafe`
>   acknowledges the risk explicitly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a job runner that executes a `Vec<Box<dyn Fn() -> i32>>`, each under
>    `catch_unwind`, and reports either the result or the panic message for every
>    job.
> 2. Build the job runner with `panic = "abort"` and observe what happens when the
>    first job panics.
> 3. Interview: Why does `catch_unwind` require `UnwindSafe`, and why is
>    `AssertUnwindSafe` nevertheless safe to use? (Hint: is the danger memory
>    unsafety, or logically inconsistent data?)

<a id="73-custom-error-types"></a>
### 7.3 Custom Error Types

A `String` is the quickest way to describe an error, but callers cannot match on
it, cannot get at its cause, and cannot treat it uniformly with other errors.
This section covers the standard trait that unifies error types, the conversions
that make `?` work across them, and the crates that remove the boilerplate.

#### Implementing std::error::Error

Error types come from everywhere: the standard library (`io::Error`,
`ParseIntError`), third-party crates, and your own code. Without a shared
interface, generic code such as a logger, an error reporter, or `Box<dyn Error>`
could do nothing with them. `std::error::Error` is that interface. It says that
an error can be:

- shown to a person, through `Display`;
- inspected by a developer, through `Debug`;
- asked for the lower-level error that caused it, through `source()`.

Simplified, the trait looks like this:

```rust
pub trait Error: Debug + Display {
    // The lower-level error that caused this one, if any
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        None
    }
    // description() and cause() also exist but are deprecated
}
```

`Debug` and `Display` are supertraits, so you implement them first; `source` has
a default, so for an error without an underlying cause the `Error` impl itself is
empty. Since Rust 1.81 the trait also lives in `core::error`, so `no_std` crates
can implement it.

The Rust API guidelines give conventions for the `Display` message, which
standard library errors follow:

- lowercase, without trailing punctuation: `invalid digit found in string`;
- concise, describing this error only, because the message is often embedded in
  a longer sentence (`error: ...`, `... caused by: ...`);
- no repetition of the underlying error's message when it is exposed through
  `source()` (see "Error Source Chains").

Errors with a single failure mode are usually structs; errors with several modes
are usually enums with one variant per mode.

```rust
use std::error::Error;
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);

// An enum error: one variant per way parsing can fail
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum ColorError {
    WrongLength(usize),
    BadDigit { position: usize, found: char },
}

impl fmt::Display for ColorError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ColorError::WrongLength(n) => write!(f, "expected 6 hex digits, found {n}"),
            ColorError::BadDigit { position, found } => {
                write!(f, "invalid hex digit {found:?} at position {position}")
            }
        }
    }
}

impl Error for ColorError {}            // no underlying cause: the defaults suffice

pub fn parse_hex(s: &str) -> Result<Rgb, ColorError> {
    let digits = s.strip_prefix('#').unwrap_or(s);
    if let Some((position, found)) = digits.char_indices().find(|(_, c)| !c.is_ascii_hexdigit()) {
        return Err(ColorError::BadDigit { position, found });
    }
    if digits.len() != 6 {
        return Err(ColorError::WrongLength(digits.len()));
    }
    // Every byte is now an ASCII hex digit, so slicing and parsing cannot fail
    let byte = |i: usize| u8::from_str_radix(&digits[i..i + 2], 16).unwrap();
    Ok(Rgb(byte(0), byte(2), byte(4)))
}

// Generic code that works with any error
fn report(e: &dyn Error) {
    println!("error: {e}");
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", parse_hex("#ff8800"));          // Ok(Rgb(255, 136, 0))

    let e = parse_hex("#ff88zz").unwrap_err();
    println!("{e}");                                 // invalid hex digit 'z' at position 4
    println!("{e:?}");                               // BadDigit { position: 4, found: 'z' }

    // Callers can still match on the variants
    match parse_hex("12345") {
        Err(ColorError::WrongLength(n)) => println!("length was {n}"),   // length was 5
        other => println!("{other:?}"),
    }

    // Because ColorError implements Error, it mixes with any other error type
    report(&e);                                      // error: invalid hex digit 'z' at position 4
    report(&"x".parse::<i32>().unwrap_err());        // error: invalid digit found in string
    let boxed: Box<dyn Error> = Box::new(e);
    println!("{boxed}");                             // invalid hex digit 'z' at position 4
}
```

| Part       | Audience                 | Content                                         |
| ---------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Display`  | End users, log readers   | Short, lowercase, this layer only               |
| `Debug`    | Developers               | Full structure; usually `#[derive(Debug)]`      |
| `source()` | Programs and reporters   | The underlying error, or `None`                 |

> Key Takeaways
> - `std::error::Error` is the common interface for errors: `Debug` + `Display` +
>   an optional `source()`.
> - Without an underlying cause, `impl Error for T {}` is all you need after the
>   two formatting traits.
> - Follow the conventions for `Display`: lowercase, no trailing punctuation, this
>   layer only.
> - Implementing `Error` makes your type usable with `Box<dyn Error>`, reporters,
>   and error-handling crates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `Error` for `struct TooLong { max: usize, actual: usize }` with the
>    message `input is 42 characters, limit is 32`.
> 2. Write `fn print_all(errors: &[&dyn Error])` and call it with a
>    `ParseIntError`, an `io::Error`, and an error of your own.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Error` require `Debug` and `Display` as supertraits
>    instead of leaving formatting optional? (Hint: what does code holding a
>    `Box<dyn Error>`, or `main` returning one, need to do with it?)

#### Error Conversion with From

A function that reads a file and parses its contents calls two APIs with two
different error types, `io::Error` and `ParseIntError`, but it can only return
one. Calling `map_err` on every line to wrap each error is noisy and repetitive.

Recall that `?` passes every error through `From::from` before returning it. That
is the hook: if your error type implements `From<io::Error>` and
`From<ParseIntError>`, then `?` converts both automatically, and the function body
contains no conversion code at all.

```text
   fs::read_to_string(p)?               text.parse::<u32>()?
            |                                   |
      Err(io::Error)                     Err(ParseIntError)
            |                                   |
  From<io::Error> for ConfigError   From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError
            \                                   /
             +-----> return Err(ConfigError) <-+
```

```rust
use std::fmt;
use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::num::ParseIntError;
use std::path::Path;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum ConfigError {
    Io(io::Error),
    Parse(ParseIntError),
    OutOfRange(u32),
}

impl fmt::Display for ConfigError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            ConfigError::Io(e) => write!(f, "cannot read config: {e}"),
            ConfigError::Parse(e) => write!(f, "invalid number: {e}"),
            ConfigError::OutOfRange(n) => write!(f, "{n} workers is outside 1..=64"),
        }
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {}

// One impl per source error type; ? will call them automatically
impl From<io::Error> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: io::Error) -> Self {
        ConfigError::Io(e)
    }
}

impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self {
        ConfigError::Parse(e)
    }
}

fn read_workers(path: &Path) -> Result<u32, ConfigError> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;          // io::Error -> ConfigError::Io
    let n: u32 = text.trim().parse()?;             // ParseIntError -> ConfigError::Parse
    if n == 0 || n > 64 {
        return Err(ConfigError::OutOfRange(n));    // constructed directly
    }
    Ok(n)
}

fn main() {
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("workers.txt");
    for content in ["8", "eight", "500"] {
        fs::write(&path, content).unwrap();
        match read_workers(&path) {
            Ok(n) => println!("workers = {n}"),
            Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
        }
    }
    // workers = 8
    // error: invalid number: invalid digit found in string
    // error: 500 workers is outside 1..=64

    if let Err(e) = read_workers(Path::new("/no/such/file")) {
        println!("error: {e}");   // error: cannot read config: No such file or directory (os error 2)
    }

    // Implementing From also gives you Into for free
    let e: ConfigError = "x".parse::<u32>().unwrap_err().into();
    println!("{}", matches!(e, ConfigError::Parse(_)));   // true
}
```

`From` is the right tool when one source type always maps to one variant with no
extra information. Reach for `map_err` instead when:

- the **same** source type must map to **different** variants depending on the
  call (reading the input file versus writing the output file are both
  `io::Error`, but they are different failures; a type can have only one
  `From<io::Error>` impl);
- you want to attach **context** that only the call site knows, such as the file
  path (see "Adding Context" in Section 7.4);
- the conversion would expose a dependency's error type through a public `From`
  impl, making it part of your API.

The orphan rule also applies: you can implement `From<io::Error>` for *your*
type, but not `From<io::Error>` for `ParseIntError`, since both are foreign.

|                     | `impl From`                         | `map_err` at the call site               |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Written             | Once per source type                | At every call                            |
| Context added       | None; it only wraps                 | Anything visible at the call site        |
| Variant choice      | Fixed: one variant per source type  | Free: any variant per call               |
| Call-site noise     | None: plain `?`                     | One closure or function per call         |

> Key Takeaways
> - `?` calls `From::from` on the error, so implementing `From<SourceError>` for
>   your type makes conversion automatic.
> - Implementing `From` also provides the matching `Into`.
> - Use `map_err` when the same source type maps to different variants or needs
>   call-site context.
> - Conversions must target a type you own; the orphan rule forbids
>   foreign-to-foreign impls.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `From<std::str::Utf8Error>` impl to `ConfigError`, then change
>    `read_workers` to use `fs::read` followed by `std::str::from_utf8`.
> 2. Design an error with `ReadInput(io::Error)` and `WriteOutput(io::Error)`
>    variants. Explain why `From` cannot express this and implement the function
>    with `map_err`.
> 3. Interview: `?` calls `From::from` even when the error types are already
>    identical. Why does that cost nothing and compile at all? (Hint: look for a
>    blanket `impl<T> From<T> for T` in the standard library.)

#### Boxed Trait Object Errors

Defining an enum, a `Display` impl, an `Error` impl, and several `From` impls is
worthwhile for a library, but heavy for a script, a prototype, a test, or the
`main` function of a small tool. In those places you often do not care *which*
error occurred, only that something failed and what the message was.

`Box<dyn Error>` is a type that can hold *any* error. The standard library
provides a blanket `impl<E: Error> From<E> for Box<dyn Error>`, so `?` converts
every error type into it automatically. It also implements `From<&str>` and
`From<String>`, so ad-hoc errors are one `.into()` away.

Two variations are common:

- `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` can cross thread boundaries and be used with
  async runtimes. Libraries that box errors usually choose this form.
- A type alias keeps signatures short:
  `type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>;`

The concrete type is not lost, only hidden: `downcast_ref::<T>()` recovers it at
runtime when you do need to branch on it.

```rust
use std::error::Error;
use std::fs;
use std::io;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

type BoxResult<T> = Result<T, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>;

fn average_from(text: &str) -> BoxResult<f64> {
    let mut total = 0i64;
    let mut count = 0;
    for line in text.lines() {
        total += line.trim().parse::<i64>()?;    // ParseIntError -> Box<dyn Error ...>
        count += 1;
    }
    if count == 0 {
        return Err("no numbers in input".into()); // &str -> Box<dyn Error ...>
    }
    Ok(total as f64 / count as f64)
}

fn average_of_file(path: &str) -> BoxResult<f64> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;        // io::Error -> Box<dyn Error ...>
    average_from(&text)
}

fn main() -> BoxResult<()> {
    println!("{}", average_from("1\n2\n6")?);    // 3

    let attempts = [average_from(""), average_from("1\nx"), average_of_file("/missing")];
    for result in attempts {
        let err = result.unwrap_err();
        // Recover the concrete type at runtime when you need to branch on it
        if let Some(pe) = err.downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>() {
            println!("parse error: {pe}");
        } else if let Some(ioe) = err.downcast_ref::<io::Error>() {
            println!("io error ({:?}): {ioe}", ioe.kind());
        } else {
            println!("other: {err}");
        }
    }
    // other: no numbers in input
    // parse error: invalid digit found in string
    // io error (NotFound): No such file or directory (os error 2)

    // Errors that are Send + Sync can travel back from another thread
    let handle = std::thread::spawn(|| average_from("4\n8"));
    println!("{:?}", handle.join().unwrap().ok());   // Some(6.0)
    Ok(())
}
```

One surprise: `Box<dyn Error>` does **not** itself implement `Error`. If it did,
the blanket `From<E: Error>` impl would overlap with the reflexive
`From<T> for T` impl when `E` is `Box<dyn Error>`. As a result, you cannot pass a
`Box<dyn Error>` to a function that requires `E: Error`. It also means `?` cannot
convert a `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` into a plain `Box<dyn Error>` (E0277),
so pick one boxed form and use it consistently. Both limitations are gaps that
`anyhow::Error` fills.

|                     | Custom enum                          | `Box<dyn Error>`                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Callers can match   | Yes, exhaustively                    | Only by downcasting at runtime            |
| Boilerplate         | `Display`, `Error`, `From` impls     | None                                      |
| Cost per error      | None beyond the value                | One heap allocation                       |
| Signature says      | Exactly which failures are possible  | "Something can fail"                      |
| Best for            | Libraries, errors callers act on     | Applications, prototypes, tests, `main`   |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Box<dyn Error>` holds any error, and `?` converts into it automatically.
> - `"message".into()` creates an ad-hoc boxed error from a string.
> - Add `+ Send + Sync` so errors can cross threads and async tasks.
> - `downcast_ref` recovers the concrete type; exhaustive matching is lost.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` that reads two numbers from
>    command-line arguments and divides them, reporting division by zero with a
>    string error.
> 2. Change `BoxResult` to drop `+ Send + Sync` and read the compiler error for
>    the `thread::spawn` call. Explain it.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Box<dyn Error>` not implement `Error`, and what practical
>    limitation results? (Hint: if it did, which two `From` impls would apply to
>    converting a `Box<dyn Error>` into a `Box<dyn Error>`?)

#### Error Source Chains

Failures happen in layers. A server fails to start because the configuration
could not be loaded, because the file could not be read, because permission was
denied. Each layer adds meaning: the bottom one knows the precise technical
reason, the top one knows what the user was trying to do. Collapsing everything
into one string loses the structure; keeping only the top error loses the cause.

`Error::source()` links the layers into a **chain**, much like a linked list:
each error points to the one beneath it, and the bottom one returns `None`. A
reporter walks the chain from top to bottom and prints each message once.

```text
   StartupError     Display: "failed to start server"
        | source()
        v
   ConfigError      Display: "could not read config file /etc/app.toml"
        | source()
        v
   io::Error        Display: "permission denied"
        | source()
        v
      None
```

The essential rule: **each error's `Display` describes only its own layer; the
cause is reachable through `source()`, not repeated in the message.** If a layer
does both, every reporter that walks the chain prints the cause twice.

```rust
use std::error::Error;
use std::fmt;
use std::io;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct ConfigError {
    path: String,
    source: io::Error,
}

impl fmt::Display for ConfigError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "could not read config file {}", self.path)   // this layer only
    }
}

impl Error for ConfigError {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        Some(&self.source)                                      // link to the cause
    }
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct StartupError {
    source: ConfigError,
}

impl fmt::Display for StartupError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str("failed to start server")
    }
}

impl Error for StartupError {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        Some(&self.source)
    }
}

fn load_config(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigError> {
    // Simulate a permission failure so the example is deterministic
    Err(ConfigError {
        path: path.to_string(),
        source: io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied, "permission denied"),
    })
}

fn start() -> Result<(), StartupError> {
    load_config("/etc/app.toml").map_err(|source| StartupError { source })?;
    Ok(())
}

// Walk the chain: a small version of what anyhow and eyre do for you
fn report(err: &dyn Error) -> String {
    let mut out = format!("error: {err}");
    let mut current = err.source();
    while let Some(cause) = current {
        out.push_str(&format!("\n  caused by: {cause}"));
        current = cause.source();
    }
    out
}

// The same walk as an iterator over every link, starting with `err` itself
fn chain<'a>(err: &'a (dyn Error + 'static)) -> impl Iterator<Item = &'a (dyn Error + 'static)> {
    std::iter::successors(Some(err), |&e| e.source())   // |&e| copies the inner reference
}

fn main() {
    let err = start().unwrap_err();
    println!("{}", report(&err));
    // error: failed to start server
    //   caused by: could not read config file /etc/app.toml
    //   caused by: permission denied

    println!("{} levels", chain(&err).count());          // 3 levels

    // Find the root cause and inspect its concrete type
    let root = chain(&err).last().unwrap();
    if let Some(io_err) = root.downcast_ref::<io::Error>() {
        println!("root kind: {:?}", io_err.kind());      // root kind: PermissionDenied
    }
}
```

| Design                          | `Display`                 | `source()`     | Reporter output                       |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Wrap and expose (recommended)   | Own layer only            | `Some(inner)`  | Each message exactly once             |
| Wrap and inline                 | `"own: {inner}"`          | `None`         | Readable, but tools cannot walk it    |
| Both (wrong)                    | `"own: {inner}"`          | `Some(inner)`  | Inner message printed twice           |

`source()` returns `&(dyn Error + 'static)` rather than a plain `&dyn Error`
because downcasting relies on `TypeId`, which only exists for `'static` types.
Errors that borrow data cannot be downcast, so the chain is restricted to owned
errors.

> Key Takeaways
> - `source()` links an error to its cause, forming a chain that ends in `None`.
> - Each `Display` describes its own layer; the cause belongs in `source()`, never
>   in both places.
> - Walk the chain with a loop or `std::iter::successors` to report every layer or
>   find the root cause.
> - Chained errors are `'static`, which is what makes `downcast_ref` possible on
>   any link.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a third wrapper layer, `ServiceError`, around `StartupError` and confirm
>    that `report` prints four lines with no duplicated text.
> 2. Write `fn root_cause(e: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> &(dyn Error + 'static)`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `source()` return `&(dyn Error + 'static)` instead of
>    `&dyn Error`? (Hint: what does `downcast_ref` need in order to compare
>    types at runtime?)

#### thiserror and anyhow

The previous topics wrote `Display`, `Error`, `source`, and `From` by hand: about
thirty lines of mechanical code per error type. Two crates by David Tolnay
remove that boilerplate, and they solve *different* problems:

- **`thiserror`** is for **defining** error types. Its derive macro generates
  exactly the impls you would write by hand, so there is no runtime cost and
  nothing of `thiserror` appears in your public API: switching back to
  hand-written impls later is not a breaking change.
- **`anyhow`** is for **handling and reporting** errors in applications. It
  provides a single opaque type, `anyhow::Error`, similar to
  `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>` but only one pointer wide, with
  built-in context messages, chain printing, and backtrace capture.

```toml
[dependencies]
thiserror = "2"
anyhow = "1"
```

| `thiserror` attribute                      | Generates                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `#[error("... {field} ... {0}")]`          | `Display`, with access to fields                       |
| `#[from]` on a field                       | `From<FieldType>` and `source()` returning that field  |
| `#[source]`, or a field named `source`     | `source()` returning that field                        |
| `#[error(transparent)]`                    | Forwards `Display` and `source()` to the single inner error |

| `anyhow` item                              | Purpose                                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `anyhow::Result<T>`                        | Alias for `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`                   |
| `.context(msg)` / `.with_context(\|\| msg)` | Wrap an error (or a `None`) with a higher-level message |
| `bail!(..)`                                | `return Err(anyhow!(..))`                              |
| `ensure!(cond, ..)`                        | `bail!` unless the condition holds                     |
| `{}` / `{:#}` / `{:?}`                     | Top message / whole chain on one line / multi-line report |

They combine naturally: typed `thiserror` errors in the lower layers, where
callers might match on them, and `anyhow` at the top, where errors are only
reported.

```rust
use anyhow::{bail, ensure, Context};
use std::io;
use std::num::ParseIntError;
use thiserror::Error;

const MAX_WORKERS: u32 = 64;

// ---- typed error, defined with thiserror ----
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum ConfigError {
    #[error("could not read config file {path}")]
    Read {
        path: String,
        source: io::Error,               // a field named `source` becomes source()
    },
    #[error("invalid worker count")]
    Parse(#[from] ParseIntError),        // From<ParseIntError> + source()
    #[error("worker count {0} is outside 1..={max}", max = MAX_WORKERS)]
    OutOfRange(u32),
}

fn read_workers(path: &str) -> Result<u32, ConfigError> {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .map_err(|source| ConfigError::Read { path: path.to_string(), source })?;
    let n: u32 = text.trim().parse()?;   // uses the generated From impl
    if n == 0 || n > MAX_WORKERS {
        return Err(ConfigError::OutOfRange(n));
    }
    Ok(n)
}

// ---- application layer, using anyhow ----
fn cost_per_worker(path: &str, jobs: &[&str]) -> anyhow::Result<u32> {
    let workers = read_workers(path).context("loading settings")?;   // typed -> anyhow
    ensure!(!jobs.is_empty(), "no jobs given");
    let mut total = 0;
    for job in jobs {
        let cost: u32 = job.parse().with_context(|| format!("bad job cost {job:?}"))?;
        if cost > 1000 {
            bail!("job cost {cost} exceeds the budget");
        }
        total += cost;
    }
    Ok(total / workers)
}

fn main() {
    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("workers.cfg");
    let path = path.to_str().unwrap();
    std::fs::write(path, "4").unwrap();

    println!("{}", cost_per_worker(path, &["100", "300"]).unwrap());   // 100

    let err = cost_per_worker(path, &["100", "abc"]).unwrap_err();
    println!("{err}");      // bad job cost "abc"
    println!("{err:#}");    // bad job cost "abc": invalid digit found in string

    println!("{}", cost_per_worker(path, &[]).unwrap_err());   // no jobs given

    std::fs::write(path, "500").unwrap();
    let err = cost_per_worker(path, &["1"]).unwrap_err();
    println!("{err:#}");    // loading settings: worker count 500 is outside 1..=64

    // The typed error survives inside anyhow::Error and can be recovered
    if let Some(ConfigError::OutOfRange(n)) = err.downcast_ref::<ConfigError>() {
        println!("out of range: {n}");   // out of range: 500
    }

    let err = cost_per_worker("/no/such/file", &["1"]).unwrap_err();
    println!("{err:?}");
    // loading settings
    //
    // Caused by:
    //     0: could not read config file /no/such/file
    //     1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
}
```

The `{:?}` report is also what you see when `main` returns
`anyhow::Result<()>` and fails: `Error: ` followed by the same multi-line chain,
plus a backtrace when `RUST_BACKTRACE` or `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE` is set.

|                        | `thiserror`                          | `anyhow`                                   |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Purpose                | Define error types                   | Propagate and report errors                |
| Result                 | Your own enum or struct              | One opaque type, `anyhow::Error`           |
| Callers can match      | Yes                                  | Only by downcasting                        |
| Appears in public API  | No (derive only)                     | Yes, if used in signatures                 |
| Context                | Fields you design                    | `.context()` strings, added at any layer   |
| Typical home           | Libraries, domain modules            | Binaries, `main`, scripts, tests           |

Related crates fill neighbouring niches: `eyre` and `color-eyre` are
`anyhow`-like with customizable, colourful reports; `snafu` combines typed errors
with context selectors; `miette` produces compiler-style diagnostics with source
snippets.

> Key Takeaways
> - `thiserror` derives `Display`, `Error`, `source`, and `From` for your own types
>   with no runtime cost and no API footprint.
> - `anyhow::Error` is an opaque, context-carrying error for application code.
> - Print `anyhow` errors with `{:#}` for a one-line chain or `{:?}` for a full
>   report.
> - Typical split: `thiserror` where callers may match, `anyhow` where errors are
>   only reported.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite `ConfigError` from "Error Conversion with From" with `thiserror` and
>    check that its messages are unchanged.
> 2. Write a CLI whose `main` returns `anyhow::Result<()>`, reads a file named on
>    the command line, and adds the path as context. Run it on a missing file and
>    read the report.
> 3. Interview: Why is returning `anyhow::Error` from a public library function
>    generally discouraged, while using `thiserror` inside the same library is
>    fine? (Hint: what can a caller do with each type, and which one is visible
>    in your API?)

<a id="74-error-design-practices"></a>
### 7.4 Error Design Practices

Knowing the mechanics is not the same as designing errors well. This section
covers the decisions that shape an error type: who consumes it, how much of it to
expose, what information it should carry, and how to keep it evolvable without
breaking callers.
