| `Rc::try_unwrap(rc)` / `Rc::into_inner(rc)` | Take `T` back out if sole owner |
| `Rc<str>`, `Rc<[T]>` | Shared immutable strings and slices in one allocation |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Rc<T>` gives a value several owners by keeping a reference count next to it
>   on the heap; the value is dropped when the last `Rc` goes away.
> - `Rc::clone` increments a counter and never copies `T`; write it as
>   `Rc::clone(&x)` to make that clear.
> - An `Rc` only hands out `&T`; mutation requires interior mutability or
>   `get_mut`/`make_mut`.
> - `Rc` is single-threaded (`!Send`, `!Sync`); use `Arc` across threads.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a small graph in which nodes `B` and `C` both hold an `Rc` to node `D`,
>    and print `Rc::strong_count` for `D` after building it and after dropping
>    `B`.
> 2. Write `fn intern(words: &[&str]) -> Vec<Rc<str>>` that returns one shared
>    `Rc<str>` per distinct word, so repeated words share an allocation. Verify
>    with `Rc::ptr_eq`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Rc<T>` implement `Deref` but not `DerefMut`, and how
>    does `Rc::get_mut` safely provide `&mut T` anyway? (Hint: what does the
>    reference count tell you at the moment of the call?)

#### Weak References and Cycles

Reference counting has a famous blind spot: **cycles**. If `A` holds an `Rc` to
`B` and `B` holds an `Rc` back to `A`, each keeps the other's count above zero.
When the rest of the program drops its handles, both counts fall to 1 but never
to 0, so neither value is ever dropped. The memory leaks. Rust considers leaking
memory safe (it cannot cause undefined behavior), so the compiler will not
stop you, but in a long-running program the leak still matters.

```text
   After dropping the external handles a and b:

        +------------------+         +------------------+
        | A  strong = 1    | ------> | B  strong = 1    |
        |    next: Rc<B>   | <------ |    prev: Rc<A>   |
        +------------------+         +------------------+
     Unreachable from the program, but each count is held up by the other: leak.
```

`Weak<T>` breaks cycles. A weak reference points at the same allocation as an
`Rc` but does not count as an owner: it increments a separate **weak count**
that keeps the memory block alive but not the value inside it. Because the
value may already be gone, a `Weak` cannot be dereferenced directly. You call
`upgrade()`, which returns `Some(Rc<T>)` if the value is still alive and `None`
if it was dropped.

The analogy is a phone number versus a house key. A key (`Rc`) keeps you
entitled to the house. A phone number (`Weak`) lets you check whether someone
still lives there, and if so, ask for a temporary key, but holding the number
does not stop the house from being sold.

The design rule is to make ownership point **one way** in any structure and use
`Weak` for the back-edges:

| Relationship | Strong (`Rc`) direction | Weak direction |
| ------------ | ----------------------- | -------------- |
| Tree | Parent to children | Child to parent |
| Doubly linked list | `next` | `prev` |
| Observer pattern | Observer list held by its owner | Subject held by observers |
| Cache | The real owner of each entry | The cache's index of entries |

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Node {
    name: String,
    parent: RefCell<Weak<Node>>,            // back-edge: does not own the parent
    children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node>>>,       // forward edges: own the children
}

impl Node {
    fn new(name: &str) -> Rc<Node> {
        Rc::new(Node {
            name: name.to_string(),
            parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()),   // empty Weak, no allocation
            children: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
        })
    }

    fn add_child(parent: &Rc<Node>, child: Rc<Node>) {
        *child.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(parent);   // Rc -> Weak
        parent.children.borrow_mut().push(child);
    }

    fn path(&self) -> String {
        match self.parent.borrow().upgrade() {   // Weak -> Option<Rc>
            Some(p) => format!("{}/{}", p.path(), self.name),
            None => self.name.clone(),
        }
    }
}

impl Drop for Node {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.name);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let leaf = Node::new("main.rs");
    {
        let root = Node::new("project");
        let src = Node::new("src");
        Node::add_child(&root, Rc::clone(&src));
        Node::add_child(&src, Rc::clone(&leaf));
        println!("{}", leaf.path());        // project/src/main.rs
        println!(
            "src: strong = {}, weak = {}",
            Rc::strong_count(&src),         // 2: `src` variable + root's children
            Rc::weak_count(&src),           // 1: leaf's parent link
        );
    }   // root dropped -> "drop project", then src's last owner -> "drop src"

    // The parent is gone, and the Weak link observes that safely.
    println!("{:?}", leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade().map(|p| p.name.clone()));   // None
    println!("{}", leaf.path());            // main.rs
}   // "drop main.rs"
```

The example uses `RefCell` to fill in the links after construction (section
9.3). When a value must hold a weak reference **to itself** from birth,
`Rc::new_cyclic` hands you the `Weak` before the `Rc` exists:

```rust
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

struct Widget {
    me: Weak<Widget>,                       // lets methods produce an Rc to self
    id: u32,
}

impl Widget {
    fn handle(&self) -> Rc<Widget> {
        self.me.upgrade().expect("widget is alive while &self exists")
    }
}

fn main() {
    let w = Rc::new_cyclic(|me| Widget { me: me.clone(), id: 9 });
    let h = w.handle();
    println!("{} {}", h.id, Rc::strong_count(&w));   // 9 2
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Rc` cycles leak: each value keeps the other's strong count above zero.
>   The compiler allows this because leaks are memory-safe.
> - `Weak<T>` observes an allocation without owning the value; `upgrade()`
>   returns `None` once the value has been dropped.
> - Keep strong references pointing one way (parent to child, owner to entry)
>   and use `Weak` for back-edges.
> - The value is dropped when the strong count hits zero; the allocation itself
>   is freed only when the weak count also hits zero.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create two `Node`s that point at each other with `Rc` (no `Weak`), give
>    `Node` a `Drop` that prints, and confirm that nothing is printed when `main`
>    ends. Then fix it with `Weak`.
> 2. Build an observer pattern: a `Subject` holds `Vec<Weak<dyn Observer>>` and
>    on `notify` skips and removes observers whose `upgrade()` fails.
> 3. Interview: An `Rc<T>` allocation contains a strong count and a weak count.
>    Why can the value `T` be dropped while the allocation is still in use?
>    (Hint: consider what an outstanding `Weak` needs to read when `upgrade` is
>    called.)

#### Arc for Threads

`Rc` is fast because it cheats on one point: it assumes only one thread ever
touches the counter. If two threads cloned the same `Rc` at the same moment,
both could read count 1, both write 2, and one increment would be lost. Later
the value would be freed while one owner was still using it, which is a
use-after-free. That is why `Rc` is `!Send`: the compiler refuses to let it
cross a thread boundary at all.

`Arc<T>` (**atomically reference counted**) is the thread-safe twin. Its API is
almost identical to `Rc`, but its counters are updated with **atomic**
instructions, which the CPU guarantees are indivisible even when several cores
access the same memory. `Arc<T>` is `Send` and `Sync` when `T` is `Send + Sync`,
so you can clone it into as many threads as you like.

Like `Rc`, an `Arc` only gives shared access (`&T`). Sharing **mutable** state
across threads requires a thread-safe interior mutability type inside it, most
often `Mutex` or `RwLock`, or atomics for simple counters. Chapter 10 covers
those in depth; the pattern you will see constantly is `Arc<Mutex<T>>`.

```rust
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    // Read-only shared data: Arc alone is enough.
    let words: Arc<Vec<String>> =
        Arc::new(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"].map(String::from).to_vec());

    // Shared mutable data: Arc for ownership, Mutex for exclusive access.
    let total_len = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0usize));

    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..3 {
        let words = Arc::clone(&words);     // one owner per thread
        let total_len = Arc::clone(&total_len);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let w = &words[i];              // Deref to Vec<String>
            *total_len.lock().unwrap() += w.len();
        }));
    }
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
    println!("total = {}", total_len.lock().unwrap());   // total = 14
    println!("owners = {}", Arc::strong_count(&words));  // owners = 1 (threads done)

    // let rc = std::rc::Rc::new(5);
    // thread::spawn(move || println!("{rc}"));
    // error[E0277]: `Rc<i32>` cannot be sent between threads safely
}
```

`Arc` is not always necessary for threads. When the threads are guaranteed to
finish before the data goes out of scope, **scoped threads** (`thread::scope`,
Chapter 10) can borrow the data directly, without any reference counting:

```rust
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["alpha", "beta", "gamma"];
    let lens: Vec<usize> = thread::scope(|s| {
        let handles: Vec<_> = words
            .iter()
            .map(|w| s.spawn(move || w.len()))  // borrows `words`; no Arc needed
            .collect();
        handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).collect()
    });                                         // all threads joined here
    println!("{lens:?}");                       // [5, 4, 5]
}
```

| | `Rc<T>` | `Arc<T>` |
| - | ------- | -------- |
| Counter updates | Plain integer operations | Atomic read-modify-write |
| Thread safety | `!Send`, `!Sync` | `Send + Sync` if `T: Send + Sync` |
| Clone cost | About a nanosecond | Higher, and much higher under contention |
| Weak variant | `std::rc::Weak` | `std::sync::Weak` |
| Typical pairing | `Rc<RefCell<T>>` | `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, `Arc<RwLock<T>>` |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Arc<T>` is `Rc<T>` with atomic counters, which makes it safe to clone and
>   drop from many threads.
> - `Arc` alone only shares read access; combine it with `Mutex`, `RwLock`, or
>   atomics to share mutable state.
> - Use `Rc` within one thread and `Arc` only when data actually crosses
>   threads; the compiler enforces this through `Send`.
> - Scoped threads can often replace `Arc` when the data outlives the threads.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Spawn four threads that each push their index into a shared
>    `Arc<Mutex<Vec<usize>>>`, then print the sorted vector.
> 2. Rewrite exercise 1 with `thread::scope` and a plain `Mutex<Vec<usize>>` with
>    no `Arc`. Explain why that compiles.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Arc<T>` require `T: Send + Sync` to be `Send`, rather
>    than just `T: Send`? (Hint: after cloning, which threads can obtain a `&T`
>    at the same time, and which thread runs `T`'s destructor?)

#### Clone Cost and Trade-offs

`.clone()` hides very different costs behind one method name. Cloning a `u64`
copies eight bytes. Cloning a `Vec<String>` allocates a new buffer and a new
heap string for every element. Cloning an `Rc<Vec<String>>` increments one
integer. Cloning an `Arc` performs an atomic operation, which is cheap when
uncontended but can become a hot spot when many cores touch the same counter.
Choosing between borrowing, cloning, and reference counting is mostly a matter
of knowing these costs.

| Operation | What actually happens | Rough cost |
| --------- | --------------------- | ---------- |
| `&T` borrow | Nothing at run time | Free |
| `Copy` types (`i32`, `char`) | Bitwise copy | Free to tiny |
| `String::clone`, `Vec::clone` | Allocate and copy every byte or element | O(n) plus allocation |
| `Rc::clone` | Non-atomic increment | About 1 ns |
| `Arc::clone` | Atomic increment | Several ns; more under contention |
| `Box<T>::clone` | Allocate and clone `T` | Same as cloning `T`, plus allocation |

The trade-offs go beyond the clone itself:

- **Borrowing is the default.** If the data clearly outlives every use, take
  `&T`. It is free and makes the code's ownership obvious.
- **Cloning is often fine.** Cloning a short `String` once at startup costs
  nothing measurable and can simplify a design considerably. Clone in cold
  paths, and avoid it inside hot loops.
- **Reference counting has hidden costs.** Every `Rc`/`Arc` value is a separate
  heap allocation, every access is an extra pointer hop, and shared data is
  immutable unless you add interior mutability (with its own overhead).
- **`Rc<str>` and `Arc<str>` beat `Rc<String>`.** The former stores the bytes
  in the same allocation as the counts (one hop); the latter points to a
  `String` that points to its bytes (two hops).

`Rc::make_mut` (and `Arc::make_mut`) combines the two worlds into
**clone-on-write**: sharing is cheap, and the first writer that is not the sole
owner pays for a private copy. Persistent data structures and undo histories
use this pattern.

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct Document {
    lines: Vec<String>,
}

fn main() {
    // Snapshots share one Document until someone edits.
    let mut current = Rc::new(Document { lines: vec!["fn main() {}".into()] });
    let snapshot = Rc::clone(&current);                 // cheap: count = 2

    Rc::make_mut(&mut current).lines.push("// edited".into());
    // `current` was shared, so make_mut cloned the Document before mutating.
    println!("{} vs {}", snapshot.lines.len(), current.lines.len());   // 1 vs 2
    println!("shared? {}", Rc::ptr_eq(&snapshot, &current));         // false

    drop(snapshot);
    Rc::make_mut(&mut current).lines.push("// again".into());  // sole owner: no clone
    println!("{}", current.lines.len());                // 3

    // Arc<str>: one allocation holding counts and bytes; clones copy no text.
    let name: Arc<str> = Arc::from("service-a");
    let tags: Vec<Arc<str>> = (0..3).map(|_| Arc::clone(&name)).collect();
    println!("{} {}", tags[2], Arc::strong_count(&name));   // service-a 4
}
```

A rule of thumb for choosing ownership of shared data:

```text
   Does one owner clearly outlive every user?
     yes -> borrow (&T)
     no  -> Is the data small, or copied rarely?
              yes -> clone it
              no  -> Is it used from several threads?
                       no  -> Rc<T>   (+ RefCell for mutation)
                       yes -> Arc<T>  (+ Mutex/RwLock/atomics for mutation)
```

Clippy can help keep clone costs visible: `clippy::redundant_clone` flags clones
that are never needed, and the opt-in `clippy::clone_on_ref_ptr` lint enforces
the `Rc::clone(&x)` spelling so that cheap pointer clones are distinguishable
from deep copies in review.

> Key Takeaways
> - `.clone()` ranges from a free bitwise copy to a deep allocation; know which
>   one you are calling.
> - Prefer borrowing, accept cheap clones in cold paths, and use `Rc`/`Arc` when
>   ownership is genuinely shared.
> - Reference counting adds an allocation, a pointer hop, and immutability; it is
>   not free even though cloning the pointer is.
> - `Rc::make_mut`/`Arc::make_mut` give clone-on-write semantics, and
>   `Rc<str>`/`Arc<str>` are the efficient way to share immutable text.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that receives a `&[String]` of 100,000 names and returns the
>    ones that start with `"A"`. Implement it once returning `Vec<String>`
>    (clones) and once returning `Vec<&str>`, and compare the timings.
> 2. Implement an undo stack for a `Vec<i32>` editor using `Rc<Vec<i32>>`
>    snapshots and `Rc::make_mut`. Count how many real clones happen across ten
>    edits with an undo after every third edit.
> 3. Interview: A service clones an `Arc<Config>` on every request and
>    profiling shows that clone as a hot spot on a 64-core machine. Why, and what
>    would you change? (Hint: consider cache-line contention on the counter, and
>    whether the request needs ownership at all.)

<a id="93-interior-mutability"></a>
### 9.3 Interior Mutability

The borrow checker's "one writer or many readers" rule is checked at compile
time, so it must reject some correct programs. Chapter 3 ended with this
motivation; this section covers the types that allow mutation through a shared
reference, from the zero-cost `Cell` to the primitive they are all built on.

#### Cell

Most of the time "shared" and "immutable" go together: if you hold `&T`, you
cannot change `T`. That is usually what you want, but sometimes a value needs to
change behind a shared reference for reasons callers do not care about: a hit
counter inside a lookup method, a "dirty" flag on a cached widget, or a node id
counter shared by several builders. Making every such method take `&mut self`
would ripple through the entire API and often be impossible, because the value
is legitimately shared.

`Cell<T>` is the simplest answer. The aliasing rule exists to prevent one piece
of code from changing data while another holds a reference **into** it. `Cell`
sidesteps the danger by **never handing out references to its contents**. You
can copy the value out (`get`), put a new value in (`set`), or swap values
(`replace`, `take`, `swap`), but you can never hold a `&T` pointing inside the
cell. With no interior references in existence, a write cannot invalidate
anything, so the operations are safe through a plain `&Cell<T>`.

Think of a pigeonhole on a shared wall. Anyone can look at the note inside and
copy it down, or swap in a new note, but nobody may keep a finger pressed on the
note while somebody else is swapping it.

| Method | Requires | Effect |
| ------ | -------- | ------ |
| `get()` | `T: Copy` | Return a copy of the value |
| `set(v)` | none | Overwrite the value (dropping the old one) |
| `replace(v)` | none | Store `v`, return the old value |
| `take()` | `T: Default` | Return the value, leave `Default::default()` |
| `swap(&other)` | none | Exchange the contents of two cells |
| `get_mut()` | `&mut self` | Ordinary `&mut T` when you have exclusive access |
| `into_inner()` | ownership | Consume the cell and return the value |

`Cell` has **zero runtime overhead**: it has the same size and layout as `T`,
and `get`/`set` compile to plain loads and stores. The price is paid in
restrictions instead: no references to the inside, `get` only for `Copy` types,
and no thread safety. `Cell<T>` is `!Sync`, so a `&Cell<T>` cannot be shared
across threads (the atomic types in `std::sync::atomic` are the thread-safe
equivalent).

```rust
use std::cell::Cell;

struct Lookup {
    entries: Vec<(&'static str, u32)>,
    hits: Cell<u32>,                        // statistics, invisible to callers
    misses: Cell<u32>,
}

impl Lookup {
    // `&self`: a logically read-only operation that still updates statistics.
    fn find(&self, key: &str) -> Option<u32> {
        let found = self.entries.iter().find(|(k, _)| *k == key).map(|&(_, v)| v);
        let counter = if found.is_some() { &self.hits } else { &self.misses };
        counter.set(counter.get() + 1);     // copy out, add, copy back in
        found
    }
}

fn main() {
    let table = Lookup {
        entries: vec![("http", 80), ("https", 443)],
        hits: Cell::new(0),
        misses: Cell::new(0),
    };
    let shared_a = &table;                  // two shared references at once
    let shared_b = &table;
    shared_a.find("http");
    shared_b.find("ftp");
    shared_a.find("https");
    println!("hits {} misses {}", table.hits.get(), table.misses.get());   // hits 2 misses 1

    // Non-Copy types work too, as long as you move values in and out.
    let name = Cell::new(String::from("draft"));
    let old = name.replace(String::from("final"));    // no reference ever escapes
    println!("{old} -> {}", name.take());             // draft -> final
    println!("{:?}", name.into_inner());              // "" (Default left by take)

    println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Cell<u64>>());   // 8: same as u64
}
```

`Cell` is also useful for its conversion helpers. `Cell::from_mut(&mut v)` turns
an exclusive reference into a `&Cell<T>` you can copy freely, and
`as_slice_of_cells` turns `&Cell<[T]>` into `&[Cell<T>]`. Together they let you
mutate a slice through several aliasing references, for example while
comparing neighbors:

```rust
use std::cell::Cell;

fn main() {
    let mut data = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5];
    let cells: &[Cell<i32>] = Cell::from_mut(&mut data[..]).as_slice_of_cells();
    // Two shared references into the same slice, both allowed to write.
    for (a, b) in cells.iter().zip(&cells[1..]) {
        if a.get() > b.get() {
            a.swap(b);                      // one bubble-sort pass
        }
    }
    println!("{data:?}");                   // [1, 3, 1, 4, 5]
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `Cell<T>` allows mutation through `&Cell<T>` by never exposing references to
>   its contents, only copying or moving whole values in and out.
> - It has no runtime cost and the same layout as `T`.
> - `get` requires `T: Copy`; for other types use `replace`, `take`, or `swap`.
> - `Cell` is `!Sync`; use atomics for the thread-safe equivalent.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Cell<bool>` "dirty" flag to a `Settings` struct so that a method
>    `set_theme(&self, ..)` marks it dirty and `save(&self)` clears it. Explain
>    why the theme itself cannot easily be a `Cell<String>` if you need to read it.
> 2. Write `fn next_id(counter: &Cell<u64>) -> u64` and use it from two closures
>    that both capture `&counter`.
> 3. Interview: Why can `Cell<T>` offer `set(&self, v: T)` safely without any
>    runtime check, while `RefCell<T>` needs a borrow counter? (Hint: what would
>    `Cell` need to give out for a write to invalidate something?)

#### RefCell and Runtime Borrow Checking

`Cell` cannot give you a reference to its contents, which rules it out for most
real data. You cannot call `push` on a `Vec` inside a `Cell` without moving the
whole vector out and back. You want an actual `&mut Vec<T>`, through a shared
handle, while keeping the guarantee that it is the only reference.

`RefCell<T>` provides exactly that by doing the borrow checker's job **at run
time**. Next to the value it keeps a small borrow state: the number of active
shared borrows, or a marker that one exclusive borrow is active. `borrow()`
returns a `Ref<T>` guard (acts like `&T`) and increments the reader count.
`borrow_mut()` returns a `RefMut<T>` guard (acts like `&mut T`) and marks the
cell as exclusively borrowed. When a guard is dropped, the state is restored.
If a request would break the rule, for example `borrow_mut()` while a `Ref` is
alive, **the program panics** instead of failing to compile.

It is like a library book with a checkout card. Many people may read it in the
reading room at the same time, or one person may take it home to annotate it,
but the librarian refuses to lend it for annotation while anyone is reading.
The difference from the compile-time borrow checker is that the librarian only
finds out at the counter, while the program is running.

```text
   RefCell<Vec<i32>>                     borrow state
   +-------------+-------------------+
   | borrow: 0   | value: [1, 2, 3]  |    0      unborrowed
   +-------------+-------------------+    n > 0  n shared Refs alive
                                          -1     one RefMut alive

   borrow()      when state >= 0  -> state += 1, returns Ref
   borrow_mut()  when state == 0  -> state = -1, returns RefMut
   otherwise                      -> panic (or Err from try_borrow*)
```

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;

struct Logger {
    lines: RefCell<Vec<String>>,
}

impl Logger {
    fn log(&self, msg: &str) {              // &self: callers share the logger
        self.lines.borrow_mut().push(msg.to_string());
    }                                       // RefMut dropped here: borrow released

    fn count(&self) -> usize {
        self.lines.borrow().len()           // temporary Ref, released at the `;`
    }
}

fn main() {
    let logger = Logger { lines: RefCell::new(Vec::new()) };
    let a = &logger;
    let b = &logger;
    a.log("start");
    b.log("connect");
    println!("{}", logger.count());         // 2

    {
        let r1 = logger.lines.borrow();     // shared borrow #1
        let r2 = logger.lines.borrow();     // shared borrow #2: fine
        println!("{} {}", r1[0], r2[1]);    // start connect
        // logger.lines.borrow_mut();       // would panic: already borrowed
        println!("{:?}", logger.lines.try_borrow_mut().is_err());   // true
    }                                       // r1, r2 dropped

    logger.lines.borrow_mut().clear();      // fine now: no other borrows
    println!("{}", logger.count());         // 0
}
```

The panic is the main risk of `RefCell`, and it almost always comes from a guard
living longer than intended. A guard bound with `let` lives until the end of its
block, and a guard created in an `if let` or `match` scrutinee lives until the
end of the whole `if let` or `match`. Calling a method that borrows the same
cell from inside that scope panics:

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;

fn main() {
    let queue = RefCell::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);

    // BUG pattern (panics): the Ref from `borrow()` lives for the whole loop.
    // for x in queue.borrow().iter() {
    //     queue.borrow_mut().push(*x);   // panicked: RefCell already borrowed
    // }

    // Fix: end the shared borrow before mutating, here by copying the data out.
    let snapshot: Vec<i32> = queue.borrow().clone();   // Ref dropped at the `;`
    for x in snapshot {
        queue.borrow_mut().push(x * 10);
    }
    println!("{:?}", queue.borrow());       // [1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 30]

    // try_borrow_mut turns the panic into a Result you can handle.
    let guard = queue.borrow();
    match queue.try_borrow_mut() {
        Ok(mut v) => v.push(0),
        Err(e) => println!("busy: {e}"),    // busy: RefCell already borrowed
    }
    drop(guard);
}
```

`Ref::map` and `RefMut::map` narrow a guard to one part of the value, so you can
return access to a field without exposing the whole structure:

```rust
use std::cell::{Ref, RefCell};

struct Cache {
    inner: RefCell<(u64, String)>,          // (version, text)
}

impl Cache {
    fn text(&self) -> Ref<'_, str> {
        Ref::map(self.inner.borrow(), |(_, s)| s.as_str())
    }
}

fn main() {
    let c = Cache { inner: RefCell::new((1, "hello".into())) };
    println!("{}", &*c.text());             // hello
}
```

| | Compile-time borrows | `RefCell<T>` |
| - | -------------------- | ------------ |
| When violations are found | Compilation | At run time (panic) |
| Runtime cost | None | One counter check and update per borrow |
| Memory cost | None | One `isize` per cell |
| Accepts | Only provably safe programs | Any program that is safe in practice |
| Thread safety | Yes | `!Sync` (single thread only) |

> Key Takeaways
> - `RefCell<T>` enforces "many readers or one writer" at run time through
>   `Ref`/`RefMut` guards, panicking on a violation.
> - A borrow lasts as long as its guard; keep guards short-lived, and never hold
>   one across a call that may borrow the same cell.
> - `try_borrow`/`try_borrow_mut` return a `Result` instead of panicking, and
>   `Ref::map`/`RefMut::map` narrow a guard to part of the value.
> - Use `RefCell` only where compile-time borrows cannot express the design;
>   its checks cost a little time and move bugs from compile time to run time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `Graph` whose `add_edge(&self, from, to)` mutates an internal
>    `RefCell<Vec<Vec<usize>>>`, and a `neighbors(&self, n) -> Ref<'_, [usize]>`
>    that uses `Ref::map`.
> 2. Reproduce the `already borrowed` panic by calling, from inside a method that
>    holds `borrow()`, another method that calls `borrow_mut()`. Fix it in two
>    different ways.
> 3. Interview: The compiler rejects a program that `RefCell` would run without a
>    panic. Give an example of such a program and explain why the static checker
>    cannot accept it. (Hint: think about borrows whose overlap depends on a
>    run-time value, such as two indices that may or may not be equal.)

#### OnceCell and LazyCell

A common kind of mutation happens **exactly once**: a configuration is loaded
on first use, an expensive lookup table is built the first time someone asks,
or a struct computes and caches a derived value. Doing this with `RefCell<Option<T>>`
works but is clumsy. Every read has to borrow, check for `None`, and handle the
first-time path, and a read can never return a plain `&T` because the guard
must stay alive.

`OnceCell<T>` captures the pattern directly. It starts empty and can be written
**at most once**. After that its value never changes again, so handing out a
plain `&T` is safe, with no guard and no counter, because nothing can ever write
to it again. `get_or_init(f)` returns the value, running `f` to fill the cell
only on the first call.

`LazyCell<T, F>` goes one step further and bundles the initializer with the cell:
you supply the closure at construction, and the first dereference runs it. It is
the "compute on first touch" variable.

Both types have thread-safe counterparts in `std::sync`, which are the ones you
need in `static` items, because a static is shared by every thread and must be
`Sync`:

| Single-threaded (`std::cell`) | Thread-safe (`std::sync`) | Initializer given |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `OnceCell<T>` | `OnceLock<T>` | At each access (`get_or_init(f)`) |
| `LazyCell<T, F>` | `LazyLock<T, F>` | At construction (`LazyCell::new(f)`) |

These types were stabilized in Rust 1.70 (`OnceCell`, `OnceLock`) and 1.80
(`LazyCell`, `LazyLock`). They replace the `once_cell` and `lazy_static` crates
that older code depends on.

```rust
use std::cell::{LazyCell, OnceCell};
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::LazyLock;

// A global, built on first access, safe to read from any thread.
static STATUS_TEXT: LazyLock<HashMap<u16, &'static str>> = LazyLock::new(|| {
    println!("(building status table)");    // runs exactly once
    HashMap::from([(200, "OK"), (404, "Not Found"), (500, "Server Error")])
});

struct Report {
    rows: Vec<f64>,
    mean: OnceCell<f64>,                    // computed lazily, then fixed
}

impl Report {
    fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
        *self.mean.get_or_init(|| {
            println!("(computing mean)");
            self.rows.iter().sum::<f64>() / self.rows.len() as f64
        })
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", STATUS_TEXT[&404]);      // (building status table) Not Found
    println!("{}", STATUS_TEXT[&200]);      // OK: already built

    let r = Report { rows: vec![2.0, 4.0, 9.0], mean: OnceCell::new() };
    println!("{}", r.mean());               // (computing mean) 5
    println!("{}", r.mean());               // 5: cached

    // `set` fails if the cell is already filled, and hands the value back.
    let cell: OnceCell<&str> = OnceCell::new();
    assert!(cell.get().is_none());
    assert_eq!(cell.set("first"), Ok(()));
    assert_eq!(cell.set("second"), Err("second"));
    println!("{:?}", cell.get());           // Some("first")

    // LazyCell: the initializer travels with the value.
    let expensive = LazyCell::new(|| (1..=20u64).product::<u64>());
    println!("ready");                      // nothing computed yet
    println!("{}", *expensive);             // 2432902008176640000
}
```

`OnceCell` is the right choice for a struct field that caches a value, because
the closure can capture `self`. `LazyCell`/`LazyLock` suit standalone values
and statics whose initializer needs no context. In a `static`, always use the
`std::sync` versions: `static X: OnceCell<..>` is rejected because `OnceCell`
is not `Sync`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `OnceCell<T>` can be written at most once, so reads return a plain `&T` with
>   no runtime borrow tracking.
> - `LazyCell<T, F>` stores its initializer and runs it on first dereference.
> - `OnceLock` and `LazyLock` are the thread-safe versions and are the ones to
>   use in `static` items.
> - These standard types replace the `lazy_static` and `once_cell` crates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace a `RefCell<Option<String>>` cache in a struct with
>    `OnceCell<String>` and compare the signatures of the accessor before and
>    after.
> 2. Create `static PRIMES: LazyLock<Vec<u32>>` holding the primes below 10,000
>    and read it from four threads; confirm with a `println!` that the
>    initializer runs once.
> 3. Interview: Why can `OnceCell::get` return `&T` without a guard, while
>    `RefCell::borrow` must return `Ref<T>`? (Hint: list every way the contents
>    of each cell can change after a reference has been handed out.)

#### UnsafeCell Foundations

`Cell`, `RefCell`, `OnceCell`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, and every atomic type all
mutate data through a shared reference. Yet Rust's most fundamental rule says
that data behind `&T` is immutable, and the optimizer relies on that: if it sees
two reads through `&T` with an unknown function call in between, it may reuse the
first result, because nothing could have changed the value. How do these types
avoid being "optimized" into wrong answers?

The answer is `UnsafeCell<T>`, the **only** legal way in Rust to obtain
mutability through a shared reference. It is a compiler-recognized ("lang
item") wrapper that tells the compiler: "data inside me may change even while
`&UnsafeCell<T>` references exist; do not assume it is immutable." Every
interior mutability type contains an `UnsafeCell` at its core.

Its API is tiny and gives no safety at all:

- `UnsafeCell::new(v)` wraps a value.
- `get(&self) -> *mut T` returns a raw pointer to the contents. Creating the
  pointer is safe; **dereferencing it is `unsafe`**.
- `get_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T` is safe, because `&mut self` already proves
  exclusive access.

The safe wrappers are the policies built around this mechanism. `Cell` ensures
no reference to the inside ever escapes. `RefCell` counts borrows. `Mutex` uses
an OS lock. In each case the `unsafe` code inside the wrapper upholds the
aliasing rule, so the outside API can be safe.

```text
   Safe API          Policy that keeps it sound            Core
   ---------------   -----------------------------------   -------------
   Cell<T>           never hand out &T to the inside   \
   RefCell<T>        runtime borrow counter             |
   OnceCell<T>       write at most once                 |--> UnsafeCell<T>
   Mutex<T>          OS / futex lock                    |
   AtomicU32         CPU atomic instructions           /
```

The rule that makes `UnsafeCell` necessary is strict: **casting `&T` to `&mut T`
(or writing through a `*const T` derived from `&T`) is undefined behavior,
always**. It is not "dangerous" or "usually fine"; the compiler is entitled to
miscompile it. If you need shared mutation in your own type, it must go through
an `UnsafeCell`.

Here is a simplified `Cell` built from scratch, showing how the pieces fit:

```rust
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;

pub struct MyCell<T> {
    value: UnsafeCell<T>,
}

// UnsafeCell<T> is !Sync, so MyCell<T> is automatically !Sync too: a &MyCell
// can never be shared between threads, which is what makes the code below sound.

impl<T: Copy> MyCell<T> {
    pub fn new(value: T) -> Self {
        MyCell { value: UnsafeCell::new(value) }
    }

    pub fn get(&self) -> T {
        // SAFETY: single-threaded (!Sync), and no reference to the contents is
        // ever handed out, so nobody can observe this read mid-write.
        unsafe { *self.value.get() }
    }

    pub fn set(&self, value: T) {
        // SAFETY: same argument as `get`; the &mut created here does not
        // outlive this statement, so it never aliases another reference.
        unsafe { *self.value.get() = value }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let c = MyCell::new(1);
    let (a, b) = (&c, &c);                  // two shared references
    a.set(a.get() + 10);
    b.set(b.get() * 2);
    println!("{}", c.get());                // 22

    // The forbidden shortcut, for contrast. Never do this:
    // let x = 5;
    // let p = &x as *const i32 as *mut i32;
    // unsafe { *p = 6 };                   // undefined behavior: x is not in an UnsafeCell
}
```

`UnsafeCell<T>` has the same in-memory layout as `T` (`#[repr(transparent)]`),
and it opts its contents out of the "`&T` is immutable" assumption, nothing more.
It does not provide synchronization, so it is `!Sync`. Types such as `Mutex`
add an explicit `unsafe impl Sync` once their lock makes cross-thread access
sound. Tools like Miri (Chapter 14) can detect code that mutates through `&T`
without an `UnsafeCell`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `UnsafeCell<T>` is the only sound way to mutate data through a shared
>   reference; all interior mutability types are built on it.
> - It tells the compiler not to assume immutability behind `&`, and its `get`
>   returns a raw pointer whose use is `unsafe`.
> - Converting `&T` into `&mut T` any other way is always undefined behavior.
> - Safe wrappers add a policy (no inner references, borrow counting, locking,
>   atomics) that makes the `unsafe` core sound.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend `MyCell<T>` with `replace(&self, v: T) -> T` using
>    `std::mem::replace` on the raw pointer, and write the `SAFETY` comment.
> 2. Try adding `pub fn get_ref(&self) -> &T` to `MyCell`, then construct a
>    sequence of calls that would make it unsound. Run it under Miri
>    (`cargo +nightly miri run`) and read the report.
> 3. Interview: Why would `unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for MyCell<T> {}` be
>    unsound, while the same impl on a spin lock wrapping `UnsafeCell<T>` can be
>    sound? (Hint: consider two threads calling `set` at the same instant.)

#### Combining Rc with RefCell

`Rc<T>` and `RefCell<T>` each solve half of a common problem. `Rc` provides
**several owners** but only shared access. `RefCell` provides **mutation
through shared access** but has a single owner. Stacked as `Rc<RefCell<T>>`,
they give you shared, mutable state in a single thread: any owner can clone the
handle, and any owner can borrow mutably as long as nobody else is borrowing at
that moment.

```text
   a: Rc ---\
             +--> [ strong=3 | weak=0 | RefCell { borrow=0 | value: Account } ]
   b: Rc ---+          ^ Rc layer: who owns it    ^ RefCell layer: who is using it now
   c: Rc ---/
```

This is how you model things such as a shared bank account referenced by
several customers, a mutable graph where nodes are referenced from several
places, or GUI widgets that several event handlers update. The order of the
layers matters:

| Type | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `Rc<RefCell<T>>` | Shared ownership of one mutable `T` (the common case) |
| `RefCell<Rc<T>>` | A slot whose shared, immutable `Rc<T>` can be swapped for another |
| `Rc<RefCell<Vec<T>>>` | One shared, mutable list |
| `Vec<Rc<RefCell<T>>>` | A list of individually shared, mutable items |
| `Arc<Mutex<T>>` | The multi-threaded equivalent of `Rc<RefCell<T>>` |

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Account {
    owner: String,
    balance: i64,
}

// A shared, mutable account handle. A type alias keeps signatures readable.
type Shared<T> = Rc<RefCell<T>>;

struct Customer {
    name: String,
    joint: Shared<Account>,
}

impl Customer {
    fn deposit(&self, amount: i64) {
        let mut acct = self.joint.borrow_mut();   // RefMut: exclusive for now
        acct.balance += amount;
        println!("{} -> {}: +{amount}, balance {}", self.name, acct.owner, acct.balance);
    }                                             // RefMut dropped: borrow released
}

fn main() {
    let account: Shared<Account> =
        Rc::new(RefCell::new(Account { owner: "Joint".into(), balance: 0 }));

    let ana = Customer { name: "Ana".into(), joint: Rc::clone(&account) };
    let ben = Customer { name: "Ben".into(), joint: Rc::clone(&account) };

    ana.deposit(100);                       // Ana -> Joint: +100, balance 100
    ben.deposit(50);                        // Ben -> Joint: +50, balance 150
    println!("{:?}", account.borrow());     // Account { owner: "Joint", balance: 150 }
    println!("{}", Rc::strong_count(&account));   // 3
}
```

A few pitfalls are specific to the combination:

- **Re-entrancy panics.** If a callback stored in shared state calls back into
  the same `Rc<RefCell<..>>` while the outer code still holds `borrow_mut()`,
  the program panics. Drop guards before calling out, or clone the data you
  need first.
- **Cycles leak.** `Rc<RefCell<T>>` makes it easy to point two nodes at each
  other. Use `Weak` for back-edges (section 9.2).
- **The `.borrow()` name clash.** If `std::borrow::Borrow` is imported,
  `rc.borrow()` on an `Rc<RefCell<T>>` resolves to `Borrow::borrow` on the
  `Rc` instead of `RefCell::borrow`, producing confusing type errors. Remove the
  import or write `RefCell::borrow(&rc)`.

```rust
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Button {
    clicks: u32,
    on_click: Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&Rc<RefCell<Button>>)>>,
}

fn click(btn: &Rc<RefCell<Button>>) {
    // Take what we need out of the borrow, then release it BEFORE calling out.
    let handlers = {
        let mut b = btn.borrow_mut();
        b.clicks += 1;
        std::mem::take(&mut b.on_click)     // move the handlers out temporarily
    };                                      // RefMut dropped here
    for h in &handlers {
        h(btn);                             // a handler may borrow `btn` freely
    }
    btn.borrow_mut().on_click = handlers;   // put them back
}

fn main() {
    let btn = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Button { clicks: 0, on_click: Vec::new() }));
    btn.borrow_mut().on_click.push(Box::new(|b| {
        println!("clicked {} times", b.borrow().clicks);   // re-entrant read: OK
    }));
    click(&btn);                            // clicked 1 times
    click(&btn);                            // clicked 2 times
}
```

`Rc<RefCell<T>>` is a legitimate tool, but code full of it is often a sign of
an object-oriented design being forced onto Rust. Common alternatives keep the
borrow checker on your side:

- **Arena and indices:** store all nodes in a `Vec<Node>` and link them by
  `usize` index (or with crates like `slotmap`); the `Vec` is the only owner.
- **Pass state explicitly:** give functions a `&mut State` parameter instead of
  having every component hold a handle to it.
- **Messages:** components send commands (an enum) to the single owner of the
  state, which applies them.

> Key Takeaways
> - `Rc<RefCell<T>>` combines shared ownership (`Rc`) with runtime-checked
>   mutation (`RefCell`) for single-threaded shared mutable state.
> - `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (or `Arc<RwLock<T>>`) is its multi-threaded counterpart.
> - Keep `borrow_mut()` guards short and release them before calling callbacks or
>   other code that may borrow the same cell.
> - Heavy use of `Rc<RefCell<T>>` is a design smell; consider arenas with
>   indices, explicit `&mut` parameters, or message passing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a doubly linked list with `Rc<RefCell<Node>>` for `next` and
>    `Weak<RefCell<Node>>` for `prev`, and implement `push_back` and a
>    function that prints the list backwards from the tail.
> 2. Reimplement the same list as an arena (`Vec<Node>` with `Option<usize>`
>    links) and compare the two implementations in length and clarity.
> 3. Interview: A colleague's single-threaded simulation uses
>    `Rc<RefCell<Entity>>` everywhere and occasionally panics with "already
>    borrowed". How would you diagnose the problem and how might you restructure
>    the code? (Hint: look for guards held across calls into other entities,
>    and consider who should own the entities.)

<a id="94-borrowed-data-abstractions"></a>
### 9.4 Borrowed Data Abstractions

The last group of types is less about where data lives and more about **how it
may be accessed**: borrowed-or-owned, fixed in place, not yet initialized, or
viewed through a different type. These tools appear throughout the standard
library's signatures, so recognizing them makes APIs much easier to read.

#### Cow for Clone-on-Write

Many functions *usually* return their input unchanged and only *sometimes* need
to modify it. Escaping HTML is a good example: most strings contain no `<` or
`&`, but a few do. If the function returns `String`, it must allocate and copy
even in the common case where nothing changed. If it returns `&str`, it cannot
return a modified string at all. Neither signature fits the real behavior.

`Cow<'a, B>` ("clone on write") is an enum that holds **either** a borrowed
reference **or** an owned value:

```rust
// Simplified from std::borrow
pub enum Cow<'a, B: ?Sized + ToOwned + 'a> {
    Borrowed(&'a B),                        // e.g. &'a str
    Owned(<B as ToOwned>::Owned),           // e.g. String
}
```

`B` is the borrowed form (`str`, `[T]`, `Path`), and `ToOwned` links it to its
owned form (`String`, `Vec<T>`, `PathBuf`). A `Cow<str>` dereferences to `&str`
either way, so callers can read it without caring which variant they got. Only
the code that needs to modify it pays for a copy: `to_mut()` clones a
`Borrowed` value into an `Owned` one on first use and returns `&mut` to it, and
`into_owned()` extracts an owned value, cloning only if necessary.

The analogy is a shared document you are reviewing. You read the original
without copying it, and you only make a personal copy once you actually need to
write a correction.

```rust
use std::borrow::Cow;

// Allocates only when the input contains something to escape.
fn escape_html(input: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    if !input.contains(['<', '>', '&']) {
        return Cow::Borrowed(input);        // fast path: zero allocation
    }
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len() + 8);
    for ch in input.chars() {
        match ch {
            '<' => out.push_str("&lt;"),
            '>' => out.push_str("&gt;"),
            '&' => out.push_str("&amp;"),
            c => out.push(c),
        }
    }
    Cow::Owned(out)
}

// Normalize in place only if needed: to_mut clones on first write.
fn ensure_trailing_slash(path: &mut Cow<'_, str>) {
    if !path.ends_with('/') {               // Deref to &str for reading
        path.to_mut().push('/');            // Borrowed -> Owned (one clone) here
    }
}

fn main() {
    for s in ["plain text", "a < b && c"] {
        match escape_html(s) {
            Cow::Borrowed(b) => println!("borrowed: {b}"),
            Cow::Owned(o) => println!("owned:    {o}"),
        }
    }
    // borrowed: plain text
    // owned:    a &lt; b &amp;&amp; c

    let mut p: Cow<str> = Cow::Borrowed("/srv/www/");
    ensure_trailing_slash(&mut p);
    println!("{} {}", p, matches!(p, Cow::Borrowed(_)));   // /srv/www/ true

    let mut q: Cow<str> = Cow::Borrowed("/srv/data");
    ensure_trailing_slash(&mut q);
    println!("{} {}", q, matches!(q, Cow::Borrowed(_)));   // /srv/data/ false

    // The standard library uses Cow where conversion is usually a no-op.
    let bytes = b"caf\xC3\xA9 \xFF";
    let text: Cow<str> = String::from_utf8_lossy(bytes);   // owned: had to replace 0xFF
    println!("{text}");                                     // café (replacement char)
    let owned: String = text.into_owned();                  // no clone: already Owned
    println!("{}", owned.len());            // 9: "é" is 2 bytes, U+FFFD is 3
}
```

`Cow` is also handy in data types that mostly hold static data but occasionally
need a computed value, such as error messages: `Cow<'static, str>` can hold a
literal like `"not found"` for free or a `format!`-ed `String` when details are
needed.

| Return type | Allocation when unchanged | Can return modified data |
| ----------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `&str` | None | No |
| `String` | Always | Yes |
| `Cow<'_, str>` | None | Yes |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Cow<'a, B>` holds either `&'a B` or `B::Owned` and dereferences to `&B` in
>   both cases.
> - It lets a function skip allocation on the common unchanged path while still
>   returning modified data when needed.
> - `to_mut()` clones only on the first write; `into_owned()` clones only if the
>   value is still borrowed.
> - `Cow<'static, str>` is a good fit for messages that are usually literals.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn strip_bom(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str>` that returns the input borrowed
>    unless it starts with `'\u{FEFF}'`. Then try to rewrite it to return `&str`
>    and decide whether `Cow` was necessary.
> 2. Define `struct AppError { code: u16, message: Cow<'static, str> }` and create
>    one error from a literal and one from `format!`.
> 3. Interview: When is returning `Cow<str>` worse than returning `String`?
>    (Hint: think about callers that always need ownership, about API
>    ergonomics, and about how often the borrowed path is actually taken.)

#### Pin and Self-Referential Types

Moving a value in Rust is a plain memory copy: the bytes go to a new address
and the old location is considered dead. That is safe for almost every type,
because ordinary values do not care where they live. It breaks for a
**self-referential** value, one that stores a pointer into itself. After a move
the pointer still holds the **old** address, so it dangles.

```text
   Before move (at 0x1000)               After move to 0x2000
   +-------------------------+           +-------------------------+
   | data: "hello"           |           | data: "hello"           |
   | ptr:  0x1000 (-> data)  |   memcpy  | ptr:  0x1000  !!!       | --> old, dead
   +-------------------------+   ----->  +-------------------------+     location
```

You rarely write such types by hand, but the compiler generates them constantly.
An `async fn` (Chapter 11) is compiled into a state machine that stores its
local variables across `.await` points. A local that borrows another local turns
into a field that points at another field of the same struct, so a
self-referential type has been created.

`Pin<P>` is the guarantee that makes such types usable. `P` is a pointer type
(`&mut T`, `Box<T>`), and `Pin<P>` promises: **the `T` this points to will not
be moved again until it is dropped**. `Pin` enforces this by not handing out
`&mut T` (which would allow `mem::swap` or `mem::replace` to move the value
out). Think of a pin in a corkboard: once a note is pinned, you may still read
it and even write on it, but you cannot slide it to a new position.

Most types do not care about being moved, and for them `Pin` is pointless. The
auto trait **`Unpin`** marks such types, and almost everything implements it:
`i32`, `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`. For an `Unpin` type, `Pin` is just a
wrapper you can freely unwrap (`Pin::new`, `Pin::get_mut`, `Pin::into_inner`).
Only `!Unpin` types (compiler-generated futures, or types that contain
`PhantomPinned`) are actually constrained.

| Operation | `T: Unpin` | `T: !Unpin` |
| --------- | ---------- | ----------- |
| Create `Pin<&mut T>` | `Pin::new(&mut t)` (safe) | `pin!(t)` or `Box::pin(t)` (safe), `Pin::new_unchecked` (unsafe) |
| Get `&T` | `pin.as_ref().get_ref()` / deref | Same (reading is always fine) |
| Get `&mut T` | `pin.get_mut()` (safe) | `get_unchecked_mut` (unsafe, must not move) |
| Move the value out | Yes | No |

There are two common ways to pin a value:

- `Box::pin(value)` puts it on the heap. A heap allocation never moves, even
  when the `Box` itself is moved, so `Pin<Box<T>>` can be passed around freely.
- `std::pin::pin!(value)` pins it on the current stack frame, giving a
  `Pin<&mut T>` without allocating. It cannot leave the frame.

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomPinned;
use std::pin::{Pin, pin};
use std::ptr::NonNull;

// A self-referential struct: `slice` points into `data`.
struct Parser {
    data: String,
    slice: Option<NonNull<str>>,            // raw pointer into `data`
    _pin: PhantomPinned,                    // opt out of Unpin: moving is unsafe
}

impl Parser {
    fn new(data: &str) -> Pin<Box<Parser>> {
        let mut boxed = Box::pin(Parser {
            data: data.to_string(),
            slice: None,
            _pin: PhantomPinned,
        });
        // The value now has its final heap address, so pointing into it is safe.
        let first_word = NonNull::from(boxed.data.split(' ').next().unwrap());
        // SAFETY: we only set a field; nothing is moved out of the pinned value.
        unsafe { boxed.as_mut().get_unchecked_mut().slice = Some(first_word) };
        boxed
    }

    fn first_word(self: Pin<&Self>) -> &str {
        // SAFETY: `slice` points into `self.data`, which cannot have moved
        // because Self is pinned and !Unpin, and `data` is never mutated.
        unsafe { self.get_ref().slice.unwrap().as_ref() }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let p = Parser::new("hello pinned world");
    let moved = p;                          // moves the Box pointer, not the Parser
    println!("{}", moved.as_ref().first_word());   // hello

    // let inner: Parser = *Pin::into_inner(moved);
    // error[E0277]: `PhantomPinned` cannot be unpinned

    // Unpin types are unaffected: Pin::new and get_mut just work.
    let mut n = 5;
    let mut pinned = Pin::new(&mut n);
    *pinned.as_mut().get_mut() += 1;        // fine: i32 is Unpin
    println!("{n}");                        // 6

    // Pinning a future on the stack, as executors and `select!` do.
    let fut = pin!(async { 40 + 2 });
    let _: Pin<&mut _> = fut;               // ready to be polled
}
```

In everyday code you meet `Pin` in three places: `Future::poll` takes
`self: Pin<&mut Self>`, executor APIs ask for `Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`, and
`tokio::select!` or manual polling needs `pin!`. Writing pinned types by hand
requires `unsafe` for **field projection** (getting `Pin<&mut Field>` from
`Pin<&mut Struct>`). The `pin-project` and `pin-project-lite` crates generate
that code soundly, and you should prefer them.

> Key Takeaways
> - A self-referential value breaks when moved, because its internal pointer
>   keeps the old address; `async fn` state machines are the main source of such
>   types.
> - `Pin<P>` guarantees the pointee will not move again until dropped, by
>   withholding `&mut T` for `!Unpin` types.
> - `Unpin` types (nearly all types) are unaffected by pinning.
> - Pin with `Box::pin` (heap, movable handle) or `pin!` (stack, local only); use
>   `pin-project` instead of hand-written `unsafe` projections.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that takes `fut: Pin<&mut impl Future<Output = u32>>` and
>    call it with a future pinned by `pin!` and with one pinned by `Box::pin`.
> 2. Remove `PhantomPinned` from `Parser`, then use `std::mem::swap` on two
>    unpinned parsers and observe that `first_word` now reads the wrong data or
>    triggers undefined behavior under Miri.
> 3. Interview: `Pin<Box<T>>` can be moved freely, so in what sense is the value
>    "pinned"? (Hint: distinguish between moving the pointer and moving the
>    pointee.)

#### ManuallyDrop and MaybeUninit

Rust's automatic resource management rests on two invariants: every value is
**initialized** before it is used, and every value is **dropped exactly once**.
Safe code never has to think about either. Low-level code sometimes must bend
them: an FFI function hands ownership of a buffer to C, a container fills an
array one element at a time, or a struct needs its fields destroyed in a
particular order. The standard library provides two wrapper types that switch
off one invariant each, under your control.

**`ManuallyDrop<T>`** wraps a value and suppresses its destructor. The value is
fully initialized and usable through `Deref`/`DerefMut`, but when the wrapper
goes out of scope nothing happens. You decide whether and when to drop it with
the `unsafe` function `ManuallyDrop::drop(&mut slot)`, or take it back with
`ManuallyDrop::into_inner`. It has the same layout as `T` and no runtime cost.

**`MaybeUninit<T>`** is storage that **may not yet hold a valid `T`**. The
compiler makes no assumptions about its contents, so it is sound to leave it
uninitialized, write to it piece by piece through raw pointers, and finally
declare it ready with the `unsafe` method `assume_init()`. Like
`ManuallyDrop`, a `MaybeUninit<T>` never drops its contents itself.

An analogy for both: ManuallyDrop is a contract with the cleaning crew saying
"do not clear this desk; I will tell you when". MaybeUninit is an empty, labeled
box in a warehouse: the shelf space is reserved, but nobody may open it
expecting goods until you mark it as filled.

| | `ManuallyDrop<T>` | `MaybeUninit<T>` |
| - | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Invariant relaxed | "Dropped exactly once" | "Always initialized" |
| Contents valid? | Always | Only after you initialize them |
| Safe to read? | Yes, via `Deref` | Only after `assume_init*` (unsafe) |
| Runs `T`'s destructor | Never automatically | Never automatically |
| Typical use | Drop order, FFI ownership transfer, unions | Buffers, arrays, out-parameters, FFI |

`ManuallyDrop` in action, controlling drop order and handing ownership away:

```rust
use std::mem::ManuallyDrop;

struct Noisy(&'static str);
impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("drop {}", self.0);
    }
}

// Fields normally drop in declaration order, which would destroy `device`
// first. A texture must be released before the device that created it.
struct Renderer {
    device: Noisy,
    texture: ManuallyDrop<Noisy>,           // excluded from automatic drop glue
}

impl Drop for Renderer {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // Runs BEFORE any field is dropped.
        // SAFETY: `texture` is dropped exactly once, here, and never used again.
        unsafe { ManuallyDrop::drop(&mut self.texture) };
    }   // afterwards the remaining fields drop automatically: `device`
}

fn main() {
    let r = Renderer {
        device: Noisy("device"),
        texture: ManuallyDrop::new(Noisy("texture")),
    };
    println!("rendering with {} on {}", r.texture.0, r.device.0);   // Deref works
    drop(r);                                // drop texture, then drop device

    // Ownership transfer: give a Vec's buffer away (for example to C code)
    // without Rust freeing it, then rebuild the Vec so it is freed properly.
    let mut v = ManuallyDrop::new(vec![1u8, 2, 3]);
    let (ptr, len, cap) = (v.as_mut_ptr(), v.len(), v.capacity());
    // ... `ptr` could now cross an FFI boundary; Rust will not free it ...
    // SAFETY: the parts come from a Vec<u8> that was never dropped or reused.
    let back = unsafe { Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, len, cap) };
    println!("{back:?}");                   // [1, 2, 3]; freed at end of scope
}
```

`MaybeUninit` in action, filling an array element by element. Without it you
would have to invent a dummy value for every slot first, which is wasteful and
impossible for types with no sensible default:

```rust
use std::mem::MaybeUninit;

struct Sensor {
    id: usize,
    name: String,                           // no cheap placeholder value exists
}

fn make_sensors() -> [Sensor; 4] {
    // An array of uninitialized slots: no Sensor values exist yet.
    let mut slots: [MaybeUninit<Sensor>; 4] = [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; 4];

    for (i, slot) in slots.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        slot.write(Sensor { id: i, name: format!("s{i}") });   // safe: just writes
    }

    // SAFETY: every element was initialized by the loop above, and
    // MaybeUninit<Sensor> has the same layout as Sensor.
    slots.map(|s| unsafe { s.assume_init() })
}

fn main() {
    let sensors = make_sensors();
    println!("{} {}", sensors[3].id, sensors[3].name);   // 3 s3

    // An out-parameter filled by a callee, as in many C APIs.
    fn fill(out: &mut MaybeUninit<u64>) {
        out.write(0xFEED);
    }
    let mut x = MaybeUninit::<u64>::uninit();
    fill(&mut x);
    let value = unsafe { x.assume_init() }; // SAFETY: `fill` always writes
    println!("{value:#x}");                 // 0xfeed

    // let bad: u64 = unsafe { MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() };
    // ^ undefined behavior: reading uninitialized memory, even for an integer
}
```

The rules are unforgiving. Calling `assume_init` on memory that is not fully
initialized is undefined behavior, even for "harmless" types like `u8` or
`bool`. A panic in the middle of initialization leaks the elements already
written (because `MaybeUninit` never drops), which is safe but must be
considered. Prefer safe alternatives such as `std::array::from_fn`,
`Vec::with_capacity` with `push`, or `Box::new_uninit` APIs whenever they fit.
The old `std::mem::uninitialized` function is deprecated because it could not
be used soundly.

Related safe functions round out the picture: `std::mem::forget(x)` leaks a
value without dropping it (always safe, since leaking is not undefined
behavior), and `std::mem::take`/`replace` move a value out of a `&mut` slot by
leaving a valid one behind.

> Key Takeaways
> - `ManuallyDrop<T>` holds a valid `T` but suppresses its destructor; you drop
>   it explicitly with `unsafe { ManuallyDrop::drop(..) }` or recover it with
>   `into_inner`.
> - `MaybeUninit<T>` is storage that may not yet contain a valid `T`; write to
>   it, then `unsafe`ly `assume_init` once every byte is initialized.
> - Both are zero-cost, layout-compatible with `T`, and never drop their
>   contents automatically.
> - Reading uninitialized memory is undefined behavior for every type; reach for
>   `array::from_fn`, `Vec`, or `mem::take` before these tools.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite `make_sensors` with `std::array::from_fn` and no `unsafe`. Which
>    situations would still require `MaybeUninit`?
> 2. Add a third field to `Renderer` that must be dropped between `texture` and
>    `device`, and verify the order with the printed messages.
> 3. Interview: Why is `std::mem::forget` a safe function even though it can
>    leak memory, file handles, and locks? (Hint: consider `Rc` cycles, and
>    what the language promises about destructors running.)

#### Borrow and AsRef Traits

Generic functions often want to accept "anything that can be viewed as a
`str`" or "anything that can be viewed as a `Path`", so that callers can pass a
`String`, a `&str`, or a `PathBuf` without converting first. The standard
library offers two traits with nearly identical signatures for this, and the
difference between them is a frequent source of confusion.

```rust
// Simplified from std
pub trait AsRef<T: ?Sized> {
    fn as_ref(&self) -> &T;
}

pub trait Borrow<Borrowed: ?Sized> {
    fn borrow(&self) -> &Borrowed;
}
```

**`AsRef<T>`** means "I can cheaply give you a `&T` view of myself". It is a
loose, conversion-oriented trait. A type may implement it for many targets:
`String` is `AsRef<str>`, `AsRef<[u8]>`, `AsRef<OsStr>`, and `AsRef<Path>`.
Its main use is ergonomic function parameters, as in `File::open<P:
AsRef<Path>>(path: P)`.

**`Borrow<T>`** makes a stronger promise: "my borrowed `&T` form is **the same
value** as me". In particular, `x.borrow()` must have the same `Hash`, `Eq`,
and `Ord` behavior as `x` itself. That promise is what lets a
`HashMap<String, V>` be looked up with a `&str`. `HashMap::get` accepts any `&Q`
where `K: Borrow<Q>`, and it hashes the `&str` expecting to land in the same
bucket as the `String` key. If the hashes could differ, lookups would silently
fail. `Borrow` also has a blanket impl `impl<T> Borrow<T> for T`, so a
`HashMap<i32, V>` can still be queried with `&i32`.

An analogy: `AsRef` is "you can look at me through this lens", and any useful
lens qualifies. `Borrow` is "this is my ID card": it must identify me exactly
as I am, because others will check identity with it.

| | `AsRef<T>` | `Borrow<T>` |
| - | ---------- | ----------- |
| Promise | Cheap reference conversion | Borrowed form is equivalent (same `Hash`/`Eq`/`Ord`) |
| Reflexive blanket impl (`T: X<T>`) | No | Yes |
| Typical consumer | Function parameters (`P: AsRef<Path>`) | Collection lookups (`HashMap::get`, `BTreeSet::contains`) |
| Example impls | `String: AsRef<str>`, `AsRef<[u8]>`, `AsRef<Path>` | `String: Borrow<str>`, `Vec<T>: Borrow<[T]>` |
| Mutable variant | `AsMut<T>` | `BorrowMut<T>` |

`ToOwned`, used by `Cow` earlier in this section, is the reverse of `Borrow`:
`str: ToOwned<Owned = String>`, with the requirement that
`String: Borrow<str>`.

```rust
use std::borrow::Borrow;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::hash::Hash;
use std::path::Path;

// AsRef: accept &str, String, &Path, PathBuf, OsString...
fn extension<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P) -> Option<String> {
    p.as_ref().extension().map(|e| e.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
}

// AsRef<[u8]>: works for &str, String, Vec<u8>, [u8; N]
fn checksum(data: impl AsRef<[u8]>) -> u32 {
    data.as_ref().iter().map(|&b| b as u32).sum()
}

// Borrow: a lookup helper with the same flexibility as HashMap::get.
fn count_of<K, Q>(map: &HashMap<K, u32>, key: &Q) -> u32
where
    K: Borrow<Q> + Hash + Eq,
    Q: Hash + Eq + ?Sized,
{
    map.get(key).copied().unwrap_or(0)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", extension("report.pdf"));                    // Some("pdf")
    println!("{:?}", extension(String::from("a/b.tar.gz")));      // Some("gz")
    println!("{:?}", extension(Path::new("/etc/hosts")));         // None

    println!("{}", checksum("AB"));                               // 131
    println!("{}", checksum(vec![1u8, 2, 3]));                    // 6
    println!("{}", checksum([10u8; 3]));                          // 30

    let mut words: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
    *words.entry("rust".to_string()).or_default() += 2;
    // String: Borrow<str>, so a &str key works without allocating a String.
    println!("{}", count_of(&words, "rust"));                     // 2
    println!("{}", words.contains_key("go"));                     // false
}
```

When to use which:

- **Writing a function parameter?** Use `AsRef` (or `impl AsRef<..>`). For
  string-like input, a plain `&str` parameter is often simpler still, because
  deref coercion already accepts `&String` and `&Box<str>`.
- **Writing a collection or a lookup API?** Use `Borrow`, and document that
  your keys rely on its `Hash`/`Eq` equivalence.
- **Implementing them for your own type?** Implement `AsRef` freely for cheap
  views. Implement `Borrow<T>` only if your type's `Hash`, `Eq`, and `Ord` agree
  exactly with `T`'s. A case-insensitive string type, for example, must not
  implement `Borrow<str>`, because `"Rust"` and `"rust"` would compare equal as
  keys but hash differently as `str`s.

> Key Takeaways
> - `AsRef<T>` is a cheap, loose reference conversion, ideal for flexible
>   function parameters such as `P: AsRef<Path>`.
> - `Borrow<T>` additionally promises that the borrowed form hashes and compares
>   exactly like the owner, which makes `HashMap<String, _>::get("key")` work.
> - `Borrow` has a reflexive blanket impl and `AsRef` does not; `ToOwned` is the
>   inverse of `Borrow`.
> - Implement `Borrow` only when `Hash`, `Eq`, and `Ord` are truly equivalent.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn read_all<P: AsRef<Path>>(paths: &[P]) -> std::io::Result<usize>`
>    that returns the total byte count of several files, and call it with a
>    `Vec<String>` and with an array of `&str`.
> 2. Create a `HashSet<Vec<u8>>` and query it with a `&[u8]` slice. Identify
>    which `Borrow` impl makes this compile.
> 3. Interview: Why does `HashMap::get` use `Borrow` rather than `AsRef` as its
>    bound? (Hint: consider a type that implements `AsRef<str>` but hashes
>    differently from the `str` it exposes.)

---

## 10. Concurrency and Parallelism

Modern machines have many cores, and programs that use only one leave most of
the hardware idle. Concurrency is notoriously hard because threads that share
memory can corrupt it in ways that are timing-dependent and nearly impossible to
reproduce. Rust's ownership system, extended by the `Send` and `Sync` traits,
turns the most dangerous of these bugs, data races, into compile errors. This
chapter covers threads, message passing, shared state, the safety guarantees
behind them, and data parallelism with Rayon.

<a id="101-threads"></a>
### 10.1 Threads

A thread is an independent sequence of execution inside a process, sharing the
process's memory with every other thread. This section covers creating threads,
giving them data, borrowing safely with scoped threads, per-thread storage, and
what happens when a thread panics.

#### Spawning and Joining Threads

A program starts with one thread, the **main thread**, which runs `main`.
Everything it does happens one step after another. When work can be split into
independent pieces (resizing a hundred images, handling several network
clients, computing while waiting for disk), running those pieces on separate
threads lets the operating system schedule them on different CPU cores at the
same time, or interleave them on one core so that a blocked task does not stall
the others.

Two terms are often confused:

- **Concurrency** is about *structure*: several tasks are in progress at
  overlapping times, possibly interleaved on a single core.
- **Parallelism** is about *execution*: several tasks literally run at the same
  instant on different cores.

A restaurant kitchen is a good picture. One chef juggling three dishes is
concurrent. Three chefs each cooking a dish are parallel. Threads give you both.

Rust's `std::thread::spawn` creates an **OS thread** (a native thread scheduled by
the kernel, with its own stack, by default 2 MiB) and runs a closure on it. It
returns a `JoinHandle<T>`, where `T` is the closure's return value. Calling
`join()` blocks the current thread until the spawned one finishes and returns
`Result<T, _>`: `Ok` with the closure's value, or `Err` if the thread panicked.

```text
   main thread  ──spawn──┬──────── work ─────── join() waits ──┬── continues
                         │                                     │
   worker thread         └── closure runs ── returns value ────┘
```

```rust
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    // spawn returns immediately; the closure runs on a new OS thread.
    let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
        for i in 1..=3 {
            println!("worker: step {i}");
            thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
        }
        42                                  // the thread's result
    });

    for i in 1..=2 {
        println!("main:   step {i}");
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
    }

    // join blocks until the worker ends and hands back its return value.
    let answer = handle.join().expect("worker panicked");
    println!("worker returned {answer}");   // worker returned 42

    // Several workers, each computing part of a result.
    let handles: Vec<thread::JoinHandle<u64>> = (0..4)
        .map(|id| thread::spawn(move || (id * 1000..(id + 1) * 1000).sum()))
        .collect();
    let total: u64 = handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().unwrap()).sum();
    println!("total = {total}");            // total = 7998000 (sum of 0..4000)

    // Threads can be named and sized with a Builder.
    let h = thread::Builder::new()
        .name("indexer".into())
        .stack_size(4 * 1024 * 1024)        // 4 MiB stack
        .spawn(|| thread::current().name().unwrap().to_string())
        .unwrap();                          // spawn can fail if the OS refuses
    println!("{}", h.join().unwrap());      // indexer
}
```

The interleaving of `main:` and `worker:` lines varies from run to run; the
operating system decides who runs when. Two more facts are essential:

- **Returning from `main` ends the process**, killing any threads that are still
  running. Forgetting to `join` is a classic reason why a worker's output
  "sometimes disappears".
- **Dropping a `JoinHandle` detaches the thread**: it keeps running, but you can
  no longer wait for it or get its result.

OS threads are not free. Each one costs a kernel object, a stack reservation,
and a few microseconds to create, and switching between them costs more. Tens
or hundreds of threads are fine. Tens of thousands of mostly idle tasks are
better served by async tasks (Chapter 11), and CPU-heavy work by a fixed pool
(section 10.5). `std::thread::available_parallelism()` reports how many threads
can usefully run at once.

> Key Takeaways
> - `thread::spawn` runs a closure on a new OS thread and returns a
>   `JoinHandle<T>`; `join()` waits for it and returns `Ok(value)` or `Err` on
>   panic.
> - Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution.
> - When `main` returns, the whole process exits, so join threads whose work
>   must finish; dropping a handle detaches the thread.
> - Use `thread::Builder` for names, stack sizes, and fallible spawning.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Spawn five threads that each print their index and the value of
>    `thread::current().id()`. Run the program several times and observe the order.
> 2. Split the computation of the sum of squares of `1..=10_000_000` across
>    `available_parallelism()` threads and compare the result with a
>    single-threaded version.
> 3. Interview: Why does Rust map `thread::spawn` directly to OS threads instead
>    of providing lightweight "green threads" like Go? (Hint: think about runtime
>    size, FFI with C code, and the zero-cost abstraction principle.)

#### Moving Data into Threads

A spawned thread may outlive the function that created it, and even the stack
frame that created its data. That is why `thread::spawn` has this signature:

```rust
// Simplified from std::thread
use std::thread::JoinHandle;

pub fn spawn<F, T>(f: F) -> JoinHandle<T>
where
    F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static,      // the closure itself
    T: Send + 'static,                      // its return value
{
    unimplemented!()
}
```

The two bounds encode exactly what can go wrong:

- **`'static`**: the closure must not borrow anything from the spawning
  function's stack, because that frame may be gone while the thread is still
  running. It must **own** everything it uses (or borrow only `'static` data).
- **`Send`**: everything the closure carries must be safe to hand to another
  thread (section 10.4).

The tool that satisfies `'static` is the **`move` closure**. By default a
closure borrows the variables it uses. `move` makes it take ownership of them,
transferring the data into the thread. Think of it as moving house: the new
thread gets the furniture itself, not the address of the old flat, which may be
demolished tomorrow.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let data = vec![1, 2, 3];

    // Without `move`, the closure would borrow `data`:
    // let h = thread::spawn(|| println!("{data:?}"));
    // error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows
    //               `data`, which is owned by the current function

    let h = thread::spawn(move || {
        let sum: i32 = data.iter().sum();   // `data` is now owned by this thread
        sum
    });
    // println!("{data:?}");                // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value
    println!("{}", h.join().unwrap());      // 6

    // Need the data in several threads? Clone it, or share it with Arc.
    let config = Arc::new(String::from("verbose=true"));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();
    for id in 0..3 {
        let config = Arc::clone(&config);   // each thread owns one Arc handle
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || format!("{id}: {config}")));
    }
    for h in handles {
        println!("{}", h.join().unwrap());  // 0: verbose=true  (then 1:, 2:)
    }
    println!("still usable here: {config}");

    // Moving out results: the return value travels back through join().
    let h = thread::spawn(|| (0..5).map(|x| x * x).collect::<Vec<u32>>());
    let squares = h.join().unwrap();        // ownership returns to main
    println!("{squares:?}");                // [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
}
```

A `move` closure moves **every** captured variable. To move some and share
others, create the values to move first (clones, `Arc` handles) and shadow the
originals inside a block, as the loop above does with `let config =
Arc::clone(&config);`. That idiom is so common it is worth memorizing.

| Need | Technique |
| ---- | --------- |
| The thread is the only user | `move` the value in |
| Several threads read the same data | `Arc<T>`, cloned per thread |
| Several threads mutate the same data | `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or atomics (section 10.3) |
| The data outlives all the threads | Borrow it with scoped threads (next topic) |
| Results flow back to the spawner | Return them from the closure, or send them on a channel |

> Key Takeaways
> - `thread::spawn` requires a `Send + 'static` closure, because the thread may
>   outlive the current stack frame.
> - `move` closures transfer ownership of captured values into the thread.
> - Clone or `Arc::clone` before the `move` to give each thread its own handle;
>   shadowing the name in the loop is the standard idiom.
> - Results come back by value through `join()`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that spawns a thread to uppercase a `String` and returns
>    it through `join()`, without cloning.
> 2. Given `let words = vec!["a", "bb", "ccc"];`, spawn one thread per word that
>    prints its length. Make it compile once using `move` and `to_string`, and
>    once using `Arc<Vec<&str>>`.
> 3. Interview: The `'static` bound on `thread::spawn` does not mean the data
>    lives forever. What does it actually require? (Hint: an owned `String` is
>    `'static`; a `&String` borrowed from a local is not.)

#### Scoped Threads

The `'static` requirement of `thread::spawn` is often more than you need. If a
function spawns threads to process a local vector and waits for all of them
before returning, the vector clearly outlives the threads. Yet `spawn` still
forces you to clone the data or wrap it in an `Arc`, because the compiler
cannot see that the threads are joined in time.

**Scoped threads** (`std::thread::scope`, stable since Rust 1.63) make that
guarantee visible to the compiler. `thread::scope(|s| { ... })` creates a scope
object `s`. Threads spawned with `s.spawn` may **borrow** any data that lives
outside the scope, because `scope` does not return until every thread spawned
inside it has finished. It is like a meeting room booked for an hour: guests may
use the room's whiteboard, because the booking guarantees all of them leave
before the room is handed back.

```text
   let data = ...;                    data lives here ─────────────────┐
   thread::scope(|s| {                                                 │
       s.spawn(|| read &data);   ── thread A ──┐                       │
       s.spawn(|| read &data);   ── thread B ──┤                       │
   });   <── implicit join of A and B ─────────┘  (scope returns)      │
   use(data);                                                          │
                                      data dropped here ───────────────┘
```

The borrow rules still apply across threads: several threads may share `&data`,
or one thread may hold `&mut` to a part, and the checker verifies this at
compile time. Splitting a slice with `chunks_mut` gives each thread its own
disjoint `&mut` region, with no locks at all.

```rust
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"];
    let mut counts = vec![0usize; words.len()];
    let mut longest_len = 0;

    thread::scope(|s| {
        // Shared borrows: both threads read `words` at the same time.
```
