>   code, enforced by ownership, borrowing, `Send`, and `Sync`.
> - Unsynchronized shared mutation, dangling cross-thread borrows, and sending
>   thread-bound types are all compile errors.
> - Deadlocks, logic race conditions, starvation, and leaks are not prevented.
> - The guarantee relies on `unsafe` code (including `unsafe impl Send/Sync`)
>   being correct.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Uncomment each of the four error cases in turn, read the compiler message,
>    and fix each one with the most appropriate tool (scoped threads, `Mutex`,
>    `Arc`, or `move`).
> 2. Write a program that compiles without warnings but deadlocks, to convince
>    yourself that the guarantee has limits.
> 3. Interview: A colleague says "Rust code can't have concurrency bugs". How
>    would you correct the statement precisely? (Hint: distinguish memory
>    safety from logical correctness, and list one example of each kind of bug
>    Rust allows.)

#### Data Race Freedom

A **data race** has a precise definition. It occurs when:

1. two or more threads access the **same memory location** concurrently,
2. at least one of the accesses is a **write**, and
3. the accesses are **not synchronized** (no lock, no atomic operation, no
   happens-before relationship between them).

In C and C++ a data race is **undefined behavior**: the compiler assumes it
never happens and optimizes accordingly, so the result is not merely "a wrong
value" but potentially torn reads (half of an old 64-bit value and half of a new
one), values that never existed, infinite loops, or corrupted heap metadata.
That is why Rust treats preventing data races as part of memory safety.

Notice how the definition lines up with Rust's rules: condition 2 (a write while
others access) is exactly what "one `&mut` **or** many `&`" forbids, and
condition 3 is what `Send`/`Sync` enforce for interior mutability. A data race
needs aliasing plus mutation without synchronization, and safe Rust never gives
you all three at once.

A **race condition** is a different and broader thing: the program's result
depends on the timing of threads, even though every individual access is
properly synchronized. Rust does **not** prevent race conditions. An example
with atomics, which cannot data race:

```rust
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::Mutex;
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    // RACE CONDITION (but no data race): load and store are each atomic, yet
    // another thread can update the value in between them.
    let racy = AtomicU64::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..8 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    let v = racy.load(Ordering::Relaxed);    // read
                    racy.store(v + 1, Ordering::Relaxed);    // write (may overwrite others)
                }
            });
        }
    });
    println!("racy:   {}", racy.load(Ordering::Relaxed));   // usually far below 800000

    // Fix 1: make the read-modify-write a single atomic operation.
    let atomic = AtomicU64::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..8 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                for _ in 0..100_000 {
                    atomic.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            });
        }
    });
    println!("atomic: {}", atomic.load(Ordering::Relaxed));  // 800000

    // Fix 2: check-then-act under one lock, so no thread can interleave.
    let seats = Mutex::new(3u32);
    let booked = AtomicU64::new(0);
    thread::scope(|s| {
        for _ in 0..10 {
            s.spawn(|| {
                let mut free = seats.lock().unwrap();   // check AND act while locked
                if *free > 0 {
                    *free -= 1;
                    booked.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                }
            });
        }
    });
    println!("booked: {}", booked.load(Ordering::Relaxed));  // 3, never more
}
```

| | Data race | Race condition |
| - | --------- | -------------- |
| Definition | Unsynchronized concurrent access with a write | Result depends on thread timing |
| Consequence | Undefined behavior (C/C++); impossible in safe Rust | Wrong but well-defined results |
| Example | Two threads doing `*p += 1` through raw pointers | Atomic `load` then `store`, or check-then-act |
| Prevented by Rust | Yes, in safe code | No |
| Fix | Synchronization (locks, atomics) | Make the whole logical operation atomic |

When `unsafe` code is involved, tools can find data races at run time:
**Miri** (Chapter 14) detects them in interpreted test runs, and the
**ThreadSanitizer** (`RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=thread"` on nightly) instruments
compiled code to catch them.

> Key Takeaways
> - A data race is two unsynchronized concurrent accesses to the same location,
>   at least one a write; in C/C++ it is undefined behavior.
> - Safe Rust is data-race-free: aliasing XOR mutability plus `Send`/`Sync` rule
>   out every case.
> - Race conditions (timing-dependent logic, such as check-then-act) remain
>   possible even with atomics and locks.
> - Fix race conditions by making the whole logical operation atomic: a single
>   read-modify-write instruction, or one critical section.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the racy counter several times and record the results. Then explain
>    why every result is still a value some thread actually wrote, and not
>    garbage.
> 2. Write a "withdraw if balance is sufficient" function using two separate
>    `lock()` calls (one to check, one to subtract) and show with many threads
>    that the balance can go negative. Fix it.
> 3. Interview: Is a program that uses only atomics with `Ordering::Relaxed`
>    free of data races? Is it free of race conditions? (Hint: apply the
>    three-part definition, then think about invariants that span two atomics.)

<a id="105-data-parallelism"></a>
### 10.5 Data Parallelism

Data parallelism applies the same operation to many pieces of data at once:
transforming every pixel, hashing every file, summing every row. This section
covers Rayon, the de facto standard library for it, the work-stealing scheduler
behind it, parallel sorting and reduction, thread pools in general, and how to
measure whether parallelism actually helped.

#### Rayon Parallel Iterators

Manually splitting work across threads is repetitive and easy to get wrong: you
must choose chunk sizes, spawn threads, collect results in the right order, and
balance the load when some items are slower than others. Most of the time the
work has a simple shape: "do this to every element". Iterators (Chapter 6)
already describe that shape for sequential code.

**Rayon** (`rayon` crate) turns iterator pipelines into parallel ones with a
one-word change: `iter()` becomes `par_iter()`. Rayon splits the input,
schedules the pieces on a global pool of worker threads (one per CPU core by
default), and combines the results. Because closures passed to it must be
`Send + Sync` where they are shared, the same compile-time checks from section
10.4 apply: if a parallel pipeline compiles, it has no data races.

Think of a stack of exam papers to grade. Sequentially, one teacher grades them
all. With Rayon, the stack is split among all available teachers, who pick up
more papers whenever they finish, and the grades are collected in the original
order at the end.

| Sequential | Parallel (Rayon) | Item type |
| ---------- | ---------------- | --------- |
| `v.iter()` | `v.par_iter()` | `&T` |
| `v.iter_mut()` | `v.par_iter_mut()` | `&mut T` |
| `v.into_iter()` | `v.into_par_iter()` | `T` |
| `(0..n)` | `(0..n).into_par_iter()` | integers |
| `v.chunks(k)` | `v.par_chunks(k)` | `&[T]` |
| any `Iterator` | `iter.par_bridge()` | unordered, from a sequential source |

Most adapters you know have parallel counterparts: `map`, `filter`,
`filter_map`, `flat_map`, `for_each`, `sum`, `min_by_key`, `any`, `all`,
`find_any`, `count`, `collect`. Two behaviors differ from sequential iterators:

- **Order of side effects is unspecified.** `for_each(|x| println!(..))` prints
  in any order. Results from `collect` on indexed sources (`Vec`, slices,
  ranges) **are** in the original order.
- **`find_any` replaces `find`** when any match will do; `find_first` exists
  but has to wait for earlier items.

```rust
// Cargo.toml: rayon = "1"
use rayon::prelude::*;                      // brings par_iter() and friends into scope

fn is_prime(n: u64) -> bool {
    n >= 2 && (2..).take_while(|d| d * d <= n).all(|d| n % d != 0)
}

fn main() {
    let numbers: Vec<u64> = (1..=2_000_000).collect();

    // Same pipeline as the sequential version, with par_iter().
    let primes = numbers.par_iter().filter(|&&n| is_prime(n)).count();
    println!("{primes} primes");            // 148933 primes

    // collect keeps the original order for indexed sources.
    let squares: Vec<u64> = (1..=5u64).into_par_iter().map(|x| x * x).collect();
    println!("{squares:?}");                // [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

    // In-place parallel mutation: each element is touched by exactly one thread.
    let mut pixels = vec![100u8; 1_000_000];
    pixels.par_iter_mut().for_each(|p| *p = p.saturating_add(50));
    println!("{}", pixels[123_456]);        // 150

    // Chunks: per-chunk work with less per-item overhead.
    let checksums: Vec<u32> = numbers
        .par_chunks(100_000)
        .map(|c| c.iter().fold(0u32, |acc, &x| acc.wrapping_add(x as u32)))
        .collect();
    println!("{} chunks", checksums.len()); // 20 chunks

    // Short-circuiting: stops other workers once a match is found.
    let big = numbers.par_iter().find_any(|&&n| n > 1_999_990 && is_prime(n));
    println!("{big:?}");                    // Some(1999993) (the only one in range)

    // Captured state must be thread-safe; this is checked at compile time.
    // let mut total = 0;
    // numbers.par_iter().for_each(|n| total += n);
    // error[E0596]: cannot borrow `total` as mutable, as it is a captured
    //               variable in a `Fn` closure
}
```

Rayon is for **CPU-bound** work. Blocking I/O inside a parallel iterator ties up
pool threads that could be computing, and async code (Chapter 11) has its own
executors. Also, parallelism has overhead: for a few thousand cheap operations,
the sequential version is often faster (see "Measuring Parallel Speedup").

> Key Takeaways
> - Rayon turns iterator pipelines parallel by swapping `iter()` for
>   `par_iter()` (or `into_par_iter`, `par_iter_mut`, `par_chunks`).
> - The `Send`/`Sync` bounds on its closures mean a compiling Rayon pipeline is
>   free of data races.
> - `collect` preserves order for indexed sources; side effects such as printing
>   happen in any order.
> - Use it for CPU-bound work with enough items to amortize the overhead.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the number of words in each of 10,000 generated strings in
>    parallel and collect the counts into a `Vec<usize>` in input order.
> 2. Parallelize a function that converts an RGB image (`Vec<[u8; 3]>`) to
>    grayscale in place with `par_iter_mut`.
> 3. Interview: Why does `numbers.par_iter().for_each(|n| total += n)` fail to
>    compile while the sequential version compiles? (Hint: which closure trait
>    does `for_each` require in Rayon, and why must the closure be shareable
>    between threads?)

#### Work Stealing

Splitting work evenly sounds easy until items differ in cost. If eight threads
each get one eighth of an array, but one eighth contains the expensive items,
seven threads finish early and sit idle while the eighth works alone. Static
splitting also cannot adapt to a machine that is busy with other programs.

Rayon uses **work stealing** to balance load dynamically. Each worker thread
has its own **double-ended queue (deque)** of tasks. A worker pushes new tasks
onto the bottom of its own deque and pops from the bottom (most recent first,
which keeps data warm in its cache). When a worker runs out of tasks, it picks
another worker at random and **steals** from the **top** of that worker's deque,
taking the oldest and therefore usually largest piece of work.

The analogy is a team of cooks, each with their own order rail. Cooks work on
their own orders, but a cook with an empty rail walks over and takes the oldest
ticket from a busy colleague's rail.

```text
   Worker 1 deque         Worker 2 deque          Worker 3 deque (empty)
   top    [ 0..500K ]  <────────────── steal ───────────  idle: steals oldest,
          [ 500K..750K]                                    largest task from W1
   bottom [ 750K..1M ]  ← W1 pops own work here
```

The core primitive is `rayon::join(a, b)`. It runs closure `a` on the current
thread and pushes `b` onto the current worker's deque, where an idle worker may
steal it. If nobody steals `b` before `a` finishes, the current thread runs `b`
itself, so an unstolen `join` costs little more than two function calls.
Parallel iterators are built by recursively splitting the input in halves with
`join` until the pieces are small, which gives work stealing a supply of tasks
of every size.

```rust
// Cargo.toml: rayon = "1"
use rayon::join;

// Divide and conquer: sum a slice by recursively splitting it.
fn par_sum(v: &[u64]) -> u64 {
    if v.len() <= 10_000 {
        return v.iter().sum();              // small enough: do it sequentially
    }
    let (left, right) = v.split_at(v.len() / 2);
    let (a, b) = join(|| par_sum(left), || par_sum(right));   // b may be stolen
    a + b
}

// Uneven work: cost grows with the index, so static splitting would be unbalanced.
fn work(i: u64) -> u64 {
    (0..i % 5_000).fold(i, |acc, x| acc.wrapping_mul(31).wrapping_add(x))
}

fn main() {
    let v: Vec<u64> = (1..=10_000_000).collect();
    println!("{}", par_sum(&v));            // 50000005000000

    use rayon::prelude::*;
    let par = (0..200_000u64).into_par_iter().map(work).reduce(|| 0, u64::wrapping_add);
    let seq = (0..200_000u64).map(work).fold(0, u64::wrapping_add);
    println!("{}", par == seq);             // true: same result, balanced by stealing

    // join returns both results; the closures may borrow local data.
    let text = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    let (words, vowels) = join(
        || text.split_whitespace().count(),
        || text.chars().filter(|c| "aeiou".contains(*c)).count(),
    );
    println!("{words} words, {vowels} vowels");   // 9 words, 11 vowels
}
```

Work stealing gives Rayon two important properties: **load balancing** is
automatic even for irregular workloads, and **nested parallelism** composes. A
parallel iterator whose closure itself uses `par_iter` simply adds more tasks
to the deques instead of oversubscribing the machine with extra threads.

> Key Takeaways
> - Each Rayon worker has its own deque; idle workers steal the oldest (largest)
>   task from a random busy worker.
> - `rayon::join(a, b)` makes `b` available for stealing while running `a`; if
>   not stolen, the same thread runs `b` cheaply.
> - Recursive splitting plus stealing balances irregular workloads
>   automatically and lets parallel code nest safely.
> - Stop splitting below a threshold, where sequential work is cheaper than task
>   overhead.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement parallel merge sort with `rayon::join`, falling back to
>    `sort_unstable` below 4,096 elements. Compare with `slice::sort`.
> 2. Write a recursive parallel Fibonacci with `join` and measure how the
>    sequential threshold affects run time.
> 3. Interview: Why does a worker take tasks from the bottom of its own deque
>    but steal from the top of others? (Hint: think about cache locality and
>    which tasks are likely to be large.)

#### Parallel Sorting and Reduction

Two operations dominate data processing: **sorting** and **reducing** (combining
many values into one, such as sum, max, histogram, or merged map). Both
parallelize well, but reduction comes with a mathematical requirement that is
easy to overlook.

**Sorting.** Rayon adds parallel versions of the slice sorts through
`ParallelSliceMut`: `par_sort` (stable), `par_sort_unstable` (usually faster),
and the `_by` and `_by_key` variants. They split the slice, sort the parts on
different workers, and merge. For millions of elements the speedup is often
several times on a multi-core machine; for small slices the sequential sort is
faster.

**Reduction.** A parallel reduction combines partial results computed on
different threads, in an order that depends on how the work was split and
stolen. That only gives a correct answer if the combining operation is:

- **associative**: `(a op b) op c == a op (b op c)`, so grouping does not
  matter, and
- given an **identity** element (`0` for addition, `1` for multiplication, an
  empty map for merging), because Rayon may start a new partial result on any
  worker.

Rayon's `reduce(identity, op)` takes both explicitly. The more flexible pair is
**`fold` + `reduce`**: `fold` builds one accumulator per split (of any type, for
example a `HashMap`), and `reduce` merges those accumulators. Picture a vote
count: each polling station tallies its own ballots (`fold`), and headquarters
adds up the station tallies (`reduce`).

```text
   items:    [a b c d | e f g h | i j k l]     split among workers
   fold:      acc1      acc2      acc3          each worker builds its own
   reduce:      \_ merge _/        |            merge in any grouping
                     \____ merge __/            -> final result
```

```rust
// Cargo.toml: rayon = "1"
use rayon::prelude::*;
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Order {
    id: u32,
    customer: &'static str,
    amount: u64,                            // cents
}

fn main() {
    // Parallel sorting
    let mut data: Vec<u64> =
        (0..5_000_000u64).map(|x| x.wrapping_mul(2654435761) % 1_000_003).collect();
    data.par_sort_unstable();
    println!("sorted: {}", data.windows(2).all(|w| w[0] <= w[1]));   // sorted: true

    let customers = ["ana", "ben", "cy"];
    let mut orders: Vec<Order> = (0..300_000u32)
        .map(|id| Order {
            id,
            customer: customers[id as usize % 3],
            amount: (id as u64 % 97) * 100,
        })
        .collect();
    orders.par_sort_by_key(|o| std::cmp::Reverse(o.amount));   // stable: ties keep id order
    println!("top order id {}", orders[0].id);   // top order id 96

    // Built-in reductions
    let total: u64 = orders.par_iter().map(|o| o.amount).sum();
    let biggest = orders.par_iter().max_by_key(|o| o.amount).unwrap();
    println!("total {total}, max {}", biggest.amount);   // total 1439920200, max 9600

    // reduce with identity: the operation must be associative.
    let max_amount = orders.par_iter().map(|o| o.amount).reduce(|| 0, u64::max);
    println!("{max_amount}");               // 9600

    // fold + reduce: per-thread HashMaps, then merge them.
    let per_customer: HashMap<&str, u64> = orders
        .par_iter()
        .fold(HashMap::new, |mut acc, o| {  // one map per split, no locking
            *acc.entry(o.customer).or_insert(0) += o.amount;
            acc
        })
        .reduce(HashMap::new, |mut a, b| {  // merge maps pairwise
            for (k, v) in b {
                *a.entry(k).or_insert(0) += v;
            }
            a
        });
    let mut rows: Vec<_> = per_customer.into_iter().collect();
    rows.sort();
    println!("{rows:?}");
    // [("ana", 479974100), ("ben", 479973400), ("cy", 479972700)]
}
```

Floating-point addition is **not** associative: `(1e20 + 1.0) - 1e20` is `0.0`,
but `1e20 - 1e20 + 1.0` is `1.0`. A parallel `sum` of `f64` values can therefore
differ in the last bits from the sequential sum, and from one run to the next.
When reproducibility matters, sum integers (for example cents), use a
compensated algorithm, or sort and sum sequentially.

| Operation | Associative? | Identity | Safe for parallel `reduce` |
| --------- | ------------ | -------- | -------------------------- |
| Integer `+`, `*` | Yes | `0`, `1` | Yes (watch for overflow) |
| `min`, `max` | Yes | Max/min value of the type | Yes |
| String concatenation | Yes (not commutative) | `""` | Yes; Rayon preserves order for indexed sources |
| Set/map union | Yes | Empty collection | Yes |
| Floating-point `+` | No | `0.0` | Approximately; results may vary slightly |
| Subtraction, average | No | none | No (compute sum and count instead) |

> Key Takeaways
> - `par_sort`, `par_sort_unstable`, and their `_by_key` variants are drop-in
>   parallel sorts for large slices.
> - Parallel reduction requires an associative operation and an identity;
>   `reduce(identity, op)` makes both explicit.
> - `fold` + `reduce` builds per-thread accumulators and then merges them,
>   avoiding locks entirely.
> - Floating-point sums are not associative, so parallel results can differ
>   slightly; use integers or compensated sums when exactness matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute a word-frequency histogram of a large text in parallel with
>    `fold` + `reduce`, and check it against a sequential version.
> 2. Compute the mean and standard deviation of ten million `f64` values in a
>    single parallel pass by reducing `(count, sum, sum_of_squares)` tuples.
> 3. Interview: Why is a lock-protected shared `HashMap` updated inside
>    `for_each` usually much slower than `fold` + `reduce`? (Hint: count how
>    many times a lock is taken, and think about contention between cores.)

#### Thread Pools

Spawning a fresh OS thread for every small task wastes time (creation costs
microseconds) and, under load, creates more threads than the machine has cores,
which then compete for CPU time and memory. A **thread pool** creates a fixed
set of worker threads once and feeds them tasks through a queue. The workers
stay alive between tasks, so the per-task cost drops to "push a closure onto a
queue", and the number of threads stays bounded.

A taxi rank is the analogy: rather than buying a new car for every passenger,
a fixed fleet of taxis waits at the rank and each one takes the next passenger
in line.

Rayon maintains a **global pool** that its parallel iterators use
automatically. Its size defaults to the number of logical CPUs and can be set
with the `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` environment variable or `ThreadPoolBuilder::
build_global` (once, at startup). For isolation, for example to stop one
subsystem from monopolizing every core, build a **custom pool** and run work in
it with `install`; every parallel iterator inside the closure uses that pool.

```rust
// Cargo.toml: rayon = "1"
use rayon::prelude::*;
use rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder;

fn main() {
    println!("global pool threads: {}", rayon::current_num_threads());   // e.g. 12

    // A dedicated pool with 2 named threads.
    let pool = ThreadPoolBuilder::new()
        .num_threads(2)
        .thread_name(|i| format!("img-worker-{i}"))
        .build()
        .expect("failed to build pool");

    let sum: u64 = pool.install(|| {
        // Every Rayon operation in here runs on `pool`, not the global pool.
        println!("inside: {}", rayon::current_num_threads());   // inside: 2
        (1..=1_000_000u64).into_par_iter().sum()
    });
    println!("{sum}");                      // 500000500000

    // Fire-and-forget tasks with a scope: tasks may borrow local data.
    let mut results = vec![0u64; 4];
    pool.scope(|s| {
        for (i, slot) in results.iter_mut().enumerate() {
            s.spawn(move |_| *slot = (i as u64 + 1) * 100);
        }
    });                                     // waits for all spawned tasks
    println!("{results:?}");                // [100, 200, 300, 400]
}
```

Understanding a pool is easier after building one. The minimal design is a
channel of boxed closures shared by N workers. Because `mpsc::Receiver` has a
single consumer, the workers share it through `Arc<Mutex<Receiver<Job>>>`, and
dropping the sender shuts the pool down gracefully:

```rust
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread::{self, JoinHandle};

type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;

pub struct ThreadPool {
    sender: Option<Sender<Job>>,
    workers: Vec<JoinHandle<()>>,
}

impl ThreadPool {
    pub fn new(size: usize) -> Self {
        assert!(size > 0);
        let (sender, receiver) = mpsc::channel::<Job>();
        let receiver: Arc<Mutex<Receiver<Job>>> = Arc::new(Mutex::new(receiver));
        let workers = (0..size)
            .map(|_| {
                let rx = Arc::clone(&receiver);
                thread::spawn(move || loop {
                    // The guard is a temporary, so the lock is released before
                    // the job runs: other workers can take jobs meanwhile.
                    let msg = rx.lock().unwrap().recv();
                    match msg {
                        Ok(job) => job(),
                        Err(_) => break,     // channel closed: shut down
                    }
                })
            })
            .collect();
        ThreadPool { sender: Some(sender), workers }
    }

    pub fn execute<F: FnOnce() + Send + 'static>(&self, f: F) {
        self.sender.as_ref().unwrap().send(Box::new(f)).unwrap();
    }
}

impl Drop for ThreadPool {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        drop(self.sender.take());           // close the channel...
        for w in self.workers.drain(..) {
            w.join().unwrap();              // ...and wait for workers to finish
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
    {
        let pool = ThreadPool::new(3);
        for i in 0..6u64 {
            let tx = tx.clone();
            pool.execute(move || tx.send(i * i).unwrap());
        }
    }                                       // pool dropped: all jobs completed
    drop(tx);
    let mut out: Vec<u64> = rx.iter().collect();
    out.sort();
    println!("{out:?}");                    // [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
}
```

| Pool | Best for | Notes |
| ---- | -------- | ----- |
| Rayon global pool | CPU-bound data parallelism | Work stealing; avoid blocking calls inside |
| Rayon custom `ThreadPool` | Isolating CPU-heavy subsystems | `install`, `scope`, `spawn` |
| Hand-written channel pool | Learning; simple background jobs | Single shared queue, no stealing |
| Async runtime (Tokio) | Many I/O-bound tasks | Plus `spawn_blocking` for blocking work (Chapter 11) |

Size pools for their workload: CPU-bound pools near the number of cores (more
threads only add switching), I/O-bound pools larger, because their threads spend
most of their time waiting.

> Key Takeaways
> - A thread pool reuses a fixed set of threads, cutting per-task cost and
>   bounding the number of threads.
> - Rayon's global pool serves all parallel iterators; `ThreadPoolBuilder` plus
>   `install` runs work on a dedicated pool.
> - A basic pool is a channel of `Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send>` jobs shared by
>   workers; dropping the sender shuts it down.
> - Size CPU-bound pools to the core count; never block a CPU pool's threads on
>   I/O.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend the hand-written `ThreadPool` so that `execute` returns a
>    `Receiver<T>` for the job's result (a minimal future).
> 2. Run two CPU-heavy Rayon computations concurrently, one in a 2-thread pool
>    and one in the global pool, and observe with `current_num_threads` which
>    pool each uses.
> 3. Interview: In the hand-written pool, why is `let msg = rx.lock().unwrap().recv();`
>    written as a separate statement instead of
>    `while let Ok(job) = rx.lock().unwrap().recv() { job() }`? (Hint: how long
>    does the temporary `MutexGuard` live in each version?)

#### Measuring Parallel Speedup

Parallel code is more complex than sequential code, and it is only worth that
complexity if it is actually faster. Intuition is unreliable here: doubling the
cores rarely halves the time, and sometimes a parallel version is slower. The
only way to know is to measure, and to understand the limits that theory
predicts.

**Speedup** is `S(n) = T(1) / T(n)`, the sequential time divided by the time
with `n` threads. **Efficiency** is `S(n) / n`, how well each extra core is used.
The ceiling is given by **Amdahl's law**: if a fraction `p` of the work can run
in parallel and the rest is sequential, then

```text
   S(n) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)          and as n -> infinity:  S = 1 / (1 - p)

   p = 0.90:  n=2 -> 1.82x   n=4 -> 3.08x   n=8 -> 4.71x   n=16 -> 6.40x   max 10x
   p = 0.99:  n=2 -> 1.98x   n=4 -> 3.88x   n=8 -> 7.48x   n=16 -> 13.9x   max 100x
```

Even 10% sequential work caps the speedup at 10x, no matter how many cores you
add. A highway is the analogy: adding lanes speeds up the open road, but if
every car must pass through a single-lane toll booth, the booth sets the limit.

Real programs fall short of Amdahl's ideal for further reasons:

| Limiting factor | Symptom | Remedy |
| --------------- | ------- | ------ |
| Task overhead | Parallel slower on small inputs | Larger chunks, `with_min_len`, sequential cutoff |
| Memory bandwidth | Simple loops stop scaling at a few cores | Do more work per byte; improve locality |
| Contention (locks, shared atomics) | Adding threads makes it slower | `fold`/`reduce`, per-thread state |
| False sharing | Per-thread counters next to each other are slow | Pad to separate cache lines |
| Load imbalance | Some cores idle at the end | Smaller tasks, work stealing |
| Other processes, frequency scaling | Noisy, unstable numbers | Repeat runs, quiet machine |

```rust
// Cargo.toml: rayon = "1"
// Run with: cargo run --release   (debug builds make timing meaningless)
use rayon::prelude::*;
use std::hint::black_box;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

fn heavy(x: u64) -> u64 {
    (0..200).fold(x, |acc, i| acc.wrapping_mul(6364136223846793005).wrapping_add(i))
}

// Best of several runs reduces noise from the OS and CPU frequency changes.
fn best_of<F: FnMut() -> u64>(runs: usize, mut f: F) -> Duration {
    (0..runs)
        .map(|_| {
            let t = Instant::now();
            black_box(f());                 // stop the optimizer deleting the work
            t.elapsed()
        })
        .min()
        .unwrap()
}

fn main() {
    let threads = rayon::current_num_threads();
    for n in [1_000u64, 100_000, 5_000_000] {
        let seq = best_of(5, || (0..n).map(heavy).fold(0, u64::wrapping_add));
        let par = best_of(5, || {
            (0..n).into_par_iter().map(heavy).reduce(|| 0, u64::wrapping_add)
        });
        let speedup = seq.as_secs_f64() / par.as_secs_f64();
        let efficiency = 100.0 * speedup / threads as f64;
        println!(
            "n = {n:>9}: seq {seq:>10.2?}  par {par:>10.2?}  \
             speedup {speedup:5.2}x  efficiency {efficiency:3.0}%"
        );
    }
    // One run on a 12-thread machine (numbers vary by hardware):
    //   n =      1000: seq  20.41µs  par   2.47ms  speedup 0.01x  (overhead dominates)
    //   n =    100000: seq   1.98ms  par 916.49µs  speedup 2.16x
    //   n =   5000000: seq  98.40ms  par  20.07ms  speedup 4.90x  (efficiency 41%)
}
```

A disciplined measuring routine:

1. **Build in release mode** and measure the code path that matters, with
   realistic input sizes.
2. **Establish a sequential baseline** using the best sequential algorithm, not
   the parallel code run on one thread.
3. **Repeat runs** and report the minimum or median; use a benchmarking
   harness such as `criterion` (Chapter 12) for statistically sound results.
4. **Scale the thread count** (`RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1,2,4,...`) and plot speedup.
   A curve that flattens early suggests a sequential fraction or a memory
   bottleneck; a curve that drops suggests contention.
5. **Profile** (`perf`, flame graphs) to see where time goes before optimizing.

> Key Takeaways
> - Speedup is `T(1) / T(n)`; efficiency is speedup per core.
> - Amdahl's law caps speedup at `1 / (1 - p)`: the sequential fraction
>   dominates as cores increase.
> - Overhead, memory bandwidth, contention, false sharing, and imbalance push
>   real results below the ideal.
> - Measure release builds against a good sequential baseline, repeat runs, and
>   scale the thread count to understand the curve.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the benchmark with `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` set to 1, 2, 4, and 8 and
>    tabulate speedup and efficiency for the largest input. Estimate `p` from
>    your numbers using Amdahl's law.
> 2. Replace `heavy` with a function that does almost no work (`x ^ 1`) and
>    explain why the speedup collapses.
> 3. Interview: A team parallelized a step that takes 30% of a request's time,
>    on an 8-core server. What is the best possible overall improvement, and
>    what would you look at next? (Hint: apply Amdahl's law with `p = 0.3`.)

## 11. Asynchronous Rust

Many programs spend most of their time waiting: for a socket to deliver bytes,
a database to answer, or a timer to fire. Dedicating an OS thread to each wait
(Chapter 10) stops scaling at a few thousand connections, while async Rust lets
one thread juggle hundreds of thousands of waiting tasks with very little memory
per task. This chapter explains how futures work under the hood, how runtimes
such as Tokio drive them, how to compose concurrent operations, and the sharp
edges (pinning, `Send` bounds, cancellation) that make async Rust powerful but
demanding.

<a id="111-async-fundamentals"></a>
### 11.1 Async Fundamentals

Async Rust is built from a small number of language features and one central
trait. This section covers the syntax, the `Future` trait, the polling and
waking protocol, the compiler's state machine transformation, and why futures
do nothing until something drives them.

#### async/await Syntax

Consider a server handling 10,000 clients. With one thread per client, each
thread spends almost all of its life blocked in `read()`, yet it still costs a
stack (typically 2–8 MiB of reserved address space) and a kernel scheduling
entry. What we really want is to say "start reading from this socket, and while
the data is not there yet, go do something useful elsewhere". Writing that by
hand with callbacks or explicit state machines is tedious and error-prone.

`async`/`await` lets you write code that *looks* sequential but can pause at
well-defined points without blocking the thread:

- **`async fn`** declares a function whose body can pause. Calling it does not
  run the body. It returns a **future**: a value representing a computation
  that will eventually produce a result.
- **`.await`** is applied to a future inside an async context. It means "run
  this future to completion; if it is not ready yet, pause *me* and let the
  thread do other work until it is".
- **`async { ... }`** blocks create an anonymous future inline, like a closure
  creates an anonymous function. `async move { ... }` takes ownership of the
  variables it captures.

An analogy: a waiter in a restaurant (the thread) takes an order to the kitchen
(starts an I/O operation). Instead of standing at the kitchen door until the
dish is ready, the waiter serves other tables and comes back when the kitchen
rings the bell. `.await` is the point where the waiter is allowed to walk away.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;

// Returns `impl Future<Output = u32>`, not `u32`.
async fn fetch_score(player: &str) -> u32 {
    // Simulated I/O: the task pauses here without blocking the thread.
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
    player.len() as u32 * 10
}

async fn total(players: &[&str]) -> u32 {
    let mut sum = 0;
    for p in players {
        sum += fetch_score(p).await;        // await: pause until the score is ready
    }
    sum
}

#[tokio::main]                              // starts a runtime that drives `main`
async fn main() {
    let t = total(&["ana", "bo"]).await;
    println!("total = {t}");                // total = 50

    // An async block: a future written inline.
    let name = String::from("carla");
    let fut = async move {                  // `move` takes ownership of `name`
        fetch_score(&name).await + 1
    };
    println!("{}", fut.await);              // 51
}
```

The signature `async fn fetch_score(player: &str) -> u32` is shorthand for:

```rust
use std::future::Future;

// The returned future borrows `player`, so it captures the lifetime 'a.
fn fetch_score<'a>(player: &'a str) -> impl Future<Output = u32> + 'a {
    async move { player.len() as u32 * 10 }
}
```

A few rules follow from this design:

| Rule | Consequence |
| ---- | ----------- |
| `.await` is only allowed inside `async fn` or `async` blocks | Synchronous code cannot await; it must hand the future to a runtime |
| `main` cannot be `async` by itself | Use `#[tokio::main]` (or similar), which wraps `main` in a runtime |
| An `async fn` that borrows arguments returns a future that borrows them too | The future cannot outlive its arguments (relevant when spawning) |
| `?` works inside async code | It returns early from the future with the error |
| Recursion needs indirection | `Box::pin(recurse(n - 1)).await` (allowed since Rust 1.77) |

Since Rust 1.85, **async closures** (`async |x| { ... }`) are stable, together
with the `AsyncFn`, `AsyncFnMut`, and `AsyncFnOnce` traits. Unlike a closure
returning an `async` block, an async closure's future may borrow from the
closure's own captures:

```rust
async fn call_twice(f: impl AsyncFn(u32) -> u32) -> u32 {
    f(1).await + f(2).await
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let offset = 10;
    let r = call_twice(async |x| x + offset).await;  // borrows `offset`
    println!("{r}");                                 // 23
}
```

Finally, `.await` works on anything that implements `IntoFuture`, not only on
`Future`. Builder-style APIs use this so that `client.get(url).timeout(t).await`
sends the request when awaited, without a final `.send()` call.

> Key Takeaways
> - `async fn` and `async` blocks produce futures; calling them does not run the
>   body.
> - `.await` drives a future to completion, pausing the current task (not the
>   thread) while it is not ready.
> - `async fn f(x: &T) -> U` desugars to `fn f<'a>(x: &'a T) -> impl Future<Output = U> + 'a`.
> - A runtime is required to start the top-level future; `#[tokio::main]`
>   provides one.
> - Async closures (`async |x| ...`) and the `AsyncFn*` traits are stable since
>   Rust 1.85.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `async fn double_after(ms: u64, x: i32) -> i32` that sleeps and
>    then returns `x * 2`. Call it three times in sequence from `main` and print
>    the elapsed time.
> 2. Rewrite `async fn len_of(s: &str) -> usize` as a plain `fn` that returns
>    `impl Future`, spelling out the lifetime. Then try to return the future
>    from a function that creates the `String` locally and explain the compiler
>    error.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `async fn` returning `T` and a
>    normal function returning `impl Future<Output = T>`? When would you
>    prefer the second form? (Hint: think about running code eagerly before the
>    future is created, and about adding bounds like `+ Send`.)

#### The Future Trait

Every async computation in Rust, whether written with `async` or by hand, is a
type implementing one trait from the standard library:

```rust
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

pub trait Future {
    type Output;                            // what the computation produces

    // Try to make progress. Never blocks.
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>;
}

pub enum Poll<T> {
    Ready(T),                               // finished, here is the value
    Pending,                                // not finished; I will ask to be woken
}
```

Why a *poll* model instead of callbacks (as in JavaScript or older C#)? With
callbacks, the operation pushes its result into a closure, which usually forces
heap allocation and shared ownership of the continuation. With polling, the
*caller* asks "are you done yet?" and the future answers. That allows futures
to be plain values on the stack or inside other futures, combined without
allocation, which is why Rust's async is a zero-cost abstraction.

The three pieces of the signature each have a job:

| Piece | Purpose |
| ----- | ------- |
| `type Output` | The value produced when the future completes |
| `self: Pin<&mut Self>` | Guarantees the future will not move in memory once polled (section 11.4) |
| `cx: &mut Context<'_>` | Carries the `Waker` the future must use to request another poll |

Writing a future by hand shows that there is no magic. This one completes
after being polled a fixed number of times:

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

struct Countdown {
    remaining: u32,
}

impl Future for Countdown {
    type Output = &'static str;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        if self.remaining == 0 {
            return Poll::Ready("liftoff");
        }
        self.remaining -= 1;                // Countdown is Unpin, so we can mutate freely
        // We are not done, but nothing external will wake us,
        // so we ask to be polled again right away.
        cx.waker().wake_by_ref();
        Poll::Pending
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let msg = Countdown { remaining: 3 }.await;   // polled 4 times in total
    println!("{msg}");                             // liftoff
}
```

The standard library also provides small building blocks so that you rarely
need a full `impl Future`:

```rust
use std::future::{self, Future};
use std::task::Poll;

async fn building_blocks() {
    let a = future::ready(5).await;                   // immediately ready
    let mut n = 0;
    let b = future::poll_fn(|cx| {                    // a future from a closure
        n += 1;
        if n < 3 {
            cx.waker().wake_by_ref();
            Poll::Pending
        } else {
            Poll::Ready(n)
        }
    })
    .await;
    println!("{a} {b}");                               // 5 3
    // future::pending::<()>().await would never complete.
}

fn takes_any_future(f: impl Future<Output = i32>) -> impl Future<Output = i32> {
    async move { f.await * 2 }                        // futures compose as values
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A future is any type implementing `Future`, with an `Output` type and a
>   `poll` method returning `Poll::Ready(value)` or `Poll::Pending`.
> - `poll` must never block; it either makes progress or reports `Pending`.
> - The pull-based design lets futures nest inside each other without heap
>   allocation.
> - `std::future::ready`, `poll_fn`, and `pending` cover many small cases
>   without a hand-written type.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a future `YieldOnce` that returns `Pending` the first time it is
>    polled (after waking itself) and `Ready(())` the second time.
> 2. Implement `struct Map<F, G> { fut: F, f: Option<G> }` that applies `G` to
>    the output of `F`. Restrict it to `F: Future + Unpin` and use
>    `Pin::new(&mut self.fut)` to poll the inner future.
> 3. Interview: Why did Rust choose a poll-based (pull) future model rather
>    than the callback-based (push) model used by JavaScript promises? (Hint:
>    compare allocations, ownership of the continuation, and how cancellation
>    works.)

#### Poll and Wakers

If `poll` returns `Pending`, who decides when to poll again? Polling in a tight
loop would burn a CPU core for nothing. Instead, Rust uses a contract:

> A future that returns `Poll::Pending` must have arranged for the `Waker` in
> the current `Context` to be called when progress is possible.

The `Waker` is a handle supplied by the executor. Calling `waker.wake()` tells
the executor "the task that owns this future is worth polling again". The
executor then puts the task back in its run queue. Think of a restaurant pager:
you register your pager (the waker) at the counter and sit down. You do not
keep asking whether your food is ready; the pager buzzes when it is.

```text
  executor                     future                    event source
     │  poll(cx)                 │                            │
     ├──────────────────────────>│ not ready:                 │
     │                           │ store cx.waker().clone() ──>│ (timer, socket,
     │<──────── Pending ─────────┤                            │  other thread)
     │  (task parked, thread     │                            │
     │   runs other tasks)       │                            │
     │                           │          event happens     │
     │<──────────────────── waker.wake() ─────────────────────┤
     │  poll(cx)                 │                            │
     ├──────────────────────────>│ ready                      │
     │<─────── Ready(value) ─────┤                            │
```

The following future completes after a delay measured by a helper thread. It
shows the full protocol: shared state, storing the latest waker, and waking
from another thread.

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Waker};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

struct Shared {
    done: bool,
    waker: Option<Waker>,
}

pub struct Delay {
    shared: Arc<Mutex<Shared>>,
    duration: Duration,
    started: bool,
}

impl Delay {
    pub fn new(duration: Duration) -> Self {
        let shared = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Shared { done: false, waker: None }));
        Delay { shared, duration, started: false }
    }
}

impl Future for Delay {
    type Output = ();

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        let mut state = self.shared.lock().unwrap();
        if state.done {
            return Poll::Ready(());
        }
        // Store the waker from *this* poll: the task may have moved to another
        // executor thread since the last poll, carrying a different waker.
        // will_wake skips the clone when the stored waker is already the same.
        if !state.waker.as_ref().is_some_and(|w| w.will_wake(cx.waker())) {
            state.waker = Some(cx.waker().clone());
        }
        drop(state);                                     // release before mutating self

        if !self.started {
            self.started = true;
            let shared = Arc::clone(&self.shared);
            let duration = self.duration;
            thread::spawn(move || {
                thread::sleep(duration);
                let mut state = shared.lock().unwrap();
                state.done = true;
                if let Some(waker) = state.waker.take() {
                    waker.wake();                        // ask the executor to poll again
                }
            });
        }
        Poll::Pending
    }
}
```

What does the *executor's* side look like? Here is a complete `block_on` that
runs one future on the current thread. Its waker simply unparks the thread:

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::pin;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};
use std::thread::{self, Thread};

struct ThreadWaker(Thread);

impl Wake for ThreadWaker {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {
        self.0.unpark();                    // resume the thread blocked in park()
    }
}

pub fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output {
    let mut fut = pin!(fut);                // pin on the stack (section 11.4)
    let waker = Waker::from(Arc::new(ThreadWaker(thread::current())));
    let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
    loop {
        match fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            Poll::Ready(v) => return v,
            Poll::Pending => thread::park(), // sleep until a waker unparks us
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    // Uses the Delay future defined above: no runtime crate involved.
    block_on(async {
        println!("waiting...");
        Delay::new(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
        println!("done");
    });
}
```

Common waker bugs are subtle because they show up as hangs rather than crashes:

| Bug | Symptom |
| --- | ------- |
| Returning `Pending` without arranging a wake-up | Task hangs forever |
| Storing only the first waker and never updating it | Hangs when the task migrates between threads or is moved by a combinator |
| Waking while still holding a lock the poller needs | Possible deadlock or lost wake-up |
| Calling `wake_by_ref` on every poll for no reason | Busy loop that burns CPU |

> Key Takeaways
> - Returning `Pending` is a promise: the future must ensure its waker will be
>   called when progress becomes possible.
> - The executor provides the `Waker` through `Context`; `wake()` reschedules
>   the task rather than polling it directly.
> - Always store the waker from the latest poll (`will_wake` avoids redundant
>   clones).
> - The `std::task::Wake` trait makes it easy to build wakers from an
>   `Arc<T>`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the `block_on` and `Delay` example. Then remove the `waker.wake()`
>    call in the helper thread and explain what you observe.
> 2. Add a counter to `block_on` that counts how many times the future is
>    polled. How many polls does a `Delay` need, and why is it not exactly one?
> 3. Interview: An engineer's custom future works in tests but occasionally
>    hangs in production on a multi-threaded runtime. The future stores the
>    waker only on its first poll. Explain the bug. (Hint: which waker is valid
>    after the task has been polled from a different context?)

#### State Machine Transformation

How can a function pause in the middle and resume later, without its own
thread and stack? The compiler rewrites every `async fn` into a **state
machine**: an enum with one variant per suspension point (`.await`). Each
variant stores exactly the local variables that are still needed after that
point. The generated `poll` method runs code until the next `.await` that
returns `Pending`, records which variant it is in, and returns.

Consider:

```rust
async fn read_value(n: u32) -> u32 {
    n * 2                                   // imagine real I/O here
}

async fn fetch_twice(a: u32) -> u32 {
    let x = read_value(a).await;            // suspension point 1
    let y = read_value(x).await;            // suspension point 2
    x + y
}
```

The compiler produces something conceptually equivalent to this hand-written
version (the real one is generated directly in MIR and has extra details):

```rust
use std::future::{self, Future, Ready};
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{ready, Context, Poll};

// Stand-in for the anonymous future returned by `read_value`.
fn read_value(n: u32) -> Ready<u32> {
    future::ready(n * 2)
}

enum FetchTwice {
    Start { a: u32 },                               // created, not yet polled
    WaitingFirst { fut: Ready<u32> },               // paused at the first .await
    WaitingSecond { x: u32, fut: Ready<u32> },      // `x` must survive this .await
    Done,
}

impl Future for FetchTwice {
    type Output = u32;

    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<u32> {
        loop {
            match &mut *self {
                FetchTwice::Start { a } => {
                    let fut = read_value(*a);
                    *self = FetchTwice::WaitingFirst { fut };
                }
                FetchTwice::WaitingFirst { fut } => {
                    // ready! returns Poll::Pending early if the inner future is not done
                    let x = ready!(Pin::new(fut).poll(cx));
                    *self = FetchTwice::WaitingSecond { x, fut: read_value(x) };
                }
                FetchTwice::WaitingSecond { x, fut } => {
                    let y = ready!(Pin::new(fut).poll(cx));
                    let result = *x + y;
                    *self = FetchTwice::Done;
                    return Poll::Ready(result);
                }
                FetchTwice::Done => panic!("future polled after completion"),
            }
        }
    }
}

fn fetch_twice(a: u32) -> FetchTwice {
    FetchTwice::Start { a }
}
```

```text
   Start ──poll──> WaitingFirst ──inner Ready──> WaitingSecond ──inner Ready──> Done
                      │   ^                         │   ^
                      └───┘ Pending                 └───┘ Pending
                    (return to executor)          (return to executor)
```

Important consequences:

- **No heap allocation per await.** The whole state lives in one value whose
  size is the size of the largest variant. Nested `async fn` calls nest their
  enums inline, so a whole request handler is often one contiguous struct.
- **Future size can grow large.** A local `[u8; 16384]` buffer that lives
  across an `.await` becomes part of the future. Check sizes with
  `std::mem::size_of_val(&fut)`; box large or deeply nested futures
  (`Box::pin(fut)`) to keep them off the stack.
- **Recursion needs boxing.** A recursive `async fn` would have to contain
  itself, giving an infinitely sized type. Boxing the recursive call adds the
  indirection.
- **Self-references appear naturally.** If a local borrows another local
  across an `.await`, the state machine stores both the data and a pointer into
  itself. Moving the future would leave that pointer dangling, which is why
  `poll` takes `Pin<&mut Self>` (section 11.4).

```rust
// Recursion: the boxed call breaks the infinite size cycle.
async fn depth(n: u32) -> u32 {
    if n == 0 { 0 } else { 1 + Box::pin(depth(n - 1)).await }
}

async fn big_buffer() {
    let buf = [0u8; 16 * 1024];             // lives across the await below
    tokio::task::yield_now().await;
    println!("{}", buf.len());
}

fn main() {
    let fut = big_buffer();
    println!("{} bytes", std::mem::size_of_val(&fut));   // a little over 16384
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The compiler turns each `async fn` into an enum-based state machine with
>   one state per `.await`.
> - Only variables live across an `.await` are stored in the future, so
>   futures are compact and need no per-await allocation.
> - Large locals held across awaits inflate future size; measure with
>   `size_of_val` and box when needed.
> - Recursive async functions require `Box::pin` on the recursive call.
> - Borrows across awaits create self-referential state, which motivates `Pin`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `async fn` with three `.await` points and sketch, on paper, the
>    enum the compiler would generate, listing which locals each variant holds.
> 2. Measure `size_of_val` of a future that holds a `Vec<u8>` across an await
>    versus one that holds a `[u8; 4096]`. Explain the difference.
> 3. Implement an async recursive directory walker signature
>    `fn walk(dir: PathBuf) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = u64> + Send>>` that
>    returns the total size of files (use `tokio::fs`).

#### Lazy Futures vs Eager Tasks

In JavaScript, calling an async function starts it immediately and returns a
promise that is already running. Rust futures are **lazy**: creating one only
builds the initial state machine (state `Start` above). Nothing runs until
someone polls it, and if the future is dropped without being polled, its body
never executes at all.

Laziness is what makes futures cheap and composable: you can build a future,
pass it around, wrap it in a timeout, or decide not to run it, all without side
effects. The cost is a classic beginner bug: forgetting `.await` and wondering
why nothing happens. The compiler helps here, since `Future` is marked
`#[must_use]`.

To make work run *eagerly*, independently of whether anyone awaits it, you
hand it to the runtime as a **task** with `spawn`. The runtime then polls it in
the background, and the returned `JoinHandle` is only a way to collect the
result.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn greet(name: &str) {
    println!("hello {name}");
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let fut = greet("lazy");                // nothing printed: just a value
    println!("before await");
    fut.await;                              // "hello lazy" is printed now

    greet("forgotten");                     // warning: unused implementer of `Future`
                                            // that must be used; it never runs

    // Eager: the task is scheduled as soon as spawn is called.
    let handle = tokio::spawn(async {
        println!("task running");
        7
    });
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await; // "task running" appears during this sleep
    println!("result = {}", handle.await.unwrap());   // result = 7
}
```

Output:

```text
before await
hello lazy
task running
result = 7
```

| Aspect | Future (`async fn` / block) | Task (`tokio::spawn`) |
| ------ | --------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Starts running | When first polled (awaited or combined) | Immediately, on the runtime |
| Driven by | Whoever owns and polls it | The runtime's scheduler |
| Runs concurrently with caller | Only if combined with `join!`/`select!` | Yes, possibly on another thread |
| Dropped before completion | Cancelled silently | Keeps running (handle drop detaches) |
| Lifetime requirement | May borrow local data | Must be `'static` (owns its data) |
| Cost | Zero allocation | One heap allocation per task |

The mental model to keep:

```text
  future = a recipe          (written down, nothing cooking yet)
  .await = cook it now, here (the current task does the work)
  spawn  = hand it to a cook (it gets done whether or not you watch)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Rust futures are lazy: no code in an `async fn` runs until the future is
>   polled.
> - Forgetting `.await` is a common bug; heed the `must_use` warning.
> - `spawn` turns a future into an eager task that the runtime drives
>   independently of the caller.
> - Awaiting a future runs it inside the current task; spawning creates a new
>   unit of concurrency with a `'static` requirement.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that creates three futures that print a message, stores
>    them in a `Vec`, and awaits only the second one. Predict the output first.
> 2. Spawn a task that prints every 100 ms, drop its `JoinHandle` immediately,
>    and sleep in `main` for 350 ms. How many lines appear, and why does the
>    printing stop when `main` returns?
> 3. Interview: A developer ported code from JavaScript and wrote
>    `let a = load_a(); let b = load_b(); (a.await, b.await)`, expecting the
>    loads to run in parallel. What actually happens in Rust, and how would you
>    fix it? (Hint: laziness, and section 11.3.)

<a id="112-runtimes"></a>
### 11.2 Runtimes

The standard library defines `Future`, but it ships no code to run futures, no
async I/O, and no timers. That job belongs to a **runtime** crate. This section
explains what a runtime is made of, how Tokio works, what the alternatives
offer, how to spawn tasks, and how to deal with code that blocks.

#### Executors and Reactors

Why does Rust not include a runtime in `std`? Because there is no single right
answer. A web server wants a multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler; an
embedded device has no threads and no heap; a GUI wants to run tasks on its
event loop. Keeping the runtime in a library lets each domain pick one, and
keeps programs that do not use async free of its cost.

A runtime combines two cooperating parts:

- **Executor**: owns the tasks and decides which one to poll next. It keeps a
  *run queue* of tasks that have been woken, pops one, calls `poll`, and
  repeats. If the queue is empty, it sleeps.
- **Reactor**: talks to the operating system's event notification mechanism
  (`epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows) and to a timer
  structure. When a socket becomes readable or a timer expires, the reactor
  calls the waker registered for it, which puts the task back in the
  executor's run queue.

```text
                      ┌──────────────────── runtime ───────────────────┐
                      │                                                │
   spawn(task) ──────>│  run queue  ──pop──>  executor: task.poll(cx)  │
                      │      ^                     │                   │
                      │      │                     │ Pending: register │
                      │      │ waker.wake()        v interest + waker  │
                      │      └────────────────  reactor  <──── OS ─────┼── epoll/kqueue/IOCP
                      │                     (I/O + timers)    events   │
                      └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

An analogy: the executor is a chef who cooks whichever order is on the ticket
rail; the reactor is the front-of-house staff who put tickets back on the rail
when a customer or supplier is ready. The chef never waits at the door.

The following is a complete (if minimal) multi-task executor using only `std`.
Each task is an `Arc<Task>`; waking a task sends it back into the run queue.

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::mpsc::{self, Receiver, Sender};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::task::{Context, Poll, Wake, Waker};

type BoxFuture = Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>>;

struct Task {
    future: Mutex<Option<BoxFuture>>,       // None once the task has completed
    queue: Sender<Arc<Task>>,               // where to re-enqueue on wake
}

impl Wake for Task {
    fn wake(self: Arc<Self>) {
        let queue = self.queue.clone();
        let _ = queue.send(self);           // schedule: back onto the run queue
    }
}

struct Executor {
    ready: Receiver<Arc<Task>>,
}

#[derive(Clone)]
struct Spawner {
    queue: Sender<Arc<Task>>,
}

fn new_runtime() -> (Executor, Spawner) {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
    (Executor { ready: rx }, Spawner { queue: tx })
}

impl Spawner {
    fn spawn(&self, fut: impl Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static) {
        let task = Arc::new(Task {
            future: Mutex::new(Some(Box::pin(fut))),
            queue: self.queue.clone(),
        });
        self.queue.send(task).unwrap();     // newly spawned tasks start "woken"
    }
}

impl Executor {
    fn run(&self) {
        // recv fails once every Sender is gone: no spawner and no pending task.
        while let Ok(task) = self.ready.recv() {
            let mut slot = task.future.lock().unwrap();
            if let Some(mut fut) = slot.take() {
                let waker = Waker::from(Arc::clone(&task));
                let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
                if fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx).is_pending() {
                    *slot = Some(fut);      // not finished: keep it until woken again
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// A future that yields once, so we can watch tasks interleave.
struct YieldOnce(bool);
impl Future for YieldOnce {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        if self.0 {
            return Poll::Ready(());
        }
        self.0 = true;
        cx.waker().wake_by_ref();           // re-enqueue behind the other tasks
        Poll::Pending
    }
}

fn main() {
    let (executor, spawner) = new_runtime();
    for id in 0..3 {
        spawner.spawn(async move {
            println!("task {id}: step 1");
            YieldOnce(false).await;
            println!("task {id}: step 2");
        });
    }
    drop(spawner);                          // otherwise run() would wait forever
    executor.run();
}
```

Output (the tasks interleave on a single thread):

```text
task 0: step 1
task 1: step 1
task 2: step 1
task 0: step 2
task 1: step 2
task 2: step 2
```

Production runtimes add a reactor, timers, multiple worker threads, per-worker
queues with work stealing (as in Rayon, section 10.5), and many optimizations,
but the core loop is exactly this one.

> Key Takeaways
> - `std` defines futures but does not run them; runtimes are libraries.
> - The executor polls woken tasks from a run queue; the reactor translates OS
>   events and timers into `wake()` calls.
> - A waker's job is to put its task back on the run queue.
> - Async is cooperative: a task gives up the thread only when it returns
>   `Pending`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend the minimal executor so `spawn` returns a handle that can be
>    awaited for the task's output (hint: share an `Arc<Mutex<Option<T>>>` plus
>    a stored waker between the task and the handle).
> 2. Add a task that never yields (an infinite loop with no `.await`) to the
>    example and observe what happens to the other tasks. Relate this to the
>    word "cooperative".
> 3. Interview: Explain the difference between an executor and a reactor, and
>    describe what happens, step by step, between a socket becoming readable
>    and the waiting task resuming. (Hint: follow the waker.)

#### Tokio Runtime

**Tokio** is the most widely used async runtime and the de facto standard for
networked services: `axum`, `hyper`, `tonic`, `reqwest`, and `sqlx` are built on
it. It provides a multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler, async networking,
timers, file system access, process management, signals, and synchronization
primitives.

Enable it in `Cargo.toml`. The `full` feature turns everything on; libraries
should enable only the features they use.

```toml
[dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
# Minimal alternative: features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros", "net", "time"]
```

The `#[tokio::main]` attribute is a convenience that builds a runtime and calls
`block_on` on your async `main`:

```rust
// What you write
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    println!("hello from the runtime");
}
```

```rust
// Roughly what it expands to
fn main() {
    tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
        .enable_all()                       // turn on the I/O and time drivers
        .build()
        .expect("failed to build runtime")
        .block_on(async {
            println!("hello from the runtime");
        })
}
```

Tokio offers two scheduler flavors:

| Flavor | How to select | Threads | Use when |
| ------ | ------------- | ------- | -------- |
| Multi-thread (default) | `#[tokio::main]` or `Builder::new_multi_thread()` | One worker per CPU core by default, work stealing | Servers and most applications |
| Current-thread | `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]` or `Builder::new_current_thread()` | Only the thread calling `block_on` | Tests, CLIs, embedding in another app, `!Send` futures |

Inside the multi-thread scheduler, each worker has a local run queue, plus
there is a global injection queue. Idle workers steal half of a busy worker's
queue. Tokio also gives each task a *cooperative budget*: after a task has
performed a certain number of operations on Tokio resources without yielding,
those resources start returning `Pending` to force it to yield, protecting
other tasks from starvation.

A TCP echo server shows the typical shape of a Tokio program: accept in a loop
and spawn one task per connection.

```rust
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
use tokio::net::TcpListener;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;
    println!("listening on 8080");

    loop {
        let (mut socket, addr) = listener.accept().await?;   // waits without blocking
        tokio::spawn(async move {                           // one task per client
            let mut buf = [0u8; 1024];
            loop {
                let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await {
                    Ok(0) => return,                         // client closed the connection
                    Ok(n) => n,
                    Err(e) => {
                        eprintln!("{addr}: read error: {e}");
                        return;
                    }
                };
                if socket.write_all(&buf[..n]).await.is_err() {
                    return;                                  // client went away mid-write
                }
            }
        });
    }
}
```

Building the runtime explicitly gives full control, and lets synchronous code
call into async code:

```rust
use tokio::runtime::Builder;

fn main() {
    let rt = Builder::new_multi_thread()
        .worker_threads(4)
        .thread_name("api-worker")
        .enable_all()
        .build()
        .unwrap();

    // A synchronous function can drive async code to completion:
    let body = rt.block_on(async { fetch_config().await });
    println!("{body}");

    // A Handle lets other threads submit work to this runtime.
    let handle = rt.handle().clone();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        handle.block_on(async { println!("from a plain thread") });
    })
    .join()
    .unwrap();
}

async fn fetch_config() -> String {
    "debug=false".to_string()
}
```

Note that calling `block_on` from *inside* a runtime worker panics with
"Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime". Inside async code, use `.await`
instead.

> Key Takeaways
> - Tokio is the dominant runtime: work-stealing scheduler plus async I/O,
>   timers, sync primitives, and more, enabled through Cargo features.
> - `#[tokio::main]` builds a runtime and `block_on`s your async `main`;
>   `Builder` gives explicit control.
> - Choose the multi-thread flavor for servers and the current-thread flavor
>   for tests, small tools, or `!Send` workloads.
> - Never call `block_on` from inside the runtime; await instead.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the echo server and connect with `nc 127.0.0.1 8080` from several
>    terminals at once. Then change the runtime to `current_thread` and verify
>    that it still serves all clients. Why does it?
> 2. Build a runtime with `Builder` that uses two worker threads named
>    `worker-N` (use `thread_name_fn`) and print `thread::current().name()`
>    from several spawned tasks.
> 3. Interview: Why might a library crate depend on `tokio` with only the
>    `sync` feature, or no Tokio at all, instead of `features = ["full"]`?
>    (Hint: compile times, binary size, and runtime coupling for users.)

#### async-std and smol

Tokio is not the only option. Different runtimes make different trade-offs in
size, API style, and threading model.

- **async-std** aimed to mirror the standard library's API in async form
  (`async_std::fs`, `async_std::net`, `task::spawn`). It was officially
  **discontinued in 2025**, and its maintainers recommend `smol` for new code.
  You will still meet it in older projects.
- **smol** is a small runtime assembled from independent crates:
  `async-executor` (task scheduling), `async-io` (reactor and timers),
  `blocking` (thread pool for blocking calls), `async-net`, `async-fs`, and
  `futures-lite`. Each piece can be used on its own.
- **Specialized runtimes** exist too: `embassy` for embedded systems without
  an OS, and `glommio` and `monoio` for thread-per-core designs built on Linux
  `io_uring`.

```rust
// smol: the same ideas with a smaller surface area.
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    smol::block_on(async {
        // spawn returns a Task<T>; dropping a smol Task CANCELS it.
        let task = smol::spawn(async { 2 + 2 });

        // Run a blocking call on smol's thread pool.
        let file_len = smol::unblock(|| std::fs::read_to_string("Cargo.toml"))
            .await
            .map(|s| s.len())
            .unwrap_or(0);

        smol::Timer::after(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
        println!("{} {file_len}", task.await);

        // To run a task in the background without awaiting it, detach it.
        smol::spawn(async { println!("background") }).detach();
    });
}
```

```rust
// async-std (legacy): std-like APIs.
#[async_std::main]
async fn main() {
    let h = async_std::task::spawn(async { 21 * 2 });
    async_std::task::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(10)).await;
    println!("{}", h.await);                // async-std handles return T, not Result
}
```

| Aspect | Tokio | smol | async-std |
| ------ | ----- | ---- | --------- |
| Status | Actively developed, dominant | Actively maintained | Discontinued (2025) |
| Design | Batteries included, feature flags | Small composable crates | `std`-mirroring API |
| Dropping a task handle | Detaches (task keeps running) | Cancels (use `.detach()`) | Detaches |
| I/O traits | `tokio::io::AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` | `futures-io` traits | `futures-io` traits |
| Ecosystem | hyper, axum, tonic, reqwest, sqlx | Smaller, runtime-agnostic crates | Legacy |

The I/O trait split is the main source of friction: a type implementing
`tokio::io::AsyncRead` does not automatically implement `futures::io::AsyncRead`.
The `tokio-util` crate's `compat` module bridges them. Library authors who want
to stay runtime-agnostic depend on the `futures` traits and avoid spawning or
sleeping directly, or let the user inject those capabilities.

> Key Takeaways
> - Runtimes are interchangeable in principle but not in practice: I/O traits,
>   timers, and spawning APIs differ.
> - async-std is discontinued; smol is the lightweight alternative built from
>   reusable crates.
> - smol's `Task` cancels on drop, while Tokio's `JoinHandle` detaches on drop.
> - Specialized runtimes target embedded (`embassy`) and `io_uring`
>   thread-per-core designs (`glommio`, `monoio`).

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Port the Tokio echo server from the previous topic to smol using
>    `smol::net::TcpListener` and `futures_lite::io`.
> 2. Write a small program that spawns a smol task, drops its handle without
>    calling `detach`, and shows that the task does not finish.
> 3. Interview: You are writing a library that needs to sleep between retries.
>    How can you avoid forcing a specific runtime on your users? (Hint: accept
>    a generic "sleep" function or future factory, or use a runtime-agnostic
>    timer crate behind a feature flag.)

#### Spawning Tasks

A single future, even with `join!`, runs inside one task and therefore on one
thread at a time. To get true parallelism across worker threads, or to let
work continue independently of the caller, you **spawn** a new task. Tasks are
the async equivalent of threads, but much lighter: a task is a heap-allocated
future plus a small header, often a few hundred bytes, so spawning a hundred
thousand of them is routine.

`tokio::spawn` has bounds that mirror `std::thread::spawn` (section 10.1):

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use tokio::task::JoinHandle;

// Simplified signature
pub fn spawn<F>(future: F) -> JoinHandle<F::Output>
where
    F: Future + Send + 'static,             // may run on any worker; may outlive caller
    F::Output: Send + 'static,
{
    unimplemented!()
}
```

- **`'static`**: the task may outlive the function that spawned it, so it must
  own its data. Use `async move` and `Arc` for shared data.
- **`Send`**: the task may migrate between worker threads at any `.await`, so
  everything it holds across an `.await` must be `Send` (section 11.4).

Awaiting a `JoinHandle` yields `Result<T, JoinError>`. The error case means the
task panicked or was aborted; a panic in a task does not bring down the
runtime.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::task::JoinSet;
use tokio::time::sleep;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Spawn and collect a result.
    let config = Arc::new(String::from("region=eu"));
    let cfg = Arc::clone(&config);
    let handle = tokio::spawn(async move {
        sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await;
        format!("loaded with {cfg}")        // `cfg` is owned by the task
    });
    println!("{}", handle.await.unwrap());

    // 2. Panics are contained in the task.
    let bad = tokio::spawn(async { panic!("boom") });
    let err = bad.await.unwrap_err();
    println!("panicked: {}", err.is_panic());   // panicked: true

    // 3. Abort a long-running task.
    let forever = tokio::spawn(async {
        loop { sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)).await; }
    });
    forever.abort();                        // cancelled at its next .await
    println!("cancelled: {}", forever.await.unwrap_err().is_cancelled());

    // 4. Many tasks: JoinSet collects results in completion order.
    let mut set = JoinSet::new();
    for id in 0..5u64 {
        set.spawn(async move {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(50 - id * 10)).await;
            id
        });
    }
    while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await {
        print!("{} ", res.unwrap());        // 4 3 2 1 0 (fastest first)
    }
    println!();
}
```

Other tools worth knowing:

| Tool | Purpose |
| ---- | ------- |
| `JoinHandle::abort()` | Request cancellation; takes effect at the task's next `.await` |
| Dropping a `JoinHandle` | Detaches: the task keeps running, its result is discarded |
| `JoinSet` | Owns a group of tasks; `join_next()` yields results as they finish; dropping it aborts them all |
| `tokio::task::yield_now()` | Voluntarily return to the scheduler in a long loop |
| `tokio::task::spawn_local` + `LocalSet` | Spawn `!Send` futures pinned to the current thread |
| `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` | Run blocking code on a separate thread pool (next topic) |

When to spawn versus simply await or `join!`:

- **Spawn** for independent units of work (one per connection, background
  jobs), for CPU parallelism across cores, or when work must continue even if
  the caller is cancelled.
- **Do not spawn** just to run two things concurrently inside one request;
  `join!` or `select!` (section 11.3) are cheaper, can borrow local data, and
  cancel cleanly with their parent.

> Key Takeaways
> - `tokio::spawn` schedules a `Send + 'static` future as an independent task
>   and returns a `JoinHandle`.
> - Awaiting a handle gives `Result<T, JoinError>`; panics and aborts are
>   reported, not propagated.
> - Dropping a Tokio `JoinHandle` detaches the task; `JoinSet` ties task
>   lifetimes to an owner and aborts them on drop.
> - Prefer `join!`/`select!` for in-request concurrency; spawn for independent
>   or parallel work.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Spawn 100,000 tasks that each sleep 1 second and then return their index;
>    sum the results with a `JoinSet` and measure total time and memory usage.
> 2. Write a function `fn spawn_logged<F>(name: &'static str, f: F)` that
>    spawns `f` and logs whether it finished, panicked, or was cancelled.
>    Determine the correct trait bounds.
> 3. Interview: A request handler spawns a task to write an audit log, then
>    returns. The client disconnects early and the handler's future is
>    dropped. Is the audit log still written? What if the code had used
>    `join!` instead? (Hint: who owns the work in each case?)

#### Blocking Code in Async Contexts

Async scheduling is **cooperative**. A worker thread can switch tasks only when
the current task returns `Pending` at an `.await`. Code that runs for a long
time without awaiting, or that blocks the thread in a system call, holds the
worker hostage: every other task scheduled on it waits. With a four-thread
runtime, four blocking calls freeze the whole application, including timers
and health checks.

Typical culprits:

| Blocking operation | Async-friendly replacement |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| `std::thread::sleep` | `tokio::time::sleep(...).await` |
| `std::fs::read`, `File::open` | `tokio::fs` (which uses `spawn_blocking` internally) |
| `std::net::TcpStream` | `tokio::net::TcpStream` |
| Synchronous database or HTTP clients | Async clients (`sqlx`, `reqwest`) or `spawn_blocking` |
| Heavy CPU work (hashing, compression, parsing large files) | `spawn_blocking`, or Rayon plus a oneshot channel |
| Holding a `std::sync::Mutex` across slow work | Shorten the critical section, or use `tokio::sync::Mutex` |

A widely used rule of thumb is that a task should not go more than about 10 to
100 microseconds between `.await` points.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::oneshot;

fn expensive_hash(data: &[u8]) -> u64 {
    // Pretend this takes 200 ms of pure CPU.
    data.iter().fold(0u64, |h, &b| h.wrapping_mul(31).wrapping_add(b as u64))
}
```
