#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // BAD: blocks a worker thread; other tasks on it stall for a second.
    // std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));

    // GOOD: yields to the scheduler while waiting.
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await;

    // spawn_blocking: runs the closure on a separate pool of threads
    // dedicated to blocking work (up to 512 by default).
    let data = vec![1u8; 10_000_000];
    let hash = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || expensive_hash(&data))
        .await
        .expect("blocking task panicked");
    println!("hash = {hash}");

    // CPU-parallel work: hand it to Rayon and await the result via oneshot.
    let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel();
    rayon::spawn(move || {
        let sum: u64 = (0..50_000_000u64).sum();
        let _ = tx.send(sum);               // receiver may have been dropped
    });
    println!("sum = {}", rx.await.unwrap());

    // block_in_place: turn the *current* worker into a blocking thread
    // (multi-thread runtime only; panics on current_thread).
    let n = tokio::task::block_in_place(|| expensive_hash(b"short input"));
    println!("{n}");
}
```

| Tool | Runs on | Best for | Caveats |
| ---- | ------- | -------- | ------- |
| `spawn_blocking` | Dedicated blocking pool | Blocking I/O, sync libraries, moderate CPU work | Needs `'static` data; cannot be aborted once started |
| Rayon + oneshot | Rayon's CPU-sized pool | Heavy, parallelizable CPU work | Extra dependency; avoid blocking I/O in Rayon |
| `block_in_place` | Current worker (others take over its queue) | Borrowing local data in a blocking call | Multi-thread runtime only |
| Dedicated `std::thread` | Its own OS thread | Long-lived blocking loops (e.g. a serial port reader) | Communicate via channels |

The opposite direction also comes up: synchronous code (inside
`spawn_blocking`, or a callback from a C library) needing to call async code.
Capture a `tokio::runtime::Handle` and call `handle.block_on(fut)` from that
non-runtime thread.

Holding a `std::sync::Mutex` in async code is fine, and usually faster than an
async mutex, *as long as the guard is not held across an `.await`* and the
critical section is short. Use `tokio::sync::Mutex` only when you genuinely
need to hold the lock while awaiting.

> Key Takeaways
> - Blocking a worker thread stalls every task scheduled on it; async relies
>   on tasks yielding frequently.
> - Use async equivalents for I/O and timers; move blocking or CPU-heavy work
>   to `spawn_blocking`, Rayon, or a dedicated thread.
> - `block_in_place` lets a multi-thread worker block without starving its
>   queue, at some cost.
> - `std::sync::Mutex` is fine in async code if the guard never lives across
>   an `.await`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run a current-thread runtime with a task printing a heartbeat every
>    100 ms. Add a second task that calls `std::thread::sleep` for 2 seconds and
>    observe the heartbeat gap. Fix it with `spawn_blocking`.
> 2. Write `async fn hash_file(path: PathBuf) -> io::Result<String>` that
>    reads the file with `tokio::fs` and computes a SHA-256 digest in
>    `spawn_blocking`.
> 3. Interview: An async service's p99 latency spikes whenever a large JSON
>    report is generated, even though CPU usage is low overall. What would you
>    suspect and how would you confirm it? (Hint: think about worker threads
>    being blocked, and tools like `tokio-console`.)

<a id="113-async-composition"></a>
### 11.3 Async Composition

The real power of async lies in combining operations: waiting for several at
once, racing them, processing sequences of values, passing messages between
tasks, and putting limits on time. This section covers the core combinators
and primitives for each.

#### join and try_join

Sequential awaits run one after another. If two requests each take 300 ms and
are independent, awaiting them in sequence takes 600 ms. **`join!`** polls
several futures *concurrently within the current task* and completes when all
of them have completed, returning a tuple of outputs. Total time becomes the
time of the slowest one.

Concurrency here does not mean parallelism. `join!` interleaves the futures on
one thread: while one is waiting on I/O, another makes progress. This is ideal
for I/O-bound work. For CPU-bound work in parallel, spawn tasks instead.

```text
 sequential:  [── users 300ms ──][── orders 200ms ──]           = 500 ms
 join!:       [── users 300ms ──]
              [── orders 200ms ──]                               = 300 ms
```

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::{sleep, Instant};

async fn fetch(name: &str, ms: u64) -> String {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    format!("{name} ok")
}

async fn load_user(id: u32) -> Result<String, String> {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
    Ok(format!("user {id}"))
}

async fn load_orders(id: u32) -> Result<Vec<u32>, String> {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
    if id == 0 { Err("no orders for guest".into()) } else { Ok(vec![7, 9]) }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let t = Instant::now();
    let a = fetch("users", 300).await;
    let b = fetch("orders", 200).await;
    println!("{a}, {b} sequential in {:?}", t.elapsed());   // ~500ms

    let t = Instant::now();
    let (a, b) = tokio::join!(fetch("users", 300), fetch("orders", 200));
    println!("{a}, {b} joined in {:?}", t.elapsed());       // ~300ms

    // try_join!: all must succeed; the first Err wins and the others are dropped.
    let (user, orders) = tokio::try_join!(load_user(1), load_orders(1))?;
    println!("{user}: {orders:?}");

    let failed = tokio::try_join!(load_user(0), load_orders(0));
    println!("{failed:?}");                 // Err("no orders for guest") after ~50ms
    Ok(())
}
```

`join!` and `try_join!` need the number of futures to be known at compile time.
For a dynamic collection, use the `futures` crate:

```rust
use futures::future::{join_all, try_join_all};
use futures::stream::{FuturesUnordered, StreamExt};

async fn price(id: u32) -> u32 { id * 100 }

async fn checked_price(id: u32) -> Result<u32, String> {
    if id == 13 { Err(format!("item {id} unavailable")) } else { Ok(id * 100) }
}

async fn demo(ids: Vec<u32>) {
    // Results in the same order as the inputs.
    let prices: Vec<u32> = join_all(ids.iter().map(|&id| price(id))).await;

    // Short-circuits on the first error.
    let checked = try_join_all(ids.iter().map(|&id| checked_price(id))).await;

    // Results in completion order, processed as soon as each one is ready.
    let mut pending: FuturesUnordered<_> = ids.iter().map(|&id| price(id)).collect();
    while let Some(p) = pending.next().await {
        println!("got {p}");
    }
    println!("{prices:?} {checked:?}");
}
```

| Combinator | Inputs | Output | On error |
| ---------- | ------ | ------ | -------- |
| `join!(a, b, ...)` | Fixed set | Tuple of all outputs | Not applicable |
| `try_join!(a, b, ...)` | Fixed set of `Result` futures | `Result<(A, B, ...), E>` | Returns first `Err`, drops the rest |
| `join_all(iter)` | Dynamic | `Vec<T>` in input order | Not applicable |
| `try_join_all(iter)` | Dynamic | `Result<Vec<T>, E>` | Returns first `Err`, drops the rest |
| `FuturesUnordered` | Dynamic, can grow | Stream of outputs in completion order | Handle per item |

A word of caution: `join_all` on thousands of futures polls all of them, which
can overwhelm a remote service. Bound concurrency with
`stream::iter(...).buffer_unordered(n)` (next topics) or a semaphore.

> Key Takeaways
> - `join!` runs futures concurrently inside the current task and waits for all
>   of them; total time is that of the slowest.
> - `try_join!` short-circuits on the first error and cancels the remaining
>   futures by dropping them.
> - `join_all` and `FuturesUnordered` handle dynamic collections; the latter
>   yields results in completion order.
> - Joined futures share one task, so they give concurrency, not CPU
>   parallelism.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fetch three simulated resources with delays 100, 200, and 300 ms, first
>    sequentially and then with `join!`, and print both durations.
> 2. Use `try_join!` with three futures where the middle one fails after
>    50 ms. Add a `Drop` impl to a guard in each future and observe which
>    futures are dropped before completion.
> 3. Interview: When would you use `tokio::join!` and when `tokio::spawn` for
>    two concurrent operations in a request handler? (Hint: consider borrowing,
>    `'static`, parallelism, and what happens if the handler is cancelled.)

#### select and Cancellation

Sometimes you want the *first* of several futures, not all of them: a response
or a timeout, a message or a shutdown signal, whichever happens first.
**`tokio::select!`** polls several futures concurrently, runs the handler of
the first one that completes, and **drops all the others**.

```rust
// General shape
tokio::select! {
    pattern1 = future1 => handler1,
    pattern2 = future2, if condition => handler2,  // optional precondition
    else => fallback,                              // all branches disabled
}
```

Key rules:

- Branches are polled in a **random order** each time, for fairness. Write
  `biased;` as the first line to poll them top to bottom instead.
- If a branch's value does not match its pattern (for example
  `Some(msg) = rx.recv()` receiving `None`), that branch is disabled and
  `select!` keeps waiting on the others.
- Futures passed by value are created fresh each time `select!` runs. To keep
  one future alive across loop iterations, pin it once and pass `&mut fut`.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio::time::sleep;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<String>(8);
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        for i in 0..5 {
            if tx.send(format!("msg {i}")).await.is_err() {
                break;                      // receiver gone: stop producing
            }
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
        }
    });

    // Created once and polled by reference, so the deadline is not reset
    // on every iteration.
    let deadline = sleep(Duration::from_millis(250));
    tokio::pin!(deadline);

    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            Some(msg) = rx.recv() => println!("got {msg}"),
            _ = &mut deadline => {
                println!("deadline reached");
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    // Output: got msg 0, got msg 1, got msg 2, deadline reached
}
```

**Cancellation in Rust is just dropping a future.** There is no exception or
cancellation token involved at the language level: when `select!` picks a
winner, the losing futures are dropped at whatever `.await` they were paused
on. Their destructors run, but no further code in their bodies executes.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::sleep;

struct Noisy(&'static str);
impl Drop for Noisy {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        println!("dropped {}", self.0);
    }
}

async fn slow() -> u32 {
    let _guard = Noisy("slow");
    sleep(Duration::from_secs(10)).await;   // cancelled while paused here
    println!("never printed");
    1
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    tokio::select! {
        v = slow() => println!("slow finished with {v}"),
        _ = sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)) => println!("timer won"),
    }
    // Output:
    // dropped slow
    // timer won
}
```

```text
  slow():   start ──> [paused at sleep(10s)] ── dropped ──> Drop for Noisy runs
                                    ^
  timer:    start ──> 50ms ──> Ready │  select! picks timer, drops slow()
```

| Approach | How cancellation happens |
| -------- | ------------------------ |
| `select!` | Losing futures are dropped |
| `tokio::time::timeout` | Inner future dropped when the deadline passes |
| `JoinHandle::abort()` | Task's future dropped at its next suspension point |
| Dropping a `JoinSet` or smol `Task` | Owned tasks aborted |
| `CancellationToken` (section 11.4) | Cooperative: the task checks the token and exits cleanly |

Because a future can stop at any `.await`, code between awaits must leave data
in a consistent state if it is abandoned there. This property, *cancellation
safety*, is covered in section 11.4. The `futures` crate also has a `select!`
macro; it requires futures to be fused (`FusedFuture`) and `Unpin`, which is
why most Tokio code uses `tokio::select!`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `select!` waits for the first of several futures, runs its handler, and
>   drops the rest.
> - Dropping a future is how Rust cancels async work: it stops at its current
>   `.await` and its destructors run.
> - Pin a future outside a loop and pass `&mut fut` to keep it alive across
>   `select!` iterations.
> - Branch order is random unless `biased;` is used; non-matching patterns
>   disable a branch.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a loop that uses `select!` to receive from two channels and exits
>    when both are closed (use the `else` branch).
> 2. Implement your own `with_timeout(fut, dur)` using `select!` and compare
>    its behavior with `tokio::time::timeout`.
> 3. Interview: In a `select!` loop, a developer writes
>    `_ = sleep(Duration::from_secs(30)) => break` to stop after 30 seconds of
>    total runtime, but the loop never stops while messages keep arriving.
>    Why? (Hint: when is the `sleep` future created?)

#### Streams and StreamExt

A future produces one value. Many async sources produce a *sequence* of values
over time: messages on a socket, rows from a database cursor, ticks of a
timer. The async counterpart of `Iterator` is **`Stream`**, defined in the
`futures` crate (the standard library has an unstable `AsyncIterator`):

```rust
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

pub trait Stream {
    type Item;

    // Ready(Some(item)): next value; Ready(None): finished; Pending: wait.
    fn poll_next(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>>;
}
```

Like `Iterator`, the raw trait has one required method and all the convenience
lives in an extension trait, **`StreamExt`**, which adds `next()`, `map`,
`filter`, `then`, `take`, `collect`, `buffer_unordered`, and more.

| `Iterator` | `Stream` |
| ---------- | -------- |
| `fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Item>` | `fn poll_next(Pin<&mut Self>, &mut Context) -> Poll<Option<Item>>` |
| `for x in iter { ... }` | `while let Some(x) = stream.next().await { ... }` |
| `iter.map(f)` | `stream.map(f)`, `stream.then(async_fn)` |
| `iter.collect::<Vec<_>>()` | `stream.collect::<Vec<_>>().await` |
| Runs synchronously | Each item may require waiting |

There are two `StreamExt` traits in common use: `futures::StreamExt` and
`tokio_stream::StreamExt`. Their methods overlap with slightly different
signatures (for example, `futures`' `filter` takes an async predicate). Import
only one per module to avoid ambiguity errors.

```rust
use futures::stream::{self, Stream, StreamExt};
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::sleep;

async fn fetch_page(url: String) -> usize {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
    url.len()
}

// Build a stream with an async generator macro (async-stream crate).
fn countdown(from: u32) -> impl Stream<Item = u32> {
    async_stream::stream! {
        for i in (1..=from).rev() {
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;
            yield i;                         // emit one item
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. From an iterator, with adapters.
    let mut s = stream::iter(1..=5)
        .map(|x| x * 10)
        .filter(|x| futures::future::ready(*x != 30));   // async predicate
    while let Some(x) = s.next().await {
        print!("{x} ");                      // 10 20 40 50
    }
    println!();

    // 2. Generated streams are usually !Unpin: pin before calling next().
    let c = countdown(3);
    tokio::pin!(c);
    while let Some(n) = c.next().await {
        print!("{n}... ");                   // 3... 2... 1...
    }
    println!();

    // 3. unfold: build a stream from state, like paging through an API.
    let pages = stream::unfold(Some(1u32), |state| async move {
        let page = state?;                   // None ends the stream
        let next = if page < 3 { Some(page + 1) } else { None };
        Some((format!("page {page}"), next))
    });
    let all: Vec<String> = pages.collect().await;
    println!("{all:?}");                     // ["page 1", "page 2", "page 3"]

    // 4. Bounded concurrency: at most 4 fetches in flight at any time.
    let urls: Vec<String> = (0..10).map(|i| format!("https://example.com/{i}")).collect();
    let sizes: Vec<usize> = stream::iter(urls)
        .map(fetch_page)                     // stream of futures
        .buffer_unordered(4)                 // run up to 4, yield as they finish
        .collect()
        .await;
    println!("fetched {} pages", sizes.len());   // ~300ms instead of ~1s
}
```

Useful sources of streams in the Tokio ecosystem:

| Source | Produces |
| ------ | -------- |
| `tokio_stream::wrappers::ReceiverStream` | Items from an `mpsc::Receiver` |
| `tokio_stream::wrappers::IntervalStream` | Timer ticks |
| `tokio_util::codec::FramedRead` | Decoded frames (lines, length-delimited messages) from a byte reader |
| `tokio::io::Lines` via `LinesStream` | Lines of text |
| Database clients (e.g. `sqlx::query(...).fetch(...)`) | Rows, one at a time |

> Key Takeaways
> - `Stream` is the async `Iterator`: `poll_next` yields `Some(item)`, `None`,
>   or `Pending`.
> - `StreamExt` provides `next`, adapters, and `collect`; do not import both the
>   `futures` and `tokio_stream` versions in one module.
> - Create streams with `stream::iter`, `unfold`, wrappers, or the
>   `async_stream::stream!` macro; pin `!Unpin` streams before calling `next`.
> - `buffer_unordered(n)` and `for_each_concurrent(n, f)` bound how many
>   futures run at once.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a stream of Fibonacci numbers with `stream::unfold` and print the
>    first 10 using `take(10)`.
> 2. Wrap an `mpsc::Receiver<String>` in `ReceiverStream`, then use
>    `chunks(3)` to process messages in batches.
> 3. Interview: You need to call an external API for 10,000 IDs without
>    exceeding 20 concurrent requests, and collect results as they arrive.
>    Sketch a solution. (Hint: a stream of futures and one adapter.)

#### Async Channels

Tasks communicate the same way threads do (section 10.2): by sending messages
rather than sharing memory. The difference is that async channels *await*
instead of blocking. A task waiting on `recv().await` frees its worker thread
for other tasks, and a sender waiting on a full bounded channel yields too.

Tokio provides four channel types, each for a distinct communication shape:

| Channel | Shape | Semantics | Typical use |
| ------- | ----- | --------- | ----------- |
| `mpsc` | Many producers, one consumer | Queue; bounded (`channel(n)`) or `unbounded_channel()` | Work queues, actor mailboxes |
| `oneshot` | One producer, one consumer | Exactly one value | Returning a response to a request |
| `broadcast` | Many producers, many consumers | Every receiver sees every message (bounded, slow receivers lag) | Event fan-out, chat rooms |
| `watch` | Many producers, many consumers | Only the latest value is kept | Configuration updates, shutdown flags, status |

A common architecture built on these is the **actor pattern**: one task owns
some state exclusively and receives commands through an `mpsc` channel.
Requests that need an answer carry a `oneshot::Sender` for the reply. No locks
are needed, because only the actor touches the state.

```rust
use tokio::sync::{mpsc, oneshot};

enum Command {
    Incr { by: u64 },
    Get { reply: oneshot::Sender<u64> },    // the "return address"
}

async fn counter_actor(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<Command>) {
    let mut count = 0;                      // state owned by this task alone
    while let Some(cmd) = rx.recv().await { // None once every Sender is dropped
        match cmd {
            Command::Incr { by } => count += by,
            Command::Get { reply } => {
                let _ = reply.send(count);  // ignore: the requester may have gone
            }
        }
    }
    println!("actor stopped");
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(32);       // bounded: send().await waits when full
    let actor = tokio::spawn(counter_actor(rx));

    let mut workers = Vec::new();
    for _ in 0..10 {
        let tx = tx.clone();                // one Sender per producer
        workers.push(tokio::spawn(async move {
            tx.send(Command::Incr { by: 1 }).await.unwrap();
        }));
    }
    for w in workers {
        w.await.unwrap();
    }

    let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = oneshot::channel();
    tx.send(Command::Get { reply: reply_tx }).await.unwrap();
    println!("count = {}", reply_rx.await.unwrap());   // count = 10

    drop(tx);                               // close the mailbox
    actor.await.unwrap();                   // "actor stopped"
}
```

`watch` and `broadcast` in brief:

```rust
use tokio::sync::{broadcast, watch};

async fn others() {
    // watch: receivers see the most recent value; intermediate ones may be skipped.
    let (cfg_tx, mut cfg_rx) = watch::channel(String::from("v1"));
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        while cfg_rx.changed().await.is_ok() {
            println!("config now {}", *cfg_rx.borrow_and_update());
        }
    });
    cfg_tx.send(String::from("v2")).unwrap();

    // broadcast: each subscriber gets its own copy of every message (T: Clone).
    let (ev_tx, mut a) = broadcast::channel::<u32>(16);
    let mut b = ev_tx.subscribe();
    ev_tx.send(1).unwrap();
    println!("{} {}", a.recv().await.unwrap(), b.recv().await.unwrap());   // 1 1
    // If a receiver falls more than 16 messages behind, recv returns
    // Err(RecvError::Lagged(n)) and skips ahead.
}
```

Bridging synchronous and async code is common: a sync thread can use
`tx.blocking_send(v)` or `rx.blocking_recv()` on a Tokio `mpsc` channel (never
from inside the runtime). Outside Tokio, `async-channel` provides
runtime-agnostic MPMC channels, and `flume` offers channels usable from both
sync and async code.

**Prefer bounded channels.** An unbounded channel accepts messages faster than
they are processed until memory runs out. A bounded channel applies
*backpressure*: producers slow down to the consumer's pace.

> Key Takeaways
> - Async channels await rather than block, freeing the worker thread.
> - Pick by shape: `mpsc` for queues, `oneshot` for single replies,
>   `broadcast` for fan-out of every message, `watch` for latest-value state.
> - The actor pattern (owned state + `mpsc` commands + `oneshot` replies)
>   avoids locks entirely.
> - Prefer bounded channels for backpressure; a closed channel is signaled by
>   `recv()` returning `None` or `send()` returning `Err`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend the counter actor with a `Reset` command and a `Get` that times out
>    after 100 ms if the actor does not respond.
> 2. Build a chat-room simulation where three tasks each subscribe to a
>    `broadcast` channel and print every message sent by the others.
> 3. Interview: Compare protecting a shared cache with `Arc<Mutex<HashMap>>`
>    versus putting it behind an actor task. What are the trade-offs in
>    latency, contention, and failure handling? (Hint: think about what
>    happens when the actor panics and when many readers arrive at once.)

#### Timeouts and Intervals

Networks are unreliable. A remote service that never answers would leave a
task waiting forever, holding memory and possibly a connection-pool slot. Every
external call in production code should have a **time limit**, and periodic
work (heartbeats, metrics flushing, cache refresh) needs a **schedule**.
Tokio's `time` module provides both, driven by the runtime's timer wheel.

| Function | Purpose |
| -------- | ------- |
| `sleep(dur)` / `sleep_until(instant)` | Pause the current task |
| `timeout(dur, fut)` | Run `fut`, give up after `dur`; returns `Result<T, Elapsed>` |
| `timeout_at(deadline, fut)` | Same, with an absolute deadline shared by several steps |
| `interval(period)` | A ticker for periodic work; `tick().await` waits for the next tick |
| `Instant` | Tokio's clock, which can be paused in tests |

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::{interval, sleep, timeout, timeout_at, Instant, MissedTickBehavior};

async fn slow_query() -> u32 {
    sleep(Duration::from_secs(5)).await;
    42
}

async fn step(ms: u64) -> u64 {
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(ms)).await;
    ms
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Per-operation timeout: on expiry the inner future is dropped.
    match timeout(Duration::from_millis(100), slow_query()).await {
        Ok(v) => println!("answer {v}"),
        Err(_elapsed) => println!("query timed out"),
    }

    // 2. One deadline for a multi-step operation (a total budget).
    let deadline = Instant::now() + Duration::from_millis(250);
    let a = timeout_at(deadline, step(100)).await;     // Ok(100)
    let b = timeout_at(deadline, step(200)).await;     // Err: only ~150ms left
    println!("{a:?} {b:?}");

    // 3. Periodic work.
    let mut ticker = interval(Duration::from_millis(100));
    ticker.set_missed_tick_behavior(MissedTickBehavior::Delay);
    for i in 0..3 {
        ticker.tick().await;                // the FIRST tick completes immediately
        println!("tick {i} at {:?}", Instant::now());
    }
}
```

Why not `loop { work().await; sleep(period).await; }`? Because the period then
*adds* to the work time, so the schedule drifts. `interval` measures from the
schedule, not from when the work finished. When work overruns a tick, the
missed-tick behavior decides what happens next:

| `MissedTickBehavior` | After a delay | Good for |
| -------------------- | ------------- | -------- |
| `Burst` (default) | Fires missed ticks back to back to catch up | Counting events where every tick matters |
| `Delay` | Restarts the schedule from now | Heartbeats, polling |
| `Skip` | Skips missed ticks, stays aligned to the original grid | Aligned sampling (every full second) |

Testing time-dependent code with real clocks is slow and flaky. Tokio can
**pause time** in tests (the `test-util` feature): sleeps then complete
instantly in virtual time, as soon as every task is idle.

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use std::time::Duration;
    use tokio::time::{sleep, Instant};

    #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]
    async fn backoff_waits_one_minute() {
        let start = Instant::now();
        sleep(Duration::from_secs(60)).await;   // returns immediately in real time
        assert!(start.elapsed() >= Duration::from_secs(60));
    }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Wrap every external call in `timeout`; on expiry the inner future is
>   dropped (cancelled).
> - Use `timeout_at` with a shared deadline to enforce a total budget over
>   several steps.
> - `interval` keeps a steady schedule; its first tick is immediate, and
>   `MissedTickBehavior` controls catch-up.
> - Paused time (`start_paused = true`) makes timer-based tests instant and
>   deterministic.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `retry<F, Fut, T, E>(f: F, attempts: u32)` with exponential backoff
>    (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms...) and a per-attempt `timeout`. Test it with
>    paused time.
> 2. Create an interval of 100 ms where each tick's work takes 250 ms. Print
>    timestamps under `Burst`, `Delay`, and `Skip` and explain the differences.
> 3. Interview: Your service calls three downstream services in sequence and
>    has a 1-second SLA. Each call has its own 1-second timeout. What is wrong
>    with this setup, and how would you fix it? (Hint: deadlines versus
>    timeouts.)

<a id="114-async-challenges"></a>
### 11.4 Async Challenges

Async Rust keeps the language's guarantees (no data races, no dangling
pointers, no hidden allocation), and some of that rigor shows up as concepts
that synchronous code never needs. This section covers pinning, async
functions in traits, `Send` bounds on futures, cancellation safety, and how to
keep task lifetimes under control.

#### Pin and Unpin in Futures

Recall from section 11.1 that an `async fn` becomes a state machine storing
the locals that live across `.await`. Now consider:

```rust
async fn parse_header() -> usize {
    let buf = [0u8; 64];
    let slice = &buf[..16];                 // a reference to another local
    tokio::task::yield_now().await;         // both `buf` and `slice` live across this
    slice.len()
}
```

The generated future contains both `buf` and `slice`, and `slice` points
*into the same future*. The future is **self-referential**. If it were moved
in memory after the first poll (say, from the stack into a `Vec`), `slice`
would still point to the old location: a dangling pointer.

```text
   before move                          after move (if it were allowed)
   ┌──────── future @ 0x1000 ──┐        ┌──────── future @ 0x2000 ──┐
   │ buf:   [ ...64 bytes... ] │<─┐     │ buf:   [ ...64 bytes... ] │
   │ slice: ptr = 0x1000 ──────┼──┘     │ slice: ptr = 0x1000 ──────┼──> freed / reused memory
   └───────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────┘
```

Rust's answer is **`Pin<P>`**, a wrapper around a pointer (`&mut T`,
`Box<T>`, ...) that promises: *the value behind this pointer will not be moved
again until it is dropped*. `Future::poll` takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`, so a
future can only be polled once it is pinned, and from then on it stays put.
Self-references are safe because the address never changes.

Most types have no self-references and do not care about being moved. They
implement the auto trait **`Unpin`**, which says "pinning has no effect on
me". For `T: Unpin`, `Pin<&mut T>` behaves exactly like `&mut T`: you can create
it with `Pin::new` and get the reference back with `get_mut`. Futures generated
by `async` are **`!Unpin`**, because they may be self-referential.

| Type | `Unpin`? | Why |
| ---- | -------- | --- |
| `i32`, `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>` | Yes | No self-references (moving a `Box` moves only the pointer) |
| `std::future::Ready<T>`, most hand-written futures | Usually yes | Plain fields |
| Futures from `async fn` / `async` blocks | No | May borrow their own locals |
| `tokio::time::Sleep` | No | Registered in an intrusive timer list |
| `Pin<Box<F>>` for any `F` | Yes | The box can move; its contents stay put |

You will meet `Pin` in three situations:

1. **Polling a future by reference** (in a `select!` loop, or with
   `stream.next()` on a generated stream). Pin it first.
2. **Storing futures in collections or struct fields**, often as
   `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send>>`.
3. **Writing your own `Future`** that wraps another future.

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::{pin, Pin};
use std::time::Duration;

async fn work() -> u32 { 7 }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Stack pinning with std::pin::pin! (or tokio::pin!): zero cost.
    let mut fut = pin!(work());             // fut: Pin<&mut impl Future>
    let v = fut.as_mut().await;             // awaiting through the pinned reference
    println!("{v}");

    // Without pinning, polling by reference fails to compile:
    // let mut f = work();
    // (&mut f).await;
    // error[E0277]: `{async fn body}` cannot be unpinned

    // 2. Heap pinning: needed to store differently typed futures together.
    let jobs: Vec<Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = u32> + Send>>> = vec![
        Box::pin(work()),
        Box::pin(async { 1 }),
        Box::pin(async {
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await;
            2
        }),
    ];
    for job in jobs {
        print!("{} ", job.await);           // 7 1 2
    }
    println!();
}
```

When you implement `Future` for a wrapper, you must decide, for each field,
whether it is **structurally pinned** (accessed as `Pin<&mut Field>`, needed
for inner futures) or not (accessed as `&mut Field`). Doing this by hand
requires `unsafe`. The `pin-project-lite` (or `pin-project`) crate generates
the safe projection for you:

```rust
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
use pin_project_lite::pin_project;

pin_project! {
    /// Wraps any future and reports how long it took.
    pub struct Timed<F> {
        #[pin]
        inner: F,                           // structurally pinned: Pin<&mut F>
        start: Option<Instant>,             // ordinary field: &mut Option<Instant>
    }
}

impl<F> Timed<F> {
    pub fn new(inner: F) -> Self {
        Timed { inner, start: None }
    }
}

impl<F: Future> Future for Timed<F> {
    type Output = (F::Output, Duration);

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        let this = self.project();          // split into per-field references
        let start = this.start.get_or_insert_with(Instant::now);
        match this.inner.poll(cx) {
            Poll::Ready(out) => Poll::Ready((out, start.elapsed())),
            Poll::Pending => Poll::Pending,
        }
    }
}

// Usage: let (value, took) = Timed::new(some_future).await;
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Futures from `async` can be self-referential, so they must not move after
>   their first poll; `Pin` encodes that promise in the type system.
> - `Unpin` types are unaffected by pinning; `async` futures and some runtime
>   types like `Sleep` are `!Unpin`.
> - Use `pin!` for zero-cost stack pinning and `Box::pin` to store or
>   type-erase futures.
> - Use `pin-project-lite` to access fields of a pinned struct safely when
>   writing future wrappers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that accepts `Vec<Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = String> + Send>>>`
>    and awaits them all with `join_all`. Fill the vector with futures of
>    three different concrete types.
> 2. Using `pin-project-lite`, implement `WithDefault<F>` that resolves to
>    `F::Output` or, if a given `Sleep` future fires first, to a default value.
> 3. Interview: Why is `Box<T>` always `Unpin` even when `T` is not, and why
>    does that make `Pin<Box<T>>` easy to move around? (Hint: what actually
>    moves when you move a box?)

#### Async Traits and Object Safety

Abstracting over async behavior is natural: a `Storage` trait with an async
`get`, or a `Handler` trait with an async `call`. Since Rust 1.75, you can write
`async fn` directly in traits:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub trait Storage {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
}

pub struct Memory(HashMap<String, String>);

impl Storage for Memory {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.0.get(key).cloned()
    }
}

// Static dispatch (generics) works perfectly.
async fn print_key(store: &impl Storage, key: &str) {
    println!("{:?}", store.get(key).await);
}
```

Under the hood, `async fn get` in a trait means
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> impl Future<Output = Option<String>>`, and each
implementation returns its **own anonymous future type**, with its own size.
That breaks dynamic dispatch:

```rust
// let stores: Vec<Box<dyn Storage>> = ...;
// error[E0038]: the trait `Storage` is not dyn compatible
//   because method `get` is `async`
```

A vtable entry must have one fixed signature, but there is no single return
type (or size) that covers every implementation's future. ("Dyn compatible" is
the current name for what used to be called "object safe".) The standard fix
is to **box the future**, giving every implementation the same return type,
`Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + '_>>`:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::sync::Arc;

type BoxFuture<'a, T> = Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send + 'a>>;

pub trait DynStorage: Send + Sync {
    fn get<'a>(&'a self, key: &'a str) -> BoxFuture<'a, Option<String>>;
}

pub struct Memory(HashMap<String, String>);

impl DynStorage for Memory {
    fn get<'a>(&'a self, key: &'a str) -> BoxFuture<'a, Option<String>> {
        Box::pin(async move { self.0.get(key).cloned() })   // one allocation per call
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let store: Arc<dyn DynStorage> =
        Arc::new(Memory(HashMap::from([("a".into(), "1".into())])));
    println!("{:?}", store.get("a").await);   // Some("1")
}
```

The `async-trait` crate generates exactly this boilerplate from `async fn`
syntax:

```rust
use async_trait::async_trait;

#[async_trait]                              // rewrites to Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>
pub trait Handler {
    async fn call(&self, req: String) -> String;
}

struct Echo;

#[async_trait]
impl Handler for Echo {
    async fn call(&self, req: String) -> String { req }
}

// Now `Box<dyn Handler>` works.
```

| Approach | Dynamic dispatch | Allocation per call | `Send` futures | Notes |
| -------- | ---------------- | ------------------- | -------------- | ----- |
| Native `async fn` in trait | No | No | Not expressible for callers by default | Best for generics; see next topic for `Send` |
| `-> impl Future<Output = T> + Send` in trait | No | No | Yes, enforced on impls | Impls may still write `async fn` |
| `#[async_trait]` | Yes | Yes (boxed) | Yes (default; `?Send` opt-out) | Mature, widely used |
| Manual `BoxFuture` | Yes | Yes | You choose | No macro, full control |
| `dynosaur` crate | Yes, alongside static | Only through `dyn` | Configurable | Generates a dyn-compatible companion type |

A practical guideline: use native `async fn` in traits when callers are
generic, and box (manually or via `async-trait`) when you need trait objects,
such as plugin registries or `Vec<Box<dyn Handler>>`. The cost of one
allocation per call is usually negligible next to the I/O the call performs.

> Key Takeaways
> - `async fn` in traits is stable since Rust 1.75 and works with static
>   dispatch.
> - Such traits are not dyn compatible, because each impl returns a differently
>   sized anonymous future.
> - Boxing the returned future (`Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'a>>`) restores
>   dynamic dispatch at the cost of one allocation per call.
> - `async-trait` automates the boxing; `dynosaur` offers dyn support alongside
>   native async traits.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Define a trait `Notifier` with `async fn notify(&self, msg: &str)` and
>    implement it for `ConsoleNotifier` and `DelayedNotifier`. Call both through
>    a generic function.
> 2. Convert `Notifier` into a dyn-compatible version with a manual
>    `BoxFuture`, store both implementations in a `Vec<Box<dyn ...>>`, and
>    notify them all concurrently.
> 3. Interview: Why can't `dyn Trait` support a method returning
>    `impl Future`, and what does boxing change? (Hint: consider what the
>    vtable needs to know about the return value at compile time.)

#### Send Bounds on Futures

On a multi-threaded runtime, a task can be paused on one worker and resumed on
another. Everything stored in the future (all locals live across `.await`) may
therefore cross threads, so `tokio::spawn` requires the future to be `Send`.

Nobody writes `impl Send` for a future. The compiler **infers** it: a future
is `Send` if every value it holds *across an `.await`* is `Send`. Values used
only between awaits do not matter, because they never exist while the task is
suspended. This leads to errors that feel surprising at first:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;

async fn not_send() {
    let rc = Rc::new(5);                    // Rc is !Send
    tokio::task::yield_now().await;         // `rc` is still alive here
    println!("{rc}");
}

async fn is_send() {
    {
        let rc = Rc::new(5);
        println!("{rc}");
    }                                       // `rc` dropped before the await
    tokio::task::yield_now().await;
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    tokio::spawn(is_send());                // fine
    // tokio::spawn(not_send());
    // error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
    //   within `{async fn body}`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<i32>`
    // note: future is not `Send` as this value is used across an await
}
```

The most common real-world case is a `std::sync::MutexGuard` held across an
`.await`. The guard is `!Send` (a mutex must be unlocked on the thread that
locked it), and holding a lock while waiting is a bad idea anyway:

```rust
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

async fn save(_v: Vec<u32>) {}

async fn bad(data: Arc<Mutex<Vec<u32>>>) {
    let mut guard = data.lock().unwrap();
    guard.push(1);
    save(guard.clone()).await;              // guard alive across await: !Send
}

async fn good(data: Arc<Mutex<Vec<u32>>>) {
    let snapshot = {
        let mut guard = data.lock().unwrap();
        guard.push(1);
        guard.clone()
    };                                      // guard dropped at end of block
    save(snapshot).await;                   // nothing !Send held here
}

// A compile-time check you can drop into tests:
fn assert_send<T: Send>(_: &T) {}

fn check() {
    let data = Arc::new(Mutex::new(vec![]));
    assert_send(&good(data.clone()));
    // assert_send(&bad(data));             // fails to compile
}
```

| Held across `.await` | Problem | Fix |
| -------------------- | ------- | --- |
| `Rc<T>`, `RefCell` borrow guards | `!Send` | Use `Arc`, or drop before the await |
| `std::sync::MutexGuard` | `!Send`, and blocks other threads | Scope the lock in a block; or `tokio::sync::Mutex` if the lock must be held while awaiting |
| Raw pointers, some FFI handles | `!Send` | Wrap in a type with a justified `unsafe impl Send`, or keep on one thread |
| `dyn Trait` without `+ Send` | `!Send` | Write `Box<dyn Trait + Send>` |

Prefer a block scope over a bare `drop(guard)` call. Explicit `drop` is
understood by current compilers (since Rust 1.74), but a block makes the
lifetime obvious to readers too.

If a future genuinely cannot be `Send`, keep it on one thread: use a
current-thread runtime, or `tokio::task::LocalSet` with `spawn_local`.

**Send bounds and async traits.** With native `async fn` in traits, a generic
caller cannot assume the returned future is `Send`:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

trait Storage {
    async fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String>;
}

fn spawn_lookup<S: Storage + Send + Sync + 'static>(s: Arc<S>) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        s.get("k").await                    // error: the future returned by `get`
    });                                     // is not known to be `Send`
}
```

Two stable fixes exist. Declare the trait method with an explicit `Send`
bound, which implementations can still satisfy with `async fn`:

```rust
use std::future::Future;

trait Storage: Send + Sync {
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> impl Future<Output = Option<String>> + Send;
}
```

Or use the `trait-variant` crate, whose `#[trait_variant::make(SendStorage: Send)]`
generates a second trait whose futures are all `Send`. A language feature,
*return type notation* (`S: Storage<get(..): Send>`), is being designed to let
callers add the bound themselves.

> Key Takeaways
> - `tokio::spawn` on a multi-thread runtime requires `Send` futures because
>   tasks migrate between threads at `.await` points.
> - A future is `Send` exactly when everything it holds across an `.await` is
>   `Send`; the error notes point to the offending value.
> - Drop `Rc`, `RefCell` guards, and `std` mutex guards before awaiting,
>   ideally by scoping them in a block.
> - For async traits used with `spawn`, require `Send` futures with
>   `-> impl Future + Send` or `trait-variant`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an async function that uses a `RefCell` and an await so it fails
>    `assert_send`, then fix it two different ways.
> 2. Run a `!Send` future (holding an `Rc` across an await) on Tokio using
>    `LocalSet` and `spawn_local`.
> 3. Interview: Why is it acceptable to use `Rc` inside an async function as
>    long as it is not held across an `.await`, even when the task runs on a
>    multi-threaded runtime? (Hint: when can a task actually switch threads?)

#### Cancellation Safety

Section 11.3 showed that cancelling a future means dropping it at its current
`.await`. That is simple and efficient, but it raises a question that
synchronous code rarely faces: *what if the future is dropped halfway through
an operation?* Any work done before the last completed `.await` stays done,
and any data the future was holding internally is lost.

A future is **cancellation safe** if dropping it before completion, and then
retrying the operation, loses nothing. The question matters most in
`select!` loops, where every iteration may cancel the futures of the losing
branches.

Consider reading a line from a socket while also watching for shutdown:

```rust
use tokio::io::{AsyncBufReadExt, BufReader};
use tokio::net::TcpStream;
use tokio::sync::watch;

async fn bad_loop(stream: TcpStream, mut shutdown: watch::Receiver<bool>) {
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);
    let mut line = String::new();
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            // NOT cancellation safe: if shutdown.changed() wins while read_line
            // has consumed half a line, that partial data is lost.
            res = reader.read_line(&mut line) => {
                if res.unwrap_or(0) == 0 { break; }
                println!("line: {line}");
                line.clear();
            }
            _ = shutdown.changed() => break,
        }
    }
}

async fn good_loop(stream: TcpStream, mut shutdown: watch::Receiver<bool>) {
    // Lines keeps its own buffer, so next_line() IS cancellation safe:
    // partial data stays inside `lines` until a full line arrives.
    let mut lines = BufReader::new(stream).lines();
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            res = lines.next_line() => match res {
                Ok(Some(line)) => println!("line: {line}"),
                _ => break,                 // EOF or error
            },
            _ = shutdown.changed() => break,
        }
    }
}
```

The general pattern: a cancellation-safe operation keeps any partial progress
in state that *outlives* the future (inside the stream or reader object), not
inside the future itself. Tokio documents cancellation safety for its methods:

| Cancellation safe | Not cancellation safe (data or position can be lost) |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `mpsc::Receiver::recv`, `broadcast::Receiver::recv` | `AsyncReadExt::read_exact`, `read_to_end`, `read_to_string` |
| `watch::Receiver::changed` | `AsyncBufReadExt::read_line`, `read_until` |
| `AsyncReadExt::read`, `AsyncWriteExt::write` | `AsyncWriteExt::write_all` (unknown how much was written) |
| `TcpListener::accept` | `mpsc::Sender::send` (the message is dropped with the future) |
| `Lines::next_line`, `StreamExt::next` on most streams | `Mutex::lock`, `Semaphore::acquire` (lose their place in the fair queue) |
| `Interval::tick`, `sleep` | Any custom `async fn` with several awaits mid-operation |

Strategies when an operation is not cancellation safe:

1. **Create the future once, outside the loop**, pin it, and poll it by
   reference (`&mut fut`) so that losing a `select!` round does not drop it.
2. **Use a stateful wrapper** (`Lines`, `FramedRead` with a codec) that buffers
   partial progress.
3. **Move the critical operation into a spawned task** so it runs to
   completion regardless of the caller (spawned tasks are not cancelled when
   their `JoinHandle` is dropped).
4. **Design for atomicity**: perform state changes after the last await, or
   use transactions, so a cancellation at any await leaves consistent state.

```rust
use tokio::sync::mpsc;
use tokio::time::{sleep, Duration};

// Strategy 1: keep the in-flight send alive across select! iterations.
async fn send_with_progress(tx: mpsc::Sender<Vec<u8>>, payload: Vec<u8>) {
    let send = tx.send(payload);            // created once
    tokio::pin!(send);
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            res = &mut send => {            // polled by reference: never dropped early
                println!("sent: {}", res.is_ok());
                break;
            }
            _ = sleep(Duration::from_millis(500)) => {
                println!("still waiting for capacity...");
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Cancellation also affects state spread across awaits in your own code. In
`debit(a).await; credit(b).await;`, cancelling between the two calls leaves
money debited but not credited. Rust's async has no `async Drop` to run
cleanup code that awaits, so such invariants must be protected by design.

> Key Takeaways
> - A future can be dropped at any `.await`; cancellation safety means doing so
>   and retrying loses nothing.
> - It matters most for branches of a `select!` loop and for futures wrapped in
>   `timeout`.
> - Check the documentation: `recv`, `accept`, `read`, and `next_line` are
>   safe; `read_exact`, `read_line`, `write_all`, and `send` are not.
> - Fix unsafe cases by reusing a pinned future, buffering progress in a
>   stateful object, spawning the critical section, or ordering side effects
>   carefully.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a `select!` loop that calls `read_exact` for a 4-byte header while
>    a 1 ms interval ticks. Send data slowly from a client and demonstrate
>    corrupted framing. Fix it with `FramedRead` and `LengthDelimitedCodec`.
> 2. Write an `async fn transfer` with two awaits, wrap it in a `timeout` that
>    fires in the middle, and show the inconsistent state. Then restructure it
>    to be safe.
> 3. Interview: What does "cancellation safe" mean for an async method, and
>    why is `mpsc::Receiver::recv` safe while `mpsc::Sender::send` is not?
>    (Hint: where does the message live while the future is pending?)

#### Structured Concurrency Patterns

`tokio::spawn` is **unstructured**: a spawned task is detached from its
creator. If the parent returns, errors out, or is cancelled, the child keeps
running, possibly forever, possibly writing to resources the parent thought it
had finished with. Errors in children are easy to lose, and at shutdown nobody
knows which tasks are still in flight.

**Structured concurrency** is the discipline that *a child task never outlives
its parent scope*. Concurrency then nests like function calls do: when a block
ends, everything it started has finished or been cancelled. You already know
two structured tools:

- `join!`/`select!` (section 11.3) are structured by construction: the
  sub-futures live inside the parent future and die with it.
- `std::thread::scope` (section 10.1) does the same for threads.

There is no fully safe async equivalent of `thread::scope` that lets spawned
tasks borrow local data. A scope future could be leaked with `mem::forget`,
ending the borrow while tasks still run, so `tokio::spawn` must require
`'static`. Instead, the ecosystem offers patterns that tie task lifetimes to an
owner:

| Tool | Crate | What it guarantees |
| ---- | ----- | ------------------ |
| `join!`, `select!`, `FuturesUnordered` | tokio / futures | Sub-futures cannot outlive the parent future |
| `JoinSet` | tokio | Owns tasks; `join_next()` collects results; dropping the set aborts all tasks |
| `CancellationToken` | tokio-util | Cooperative cancellation broadcast to a tree of tasks (`child_token()`) |
| `TaskTracker` | tokio-util | Wait until a group of tasks has finished (`close()` then `wait()`) |
| Scoped-task crates (`moro`, `async-scoped`) | third party | Borrowing tasks with restrictions or `unsafe` caveats |

The usual production recipe for a service is: a `CancellationToken` to signal
shutdown, a `TaskTracker` (or `JoinSet`) to wait for every task to finish, and
a timeout to bound how long shutdown may take.

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::{interval, sleep, timeout};
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;
use tokio_util::task::TaskTracker;

async fn worker(id: u32, token: CancellationToken) {
    let mut ticker = interval(Duration::from_millis(200));
    loop {
        tokio::select! {
            _ = token.cancelled() => {
                println!("worker {id}: flushing and exiting");
                sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await;   // graceful cleanup
                return;
            }
            _ = ticker.tick() => println!("worker {id}: tick"),
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let token = CancellationToken::new();
    let tracker = TaskTracker::new();

    for id in 0..3 {
        // child_token: cancelled when the parent is, but can be cancelled alone.
        tracker.spawn(worker(id, token.child_token()));
    }
    tracker.close();                        // no more tasks; wait() may now complete

    // In a real server: tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await.unwrap();
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(500)).await;
    println!("shutdown requested");
    token.cancel();                         // tell every worker to stop

    // Structured exit: main does not return until all children are done,
    // but gives up after 5 seconds rather than hanging forever.
    if timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), tracker.wait()).await.is_err() {
        eprintln!("some tasks did not stop in time");
    }
    println!("all workers stopped");
}
```

For fan-out work whose results matter, `JoinSet` gives structure plus error
propagation:

```rust
use tokio::task::JoinSet;

async fn fetch(id: u32) -> Result<String, String> {
    if id == 3 { Err(format!("item {id} failed")) } else { Ok(format!("item {id}")) }
}

async fn fetch_all(ids: Vec<u32>) -> Result<Vec<String>, String> {
    let mut set = JoinSet::new();
    for id in ids {
        set.spawn(fetch(id));               // runs in parallel on worker threads
    }
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await {
        let item = res.map_err(|e| e.to_string())??;   // JoinError, then app error
        out.push(item);
    }
    Ok(out)
    // On early return via `?`, `set` is dropped and the remaining tasks are
    // aborted, so no orphaned work survives the failed call.
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Plain `spawn` is unstructured: tasks can outlive and silently outfail
>   their creator.
> - Structured concurrency means children finish or are cancelled before the
>   parent scope ends; `join!`, `select!`, and `JoinSet` provide it.
> - Safe borrowing scoped tasks are not possible in async Rust because futures
>   can be leaked, which is why spawned tasks need `'static`.
> - For services, combine `CancellationToken` (signal), `TaskTracker` or
>   `JoinSet` (wait), and a timeout (bound) for graceful shutdown.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a program that spawns detached background tasks so that all of
>    them are owned by a `JoinSet` and the first error cancels the others.
> 2. Implement graceful shutdown for the echo server from section 11.2: stop
>    accepting on Ctrl-C, let open connections finish their current message,
>    and exit after at most 10 seconds.
> 3. Interview: Why can `std::thread::scope` let threads borrow stack data
>    safely while an async equivalent cannot offer the same API? (Hint:
>    consider what `mem::forget` does to a future versus a blocking function
>    call.)

---

## 12. Testing, Documentation, and Quality

The compiler rules out whole classes of bugs, but it cannot tell whether your
function computes the right answer, whether a refactor kept behaviour intact, or
whether a change made the hot path twice as slow. This chapter covers the tools
Rust provides for those questions: the built-in test harness, advanced testing
techniques (doc tests, property testing, fuzzing, mocking, snapshots, coverage),
benchmarking and profiling, and writing documentation that is itself tested.
Together they turn "it compiles" into "it is correct, fast enough, and usable by
others".

<a id="121-testing-fundamentals"></a>
### 12.1 Testing Fundamentals

Rust ships a test framework in the toolchain itself: no runner to install and no
configuration to write. This section covers how unit and integration tests are
written, where they live, how to express expected failures, and how to select
which tests run.

#### Unit Tests and #[test]

Imagine changing a parsing function to support a new syntax. Without tests, the
only way to know whether the old inputs still work is to try them all by hand,
every time. A **unit test** automates that check: a small function that calls
one piece of code with known input and asserts on the output. Run hundreds of
them in a second and you can refactor without fear.

In Rust, a test is any function annotated with `#[test]`. When you run
`cargo test`, Cargo compiles your crate a second time with the `test` cfg
enabled and links it against **libtest**, the built-in harness. libtest
collects every `#[test]` function, runs them on a pool of threads, and reports
which passed. A test **passes if it returns normally** and **fails if it
panics**; the assertion macros are just convenient ways to panic with a useful
message.

By convention, unit tests live in the same file as the code they test, inside a
`tests` module guarded by `#[cfg(test)]` so that it is compiled only for
`cargo test`, never into your real binary:

```rust
// src/lib.rs

/// Splits `"key=value"` into its two parts, trimming whitespace.
pub fn parse_kv(line: &str) -> Option<(&str, &str)> {
    let (k, v) = line.split_once('=')?;
    let (k, v) = (k.trim(), v.trim());
    if k.is_empty() { None } else { Some((k, v)) }
}

fn normalize_key(k: &str) -> String {      // private helper
    k.to_ascii_lowercase().replace('-', "_")
}

#[cfg(test)]                                // compiled only by `cargo test`
mod tests {
    use super::*;                           // bring the parent's items, private ones too

    #[test]
    fn splits_and_trims() {
        assert_eq!(parse_kv(" port = 8080 "), Some(("port", "8080")));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_missing_key() {
        assert_eq!(parse_kv("=8080"), None);
        assert!(parse_kv("no equals sign").is_none());
    }

    #[test]
    fn private_functions_are_testable() {
        // Child modules can see their parent's private items.
        assert_eq!(normalize_key("Max-Conn"), "max_conn");
    }
}
```

The assertion macros:

| Macro | Panics when | On failure prints |
| ----- | ----------- | ----------------- |
| `assert!(cond)` | `cond` is `false` | The condition's source text |
| `assert_eq!(a, b)` | `a != b` | Both values with `{:?}` (`left`, `right`) |
| `assert_ne!(a, b)` | `a == b` | Both values with `{:?}` |
| `debug_assert!` and friends | Same, but only when debug assertions are on | Same |
| `assert!(matches!(v, Pattern))` | `v` does not match the pattern | The condition's source text |

All of them accept an optional format string, which is the cheapest way to make
failures easy to diagnose:

```rust
#[test]
fn every_line_parses() {
    let config = "host = example.com\nport = 8080\nmode = fast";
    for (n, line) in config.lines().enumerate() {
        // Without the message you learn only that *some* line failed.
        assert!(parse_kv(line).is_some(), "line {} did not parse: {line:?}", n + 1);
    }
}
```

Running the suite:

```text
$ cargo test
   Compiling kv v0.1.0 (/home/user/kv)
    Finished `test` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.61s
     Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/kv-3f2a9c1d)

running 4 tests
test tests::private_functions_are_testable ... ok
test tests::rejects_missing_key ... ok
test tests::splits_and_trims ... ok
test tests::every_line_parses ... ok

test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

   Doc-tests kv
...
```

Two harness behaviours surprise newcomers:

- **Output is captured.** `println!` inside a passing test is swallowed so the
  report stays readable; it is shown only for failing tests. Use
  `cargo test -- --nocapture` to see it live, or `-- --show-output` to print
  the captured output of passing tests after they finish.
- **Tests run in parallel**, one thread per test, up to the number of CPUs.
  Tests that share global state (the current directory, environment variables,
  a fixed file path, a port) can interfere with each other. Prefer giving each
  test its own resources (a temporary directory, port `0`); as a last resort,
  run serially with `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`. Note that since the 2024
  edition, `std::env::set_var` is `unsafe` precisely because changing the
  environment while other threads read it is a data race.

Arguments before `--` go to Cargo; arguments after `--` go to the test binary.

> Key Takeaways
> - A test is a `#[test]` function; it passes if it returns and fails if it
>   panics.
> - Unit tests go in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file and can test
>   private items through `use super::*`.
> - `assert_eq!` prints both values on failure; add a custom message whenever
>   the values alone will not explain the failure.
> - The harness captures output and runs tests in parallel: avoid shared global
>   state, or use `--nocapture` and `--test-threads=1` when debugging.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function `fn word_count(s: &str) -> usize` and four unit tests
>    covering empty input, a single word, repeated whitespace, and Unicode
>    words.
> 2. Write a test that prints with `println!`, make it fail, and compare the
>    output of `cargo test`, `cargo test -- --nocapture`, and
>    `cargo test -- --show-output`.
> 3. Interview: Two tests pass individually but fail intermittently when run
>    together. What is the most likely cause, and how would you fix it properly
>    rather than with `--test-threads=1`? (Hint: think about what the harness
>    runs concurrently and what state those tests might share.)

#### Integration Tests

Unit tests check pieces from the inside. They can call private functions, so
they can pass even when the public API is awkward or broken. **Integration
tests** check the crate from the outside, exactly as a user would: they can only
call `pub` items, through the crate's name.

Cargo treats every `.rs` file directly inside a top-level `tests/` directory as
a separate **test crate** that depends on your library:

```text
kv/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   └── lib.rs            library under test
└── tests/
    ├── parsing.rs        test crate #1 -> its own binary
    ├── config_file.rs    test crate #2 -> its own binary
    └── common/
        └── mod.rs        shared helpers; NOT a test crate (it is in a subdirectory)
```

```rust
// tests/common/mod.rs: helpers shared by several test files
use std::path::PathBuf;

pub fn fixture(name: &str) -> PathBuf {
    // CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR is the package root, regardless of the working directory.
    PathBuf::from(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("tests/fixtures").join(name)
}
```

```rust
// tests/config_file.rs
mod common;                                  // pull in tests/common/mod.rs

use kv::parse_kv;                            // only the public API is reachable

#[test]
fn parses_the_sample_config() {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(common::fixture("sample.conf")).unwrap();
    let pairs: Vec<_> = text.lines().filter_map(parse_kv).collect();
    assert_eq!(pairs.first(), Some(&("host", "example.com")));
}
```

Why `tests/common/mod.rs` rather than `tests/common.rs`? Every top-level file in
`tests/` becomes a test binary, so `tests/common.rs` would show up in the output
as a crate with "running 0 tests". Files in subdirectories are ignored by test
discovery and can be included as modules.

Things to know about integration tests:

| Aspect | Behaviour |
| ------ | --------- |
| Visibility | Only `pub` items; `#[cfg(test)]` items of the library are **not** visible, because the library is compiled normally for them |
| Dependencies | `[dependencies]` and `[dev-dependencies]` |
| Binary crates | A `src/main.rs`-only crate cannot be imported; move logic to `src/lib.rs`, or run the executable |
| Running one file | `cargo test --test config_file` |
| Build cost | Each file is linked into its own executable; many files mean many link steps |

To test a binary end to end, run the compiled executable. Cargo builds the
package's binaries before integration tests and exposes their paths through
`CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>`:

```rust
// tests/cli.rs: exercise the real `kv` executable
use std::process::Command;

#[test]
fn prints_value_for_key() {
    let out = Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_kv"))   // path set by Cargo at compile time
        .args(["get", "port", "tests/fixtures/sample.conf"])
        .output()
        .expect("failed to run binary");

    assert!(out.status.success());
    assert_eq!(String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).trim(), "8080");
}
```

The `assert_cmd` crate wraps this pattern with fluent assertions on exit codes
and output.

For larger suites, link time adds up. A common pattern is a single integration
test crate with modules, which links once:

```text
tests/
└── it/
    ├── main.rs        mod parsing; mod config_file; mod cli;
    ├── parsing.rs
    ├── config_file.rs
    └── cli.rs
```

Cargo discovers `tests/it/main.rs` as one test target named `it`.

> Key Takeaways
> - Each top-level file in `tests/` is a separate crate that sees only the
>   library's public API.
> - Shared helpers go in `tests/common/mod.rs` (a subdirectory), not
>   `tests/common.rs`.
> - Integration tests need a library target; test binaries end to end through
>   `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_<name>")`.
> - Many test files mean many link steps; a single `tests/it/main.rs` crate
>   with modules scales better.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Move the tests of a small library that only exercise public functions
>    from `src/lib.rs` into `tests/api.rs`. Which tests could not be moved, and
>    why?
> 2. Add a `tests/common/mod.rs` with a helper that creates a temporary
>    directory containing a config file (use the `tempfile` crate), and use it
>    from two different test files.
> 3. Interview: You add `#[cfg(test)] pub fn test_only_constructor()` to your
>    library, but your integration test cannot find it. Why? (Hint: how is the
>    library compiled when an integration test links against it?)

#### Test Organization and Modules

A test suite is code, and it rots like code. Good organization makes it obvious
where a test for a given behaviour belongs, keeps test-only code out of
production builds, and keeps the suite fast enough that people actually run it.

Rust has several kinds of test, each with its own place:

| Kind | Location | Can access | Compiled as | Run by |
| ---- | -------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------ |
| Unit | `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` beside the code | Everything in the module tree, private included | Part of the library/binary test build | `cargo test --lib` / `--bins` |
| Integration | `tests/*.rs` | Public API | One crate per file | `cargo test --test NAME` / `--tests` |
| Doc | Code blocks in `///` and `//!` | Public API | One crate per example (or merged) | `cargo test --doc` |
| Examples | `examples/*.rs` | Public API | Binaries | Compiled (not run) by `cargo test` |
| Benchmarks | `benches/*.rs` | Public API | Release-mode binaries | `cargo bench` |

When a module's tests grow long, move them into their own file but keep them a
child module, so they still see private items:

```text
src/
├── lib.rs
├── parser.rs          ends with:  #[cfg(test)] mod tests;
└── parser/
    └── tests.rs       the body of parser::tests (no `mod tests { }` wrapper)
```

```rust
// src/parser/tests.rs
use super::*;          // `super` is still `parser`, so private items are visible

#[test]
fn tokenizes_numbers() {
    assert_eq!(tokenize("12 + 3").len(), 3);
}
```

Test-only code in the library belongs behind `#[cfg(test)]`, and test-only
dependencies belong in `[dev-dependencies]`, which are never compiled into
users' builds:

```rust
pub struct Config {
    pub port: u16,
    pub host: String,
}

#[cfg(test)]
impl Config {
    // A builder that only tests need; absent from release builds.
    pub(crate) fn for_test() -> Self {
        Config { port: 0, host: "127.0.0.1".into() }
    }
}
```

**Table-driven tests** keep many similar cases readable. A loop with a
descriptive message works with no dependencies; the `rstest` crate turns each
case into a separately reported test:

```rust
#[test]
fn parse_kv_cases() {
    let cases = [
        ("a=1", Some(("a", "1"))),
        (" a = 1 ", Some(("a", "1"))),
        ("=1", None),
        ("a", None),
    ];
    for (input, expected) in cases {
        assert_eq!(parse_kv(input), expected, "input: {input:?}");
    }
}

// With rstest (dev-dependency): each #[case] is its own test, e.g. kv_cases::case_3
#[rstest::rstest]
#[case("a=1", Some(("a", "1")))]
#[case(" a = 1 ", Some(("a", "1")))]
#[case("=1", None)]
fn kv_cases(#[case] input: &str, #[case] expected: Option<(&str, &str)>) {
    assert_eq!(parse_kv(input), expected);
}
```

Naming matters because test names are what you read in failure reports and what
you filter on. Prefer names that state the behaviour (`rejects_missing_key`,
`retries_after_timeout`) over names that repeat the function (`test_parse_1`).
Grouping with nested modules gives filterable paths such as
`parser::tests::numbers::rejects_leading_zero`.

> Key Takeaways
> - Unit tests sit beside the code, integration tests in `tests/`, examples in
>   `examples/`, benchmarks in `benches/`; doc tests live in doc comments.
> - Long unit test modules can move to `src/<module>/tests.rs` and still see
>   private items.
> - Keep test helpers behind `#[cfg(test)]` and test libraries in
>   `[dev-dependencies]`.
> - Use table-driven tests (or `rstest`) for many similar cases, and give tests
>   behaviour-describing names.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a module with an inline `mod tests` and move its tests to
>    `src/<module>/tests.rs` without changing any test.
> 2. Convert five near-identical tests into a single table-driven test, then
>    into an `rstest` test, and compare the failure output of each when one
>    case breaks.
> 3. Interview: Where would you put a test that checks a private invariant of a
>    data structure, and where would you put a test that checks a user-facing
>    workflow? Justify each choice. (Hint: consider what each location can see
>    and what breaks when internals are refactored.)

#### should_panic and Result Tests

Some behaviour is *supposed* to fail: indexing past the end, constructing an
invalid value, parsing garbage. Testing only the happy path leaves those
contracts unchecked. Rust offers two ways to write tests about failure, matching
its two failure mechanisms (Chapter 7): panics and `Result`.

**`#[should_panic]`** inverts the pass condition: the test passes only if the
body panics. Always add `expected = "..."`, a substring the panic message must
contain. Otherwise the test also passes when the code panics for an unrelated
reason, such as an `unwrap()` on the wrong line:

```rust
pub struct Stack<T> {
    items: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T> Stack<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self { Stack { items: Vec::new() } }
    pub fn push(&mut self, x: T) { self.items.push(x) }
    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> { self.items.pop() }

    /// # Panics
    /// Panics if the stack is empty.
    pub fn peek(&self) -> &T {
        self.items.last().expect("peek on empty stack")
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    #[should_panic(expected = "empty stack")]   // substring of the panic message
    fn peek_on_empty_panics() {
        Stack::<i32>::new().peek();
    }
}
```

**Result-returning tests** let you use `?` instead of `unwrap()`. The test
fails if it returns `Err`, and the harness prints the error's `Debug`
representation:

```rust
use std::error::Error;

#[test]
fn reads_port_from_config() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let text = "port = 8080";
    let (_, value) = parse_kv(text).ok_or("no key/value pair")?;
    let port: u16 = value.parse()?;           // ParseIntError converts into Box<dyn Error>
    assert_eq!(port, 8080);
    Ok(())
}
```

To assert that a function *returns* an error, which is what you usually want for
`Result`-based APIs, check the value directly. Matching on the error variant is
more robust than comparing message strings:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub enum PortError { Empty, NotANumber, Reserved(u16) }

pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, PortError> {
    let s = s.trim();
    if s.is_empty() { return Err(PortError::Empty); }
    let n: u16 = s.parse().map_err(|_| PortError::NotANumber)?;
    if n < 1024 { Err(PortError::Reserved(n)) } else { Ok(n) }
}

#[test]
fn rejects_reserved_ports() {
    assert_eq!(parse_port("80"), Err(PortError::Reserved(80)));
    assert!(matches!(parse_port("http"), Err(PortError::NotANumber)));
}
```

| Approach | Use when | Caveat |
| -------- | -------- | ------ |
| `#[should_panic(expected = ...)]` | The documented contract is a panic | Must return `()`; cannot be combined with a `Result` return type |
| `-> Result<(), E>` with `?` | Setup steps are fallible and you want concise code | Error location is lost; the report shows only the `Debug` of the error |
| `assert_eq!(f(x), Err(...))` / `matches!` | The API returns `Result` and the error is part of the contract | Requires `PartialEq` for `assert_eq!` |
| `std::panic::catch_unwind` | You need to check a panic and then continue the test | Requires `UnwindSafe` closures; rarely needed |

Tests always unwind on panic: Cargo ignores `panic = "abort"` for test and bench
builds, because the harness relies on catching each test's panic.

> Key Takeaways
> - `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]` passes only if the body panics with a
>   message containing the substring; always include `expected`.
> - Tests may return `Result<(), E>` (with `E: Debug`) so that `?` works;
>   returning `Err` fails the test.
> - For `Result`-based APIs, assert on the returned error variant rather than
>   using `should_panic`.
> - `should_panic` tests must return `()`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32` that panics with "division by
>    zero" and test it with `should_panic`. Then change the panic message and
>    observe what happens to the test.
> 2. Rewrite three tests that use several `.unwrap()` calls into
>    `Result`-returning tests with `?`. Compare the failure output of both
>    styles.
> 3. Interview: Why is `#[should_panic]` without `expected` considered a weak
>    test? Describe a bug it would fail to catch. (Hint: what else in the test
>    body could panic?)

#### Ignoring and Filtering Tests

As a suite grows, running everything on every save becomes slow, and some tests
need resources (a database, the network, ten minutes of CPU) that are not
always available. libtest lets you mark tests as ignored by default and select
tests by name, so the fast feedback loop and the exhaustive CI run can use the
same suite.

`#[ignore]` excludes a test from normal runs while keeping it compiled, so it
cannot silently stop building. A reason string documents why:

```rust
#[test]
#[ignore = "needs a running PostgreSQL; run with `cargo test -- --ignored`"]
fn migrates_real_database() {
    // ...
}

#[test]
#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]               // ignored only when running under Miri (Chapter 14)
fn uses_the_filesystem() {
    // ...
}
```

Filtering by name uses a substring match on the full test path
(`module::submodule::test_name`):

```bash
cargo test parse                       # every test whose path contains "parse"
cargo test -- parse config             # several filters: matches either one
cargo test -- --exact tests::parse_kv  # exactly this path, no substring matching
cargo test -- --skip slow              # everything except paths containing "slow"
cargo test -- --ignored                # ONLY the ignored tests
cargo test -- --include-ignored        # everything, ignored or not
cargo test -- --list                   # list test names without running them
```

Cargo-level flags select which *targets* are built and run, before libtest
filters by name:

| Command | Runs |
| ------- | ---- |
| `cargo test --lib` | Unit tests of the library only |
| `cargo test --test cli` | Only the integration test crate `tests/cli.rs` |
| `cargo test --tests` | All unit and integration tests, no doc tests |
| `cargo test --doc` | Only doc tests |
| `cargo test -p kv-core` | Only one workspace member |
| `cargo test --no-fail-fast` | Keep running other test binaries after one fails |

The output tells you what the filter excluded:

```text
running 2 tests
test tests::parse_kv_cases ... ok
test tests::splits_and_trims ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 8 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
```

Many projects use **cargo-nextest** (`cargo nextest run`) as a faster test
runner. It runs each test in its own process, which isolates global state and
makes per-test timeouts and retries possible, and it produces clearer output for
large suites. It does not run doc tests, so CI usually runs `cargo nextest run`
followed by `cargo test --doc`.

A typical split:

```text
local edit loop:   cargo test parser            (seconds, one area)
pre-push:          cargo test                   (whole fast suite)
CI:                cargo test -- --include-ignored  (or nextest + doc tests)
nightly CI job:    slow, ignored, and external-service tests
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `#[ignore = "reason"]` keeps slow or resource-dependent tests compiled but
>   out of the default run; `--ignored` or `--include-ignored` runs them.
> - Name filters are substring matches on the full test path; `--exact` and
>   `--skip` refine them.
> - Arguments before `--` select Cargo targets (`--lib`, `--test`, `--doc`);
>   arguments after `--` go to libtest.
> - cargo-nextest offers process-per-test isolation and better reporting but
>   does not run doc tests.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Mark one test `#[ignore]` with a reason, then run the suite three ways:
>    default, `--ignored`, and `--include-ignored`. Explain the counts.
> 2. Using only filters, run every test in the `parser` module except those
>    whose names contain `unicode`.
> 3. Interview: Your CI runs `cargo test` and takes 25 minutes, mostly because
>    of a few end-to-end tests. How would you restructure the suite and the CI
>    pipeline so developers get fast feedback without losing coverage? (Hint:
>    think about `#[ignore]`, separate jobs, and test targets.)

<a id="122-advanced-testing"></a>
### 12.2 Advanced Testing

Hand-written example-based tests check the cases you thought of. This section
covers techniques that reach further: documentation that is tested, inputs
generated by the thousand, fuzzers that hunt for crashes, test doubles that
isolate code from the outside world, snapshots for large outputs, and coverage
reports that show what the suite never touched.

#### Doc Tests

Chapters 1 and 8 introduced the headline feature: code blocks in doc comments
are compiled and run by `cargo test`. This topic covers how that works and the
controls you need to write doc examples that are honest, readable, and fast.

**How rustdoc runs an example.** Each fenced code block is treated as a small
program *outside* your crate. Roughly, rustdoc:

1. Adds `extern crate your_crate;` (so `use your_crate::...` works).
2. Wraps the code in `fn main() { ... }` unless it already contains one.
3. Compiles it, runs it, and treats a panic as a failure.

```text
/// ```                               What rustdoc compiles (simplified):
/// use kv::parse_kv;                 extern crate kv;
/// assert_eq!(                       fn main() {
///     parse_kv("a=1"),                  use kv::parse_kv;
///     Some(("a", "1")));                assert_eq!(parse_kv("a=1"), Some(("a", "1")));
/// ```                               }
```
