Because examples are external code, they see only the public API, which makes
them a good check that the public API is actually usable. Examples on private
items still run, but they cannot call those items.

**Hidden lines.** Lines starting with `# ` (hash, space) are compiled but not
shown in the rendered documentation. Use them for setup that would distract the
reader:

```rust
/// Reads the configured port.
///
/// ```
/// # use std::error::Error;
/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {   // hidden: enables `?` below
/// let port: u16 = "8080".parse()?;
/// assert_eq!(port, 8080);
/// # Ok(())
/// # }
/// ```
pub fn port() {}
```

There is a shorter idiom for `?`: if the block ends with an `Ok(())` whose error
type is spelled out, rustdoc wraps it in a function returning `Result`:

```rust
/// ```
/// let port: u16 = "8080".parse()?;
/// assert_eq!(port, 8080);
/// Ok::<(), std::num::ParseIntError>(())      // turbofish names the error type
/// ```
pub fn port_short() {}
```

**Code block attributes** control what rustdoc does with a block:

| Fence | Compiled | Run | Use for |
| ----- | -------- | --- | ------- |
| `` ```rust `` or `` ``` `` | Yes | Yes | Normal examples (the default) |
| `` ```no_run `` | Yes | No | Examples that need the network, a server, or run forever |
| `` ```should_panic `` | Yes | Must panic | Demonstrating a documented panic |
| `` ```compile_fail `` | Must fail | No | Showing what the type system forbids |
| `` ```compile_fail,E0382 `` | Must fail with that error code | No | A more precise `compile_fail` |
| `` ```ignore `` | No | No | Pseudo-code; avoid, since it is never checked |
| `` ```text `` (or any non-Rust language) | No | No | Shell sessions, output, config files |
| `` ```edition2021 `` | Yes, with that edition | Yes | Edition-specific behaviour |
| `` ```standalone_crate `` | As its own crate | Yes | Examples that must not be merged (see below) |

```rust
/// A `Token` cannot be used after it has been consumed:
///
/// ```compile_fail,E0382
/// let t = auth::Token::new("secret");
/// auth::consume(t);
/// auth::consume(t);                  // error[E0382]: use of moved value
/// ```
///
/// Connecting needs a live server, so this example is only compiled:
///
/// ```no_run
/// let session = auth::connect("db.internal:5432")?;
/// # Ok::<(), auth::Error>(())
/// ```
pub mod docs_only {}
```

`compile_fail` tests are useful but fragile: the block passes if it fails to
compile for *any* reason, including a typo. Adding the error code makes the
check meaningful.

**Merged doc tests (2024 edition).** Historically each example was compiled as
its own executable, which made doc tests the slowest part of many suites. In
the 2024 edition, rustdoc merges compatible examples into a single binary and
runs them together; you can see this in the output:

```text
   Doc-tests kv

running 7 tests
.......
test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

running 3 tests                    <- examples that must stay standalone
i..
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.08s

all doctests ran in 0.29s; merged doctests compilation took 0.20s
```

Examples that use crate-level attributes (`#![...]`), `compile_fail`, or that
are marked `standalone_crate` are still compiled separately.

> Key Takeaways
> - Each doc example is compiled as an external crate wrapped in `fn main`, so
>   it exercises only the public API.
> - Hide setup with `# ` lines; enable `?` with a hidden `main` returning
>   `Result` or a trailing `Ok::<(), E>(())`.
> - Choose the right fence: `no_run` for side effects, `compile_fail,EXXXX` for
>   type-system guarantees, `text` for non-Rust content; avoid `ignore`.
> - The 2024 edition merges doc tests into one binary, which makes them much
>   faster to run.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a doc example that uses `?` twice, first with a hidden `main`, then
>    with the trailing `Ok::<(), E>(())` idiom. Check the rendered output with
>    `cargo doc --open`.
> 2. Write a `compile_fail` example demonstrating that your type is not `Send`,
>    then add the matching error code and confirm the test still passes.
> 3. Interview: A colleague marks every failing doc example `ignore` "to get CI
>    green". What are the risks, and which attributes would you use instead?
>    (Hint: compare what `ignore`, `no_run`, and `text` each verify.)

#### Property-Based Testing

Example-based tests check the inputs you thought of, and bugs tend to hide in
the inputs you did not: empty strings, `i32::MIN`, a single repeated byte,
Unicode combining characters. **Property-based testing** turns the problem
around. Instead of writing inputs and expected outputs, you state a
**property** that must hold for *all* valid inputs, and the framework generates
hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.

When it finds a failing input, the framework **shrinks** it: it repeatedly
tries simpler versions (shorter vectors, smaller numbers) that still fail, and
reports the minimal one. You get `[0, 0]` instead of a 300-element vector of
noise.

An analogy: example tests are a checklist inspector, while property tests are a
crash-test lab that throws thousands of randomized collisions at the car and
then reports the simplest collision that broke it.

The most widely used crate is `proptest` (`quickcheck` is a smaller
alternative):

```toml
[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"
```

```rust
// A run-length encoder: "aaab" -> [(b'a', 3), (b'b', 1)]
pub fn encode(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<(u8, u8)> {
    let mut out: Vec<(u8, u8)> = Vec::new();
    for &b in input {
        match out.last_mut() {
            Some((last, n)) if *last == b && *n < u8::MAX => *n += 1,
            _ => out.push((b, 1)),
        }
    }
    out
}

pub fn decode(runs: &[(u8, u8)]) -> Vec<u8> {
    runs.iter()
        .flat_map(|&(b, n)| std::iter::repeat_n(b, n as usize))
        .collect()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use proptest::prelude::*;

    proptest! {
        // Each test runs 256 random cases by default; raise it for this block.
        #![proptest_config(ProptestConfig::with_cases(1000))]

        #[test]
        fn roundtrip(data in prop::collection::vec(any::<u8>(), 0..1000)) {
            // Property: decoding an encoding gives back the original.
            prop_assert_eq!(decode(&encode(&data)), data);
        }

        #[test]
        fn runs_are_never_empty_or_adjacent_duplicates(data in prop::collection::vec(0u8..4, 0..500)) {
            // Small alphabet (0..4) makes long runs and repeats likely.
            let runs = encode(&data);
            for w in runs.windows(2) {
                // Equal neighbours are only allowed when the first run is full.
                prop_assert!(w[0].0 != w[1].0 || w[0].1 == u8::MAX);
            }
            prop_assert!(runs.iter().all(|&(_, n)| n > 0));
        }
    }
}
```

Note the `*n < u8::MAX` guard. Without it, a run of 256 identical bytes
overflows the counter. That is exactly the kind of bug an example-based suite
misses and a property test finds within seconds.

**Strategies** describe how to generate values. They compose:

```rust
use proptest::prelude::*;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Cmd { Push(i32), Pop }

// A strategy for one command, then for a whole program of commands.
fn cmd() -> impl Strategy<Value = Cmd> {
    prop_oneof![
        any::<i32>().prop_map(Cmd::Push),   // transform generated values
        Just(Cmd::Pop),                     // a constant
    ]
}

proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn stack_matches_vec_model(cmds in prop::collection::vec(cmd(), 0..100)) {
        // Model-based testing: compare the real type against a trusted "oracle".
        let mut real = Stack::new();
        let mut model: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
        for c in cmds {
            match c {
                Cmd::Push(x) => { real.push(x); model.push(x); }
                Cmd::Pop => prop_assert_eq!(real.pop(), model.pop()),
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Common shapes of properties:

| Property | Example |
| -------- | ------- |
| Round trip | `decode(encode(x)) == x`; `parse(format(x)) == x` |
| Oracle / model | Optimized implementation agrees with a slow, obviously correct one |
| Invariant | Output is sorted; a tree stays balanced; length is preserved |
| Idempotence | `normalize(normalize(x)) == normalize(x)` |
| Metamorphic | `search(q)` results are a superset of `search(q + " extra_term")` |
| No crash | Arbitrary input returns `Ok` or `Err`, never panics |

When a case fails, proptest records the seed in a
`proptest-regressions/<module>.txt` file. Commit it: every later run replays
those cases first, so a bug once found stays covered.

> Key Takeaways
> - Property tests state rules that hold for all inputs; the framework
>   generates inputs and shrinks failures to a minimal counterexample.
> - Round trips, oracles, and invariants are the most productive properties.
> - Strategies compose with `prop_map`, `prop_oneof!`, and collection
>   strategies; constrain them to valid inputs rather than filtering heavily.
> - Commit `proptest-regressions/` so past failures are always re-tested.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a property test for a function that reverses the words in a
>    sentence: reversing twice should give the original (after whitespace
>    normalization).
> 2. Implement a sorted-insert function for `Vec<i32>` and check it against the
>    oracle "push, then `sort`".
> 3. Interview: How does shrinking work, and why does it matter more than the
>    random generation itself when debugging? (Hint: think about what you would
>    do with a failing 800-element input.)

#### Fuzzing with cargo-fuzz

Property testing generates inputs from a strategy you design. **Fuzzing** goes
further for code that consumes untrusted bytes, such as parsers, decoders, and
protocol handlers. A coverage-guided fuzzer watches which branches each input
reaches. Inputs that reach new code are kept and mutated further, so over
millions of executions it digs into corners no one thought to test. In Rust,
safe code cannot corrupt memory, but a fuzzer still finds panics, arithmetic
overflow, infinite loops, excessive allocation, and memory bugs in `unsafe`
code.

```text
            +-----------+     mutate      +-------------+
            |  corpus   | --------------> |  new input  |
            | (inputs)  |                 +------+------+
            +-----^-----+                        |
                  | keep if new                  v
                  | coverage            +-----------------+
                  +-------------------- | fuzz target     | -- panic/crash --> artifacts/
                                        | (instrumented)  |
                                        +-----------------+
```

`cargo-fuzz` drives LLVM's **libFuzzer**. It needs a nightly toolchain (it uses
sanitizer flags) and works on Linux and macOS.

```bash
cargo install cargo-fuzz
cargo fuzz init                  # creates fuzz/ (a separate crate) with a first target
cargo fuzz add parse_config      # adds fuzz/fuzz_targets/parse_config.rs
```

A fuzz target is a function that receives arbitrary bytes and calls your code:

```rust
// fuzz/fuzz_targets/parse_config.rs
#![no_main]                                   // libFuzzer provides main()
use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;

fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
    // Only valid UTF-8 is interesting for a text parser.
    if let Ok(text) = std::str::from_utf8(data) {
        // Must never panic, whatever the input. Errors are fine.
        let _ = kv::Config::parse(text);
    }
});
```

```bash
cargo +nightly fuzz run parse_config                       # runs until a crash or Ctrl-C
cargo +nightly fuzz run parse_config -- -max_total_time=300  # bound it (for CI)
```

When it finds a crash, libFuzzer saves the input and prints how to reproduce it:

```text
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/config.rs:41:27:
attempt to subtract with overflow
==12345== ERROR: libFuzzer: deadly signal
artifact_prefix='fuzz/artifacts/parse_config/'; Test unit written to
    fuzz/artifacts/parse_config/crash-5f1c0a...

Reproduce with:
    cargo fuzz run parse_config fuzz/artifacts/parse_config/crash-5f1c0a...

Minimize test case with:
    cargo fuzz tmin parse_config fuzz/artifacts/parse_config/crash-5f1c0a...
```

By default cargo-fuzz builds with optimizations *and* debug assertions, so
integer overflow panics instead of wrapping silently. Once fixed, turn the
minimized input into an ordinary regression test.

**Structured fuzzing.** For APIs that take structured values rather than bytes,
derive `arbitrary::Arbitrary` and let the fuzzer build typed inputs from its raw
bytes:

```rust
#![no_main]
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;

#[derive(Debug, Arbitrary)]
enum Op { Insert(u16, u32), Remove(u16), Get(u16) }

fuzz_target!(|ops: Vec<Op>| {
    // Differential fuzzing: our map must behave exactly like std's.
    let mut ours = kv::SmallMap::new();
    let mut reference = std::collections::BTreeMap::new();
    for op in ops {
        match op {
            Op::Insert(k, v) => assert_eq!(ours.insert(k, v), reference.insert(k, v)),
            Op::Remove(k) => assert_eq!(ours.remove(&k), reference.remove(&k)),
            Op::Get(k) => assert_eq!(ours.get(&k), reference.get(&k)),
        }
    }
});
```

| | Property testing (proptest) | Fuzzing (cargo-fuzz) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input generation | Random, from a strategy you define | Mutation guided by code coverage |
| Runs | Hundreds of cases, inside `cargo test` | Millions, for minutes to days |
| Toolchain | Stable | Nightly (sanitizers) |
| Best for | Logic properties, every commit | Parsers and decoders of untrusted input |
| Failure output | Shrunk counterexample | Crash file, minimized with `tmin` |

> Key Takeaways
> - Coverage-guided fuzzers mutate inputs that reach new code, finding panics,
>   overflows, hangs, and `unsafe` memory bugs.
> - `cargo fuzz init` / `add` / `run` manage targets in a separate `fuzz/`
>   crate; it requires nightly.
> - Crashes are saved under `fuzz/artifacts/`; minimize with `cargo fuzz tmin`
>   and keep them as regression tests.
> - Derive `Arbitrary` for structured inputs and compare against a reference
>   implementation (differential fuzzing).

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a fuzz target for a function that parses `"HH:MM"` times. Run it for
>    five minutes and fix anything it finds.
> 2. Write a structured fuzz target that checks a custom ring buffer against
>    `VecDeque`.
> 3. Interview: Safe Rust prevents memory corruption, so why do Rust projects
>    still fuzz their parsers? (Hint: list the failure modes that remain in safe
>    code, and think about what an attacker controls.)

#### Mocking and Test Doubles

Code that sends email, calls an HTTP API, reads the clock, or writes to a
database is hard to test: real dependencies are slow, flaky, costly, or have
side effects. A **test double** stands in for the real dependency during a test,
the way a stunt double stands in for an actor.

Languages with runtime reflection can swap dependencies behind your back
("monkeypatching"). Rust cannot, and that is a design advantage: the substitution
point, the **seam**, has to be explicit. The idiomatic seam is a **trait**. Code
depends on the trait, production passes the real implementation, and tests pass
a double.

| Double | What it does | Example |
| ------ | ------------ | ------- |
| Dummy | Fills a parameter, never used | `NoopLogger` |
| Stub | Returns canned answers | `FixedClock(1_700_000_000)` |
| Fake | Working but simplified implementation | In-memory repository backed by a `HashMap` |
| Spy | Records calls for later assertions | Mailer that pushes messages into a `Vec` |
| Mock | Pre-programmed with expectations, verifies them | `mockall` mock expecting `send` exactly once |

```rust
pub trait Clock {
    fn now_secs(&self) -> u64;
}

pub trait Mailer {
    fn send(&self, to: &str, body: &str) -> Result<(), String>;
}

// The code under test depends on traits, not concrete services.
pub struct Reminder<'a, C: Clock, M: Mailer> {
    pub clock: &'a C,
    pub mailer: &'a M,
}

impl<C: Clock, M: Mailer> Reminder<'_, C, M> {
    pub fn remind_if_due(&self, due: u64, user: &str) -> Result<bool, String> {
        if self.clock.now_secs() < due {
            return Ok(false);
        }
        self.mailer.send(user, "Your task is due")?;
        Ok(true)
    }
}
```

Hand-written doubles are often all you need:

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use std::cell::RefCell;

    struct FixedClock(u64);                              // stub
    impl Clock for FixedClock {
        fn now_secs(&self) -> u64 { self.0 }
    }

    #[derive(Default)]
    struct SpyMailer { sent: RefCell<Vec<(String, String)>> }   // spy
    impl Mailer for SpyMailer {
        fn send(&self, to: &str, body: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
            // RefCell: `send` takes &self, but the spy must record (Chapter 9).
            self.sent.borrow_mut().push((to.into(), body.into()));
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn sends_when_due() {
        let mailer = SpyMailer::default();
        let r = Reminder { clock: &FixedClock(100), mailer: &mailer };
        assert_eq!(r.remind_if_due(100, "ana"), Ok(true));
        assert_eq!(mailer.sent.borrow().len(), 1);
    }

    #[test]
    fn stays_quiet_before_due() {
        let mailer = SpyMailer::default();
        let r = Reminder { clock: &FixedClock(99), mailer: &mailer };
        assert_eq!(r.remind_if_due(100, "ana"), Ok(false));
        assert!(mailer.sent.borrow().is_empty());
    }
}
```

For traits with many methods, or when you need call-count and argument
expectations, **`mockall`** generates mocks from the trait definition:

```rust
// The mock type MockMailer is generated only in test builds.
#[cfg_attr(test, mockall::automock)]
pub trait Mailer {
    fn send(&self, to: &str, body: &str) -> Result<(), String>;
}

#[test]
fn propagates_mailer_errors() {
    let mut mailer = MockMailer::new();
    mailer.expect_send()
        .withf(|to, _body| to == "bo")              // argument matcher
        .times(1)                                   // verified when the mock is dropped
        .returning(|_, _| Err("smtp down".into())); // canned response

    let r = Reminder { clock: &FixedClock(500), mailer: &mailer };
    assert_eq!(r.remind_if_due(100, "bo"), Err("smtp down".to_string()));
}
```

Other seams worth knowing:

- **HTTP:** point the client at a local mock server (`wiremock`, `httpmock`)
  instead of mocking the client type. This also tests serialization and status
  handling.
- **Time in async code:** `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` freezes Tokio's
  clock and auto-advances it, so a 30-second timeout test finishes instantly.
- **Filesystem:** use a real temporary directory (`tempfile::tempdir()`); it is
  fast and avoids mocking `std::fs`.

Over-mocking has a cost. Tests that assert every call couple themselves to the
implementation and break on harmless refactors. Prefer fakes and real
lightweight dependencies, and use strict mocks only where the interaction *is*
the behaviour, such as "the payment API is called exactly once".

> Key Takeaways
> - Rust has no monkeypatching; make dependencies explicit through traits
>   (generic parameters or `dyn Trait`) and substitute doubles in tests.
> - Hand-written stubs, fakes, and spies cover most needs; `mockall` generates
>   mocks with argument matchers and call-count verification.
> - Prefer real lightweight substitutes (temp dirs, local HTTP servers, paused
>   clocks) over mocking library types.
> - Mock interactions only when the interaction itself is the contract.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Refactor a function that calls `std::time::SystemTime::now()` directly so
>    that it receives a `Clock`, and test both branches of its time-dependent
>    logic.
> 2. Write an in-memory fake for a `UserRepository` trait (`get`, `insert`,
>    `delete`) and use it to test a service that registers users.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between a stub and a mock, and why can
>    heavy use of mocks make a codebase harder to refactor? (Hint: think about
>    whether a test checks *outcomes* or *interactions*.)

#### Snapshot Testing

Some outputs are large and structured: a rendered error message, a pretty-printed
AST, a JSON API response, a CLI's help text. Writing `assert_eq!` against a
hand-typed 40-line string is tedious, and updating it after an intentional
change is worse. **Snapshot testing** records the output once, stores it
alongside the tests, and on later runs compares new output against the stored
snapshot. When output changes, you *review the diff* and either accept it or
fix the code.

The standard crate is **`insta`**, paired with the `cargo-insta` CLI:

```toml
[dev-dependencies]
insta = { version = "1", features = ["json", "redactions"] }
```

```bash
cargo install cargo-insta
```

```rust
#[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize)]
struct Report { id: u64, created: String, warnings: Vec<String> }

#[test]
fn renders_error_message() {
    let err = kv::Config::parse("port = abc").unwrap_err();
    // Stored in src/snapshots/<crate>__tests__renders_error_message.snap
    insta::assert_snapshot!(err.to_string());
}

#[test]
fn ast_shape() {
    // Snapshot of the Debug representation (pretty-printed).
    insta::assert_debug_snapshot!(kv::parse_kv("a = b"));
}

#[test]
fn inline_snapshot() {
    // Inline: the expected value lives in the source; cargo-insta rewrites it.
    insta::assert_snapshot!(format!("{:?}", kv::encode(b"aaab")), @"[(97, 3), (98, 1)]");
}

#[test]
fn report_json() {
    let r = Report { id: 7, created: "2026-10-13T09:00:00Z".into(), warnings: vec![] };
    // Redactions replace volatile fields so the snapshot is stable.
    insta::assert_json_snapshot!(r, { ".created" => "[timestamp]" });
}
```

The workflow:

```text
1. Write the test with no snapshot yet  -> test fails, writes a .snap.new file
2. cargo insta review                   -> shows each new/changed snapshot as a diff
                                           a = accept, r = reject, s = skip
3. Commit the accepted .snap files      -> they are the expected output from now on
4. Later change alters output           -> test fails with a colored diff
5. Intentional? cargo insta review      -> accept. Bug? fix the code.
```

`cargo insta test --review` runs the tests and opens the review in one step. In
CI (detected through the `CI` environment variable), insta does not write
pending snapshot files; it simply fails on mismatch.

| Use snapshots for | Avoid snapshots for |
| ----------------- | ------------------- |
| Error and diagnostic messages | Small values where `assert_eq!` is clearer |
| Serialized formats (JSON, YAML, TOML) | Output containing timestamps or random IDs (unless redacted) |
| Pretty-printed ASTs and IRs | Checking a single important field among many |
| CLI help and output | Anything where reviewers will accept diffs without reading them |

The main danger is "snapshot fatigue": accepting changed snapshots without
reading them turns the test into a record of whatever the code does, bugs
included. Keep snapshots small and focused so diffs stay reviewable. Related
tools include `expect-test` (inline snapshots with `UPDATE_EXPECT=1`) and
`trybuild`, which snapshots *compiler errors* and is the standard way to test
procedural macros (Chapter 13).

> Key Takeaways
> - Snapshot tests store expected output in files (or inline) and fail with a
>   diff when output changes.
> - `cargo insta review` turns intentional changes into a quick, reviewable
>   accept/reject step.
> - Use redactions for timestamps and IDs so snapshots are deterministic.
> - Snapshots only protect you if humans actually read the diffs; keep them
>   focused.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a snapshot test for the `Debug` output of a nested struct, change one
>    field name, and walk through `cargo insta review`.
> 2. Snapshot a JSON response that includes a UUID and a timestamp, using
>    redactions to keep it stable.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose a snapshot test over a set of targeted
>    `assert_eq!` checks, and what process prevents snapshots from silently
>    blessing regressions? (Hint: think about output size and code review.)

#### Code Coverage

How do you know which code your tests never exercise? **Code coverage**
instruments the program to record which lines, regions, and branches execute
during the test run, then reports the gaps. It is a flashlight for finding
untested code, not a score that proves correctness.

Rust has **source-based coverage** built into the compiler
(`-C instrument-coverage`), which uses LLVM to map counters precisely back to
source regions, including individual sub-expressions. The convenient front end
is **`cargo-llvm-cov`**:

```bash
rustup component add llvm-tools-preview
cargo install cargo-llvm-cov

cargo llvm-cov                              # run tests, print a per-file summary
cargo llvm-cov --open                       # HTML report with highlighted source
cargo llvm-cov --lcov --output-path lcov.info   # for Codecov, Coveralls, IDE plugins
cargo llvm-cov --fail-under-lines 80        # fail CI if line coverage drops below 80%
cargo llvm-cov nextest                      # same, using cargo-nextest as the runner
```

```text
(abridged: the real report also has function and branch columns)
Filename          Regions  Missed Regions  Cover   Lines  Missed Lines  Cover
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
src/config.rs         48               6  87.50%     102            9  91.18%
src/parser.rs         95              21  77.89%     188           33  82.45%
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                143              27  81.12%     290           42  85.52%
```

What the metrics mean:

| Metric | Counts as covered when | Blind spot |
| ------ | ---------------------- | ---------- |
| Line | Any code on the line ran | `if a && b { .. }` on one line looks fully covered even if `b` was never evaluated |
| Region | Each source region (sub-expression, block) ran | Does not say both outcomes of a condition were seen |
| Branch | Both the true and false side of each condition ran | Requires nightly at the time of writing (`-Z coverage-options=branch`) |

The alternative tool, **`cargo-tarpaulin`**, is popular on Linux CI and
supports both its own ptrace-based engine and LLVM coverage.

Reading a report well:

- **Uncovered error paths** are the most valuable finding: they show which
  failures have never been exercised, which is where production incidents come
  from.
- **100% coverage does not mean correct.** A test that calls a function and
  asserts nothing still "covers" it. **Mutation testing** (`cargo-mutants`)
  checks the assertions instead: it changes your code (replaces `<` with `<=`,
  makes a function return `Default::default()`) and reports mutations that no
  test caught.
- **Ratchet, do not mandate.** A rule like "coverage must not decrease" works
  better than a fixed high target, which encourages assertion-free tests.

```text
Coverage answers:     "Did the tests RUN this code?"
Mutation testing:     "Would the tests NOTICE if this code were wrong?"
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `-C instrument-coverage` provides precise source-based coverage;
>   `cargo llvm-cov` wraps it with HTML, LCOV, and threshold options.
> - Line coverage can hide unevaluated conditions; region and branch coverage
>   are finer grained.
> - Use coverage to find untested code, especially error paths, not as proof
>   of correctness.
> - Complement coverage with mutation testing (`cargo-mutants`) to measure
>   whether assertions are meaningful.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `cargo llvm-cov --open` on a project, find one uncovered error branch,
>    and write a test that reaches it.
> 2. Write a test that reaches 100% coverage of a small function while
>    asserting nothing useful, then run `cargo mutants` on it and explain the
>    surviving mutants.
> 3. Interview: A manager proposes requiring 95% line coverage on every pull
>    request. What would you suggest instead, and why? (Hint: think about what
>    coverage measures, what it incentivizes, and the cost of the last 10%.)

<a id="123-benchmarking-and-profiling"></a>
### 12.3 Benchmarking and Profiling

Performance work without measurement is guesswork, and naive measurement is
often worse than guesswork because it looks authoritative. This section covers
how to benchmark Rust code with statistical rigor, how to choose the right scale
of benchmark, how to find where time and memory actually go, and how to tell a
real improvement from noise.

#### Criterion Benchmarks

The obvious approach, wrapping code in `Instant::now()` and printing the
elapsed time, is unreliable. One run says nothing about variance. The optimizer
may delete code whose result is unused. The first iterations run with cold
caches. And when the number changes after an edit, you cannot tell whether the
change is real.

Rust's built-in `#[bench]` attribute is still nightly-only, so the ecosystem
standard is **Criterion.rs**. It warms up the code, runs it many times, applies
statistics to the samples, and compares each run with the previous one to tell
you whether performance changed significantly.

Setup: benchmarks live in `benches/`, and each needs `harness = false` because
Criterion supplies its own `main`:

```toml
[dev-dependencies]
criterion = { version = "0.8", features = ["html_reports"] }

[[bench]]
name = "rle"              # benches/rle.rs
harness = false           # use Criterion's main, not libtest's
```

```rust
// benches/rle.rs
use criterion::{criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};
use std::hint::black_box;

fn bench_encode(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let input = vec![7u8; 4096];
    c.bench_function("encode 4 KiB", |b| {
        // b.iter runs the closure many times and measures each batch.
        // black_box hides the value from the optimizer so the work is not
        // constant-folded or deleted.
        b.iter(|| kv::encode(black_box(&input)))
    });
}

criterion_group!(benches, bench_encode);   // a named group of benchmark functions
criterion_main!(benches);                  // generates main()
```

```bash
cargo bench                          # all benchmarks (built with the `bench` profile: optimized)
cargo bench --bench rle              # one bench target
cargo bench -- encode                # filter benchmarks by name (a regex)
```

```text
encode 4 KiB            time:   [9.6130 µs 9.7075 µs 9.8105 µs]
                        change: [−2.1270% −0.5640% +0.9820%] (p = 0.48 > 0.05)
                        No change in performance detected.
Found 3 outliers among 100 measurements (3.00%)
  1 (1.00%) low mild
  1 (1.00%) high mild
  1 (1.00%) high severe
```

The `time` line shows a **confidence interval**: lower bound, best estimate,
and upper bound for the time per iteration. The `change` line compares against
the previous run, with a p-value saying whether the difference is statistically
significant. An HTML report with plots is written to
`target/criterion/report/index.html`.

**Parameterized benchmarks and setup.** Groups compare implementations across
input sizes. `iter_batched` keeps per-iteration setup, such as cloning input
that the benchmark consumes, out of the measurement:

```rust
use criterion::{BatchSize, BenchmarkId, Criterion, Throughput};

fn bench_sort(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("sort");
    for n in [1_000usize, 10_000, 100_000] {
        // Pseudo-random data, generated once per size (outside the timing).
        let data: Vec<u64> = (0..n as u64)
            .map(|x| x.wrapping_mul(0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15))
            .collect();
        group.throughput(Throughput::Elements(n as u64));   // report elements/second too

        group.bench_with_input(BenchmarkId::new("stable", n), &data, |b, d| {
            // setup closure (not timed), then routine (timed) consuming its output
            b.iter_batched(|| d.clone(), |mut v| v.sort(), BatchSize::LargeInput)
        });
        group.bench_with_input(BenchmarkId::new("unstable", n), &data, |b, d| {
            b.iter_batched(|| d.clone(), |mut v| v.sort_unstable(), BatchSize::LargeInput)
        });
    }
    group.finish();
}
```

This produces IDs like `sort/unstable/10000`, a throughput line
(`thrpt: [41.694 Melem/s ...]`), and comparison plots across sizes in the HTML
report.

**Baselines** make before/after comparisons across branches explicit:

```bash
git switch main     && cargo bench -- --save-baseline main
git switch feature  && cargo bench -- --baseline main     # compare against main's numbers
```

Other benchmark harnesses:

| Tool | Measures | Strength |
| ---- | -------- | -------- |
| Criterion.rs | Wall-clock time with statistics | Mature, rich reports, baselines |
| `divan` | Wall-clock time | Attribute-based (`#[divan::bench]`), concise, also tracks allocations |
| `gungraun` (formerly `iai-callgrind`) | Instruction counts and cache simulation under Valgrind | Deterministic numbers, ideal for CI |
| `#[bench]` (nightly) | Wall-clock time | Built in, but unstable and minimal |

> Key Takeaways
> - Use Criterion in `benches/` with `harness = false`; it handles warm-up,
>   sampling, statistics, and change detection.
> - Wrap inputs (and if needed outputs) in `std::hint::black_box` so the
>   optimizer cannot delete or precompute the work.
> - Use groups, `BenchmarkId`, and `Throughput` to compare implementations
>   across sizes; use `iter_batched` to keep setup out of the measurement.
> - Save and compare named baselines for branch-to-branch comparisons.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Benchmark `String::push_str` in a loop versus `format!` versus
>    `[..].concat()` for joining 100 short strings.
> 2. Write a benchmark group that compares a linear search and a binary search
>    over sorted vectors of 10, 1,000, and 100,000 elements. Find the crossover
>    point.
> 3. Interview: Why does a naive benchmark of a pure function sometimes report
>    0 ns per iteration, and what does `black_box` do about it? (Hint: think
>    about what the optimizer may assume about unused results and constant
>    inputs.)

#### Micro vs Macro Benchmarks

A benchmark answers a question, and different questions need different scales.
A **micro benchmark** measures a tiny unit, such as one function or one data
structure operation, in isolation and in a tight loop. A **macro benchmark**
measures a whole workload: the CLI processing a real file, the server handling
realistic traffic. Confusing the two is one of the most common ways to "optimize"
something that does not matter.

| | Micro benchmark | Macro benchmark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | One function or operation | End-to-end program or request |
| Tools | Criterion, divan, gungraun | `hyperfine`, load generators (`oha`, `wrk`, k6), production metrics |
| Precision | Nanosecond-level, low variance | Millisecond-level, higher variance |
| Realism | Low: hot caches, same input every time, no I/O contention | High: real data, real I/O, real interactions |
| Answers | "Is implementation A faster than B?" | "Is the program faster for users?" |
| Typical trap | Optimizing something that is 1% of the runtime | Too noisy to detect small changes |

The traps of micro benchmarks, which all make results look better than reality:

- **Warm caches.** The same small input is reused, so it sits in L1 cache. In
  production the data might come from main memory, 50 to 100 times slower.
- **Trained branch predictor.** Repeating one input lets the CPU predict every
  branch perfectly.
- **Dead code and constant folding.** Without `black_box`, the compiler may
  compute the answer once, or not at all.
- **Unrepresentative inputs.** Sorting already-sorted data, or hashing 8-byte
  keys when production keys are 200 bytes.

**Amdahl's law** explains why the macro view matters. If a function accounts
for a fraction `p` of total runtime and you make it `s` times faster, the
overall speedup is `1 / ((1 - p) + p / s)`:

```text
Function is 5% of runtime, made 10x faster:   1 / (0.95 + 0.005) = 1.047  -> 4.7% faster overall
Function is 60% of runtime, made 2x faster:   1 / (0.40 + 0.30)  = 1.43   -> 43% faster overall
```

A practical workflow combines both scales:

```text
1. Macro: measure the real workload        -> "the import takes 4.2 s"
2. Profile it (next topic)                 -> "62% is in parse_record"
3. Micro: benchmark parse_record alone     -> iterate quickly on alternatives
4. Macro again: confirm the user-visible   -> "the import now takes 2.6 s"
   improvement
```

For command-line programs, **hyperfine** is the standard macro tool. It runs
commands repeatedly, handles warm-up, and reports mean, deviation, and
relative speed:

```bash
cargo build --release
hyperfine --warmup 3 \
    './old-kv big.conf' \
    './target/release/kv big.conf'
```

```text
Benchmark 1: ./old-kv big.conf
  Time (mean ± σ):     412.3 ms ±   6.1 ms    [User: 380.2 ms, System: 30.9 ms]
  Range (min … max):   404.8 ms … 423.0 ms    10 runs

Benchmark 2: ./target/release/kv big.conf
  Time (mean ± σ):     314.9 ms ±   4.4 ms    [User: 284.0 ms, System: 30.1 ms]
  Range (min … max):   309.2 ms … 322.7 ms    10 runs

Summary
  ./target/release/kv big.conf ran
    1.31 ± 0.03 times faster than ./old-kv big.conf
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Micro benchmarks compare implementations precisely; macro benchmarks tell
>   you whether users benefit.
> - Micro results flatter code through warm caches, trained branch predictors,
>   and unrealistic inputs.
> - Amdahl's law: overall speedup is bounded by the fraction of runtime you
>   improved.
> - Measure the whole workload, profile, micro-optimize the hotspot, then
>   confirm with the whole workload again.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a micro benchmark for a JSON-parsing function using one small input,
>    then a macro benchmark that parses a 50 MB file with hyperfine. Compare how
>    a change to the function affects each.
> 2. Benchmark a `HashMap` lookup with 10 keys and with 10 million keys. Explain
>    the difference in time per lookup.
> 3. Interview: A colleague's PR makes a hashing function 3x faster in a
>    Criterion benchmark, but the service's p99 latency does not move. Give
>    three possible explanations. (Hint: Amdahl, caches, and what dominates a
>    request's latency.)

#### Flamegraphs and perf

Benchmarks tell you *how long* something takes; a **profiler** tells you
*where* the time goes. Intuition about hotspots is wrong surprisingly often:
the slow part is frequently an innocent-looking `clone`, a hash function, or
an allocation inside a loop.

A **sampling profiler** interrupts the program many times per second (for
example 1,000 Hz) and records the call stack each time. Functions that appear in
many samples are where the program spends its time. Overhead is low and no code
changes are needed, but the binary needs **debug symbols** to map addresses back
to function names.

```toml
# Cargo.toml: a dedicated profile (Chapter 8) - release speed plus symbols
[profile.profiling]
inherits = "release"
debug = true
```

On Linux, the standard tool is `perf`:

```bash
cargo build --profile profiling
perf record -g --call-graph dwarf ./target/profiling/kv big.conf   # sample with call stacks
perf report                                                         # interactive breakdown
```

```text
  Children      Self  Symbol
-   71.20%     0.40%  kv::run
   - 70.80% kv::run
      - 52.10% kv::parse_record
           31.70% alloc::string::String::push_str
           12.20% core::str::<impl str>::trim
      - 18.30% kv::index::build
           15.10% hashbrown::map::HashMap::insert
```

"Self" is time spent in the function's own code; "Children" includes everything
it calls.

**Flame graphs** turn thousands of stack samples into one picture. Install the
Cargo wrapper with `cargo install flamegraph`; it uses `perf` on Linux and
DTrace on macOS:

```bash
cargo flamegraph --profile profiling --bin kv -- big.conf     # writes flamegraph.svg
cargo flamegraph --bench rle -- --bench --profile-time 10     # profile a Criterion benchmark
```

```text
              [push_str ]   [ trim ]  [ HashMap::insert ]
         [        parse_record       ][    index::build     ][fmt]
         [                       kv::run                           ][ read_file ]
         [                             main                                     ]
         <------------------------- 100% of samples --------------------------->
```

How to read it:

| Feature | Meaning |
| ------- | ------- |
| Y axis | Stack depth: each box's caller is directly below it |
| Box width | Fraction of samples containing that function, i.e. its share of time |
| X axis | **Not** time; boxes are sorted alphabetically to merge identical stacks |
| Wide box with nothing on top | Time spent in that function's own code: a hotspot |
| Wide "towers" | Expensive call paths worth investigating first |
| Color | Usually random warm tones, with no meaning |

Practical notes:

- **samply** (`samply record ./target/profiling/kv big.conf`) works on Linux,
  macOS, and Windows and opens the result in the Firefox Profiler UI, with a
  timeline, call tree, and flame graph.
- **Inlining hides functions.** Inlined callees are attributed to their caller.
  If a stack looks implausibly flat, that is usually why.
- **Broken stacks** often mean the unwinder could not walk the frames.
  `--call-graph dwarf` or building with `RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes"`
  helps.
- **Permissions.** On Linux, `perf` may require lowering
  `kernel.perf_event_paranoid` (`sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1`).
- **Profile release builds.** Debug builds have entirely different hotspots,
  such as un-inlined iterator adapters.

> Key Takeaways
> - Sampling profilers record call stacks periodically; they need debug symbols
>   but not code changes.
> - Use a `profiling` profile (`inherits = "release"`, `debug = true`) so
>   profiles reflect optimized code with readable names.
> - In a flame graph, width is time and height is call depth; the x axis is not
>   chronological.
> - `perf` plus `cargo flamegraph` on Linux, or `samply` everywhere, covers most
>   needs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Profile a program that counts word frequencies in a large text file with
>    `cargo flamegraph`. Identify the widest leaf box and optimize it.
> 2. Profile the same program in a debug build and compare the flame graphs.
>    Which functions appear only in the debug profile, and why?
> 3. Interview: A flame graph shows `memcpy` as 25% of samples, called from
>    many places. How would you find out which Rust code is responsible, and
>    what are common causes in Rust? (Hint: look below `memcpy` in the stacks;
>    think about large values moved by value and `clone`.)

#### Allocation Profiling

A CPU profile may show time spread thinly across `malloc`, `free`, `memcpy`,
and page faults, with no single hotspot. That is often the signature of
**excessive allocation**. Each heap allocation costs a call into the allocator,
possible synchronization, cache misses on fresh memory, and later a `free`. In a
hot loop, a stray `to_string()` can cost more than the actual work.

Allocation profilers answer: *how many* allocations, *how many bytes*, *peak
memory*, and *which call stacks* allocate.

| Tool | How it works | Platforms |
| ---- | ------------ | --------- |
| `dhat` crate | Replaces the global allocator in your binary; writes a JSON profile | All |
| heaptrack | Intercepts `malloc`/`free` of an unmodified binary; GUI analysis | Linux |
| Valgrind DHAT (`valgrind --tool=dhat`) | Runs the binary on a simulated CPU; slow but detailed | Linux |
| Instruments (Allocations) | System profiler | macOS |
| Counting allocator (hand-written) | Wraps `System` and counts calls | All; good for tests |

**dhat-rs** is the most portable option. It is enabled through a feature so it
never ships in normal builds:

```toml
[dependencies]
dhat = "0.3"

[features]
dhat-heap = []          # cargo run --release --features dhat-heap

[profile.release]
debug = 1               # line tables, so stacks have file:line information
```

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "dhat-heap")]
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: dhat::Alloc = dhat::Alloc;      // route every allocation through dhat

fn main() {
    #[cfg(feature = "dhat-heap")]
    let _profiler = dhat::Profiler::new_heap();  // writes dhat-heap.json when dropped

    let mut words = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..1000 {
        words.push(format!("word{i}"));          // one heap allocation per String
    }
}
```

```text
dhat: Total:     57,056 bytes in 1,009 blocks
dhat: At t-gmax: 32,576 bytes in 1,001 blocks
dhat: At t-end:  0 bytes in 0 blocks
dhat: The data has been saved to dhat-heap.json, and is viewable with dhat/dh_view.html
```

`Total` is every allocation made; `t-gmax` is the moment of peak heap usage;
`t-end` is what was still allocated at exit. Open the JSON file in the DHAT
viewer (`dh_view.html`, shipped with Valgrind and hosted online) to see the
allocating call stacks sorted by bytes or block count. Here the 1,000 `String`s
plus nine buffers for the growing `Vec` (capacity 4, 8, 16, ..., 1024) explain
the 1,009 blocks. At the peak, 1,001 blocks are live: every string plus the
final `Vec` buffer. `Vec::with_capacity(1000)` would remove eight of the
allocations.

**Allocation regression tests.** A counting global allocator can assert that a
hot function does not allocate at all. Put it in its own integration test file,
since it replaces the allocator for that whole test binary:

```rust
// tests/allocations.rs
use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout, System};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};

struct Counting;
static ALLOCATIONS: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for Counting {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        ALLOCATIONS.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        unsafe { System.alloc(layout) }          // delegate to the system allocator
    }
    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        unsafe { System.dealloc(ptr, layout) }
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: Counting = Counting;

fn allocations_during<R>(f: impl FnOnce() -> R) -> (R, usize) {
    let before = ALLOCATIONS.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
    let r = f();
    (r, ALLOCATIONS.load(Ordering::Relaxed) - before)
}

// Keep this the only test in the file: parallel tests would allocate
// concurrently and pollute the global counter.
#[test]
fn parse_kv_is_allocation_free() {
    let (result, n) = allocations_during(|| kv::parse_kv("port = 8080"));
    assert_eq!(result, Some(("port", "8080")));
    assert_eq!(n, 0, "parse_kv should borrow from its input, not allocate");
}
```

Common sources of avoidable allocation, and their fixes:

| Pattern | Fix |
| ------- | --- |
| `s.to_string()` / `format!` only to compare or look up | Borrow: `&str`, `Cow<str>`, `HashMap::get` with `&str` keys |
| `Vec::new()` then many `push` calls with a known size | `Vec::with_capacity(n)` |
| New `Vec`/`String` per loop iteration | Hoist it out of the loop and `clear()` it each time |
| `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` just to iterate again | Keep it as an iterator chain |
| `clone()` to satisfy the borrow checker | Restructure borrows, or share with `Rc`/`Arc` |
| Many tiny short-lived objects | Small-buffer types (`smallvec`) or an arena (`bumpalo`) |

> Key Takeaways
> - Allocation-heavy code shows up as time spread across allocator functions
>   rather than one hotspot.
> - `dhat` reports total, peak (`t-gmax`), and leaked (`t-end`) memory with
>   allocating stacks; gate it behind a feature.
> - A counting `#[global_allocator]` in a dedicated test file turns "this does
>   not allocate" into an enforced regression test.
> - Most fixes are about borrowing instead of owning, pre-sizing, and reusing
>   buffers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Profile a log-processing program with dhat, find the call site with the
>    most blocks, and reduce its allocations by at least 90%.
> 2. Write an allocation regression test asserting that a tokenizer returning
>    `&str` slices performs zero allocations for a 1 KB input.
> 3. Interview: Why can reducing allocations speed up a multi-threaded program
>    more than a single-threaded one? (Hint: think about what a general-purpose
>    allocator must coordinate between threads, and about cache lines.)

#### Interpreting Benchmark Noise

Run the same benchmark twice without changing a line of code, and you will get
two different numbers. Sometimes the difference is dramatic. Here is real
output from running the `encode 4 KiB` benchmark above twice in a row on a
laptop, with no code change in between:

```text
first run:   encode 4 KiB   time:   [19.435 µs 20.099 µs 20.808 µs]

second run:  encode 4 KiB   time:   [9.6130 µs 9.7075 µs 9.8105 µs]
                            change: [−52.127% −50.564% −48.982%] (p = 0.00 < 0.05)
                            Performance has improved.
```

Criterion reported a statistically significant 50% improvement for identical
code. The statistics were not wrong: the *machine* changed between runs (CPU
frequency, background load, thermal state). Statistics can only tell you that
two sets of samples differ, not *why*. Interpreting benchmarks is mostly about
controlling and recognizing those other causes.

Sources of noise:

| Source | Effect | Mitigation |
| ------ | ------ | ---------- |
| CPU frequency scaling and turbo boost | Speed varies with temperature and load, often by 2x | Disable turbo, fix the governor (`cpupower frequency-set -g performance`), let the machine cool |
| Other processes | Steal CPU time and cache | Close browsers and IDE indexers; benchmark on an idle machine |
| Virtual machines and cloud CI | Noisy neighbours, shared caches | Use instruction counts (gungraun) in CI, wall clock only on dedicated hardware |
| Code layout and alignment | Unrelated changes shift hot loops across cache lines, ±5% or more | Distrust small changes; confirm with several builds or a macro benchmark |
| Memory layout (ASLR, environment size) | Different stack/heap addresses change cache behaviour | Repeat runs; compare distributions, not single numbers |
| Thread scheduling and migration | Cold caches after moving cores | Pin the process: `taskset -c 2 cargo bench` |

What Criterion's output tells you, and what it does not:

```text
time:   [9.6130 µs 9.7075 µs 9.8105 µs]
         ^ lower      ^ estimate  ^ upper    95% confidence interval of the mean

change: [−2.12% −0.56% +0.98%] (p = 0.48 > 0.05)
         interval includes 0 and p > 0.05     -> "No change in performance detected."

Found 6 outliers among 100 measurements (6.00%)
  4 (4.00%) high mild                         -> some samples were slow:
  2 (2.00%) high severe                          interrupts, other processes
```

- **Confidence interval width** is your precision. If the interval is ±10%,
  you cannot detect a 3% change, however many times you rerun.
- **p-value** below the significance level (default `0.05`) means the
  difference is unlikely to be random sampling variation. It does not mean the
  difference is large or that your code caused it.
- **Noise threshold** (default 1%): changes smaller than this are reported as
  "within noise threshold" even when statistically significant.
- **Outliers**, especially many "high severe" ones, indicate interference
  during measurement. A few percent is normal; 20% suggests a noisy machine.

```text
A real improvement:          Noise:

  before   |  ####              before   |   ######
  after    |####                after    |  ######
           +-----------> time            +-----------> time
  distributions separated      distributions overlap heavily
```

A disciplined procedure:

1. **Stabilize the machine** before trusting any number: plugged in, idle,
   turbo disabled if possible.
2. **Measure the noise floor**: run the unchanged benchmark several times and
   see how much it varies. Changes smaller than that range are not evidence.
3. **Interleave A/B comparisons** (baseline, change, baseline, change) instead
   of measuring each once, so drift affects both equally.
4. **Prefer deterministic metrics in CI**: instruction counts from
   `gungraun` vary by fractions of a percent where wall-clock time varies by
   10% or more.
5. **Confirm with a macro benchmark.** A 3% micro-improvement that disappears
   end to end was probably layout noise or irrelevant (Amdahl).
6. **Report distributions, not single numbers**: median and spread, or
   Criterion's interval.

Criterion's statistical knobs can be changed when a benchmark is noisy by
nature:

```rust
use criterion::Criterion;
use std::time::Duration;

fn config() -> Criterion {
    Criterion::default()
        .sample_size(200)                         // default 100
        .measurement_time(Duration::from_secs(10)) // default 5 s
        .warm_up_time(Duration::from_secs(3))      // default 3 s
        .noise_threshold(0.03)                     // ignore changes under 3% (default 1%)
        .significance_level(0.01)                  // stricter than the default 0.05
}

criterion::criterion_group! {
    name = benches;
    config = config();
    targets = bench_encode
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Identical code can produce significantly different timings; machine state
>   (frequency, load, layout) is often the cause, not your change.
> - Read the confidence interval as your precision, the p-value as "probably
>   not random", and the noise threshold as "too small to care".
> - Establish the noise floor, interleave A/B runs, and pin or quiet the
>   machine before trusting small differences.
> - In shared CI, prefer instruction-count benchmarks; confirm micro-level wins
>   with macro benchmarks.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run one Criterion benchmark ten times without changing code and record
>    the reported changes. What is the noise floor on your machine?
> 2. Repeat the experiment while compiling a large project in the background,
>    and then with the process pinned to one core with `taskset`. Compare the
>    outlier counts.
> 3. Interview: A benchmark in CI reports a 4% regression on a pull request
>    that only changed documentation. How do you explain this to the team, and
>    how would you redesign the CI benchmarking setup? (Hint: noise floor,
>    shared runners, and deterministic metrics.)

<a id="124-documentation"></a>
### 12.4 Documentation

In Rust, documentation is part of the product: it ships on docs.rs for every
published crate, and its examples are tested. Chapter 1 introduced doc comment
syntax and Chapter 8 the `cargo doc` tool. This section covers how to write
documentation well: the conventions readers expect, linking between items,
runnable examples, the crate's front page, and configuring how docs.rs builds
it.

#### Doc Comment Conventions

Readers come to API documentation with specific questions: *What does this do?
How do I call it? What can go wrong?* Rust's ecosystem has settled on a shared
structure that answers them in a predictable order, so a reader who knows the
standard library's docs can navigate any crate's docs.

The anatomy of a well-documented item:

```rust
/// Parses a duration such as `"1h30m"` or `"45s"` into a [`Duration`].
///
/// Units are `h`, `m`, and `s`, and may appear at most once each, in that
/// order. Whitespace is not allowed. Use [`format_duration`] for the inverse.
///
/// # Examples
///
/// ```
/// use std::time::Duration;
/// use timefmt::parse_duration;
///
/// assert_eq!(parse_duration("1h30m")?, Duration::from_secs(5400));
/// assert_eq!(parse_duration("45s")?, Duration::from_secs(45));
/// # Ok::<(), timefmt::ParseError>(())
/// ```
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns [`ParseError::Empty`] if `s` is empty, and
/// [`ParseError::BadUnit`] if it contains a unit other than `h`, `m`, or `s`.
///
/// # Panics
///
/// Panics if the total number of seconds overflows `u64`.
pub fn parse_duration(s: &str) -> Result<Duration, ParseError> {
    // ...
}
```

1. **Summary line.** One sentence, ending with a period, saying what the item
   does. rustdoc shows this first paragraph alone in module listings and search
   results, so it must make sense on its own.
2. **Details.** Behaviour, edge cases, relationships to other items.
3. **Standard sections**, as `#` headings in this conventional order:

| Section | When to include | Enforced by |
| ------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `# Examples` | Every public item where usage is not utterly obvious | Code review (rustdoc's `missing_doc_code_examples` lint is nightly-only) |
| `# Errors` | Functions returning `Result`: which errors, and when | `clippy::missing_errors_doc` (pedantic) |
| `# Panics` | Functions that can panic on some input | `clippy::missing_panics_doc` (pedantic) |
| `# Safety` | Every `unsafe fn` and `unsafe trait`: the caller's obligations | `clippy::missing_safety_doc` (warn by default) |
| Optional: `# Performance`, `# Platform-specific behavior` | Complexity guarantees, OS differences | Convention |

Style conventions, from the Rust API Guidelines and the standard library:

- Use the **third person, present tense**: "Returns the number of elements",
  not "Return..." or "This function will return...".
- Put identifiers in backticks and link them (next topic).
- Document **what and why**, not how. Implementation details belong in `//`
  comments inside the body.
- Document every public item: types, **fields**, **enum variants**, trait
  methods, modules (`//!` at the top of the module file), and constants.
- In examples, prefer `?` over `unwrap()`. Readers copy examples, so they
  should model good error handling.

A weak doc versus a strong one:

```rust
// Weak: restates the signature and hides what a reader needs to know.
/// This function gets the user.
pub fn get_user(id: u64) -> Option<User> { todo!() }

// Strong: behaviour, edge cases, and cost.
/// Returns the user with the given `id`, or `None` if no such user exists.
///
/// Results are served from an in-memory cache; a cache miss reads from the
/// database and may take several milliseconds.
pub fn get_user_cached(id: u64) -> Option<User> { todo!() }
```

`///` is sugar for the `#[doc = "..."]` attribute. That matters when
documentation must be computed, for example in macro-generated code:

```rust
macro_rules! int_parser {
    ($name:ident, $t:ty) => {
        #[doc = concat!("Parses a decimal `", stringify!($t), "`.")]   // per-type docs
        pub fn $name(s: &str) -> Option<$t> { s.parse().ok() }
    };
}
int_parser!(parse_u8, u8);       // documented as: Parses a decimal `u8`.
int_parser!(parse_i64, i64);
```

To make missing documentation a build error in a library, combine the compiler
lint with Clippy's section lints:

```rust
// lib.rs
#![warn(missing_docs)]                 // every public item needs a doc comment
#![warn(clippy::missing_errors_doc, clippy::missing_panics_doc)]
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Start with a one-sentence summary that stands alone in search results,
>   then details, then the standard sections.
> - Use `# Examples`, `# Errors`, `# Panics`, and `# Safety` (mandatory for
>   `unsafe` items) consistently; Clippy can enforce them.
> - Write in the third person present tense, document fields and variants, and
>   use `?` in examples.
> - `///` is the `#[doc]` attribute, which lets macros generate documentation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Document a function that returns `Result` and can panic, with all four
>    standard sections. Run `cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic` before and
>    after.
> 2. Find a public item in one of your projects whose docs merely restate its
>    name, and rewrite them to explain behaviour and edge cases.
> 3. Interview: Why does every `unsafe fn` need a `# Safety` section, and what
>    exactly should it contain? (Hint: think about who must uphold the
>    invariants and what happens if they do not; see Chapter 14.)

#### Intra-Doc Links

Documentation that mentions `Duration` or `ParseError::BadUnit` should let the
reader click through to them. Writing raw HTML links (`../struct.Foo.html`) is
brittle: the paths change when items move, and they cannot point into other
crates reliably. **Intra-doc links** let you link to items *by their Rust
path*. rustdoc resolves the path like the compiler would and generates the
correct URL, even into dependencies' docs on docs.rs.

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::time::Duration;

/// A cache of parsed values, keyed by name.
///
/// - Built on [`HashMap`] (resolved through the `use` above)
/// - Create one with [`Cache::new`], add entries with [`insert`](Cache::insert)
/// - Entries expire after a [`Duration`]; see [`Self::ttl`]
/// - Errors are reported as [`crate::error::CacheError`]
/// - Uses the [`parse_kv()`] function and the [`log!`] macro
/// - Free text pointing anywhere: see [the module docs][mod-docs]
///
/// [mod-docs]: crate::cache
pub struct Cache {
    ttl: Duration,
    entries: HashMap<String, String>,
}
```

| Syntax | Links to |
| ------ | -------- |
| ``[`Name`]`` | The item `Name`, resolved in the current scope |
| ``[`path::to::Item`]`` | A full or relative path (`crate::`, `super::`, `self::` work) |
| ``[`Type::method`]`` | A method or associated item |
| ``[`Self::method`]`` | Associated item of the documented type (inside `impl` and type docs) |
| ``[text](path::Item)`` | Custom link text with a Rust path as target |
| ``[text][label]`` + `[label]: path::Item` | Reference-style link, keeps long paths out of prose |
| ``[`f()`]`` / ``[`m!`]`` | Disambiguates a function / macro |
| ``[`struct@Foo`]``, ``[`fn@foo`]``, ``[`mod@foo`]``, ``[`macro@foo`]``, ``[`prim@str`]`` | Explicit disambiguators when names clash |

Disambiguation is needed when one name refers to several things, such as a
struct `Point` and a function `point`, or a module and a macro with the same
name. rustdoc reports an ambiguity warning and suggests the fix.

Links are checked at doc-build time. A link that does not resolve is a warning
by default, which CI should turn into an error:

```text
$ RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps
error: unresolved link to `Missing`
   --> src/lib.rs:195:7
    |
195 | /// [`Missing`]
    |       ^^^^^^^ no item named `Missing` in scope
    |
    = help: to escape `[` and `]` characters, add '\' before them like `\[` or `\]`
    = note: `-D rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links` implied by `-D warnings`
```

This turns renames into doc-build failures, so docs cannot silently point at
items that no longer exist. Two subtleties:

- Links resolve **in the scope of the documented item**, so a `use` statement
  that exists only for the docs may trigger an "unused import" warning.
  Writing the full path in the link (``[`std::time::Duration`]``) avoids it.
- Linking from public docs to a **private** item triggers
  `rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links`, because readers of the public docs cannot
  follow the link.

> Key Takeaways
> - Intra-doc links (``[`Path`]``) link items by Rust path; rustdoc computes
>   the URL, including into dependencies.
> - Use `Self::`, `crate::`, custom text `[text](Path)`, and reference-style
>   links for readable prose.
> - Disambiguate with `fn@`, `struct@`, `macro@`, `()` or `!` when names clash.
> - Build docs with `-D warnings` in CI so broken links fail the build.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Convert every backticked type name in a module's docs into an intra-doc
>    link, then rename one of the types and observe the doc build fail.
> 2. Create a struct `Config` and a function `config()` in the same module and
>    write a doc comment linking to each unambiguously.
> 3. Interview: Why are intra-doc links preferable to hard-coded HTML links in
>    a library that will be published on docs.rs? (Hint: think about renames,
>    re-exports, and links into other crates' versions.)

#### Examples Directory

Doc examples show how to use *one item*. Real users also need to see how the
pieces fit together: build a client, configure it, handle errors, shut down
cleanly. That is the job of the `examples/` directory (Chapter 8 introduced it
as a Cargo target kind): complete, runnable programs that demonstrate
realistic workflows.

```text
kv/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/lib.rs
└── examples/
    ├── basic.rs               cargo run --example basic
    ├── watch_file.rs          cargo run --example watch_file --features watch
    └── http_server/           multi-file example
        ├── main.rs            cargo run --example http_server
        └── routes.rs
```

```rust
// examples/basic.rs
//! Loads a config file and prints every key.
//!
//! Run with:
//!     cargo run --example basic -- path/to/app.conf

use std::error::Error;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let path = std::env::args().nth(1).ok_or("usage: basic <file>")?;
    let config = kv::Config::load(&path)?;       // public API only, like a user
    for (key, value) in config.iter() {
        println!("{key} = {value}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

```toml
# Examples can use [dev-dependencies] (e.g. tokio, clap) without
# forcing them on users of the library.
[dev-dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }

[[example]]
name = "watch_file"
required-features = ["watch"]     # skipped unless the feature is enabled
```

How the three kinds of runnable documentation compare:

| | Doc examples | `examples/` | Integration tests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audience | API readers | New users, evaluators | Maintainers |
| Scope | One item | A complete workflow | A behaviour, with assertions |
| Verified by `cargo test` | Compiled and run | Compiled only | Compiled and run |
| Can use dev-dependencies | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Typical length | 3 to 15 lines | 30 to 200 lines | Varies |

Guidelines for good examples:

- **Start each file with a `//!` comment** saying what it demonstrates and the
  exact command to run it.
- **Order them by difficulty** and mention them from the crate docs
  ("see `examples/basic.rs`"). Readers do not find examples on their own.
- **Keep them compiling in CI.** `cargo test` builds them, but examples
  with `required-features` are skipped unless the features are enabled, so CI
  should also run `cargo build --examples --all-features`.
- **Use realistic error handling** (`?`, `main` returning `Result`) because
  examples are copied into production code.

docs.rs can also show **scraped examples**: rustdoc finds calls to each
function in your `examples/` and displays them on that function's page. The
feature is unstable and enabled through docs.rs metadata (next topics):
`cargo-args = ["-Zunstable-options", "-Zrustdoc-scrape-examples"]`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `examples/` holds complete programs that show workflows; doc examples show
>   individual items.
> - Examples use only the public API and may use `[dev-dependencies]`.
> - `cargo test` compiles examples but does not run them; gate optional ones
>   with `required-features` and build them all in CI.
> - Document each example's purpose and run command at the top, and link to
>   examples from the crate docs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `examples/quickstart.rs` for a library you maintain that goes
>    from configuration to a successful result in under 40 lines.
> 2. Add an example that requires an optional feature, declare it with
>    `required-features`, and verify the behaviour of `cargo run --example`
>    with and without the feature.
> 3. Interview: What belongs in a doc example, what belongs in `examples/`, and
>    what belongs in an integration test? (Hint: consider audience, scope, and
>    whether results are asserted.)

#### README and Crate-Level Docs

A crate has two front doors. The **README** is what people see on GitHub and
crates.io when deciding whether to use the crate. The **crate-level
documentation** (`//!` at the top of `src/lib.rs`) is the first page of the API
docs on docs.rs, read by people who have already decided and want to start.
Both should answer, within seconds: *what is this, why would I use it, and what
does the simplest use look like?*

A proven structure for crate-level docs:

```rust
//! Fast, zero-copy parsing of `key = value` configuration files.
//!
//! `kv` reads configuration without allocating for keys or values, validates
//! it against an optional schema, and reports errors with line numbers.
//!
//! # Quick start
//!
//! ```
//! let config = kv::Config::parse("host = example.com\nport = 8080")?;
//! assert_eq!(config.get("port"), Some("8080"));
//! # Ok::<(), kv::Error>(())
//! ```
//!
//! # Overview
//!
//! - [`Config`]: a parsed file; borrow values with [`Config::get`]
//! - [`Schema`]: optional validation rules
//! - [`Error`]: everything that can go wrong, with source locations
//!
//! # Feature flags
//!
//! | Feature | Default | Enables |
//! |---------|---------|---------|
//! | `serde` | no      | `Deserialize` into your own structs |
//! | `watch` | no      | Reloading when the file changes |
//!
//! # Minimum supported Rust version
//!
//! Rust 1.85 or newer.
//!
//! See the `examples/` directory for complete programs.
```

**Sharing one source.** Maintaining two near-identical texts invites drift.
You can make the README *be* the crate docs:

```rust
// src/lib.rs
#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]     // README becomes the crate docs, and its
                                           // ```rust blocks become doc tests
```

Things to watch with this approach:

- README code blocks are now doc tests. Mark shell snippets as ` ```sh ` or
  ` ```text `, or they will be compiled as Rust and fail.
- Relative links in the README (`[guide](docs/guide.md)`) work on GitHub but
  not on docs.rs. Use absolute URLs.
- Badges and HTML that look right on GitHub may render oddly in rustdoc.

If you prefer separate texts but still want the README's examples tested, a
`#[cfg(doctest)]` item includes it only when collecting doc tests:

```rust
// src/lib.rs: tests README examples without making the README the crate docs
#[cfg(doctest)]
#[doc = include_str!("../README.md")]
struct ReadmeDoctests;
```

The reverse direction, generating the README from the crate docs, is handled
by tools such as `cargo-rdme`, which can also check in CI that the two are in
sync.

| Concern | README | Crate-level docs |
| ------- | ------ | ---------------- |
| Shown on | GitHub, crates.io | docs.rs (crate root page) |
| Audience | Evaluators: "should I use this?" | Users: "how do I start?" |
| Typical content | Pitch, installation, quick example, badges, license, contributing | Quick start, concepts, links to key types, feature flags, MSRV |
| Links | URLs | Intra-doc links |
| Tested | Only if included in doc tests | Always (it is a doc comment) |

In `Cargo.toml`, `readme = "README.md"` sets the file crates.io displays (Cargo
picks up `README.md` automatically if present), and `documentation` can point
to a custom docs URL. Without it, crates.io links to docs.rs.

> Key Takeaways
> - The README sells and orients; crate-level `//!` docs onboard users of the
>   API. Both need a one-line pitch and a minimal working example.
> - Structure crate docs as summary, quick start, overview of key types,
>   feature flags, and MSRV.
> - `#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]` shares one source and tests the
>   README's examples; mark non-Rust blocks and use absolute links.
> - `#[cfg(doctest)]` with `include_str!` tests README examples without making
>   it the crate docs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write crate-level docs for a library following the structure above,
>    including a feature-flag table, and view them with `cargo doc --open`.
> 2. Include your README with `#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]`, run
>    `cargo test --doc`, and fix every block that fails.
> 3. Interview: A crate's README example stopped compiling two releases ago
>    and nobody noticed. What process change would have caught it? (Hint:
>    consider which documentation `cargo test` actually executes.)

#### docs.rs Configuration

Every version of every crate published to crates.io gets documentation built
automatically on **docs.rs**. That is convenient, but the build happens on
docs.rs's machines with its defaults. Unless told otherwise, it documents only
the **default features**, for one target (`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`), with a
**nightly** rustdoc, in a sandbox **without network access**. If your crate's
most interesting API sits behind optional features, or only exists on Windows,
the hosted docs will simply omit it.

Configuration lives in `Cargo.toml` under `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`, which
Cargo itself ignores:

```toml
[package.metadata.docs.rs]
all-features = true                       # document everything, including optional APIs
# features = ["serde", "watch"]           # ...or a specific list
# no-default-features = true
rustdoc-args = ["--cfg", "docsrs"]        # lets the code detect a docs.rs build
targets = ["x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]  # extra platforms
# default-target = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
```

docs.rs passes `--cfg docsrs` itself; many crates still list it explicitly,
which is harmless and also documents the intent.

**Feature badges with `doc(cfg)`.** When everything is documented, readers need
to know which items need a feature or platform. rustdoc can render a note such
as *"Available on crate feature `serde` only."* next to the item. The attribute
behind this, `doc_cfg`, is still nightly-only, so it is enabled only when
`docsrs` is set: docs.rs uses nightly, while normal users build on stable and
never see the attribute.

```rust
// lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]   // only on docs.rs (nightly)

#[cfg(feature = "serde")]
#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "serde")))]   // explicit badge
pub mod serde_support {
    //! `Deserialize` integration.
}

#[cfg(windows)]
#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(windows)))]   // "Available on Windows only."
pub fn registry_config() {}
```

```text
Rendered on docs.rs:

  pub mod serde_support
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Available on crate feature serde only.           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  `Deserialize` integration.
```

Recent nightlies merged the former `doc_auto_cfg` feature into `doc_cfg`, so
with `feature(doc_cfg)` enabled rustdoc also infers badges from plain `#[cfg]`
attributes. The explicit `doc(cfg(...))` form still works and is useful when
the inferred condition is not what you want to show.

**Preview locally** with the same settings before publishing:

```bash
RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly doc --all-features --no-deps --open
```

**Build-environment pitfalls**:

| Problem on docs.rs | Cause | Fix |
| ------------------ | ----- | --- |
| Build fails in `build.rs` | No network; native library or tool not installed | Check the `DOCS_RS` environment variable in `build.rs` and skip the native build |
| Feature-gated items missing | Only default features are built | `all-features = true` or a `features` list |
| Platform-specific API missing | Only the default target is built | Add it to `targets` |
| Build times out | Heavy dependencies or build scripts | Disable expensive features for docs; skip work when `DOCS_RS` is set |
| `#![feature(...)]` error on stable | Unconditional nightly feature | Gate with `cfg_attr(docsrs, ...)` |

```rust
// build.rs: skip compiling the bundled C library on docs.rs
fn main() {
    if std::env::var_os("DOCS_RS").is_some() {
        return;                         // docs only need the Rust API, not a linkable library
    }
    // ... compile and link the native library ...
}
```

Once published, a version's docs.rs page cannot be edited. Fixing the
configuration requires publishing a new version, so preview locally first.

> Key Takeaways
> - docs.rs builds docs for every published version with default features,
>   one target, a nightly rustdoc, and no network access.
> - Configure it with `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`: `all-features`, `features`,
>   `targets`, `rustdoc-args`.
> - Gate nightly-only doc features with `#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]`
>   and mark feature- or platform-specific items with `doc(cfg(...))`.
> - Make `build.rs` skip native work when `DOCS_RS` is set, and preview with
>   `RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly doc --all-features`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `[package.metadata.docs.rs]` to a crate with optional features, add
>    `doc(cfg)` badges, and preview the result locally with nightly.
> 2. Write a `build.rs` that compiles a small C file with the `cc` crate but
>    skips it when `DOCS_RS` is set, and verify the skip by setting the
>    variable locally.
> 3. Interview: A user reports that a function from your crate's README "does
>    not exist" on docs.rs, although it compiles fine for them. What are the
>    likely causes, and how do you fix them for the next release? (Hint: think
>    about features, targets, and what docs.rs builds by default.)

---

## 13. Metaprogramming

Metaprogramming is writing code that writes or checks code. Rust has two
macro systems: **declarative macros** (`macro_rules!`), which rewrite code by
pattern matching, and **procedural macros**, which are compiler plugins that
transform token streams with ordinary Rust code. It also has a set of
compile-time tools: `const fn`, the type system, static assertions and build
scripts. Together they remove boilerplate, embed small domain-specific
languages, and move checks from run time to compile time, which is how crates
such as `serde`, `tokio`, `clap` and `sqlx` give concise APIs without runtime
cost.

<a id="131-declarative-macros"></a>
### 13.1 Declarative Macros

Declarative macros, also called "macros by example", match input tokens
against patterns and replace them with a template. They are the first tool to
reach for when a function cannot express what you need: a variable number of
arguments, new items, or code that must be inlined at the call site.

#### macro_rules! Syntax

Functions abstract over *values*. Some repetition cannot be expressed that way:
`vec![1, 2, 3]` takes any number of arguments, `println!` checks its format
string against its arguments at compile time, and a macro can define structs,
impls or whole modules. A function cannot do any of that. A **declarative
macro** fills that gap: it receives source code (as tokens) and produces source
code, before type checking happens.

A useful analogy is a mail-merge template. You write a template with holes
(`$x`), the compiler matches the invocation against the patterns you listed,
fills the holes with the matched pieces, and then compiles the result as if you
had written it by hand.

```rust
macro_rules! square {
    //  matcher          transcriber
    ($x:expr) => { $x * $x };
}

fn main() {
    let n = square!(2 + 3);   // expands to: (2 + 3) * (2 + 3)
    println!("{n}");          // 25, not 2 + 3 * 2 + 3 = 11
}
```

The anatomy of a definition:

```text
macro_rules! NAME {
    ( MATCHER_1 ) => { TRANSCRIBER_1 };     <- rule 1, tried first
    ( MATCHER_2 ) => { TRANSCRIBER_2 };     <- rule 2, tried if rule 1 fails
}

MATCHER      literal tokens to match, plus metavariables `$name:fragment`
TRANSCRIBER  the code to produce; `$name` is replaced by what it matched
```

Unlike the C preprocessor, Rust macros operate on **token trees**, not text,
and they expand into syntax tree nodes. The `$x:expr` above captured
`2 + 3` as a *single expression node*, so the expansion behaves as if it were
