parenthesised. Operator precedence cannot leak in or out.

Where expansion fits in compilation:

```text
source text
   │  lexing
   ▼
tokens ── parsing ──► AST containing unexpanded macro calls (kept as token trees)
                          │
                          │  expansion: match rules, substitute, re-parse,
                          │  repeat until no macro calls remain
                          ▼
                       full AST ──► name resolution ──► type checking ──► ...
```

Expansion happens **before** types exist, so a macro cannot ask "what type is
this expression?". It can only look at tokens.

**Rules are tried in order** and the first one that matches wins, so put
specific rules before general ones. A macro with several rules:

```rust
macro_rules! hashmap {
    // Rule 1: empty invocation.
    () => {
        ::std::collections::HashMap::new()
    };
    // Rule 2: one or more `key => value` pairs, optional trailing comma.
    ($($key:expr => $value:expr),+ $(,)?) => {{
        let mut map = ::std::collections::HashMap::new();
        $( map.insert($key, $value); )+        // repeated once per pair
        map                                    // the block's value
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let ages = hashmap! { "ada" => 36, "alan" => 41, };
    let empty: std::collections::HashMap<u8, u8> = hashmap!();
    println!("{} {}", ages.len(), empty.len());   // 2 0
}
```

Note the **double braces** in rule 2. The outer pair delimits the transcriber;
the inner pair is part of the output, a block expression. Without it, the macro
would expand to several statements, which is not valid where an expression is
expected (`let ages = ...`).

Invocation details worth knowing:

| Aspect | Rule |
| ------ | ---- |
| Delimiters | `m!(...)`, `m![...]` and `m!{...}` are equivalent; convention: `[]` for collections, `{}` for item-like blocks, `()` otherwise |
| Item position | `m!(...)` and `m![...]` need a trailing `;` when used as an item or statement; `m!{...}` does not |
| Where macros may appear | Expressions, statements, items, patterns, types, and inside `impl`/`trait` blocks |
| Visibility of definition | A `macro_rules!` macro is usable only *after* its definition in the source (see Exporting Macros) |
| Recursion | Allowed; limited by `#![recursion_limit = "..."]`, default 128 |

A classic pitfall is **multiple evaluation**. The argument is pasted wherever
`$x` appears, so side effects run as many times as it is mentioned:

```rust
macro_rules! square_once {
    ($x:expr) => {
        match $x {
            v => v * v,      // bind once, use twice: `$x` is evaluated exactly once
        }
    };
}

fn main() {
    let mut calls = 0;
    let mut next = || { calls += 1; calls };
    println!("{}", square!(next()));       // next() * next() = 1 * 2 = 2
    let mut calls = 0;
    let mut next = || { calls += 1; calls };
    println!("{}", square_once!(next()));  // 1
}
```

The `match` form is preferred over `{ let v = $x; v * v }` because `match`
keeps temporaries in `$x` alive for the whole expression, exactly as
`assert_eq!` does in the standard library.

To see what a macro produced, use `cargo expand` (Chapter 8), which prints the
crate after expansion. It is the first debugging tool for every macro problem.

> Key Takeaways
> - `macro_rules!` maps token patterns (matchers) to code templates
>   (transcribers); rules are tried top to bottom, first match wins.
> - Macros operate on token trees and produce syntax nodes, so captured
>   expressions keep their grouping; there are no textual precedence bugs.
> - Expansion happens before type checking: macros see tokens, never types.
> - Use `{{ ... }}` when a macro must expand to a block expression, and bind
>   arguments once (`match $x { v => ... }`) to avoid multiple evaluation.
> - `cargo expand` shows the generated code.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `min!` that accepts one or more expressions and returns the smallest.
>    Check with `cargo expand` that each argument appears exactly once in the
>    output.
> 2. Write `hashset!` modelled on `hashmap!` above, supporting an empty
>    invocation and a trailing comma. Then swap the order of its two rules and
>    explain whether anything changes.
> 3. Interview: Why does `square!(2 + 3)` evaluate to 25 in Rust when the
>    equivalent C macro `#define SQUARE(x) x * x` gives 11? (Hint: compare what
>    each preprocessor operates on, text or syntax.)

#### Fragment Specifiers

A matcher must say *what kind* of syntax each metavariable captures. That is
the job of the **fragment specifier** after the colon in `$name:spec`. It tells
the macro parser how much input to consume: `$e:expr` swallows a whole
expression such as `a + f(b)[0]`, while `$t:tt` takes exactly one token tree.

| Specifier | Matches | Example input |
| --------- | ------- | ------------- |
| `expr` | An expression | `x + 1`, `f(a)`, `{ 3 }` |
| `expr_2021` | An expression, excluding `_` and `const { }` (edition 2021 behaviour) | `x + 1` |
| `ident` | An identifier or keyword (raw identifiers allowed) | `foo`, `r#type`, `self` |
| `ty` | A type | `Vec<u8>`, `&'a str`, `impl Fn()` |
| `path` | A type-style path | `std::io::Error`, `Vec::<u8>::new` |
| `pat` | A pattern, including top-level `A \| B` (edition 2021+) | `Some(x)`, `1..=5`, `A \| B` |
| `pat_param` | A pattern without top-level `\|` | `Some(x)` |
| `stmt` | A statement without its trailing semicolon | `let x = 1` |
| `block` | A block | `{ do_it(); 3 }` |
| `item` | An item | `fn f() {}`, `struct S;` |
| `literal` | A literal, optionally preceded by `-` | `42`, `-1.5`, `"hi"`, `b'a'` |
| `lifetime` | A lifetime | `'a`, `'static` |
| `meta` | The contents of an attribute | `derive(Debug)`, `doc = "text"` |
| `vis` | A visibility, possibly empty | `pub`, `pub(crate)`, nothing |
| `tt` | A single token tree: one token, or a `()`/`[]`/`{}` group with its contents | `+`, `foo`, `(a, b)` |

In edition 2024, `expr` also matches the `_` expression and `const { ... }`
blocks. `expr_2021` preserves the old behaviour for macros that depended on it.

Specifiers make macros generate real items. Here `vis`, `ident`, `ty` and
`meta` let a macro define a newtype with conversions, passing attributes and doc
comments through (doc comments are `#[doc = "..."]` attributes):

```rust
macro_rules! newtype {
    ($(#[$meta:meta])* $vis:vis $name:ident($inner:ty);) => {
        $(#[$meta])*                                 // re-emit doc comments and derives
        $vis struct $name($inner);

        impl ::core::convert::From<$inner> for $name {
            fn from(value: $inner) -> Self { $name(value) }
        }

        impl $name {
            $vis fn into_inner(self) -> $inner { self.0 }
        }
    };
}

newtype! {
    /// A user identifier.
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
    pub UserId(u64);
}

fn main() {
    let id: UserId = 7.into();
    println!("{id:?} {}", id.into_inner());   // UserId(7) 7
}
```

**Follow-set restrictions.** To keep macros forward compatible with future
syntax, some fragments may only be followed by certain tokens. The compiler
rejects ambiguous matchers at definition time:

```text
error: `$a:expr` is followed by `$b:expr`, which is not allowed for `expr` fragments
 --> src/main.rs:1:29
  |
1 | macro_rules! bad { ($a:expr $b:expr) => {}; }
  |                             ^^^^^^^ not allowed after `expr` fragments
  |
  = note: allowed there are: `=>`, `,` or `;`
```

| Fragment | May be followed by |
| -------- | ------------------ |
| `expr`, `stmt` | `=>` `,` `;` |
| `pat` | `=>` `,` `=` `if` `in` |
| `pat_param` | `=>` `,` `=` `\|` `if` `in` |
| `ty`, `path` | `=>` `,` `=` `\|` `;` `:` `>` `>>` `[` `{` `as` `where`, or a `block` fragment |
| `vis` | `,`, an identifier, a type, or an `ident`/`ty`/`path` fragment |
| all others | Anything |

**Captured fragments are opaque.** Once input is parsed as `expr`, `ty`,
`pat` and so on, it becomes a single syntax node. If you forward it to another
macro, that macro can no longer match its individual tokens. Only `ident`,
`lifetime` and `tt` forward transparently:

```rust
macro_rules! is_zero_literal {
    (0) => { true };
    ($($t:tt)*) => { false };
}
macro_rules! via_expr { ($e:expr) => { is_zero_literal!($e) }; }
macro_rules! via_tt   { ($t:tt)   => { is_zero_literal!($t) }; }

fn main() {
    println!("{} {}", via_expr!(0), via_tt!(0));   // false true
}
```

This is why macros that delegate to helper macros usually capture `tt`, and
choose a precise specifier only at the point where the input is finally used.

> Key Takeaways
> - The fragment specifier decides how much input a metavariable consumes and
>   what syntax node it becomes.
> - Use precise specifiers (`expr`, `ty`, `ident`) for clear errors; use `tt`
>   for flexible or forwarded input.
> - Follow-set rules restrict what may come after `expr`, `stmt`, `pat`, `ty`,
>   `path` and `vis`; usually a `,`, `;` or `=>` separator fixes it.
> - Captured fragments other than `ident`, `lifetime` and `tt` are opaque to
>   macros they are forwarded to.
> - In edition 2024, `expr` also accepts `_` and `const { }`; `expr_2021` keeps
>   the older behaviour.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `getter!(Struct, field: Type)` that generates
>    `impl Struct { pub fn field(&self) -> &Type { &self.field } }`. Which
>    specifiers do you need for each part?
> 2. Write a macro `matches_any!(value, P1 | P2 | ...)` that returns `true` if
>    `value` matches any of the patterns, capturing each alternative separately
>    with a `|` separator. Try both `pat` and `pat_param` and explain why only
>    one of them is accepted.
> 3. Interview: A macro `outer!($e:expr)` forwards `$e` to `inner!`, which has a
>    rule matching the literal `true`. Calling `outer!(true)` never hits that
>    rule. Why? (Hint: think about what `$e` is once it has been parsed.)

#### Repetition Patterns

Many useful macros accept "a list of things": `vec![1, 2, 3]`, a set of
`key => value` pairs, a list of struct fields. **Repetitions** express this.
In the matcher, `$( ... ) sep op` matches the inner pattern repeatedly; in the
transcriber, `$( ... ) sep op` emits the inner template once per match.

| Operator | Meaning | Separator allowed |
| -------- | ------- | ----------------- |
| `*` | Zero or more | Yes, e.g. `$($x:expr),*` |
| `+` | One or more | Yes, e.g. `$($x:expr);+` |
| `?` | Zero or one | No |

Think of a repetition as a loop the compiler runs for you. Every metavariable
captured inside `$( ... )` becomes a list, and the transcriber's `$( ... )`
walks all lists in lockstep.

```rust
macro_rules! record {
    // name { field: Type, field: Type, ... }   trailing comma optional
    ($name:ident { $($field:ident : $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {
        #[derive(Debug, Default)]
        pub struct $name {
            $( pub $field: $ty, )*                  // one line per field
        }

        impl $name {
            pub const FIELDS: &'static [&'static str] =
                &[ $( stringify!($field) ),* ];    // ["x", "y", "z"]
        }
    };
}

record!(Point3 { x: f64, y: f64, z: f64 });
```

`$(,)?` is the standard idiom for "optional trailing comma". Notice that the
separator `,` inside `$( pub $field: $ty, )*` is part of the repeated body, so
every field gets a comma. In `$( stringify!($field) ),*` it is a *separator*, so
there is none after the last element.

**Nesting.** Repetitions can nest, and each metavariable must be used at the
same depth it was captured:

```rust
macro_rules! enum_groups {
    ($( $group:ident => [ $($member:ident),* $(,)? ] );* $(;)?) => {
        $(                                             // outer: once per group
            #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
            pub enum $group { $($member),* }           // inner: once per member

            impl $group {
                pub const ALL: &'static [$group] = &[ $($group::$member),* ];
            }
        )*
    };
}

enum_groups! {
    Fruit => [Apple, Pear];
    Veg   => [Leek, Kale, Pea];
}
// Fruit::ALL == [Apple, Pear], Veg::ALL.len() == 3
```

Inside the inner repetition, `$group` (depth 1) is repeated alongside
`$member` (depth 2); that is allowed because it is a single value at that
level. Two metavariables at the same depth used in one repetition must have
**the same length**, or expansion fails:

```text
error: meta-variable `k` repeats 2 times, but `v` repeats 3 times
 --> src/main.rs:5:60
  |
5 | macro_rules! pairs { ($($k:ident),* ; $($v:expr),*) => { [$( (stringify!($k), $v) ),*] }; }
  |                                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

**Recursion** handles cases a single repetition cannot, such as a fold:

```rust
macro_rules! max {
    ($x:expr $(,)?) => { $x };                         // base case
    ($x:expr, $($rest:expr),+ $(,)?) => {{             // recursive case
        let first = $x;
        let rest = max!($($rest),+);
        if first > rest { first } else { rest }
    }};
}
// max!(3, 9, 4,) == 9
```

Two more advanced idioms appear in real-world macros:

- **Counting** without recursion, so it works for long lists and in `const`
  contexts:

  ```rust
  macro_rules! replace_expr { ($_t:tt $sub:expr) => { $sub }; }
  macro_rules! count_tts {
      // Builds `[(), (), ...]` with one `()` per token, then takes its length.
      ($($tts:tt)*) => { <[()]>::len(&[ $( replace_expr!($tts ()) ),* ]) };
  }
  const N: usize = count_tts!(a b c d);   // 4
  ```

- **TT munchers** consume input a few tokens at a time and recurse on the rest.
  They can parse grammars that a single matcher cannot, such as a list whose
  elements have different shapes. **Internal rules**, conventionally prefixed
  with `@`, keep an accumulator:

  ```rust
  macro_rules! html_attrs {
      // Done: emit everything accumulated so far.
      (@acc [$($done:tt)*]) => { vec![$($done)*] };
      // `key = "value"` followed by optional `, rest`
      (@acc [$($done:tt)*] $key:ident = $value:literal $(, $($rest:tt)*)?) => {
          html_attrs!(@acc [$($done)* (stringify!($key), $value.to_string()),] $($($rest)*)?)
      };
      // bare `key` (boolean attribute) followed by optional `, rest`
      (@acc [$($done:tt)*] $key:ident $(, $($rest:tt)*)?) => {
          html_attrs!(@acc [$($done)* (stringify!($key), String::new()),] $($($rest)*)?)
      };
      // Public entry point: start with an empty accumulator.
      ($($input:tt)*) => { html_attrs!(@acc [] $($input)*) };
  }

  // [("id", "main"), ("hidden", ""), ("tabindex", "3")]
  let attrs = html_attrs!(id = "main", hidden, tabindex = 3);
  ```

TT munchers recurse once per element, so they are quadratic in compile time and
bounded by the recursion limit. When a macro needs more than a short muncher,
a procedural macro is usually clearer (section 13.2).

> Key Takeaways
> - `$( ... ) sep op` repeats a pattern; `*` is zero or more, `+` is one or
>   more, `?` is optional and takes no separator.
> - Metavariables captured in a repetition must be expanded inside a
>   repetition of the same depth; parallel lists must have equal length.
> - `$(,)?` accepts an optional trailing comma; `stringify!` turns captured
>   tokens into a string literal.
> - Recursion, internal `@rules` and TT munchers handle irregular input, at
>   the cost of compile time and readability.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `my_vec!` supporting both `my_vec![a, b, c]` and `my_vec![value; n]`,
>    like the standard `vec!`. Which rule must come first, and why?
> 2. Write `bitflags_lite!(Name: u8 { A = 0b001, B = 0b010, C = 0b100 })` that
>    generates a struct with one associated constant per flag and an `ALL`
>    constant containing their bitwise OR.
> 3. Interview: Why do experienced macro authors avoid recursive TT munchers
>    for inputs that may contain hundreds of elements, and what are the
>    alternatives? (Hint: count how many expansions happen and what the default
>    recursion limit is.)

#### Macro Hygiene

When a macro introduces a variable, could it accidentally capture or shadow a
variable at the call site? In C, yes: a macro that declares `tmp` breaks any
caller who also uses `tmp`. **Hygiene** is the property that names introduced
by a macro do not collide with names at the invocation site.

Rust attaches a **syntax context** to every identifier, recording where it was
written. Two identifiers with the same spelling but different contexts are
different names. Think of it as each identifier carrying an invisible colour:
the macro's `tmp` is blue, the caller's `tmp` is red, and they never match.

```rust
macro_rules! double_then_add {
    ($x:expr, $y:expr) => {{
        let tmp = $x * 2;     // the macro's own `tmp`
        tmp + $y
    }};
}

fn main() {
    let tmp = 10;                                // the caller's `tmp`
    println!("{}", double_then_add!(tmp, 1));    // 21: no confusion between the two
}
```

Hygiene also works in the other direction: code passed in by the caller cannot
see the macro's locals.

```rust
macro_rules! using_a {
    ($e:expr) => {{ let a = 42; $e }};
}

fn main() {
    let four = using_a!(a / 10);   // error[E0425]: cannot find value `a`
}
```

```text
help: an identifier with the same name is defined here, but is not accessible due to macro hygiene
 --> src/main.rs:1:44
  |
1 | macro_rules! using_a { ($e:expr) => {{ let a = 42; $e }}; }
  |                                            ^
```

To deliberately share a name, the **caller provides the identifier**, so it
carries the caller's context:

```rust
macro_rules! using_a {
    ($a:ident, $e:expr) => {{ let $a = 42; $e }};
}
let four = using_a!(a, a / 10);    // 4
```

The same rule explains a common surprise: `self` behaves like a local
variable, so a macro cannot use `self` unless it receives it as an argument
(`bump!(self)` with `($s:ident) => { $s.n += 1 }`).

Rust's `macro_rules!` hygiene is **partial** ("mixed-site"). Only some names
are resolved where the macro was defined:

| Name kind | Resolved at | Consequence |
| --------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| Local variables, labels, `$crate` | Definition site | Macro locals and caller locals never collide |
| Functions, types, traits, modules, macros, fields, methods | Invocation site | A path in the macro body is looked up where the macro is *called* |

The second row is where macros break in practice. A macro body that says
`HashMap::new()` works only where the caller has imported `HashMap`. A macro
that says `Option::Some(x)` breaks if the caller has a type named `Option` in
scope. Defensive macro code therefore uses **absolute paths**:

```rust
macro_rules! try_parse {
    ($s:expr) => {
        match ::core::str::FromStr::from_str($s) {
            ::core::result::Result::Ok(v) => ::core::option::Option::Some(v),
            ::core::result::Result::Err(_) => ::core::option::Option::None,
        }
    };
}
```

The leading `::` means "a crate named `core`" and cannot be shadowed by a local
module called `core`. For items from your own crate, use `$crate::` (next
topic).

| Situation | Write |
| --------- | ----- |
| Standard library item | `::core::...`, `::alloc::...` or `::std::...` |
| Item from the macro's own crate | `$crate::path::to::item` |
| Name the caller should be able to use | Take it as an `$name:ident` argument |
| Temporary variable inside the macro | A plain `let` is fine; hygiene protects it |

> Key Takeaways
> - Hygiene keeps a macro's local variables and labels separate from the
>   caller's, even when they share a spelling.
> - It is partial: item paths (functions, types, macros) are resolved at the
>   call site, so use absolute paths (`::core::...`, `$crate::...`).
> - To introduce a name the caller can use, take the identifier as an
>   `ident` argument.
> - `self` is hygienic like a local; pass it in explicitly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `swap!(a, b)` macro using a temporary variable. Prove that it
>    works when the caller's variables are themselves named `tmp`.
> 2. Write a macro that calls `HashMap::new()` without a path prefix, then call
>    it from a module that does not import `HashMap`. Fix it with an absolute
>    path.
> 3. Interview: Rust macro hygiene is described as "mixed-site". Which names are
>    hygienic and which are not, and how does that affect a library author
>    writing exported macros? (Hint: compare a `let` binding in the macro with a
>    call to a helper function defined in the library.)

#### Exporting Macros

Macros are not items like functions, and their scoping rules carry history.
Inside a crate, `macro_rules!` macros use **textual scoping**: a macro is
visible from its definition *downward* in source order, including into child
modules declared after it. To use a macro in other crates, it must be
**exported**, which adds a second, path-based way to name it.

```text
src/lib.rs                               textual scope of `helper!`
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mod early;            // cannot see helper!
macro_rules! helper { ... }  ──────────┐
fn a() { helper!(); }  // OK            │
mod later;            // OK inside      │  everything after the
                      // later.rs too   │  definition, in source order
───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Mechanism | Effect | Typical use |
| --------- | ------ | ----------- |
| Textual order | Visible after the definition in the same file and in later child modules | Small private helpers |
| `#[macro_use] mod macros;` | Extends the module's macros into the parent, after the `mod` line | A crate-private `macros.rs` declared first in `lib.rs` |
| `pub(crate) use name;` after the definition | Makes the macro nameable by path (`crate::module::name!`) inside the crate | Crate-private macros used across modules, without ordering concerns |
| `#[macro_export]` | Places the macro at the **crate root** of the public API: `mylib::name!` | Public macros |

`#[macro_export]` always exports at the crate root, regardless of the module
the macro is written in. A public macro then needs two things to work for its
users:

1. **`$crate`** to refer to items of the defining crate. It expands to the
   correct path to your crate, even if the user renamed the dependency in
   `Cargo.toml`.
2. **Every item it references must be public**, because the expansion is
   compiled inside the user's crate. Items that exist only for macros are
   public but hidden from documentation.

```rust
// mylib/src/lib.rs
mod macros;     // #[macro_export] macros inside still live at the crate root

/// Implementation details used by exported macros. Not part of the API.
#[doc(hidden)]
pub mod __private {
    pub use std::collections::HashMap;
}
```

```rust
// mylib/src/macros.rs
/// Creates a `HashMap` from `key => value` pairs.
///
/// ```
/// let m = mylib::hashmap! { "a" => 1, "b" => 2 };
/// assert_eq!(m["b"], 2);
/// ```
#[macro_export]
macro_rules! hashmap {
    ($($k:expr => $v:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut map = $crate::__private::HashMap::new();   // works under any crate name
        $( map.insert($k, $v); )*
        map
    }};
}
```

```rust
// a user's crate (edition 2018 or later)
use mylib::hashmap;            // macros are imported like any other item

fn main() {
    let ports = hashmap! { "http" => 80, "https" => 443 };
}
```

Practical guidance for public macros:

- **Helper macros** used by your public macro must also be `#[macro_export]`.
  Mark them `#[doc(hidden)]`, give them a `__` prefix, and call them as
  `$crate::__helper!(...)`.
- **The accepted syntax is public API.** Removing a rule or tightening a
  fragment specifier is a breaking change under semver (Chapter 8).
- **Test from the outside.** Doc tests (Chapter 12) compile as an external
  crate, so they catch a missing `$crate` or a private item that unit tests
  inside the crate cannot.
- **Legacy forms.** You may still see `#[macro_use] extern crate foo;` (edition
  2015) and `#[macro_export(local_inner_macros)]`; neither is needed in modern
  code.

> Key Takeaways
> - Inside a crate, `macro_rules!` macros are textually scoped: define before
>   use, or re-export with `pub(crate) use name;` for path-based access.
> - `#[macro_export]` publishes a macro at the crate root; users `use
>   mylib::name;`.
> - Exported macros must reach your items through `$crate::` and only through
>   public (often `#[doc(hidden)]`) paths.
> - A macro's accepted syntax is part of your semver contract; test it with doc
>   tests.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a library with a `macros.rs` module containing a `#[macro_export]`
>    macro that calls a private helper function. Use it from a doc test, observe
>    the error, and fix it with `$crate` and a `#[doc(hidden)]` public path.
> 2. Define a crate-internal macro in `src/util.rs` and use it from a module
>    declared *before* `util` in `lib.rs`, using `pub(crate) use`.
> 3. Interview: Why is `$crate` necessary at all; why not write `mylib::` in the
>    macro body? (Hint: consider how users can rename dependencies in
>    `Cargo.toml`, and what happens when the macro is used inside `mylib`
>    itself.)

<a id="132-procedural-macros"></a>
### 13.2 Procedural Macros

Procedural macros are Rust functions that the compiler runs during
compilation. They receive code as a stream of tokens and return new tokens.
Because they are ordinary Rust, they can parse arbitrary syntax, inspect type
definitions and produce detailed errors. This is how `#[derive(Serialize)]`,
`#[tokio::main]` and `sqlx::query!` work.

#### Derive Macros

`#[derive(Debug)]` saves you from writing a `Debug` impl by hand for every
struct. The standard derives cover a few built-in traits. **Custom derive
macros** let any library offer the same convenience for its own traits: you
annotate a type, and the macro reads the type definition and generates an
`impl`.

A procedural macro is a **compiler plugin**. It is compiled for the host
machine, loaded by `rustc` as a dynamic library, and called with the tokens of
the annotated item. This imposes a structural rule: procedural macros live in
their **own crate**, with `proc-macro = true`, and that crate can export *only*
procedural macros.

```text
workspace
├── fieldnames/                 the library users depend on
│   └── src/lib.rs              pub trait FieldNames + re-export of the derive
└── fieldnames-derive/          proc-macro = true; compiled for the HOST
    └── src/lib.rs              #[proc_macro_derive(FieldNames)]

user crate ──depends on──► fieldnames ──(feature "derive")──► fieldnames-derive
```

```toml
# fieldnames-derive/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "fieldnames-derive"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
proc-macro = true          # this crate is a compiler plugin

[dependencies]
proc-macro2 = "1"
quote = "1"
syn = "2"                  # syn 3 also works for every example in this chapter
```

```toml
# fieldnames/Cargo.toml: the facade crate, serde-style
[dependencies]
fieldnames-derive = { path = "../fieldnames-derive", optional = true }

[features]
derive = ["dep:fieldnames-derive"]
```

The facade crate defines the trait and re-exports the derive under the same
name. Macros live in a separate namespace from types and traits, so one `use`
brings in both:

```rust
// fieldnames/src/lib.rs
/// Types that can list the names of their fields.
pub trait FieldNames {
    const FIELD_NAMES: &'static [&'static str];
}

#[cfg(feature = "derive")]
pub use fieldnames_derive::FieldNames;     // same name, macro namespace
```

The derive macro itself. A derive receives the item's tokens and returns tokens
that the compiler **appends** after the item; it cannot modify or remove the
original definition.

```rust
// fieldnames-derive/src/lib.rs
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::ext::IdentExt;                     // for `unraw()`
use syn::{parse_macro_input, Data, DeriveInput, Fields};

// `attributes(field_names)` registers a *helper attribute*: the compiler accepts
// `#[field_names(...)]` on fields of types that derive FieldNames.
#[proc_macro_derive(FieldNames, attributes(field_names))]
pub fn derive_field_names(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // 1. Parse the raw tokens into a syntax tree describing the type.
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);

    // 2. Do the real work in a function that can return errors.
    expand(input)
        .unwrap_or_else(syn::Error::into_compile_error)
        .into()                              // proc_macro2 -> proc_macro
}

fn expand(input: DeriveInput) -> syn::Result<proc_macro2::TokenStream> {
    let Data::Struct(data) = &input.data else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
            &input.ident,
            "FieldNames can only be derived for structs",
        ));
    };
    let Fields::Named(fields) = &data.fields else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
            &data.fields,
            "FieldNames requires named fields",
        ));
    };

    let mut names = Vec::new();
    for field in &fields.named {
        if is_skipped(field)? {
            continue;
        }
        // `r#type` should be listed as "type".
        names.push(field.ident.as_ref().unwrap().unraw().to_string());
    }

    let name = &input.ident;
    // Carry the struct's generics over to the impl: `impl<T: Clone> X<T>`.
    let (impl_generics, ty_generics, where_clause) = input.generics.split_for_impl();

    // 3. Generate the output. `#(#names),*` repeats once per element.
    Ok(quote! {
        impl #impl_generics ::fieldnames::FieldNames for #name #ty_generics #where_clause {
            const FIELD_NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &[#(#names),*];
        }
    })
}

/// True if the field carries `#[field_names(skip)]`.
fn is_skipped(field: &syn::Field) -> syn::Result<bool> {
    let mut skip = false;
    for attr in &field.attrs {
        if attr.path().is_ident("field_names") {
            attr.parse_nested_meta(|meta| {
                if meta.path.is_ident("skip") {
                    skip = true;
                    Ok(())
                } else {
                    Err(meta.error("expected `skip`"))
                }
            })?;
        }
    }
    Ok(skip)
}
```

Using it, and what `cargo expand` shows:

```rust
use fieldnames::FieldNames;

#[derive(FieldNames)]
struct User {
    id: u64,
    name: String,
    r#type: String,
    #[field_names(skip)]
    password_hash: String,
}

#[derive(FieldNames)]
struct Wrapper<T: Clone> { inner: T, count: usize }

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", User::FIELD_NAMES);                           // ["id", "name", "type"]
    println!("{:?}", <Wrapper<u8> as FieldNames>::FIELD_NAMES);    // ["inner", "count"]
}
```

```rust
// cargo expand (excerpt)
impl ::fieldnames::FieldNames for User {
    const FIELD_NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &["id", "name", "type"];
}
impl<T: Clone> ::fieldnames::FieldNames for Wrapper<T> {
    const FIELD_NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &["inner", "count"];
}
```

Points that trip up first-time derive authors:

- **No `$crate` in procedural macros.** The generated code names the facade
  crate by an absolute path (`::fieldnames::...`). This assumes users did not
  rename the dependency; the `proc-macro-crate` crate can look up the actual
  name in the user's `Cargo.toml` when that matters.
- **Generics.** Forgetting `split_for_impl` produces an impl that does not
  compile for generic types. Real derives such as `Clone` also add bounds
  (`T: Clone`) to the where clause; decide deliberately whether yours needs
  them.
- **Compile-time cost.** `syn` with full parsing is one of the heaviest
  dependencies in the ecosystem. Every proc-macro crate adds to clean build
  times, which is why facade crates put derives behind a feature.

> Key Takeaways
> - A derive macro is `#[proc_macro_derive(Name, attributes(helpers))]` on a
>   `fn(TokenStream) -> TokenStream` in a `proc-macro = true` crate.
> - Its output is appended after the item; the item itself is untouched.
> - Ship it serde-style: a facade crate with the trait plus an optional
>   `derive` feature that re-exports the macro under the same name.
> - Use absolute paths (`::yourcrate::Trait`) and propagate generics with
>   `split_for_impl`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend `FieldNames` with a `#[field_names(rename = "...")]` helper
>    attribute. Reject an attribute that sets both `skip` and `rename`.
> 2. Write `#[derive(VariantNames)]` for fieldless enums that generates
>    `const VARIANTS: &'static [&'static str]`. Report an error if a variant
>    carries data.
> 3. Interview: Why must procedural macros live in a separate crate, and why
>    can that crate export nothing but macros? (Hint: think about which machine
>    the crate is compiled for and how the compiler loads it.)

#### Attribute Macros

Derives can only add code next to an item. Sometimes you want to *change* the
item: wrap a function body with timing, turn `async fn main` into a function
that starts a runtime (`#[tokio::main]`), or register a handler in a routing
table (`#[get("/users")]`). **Attribute macros** receive the annotated item and
return a *replacement* for it.

```text
#[timed(label = "db")]     ──►  attr: TokenStream  = `label = "db"`
async fn query() { ... }   ──►  item: TokenStream  = `async fn query() { ... }`

macro returns TokenStream  ──►  replaces the original item entirely
```

The signature takes two streams: the attribute's arguments and the item.
Because the output *replaces* the input, a macro that returns an empty stream
deletes the item. Forgetting to re-emit it is the most common mistake.

```rust
// macros/src/lib.rs   (proc-macro crate; syn with features = ["full"] to parse fns)
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, parse_quote, ItemFn, LitStr};

#[proc_macro_attribute]
pub fn timed(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the attribute's own arguments: `#[timed]` or `#[timed(label = "...")]`.
    let mut label: Option<LitStr> = None;
    let args_parser = syn::meta::parser(|meta| {
        if meta.path.is_ident("label") {
            label = Some(meta.value()?.parse()?);   // `= "some text"`
            Ok(())
        } else {
            Err(meta.error("unsupported option; expected `label = \"...\"`"))
        }
    });
    parse_macro_input!(attr with args_parser);

    // Parse the annotated item; anything but a function is rejected with an error.
    let mut func = parse_macro_input!(item as ItemFn);
    let label = match label {
        Some(lit) => lit.value(),
        None => func.sig.ident.to_string(),          // default: the function's name
    };

    // Wrap the original body: a guard reports on drop, so every exit path
    // (normal return, `?`, early `return`, panic) is measured.
    let body = &func.block;
    let new_body: syn::Block = parse_quote! {{
        struct __TimedGuard(&'static str, ::std::time::Instant);
        impl ::core::ops::Drop for __TimedGuard {
            fn drop(&mut self) {
                ::std::eprintln!("[timed] {} took {:?}", self.0, self.1.elapsed());
            }
        }
        let _guard = __TimedGuard(#label, ::std::time::Instant::now());
        #body
    }};
    *func.block = new_body;

    // Attributes, visibility and signature are re-emitted untouched.
    quote!(#func).into()
}
```

```rust
use macros::timed;

#[timed]
fn load_config(path: &str) -> std::io::Result<String> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)            // `?`-style errors are still timed
}

#[timed(label = "checksum")]
fn checksum(data: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    data.iter().map(|&b| b as u32).sum()
}

// stderr:
// [timed] load_config took 15.6µs
// [timed] checksum took 367ns
```

Design decisions in this example that generalise:

- **Modify the parsed item, then print it.** Mutating `func.block` and
  emitting `#func` keeps every other part (attributes, generics, `async`,
  `unsafe`, doc comments) exactly as written. Rebuilding the function from
  hand-picked fields silently drops whatever you forgot.
- **Wrap with a drop guard rather than a closure.** Moving the body into a
  closure changes the meaning of `return`, `?` and `.await`; a guard does not.
  `let _guard` keeps the guard alive to the end of the scope, while
  `let _ = ...` would drop it immediately.
- **Reject what you do not support.** `#[timed]` on a struct produces
  `error: expected 'fn'` from `parse_macro_input!`, pointing at the struct.
- **Order matters.** Attribute macros expand top to bottom: the first one
  receives the item with the attributes below it still attached, as tokens.

| Aspect | Derive macro | Attribute macro |
| ------ | ------------ | --------------- |
| Declared with | `#[proc_macro_derive(Name)]` | `#[proc_macro_attribute]` |
| Applies to | `struct`, `enum`, `union` | Any item (and some statements and expressions on nightly) |
| Receives | The item | Its own arguments and the item |
| Output | Appended after the item | Replaces the item |
| Can take arguments | Only via helper attributes | Yes: `#[name(args)]` |
| Typical uses | Trait impls (`Serialize`, `Error`) | Wrapping (`#[tokio::main]`, `#[instrument]`), registration (`#[get]`), test frameworks (`#[rstest]`) |

> Key Takeaways
> - `#[proc_macro_attribute] fn(attr, item) -> TokenStream` receives the
>   attribute arguments and the item, and its output replaces the item.
> - Re-emit the item; the cleanest way is to parse it, mutate the parsed tree,
>   and print it back.
> - `syn::meta::parser` parses `key = value` style arguments with good errors.
> - Prefer guards over closures when wrapping bodies, so `return`, `?` and
>   `.await` keep their meaning.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `threshold_ms = 100` option to `#[timed]` so it only prints when the
>    call takes longer than the threshold.
> 2. Write `#[retry(times = 3)]` for functions returning `Result`, re-running
>    the body until it succeeds or the attempts run out. Report a compile error
>    when the function's return type is not written as `Result<...>`.
> 3. Interview: How does `#[tokio::main]` let you write `async fn main` when
>    `main` cannot be async? Sketch the code it generates. (Hint: the macro
>    rewrites the signature and the body.)

#### Function-Like Macros

`macro_rules!` handles many call-style macros, but it can only rearrange
tokens it is given. It cannot read a file, validate an SQL string, compute a
value from a string literal, or parse a grammar too irregular for patterns.
**Function-like procedural macros** are invoked like `macro_rules!` macros,
`name!(...)`, but run arbitrary Rust code on their input.

The signature is the simplest of the three: one stream in, one stream out. The
example below decodes a hex string **at compile time** and validates it,
producing a byte-array literal. Invalid input becomes a compile error pointing
at the string.

```rust
// macros/src/lib.rs
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, LitStr};

#[proc_macro]
pub fn hex(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let lit = parse_macro_input!(input as LitStr);      // accept exactly one string literal
    match decode_hex(&lit.value()) {
        Ok(bytes) => quote! { [#(#bytes),*] }.into(),    // `[127u8, 69u8, ...]`
        Err(msg) => syn::Error::new(lit.span(), msg).to_compile_error().into(),
    }
}

fn decode_hex(s: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>, String> {
    let digits: Vec<char> = s.chars().filter(|c| !c.is_whitespace()).collect();
    if digits.len() % 2 != 0 {
        return Err(format!("expected an even number of hex digits, found {}", digits.len()));
    }
    digits
        .chunks(2)
        .map(|pair| {
            let pair: String = pair.iter().collect();
            u8::from_str_radix(&pair, 16).map_err(|_| format!("`{pair}` is not a hex byte"))
        })
        .collect()
}
```

```rust
const ELF_MAGIC: [u8; 4] = macros::hex!("7f45 4c46");   // [127, 69, 76, 70]
const BAD: [u8; 3] = macros::hex!("abcde");
```

```text
error: expected an even number of hex digits, found 5
 --> src/main.rs:2:35
  |
2 | const BAD: [u8; 3] = macros::hex!("abcde");
  |                                   ^^^^^^^
```

Function-like macros are the tool for **embedded languages**: `html!` in Yew,
`sqlx::query!` (which checks SQL against a live database schema at compile
time), `include_str!`-like file readers, and parsers for custom syntax such as
the routing table built in the "syn and quote Crates" topic.

Choosing between the two kinds of function-style macro:

| Need | `macro_rules!` | `#[proc_macro]` |
| ---- | -------------- | --------------- |
| Rearranging tokens, variadic arguments | Ideal | Overkill |
| Same crate as the code using it | Yes | No, separate proc-macro crate |
| Computation on input (decode, hash, validate) | Very limited | Arbitrary Rust code |
| Reading files or the environment | Only via built-ins like `include_str!` | Yes (keep it deterministic) |
| Error messages | Rule mismatch, or `compile_error!` | Precise, custom, multi-span |
| Compile-time cost | Low | Builds `syn`; runs a plugin |

Before writing a procedural macro, check whether `const fn` (section 13.3) can
do the job. The popular `hex-literal` crate moved from a procedural macro to
a declarative macro plus `const fn`, removing the proc-macro dependency for
its users.

> Key Takeaways
> - `#[proc_macro] fn(TokenStream) -> TokenStream` defines `name!(...)`; its
>   output replaces the invocation.
> - Use it for computation and validation on input, and for embedded languages
>   whose grammar patterns cannot express.
> - Turn invalid input into compile errors with spans pointing at the
>   offending tokens.
> - Prefer `macro_rules!` or `const fn` when they suffice; they are cheaper to
>   compile and live in the same crate.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `bin!("1010 0001")` that produces a `u8` or a byte array, with an
>    error for any character other than `0`, `1` or whitespace.
> 2. Write `env_or!("NAME", "default")` that expands to the value of an
>    environment variable at compile time, or to the default. Compare it with
>    the built-in `option_env!`.
> 3. Interview: Your team wants a macro that validates SQL strings against the
>    database schema at compile time. What are the operational consequences for
>    builds, CI and offline development? (Hint: look at how `sqlx` handles the
>    no-database case.)

#### TokenStream Manipulation

All three kinds of procedural macro speak the same language: a
**`TokenStream`**, a sequence of **token trees**. Before reaching for parsing
libraries, it is worth knowing what is inside, because that is what you are
really producing.

A token tree is one of four things:

| Variant | Represents | Examples |
| ------- | ---------- | -------- |
| `Ident` | An identifier or keyword | `foo`, `fn`, `r#type` |
| `Punct` | A single punctuation character, with spacing | `+`, `=`, `#`, `'` (of a lifetime) |
| `Literal` | A literal | `2`, `"text"`, `b'x'`, `1.5f32` |
| `Group` | A delimited sub-stream | `( ... )`, `[ ... ]`, `{ ... }` |

Multi-character operators are sequences of `Punct`s. **Spacing** records
whether the next character is glued on (`Joint`) or not (`Alone`). Groups make
the stream a **tree**: the contents of brackets are nested.

```text
input:  a += (b * 2)

TokenStream
├── Ident   a
├── Punct   '+'  Joint          `+` glued to the next char: forms `+=`
├── Punct   '='  Alone
└── Group   Parenthesis
    └── TokenStream
        ├── Ident   b
        ├── Punct   '*'  Alone
        └── Literal 2
```

Every token also carries a **`Span`**: its location in the source plus hygiene
information. Spans decide where errors point and how identifiers resolve:

| Span | Resolves names like | Use for |
| ---- | ------------------- | ------- |
| `Span::call_site()` | Code written at the invocation | Default; names the user can see and refer to |
| `Span::mixed_site()` | `macro_rules!`: locals at definition site, items at call site | Temporaries that must not clash with user variables |
| A token's own `.span()` | Wherever that token was written | Error messages and re-emitted user tokens |

Two crates provide these types. `proc_macro` is the compiler's own API; it
exists only *inside* a running proc macro, so code using it cannot run in unit
tests. `proc_macro2` mirrors the same API and works anywhere. The standard
practice is to write logic against `proc_macro2` and convert at the boundary
with `.into()`.

Manipulating tokens directly, without `syn`: a function that renames an
identifier everywhere, recursing into groups and preserving spans so that
errors still point at the user's code.

```rust
use proc_macro2::{Group, Ident, TokenStream, TokenTree};

/// Replaces every identifier `from` with `to`, descending into groups.
pub fn rename(input: TokenStream, from: &str, to: &str) -> TokenStream {
    input
        .into_iter()
        .map(|tree| match tree {
            TokenTree::Ident(ident) if ident == from => {
                TokenTree::Ident(Ident::new(to, ident.span()))   // keep the span
            }
            TokenTree::Group(group) => {
                let inner = rename(group.stream(), from, to);     // recurse into ( ) [ ] { }
                let mut new = Group::new(group.delimiter(), inner);
                new.set_span(group.span());
                TokenTree::Group(new)
            }
            other => other,                                      // Punct, Literal: unchanged
        })
        .collect()                                               // TokenStream: FromIterator
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn renames_inside_groups() {
        // `TokenStream: FromStr` makes test input easy to write.
        let input: TokenStream = "x + f(x, [y, x])".parse().unwrap();
        // Display separates tokens with spaces; only token content matters.
        assert_eq!(rename(input, "x", "z").to_string(), "z + f (z , [y , z])");
    }
}
```

Hand-written token code is fine for simple transformations, but reconstructing
a Rust *grammar* this way (where does an expression end? which `<` opens
generics?) is error-prone. In practice:

- **Parse** input with `syn`, which turns tokens into a typed syntax tree.
- **Generate** output with `quote!`, which turns Rust-like templates into
  tokens.
- Drop to raw `TokenTree`s only for token-level tasks: renaming, scanning,
  or forwarding input you do not need to understand.

> Key Takeaways
> - A `TokenStream` is a tree of `Ident`, `Punct`, `Literal` and `Group`
>   tokens; multi-character operators are joint `Punct`s.
> - Spans carry location and hygiene; preserve user spans so errors point at
>   user code.
> - Write logic against `proc_macro2` for testability; convert to and from
>   `proc_macro` at the macro entry point.
> - Raw token manipulation suits token-level tasks; use `syn` and `quote` for
>   anything grammar-aware.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that counts the identifiers, punctuation tokens and
>    literals in a `proc_macro2::TokenStream`, including those inside groups.
>    Test it on `"fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }"`.
> 2. Print the token trees of `x -> y`, `'a` and `a::b` with `{:?}`, and
>    explain the `Spacing` of each `Punct`.
> 3. Interview: Why can't a function that takes a `proc_macro::TokenStream` be
>    unit tested with `cargo test`, and how do real proc-macro crates structure
>    their code around that? (Hint: where does the `proc_macro` crate get its
>    implementation from?)

#### syn and quote Crates

Almost every procedural macro is built from the same three crates, each with
one responsibility:

```text
 proc_macro::TokenStream
          │  .into()
          ▼
 proc_macro2::TokenStream ──syn::parse──► syntax tree (DeriveInput, ItemFn, Expr, ...)
                                                 │  inspect, transform
                                                 ▼
 proc_macro2::TokenStream ◄──quote!──── templates with #interpolations
          │  .into()
          ▼
 proc_macro::TokenStream
```

**syn** is a complete parser for Rust syntax. Its most used entry points:

| Type | Parses | Typical macro |
| ---- | ------ | ------------- |
| `DeriveInput` | A struct, enum or union definition | Derive macros |
| `ItemFn`, `ItemStruct`, `Item` | Items | Attribute macros |
| `Expr`, `Type`, `Path`, `LitStr`, `Ident` | Expressions, types, paths, literals | Building blocks for custom parsers |
| `Attribute` + `parse_nested_meta` | `#[name(key = value, flag)]` | Helper attributes |

A `DeriveInput` mirrors the shape of a type definition:

```text
DeriveInput
├── attrs:    Vec<Attribute>           #[derive(...)], #[serde(...)], doc comments
├── vis:      Visibility               pub, pub(crate), inherited
├── ident:    Ident                    the type's name
├── generics: Generics                 <T: Clone, 'a, const N: usize> + where clause
└── data:     Data
    ├── Struct(DataStruct { fields: Fields::Named | Fields::Unnamed | Fields::Unit })
    ├── Enum(DataEnum { variants: [Variant { ident, fields, discriminant }] })
    └── Union(DataUnion { fields })

Field { attrs, vis, ident: Option<Ident>, ty: Type }   (ident is None for tuple fields)
```

`syn` compiles only what you enable. The defaults (`derive`, `parsing`,
`printing`, `proc-macro`, `clone-impls`) handle `DeriveInput`; parsing function
bodies, items or arbitrary expressions needs `full`.

| Feature | Adds |
| ------- | ---- |
| `full` | All item and expression types (`ItemFn`, `Block`, `Stmt`, ...) |
| `visit`, `visit-mut`, `fold` | Generic traversals of the syntax tree |
| `extra-traits` | `Debug`, `Eq`, `Hash` on syntax types: useful when debugging |

**quote** turns a template into tokens. Inside `quote! { ... }`:

| Syntax | Meaning |
| ------ | ------- |
| `#var` | Interpolate anything implementing `ToTokens` (syntax nodes, `Ident`, strings, integers) |
| `#(#items)*` | Repeat for each element of an iterator |
| `#(#items),*` | Repeat with `,` as separator |
| `#(#keys => #values),*` | Iterate several iterators in lockstep |
| `format_ident!("{}Builder", name)` | Build a new identifier |
| `quote_spanned!(span=> ...)` | Give generated tokens a chosen span (see Compile-Time Error Reporting) |
| `parse_quote!(...)` | `quote!` followed by parsing into an inferred syn type |

Strings interpolate as string literals and integers as suffixed literals
(`404` becomes `404u16`), so values computed in the macro land in the output
correctly escaped.

**Custom grammars.** For function-like macros, you can implement
`syn::parse::Parse` for your own types. Then `syn` handles tokens, lookahead and
error messages, and you describe only the grammar. Here is a small routing DSL:

```rust
use proc_macro2::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
use syn::{Ident, LitStr, Path, Token};

// Grammar:  routes! { GET "/users" => list_users, POST "/users" => create_user }
pub struct RouteTable {
    routes: Punctuated<Route, Token![,]>,       // `Route, Route, ...`
}

struct Route {
    method: Ident,
    path: LitStr,
    handler: Path,
}

impl Parse for Route {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> syn::Result<Self> {
        let method: Ident = input.parse()?;      // each parse() advances the cursor
        if !["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"].iter().any(|m| method == m) {
            return Err(syn::Error::new(method.span(), "expected GET, POST, PUT or DELETE"));
        }
        let path: LitStr = input.parse()?;
        if !path.value().starts_with('/') {
            return Err(syn::Error::new(path.span(), "route paths must start with `/`"));
        }
        input.parse::<Token![=>]>()?;            // `Token![=>]` is the type of that token
        let handler: Path = input.parse()?;
        Ok(Route { method, path, handler })
    }
}

impl Parse for RouteTable {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> syn::Result<Self> {
        // Zero or more `Route`s separated by commas, trailing comma allowed.
        Ok(RouteTable { routes: Punctuated::parse_terminated(input)? })
    }
}

pub fn expand(table: RouteTable) -> TokenStream {
    let arms = table.routes.iter().map(|r| {
        let method = r.method.to_string();
        let (path, handler) = (&r.path, &r.handler);
        quote! { (#method, #path) => ::core::option::Option::Some(#handler as fn() -> String) }
    });
    quote! {
        |method: &str, path: &str| -> ::core::option::Option<fn() -> String> {
            match (method, path) {
                #(#arms,)*
                _ => ::core::option::Option::None,
            }
        }
    }
}
```

```rust
// In the proc-macro crate's lib.rs: the thin entry point.
#[proc_macro]
pub fn routes(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let table = parse_macro_input!(input as dsl::RouteTable);
    dsl::expand(table).into()
}
```

```rust
// User code
let router = routes! {
    GET "/users" => list_users,
    POST "/users" => create_user,
};
assert_eq!(router("GET", "/users").map(|h| h()), Some("all users".to_string()));
```

**Testing macro logic** works best on `proc_macro2` types, without the
compiler in the loop. `syn::parse_quote!` builds input, and the `prettyplease`
crate formats output for snapshot tests (Chapter 12). Add `insta`,
`prettyplease` and `syn` with the `full` feature (needed for `syn::File`) as
dev-dependencies:

```rust
#[test]
fn expands_field_names() {
    let input: syn::DeriveInput = syn::parse_quote! {
        struct P { x: f64, #[field_names(skip)] cache: u8 }
    };
    let output = expand(input).unwrap();
    let file: syn::File = syn::parse2(output).unwrap();
    insta::assert_snapshot!(prettyplease::unparse(&file));
}
```

A note on versions: syn 2 is what most published crates depend on, and syn 3
(2026) is also available. Every example in this chapter compiles unchanged
with both. Newer syn versions add fields to syntax-tree structs (for example,
`ItemFn` gained `modifiers` in syn 3), so prefer mutating parsed nodes, or
`..` in destructuring patterns, over listing every field.

> Key Takeaways
> - `syn` parses tokens into typed syntax trees; `quote!` turns templates back
>   into tokens; `proc_macro2` connects them and makes the logic testable.
> - Enable `syn`'s `full` feature only when you parse items or expressions
>   beyond type definitions.
> - `quote!` interpolates with `#var` and repeats with `#(...)*`;
>   `format_ident!` creates identifiers.
> - Implement `Parse` to define a DSL grammar; `syn` supplies tokens,
>   punctuation helpers and error reporting.
> - Test expansion functions directly with `parse_quote!` and snapshot the
>   `prettyplease` output.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend the `routes!` grammar with an optional `as name` suffix and
>    generate a `const` with the route's path for each named route.
> 2. Using `syn::visit_mut::VisitMut`, write an attribute macro that replaces
>    every `.unwrap()` call in a function body with
>    `.expect("<function name>")`.
> 3. Interview: Why do proc-macro crates usually depend on both `proc_macro`
>    and `proc_macro2`, and what would break if they used only `proc_macro`?
>    (Hint: think about tests and about the interfaces of `syn` and `quote`.)

#### Compile-Time Error Reporting

A macro runs on someone else's code, and that code will often be wrong. If the
macro panics, the user sees `error: proc-macro derive panicked` with a message
and no location. If the generated code fails to type-check, the error points at
`#[derive(...)]` with no hint which field caused it. Good macros report errors
**at the user's tokens**, say what is expected, and report all problems in one
compile.

There are three levels of tooling.

**1. Errors in `macro_rules!`: `compile_error!`.** A fallback rule can turn
unexpected input into a readable message:

```rust
macro_rules! bits_type {
    (8) => { u8 };
    (16) => { u16 };
    (32) => { u32 };
    ($other:tt) => {
        compile_error!(concat!("unsupported width: ", stringify!($other), "; use 8, 16 or 32"))
    };
}
let x: bits_type!(64) = 1;   // error: unsupported width: 64; use 8, 16 or 32
```

The same built-in, guarded by `cfg`, rejects invalid feature combinations:

```rust
#[cfg(all(feature = "rustls", feature = "native-tls"))]
compile_error!("features `rustls` and `native-tls` are mutually exclusive");
```

**2. Errors in procedural macros: `syn::Error`.** It holds a message and a
span (or a start and end span, with `new_spanned`). `to_compile_error()`
converts it into tokens that invoke `compile_error!` at that span, which you
return instead of the expansion. Structure macros so that errors propagate
with `?`:

```rust
#[proc_macro_derive(Builder, attributes(builder))]
pub fn derive_builder(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);   // parse errors return early
    expand_builder(input)
        .unwrap_or_else(syn::Error::into_compile_error)     // one place converts errors
        .into()
}
```

| Constructor | Points at |
| ----------- | --------- |
| `syn::Error::new(span, msg)` | One token's span, e.g. `lit.span()` |
| `syn::Error::new_spanned(&node, msg)` | The whole syntax node, first to last token |
| `meta.error(msg)` (inside `parse_nested_meta`) | The attribute key being parsed |
| `err.combine(other)` | Merges several errors; all are reported |

Reporting every problem at once saves the user a compile-fix cycle per error.
Accumulate rather than return on the first failure:

```rust
let mut errors: Option<syn::Error> = None;
for field in &fields.named {
    match builder_default(field) {          // parses #[builder(...)] on one field
        Ok(d) => { /* ... */ }
        Err(e) => match &mut errors {
            Some(all) => all.combine(e),    // keep going, collect everything
            None => errors = Some(e),
        },
    }
}
if let Some(e) = errors {
    return Err(e);
}
```

```text
error: unknown builder option; expected `default`
 --> src/main.rs:3:24
  |
3 | struct Cfg { #[builder(defualt)] a: u8, #[builder(each = "x")] b: Vec<u8> }
  |                        ^^^^^^^

error: unknown builder option; expected `default`
 --> src/main.rs:3:51
  |
3 | struct Cfg { #[builder(defualt)] a: u8, #[builder(each = "x")] b: Vec<u8> }
  |                                                   ^^^^
```

**3. Errors in generated code: spans and diagnostics attributes.** Many
mistakes surface only during type checking, after the macro has finished, for
example a field type that does not implement a required trait. By default the
generated tokens carry the call-site span, so the error points at the
`derive`. `quote_spanned!` assigns the span of the user's tokens instead:

```rust
#[proc_macro_derive(Inspect)]
pub fn derive_inspect(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    let name = &input.ident;
    let Data::Struct(data) = &input.data else {
        return syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "Inspect supports only structs")
            .to_compile_error()
            .into();
    };
    let entries = data.fields.iter().map(|f| {
        let ident = f.ident.as_ref().unwrap();
        // Tokens built here carry the span of the field's type, so a type
        // error is reported on that field instead of on `#[derive(Inspect)]`.
        quote_spanned! {f.ty.span()=>
            (::core::stringify!(#ident), ::std::format!("{:?}", &self.#ident))
        }
    });
    let (impl_g, ty_g, where_c) = input.generics.split_for_impl();
    quote! {
        impl #impl_g #name #ty_g #where_c {
            pub fn inspect(&self) -> ::std::vec::Vec<(&'static str, ::std::string::String)> {
                ::std::vec![#(#entries),*]
            }
        }
    }
    .into()
}
```

```text
error[E0277]: `Secret` doesn't implement `Debug`
 --> src/main.rs:4:27
  |
4 | struct Account { id: u32, key: Secret }
  |                           ^^^^^------
  |                           |    |
  |                           |    in this macro invocation
  |                           `Secret` cannot be formatted using `{:?}` because it doesn't implement `Debug`
```

For trait-bound errors, the trait's author can also customise the message with
`#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` (stable since Rust 1.78). This is valuable
when a missing derive is the usual cause:

```rust
#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
    message = "`{Self}` is not a registered component",
    label = "this type is missing `#[derive(Component)]`",
    note = "components must be declared with `#[derive(Component)]`"
)]
pub trait Component {}
```

```text
error[E0277]: `Position` is not a registered component
 --> src/main.rs:9:19
  |
9 | fn main() { spawn(Position); }
  |             ----- ^^^^^^^^ this type is missing `#[derive(Component)]`
  = note: components must be declared with `#[derive(Component)]`
```

**Testing error messages.** Error output is part of a macro's user
experience, so lock it down with **trybuild** UI tests. Each file in
`tests/ui/` is compiled; `compile_fail` cases must fail, with output matching
a committed `.stderr` file:

```rust
// macros/tests/ui.rs      ([dev-dependencies] trybuild = "1")
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild::TestCases::new();
    t.pass("tests/ui/hex-ok.rs");
    t.compile_fail("tests/ui/*-fail.rs");
}
```

```text
$ TRYBUILD=overwrite cargo test --test ui     # (re)generate the .stderr files
$ cargo test --test ui                         # later runs compare against them
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Never panic for user errors in a proc macro; return
>   `syn::Error::to_compile_error()` with a span on the offending tokens.
> - Funnel errors through one `expand(...) -> syn::Result<...>` function and
>   `combine` them to report every problem in one build.
> - Use `quote_spanned!` so type errors in generated code point at the user's
>   field or expression; use `#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]` to explain
>   missing trait impls.
> - `compile_error!` serves the same purpose in `macro_rules!` and for invalid
>   `cfg` combinations.
> - Test diagnostics with trybuild and committed `.stderr` snapshots.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Make the `FieldNames` derive report *every* invalid `#[field_names(...)]`
>    attribute in one compile using `syn::Error::combine`, and add trybuild
>    tests for a tuple struct, an enum and an unknown option.
> 2. Write a derive that requires every field to implement `Clone`, and use
>    `quote_spanned!` so that the error points at the non-`Clone` field.
> 3. Interview: A user reports that your derive fails with "proc-macro derive
>    panicked: called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value". What was likely
>    wrong in their code, and how would you change the macro? (Hint: which
>    syn nodes have optional parts, and what should happen instead of
>    `unwrap()`?)

<a id="133-compile-time-techniques"></a>
### 13.3 Compile-Time Techniques

Macros generate code, but much of compile-time programming in Rust needs no
macros at all. The compiler can evaluate functions, the type system can encode
rules, and build scripts can generate code from data. This section covers
these techniques, which turn runtime failures into build failures.

#### const fn and const Evaluation

Some values are known before the program runs: lookup tables, configuration
defaults, sizes derived from other constants. Computing them at startup costs
time, and computing them by hand in a spreadsheet and pasting the result
invites mistakes. **Const evaluation** lets the compiler run ordinary Rust
code during compilation and embed the result in the binary.

Chapter 2 introduced `const fn`: a function that *may* be evaluated at compile
time when called from a **const context**, and that behaves like a normal
function at run time. The const contexts are:

| Const context | Example |
| ------------- | ------- |
| `const` item initializer | `const TABLE: [u32; 256] = crc32_table();` |
| `static` item initializer | `static GREETING: &str = make_greeting();` |
| Array length / repeat count | `[0u8; kib(4)]` |
| Const generic argument | `Buffer::<{ 2 * PAGE }>` |
| Enum discriminant | `enum E { A = base() + 1 }` |
| Inline `const { ... }` block (Rust 1.79) | `const { assert!(N > 0) }` |

The compiler contains an interpreter for Rust's mid-level IR (the same engine
that powers Miri, Chapter 14). Inside a const context it runs your function
step by step, and the result becomes data in the binary:

```rust
/// CRC-32 (IEEE) lookup table, computed by the compiler.
const fn crc32_table() -> [u32; 256] {
    let mut table = [0u32; 256];
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < 256 {                       // `for` is not allowed: it uses the Iterator trait
        let mut crc = i as u32;
        let mut bit = 0;
        while bit < 8 {
            crc = if crc & 1 != 0 { (crc >> 1) ^ 0xEDB8_8320 } else { crc >> 1 };
            bit += 1;
        }
        table[i] = crc;
        i += 1;
    }
    table
}

static CRC_TABLE: [u32; 256] = crc32_table();      // baked into the binary's data

pub fn crc32(data: &[u8]) -> u32 {
    let mut crc = !0u32;
    for &b in data {                               // runtime code: `for` is fine here
        crc = CRC_TABLE[((crc ^ b as u32) & 0xFF) as usize] ^ (crc >> 8);
    }
    !crc
}
```

**A panic during const evaluation is a compile error.** This turns `const fn`
into a validation tool: parse and check values while building, and a bad value
stops the build instead of crashing in production.

```rust
/// Parses a decimal port number; panics (= compile error in const context) if invalid.
const fn parse_port(s: &str) -> u16 {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    assert!(!bytes.is_empty(), "port must not be empty");
    let mut value: u32 = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < bytes.len() {
        let d = bytes[i];
        assert!(d.is_ascii_digit(), "port must contain only digits");
        value = value * 10 + (d - b'0') as u32;
        assert!(value <= 65535, "port out of range");
        i += 1;
    }
    value as u16
}

// Optionally overridden at build time: APP_PORT=9000 cargo build
const DEFAULT_PORT: u16 = parse_port(match option_env!("APP_PORT") {
    Some(port) => port,
    None => "8080",
});
```

```text
$ APP_PORT=80a0 cargo build
error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: port must contain only digits
  --> src/main.rs:20:27
   |
20 |   const DEFAULT_PORT: u16 = parse_port(match option_env!("APP_PORT") {
   |  ___________________________^
21 | |     Some(port) => port,
22 | |     None => "8080",
23 | | });
   | |__^ evaluation of `DEFAULT_PORT` failed inside this call
```

**What is allowed** has grown with almost every release. As of Rust 1.98:

| Feature in `const fn` | Status |
| --------------------- | ------ |
| `let`, `if`, `match`, `loop`, `while` | Stable (1.46) |
| `panic!`, `assert!` with a literal message | Stable (1.57) |
| Trait bounds on generic parameters (`T: Copy`) | Stable (1.61), but the trait's methods cannot be called |
| `&mut` references and mutation through them | Stable (1.83) |
| Floating-point arithmetic | Stable (1.82) |
| Many std helpers: `u8::from_str_radix`, `str::as_bytes`, `Option::unwrap`, `Mutex::new`, `size_of` | Stable (check for "const" in the docs) |
| `for` loops, `?`, `==` on non-primitive types, closures, trait method calls | Not stable (they go through traits) |
| Heap allocation (`Vec::push`, `String::from`) | Not allowed |

Since `==` on `&str` is not const, compare bytes in a `while` loop. Since `for`
is not const, iterate with an index.

Choosing between the ways of defining "global" values:

| | `const` | `static` | `static` + `LazyLock` (Rust 1.80) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Evaluated | At compile time | At compile time | On first access, at run time |
| Memory | Inlined at each use; no fixed address | One fixed address | One fixed address |
| Can allocate (`Vec`, `HashMap`, `Regex`) | No | No | Yes |
| Shared mutable state | No: each use is a fresh copy | Via `Mutex`, atomics | Via `Mutex`, atomics |
| Use for | Numbers, small tables, validated config | Large tables (avoid copies), global state | Expensive or allocating initialization |

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::LazyLock;

// Cannot be const: HashMap allocates. Computed once, on first use.
static KEYWORDS: LazyLock<HashMap<&'static str, u8>> =
    LazyLock::new(|| [("fn", 1), ("let", 2), ("match", 3)].into_iter().collect());
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `const fn` can be called at compile time from const contexts (`const`,
>   `static`, array lengths, const generics, `const { }` blocks) and at run time
>   like any function.
> - A panic during const evaluation is a compile error, which makes `const fn`
>   a tool for build-time validation.
> - Const code cannot allocate or call trait methods; use `while` loops,
>   indexing and byte comparisons instead of iterators and `==` on strings.
> - Use `const` for small values, `static` for large tables or shared state,
>   and `LazyLock` when initialization must allocate.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `const fn is_prime(n: u64) -> bool` and use it in
>    `const _: () = assert!(is_prime(1_000_003));`. Then make the assertion fail
>    and read the error.
> 2. Write a `const fn` that builds a 256-entry table mapping each ASCII byte to
>    its uppercase version, and use it in a `to_upper` function. Compare its
>    speed against `u8::to_ascii_uppercase`.
> 3. Interview: What is the difference between `const` and `static` in Rust,
>    and why might a large lookup table be better as a `static`? (Hint: what
>    happens to a `const` at each place it is used?)

#### Type-State Programming

Many APIs have a protocol: open before reading, authenticate before querying,
submit an order before paying. A runtime check (`if !self.submitted { return
Err(...) }`) catches violations only when that code path runs. **Type-state
programming** encodes the state of a value in its **type**, so that calling
an operation in the wrong state is a compile error. Phantom types (Chapter 4)
introduced the idea; Chapter 16 covers it as a design pattern. Here the focus is
the compile-time mechanics and their cost.

Think of a vending machine whose buttons physically disappear when they do not
apply: the "dispense" button does not exist until you have paid. Each state is a
different type, and each type only *has* the methods valid in that state.

```text
Order<Draft> ──submit()──► Order<Submitted> ──pay(receipt)──► Order<Paid>
   add()                                                      receipt()
   total()                    total()                          total()
```

```rust
mod state {
    // Sealed: other crates cannot invent new states.
    mod sealed { pub trait Sealed {} }

    pub trait OrderState: sealed::Sealed {}

    pub struct Draft;                                   // zero-sized marker
    pub struct Submitted;                               // zero-sized marker
    pub struct Paid { pub receipt: String }             // a state can carry data

    impl sealed::Sealed for Draft {}
    impl sealed::Sealed for Submitted {}
    impl sealed::Sealed for Paid {}
    impl OrderState for Draft {}
    impl OrderState for Submitted {}
    impl OrderState for Paid {}
}
use state::{Draft, OrderState, Paid, Submitted};

pub struct Order<S: OrderState> {
    items: Vec<(String, u32)>,          // (product, cents)
    state: S,
}

// Available in every state.
impl<S: OrderState> Order<S> {
    pub fn total(&self) -> u32 {
        self.items.iter().map(|(_, cents)| cents).sum()
    }
}

impl Order<Draft> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Order { items: Vec::new(), state: Draft }
    }
    pub fn add(mut self, product: &str, cents: u32) -> Self {
        self.items.push((product.to_owned(), cents));
        self
    }
    pub fn submit(self) -> Order<Submitted> {        // consumes the draft
        Order { items: self.items, state: Submitted }
    }
}

impl Order<Submitted> {
    pub fn pay(self, receipt: &str) -> Order<Paid> {
        Order { items: self.items, state: Paid { receipt: receipt.to_owned() } }
    }
}

impl Order<Paid> {
    pub fn receipt(&self) -> &str {
        &self.state.receipt                          // only paid orders have one
    }
}

fn main() {
    let order = Order::new().add("book", 1_500).add("pen", 250).submit();
    // order.add("mug", 900);          // does not compile, see below
    let paid = order.pay("R-1029");
    println!("{} {}", paid.total(), paid.receipt());   // 1750 R-1029
}
```

```text
error[E0599]: no method named `add` found for struct `Order<Submitted>` in the current scope
  |
  = note: the method was found for `Order<Draft>`
```

Three properties make this work:

- **Transitions consume `self`.** `submit(self)` moves the draft, so the old
  value cannot be used afterwards. Ownership (Chapter 3) guarantees there is
  never a stale `Order<Draft>` alias of a submitted order.
- **State markers are zero-sized.** `Draft` and `Submitted` occupy no memory,
  so the type-state costs nothing at run time. You can prove it at compile
  time:

  ```rust
  const _: () = assert!(size_of::<Order<Draft>>() == size_of::<Vec<(String, u32)>>());
  ```

- **Sealing** the state trait guarantees that the set of states is closed, so
  `Order<SomethingElse>` cannot be constructed outside the module.

The limits are equally important:

| Limitation | Consequence | Workaround |
| ---------- | ----------- | ---------- |
| The state must be known at compile time | You cannot pick the state from runtime data (e.g. a database row) | Wrap the states in an enum: `enum AnyOrder { Draft(Order<Draft>), Paid(Order<Paid>), ... }` |
| Different states are different types | You cannot store mixed states in one `Vec` | The same enum wrapper, or a trait object |
| Every transition rebuilds the struct | Verbose with many fields | Keep shared data in an inner struct and move it as one field |
| Many states multiply impl blocks | API docs become harder to read | Use type-state only where misuse is costly |

> Key Takeaways
> - Type-state encodes a protocol's state as a type parameter, so invalid
>   calls do not compile; each state's `impl` block lists exactly the valid
>   operations.
> - Transitions take `self` by value, so ownership forbids using the old state.
> - Zero-sized markers make the technique free at run time; states may also
>   carry data that exists only in that state.
> - Seal the state trait, and convert to an enum at boundaries where the state
>   is only known at run time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model a TCP-like `Connection` with states `Closed`, `Open` and
>    `Authenticated`, where `send` exists only on `Authenticated` and `close`
>    works from any open state.
> 2. Add a `cancel()` method available on both `Draft` and `Submitted` orders,
>    but not on `Paid` ones, without duplicating its body. (Hint: a second
>    sealed trait implemented by the cancellable states.)
> 3. Interview: An order's state is loaded from a database at run time. How do
>    you combine that with a type-state API that requires the state to be known
>    at compile time? (Hint: where does the `match` happen, and how many times?)

#### Builder Pattern Generation

Structs with many fields, several of them optional, make constructors painful:
`Command::new("cargo", vec![], None, None, false, 30)` is unreadable and breaks
whenever a field is added. The **builder pattern** (covered as a design pattern
in Chapter 16) replaces it with named, chainable setters. Writing a builder by
hand is pure boilerplate: a mirror struct with optional fields, one setter per
field, and a `build` method. That makes it a classic target for a **derive
macro**.

There are two families of generated builder:

| | Runtime-checked builder | Type-state builder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing required field | `build()` returns `Err` | Compile error: `build` does not exist yet |
| Generated type | One builder struct | A builder generic over "set / unset" markers per field |
| Error messages | Simple | Long generic types; crates work hard to improve them |
| Crates | `derive_builder` | `typed-builder`, `bon` |

**A runtime-checked builder derive.** The macro below generates the builder
from the struct definition. `Option<T>` fields become optional,
`#[builder(default)]` fields fall back to `Default`, and everything else is
required.

```rust
// macros/src/lib.rs (proc-macro crate)
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::{format_ident, quote};
use syn::{parse_macro_input, Data, DeriveInput, Fields, GenericArgument, PathArguments, Type};

#[proc_macro_derive(Builder, attributes(builder))]
pub fn derive_builder(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    expand_builder(input)
        .unwrap_or_else(syn::Error::into_compile_error)
        .into()
}

fn expand_builder(input: DeriveInput) -> syn::Result<proc_macro2::TokenStream> {
    let name = &input.ident;
    let vis = &input.vis;
    let builder = format_ident!("{name}Builder");          // `Command` -> `CommandBuilder`

    if !input.generics.params.is_empty() {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(&input.generics, "generic structs are not supported"));
    }
    let Data::Struct(data) = &input.data else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(name, "Builder can only be derived for structs"));
    };
    let Fields::Named(fields) = &data.fields else {
        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(&data.fields, "Builder requires named fields"));
    };

    let mut storage = Vec::new();   // fields of the builder struct
    let mut setters = Vec::new();   // one method per field
    let mut inits = Vec::new();     // expressions used by build()

    for field in &fields.named {
        let ident = field.ident.as_ref().unwrap();          // named fields always have one
        let ty = &field.ty;

        if let Some(inner) = option_inner(ty) {
            // `Option<T>` field: optional, setter takes `T`.
            storage.push(quote! { #ident: #ty });
            setters.push(setter(vis, ident, inner));
            inits.push(quote! { #ident: self.#ident });
        } else {
            storage.push(quote! { #ident: ::core::option::Option<#ty> });
            setters.push(setter(vis, ident, ty));
            if builder_default(field)? {
                inits.push(quote! { #ident: self.#ident.unwrap_or_default() });
            } else {
                let msg = format!("missing required field `{ident}`");
                inits.push(quote! { #ident: self.#ident.ok_or(#msg)? });
            }
        }
    }

    let idents = fields.named.iter().map(|f| &f.ident);
    Ok(quote! {
        #vis struct #builder {
            #(#storage),*
        }

        impl #name {
            #vis fn builder() -> #builder {
                #builder { #(#idents: ::core::option::Option::None),* }
            }
        }

        impl #builder {
            #(#setters)*

            #vis fn build(self) -> ::core::result::Result<#name, &'static str> {
                ::core::result::Result::Ok(#name { #(#inits),* })
            }
        }
    })
}

fn setter(vis: &syn::Visibility, ident: &syn::Ident, ty: &Type) -> proc_macro2::TokenStream {
    quote! {
        #vis fn #ident(mut self, value: impl ::core::convert::Into<#ty>) -> Self {
            self.#ident = ::core::option::Option::Some(value.into());
            self
        }
    }
}

/// `Option<T>` -> `Some(T)`; any other type -> `None`.
fn option_inner(ty: &Type) -> Option<&Type> {
    let Type::Path(tp) = ty else { return None };
    let last = tp.path.segments.last()?;
    if tp.qself.is_some() || last.ident != "Option" {
        return None;
    }
    let PathArguments::AngleBracketed(args) = &last.arguments else { return None };
    match args.args.first()? {
        GenericArgument::Type(inner) => Some(inner),
        _ => None,
    }
}
