| `PhantomData<T>` | Tells the compiler a type acts as if it held a `T` |
| `[T; 0]` | Zero-length array, aligned like `T` |
| Closures with no captures, function items | Each is a distinct zero-sized type, so calls can be inlined |

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;
use std::mem::size_of;

struct Meters;
struct Feet;

/// A length tagged with its unit at the type level.
struct Length<Unit> {
    value: f64,
    _unit: PhantomData<Unit>,     // zero bytes, but Length<Meters> != Length<Feet>
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", size_of::<()>());                 // 0
    println!("{}", size_of::<Meters>());             // 0
    println!("{}", size_of::<Length<Meters>>());     // 8: only the f64
    println!("{}", size_of::<[u64; 0]>());           // 0
    let f = |x: i32| x + 1;
    println!("{}", size_of_val(&f));                 // 0: no captures
    let _ = Length::<Feet> { value: 1.0, _unit: PhantomData };
}
```

`PhantomData<T>` has three distinct jobs, chosen by how you write it:

| Form | Effect |
| ---- | ------ |
| `PhantomData<T>` | Acts as if the type owns a `T`: affects drop check, `Send`/`Sync` and covariance |
| `PhantomData<&'a T>` | Ties the type to lifetime `'a`, for raw-pointer wrappers that borrow |
| `PhantomData<fn() -> T>` | Mentions `T` without ownership: covariant, always `Send`/`Sync` |
| `PhantomData<*const ()>` | Makes a type `!Send` and `!Sync` |

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;

/// A borrowed view over raw memory. The PhantomData makes the borrow checker
/// enforce that the view does not outlive the slice it came from.
pub struct RawView<'a> {
    ptr: *const u8,
    len: usize,
    _borrow: PhantomData<&'a [u8]>,
}

impl<'a> RawView<'a> {
    pub fn new(data: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
        RawView { ptr: data.as_ptr(), len: data.len(), _borrow: PhantomData }
    }
    pub fn first(&self) -> Option<u8> {
        // SAFETY: ptr/len come from a live &'a [u8] (guaranteed by `'a`).
        (self.len > 0).then(|| unsafe { *self.ptr })
    }
}

fn main() {
    let v = vec![9u8, 8];
    let view = RawView::new(&v);
    println!("{:?}", view.first());
    // drop(v); println!("{:?}", view.first());   // error: `v` is still borrowed
}
```

ZSTs need care in unsafe code, because "zero bytes" breaks assumptions that
work for every other type:

- **Allocation.** `Vec<()>` never allocates; its capacity is `usize::MAX`.
  Calling `GlobalAlloc::alloc` with a zero-sized layout is UB, so generic
  collections must special-case `size_of::<T>() == 0`.
- **Pointers.** Zero-sized reads and writes are valid through any pointer, but
  a *reference* `&T` to a ZST must still be non-null and aligned. Use
  `NonNull::<T>::dangling()`, which is non-null and aligned, as the "address".
- **Pointer arithmetic.** `p.add(1)` moves by `size_of::<T>()` bytes, which is
  zero, so a loop `while p != end { p = p.add(1) }` never terminates. Slice
  iterators count elements instead of comparing addresses for ZSTs.

**Uninhabited types** are a related idea: types with *no* values, such as
`enum Void {}`, `std::convert::Infallible` and `!`. They are also zero-sized,
but a value of them can never exist, so code after one is unreachable.
`Result<T, Infallible>` has the same size as `T`, and a `match` on it needs no
`Err` arm.

> Key Takeaways
> - Types with a single value are zero-sized; they carry information in the
>   type system at no run-time cost.
> - `PhantomData` tells the compiler how a type relates to `T` or `'a`
>   (ownership, borrowing, variance, auto traits) without storing anything.
> - Generic unsafe code must handle ZSTs: never allocate them, use
>   `NonNull::dangling()` for their address, and do not iterate by comparing
>   pointers.
> - Uninhabited types (`!`, `Infallible`, empty enums) have no values at all and
>   make impossible states unrepresentable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement `Length<Unit>` with a method `to_feet(self) -> Length<Feet>`
>    available only on `Length<Meters>`. Confirm with `size_of` that the
>    wrapper costs nothing.
> 2. Write a function `fn first_raw<T>(v: &[T]) -> *const T` and test it on
>    `&[(); 3]` and an empty `&[u32]`. Which pointers do you get, and are they
>    safe to turn into references?
> 3. Interview: Your generic ring buffer works for every type except `()`, where
>    it hangs. What is the likely cause? (Hint: compute `p.add(1)` when
>    `size_of::<T>() == 0`.)

<a id="143-foreign-function-interface"></a>
### 14.3 Foreign Function Interface

The **foreign function interface (FFI)** lets Rust call code written in other
languages and be called by them, using the C calling convention as the common
language. This section covers declarations and ABIs, both directions of calls,
the tools that generate bindings, and the most common source of FFI bugs:
ownership of memory that crosses the boundary.

#### extern Blocks and ABI

Operating systems, databases, codecs and GPU drivers expose C interfaces. To
use them, Rust needs two things the C header normally provides: the
**signature** of each function, and the **ABI** (application binary
interface), meaning the low-level rules for a call: which registers hold the
arguments, who cleans up the stack, how structs are returned. Think of the ABI
as the shape of the plug and socket. If the two sides disagree, the call still
"goes through", but the arguments end up in the wrong places.

An `extern` block declares functions implemented elsewhere. Since edition 2024
the block itself must be written `unsafe extern`, because the compiler cannot
check that your declaration matches the real function:

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_double, c_int};

#[link(name = "m")]                 // link against libm (Unix); Cargo build scripts can do this too
unsafe extern "C" {
    // `safe`: we promise that calling it is safe for every input,
    // so callers need no unsafe block.
    pub safe fn cos(x: c_double) -> c_double;

    // Unmarked (or `unsafe`): calling requires unsafe, because `exp` must be
    // a valid pointer.
    pub fn frexp(x: c_double, exp: *mut c_int) -> c_double;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", cos(0.0));                      // 1, no unsafe needed

    let mut exp: c_int = 0;
    // SAFETY: `exp` is a valid, writable c_int for the duration of the call.
    let mantissa = unsafe { frexp(8.0, &mut exp) };
    println!("{mantissa} * 2^{exp}");              // 0.5 * 2^4
}
```

The string after `extern` selects the ABI:

| ABI string | Meaning |
| ---------- | ------- |
| `"C"` | The platform's C calling convention; the default choice for FFI |
| `"system"` | The OS API convention: `stdcall` on 32-bit Windows, `"C"` elsewhere; use for Win32 APIs |
| `"C-unwind"`, `"system-unwind"` | As above, but unwinding (Rust panics, C++ exceptions) may cross the call |
| `"Rust"` | The default for Rust functions; unstable and unspecified, never use across FFI |
| `"efiapi"`, `"sysv64"`, `"win64"`, `"aapcs"`, ... | Specific conventions for firmware or particular architectures |

The same strings apply to function *definitions* and function *pointer types*:

```rust
use std::ffi::c_int;

// A Rust function callable with the C ABI (for callbacks, or exported to C).
extern "C" fn double_it(x: c_int) -> c_int {
    x * 2
}

fn main() {
    let f: extern "C" fn(c_int) -> c_int = double_it;     // C-compatible fn pointer
    let maybe: Option<extern "C" fn(c_int) -> c_int> = Some(f); // nullable, same size
    println!("{}", maybe.map_or(0, |g| g(21)));          // 42
}
```

**Unwinding.** If a Rust panic tries to unwind out of an `extern "C"` function,
the process aborts (guaranteed since Rust 1.81). A C++ exception entering Rust
through an `"C"` declaration is UB. If unwinding across the boundary is
intended, both sides must use `"C-unwind"`.

**Which types may cross?** Only types whose layout C understands. The
`improper_ctypes` lint warns about the rest in `extern` declarations.

| FFI-safe | Not FFI-safe |
| -------- | ------------ |
| `i8`..`i64`, `u8`..`u64`, `isize`/`usize`, `f32`, `f64` | `i128`/`u128` (no stable C equivalent on all targets) |
| `c_int`, `c_long`, `c_char`, ... from `std::ffi` | `char` (a Unicode scalar, not a C `char`) |
| `bool` (C `_Bool`) | `&str`, `String`, `&[T]`, `Vec<T>` |
| `*const T`, `*mut T` | Trait objects `&dyn Trait`, `Box<dyn Trait>` |
| `&T`, `&mut T`, `Box<T>` (as non-null pointers, `T: Sized`) | Tuples, ordinary structs and enums (unspecified layout) |
| `#[repr(C)]` structs, unions and enums; `#[repr(transparent)]` wrappers | `Option<T>` in general |
| `Option<&T>`, `Option<Box<T>>`, `Option<NonNull<T>>`, `Option<extern "C" fn>` | Zero-sized types other than in `repr(C)` structs |

C's integer types differ in size by platform (`long` is 32 bits on Windows and
64 bits on Linux), so use the `std::ffi` aliases (`c_long`, `c_ulong`), not a
fixed Rust type. C `size_t` corresponds to `usize` on all mainstream targets.

C variadic functions such as `printf` can be declared with `...`. Only types
that survive C's default argument promotions may be passed (`c_int`, `c_long`,
`c_double`, pointers; not `f32` or `i8`):

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, c_int};

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn printf(format: *const c_char, ...) -> c_int;
}

fn main() {
    // SAFETY: the format string is NUL-terminated and matches the arguments.
    unsafe { printf(c"%d + %d = %d\n".as_ptr(), 2, 3, 2 + 3) };
}
```

`c"..."` is a C string literal (Rust 1.77): a `&'static CStr` with the
trailing NUL included.

> Key Takeaways
> - `unsafe extern "C" { ... }` declares foreign functions; the declaration is
>   a promise, so it must match the real signature exactly.
> - Mark items in the block `safe fn` only when every possible input is safe;
>   otherwise calls require `unsafe`.
> - `"C"` is the ABI for FFI; `"system"` for Windows APIs; `"C-unwind"` when
>   panics or exceptions may cross the boundary, which otherwise aborts or is
>   UB.
> - Only FFI-safe types may cross: C integer aliases, raw pointers, `repr(C)`
>   types and nullable-pointer `Option`s; never `String`, slices or trait
>   objects.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Declare and call `abs`, `strtol` and `getenv` from the C library.
>    Which can be `safe fn`, and which must stay unsafe? Justify each choice.
> 2. Declare a function that takes `&str` in an `extern "C"` block and read the
>    `improper_ctypes` warning. Change the declaration to an FFI-safe pointer
>    and length pair.
> 3. Interview: A C function is declared in Rust as returning `i32`, but the C
>    code returns `long`. Tests pass on Linux CI but the program misbehaves on
>    Windows. Explain. (Hint: compare `long` across platforms and think about
>    which half of a register holds the value.)

#### Calling C from Rust

A raw `extern` declaration is unsafe to use and awkward: raw pointers, C
strings, error codes, out-parameters. The standard practice is to write a
**safe wrapper** for each foreign function, so `unsafe` appears in one place
and the rest of the program uses ordinary Rust types. Every wrapper does the
same job: convert Rust types to C types, uphold the C function's
preconditions, call it, and convert the results back, turning error codes into
`Result`.

Suppose a small C library:

```c
// csrc/stats.c
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

// Mean of `len` values. Sets *ok to 0 (and returns 0.0) when len == 0.
double stats_mean(const double *values, size_t len, int *ok) {
    if (len == 0) { *ok = 0; return 0.0; }
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += values[i];
    *ok = 1;
    return sum / (double)len;
}

// Writes "Hello, <name>!" into buf (capacity cap, including the NUL).
// Returns the length the full message needs, excluding the NUL, like snprintf.
size_t stats_greet(const char *name, char *buf, size_t cap) {
    int n = snprintf(buf, cap, "Hello, %s!", name);
    return n < 0 ? 0 : (size_t)n;
}
```

Cargo compiles and links it through a build script and the `cc` crate
(Chapter 8 covers build scripts):

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[build-dependencies]
cc = "1"
```

```rust
// build.rs
fn main() {
    cc::Build::new().file("csrc/stats.c").compile("stats");   // builds libstats.a, links it
    println!("cargo::rerun-if-changed=csrc/stats.c");
}
```

The Rust side: raw declarations kept private, safe wrappers public.

```rust
// src/lib.rs
use std::ffi::{c_char, c_int, CStr, CString, NulError};

mod ffi {
    use super::*;
    unsafe extern "C" {
        pub fn stats_mean(values: *const f64, len: usize, ok: *mut c_int) -> f64;
        pub fn stats_greet(name: *const c_char, buf: *mut c_char, cap: usize) -> usize;
    }
}

/// Arithmetic mean, or `None` for an empty slice.
pub fn mean(values: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> {
    let mut ok: c_int = 0;
    // SAFETY: the pointer and length describe a valid slice (an empty slice
    // gives a dangling but non-null pointer, which C never reads since len
    // is 0); `ok` is a valid out-parameter.
    let m = unsafe { ffi::stats_mean(values.as_ptr(), values.len(), &mut ok) };
    (ok != 0).then_some(m)
}

/// Builds a greeting through the C library.
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> Result<String, NulError> {
    let name = CString::new(name)?;          // appends NUL; fails on interior NUL bytes
    let mut buf = vec![0u8; 8];              // deliberately small to exercise the retry
    loop {
        // SAFETY: `name` is NUL-terminated and alive; `buf` has `buf.len()`
        // writable bytes.
        let needed = unsafe {
            ffi::stats_greet(name.as_ptr(), buf.as_mut_ptr().cast(), buf.len())
        };
        if needed < buf.len() {
            let text = CStr::from_bytes_until_nul(&buf).expect("C wrote a NUL");
            return Ok(text.to_string_lossy().into_owned());
        }
        buf.resize(needed + 1, 0);           // grow and try again
    }
}
```

```rust
// src/main.rs
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", ffi_demo::mean(&[1.0, 2.0, 6.0]));   // Some(3.0)
    println!("{:?}", ffi_demo::mean(&[]));                // None
    println!("{:?}", ffi_demo::greet("Ferris"));          // Ok("Hello, Ferris!")
    println!("{:?}", ffi_demo::greet("a\0b").is_err());   // true
}
```

**Strings** are the most frequent conversion. C strings are NUL-terminated
byte arrays with no encoding guarantee; Rust strings are UTF-8 with a length.

| Type | Owned or borrowed | Use |
| ---- | ----------------- | --- |
| `&str` / `String` | Borrowed / owned | Rust text: UTF-8, length-prefixed, may contain `\0` |
| `&CStr` | Borrowed | A C string you received: `CStr::from_ptr(p)`, then `to_str()` or `to_string_lossy()` |
| `CString` | Owned | A C string you send: `CString::new(s)?`, then `.as_ptr()` |
| `c"..."` | `&'static CStr` | Literal C strings |
| `&OsStr` / `OsString` | Borrowed / owned | Platform strings (file names, environment) |

**Callbacks.** Many C APIs take function pointers. Pass an `extern "C" fn`;
the classic example is `qsort`:

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_int, c_void};

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn qsort(
        base: *mut c_void,
        count: usize,
        size: usize,
        compare: unsafe extern "C" fn(*const c_void, *const c_void) -> c_int,
    );
}

unsafe extern "C" fn compare_i32(a: *const c_void, b: *const c_void) -> c_int {
    // SAFETY: qsort passes pointers to elements of our i32 array.
    let (a, b) = unsafe { (*a.cast::<i32>(), *b.cast::<i32>()) };
    a.cmp(&b) as c_int                       // Ordering is -1, 0 or 1
}

fn main() {
    let mut v = [5, 1, 4, 2, 3];
    // SAFETY: base/count/size describe `v`; the comparator matches the element type.
    unsafe {
        qsort(v.as_mut_ptr().cast(), v.len(), size_of::<i32>(), compare_i32);
    }
    println!("{v:?}");                       // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
}
```

To pass a closure (with captured state) instead of a plain function, C APIs
usually take a `void *user_data` argument next to the callback. That pattern,
the *trampoline*, is shown in Ownership Across FFI Boundaries.

**Errors.** C reports failure through return codes, null pointers, out
parameters or `errno`. Turn each into a `Result` inside the wrapper. For
`errno`-style APIs, read it immediately after the call with
`std::io::Error::last_os_error()`, before anything else can overwrite it.

> Key Takeaways
> - Keep raw `extern` declarations private and expose safe wrappers that
>   convert types, check preconditions and map errors to `Result`.
> - Use the `cc` crate in `build.rs` to compile C sources into the crate.
> - Convert strings with `CString` (outgoing) and `CStr` (incoming); a Rust
>   `&str` is not NUL-terminated.
> - Pass `extern "C" fn` items as callbacks; closures need a trampoline and a
>   user-data pointer.
> - Read `errno` with `io::Error::last_os_error()` immediately after the call.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `int stats_minmax(const double *v, size_t len, double *min, double
>    *max)` to the C library (returning -1 for an empty input) and write a safe
>    `minmax(&[f64]) -> Option<(f64, f64)>` wrapper.
> 2. Wrap the C function `getenv` as `fn env_var(name: &str) -> Option<String>`.
>    Consider interior NULs, null returns and non-UTF-8 values. Why is
>    `getenv` not thread-safe, and should your wrapper be `unsafe` because of
>    it?
> 3. Interview: Why should the raw FFI declarations be private and the safe
>    wrappers public, rather than exposing both? (Hint: think about where the
>    preconditions are checked, and how many places a reviewer must look at.)

#### Exposing Rust to C

The other direction is just as common: a Rust library used from a C, C++,
Python or Swift program. Rust can produce a C-compatible library if three
things line up: functions use the **C ABI**, their **symbol names** are not
mangled, and the crate is built as a **C-compatible library**.

```text
 Rust crate                          C program
 ──────────                          ─────────
 #[unsafe(no_mangle)]                counter.h  (declarations)
 pub extern "C" fn counter_new()     main.c     calls counter_new()
         │                                     │
         ▼  crate-type = cdylib/staticlib      ▼  cc main.c -lcounter
 libcounter.so / libcounter.a  ─────── linker ──────►  executable
```

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "counter"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "staticlib", "rlib"]   # .so/.dll, .a/.lib, and Rust tests
```

Rust's default symbol names are mangled (`_ZN7counter11counter_new17h...E`)
so that generic and overloaded items get unique names. `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`
keeps the plain name. It is an unsafe attribute since edition 2024 because two
symbols with the same name in one program is UB.

A complete library using the **opaque handle** pattern, the standard way to
give C an object it can hold but not inspect:

```rust
// src/lib.rs
use std::ffi::{c_char, c_int, CStr};
use std::panic::catch_unwind;

/// Internal Rust type. Not repr(C): C only ever sees a pointer to it.
pub struct Counter {
    count: u64,
    step: u64,
}

/// Creates a counter. Free it with `counter_free`.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn counter_new(step: u64) -> *mut Counter {
    Box::into_raw(Box::new(Counter { count: 0, step }))  // ownership moves to the caller
}

/// Adds `step` and returns the new value, or 0 if `counter` is null.
///
/// # Safety
/// `counter` must be null or a live pointer from `counter_new`, not used
/// concurrently from another thread.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn counter_increment(counter: *mut Counter) -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: caller guarantees a valid, exclusive pointer or null.
    let Some(c) = (unsafe { counter.as_mut() }) else { return 0 };
    c.count += c.step;
    c.count
}

/// Parses `text` as the new step. Returns 0 on success, -1 on bad input,
/// -2 on an internal error (a caught panic).
///
/// # Safety
/// `counter` as above; `text` must be a NUL-terminated string.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn counter_set_step(counter: *mut Counter, text: *const c_char) -> c_int {
    if counter.is_null() || text.is_null() {
        return -1;
    }
    let result = catch_unwind(|| {
        // SAFETY: both pointers were checked for null; validity is the caller's duty.
        let text = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(text) };
        let c = unsafe { &mut *counter };
        match text.to_str().ok().and_then(|s| s.trim().parse().ok()) {
            Some(step) => { c.step = step; 0 }
            None => -1,
        }
    });
    result.unwrap_or(-2)                      // never let a panic reach C
}

/// Frees a counter. Passing null is allowed and does nothing.
///
/// # Safety
/// `counter` must be null or come from `counter_new`, and not be used afterwards.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn counter_free(counter: *mut Counter) {
    if !counter.is_null() {
        // SAFETY: the pointer came from Box::into_raw and is freed exactly once.
        drop(unsafe { Box::from_raw(counter) });
    }
}
```

The matching C header and program (the cbindgen topic below shows how to
generate the header instead of writing it):

```c
/* counter.h */
#include <stdint.h>
typedef struct Counter Counter;              /* opaque: C never sees the fields */
Counter *counter_new(uint64_t step);
uint64_t counter_increment(Counter *counter);
int counter_set_step(Counter *counter, const char *text);
void counter_free(Counter *counter);

/* main.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include "counter.h"
int main(void) {
    Counter *c = counter_new(2);
    counter_increment(c);
    counter_set_step(c, "10");
    printf("%llu\n", (unsigned long long)counter_increment(c));   /* 12 */
    counter_free(c);
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
cargo build --release
# Dynamic: link against target/release/libcounter.so
cc main.c -Itarget/release -Ltarget/release -lcounter -o main
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=target/release ./main

# Static: libcounter.a needs the system libraries Rust's std uses
cargo rustc --release --lib -- --print native-static-libs   # prints the -l flags below
cc main.c target/release/libcounter.a -lgcc_s -lutil -lrt -lpthread -lm -ldl -lc -o main
```

Design rules for a C-facing API:

| Rule | Reason |
| ---- | ------ |
| Accept and check null pointers | C callers pass null by mistake; failing cleanly is cheap |
| Return error codes (or a status struct), never panic | Unwinding out of `extern "C"` aborts the whole process |
| Give every allocating function a matching `*_free` | C must not free Rust memory with `free()` (next topics) |
| Keep Rust types opaque; expose `repr(C)` only for plain data | The default layout is not stable and may hold non-FFI-safe fields |
| Mark functions taking raw pointers `unsafe extern "C"` with `# Safety` docs | Documents the contract for Rust callers; C ignores it |
| Prefix symbol names (`counter_`) | C has a single global namespace |

`catch_unwind` only catches unwinding panics. If the crate is built with
`panic = "abort"`, panics abort before reaching it. Either way, the program
cannot continue after a panic escapes into C, so catching at every exported
function is the robust choice.

> Key Takeaways
> - Export with `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn` and build with
>   `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` or `["staticlib"]`.
> - Hand objects to C as opaque pointers from `Box::into_raw`, and provide a
>   `*_free` function that calls `Box::from_raw` exactly once.
> - Check for null, convert C strings with `CStr`, and return error codes.
> - Never let a panic reach C: wrap bodies in `catch_unwind`.
> - Linking a static Rust library needs the extra system libraries reported by
>   `--print native-static-libs`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the `counter` library as both `cdylib` and `staticlib`, and link the
>    C program against each. Inspect the exported symbols with `nm -D
>    libcounter.so | grep counter_`, then remove `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` from one
>    function and inspect again.
> 2. Add `counter_label(const Counter *c) -> const char *` returning a label
>    that stays valid until the next call that modifies the counter. Where must
>    the string live, and what does the header comment need to say?
> 3. Interview: An exported Rust function calls `.unwrap()` on user input, and
>    the C application crashes with an abort instead of an error. Why does it
>    abort rather than unwind, and how would you design the API instead? (Hint:
>    look at what happens to a panic at an `extern "C"` boundary.)

#### Binding Generation with bindgen

Writing `extern` declarations by hand is fine for three functions and
error-prone for three hundred: every struct field, `#define` constant and
platform-specific `typedef` must be copied exactly. **bindgen** reads C (and
some C++) headers with libclang and generates the Rust declarations
automatically, so the header stays the single source of truth.

```text
wrapper.h ──► bindgen (libclang parses it) ──► bindings.rs in OUT_DIR
                                                    │ include!
                                                    ▼
                                               zlib-sys crate (raw, unsafe)
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
                                               zlib crate (safe wrappers)
```

Usually bindgen runs in `build.rs`, so bindings always match the headers
installed on the build machine:

```c
/* wrapper.h: list every header you want bindings for */
#include <zlib.h>
```

```toml
# Cargo.toml of the -sys crate
[package]
name = "zlib-sys"
links = "z"                 # declares the native library; only one crate may link it

[build-dependencies]
bindgen = "0.72"
```

```rust
// build.rs
use std::{env, path::PathBuf};

fn main() {
    println!("cargo::rustc-link-lib=z");             // link libz
    println!("cargo::rerun-if-changed=wrapper.h");

    let bindings = bindgen::Builder::default()
        .header("wrapper.h")
        .allowlist_function("zlibVersion|compress2?|uncompress|compressBound")
        .allowlist_var("Z_.*")                       // constants such as Z_OK
        .rust_edition(bindgen::RustEdition::Edition2024)   // emit `unsafe extern`
        .parse_callbacks(Box::new(bindgen::CargoCallbacks::new())) // rerun when headers change
        .generate()
        .expect("unable to generate bindings");

    let out = PathBuf::from(env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap());
    bindings.write_to_file(out.join("bindings.rs")).expect("cannot write bindings");
}
```

```rust
// src/lib.rs of zlib-sys
#![allow(non_upper_case_globals, non_camel_case_types, non_snake_case)]
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/bindings.rs"));
```

What the generated file looks like (abridged):

```rust
pub const Z_OK: u32 = 0;
pub const Z_BUF_ERROR: i32 = -5;
pub type Bytef = ::std::os::raw::c_uchar;
pub type uLong = ::std::os::raw::c_ulong;
pub type uLongf = uLong;
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub fn zlibVersion() -> *const ::std::os::raw::c_char;
    pub fn compressBound(sourceLen: uLong) -> uLong;
    pub fn compress(
        dest: *mut Bytef,
        destLen: *mut uLongf,
        source: *const Bytef,
        sourceLen: uLong,
    ) -> ::std::os::raw::c_int;
}
```

A safe crate then wraps the raw one, exactly as in Calling C from Rust:

```rust
use std::ffi::CStr;

pub fn version() -> &'static str {
    // SAFETY: zlibVersion returns a pointer to a static NUL-terminated string.
    let v = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(zlib_sys::zlibVersion()) };
    v.to_str().expect("zlib version is ASCII")
}

pub fn compress(input: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, i32> {
    // SAFETY: compressBound is a pure computation with no preconditions.
    let mut len = unsafe { zlib_sys::compressBound(input.len() as _) };  // worst-case size
    let mut out = vec![0u8; len as usize];
    // SAFETY: `out` has `len` writable bytes; `input` is a valid slice.
    let rc = unsafe {
        zlib_sys::compress(out.as_mut_ptr(), &mut len, input.as_ptr(), input.len() as _)
    };
    if rc != zlib_sys::Z_OK as i32 {
        return Err(rc);
    }
    out.truncate(len as usize);              // C told us how many bytes it wrote
    Ok(out)
}
```

The **`-sys` crate convention**: `foo-sys` contains only the raw bindings
and the build logic that finds or builds `libfoo` (often with `pkg-config` or
by compiling a vendored copy with `cc`). A separate `foo` crate provides the
safe API. The `links = "foo"` key ensures only one version of the native
library is linked into a program, and lets dependent crates read metadata the
build script exports.

Useful builder options:

| Option | Effect |
| ------ | ------ |
| `allowlist_function`/`_type`/`_var` | Generate only matching items (and what they depend on); keeps output small |
| `blocklist_item` | Skip an item, for example to define it by hand |
| `opaque_type("T")` | Emit `T` as an array of bytes of the right size, hiding its fields |
| `default_enum_style(EnumVariation::...)` | C enums as constants (default), newtypes, or Rust enums |
| `derive_default(true)`, `derive_debug(true)` | Add derives to generated structs |
| `layout_tests(true)` (default) | Emit compile-time checks that sizes and offsets match what clang computed |

Generating C enums as **Rust enums** (`EnumVariation::Rust`) is a trap: if the C
library ever returns a value that is not one of the variants (a newer library
version, a bit flag combination), the Rust program has UB. The default
constants, or `NewType`, are safe for any value.

bindgen can also be used from the command line, to generate a file once and
commit it (no libclang needed for downstream builds):

```bash
cargo install bindgen-cli
bindgen wrapper.h --allowlist-function 'compress.*' -o src/bindings.rs
```

> Key Takeaways
> - bindgen generates Rust declarations from C headers with libclang, keeping
>   the header the source of truth.
> - Run it from `build.rs` writing into `OUT_DIR`, or once from the CLI and
>   commit the output; use allowlists to limit what is generated.
> - Follow the `-sys` convention: raw bindings and linking in `foo-sys`, safe
>   wrappers in `foo`, and `links = "foo"` in the manifest.
> - Keep the generated layout tests, and do not generate C enums as Rust enums
>   unless the C side truly cannot produce other values.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate bindings for `<time.h>` (allowlist `time`, `localtime_r`,
>    `strftime` and `struct tm`) and write a safe `fn now_formatted(fmt: &str)
>    -> String`.
> 2. Write a header with `enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE };` and a function
>    returning it. Generate bindings with the default style, `NewType` and
>    `Rust`, and compare. Which one can be used safely if the C function
>    returns 7?
> 3. Interview: Why does a `-sys` crate set `links = "..."` in `Cargo.toml`, and
>    what goes wrong if two crates in a dependency graph each bundle and link
>    their own copy of the same C library? (Hint: think about duplicate symbols
>    and global state in the C library.)

#### cbindgen for Headers

For the opposite direction, a Rust library used from C, the C side needs a
header. Writing it by hand duplicates every signature, and the header silently
drifts from the code. **cbindgen** reads your Rust source and generates the
header from the exported items: `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` functions,
and `#[repr(C)]`/`#[repr(transparent)]` types and constants they use. Types
that are not `repr(C)` become opaque forward declarations, which is exactly
the opaque handle pattern.

Configuration lives in `cbindgen.toml` at the crate root:

```toml
# cbindgen.toml
language = "C"                       # or "C++" (also "Cython")
include_guard = "COUNTER_H"
autogen_warning = "/* Generated by cbindgen. Do not edit by hand. */"
documentation = true                 # copy /// doc comments into the header
cpp_compat = true                    # wrap declarations in extern "C" for C++ users

[export]
prefix = ""                          # optional prefix for every exported type name
```

Running it from the command line:

```bash
cargo install cbindgen
cbindgen --config cbindgen.toml --crate counter --output include/counter.h
```

Or from `build.rs`, so the header is regenerated on every build:

```rust
// build.rs (with cbindgen in [build-dependencies])
fn main() {
    let crate_dir = std::env::var("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR").unwrap();
    let config = cbindgen::Config::from_file("cbindgen.toml").unwrap();
    cbindgen::generate_with_config(&crate_dir, config)
        .expect("unable to generate header")
        .write_to_file("include/counter.h");
    println!("cargo::rerun-if-changed=src/lib.rs");
}
```

For the `counter` library from Exposing Rust to C, plus a `repr(C)` struct, the
generated header looks like this (abridged):

```rust
#[repr(C)]
pub struct Stats {
    pub count: u64,
    pub step: u64,
}

/// Returns a snapshot of the counter's state.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn counter_stats(counter: *const Counter) -> Stats { /* ... */ }
```

```c
/* Generated by cbindgen. Do not edit by hand. */
#ifndef COUNTER_H
#define COUNTER_H

#include <stdarg.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct Counter Counter;          /* not repr(C): opaque */

typedef struct Stats {                   /* repr(C): fields exposed */
  uint64_t count;
  uint64_t step;
} Stats;

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

/**
 * Creates a counter. Free it with `counter_free`.
 */
Counter *counter_new(uint64_t step);

uint64_t counter_increment(Counter *counter);

int counter_set_step(Counter *counter, const char *text);

/**
 * Returns a snapshot of the counter's state.
 */
Stats counter_stats(const Counter *counter);

void counter_free(Counter *counter);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

#endif /* COUNTER_H */
```

How Rust types map:

| Rust | Generated C |
| ---- | ----------- |
| `u64`, `i32`, `bool`, `f64` | `uint64_t`, `int32_t`, `bool`, `double` |
| `*const T` / `*mut T` | `const T *` / `T *` |
| `Option<extern "C" fn(i32)>` | `void (*)(int32_t)` (nullable) |
| `#[repr(C)] struct` | `typedef struct { ... }` with fields |
| `#[repr(C)] enum` / `#[repr(u8)] enum` | `enum` (or `typedef uint8_t` plus constants) |
| Non-`repr(C)` struct | `typedef struct X X;` (opaque) |
| `pub const MAX: u32 = 8;` | `#define MAX 8` |

cbindgen generates C declarations; it does not make anything safe. For richer
interop, other tools generate both sides:

| Tool | Target | Approach |
| ---- | ------ | -------- |
| cbindgen | C, C++ | Header from Rust's `extern "C"` items |
| cxx | C++ | Declare a bridge module once; generates safe Rust and C++ glue, supports `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr`, `Vec` |
| PyO3 / maturin | Python | Native Python modules from annotated Rust |
| UniFFI | Kotlin, Swift, Python | Bindings from an interface definition, used for mobile apps |
| wasm-bindgen | JavaScript | WebAssembly interop (Chapter 16) |

> Key Takeaways
> - cbindgen generates a C or C++ header from `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"`
>   functions and `repr(C)` types, so the header cannot drift from the code.
> - Non-`repr(C)` types become opaque `typedef struct X X;` declarations.
> - Configure with `cbindgen.toml`; run from the CLI or from `build.rs`.
> - For C++ with standard library types, prefer `cxx`; for Python, Kotlin or
>   Swift, use PyO3 or UniFFI.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate the header for the `counter` crate with cbindgen, then add a
>    `#[repr(C)] pub enum CounterError { Ok, Null, BadInput, Panic }` and change
>    `counter_set_step` to return it. Inspect how the enum appears in C.
> 2. Configure cbindgen to emit C++ (`language = "C++"`) and compile a small
>    C++ program against the result.
> 3. Interview: Your team commits the generated header to the repository. How
>    would you make CI fail when someone changes an exported function but
>    forgets to regenerate the header? (Hint: generate it in CI and compare.)

#### Ownership Across FFI Boundaries

Rust's ownership rules end at the boundary. The C compiler knows nothing about
`Drop`, lifetimes or borrows, so every pointer that crosses must come with an
answer to two questions: **who frees it**, and **how long is it valid**?
Getting either wrong produces the classic C bugs (leaks, double frees,
use-after-free) in a Rust program. A good mental model is a library loan:
either the book is lent (borrowed for the call, returned when the call ends),
or ownership is transferred with a receipt saying who must eventually dispose
of it.

**Rule 1: memory goes back to the allocator that produced it.** Rust's
allocator and C's `malloc` may be different (and are, if you set a custom
`#[global_allocator]`). Freeing a `Box` with C `free()`, or a `malloc`ed
buffer with `Box::from_raw`, is UB.

```text
 allocated by                      freed by
 ────────────                      ────────
 Box::into_raw / CString::into_raw ──► Rust: Box::from_raw / CString::from_raw
                                        (exported as foo_free for C to call)
 C malloc / library foo_create      ──► C: free / foo_destroy
                                        (called from a Rust Drop impl)
```

The standard patterns, by direction:

| Situation | Owned (transfer) | Borrowed (for the call only) |
| --------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Rust object to C | `Box::into_raw`; C calls `foo_free`, which does `Box::from_raw` | `&x as *const T` or `&raw const x` |
| Rust string to C | `CString::into_raw`; C calls `string_free`, which does `CString::from_raw` | Keep the `CString` alive, pass `.as_ptr()` |
| Rust buffer to C | `Box<[T]>` via `Box::into_raw`, pass pointer and length; free reconstructs it | `slice.as_ptr()`, `slice.len()` |
| C object to Rust | Wrap the pointer in a type whose `Drop` calls the C destructor | `&*ptr` or `CStr::from_ptr`, copy out before the call returns if needed |

Returning a string to C, with its matching free function:

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, CString};

/// Returns a newly allocated greeting. Free it with `greeting_free`.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn greeting_new() -> *mut c_char {
    CString::new("hello from Rust").unwrap().into_raw()   // C now owns it
}

/// # Safety
/// `s` must be null or a pointer returned by `greeting_new`, freed only once.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn greeting_free(s: *mut c_char) {
    if !s.is_null() {
        // SAFETY: reconstitutes the CString created in greeting_new.
        drop(unsafe { CString::from_raw(s) });
    }
}
```

**Rule 2: a borrowed pointer is valid only as long as its owner.** The
compiler cannot track a lifetime through a raw pointer. The best-known
instance:

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, CString};

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn puts(s: *const c_char) -> i32;
}

fn main() {
    // BUG: the CString is a temporary, dropped at the end of this statement,
    // so `p` dangles before it is used.
    let p = CString::new("dangling").unwrap().as_ptr();
    let _ = p;                                // passing `p` to C here would be UB

    // FIX: bind the owner to a variable that outlives the call.
    let owned = CString::new("fine").unwrap();
    unsafe { puts(owned.as_ptr()) };
}
```

**Wrapping a C-owned resource.** When C gives you an object with a `create` /
`destroy` pair, wrap it in a Rust type with a `Drop` implementation, and use
lifetimes to express rules the C documentation states in prose. Suppose a C
library with this API (documentation: "the string returned by `db_get` is
valid until the next call on the same handle"):

```c
typedef struct db db;
db *db_open(const char *path);                    /* NULL on failure */
const char *db_get(db *handle, const char *key);  /* NULL if absent */
void db_close(db *handle);
```

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_char, CStr, CString};
use std::marker::{PhantomData, PhantomPinned};
use std::ptr::NonNull;

/// Opaque C type: zero-sized, cannot be constructed, !Send, !Sync, !Unpin.
#[repr(C)]
pub struct RawDb {
    _private: [u8; 0],
    _marker: PhantomData<(*mut u8, PhantomPinned)>,
}

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn db_open(path: *const c_char) -> *mut RawDb;
    fn db_get(handle: *mut RawDb, key: *const c_char) -> *const c_char;
    fn db_close(handle: *mut RawDb);
}

pub struct Db {
    raw: NonNull<RawDb>,          // INVARIANT: a live handle from db_open
}

impl Db {
    pub fn open(path: &str) -> Option<Db> {
        let path = CString::new(path).ok()?;
        // SAFETY: `path` is a valid C string for the duration of the call.
        let raw = unsafe { db_open(path.as_ptr()) };
        NonNull::new(raw).map(|raw| Db { raw })     // null means failure
    }

    /// `&mut self` in the signature encodes "valid until the next call":
    /// while the returned &CStr is alive, no other method can be called.
    pub fn get(&mut self, key: &CStr) -> Option<&CStr> {
        // SAFETY: the handle is live (invariant) and `key` is NUL-terminated.
        let value = unsafe { db_get(self.raw.as_ptr(), key.as_ptr()) };
        // SAFETY: non-null results point to a C string valid until the next
        // call on this handle, which the borrow of `self` rules out.
        (!value.is_null()).then(|| unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(value) })
    }
}

impl Drop for Db {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // SAFETY: the handle is live and is closed exactly once, here.
        unsafe { db_close(self.raw.as_ptr()) };
    }
}
```

The `RawDb` definition is the recommended way to declare an opaque C type. A
`[u8; 0]` field makes it impossible to construct in Rust, and the
`PhantomData` removes `Send`, `Sync` and `Unpin`, which is the right default
for an unknown C object. Add `unsafe impl Send for Db {}` only if the C
documentation says handles may move between threads.

**Callbacks with state (trampolines).** C callbacks receive a `void *user_data`
argument chosen by the caller. To pass a Rust closure, give C a pointer to the
closure as user data, and a generic `extern "C"` function that casts it back
and calls it:

```c
/* C API: calls cb(value, user_data) for every stored value */
void for_each_value(void (*cb)(int value, void *user_data), void *user_data);
```

```rust
use std::ffi::{c_int, c_void};

unsafe extern "C" {
    fn for_each_value(
        cb: unsafe extern "C" fn(value: c_int, user_data: *mut c_void),
        user_data: *mut c_void,
    );
}

pub fn for_each<F: FnMut(i32)>(mut f: F) {
    // One trampoline is instantiated per closure type F.
    unsafe extern "C" fn trampoline<F: FnMut(i32)>(value: c_int, user_data: *mut c_void) {
        // SAFETY: user_data is the `&mut F` passed below, alive for the call.
        let f = unsafe { &mut *user_data.cast::<F>() };
        f(value);                               // a panic here aborts (extern "C")
    }

    // SAFETY: the closure lives on this stack frame until for_each_value
    // returns, and C does not keep the pointer after returning.
    unsafe { for_each_value(trampoline::<F>, (&raw mut f).cast()) };
}

// Usage: closures can capture and mutate local state.
// let mut total = 0;
// for_each(|v| total += v);
```

If C stores the callback and calls it *later* (an event loop, a signal
handler), the closure must outlive the registration: box it, pass
`Box::into_raw`, and free it with `Box::from_raw` when the callback is
unregistered.

Ownership checklist for every pointer in an FFI signature:

| Question | Where the answer goes |
| -------- | --------------------- |
| Who allocates, and who frees? | Function docs, and a `*_free` function or a `Drop` impl |
| How long is a borrowed pointer valid? | Rust lifetimes in the safe wrapper (`&self`, `&mut self`, `PhantomData<&'a T>`) |
| May it be null? | `Option<NonNull<T>>`, or a null check |
| May it be used from another thread? | `Send`/`Sync` impls (or their absence) on the wrapper |
| Does C keep the pointer after returning? | Box and leak until an explicit unregister call |

> Key Takeaways
> - Every pointer that crosses FFI needs a documented owner and a documented
>   validity period.
> - Free memory with the allocator that allocated it: export `*_free` functions
>   for Rust allocations, call the C destructor from `Drop` for C allocations.
> - Keep owners (such as `CString`) alive while C uses their pointers;
>   `CString::new(..).unwrap().as_ptr()` dangles immediately.
> - Encode C's lifetime rules as Rust lifetimes in safe wrappers (for example
>   `&mut self` for "valid until the next call").
> - Pass closures to C with a generic trampoline and a user-data pointer; box
>   them if C keeps the callback.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the `db` C library (an in-memory key-value array is enough),
>    compile it with `cc`, and write tests showing that the `Db` wrapper
>    rejects (at compile time) holding a value across a second `get` call.
> 2. Add `pub fn values(&self) -> Vec<i32>` built on `for_each`, then change the
>    C library so that it stores the callback for later use. What breaks in the
>    Rust wrapper, and how do you fix it?
> 3. Interview: A Rust library returns `Vec<u8>` data to C by calling
>    `as_mut_ptr()` and `mem::forget`, and C later calls `free()` on it. It
>    works in testing. What is wrong, and what should the API look like?
>    (Hint: think about allocators, capacity, and who knows the length.)

<a id="144-verification-tools"></a>
### 14.4 Verification Tools

Undefined behavior often produces no visible symptom until a different
compiler version, optimization level or CPU exposes it, so ordinary tests are
not enough to show that unsafe code is correct. This section covers the tools
that detect UB at run time, the aliasing models they check against, and the
review and documentation practices that keep unsafe code auditable.

#### Miri Interpreter

A test that passes proves the code produced the right output *this time*, not
that it was free of UB. Reading one byte past an allocation usually returns
some harmless garbage; a use-after-free usually finds the old value still
there. **Miri** closes that gap. It is an interpreter for Rust's mid-level
intermediate representation (MIR) that executes your program while tracking,
for every byte, whether it is allocated, initialized, which pointer may access
it, and with what permissions. It is like running the program with a strict
referee watching every memory access, instead of only checking the final
score.

```bash
rustup +nightly component add miri      # Miri needs a nightly toolchain
cargo +nightly miri test                # run the test suite under Miri
cargo +nightly miri run                 # run the binary under Miri
cargo +nightly miri test parser::       # filter tests as usual
```

A use-after-free that passes ordinary tests:

```rust
fn main() {
    let p: *const i32 = {
        let b = Box::new(42);
        &*b as *const i32
    };                                      // the Box is freed here
    println!("{}", unsafe { *p });          // natively: prints 42 or garbage, rarely crashes
}
```

Under Miri (output abridged):

```text
error: Undefined Behavior: memory access failed: alloc1001 has been freed,
       so this pointer is dangling
 --> src/main.rs:6:29
  |
6 |     println!("{}", unsafe { *p });
  |                             ^^ Undefined Behavior occurred here
  |
help: alloc1001 was allocated here:
 --> src/main.rs:3:17
help: alloc1001 was deallocated here:
 --> src/main.rs:5:5
```

What Miri detects:

| Detected | Examples |
| -------- | -------- |
| Out-of-bounds and use-after-free accesses | `ptr.add(len)` read, dangling `&T` |
| Reads of uninitialized memory | `MaybeUninit::assume_init` too early |
| Invalid values | `bool` with value 2, bad enum discriminant, null reference |
| Misaligned accesses | `*(p as *const u32)` on an odd address |
| Aliasing violations | Two `&mut`, writing behind a live `&T` (Stacked or Tree Borrows) |
| Data races | Unsynchronized concurrent access, including weak memory effects |
| Memory leaks | Reported at the end of the run |
| Incorrect `unsafe` API use | Wrong layout passed to `dealloc`, overlapping `copy_nonoverlapping` |

Useful flags go in the `MIRIFLAGS` environment variable:

| Flag | Effect |
| ---- | ------ |
| `-Zmiri-tree-borrows` | Check against Tree Borrows instead of Stacked Borrows |
| `-Zmiri-strict-provenance` | Reject integer-to-pointer casts that lose provenance |
| `-Zmiri-many-seeds=0..32` | Repeat the run with many random seeds (thread schedules, addresses) |
| `-Zmiri-disable-isolation` | Allow access to the real file system, clock and environment |
| `-Zmiri-ignore-leaks` | Do not fail on leaked memory |

Miri can also interpret code for a target you do not have, which is the easiest
way to test endianness and 32-bit assumptions:

```bash
cargo +nightly miri test --target s390x-unknown-linux-gnu   # big-endian, 64-bit
cargo +nightly miri test --target i686-unknown-linux-gnu    # little-endian, 32-bit
```

Limitations, and how to deal with them:

| Limitation | Workaround |
| ---------- | ---------- |
| Orders of magnitude slower than native code | Shrink inputs with `cfg!(miri)`; skip heavy tests with `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]` |
| Cannot call most foreign (C) functions or inline assembly | Test the Rust logic separately; use sanitizers for the FFI part |
| Only checks paths that actually execute | Combine with fuzzing, property tests, many seeds |
| Isolated from the OS by default | `-Zmiri-disable-isolation`, or mock I/O in tests |

```rust
#[test]
fn fill_large_buffer() {
    let n = if cfg!(miri) { 100 } else { 1_000_000 };  // keep Miri runs fast
    let v: Vec<u64> = (0..n).collect();
    assert_eq!(v.len() as u64, n);
}

#[test]
#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]                 // calls into C, which Miri cannot run
fn calls_zlib() { /* ... */ }
```

Run Miri in CI for every crate that contains `unsafe`. It is the closest thing
Rust has to a UB checker for the language itself.

> Key Takeaways
> - Miri interprets Rust code and checks each operation against the language
>   rules, so it finds UB that ordinary tests miss.
> - Run it with `cargo +nightly miri test`; configure it with `MIRIFLAGS`, for
>   example Tree Borrows, strict provenance and many seeds.
> - It detects out-of-bounds and dangling accesses, uninitialized reads,
>   invalid values, aliasing violations, data races and leaks.
> - It is slow, cannot run most FFI, and only checks executed paths: shrink
>   inputs under `cfg!(miri)` and pair it with sanitizers and fuzzing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run Miri on the use-after-free above, on the `add_twice` example from
>    14.1, and on the `transmute::<u8, bool>` example. Record the error each one
>    reports.
> 2. Add Miri to a CI workflow for one of your crates, with
>    `-Zmiri-many-seeds=0..8`, and mark any test that does I/O or FFI with
>    `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]`.
> 3. Interview: All tests pass under `cargo test` and under Miri. Can you
>    conclude that the crate has no undefined behavior? (Hint: think about
>    which inputs, code paths and schedules were exercised, and about FFI.)

#### Sanitizers

Miri cannot run C code, real system calls or large workloads. **Sanitizers**
fill that gap from the other side: the compiler adds checks to the native
machine code, so the program runs at close to full speed (typically 2-5x
slower, plus extra memory) and can include C and C++ code compiled with the same
instrumentation. They are the same tools C and C++ developers use, provided by
LLVM, and they require a nightly toolchain in Rust.

| Sanitizer | Flag | Detects | Notes |
| --------- | ---- | ------- | ----- |
| AddressSanitizer (ASan) | `-Zsanitizer=address` | Heap, stack and global out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free, leaks on Linux | The most generally useful one |
| ThreadSanitizer (TSan) | `-Zsanitizer=thread` | Data races | Needs `-Zbuild-std` so the standard library is instrumented too |
| MemorySanitizer (MSan) | `-Zsanitizer=memory` | Reads of uninitialized memory | Needs `-Zbuild-std`, and *all* code (including C) instrumented |
| LeakSanitizer (LSan) | `-Zsanitizer=leak` | Memory leaks only | Low overhead |
| HWASan | `-Zsanitizer=hwaddress` | Like ASan, using pointer tagging | AArch64 only |
| CFI, KCFI, SafeStack, ShadowCallStack | various | Control-flow hijacking | Production hardening, not testing |

Running tests with ASan:

```bash
# --target makes RUSTFLAGS apply to your code but not to build scripts and proc macros
RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address" \
    cargo +nightly test --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

# TSan needs an instrumented standard library
rustup +nightly component add rust-src
RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=thread" \
    cargo +nightly test -Zbuild-std --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

The same use-after-free as in the Miri topic, reported by ASan (abridged):

```text
==48213==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x502000000010
READ of size 4 at 0x502000000010 thread T0
    #0 0x55d1c3a1 in demo::main src/main.rs:6:29
0x502000000010 is located 0 bytes inside of 4-byte region
freed by thread T0 here:
    #1 0x55d1c2f0 in core::ptr::drop_in_place<Box<i32>> ...
previously allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 0x55d1c260 in alloc::boxed::Box<i32>::new ...
```

For mixed Rust and C crates, instrument the C side as well. The `cc` crate
reads `CFLAGS`:

```bash
CFLAGS="-fsanitize=address" RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address" \
    cargo +nightly test --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

Which tool for which job:

| | Miri | ASan | TSan | Valgrind |
| - | ---- | ---- | ---- | -------- |
| Toolchain | Nightly | Nightly | Nightly | Stable (any binary) |
| Speed | Very slow | ~2x | ~5-15x | ~20-50x |
| Runs C/FFI code | No | Yes (if instrumented) | Yes (if instrumented) | Yes |
| Aliasing (`&mut` uniqueness) | Yes | No | No | No |
| Invalid values (`bool` = 2) | Yes | No | No | No |
| Out-of-bounds, use-after-free | Yes | Yes | No | Heap only |
| Data races | Yes | No | Yes | With Helgrind/DRD |
| Uninitialized reads | Yes | No | No | Yes (Memcheck) |

Sanitizers check what the *machine code* does, so they cannot see
Rust-specific rules such as aliasing or validity; Miri checks the *language*
rules but cannot run everything. Use both. Fuzzing (`cargo fuzz`, Chapter 12)
enables ASan by default, which makes it one of the most effective ways to
explore unusual inputs into unsafe code.

> Key Takeaways
> - Sanitizers instrument native code: fast enough for real workloads, and able
>   to cover C code in the same process.
> - ASan finds out-of-bounds and use-after-free bugs, TSan data races, MSan
>   uninitialized reads; TSan and MSan need `-Zbuild-std`.
> - Pass `--target` explicitly so build scripts and proc macros are not
>   instrumented, and set `CFLAGS` to instrument C sources too.
> - Sanitizers cannot see Rust's aliasing or validity rules; combine them with
>   Miri.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the use-after-free example under ASan and under Valgrind (on a stable
>    build). Compare the reports and the run time.
> 2. Write a program where two threads increment a `static mut` counter, and
>    confirm that TSan reports the race. Fix it with `AtomicU64` and run again.
> 3. Interview: Your crate wraps a C library and Miri cannot run its tests.
>    How do you still get confidence that the FFI layer is free of memory
>    errors? (Hint: which tools can see both the Rust and C sides of a call?)

#### Stacked and Tree Borrows Models

The aliasing rules of 14.1 ("a live `&mut` is unique") are easy to state for
references the borrow checker sees. But what exactly is allowed when raw
pointers and references are mixed in unsafe code? The Rust language has not
finished answering that question. To check unsafe code anyway, Miri implements
two candidate **aliasing models**, precise sets of rules that define which
accesses are UB. Following them is how you write unsafe code that will stay
correct whatever the final rules are.

**Stacked Borrows** (the default in Miri) gives every pointer a *tag* and keeps,
for every memory location, a **stack** of tags that may currently access it.
Creating a reference or raw pointer pushes its tag. Using a pointer is allowed
only if its tag is in the stack, and it removes (pops) everything above it,
because those later borrows have now been invalidated.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut x = 0;
    let p = &raw mut x;              // stack(x): [x, p]
    let r = unsafe { &mut *p };      // stack(x): [x, p, r]    r derived from p
    *r = 1;                          // r is in the stack: OK
    unsafe { *p = 2 };               // p used: pop r -> [x, p]
    *r = 3;                          // UB: r is no longer in the stack
}
```

```text
step                   stack for x (bottom → top)     result
let p = &raw mut x     x, p                           ok
let r = &mut *p        x, p, r                        ok
*r = 1                 x, p, r                        ok (r on stack)
*p = 2                 x, p          (r popped)       ok (p on stack)
*r = 3                 x, p                           UB: r not found
```

The rule matches intuition: using the "parent" pointer `p` ends the
"child" borrow `r`, exactly as using `x` would end a `&mut x` in safe code. The
fix is to stop using `r` once `p` is used again, or to do all accesses through
one of them.

**Tree Borrows** is a newer model (selected with `-Zmiri-tree-borrows`). It
records the parent-child relationship of pointers as a **tree** instead of a
stack, and gives each pointer a *permission* per location (such as Reserved,
Active, Frozen, Disabled) that changes as other pointers are used. It forbids
the same core violations (the example above is UB under both), but accepts a
number of patterns that are common in real code and that Stacked Borrows
rejects.

The best-known difference: under Stacked Borrows, a raw pointer derived from a
reference may only access the memory that reference covered.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut arr = [0i32; 4];

    // Pointer derived from a reference to ONE element:
    let p = &mut arr[0] as *mut i32;
    unsafe { *p.add(1) = 5 };        // Stacked Borrows: UB (outside arr[0])
                                     // Tree Borrows: accepted

    // Pointer derived from the whole array: fine under both models.
    let q = arr.as_mut_ptr();
    unsafe { *q.add(1) = 5 };
    println!("{arr:?}");
}
```

| | Stacked Borrows | Tree Borrows |
| - | --------------- | ------------ |
| Structure per location | Stack of tags | Tree of tags with permissions |
| Miri flag | Default | `-Zmiri-tree-borrows` |
| Two live `&mut` used interleaved | UB | UB |
| Writing behind a live `&T` | UB | UB |
| Raw pointer from `&mut a[0]` accessing `a[1]` | UB | Allowed |
| `&mut` that has not yet been written to, while others read | UB | Allowed (Reserved state) |
| Overall | Stricter, older, more studied | More permissive, closer to how code is written |

Neither model is yet the official definition. Practical guidance that is
correct under both:

- Derive pointers that cover a whole buffer from the whole buffer
  (`as_mut_ptr()`, `&raw mut`), not from a reference to its first element.
- Do not interleave uses of a raw pointer and of references derived from it;
  finish with one before using the other.
- Keep references created from raw pointers short-lived, ideally a single
  expression.
- Prefer raw pointer operations (`ptr.add(i).write(v)`) inside loops over
  turning each element into a `&mut`.
- Run Miri with both models; if code passes Stacked Borrows, it is very likely
  to stay valid.

> Key Takeaways
> - The exact aliasing rules for unsafe code are not final; Miri checks against
>   two candidate models, Stacked Borrows (default) and Tree Borrows.
> - Stacked Borrows keeps a stack of tags per location; using a pointer pops
>   every borrow created after it, and using a popped tag is UB.
> - Tree Borrows tracks a tree of pointers with permissions; it rejects the same
>   core violations but allows more real-world patterns.
> - Derive pointers from the whole allocation, avoid interleaving raw pointers
>   with references derived from them, and test with both models.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Trace the stack for each location in this code by hand, then check with
>    Miri: `let mut v = [1, 2]; let a = &mut v as *mut [i32; 2] as *mut i32;
>    let b = &mut v[1]; unsafe { *a = 9 }; *b = 8;`
> 2. Write a function that swaps the first and last element of a `&mut [T]`
>    using raw pointers, once deriving pointers from `&mut s[0]` and
>    `&mut s[len - 1]`, once from `s.as_mut_ptr()`. Run both under both models.
> 3. Interview: Why would a language deliberately leave its aliasing rules
>    unfinished, and how should library authors write unsafe code in the
>    meantime? (Hint: weigh optimization opportunities against existing code
>    that must stay valid.)

#### Auditing unsafe Code

Every `unsafe` block is a place where a human, not the compiler, vouches for
correctness, so it needs a human check. **Auditing** means finding all unsafe
code that ends up in your program (yours and your dependencies'), keeping it
small, and reviewing each block against a consistent checklist. The goal is not
zero `unsafe`; it is that every remaining block is necessary, justified and
checked.

**Step 1: measure.** Know where unsafe code is:

```bash
cargo install cargo-geiger
cargo geiger                       # unsafe usage per crate in the dependency tree

grep -rn "unsafe" src/ | wc -l     # crude, but a useful trend metric for your own crate
```

For dependencies, `cargo vet` (records who audited which crate version) and
`cargo crev` (shared community reviews) turn "we trust this crate" into an
explicit, reviewable decision. `cargo audit` and `cargo deny` (Chapter 8) report
crates with known soundness advisories.

**Step 2: let lints enforce the rules.** Configure them once for the whole
workspace:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[lints.rust]
unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny"          # every unsafe op needs its own block
unsafe_code = "deny"                     # opt in per module with #[allow(unsafe_code)]

[lints.clippy]
undocumented_unsafe_blocks = "deny"      # every unsafe block needs // SAFETY:
missing_safety_doc = "deny"              # every pub unsafe fn needs # Safety (warn by default)
multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block = "warn"   # one justification per operation
ptr_as_ptr = "warn"                      # prefer .cast() over `as` between pointer types
borrow_as_ptr = "warn"                   # prefer &raw const over &x as *const T
transmute_ptr_to_ref = "deny"            # prefer &*ptr over transmute
```

**Step 3: shrink the unsafe surface.** Many unsafe blocks can be replaced by
safe APIs that did not exist when the code was written:

| Unsafe pattern | Safe replacement |
| -------------- | ---------------- |
| Two `&mut` into one slice via raw pointers | `split_at_mut`, `chunks_exact_mut`, `get_disjoint_mut` |
| `set_len` after writing through a pointer | `Vec::spare_capacity_mut` with `MaybeUninit::write`, or `extend` |
| `get_unchecked` in a loop | Iterators (bounds checks disappear), or one `assert!` before the loop |
| `transmute` between plain-data types | `bytemuck` or `zerocopy` |
| `static mut` | `AtomicU64`, `Mutex`, `OnceLock`, `LazyLock` |
| `mem::uninitialized`, `mem::zeroed` for arrays | `MaybeUninit`, `[const { None }; N]`, `array::from_fn` |

**Step 4: review each block.** A checklist that covers most unsafe code:

| Check | Question |
| ----- | -------- |
| Necessity | Can this be done with a safe API at acceptable cost? |
| Preconditions | Does the `SAFETY` comment address *every* requirement in the called function's `# Safety` section? |
| Pointers | Non-null, aligned, in bounds, initialized, valid value, and still alive? |
| Aliasing | Could a `&mut` overlap anything else? Is anything written behind a `&`? |
| Invariants | Which type invariants does this rely on, and can any safe code in the module break them? |
| Panics | If any call in between panics, is everything left in a valid state? |
| Threads | Are `Send`/`Sync` impls justified? Can two threads reach this code at once? |
| Generics | Does it hold for zero-sized types, `!Sized` types, types with `Drop`, and malicious trait impls? |
| Tests | Is it covered by tests that run under Miri? |

An audit in practice. This function compiles and passes tests on most
machines:

```rust
pub fn as_u32s(bytes: &[u8]) -> &[u32] {
    // SAFETY: every bit pattern is a valid u32.
    unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(bytes.as_ptr() as *const u32, bytes.len() / 4) }
}
```

The checklist finds the problem: the `SAFETY` comment covers validity but not
**alignment**, which `from_raw_parts` requires. In a debug build, the standard
library's precondition checks catch it at run time when the slice starts at an
odd address:

```text
thread 'main' panicked at src/lib.rs:3:14:
unsafe precondition(s) violated: slice::from_raw_parts requires the pointer
to be aligned and non-null, and the total size of the slice not to exceed
`isize::MAX`
```

These checks are a useful first line of defence, but they are optional,
compiled out in release builds, and cover only some preconditions. The fix
removes the unsafe code entirely:

```rust
pub fn as_u32s(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<&[u32]> {
    // Safe: returns None if the slice is misaligned or its length is not a
    // multiple of 4.
    bytemuck::try_cast_slice(bytes).ok()
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Measure unsafe code in your crate and dependencies (`cargo geiger`,
>   `cargo vet`, `cargo audit`).
> - Enforce documentation and granularity with lints: `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn`,
>   `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `missing_safety_doc`.
> - Replace unsafe code with safe standard or ecosystem APIs whenever possible.
> - Review every block against a checklist: preconditions, pointer validity,
>   aliasing, invariants, panics, threads, generics and Miri coverage.
> - Debug-build precondition checks catch some misuse, but cannot be relied on.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `cargo geiger` on a project with at least ten dependencies. Pick the
>    dependency with the most unsafe code and read one of its unsafe blocks.
>    Can you find its `SAFETY` justification?
> 2. Enable the lint configuration above on one of your crates and fix every
>    warning. How many unsafe blocks could you remove entirely?
> 3. Interview: You are asked to approve a pull request that adds 30 lines of
>    unsafe code to speed up a parser by 15%. What would you ask for before
>    approving? (Hint: benchmarks, alternatives, invariants, tests, Miri.)

#### Documenting Safety Invariants

Unsafe code is correct only relative to assumptions, and assumptions that
exist only in the author's head are lost the first time someone else edits the
code. Documentation is therefore part of the correctness argument, not
decoration. Rust has settled conventions for three kinds of safety
documentation, each written for a different reader:

| Where | Form | Reader | Content |
| ----- | ---- | ------ | ------- |
| `unsafe fn`, `unsafe trait` | `/// # Safety` doc section | Callers, implementers | The conditions *they* must uphold |
| `unsafe { }` block, `unsafe impl` | `// SAFETY:` comment directly above | Reviewers, future maintainers | *Why* the conditions hold at this spot |
| Types with invariants | Doc comment or `// INVARIANT:` on fields | Anyone editing the module | What must always be true about the fields |

A complete example: an ASCII-only string type.

```rust
/// An owned string that contains only ASCII bytes.
pub struct AsciiString {
    /// INVARIANT: every byte is < 0x80. Code in this module that mutates
    /// `bytes` must preserve this; `as_str` relies on it for UTF-8 validity.
    bytes: Vec<u8>,
}

impl AsciiString {
    /// Validates `bytes` and wraps them.
    pub fn new(bytes: Vec<u8>) -> Option<Self> {
        bytes.is_ascii().then_some(AsciiString { bytes })   // establishes the invariant
    }

    /// Wraps `bytes` without checking them.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Every byte in `bytes` must be less than `0x80`. Violating this makes
    /// [`AsciiString::as_str`] produce a `&str` that is not valid UTF-8,
    /// which is undefined behavior.
    pub unsafe fn from_bytes_unchecked(bytes: Vec<u8>) -> Self {
        debug_assert!(bytes.is_ascii());
        AsciiString { bytes }
    }

    /// Appends an ASCII character.
    ///
    /// # Panics
    ///
    /// Panics if `c` is not ASCII.
    pub fn push(&mut self, c: char) {
        assert!(c.is_ascii(), "not ASCII: {c:?}");          // preserves the invariant
        self.bytes.push(c as u8);
    }

    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        // SAFETY: ASCII is a subset of UTF-8, and `bytes` is all ASCII by the
        // type invariant (established in `new`/`from_bytes_unchecked`,
        // preserved by `push`).
        unsafe { std::str::from_utf8_unchecked(&self.bytes) }
    }

    /// Mutable access to the raw bytes.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The caller must leave every byte less than `0x80` before the borrow
    /// ends.
    pub unsafe fn as_bytes_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<u8> {
        &mut self.bytes
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut s = AsciiString::new(b"abc".to_vec()).unwrap();
    s.push('d');
    // SAFETY: we only uppercase ASCII letters, which stay ASCII.
    unsafe { s.as_bytes_mut().make_ascii_uppercase() };
    println!("{}", s.as_str());                              // ABCD
}
```

Note why `as_bytes_mut` is an `unsafe fn` even though its body contains no
unsafe operation: it hands out the ability to break the invariant, so it makes
`as_str` unsound unless callers keep their side of the contract. This is the
safety-invariant idea from 14.1 in action.

Writing a good `SAFETY` comment:

| Weak | Strong |
| ---- | ------ |
| `// SAFETY: this is safe` | `// SAFETY: i < self.len (checked on line 12), so get_unchecked's bound holds` |
| `// SAFETY: trust me, the pointer is fine` | `// SAFETY: ptr comes from Box::into_raw in new() and is freed only in Drop` |
| `// SAFETY: see above` | One comment per block, naming each precondition of the callee |

Guidelines:

- **Mirror the callee's contract.** Read the `# Safety` section of the function
  you call, and address each point in your comment.
- **Point at the evidence**: the check, the invariant, or the caller's
  obligation that makes each point true.
- **Document invariants where they are established and where they are
  relied on.** A reader of `as_str` should be able to find the code that
  guarantees the invariant.
- **State the consequence** in `# Safety` sections: what goes wrong (which UB)
  if the condition is broken, so callers understand the stakes.
- **Keep `# Panics` and `# Safety` separate.** A panic is a defined outcome; a
  safety violation is UB.
- **Document `unsafe impl Send`/`Sync`** with the thread-safety argument, and
  `unsafe trait`s with the exact obligations of implementers.

A template for a public unsafe function:

```rust
/// One-line summary.
///
/// Longer description of what the function does.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// - `ptr` must be non-null, aligned, and valid for reads of `len` elements.
/// - The memory must not be mutated for the lifetime `'a`.
/// - `len * size_of::<T>()` must not exceed `isize::MAX`.
///
/// Violating any of these is undefined behavior.
pub unsafe fn view<'a, T>(ptr: *const T, len: usize) -> &'a [T] {
    // SAFETY: the caller upholds exactly the requirements of
    // `slice::from_raw_parts`, which are restated above.
    unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) }
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Use `# Safety` doc sections for obligations on callers and implementers,
>   `// SAFETY:` comments for why each unsafe block is correct, and documented
>   invariants on fields that unsafe code relies on.
> - A `SAFETY` comment should name each precondition of the callee and point to
>   the evidence that it holds.
> - A function that lets callers break a type invariant must be `unsafe`, even
>   with no unsafe operation in its body.
> - Keep `# Panics` (defined behavior) separate from `# Safety` (UB if
>   violated), and enforce documentation with Clippy lints.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8]` and `pub fn pop(&mut self) ->
>    Option<char>` to `AsciiString`, with comments showing how each one
>    preserves or relies on the invariant. Which, if any, need `unsafe`?
> 2. Take the `TinyVec` from 14.1 and document it fully: field invariants,
>    `SAFETY` comments, and a `# Safety` section for a new `unsafe fn
>    set_len(&mut self, n: usize)`.
> 3. Interview: A reviewer says, "This `unsafe fn` contains no unsafe code, so
>    remove the `unsafe` keyword." When is that advice wrong? (Hint: what can
>    callers of the function break, and which other code relies on it?)

---

## 15. Performance and Low-Level Control

Rust compiles to native code with no garbage collector and no runtime, so its
performance ceiling is that of C and C++; reaching that ceiling still depends on
choices the compiler cannot make for you: how often you allocate, what the
optimizer can see, and how your data is laid out in memory. This chapter covers
the optimization techniques that matter most in practice, the data-oriented
design patterns that keep the CPU's caches busy, and the `no_std` world, where
there is no operating system at all and Rust runs directly on a microcontroller.
Measuring comes first: everything here assumes the benchmarking and profiling
workflow from Chapter 12.

<a id="151-optimization-techniques"></a>
### 15.1 Optimization Techniques

This section covers the main ways to make a correct Rust program faster:
allocating less, guiding inlining, widening what the optimizer sees with LTO,
PGO and codegen settings, removing bounds checks, and using the CPU's vector
units.

#### Avoiding Unnecessary Allocation

A heap allocation looks free in source code (`String::new()`, `vec![]`,
`.to_string()`), but each one has a real cost. The allocator has to find a free
block, update its bookkeeping and, in multi-threaded programs, coordinate with
other threads; later the block has to be freed again. The new memory is often
not in the CPU cache, so the first touch of it is slow. A single allocation
takes tens of nanoseconds, and a hot loop that allocates on every iteration can
spend most of its time in `malloc` and `free` rather than in your code.

Think of the allocator as a hardware store. Buying one screw is cheap, but a
trip to the store for every screw you need dwarfs the time spent driving them
in. The fixes are the same as in a workshop: buy in bulk up front
(`with_capacity`), keep a box of screws on the bench and reuse it (buffer
reuse), or borrow your neighbour's instead of buying (`&str`, `Cow`).

Chapter 12 showed how to *find* allocation hotspots with `dhat` and a counting
allocator, and listed the common fixes. This topic explains the techniques
behind those fixes.

**1. Pre-size collections.** A `Vec` that grows by `push` doubles its capacity
each time it fills up, copying every element to the new buffer:

```text
push #   capacity   reallocation?
1        4          yes (first allocation)
5        8          yes, copies 4 elements
9        16         yes, copies 8 elements
17       32         yes, copies 16 elements
...
n        ~n         log2(n) reallocations in total
```

Pushing is amortized O(1), but if you know the final size, `with_capacity` (or
`reserve`) does the whole job with a single allocation and no copies:

```rust
fn squares(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(n);    // one allocation, exact size
    for i in 0..n as u64 {
        out.push(i * i);                    // never reallocates
    }
    out
}

// Even better: iterators over ranges know their length, so collect()
// pre-allocates on its own.
fn squares_iter(n: usize) -> Vec<u64> {
    (0..n as u64).map(|i| i * i).collect()
}
```

**2. Reuse buffers across iterations.** `clear()` sets the length to zero but
keeps the capacity, so a buffer that is hoisted out of a loop reaches its
largest needed size once and then never allocates again:

```rust
use std::io::{self, BufRead};

fn count_long_lines(input: impl BufRead) -> io::Result<usize> {
    let mut reader = input;
    let mut line = String::new();            // allocated once, outside the loop
    let mut count = 0;

    // read_line appends into an existing String instead of returning a new one
    while reader.read_line(&mut line)? != 0 {
        if line.trim_end().len() > 80 {
            count += 1;
        }
        line.clear();                        // keep the capacity, drop the contents
    }
    Ok(count)
}
```

Compare this with `for line in reader.lines()`, which allocates a fresh
`String` per line. The same pattern applies to scratch `Vec`s in parsers,
encoders and simulation steps.

**3. Borrow instead of own.** Many allocations exist only because a function
signature demands ownership. Take `&str` or `&[T]` when you only read, and
return borrowed slices of the input when you can. When a function *sometimes*
needs to modify its input, `Cow` (clone-on-write) allocates only in that case:

```rust
use std::borrow::Cow;

/// Replaces tabs with four spaces; allocates only if a tab is present.
fn expand_tabs(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
    if s.contains('\t') {
        Cow::Owned(s.replace('\t', "    "))  // rare path: allocate
    } else {
        Cow::Borrowed(s)                     // common path: zero allocations
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = expand_tabs("no tabs here");     // Borrowed
    let b = expand_tabs("\tindented");       // Owned
    println!("{a} | {b}");
}
```

**4. Write into existing buffers instead of formatting new ones.** `format!`
always returns a new `String`. When you build output piece by piece, `write!`
into one buffer instead:

```rust
use std::fmt::Write;

fn render(rows: &[(u32, &str)]) -> String {
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(rows.len() * 16);   // rough estimate
    for (id, name) in rows {
        // writes into `out`; no temporary String per row
        writeln!(out, "{id:>5}  {name}").unwrap();          // fmt::Write to a String cannot fail
    }
    out
}
```

**5. Prefer iterator chains to intermediate collections.** Every
`.collect::<Vec<_>>()` that is immediately iterated again is an allocation that
does nothing useful. Keep the chain lazy, and collect once at the end, if at
all.

**6. Pick the right owned type.** A few smaller decisions also add up:

| Situation | Choice | Why |
| --------- | ------ | --- |
| A string that never changes after creation | `Box<str>` instead of `String` | 16 bytes instead of 24; no spare capacity |
| An immutable string shared by many owners | `Arc<str>` / `Rc<str>` | Cloning bumps a counter instead of copying bytes |
| Moving a value out of a `&mut` field | `std::mem::take` / `mem::replace` | Avoids `clone()` |
| Removing many elements | `retain` / `drain(..)` | One pass, no new `Vec` |
| Many small, short-lived objects | Small-vector types or arenas (15.2) | Avoid the allocator entirely |

`shrink_to_fit` gives memory back but itself reallocates, so call it only on
long-lived collections that will not grow again.

> Key Takeaways
> - Allocation costs allocator work, a later free, and cache misses; it matters
>   most in hot loops.
> - Pre-size with `with_capacity`/`reserve`, and reuse buffers with `clear()`,
>   which keeps capacity.
> - Borrow (`&str`, `&[T]`) when you only read, and use `Cow` when a function
>   only sometimes needs to own.
> - `write!` into an existing `String` instead of building many `format!`
>   temporaries, and avoid `collect()` calls that are immediately re-iterated.
> - Confirm every fix with a measurement (Chapter 12); not every allocation is
>   worth removing.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that splits a text into words and returns the ten most
>    frequent ones. Implement it once with `String` keys and once with `&str`
>    keys borrowed from the input, and count the allocations of each with the
>    counting allocator from Chapter 12.
