> 2. Rewrite a loop that uses `reader.lines()` to use a single reused `String`
>    with `read_line`. Benchmark both on a 100 MB file.
> 3. Interview: A function `fn normalize(s: String) -> String` is called a
>    million times, and in 99% of calls it returns its input unchanged. How
>    would you redesign its signature? (Hint: think about who should pay for
>    the allocation, and when.)

#### Inlining and Attributes

A function call has a small direct cost (saving registers, jumping, returning),
but its larger cost is indirect: the optimizer mostly works one function at a
time, so a call is a wall it cannot see through. **Inlining** copies the body
of the callee into the caller, and that removes the wall. Once `len()` is
inlined into a loop, the compiler can hoist it out of the loop; once a closure
is inlined into `map`, the whole iterator chain collapses into a simple loop
that may then be vectorized. Most of Rust's "zero-cost abstractions" are zero
cost *because* of inlining.

The analogy is a recipe that says "make the sauce (see page 42)". A cook who
copies the sauce instructions into the main recipe can spot that both steps
need chopped onions and do them together. A cook who flips to page 42 every
time cannot.

Inlining also has a cost: every inlined copy makes the binary bigger, and a
bloated hot loop can stop fitting in the instruction cache. LLVM therefore
decides with heuristics. Rust gives you attributes to inform those decisions:

| Attribute | Meaning |
| --------- | ------- |
| `#[inline]` | Make the body available to other crates, and hint that inlining is worthwhile |
| `#[inline(always)]` | Strongly request inlining at every call site (still not guaranteed) |
| `#[inline(never)]` | Never inline; useful for slow paths, profiling and stack traces |
| `#[cold]` | This function is rarely called: optimize callers for the path that avoids it |
| `#[track_caller]` | Panics inside report the caller's location (adds a hidden argument) |
| `#[target_feature(enable = "...")]` | Compile this function with extra CPU features (see SIMD below) |

**Inlining across crates.** Within one crate, LLVM can inline anything it
likes. Across crates it can only inline what it has the body of:

```text
Function kind                          Inlinable in other crates?
-------------------------------------  ---------------------------------------
Generic fn / generic impl method       Yes: it is monomorphized in the caller's crate
Non-generic fn marked #[inline]        Yes: its body is shipped in the crate metadata
Very small non-generic fn              Usually: rustc exports tiny leaf functions automatically
Other non-generic fn                   Only with LTO (see next topic)
```

This is why the standard library puts `#[inline]` on small non-generic
functions such as `String::len` and trait impls for concrete types. In
your own code, `#[inline]` matters mostly on small public functions of a
*library* crate that are called in hot loops from other crates. Inside a binary
crate it rarely changes anything.

**Splitting hot and cold paths.** A common, effective pattern is to keep the
fast path small, so it inlines well, and move the rare, bulky path into a
separate function marked `#[cold]` and `#[inline(never)]`:

```rust
pub struct Buffer {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    pos: usize,
}

impl Buffer {
    #[inline]                               // tiny and hot: let callers inline it
    pub fn read_u8(&mut self) -> u8 {
        if self.pos < self.data.len() {     // the branch that almost always runs
            let b = self.data[self.pos];
            self.pos += 1;
            b
        } else {
            self.refill_and_read()          // a single call instead of bulky code
        }
    }

    #[cold]                                 // tells LLVM this branch is unlikely
    #[inline(never)]                        // keeps the slow code out of every caller
    fn refill_and_read(&mut self) -> u8 {
        // ... read more data from disk or the network, handle EOF, etc.
        panic!("end of buffer")
    }
}
```

`#[cold]` also changes code layout: the compiler places the cold branch away
from the hot code, so the hot loop stays compact in the instruction cache, and
it predicts the branch as not taken. Functions that panic are treated as cold
automatically.

**Rules of thumb:**

- Do not sprinkle `#[inline(always)]` everywhere. It increases compile time and
  code size and can make code slower. Reach for it only after a profile shows
  a call that LLVM refused to inline and a benchmark shows that forcing it
  helps.
- Use `#[inline(never)]` temporarily to make a function show up as its own
  entry in a profiler or flamegraph.
- Inspect the result with `cargo asm` (the `cargo-show-asm` tool) or Compiler
  Explorer (godbolt.org) rather than guessing.

```bash
cargo install cargo-show-asm
cargo asm --lib mycrate::Buffer::read_u8      # assembly of one function, release build
cargo asm --lib --llvm mycrate::Buffer::read_u8   # the LLVM IR instead
```

If the function disappears from the list of symbols, it was inlined into all
its callers.

> Key Takeaways
> - Inlining's main benefit is that it lets the optimizer see across function
>   boundaries; the saved call overhead is secondary.
> - Generic functions are always inlinable across crates; non-generic ones
>   need `#[inline]` (or LTO), except very small leaf functions.
> - `#[inline]` is a hint and an export of the body, `#[inline(always)]` a
>   strong request; neither is guaranteed.
> - Split hot and cold paths: a small `#[inline]` fast path plus a `#[cold]
>   #[inline(never)]` slow path.
> - Check what the compiler did with `cargo asm` before and after adding
>   attributes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create a library crate with a non-generic `pub fn add_one(x: u32) -> u32`
>    that does a little more work (for example, a checked add with a custom
>    error), call it in a loop from a binary crate, and compare the assembly of
>    the loop with and without `#[inline]`.
> 2. Take a parser function with a rarely taken error branch that builds a
>    detailed error message. Move the message-building into a `#[cold]`
>    function and compare the size of the hot function with `cargo asm`.
> 3. Interview: Why is `#[inline]` important for small public functions in a
>    library, but usually pointless in a binary crate? (Hint: what does the
>    compiler have access to when it compiles the calling crate?)

#### Link-Time Optimization

Rust compiles each crate separately, and by default the optimizer only sees
one crate (or one piece of a crate, see codegen units below) at a time. A
non-generic function in a dependency is opaque: it cannot be inlined, the
caller cannot benefit from knowing that it never returns `None`, and a function
that nobody in the final program calls cannot always be discarded early.

**Link-time optimization (LTO)** delays part of the optimization until link
time, when all the crates of the program are known. Instead of linking finished
machine code, rustc hands LLVM the intermediate representation of every crate,
and LLVM optimizes them as one program.

```text
Without LTO: each crate is optimized alone, then the machine code is linked

  crate A ──► optimize ──► machine code ──┐
  crate B ──► optimize ──► machine code ──┼──► link ──► binary
  std     ──► (shipped precompiled) ──────┘

With LTO: every crate is handed over as LLVM IR and optimized as one program

  crate A ──► LLVM IR ──┐
  crate B ──► LLVM IR ──┼──► optimize together ──► link ──► binary
  std     ──► LLVM IR ──┘    (cross-crate inlining, dead code removal)
```

It is like proofreading a book. Proofreading each chapter on its own catches
typos, but only a pass over the whole book notices that chapter 3 and chapter
9 explain the same thing and one of them can go.

Cargo exposes LTO through the `lto` setting of a profile (Chapter 8 listed
it):

| Setting | Meaning | Build cost | Typical effect |
| ------- | ------- | ---------- | -------------- |
| `lto = false` (default) | "Thin local" LTO: across the codegen units of *one* crate only | None | Baseline |
| `lto = "off"` | No LTO at all | Lowest | Slightly slower than the default |
| `lto = "thin"` | ThinLTO across all crates: summaries plus parallel, selective imports | Moderate | Most of fat LTO's speed-up |
| `lto = "fat"` or `true` | Merge every crate into one module and optimize it | High, single-threaded, memory hungry | Best runtime speed and smallest binary |

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[profile.release]
lto = "thin"            # a good default for most release builds

[profile.dist]          # for the binaries you actually ship
inherits = "release"
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
```

How much it helps depends on the program. Code that makes many small calls
into dependencies (parsers, serializers, numeric code calling small library
functions) often speeds up by 5-20% and shrinks noticeably. Programs whose time
is spent in a few big functions, or in I/O, see little change.

LTO only optimizes what it receives as LLVM IR. Two consequences:

- Code from C libraries linked into your program is still opaque. To optimize
  across the language boundary, build both sides with LLVM (rustc and a
  matching `clang`) and use **cross-language LTO** with
  `-C linker-plugin-lto` (plus `-flto=thin` on the C side). This needs
  matching LLVM versions and is mainly used by large mixed codebases such as
  browsers.
- LTO does not fix algorithmic problems; it gives the optimizer more to look
  at, nothing more.

Check the effect on binary size and speed instead of assuming it:

```bash
cargo build --release && ls -l target/release/myapp
cargo build --profile dist && ls -l target/dist/myapp
hyperfine 'target/release/myapp input.txt' 'target/dist/myapp input.txt'
```

> Key Takeaways
> - LTO lets LLVM optimize across crate boundaries at link time, enabling
>   cross-crate inlining and removing dead code.
> - The default (`false`) only optimizes across codegen units of one crate;
>   `"thin"` is a good speed/build-time balance; `"fat"` gives the most at the
>   highest build cost.
> - Use a separate profile (for example `dist`) for expensive settings so
>   everyday release builds stay fast.
> - Optimizing across C and Rust needs cross-language LTO with matching LLVM
>   versions.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a project that uses `serde_json` with `lto = "off"`, `false`,
>    `"thin"` and `"fat"`. Record build time, binary size and the runtime of a
>    parsing benchmark in a table.
> 2. Add a `dist` profile that inherits from `release`, enables fat LTO and one
>    codegen unit, and wire it into a CI release job.
> 3. Interview: Your team enabled fat LTO and the release build went from 2 to
>    9 minutes, with a 3% runtime gain. How would you decide whether to keep it,
>    and what middle ground exists? (Hint: consider who runs which build how
>    often, and the `thin` and profile options.)

#### Codegen Units and PGO

**Codegen units** are the other half of the "how much does the optimizer see"
question. To compile one large crate quickly, rustc splits it into several
chunks, the codegen units, and runs LLVM on them in parallel. The price is the
same as for separate crates: a function in one unit cannot be inlined into
another unit unless the default thin-local LTO manages to recover it.

```text
                 ┌── unit 1 ──► LLVM ──┐
 crate source ───┼── unit 2 ──► LLVM ──┼──► object files ──► link
                 └── unit N ──► LLVM ──┘
                    (parallel; less cross-unit optimization as N grows)
```

| Profile | Default `codegen-units` | Reasoning |
| ------- | ----------------------- | --------- |
| `dev` | 256 (with incremental compilation) | Fastest rebuilds |
| `release` | 16 | Parallel build, decent optimization |
| Tuned release | 1 | Whole crate optimized as one unit; slowest build |

`codegen-units = 1` typically gives a few percent of speed and a smaller
binary. It pairs naturally with LTO in a dedicated shipping profile, as shown
above.

**Profile-guided optimization (PGO)** answers a different question: not *how
much* the optimizer sees, but *what it knows about how the program behaves*.
Without data, the compiler has to guess which branches are taken, which
functions are hot, and which `match` arms are common. PGO replaces the guesses
with measurements in three steps:

```text
1. Instrumented build   ──►  a binary that counts branches and calls
2. Training run         ──►  run representative workloads; write .profraw files
3. Optimized build      ──►  recompile using the merged profile:
                             hot code inlined and laid out together,
                             cold code moved away, branches arranged by real frequency
```

The analogy is a supermarket that rearranges its shelves after a month of
till receipts: what people actually buy most goes near the entrance.

The manual workflow uses rustc flags and LLVM's `llvm-profdata` tool:

```bash
# Tool that merges raw profiles (matches the toolchain's LLVM version)
rustup component add llvm-tools-preview

# 1. Instrumented build
RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-generate=/tmp/pgo-data" \
    cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

# 2. Training: run realistic workloads (several, if the program has several modes)
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/myapp bench-input-1.json
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/myapp bench-input-2.json

# 3. Merge the raw profiles, then rebuild using them
~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/llvm-profdata \
    merge -o /tmp/pgo-data/merged.profdata /tmp/pgo-data
RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-use=/tmp/pgo-data/merged.profdata" \
    cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

Passing `--target` explicitly keeps `RUSTFLAGS` away from build scripts and
procedural macros, which do not need instrumentation. The `cargo-pgo` tool
wraps the same steps and can also apply **BOLT**, a post-link optimizer that
reorders machine code using a profile:

```bash
cargo install cargo-pgo
cargo pgo build                 # instrumented build
cargo pgo run -- bench-input-1.json
cargo pgo optimize              # rebuild with the gathered profile
```

Gains of 10-20% are common for branchy code such as compilers, interpreters,
parsers and databases; the Rust compiler itself is built with PGO and BOLT.
Numeric kernels that are already branch-free gain little. The main risk is a
**non-representative training set**: if you train on a workload that is unlike
production, you optimize for the wrong paths, and production can get slower.

> Key Takeaways
> - More codegen units mean faster parallel builds but less optimization;
>   `codegen-units = 1` maximizes optimization within a crate.
> - PGO feeds measured branch and call frequencies back into the compiler:
>   instrument, train, rebuild.
> - Training workloads must resemble production, or PGO optimizes the wrong
>   paths.
> - `cargo-pgo` automates PGO and BOLT; keep PGO builds in CI where the
>   training run can be repeated reliably.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a CPU-bound program (for example, a JSON-to-CSV converter) with
>    `codegen-units` set to 16 and to 1, and compare build times and runtime.
> 2. Apply PGO to the same program by hand with `-Cprofile-generate` and
>    `-Cprofile-use`, then with `cargo pgo`. Measure the speed-up with
>    `hyperfine`.
> 3. Interview: An interpreter got 15% faster with PGO in benchmarks but 5%
>    slower in production. What is the most likely cause, and how would you fix
>    the build process? (Hint: what did the instrumented binary actually
>    observe?)

#### Bounds Check Elimination

Indexing a slice with `v[i]` is checked: if `i >= v.len()`, the program panics
instead of reading memory outside the buffer. This is one of Rust's core safety
guarantees, and in C the same out-of-range read would be a silent bug or a
security hole.

A bounds check is a comparison and a branch. On its own it is cheap, because
the branch is almost always predicted correctly. The real cost is indirect:

- The possible panic is a side effect, so the compiler must keep the exact
  order of loop iterations up to the panic. That often prevents
  **vectorization** (processing 4-16 elements per instruction).
- The panic path adds code, which can stop a small function from being inlined.

The good news is that LLVM removes checks it can *prove* unnecessary. Your job
is to write code where the proof is easy, much like giving a security guard a
guest list at the door so they stop checking every badge in every corridor.

**1. Use iterators instead of indices.** An iterator over a slice cannot go out
of bounds by construction, so there is nothing to check:

```rust
// Indexed: a check on every access unless LLVM can prove i < a.len()
// and i < b.len()
pub fn dot_indexed(a: &[f32], b: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let mut sum = 0.0;
    for i in 0..a.len() {
        sum += a[i] * b[i];          // b[i] is checked: b may be shorter than a
    }
    sum
}

// Iterator: zip stops at the shorter slice, no checks needed
pub fn dot_zip(a: &[f32], b: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    a.iter().zip(b).map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum()
}
```

**2. Prove the length once, up front.** When you need indices (for example,
because you access `i` and `i + 1`), an assertion or a re-slice before the loop
gives LLVM the fact it needs. One check replaces many:

```rust
pub fn add_into(dst: &mut [u32], a: &[u32], b: &[u32]) {
    let n = dst.len();
    let (a, b) = (&a[..n], &b[..n]);     // two checks here, then none inside the loop
    for i in 0..n {
        dst[i] = a[i] + b[i];            // LLVM now knows a.len() == b.len() == n
    }
}

pub fn deltas(xs: &[i64], out: &mut [i64]) {
    assert!(out.len() + 1 >= xs.len()); // one check, with a clear message on failure
    for i in 1..xs.len() {
        out[i - 1] = xs[i] - xs[i - 1];  // provably in range for both slices
    }
}
```

**3. Use fixed-size chunks.** `chunks_exact(N)` yields slices that are known to
have exactly `N` elements, and `as_chunks::<N>()` (Rust 1.88+) yields
`&[T; N]` arrays, whose length is part of the type:

```rust
pub fn sum_by_4(xs: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    let (chunks, rest) = xs.as_chunks::<4>();          // &[[u32; 4]], &[u32]
    let mut acc = [0u32; 4];
    for c in chunks {
        for k in 0..4 {
            acc[k] = acc[k].wrapping_add(c[k]);         // array index with constant
        }                                               // bound: no check
    }
    acc.iter().chain(rest).fold(0, |s, x| s.wrapping_add(*x))
}
```

**4. Last resort: `get_unchecked`.** When a profile proves that a check
remains and matters, and you can prove the index is in range, the unchecked
accessors skip the check. This is `unsafe`, needs a `SAFETY` comment (Chapter
14), and should be covered by a `debug_assert!` so tests still catch mistakes:

```rust
pub fn gather(table: &[u8; 256], idx: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    // No unsafe needed: a u8 index into a 256-element array is always in range,
    // and LLVM knows it.
    idx.iter().map(|&i| table[i as usize]).collect()
}

pub fn lookup(table: &[u32], keys: &[usize]) -> u64 {
    let mut s = 0u64;
    for &k in keys {
        debug_assert!(k < table.len());
        // SAFETY: every key was validated against table.len() when `keys`
        // was built (see KeySet::new), so k is in bounds.
        s += unsafe { *table.get_unchecked(k) } as u64;
    }
    s
}
```

The `gather` example shows an often-forgotten fact: choosing types that encode
the range (`u8` into a 256-entry table, arrays instead of slices) removes checks
without any `unsafe`.

To verify that a check is gone, look for the call to the panic function in the
assembly:

```bash
cargo asm --lib mycrate::add_into | grep -c panic_bounds_check   # 0 means eliminated
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Bounds checks are cheap branches, but they can block vectorization and
>   inlining in hot loops.
> - Iterators (`iter`, `zip`, `chunks_exact`, `windows`) avoid checks by
>   construction.
> - Re-slice or `assert!` lengths before a loop so one check replaces many.
> - Types that encode the range (fixed-size arrays, `u8` indices into
>   256-element tables) remove checks safely.
> - `get_unchecked` is a last resort: `unsafe`, documented, guarded by
>   `debug_assert!`, and justified by a profile.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write `fn prefix_sums(xs: &[u64]) -> Vec<u64>` with indexing, compile it,
>    and count `panic_bounds_check` calls with `cargo asm`. Then rewrite it so
>    the count drops to zero without `unsafe`.
> 2. Implement a 3x3 box blur over a grayscale image stored as a flat
>    `Vec<u8>`. Use re-slicing of the three input rows to remove the bounds
>    checks in the inner loop, and benchmark the before/after versions.
> 3. Interview: Why can a loop with `v[i]` fail to vectorize even though the
>    bounds check almost never fails? (Hint: consider what must be true of the
>    program state at the exact moment of the panic.)

#### SIMD and Intrinsics

Modern CPUs contain **vector units** that apply one instruction to several
values at once: **S**ingle **I**nstruction, **M**ultiple **D**ata. A 256-bit
AVX2 register holds eight `f32` or thirty-two `u8` values, so one addition
instruction does eight or thirty-two additions:

```text
scalar add:   a0 + b0 = c0                          (1 result per instruction)

AVX add:      ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐
              │a0│a1│a2│a3│a4│a5│a6│a7│
            + │b0│b1│b2│b3│b4│b5│b6│b7│
            = │c0│c1│c2│c3│c4│c5│c6│c7│            (8 results per instruction)
              └──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘
                  one 256-bit register
```

It is the difference between a cashier who scans one item at a time and a
checkout that scans the whole basket at once. For data-parallel work (image
processing, audio, compression, parsing, hashing, numeric kernels) the speed-up
can be 4-16x.

Rust offers three levels, from easiest to most control:

| Level | How | Portability | Stable Rust? |
| ----- | --- | ----------- | ------------ |
| Auto-vectorization | Write simple loops; the compiler vectorizes them | Any target | Yes |
| Portable SIMD | `std::simd` types such as `f32x8` | Any target | No (nightly feature) |
| Intrinsics | `std::arch::x86_64::_mm256_add_ps`, `std::arch::aarch64::vaddq_f32`, ... | One architecture | Yes |

Crates such as `wide` and `pulp` provide portable SIMD types on stable Rust
today.

**Level 1: help the auto-vectorizer.** LLVM vectorizes loops that are simple,
free of bounds checks (previous topic), and free of hidden dependencies between
iterations. It can only use instructions that the *target CPU* supports, and
the default `x86_64` target is the 2003 baseline with SSE2. Enabling a newer
level unlocks AVX2:

```toml
# .cargo/config.toml: for binaries deployed only to CPUs from about 2015 on
[build]
rustflags = ["-C", "target-cpu=x86-64-v3"]    # AVX2, FMA, BMI2
```

There is a catch for floating point. Integer addition is associative, so the
compiler may reorder a sum into eight parallel lanes. Floating-point addition
is not associative (`(a + b) + c` can differ from `a + (b + c)`), so the
compiler must keep the sequential order and will **not** vectorize a plain
`f32` sum. You can opt in by reordering the work yourself, with several
independent accumulators:

```rust
pub fn sum_f32(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    let (chunks, rest) = xs.as_chunks::<8>();
    let mut acc = [0.0f32; 8];                  // 8 independent partial sums
    for c in chunks {
        for k in 0..8 {
            acc[k] += c[k];                     // lanes do not depend on each other:
        }                                       // LLVM can map acc to one vector register
    }
    acc.iter().sum::<f32>() + rest.iter().sum::<f32>()
}
```

The result may differ from the sequential sum in the last bits, which is
exactly the freedom the compiler was not allowed to take on its own.

**Level 3: intrinsics with runtime detection.** Intrinsics map one-to-one to
CPU instructions. Because a binary may run on a CPU that lacks the instruction,
the usual pattern is: compile one function with the feature enabled through
`#[target_feature]`, check at runtime whether the CPU supports it, and fall back
otherwise.

```rust
#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
#[target_feature(enable = "avx")]
fn sum_avx(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    use std::arch::x86_64::*;

    let (chunks, rest) = xs.as_chunks::<8>();
    let mut acc = _mm256_setzero_ps();                 // 8 lanes of 0.0
    for c in chunks {
        // SAFETY: `c` is exactly 8 f32s (32 bytes) of valid memory, and
        // loadu has no alignment requirement.
        let v = unsafe { _mm256_loadu_ps(c.as_ptr()) };
        acc = _mm256_add_ps(acc, v);                   // safe: AVX is enabled here
    }
    let mut lanes = [0.0f32; 8];
    // SAFETY: `lanes` has room for exactly 8 f32s.
    unsafe { _mm256_storeu_ps(lanes.as_mut_ptr(), acc) };
    lanes.iter().sum::<f32>() + rest.iter().sum::<f32>()
}

pub fn sum(xs: &[f32]) -> f32 {
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    {
        if is_x86_feature_detected!("avx") {           // checks CPUID once, then caches
            // SAFETY: we just checked that the CPU supports AVX.
            return unsafe { sum_avx(xs) };
        }
    }
    xs.iter().sum()                                     // portable fallback
}
```

The safety rules around this pattern:

- Since Rust 1.86, a function with `#[target_feature]` can be a safe `fn`, but
  *calling* it from code that does not itself enable the feature is `unsafe`:
  running AVX instructions on a CPU without AVX is undefined behaviour. The
  runtime check is what makes the call sound.
- Since Rust 1.87, intrinsics that only operate on register values (such as
  `_mm256_add_ps`) are safe to call inside a function that enables the
  required feature. Intrinsics that read or write memory through raw pointers
  (`loadu`, `storeu`) remain `unsafe`.
- `is_x86_feature_detected!` (and `is_aarch64_feature_detected!`) need `std`.
  If the whole binary is compiled with the feature (`target-cpu` or
  `-C target-feature=+avx2`), `cfg!(target_feature = "avx2")` is true at
  compile time and no runtime check is needed.

Before writing intrinsics, check whether auto-vectorization or a crate
(`memchr` for byte search, `simd-json`, `wide`) already does the job.
Intrinsics are fast but cost the most maintenance: one implementation per
architecture, plus tests that run each path.

> Key Takeaways
> - SIMD processes several values per instruction; data-parallel kernels can
>   gain 4-16x.
> - Start with auto-vectorization: simple loops, no bounds checks, and a
>   suitable `target-cpu` level.
> - Floating-point reductions do not vectorize by themselves; use several
>   accumulators to allow it explicitly.
> - Intrinsics live in `std::arch`; combine `#[target_feature]` with runtime
>   detection and a scalar fallback.
> - Calling a target-feature function is unsafe unless the caller enables the
>   same feature; memory-touching intrinsics are always unsafe.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function that counts how many bytes in a `&[u8]` equal a given
>    byte. Check with `cargo asm` whether it vectorizes with the default target
>    and with `target-cpu=x86-64-v3`.
> 2. Implement `sum_f32` with one accumulator and with eight, benchmark both
>    on 10 million elements, and explain the difference in both speed and
>    result.
> 3. Interview: Your library uses AVX2 intrinsics and a user reports "illegal
>    instruction" crashes on some machines. What went wrong, and how do you
>    restructure the code? (Hint: compile-time versus runtime knowledge of the
>    CPU.)

<a id="152-data-oriented-design"></a>
### 15.2 Data-Oriented Design

Data-oriented design starts from the data and the way the hardware moves it,
rather than from objects and their behaviour; this section covers the cache
effects behind it and the layouts and allocation strategies that follow from
it.

#### Cache Locality

A modern CPU can do an addition in a fraction of a nanosecond, but fetching a
value from main memory takes around 100 nanoseconds, long enough for hundreds
of additions. To hide this gap, CPUs keep recently used memory in a hierarchy
of small, fast **caches**:

| Level | Typical size | Approx. latency | Analogy |
| ----- | ------------ | --------------- | ------- |
| Registers | ~1 KB | 0 cycles | In your hand |
| L1 cache | 32-64 KB per core | ~1 ns (4 cycles) | On your desk |
| L2 cache | 0.5-2 MB per core | ~4 ns | In the desk drawer |
| L3 cache | 8-64 MB shared | ~10-20 ns | On the bookshelf |
| Main memory (DRAM) | GBs | ~80-100 ns | In the library across town |

Memory moves between these levels in fixed blocks called **cache lines**,
64 bytes on almost all current CPUs. Reading one `u8` brings in the 63 bytes
around it too. Programs are fast when they exploit two kinds of **locality**:

- **Spatial locality:** after using one address, use its neighbours. The rest
  of the cache line is already there, and the hardware **prefetcher** notices
  sequential access and fetches the following lines before you ask.
- **Temporal locality:** reuse data soon, while it is still cached.

A program's speed is therefore often decided by *how* it walks memory, not by
how many instructions it runs. The classic demonstration is a 2-D grid stored
row by row in a flat `Vec`:

```rust
const N: usize = 4096;

// Element (row, col) lives at index row * N + col: rows are contiguous.
fn sum_row_major(grid: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    let mut s = 0.0;
    for row in 0..N {
        for col in 0..N {
            s += grid[row * N + col];     // consecutive addresses: every byte of
        }                                 // each cache line is used, prefetch works
    }
    s
}

fn sum_col_major(grid: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    let mut s = 0.0;
    for col in 0..N {
        for row in 0..N {
            s += grid[row * N + col];     // jumps 32 KB each step: one useful value
        }                                 // per cache line, constant cache misses
    }
    s
}
```

Both functions do exactly the same arithmetic, yet the column-major version is
typically several times slower, because for each 8-byte value it uses it
fetches a whole 64-byte line and throws the rest away.

The same principle explains several Rust performance rules:

```text
Vec<T>                  [ T ][ T ][ T ][ T ][ T ]           one contiguous block:
                                                            sequential, prefetchable

Vec<Box<T>>             [ptr][ptr][ptr][ptr]                every element is a separate
                          │    │    │    └──► T  (somewhere)   allocation: each access
                          │    │    └──► T  (elsewhere)        may be a cache miss
                          ▼    ▼
                          T    T

LinkedList<T>           T ──► T ──► T ──► T                 the next address is only known
                                                            after loading the current node
```

- Prefer `Vec<T>` to `Vec<Box<T>>` and to `LinkedList<T>`; even for inserts in
  the middle, a `Vec` often wins until it is very large.
- Prefer enums to `Box<dyn Trait>` in hot collections (Chapter 5): an enum is
  stored inline, while trait objects are scattered on the heap.
- Keep frequently used ("hot") fields together, and move rarely used ("cold")
  fields behind a `Box` or into a separate collection, so more hot data fits
  in each cache line.
- In multi-threaded code, avoid **false sharing**: two threads writing to
  different variables in the *same* cache line slow each other down (Chapter
  10). Align per-thread data to 64 bytes, for example with
  `#[repr(align(64))]` or `crossbeam_utils::CachePadded`.

```rust
use std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64;

#[repr(align(64))]                 // each counter gets its own cache line
struct PaddedCounter(AtomicU64);

struct Stats {
    per_thread: [PaddedCounter; 8],   // threads no longer invalidate each other's lines
}
```

Tools such as `perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references` (Linux) or
`cachegrind` show whether cache misses are actually your problem before you
restructure anything.

> Key Takeaways
> - Main memory is about 100x slower than L1 cache; caches move data in
>   64-byte lines.
> - Sequential access uses whole cache lines and lets the prefetcher work;
>   scattered access wastes most of each line.
> - Contiguous `Vec<T>` and inline enums beat pointer-heavy structures
>   (`Vec<Box<T>>`, linked lists, trait objects) in hot loops.
> - Separate hot from cold fields, and pad per-thread data to avoid false
>   sharing.
> - Confirm cache problems with hardware counters before redesigning.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Benchmark `sum_row_major` against `sum_col_major` for `N` = 256, 1024
>    and 4096, and explain why the gap grows with `N`.
> 2. Fill a `Vec<u64>` and a `LinkedList<u64>` with 10 million values, then
>    time a full traversal of each. Repeat with the list built in random order
>    of allocation.
> 3. Interview: Two threads each increment their own `AtomicU64`, stored side
>    by side in a struct, and the program is slower than with one thread. Why?
>    (Hint: what is the unit at which cores keep their caches coherent?)

#### Struct of Arrays vs Array of Structs

Object-oriented habits put everything about one entity in one struct and then
keep a collection of those structs. This is an **Array of Structs (AoS)**. The
alternative, **Struct of Arrays (SoA)**, keeps one array per field, with the
`i`-th element of every array belonging to entity `i`.

Picture a school's records. AoS is a filing cabinet with one folder per pupil:
perfect when you need everything about Alice. SoA is one register per subject:
perfect when you need every pupil's maths grade, because you read one list from
top to bottom instead of opening every folder.

```rust
// Array of Structs
struct Particle {
    pos: [f32; 3],      // 12 bytes
    vel: [f32; 3],      // 12 bytes
    mass: f32,          //  4 bytes
    color: [u8; 4],     //  4 bytes
    name: String,       // 24 bytes
}                       // 56 bytes per particle
type ParticlesAoS = Vec<Particle>;

// Struct of Arrays
struct ParticlesSoA {
    pos: Vec<[f32; 3]>,
    vel: Vec<[f32; 3]>,
    mass: Vec<f32>,
    color: Vec<[u8; 4]>,
    name: Vec<String>,
}
```

The difference shows when a hot loop touches only some of the fields:

```text
Updating positions (reads pos + vel = 24 of 56 bytes per particle)

AoS memory:  |pos vel mass color name|pos vel mass color name|pos vel ...
              ^^^^^^^                 ^^^^^^^
              useful                  useful        -> ~43% of each cache line is useful

SoA memory:  pos: |p0|p1|p2|p3|p4|p5|...            -> 100% useful, contiguous
             vel: |v0|v1|v2|v3|v4|v5|...            -> 100% useful, contiguous
```

```rust
impl ParticlesSoA {
    fn integrate(&mut self, dt: f32) {
        // Only the two arrays that matter are touched; the loop is simple
        // and bounds-check free, so it auto-vectorizes well.
        for (p, v) in self.pos.iter_mut().zip(&self.vel) {
            p[0] += v[0] * dt;
            p[1] += v[1] * dt;
            p[2] += v[2] * dt;
        }
    }

    fn push(&mut self, pos: [f32; 3], vel: [f32; 3], mass: f32, color: [u8; 4], name: String) {
        // The invariant "all Vecs have the same length" is maintained here,
        // in one place.
        self.pos.push(pos);
        self.vel.push(vel);
        self.mass.push(mass);
        self.color.push(color);
        self.name.push(name);
    }
}
```

Neither layout is always better:

| Aspect | AoS (`Vec<Struct>`) | SoA (struct of `Vec`s) |
| ------ | ------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Loop touching few fields | Wastes cache on unused fields | Uses every fetched byte |
| Access to a whole entity | One cache line or two | One line per field |
| SIMD friendliness | Poor (fields interleaved) | Good (same field contiguous) |
| Adding or removing entities | One push or remove | Must update every array in sync |
| Ergonomics | Natural; borrow one `&mut Particle` | No single "entity" reference; invariant to keep |
| Typical users | Business logic, small collections | Games (ECS), physics, analytics, columnar databases |

Practical middle grounds:

- **Hot/cold splitting:** keep an AoS of the hot fields (`pos`, `vel`) and a
  separate `Vec` for cold ones (`name`). This captures most of the gain with
  little restructuring.
- **AoSoA (tiled):** store small fixed-size blocks, such as 8 positions
  followed by 8 velocities, which matches SIMD width while keeping related data
  close together.
- **Derive macros:** crates such as `soa_derive` generate the SoA container,
  iterators and push/remove methods from a normal struct definition, so the
  synchronization invariant is maintained by generated code.
- **Entity Component Systems:** game engines such as Bevy store components in
  SoA-like tables, and are built on exactly this idea.

Rust's default struct layout already reorders fields to minimize padding
(Chapter 14), but it never splits a struct apart; only you can choose SoA.

> Key Takeaways
> - AoS keeps each entity together; SoA keeps each field together.
> - SoA wins when hot loops read a few fields of many entities, and enables
>   SIMD; AoS wins when you mostly handle whole entities.
> - SoA requires keeping parallel arrays the same length; encapsulate that
>   invariant in one type, or generate it with a derive macro.
> - Hot/cold splitting is a cheap first step that often captures most of the
>   benefit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the particle system in both layouts with 1 million particles
>    and benchmark the `integrate` step. Then add a `name` field of type
>    `String` and measure again.
> 2. Add `fn swap_remove(&mut self, i: usize)` to `ParticlesSoA` that keeps all
>    arrays consistent, and write a test that checks the invariant after random
>    operations.
> 3. Interview: A game's update loop reads position and velocity for 100,000
>    entities but rarely touches their 200-byte inventory. What layout change
>    would you propose, and how would you prove it helped? (Hint: estimate the
>    bytes fetched per entity before and after.)

#### Arena and Slab Allocation

A general-purpose allocator must handle any size, any lifetime and any order of
frees, and that flexibility has a price on every call. Many programs do not
need it. A compiler allocates thousands of syntax-tree nodes that all die
together when the file is done; a request handler allocates temporary data that
all dies when the request ends; a server tracks connections that are all the
same type and come and go individually. Specialized allocators exploit these
patterns.

**Arenas (bump allocation)** grab a large chunk of memory and hand out pieces
by moving a pointer forward. Nothing is freed individually; the whole arena is
released at once.

```text
chunk:  [ node A | node B | node C |            free space            ]
                                   ^
                                   bump pointer: alloc = "return ptr; ptr += size"

drop(arena)  ->  the whole chunk is released in one call
```

It is like a notepad where you only ever write on the next free line and, when
you are done, throw the whole pad away: no erasing, no searching for space.
Allocation is a few instructions, consecutive allocations sit next to each
other in memory (good locality), and freeing a million nodes costs nothing.

The `bumpalo` crate provides a general bump arena. Values borrow from the
arena, so the borrow checker guarantees that nothing outlives it:

```rust
// Cargo.toml: bumpalo = "3"
use bumpalo::Bump;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Expr<'a> {
    Num(i64),
    Add(&'a Expr<'a>, &'a Expr<'a>),     // children are plain references into the arena
    Mul(&'a Expr<'a>, &'a Expr<'a>),
}

fn eval(e: &Expr<'_>) -> i64 {
    match e {
        Expr::Num(n) => *n,
        Expr::Add(a, b) => eval(a) + eval(b),
        Expr::Mul(a, b) => eval(a) * eval(b),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let arena = Bump::new();

    // (2 + 3) * 4: every node is a pointer bump, no malloc per node
    let two = arena.alloc(Expr::Num(2));
    let three = arena.alloc(Expr::Num(3));
    let sum = arena.alloc(Expr::Add(two, three));
    let four = arena.alloc(Expr::Num(4));
    let product = arena.alloc(Expr::Mul(sum, four));

    println!("{}", eval(product));      // 20
}                                       // arena dropped: all nodes freed at once
```

Two things to know about `bumpalo`:

- `Bump` does **not** run destructors of the values in it. Store plain data, or
  use `bumpalo::boxed::Box` for values that need `Drop`. `typed-arena`, which
  holds values of a single type, does run destructors.
- With its `collections` feature it offers arena-backed `Vec` and `String`, and
  `reset()` reuses the memory for the next batch (for example, the next
  request or frame) without returning it to the OS.

**Slabs** solve a different pattern: many objects of *one* type that are
inserted and removed individually, in any order. A slab is a `Vec` of slots
plus a free list of empty slots. Inserting returns a `usize` key; removing puts
the slot back on the free list, so its memory is reused by the next insert.

```text
slots:  [ conn#0 | free | conn#2 | free | conn#4 ]
free list: 3 -> 1 -> end           next insert reuses slot 3, without allocating
```

```rust
// Cargo.toml: slab = "0.4"
use slab::Slab;

struct Connection {
    peer: String,
    bytes_in: u64,
}

fn main() {
    let mut conns: Slab<Connection> = Slab::with_capacity(1024);

    let a = conns.insert(Connection { peer: "10.0.0.1".into(), bytes_in: 0 });
    let b = conns.insert(Connection { peer: "10.0.0.2".into(), bytes_in: 0 });

    conns[a].bytes_in += 512;             // O(1) access by key
    conns.remove(b);                      // slot b goes on the free list

    let c = conns.insert(Connection { peer: "10.0.0.3".into(), bytes_in: 0 });
    assert_eq!(b, c);                     // the freed slot (and key) is reused

    for (key, conn) in &conns {
        println!("{key}: {} ({} bytes)", conn.peer, conn.bytes_in);
    }
}
```

The `assert_eq!(b, c)` line shows the slab's main hazard: a key can be reused
for a different object. Code that keeps a stale key around silently accesses
the wrong connection. Generational indices (see Index-Based Graph Structures,
below) fix this.

| Tool | Best for | Frees individually? | Runs `Drop`? |
| ---- | -------- | ------------------- | ------------ |
| `bumpalo::Bump` | Mixed types with one shared lifetime (ASTs, per-request data) | No | No (by default) |
| `typed-arena::Arena<T>` | Many values of one type with one shared lifetime | No | Yes |
| `slab::Slab<T>` | One type, individual insert/remove, `usize` keys | Yes (slot reuse) | Yes |
| `slotmap::SlotMap<K, V>` | Like a slab, but keys detect reuse | Yes | Yes |
| Global allocator swap (`mimalloc`, Chapter 14) | Whole-program speed-up with no code changes | Yes | Yes |

> Key Takeaways
> - Arenas allocate by bumping a pointer and free everything at once: very
>   fast, with good locality, for data that shares one lifetime.
> - Arena references borrow from the arena, so the borrow checker prevents
>   use after the arena is gone.
> - `bumpalo` does not run destructors by default; `typed-arena` does.
> - Slabs store one type in reusable slots addressed by `usize` keys; keys can
>   be reused, so stale keys are a logic bug to guard against.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a tiny arithmetic parser that builds the `Expr` tree above in a
>    `Bump`, then parse 100,000 expressions with and without the arena (using
>    `Box<Expr>` instead) and compare the runtime.
> 2. Use `Slab` to implement a timer wheel or a simple connection table with
>    `open`, `close` and `send` operations, and write a test showing the stale
>    key problem.
> 3. Interview: Why does a per-request arena usually make a web service faster,
>    and what kind of data must never be put into it? (Hint: think about the
>    request's lifetime and about values that must outlive the request or need
>    destructors.)

#### Small Vector Optimization

Collections often hold just a few elements. Most function calls have fewer than
four arguments, most identifiers are shorter than 24 bytes, and most HTTP
headers have one value. A `Vec` always stores its elements on the heap, so even
a one-element `Vec` costs an allocation and a pointer dereference.

**Small vector optimization** stores up to `N` elements *inline*, inside the
value itself, and only switches ("spills") to a heap allocation when more are
needed. It is like a wallet with a few card slots: the common case fits, and
you only need a separate card holder when you carry more cards than slots.

```text
Vec<u32> (24 bytes on the stack)       SmallVec<[u32; 4]> holding 3 items
┌─────┬─────┬─────┐                    ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ ptr │ cap │ len │                    │ len=3 │ 7 │ 9 │ 4 │ (unused)  │   no heap at all
└──┬──┴─────┴─────┘                    └───────────────────────────────┘
   ▼
 heap: [7, 9, 4]                       after pushing a 5th item: spills to the heap,
                                       then behaves like a Vec
```

The most common crates:

| Crate / type | Inline storage | Behaviour when full | Notes |
| ------------ | -------------- | ------------------- | ----- |
| `smallvec::SmallVec<[T; N]>` | Up to `N` | Spills to the heap | Most widely used; used inside rustc and Servo |
| `arrayvec::ArrayVec<T, N>` | Exactly up to `N` | `push` panics, `try_push` returns an error | Never allocates; works in `no_std` |
| `tinyvec::TinyVec<[T; N]>` | Up to `N` | Spills to the heap | 100% safe code; requires `T: Default` |
| `compact_str::CompactString` | Up to 24 bytes of a string | Spills to the heap | Same size as `String` |

```rust
// Cargo.toml: smallvec = "1"
use smallvec::{smallvec, SmallVec};

/// Most tokens have at most 4 attributes, so this almost never allocates.
type Attrs = SmallVec<[u32; 4]>;

fn main() {
    let mut a: Attrs = smallvec![1, 2, 3];
    assert!(!a.spilled());                 // still stored inline

    a.push(4);
    assert!(!a.spilled());                 // exactly 4: still inline

    a.push(5);
    assert!(a.spilled());                  // 5th element: moved to the heap

    // The API mirrors Vec: Deref to a slice, iteration, extend, etc.
    let total: u32 = a.iter().sum();
    println!("{total}, {} bytes on the stack", std::mem::size_of::<Attrs>());
}
```

`ArrayVec` is the right choice when a hard upper bound is part of the design
(for example, "at most 8 path segments") or there is no heap at all:

```rust
// Cargo.toml: arrayvec = "0.7"
use arrayvec::ArrayVec;

fn parse_octets(s: &str) -> Option<ArrayVec<u8, 4>> {
    let mut out = ArrayVec::new();
    for part in s.split('.') {
        out.try_push(part.parse().ok()?).ok()?;   // a 5th octet is an error, not a panic
    }
    out.is_full().then_some(out)                  // exactly 4 octets
}
```

The optimization is not free, and it is easy to make things worse:

- **The value gets bigger.** `SmallVec<[u64; 16]>` is about 136 bytes, compared
  with 24 for a `Vec`. Moving it copies all of that, and a `Vec` of them
  wastes memory when most are empty. Keep `N` small.
- **Every access has a branch** ("inline or spilled?"). If most instances
  spill anyway, you pay the branch and the larger size and still allocate.
- **Choose `N` from data.** Log or histogram real lengths first, then pick the
  `N` that covers most cases (for example, the 90th or 95th percentile).

> Key Takeaways
> - Small-vector types store up to `N` elements inline and only allocate when
>   they overflow.
> - `SmallVec` spills to the heap; `ArrayVec` has a fixed capacity and never
>   allocates; `CompactString` does the same for strings.
> - The value grows by `N` elements, and each access branches on inline versus
>   heap, so keep `N` small and pick it from measured length distributions.
> - Use it where many short collections are created on hot paths, not as a
>   general replacement for `Vec`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Print `size_of` for `Vec<u32>`, `SmallVec<[u32; 2]>`,
>    `SmallVec<[u32; 8]>`, `ArrayVec<u32, 8>` and `CompactString`, and explain
>    each number.
> 2. Write a tokenizer that stores the characters of each identifier in a
>    `String`, then in a `CompactString`. Measure allocations with the counting
>    allocator from Chapter 12 on a real source file.
> 3. Interview: After replacing `Vec<Item>` with `SmallVec<[Item; 32]>` in a
>    struct stored in a large `HashMap`, memory use tripled and lookups got
>    slower. What happened? (Hint: compute the size of the struct before and
>    after, and think about how many of those maps' values ever hold 32
>    items.)

#### Index-Based Graph Structures

Graphs, trees with parent links, doubly linked lists and observer networks all
contain cycles or shared references. In languages with a garbage collector you
simply let objects point at each other. In Rust, references must have a single
owner and a provable lifetime, so the direct translation needs
`Rc<RefCell<Node>>` plus `Weak` for back edges (Chapter 9). That works, but it
is verbose, every access pays for runtime borrow checks and reference counts,
and every node is a separate heap allocation scattered in memory.

The data-oriented alternative is to store all nodes in one `Vec` and replace
pointers with **indices** into it. The `Vec` is the single owner of every
node; an edge is just a number.

```text
Pointer graph:                     Index graph:
                                   nodes: [ A | B | C | D ]
  A ──► B                                   0   1   2   3
  │     │                          edges of A (0): [1, 2]
  ▼     ▼                          edges of B (1): [3]
  C ──► D                          edges of C (2): [3]
                                   edges of D (3): []
```

It is like a city map that labels each building with a number and lists
streets as "from 3 to 7", instead of tying a piece of string between buildings.

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct NodeId(u32);              // a newtype: cannot be confused with other integers

pub struct Graph<T> {
    nodes: Vec<T>,                   // node payloads, contiguous
    adj: Vec<Vec<NodeId>>,           // adj[i] = outgoing edges of node i
}

impl<T> Graph<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Graph { nodes: Vec::new(), adj: Vec::new() }
    }

    pub fn add_node(&mut self, value: T) -> NodeId {
        let id = NodeId(self.nodes.len() as u32);
        self.nodes.push(value);
        self.adj.push(Vec::new());
        id
    }

    pub fn add_edge(&mut self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) {
        self.adj[from.0 as usize].push(to);   // cycles are fine: they are just numbers
    }

    pub fn neighbors(&self, n: NodeId) -> impl Iterator<Item = NodeId> + '_ {
        self.adj[n.0 as usize].iter().copied()
    }

    pub fn get_mut(&mut self, n: NodeId) -> &mut T {
        &mut self.nodes[n.0 as usize]         // ordinary &mut: no RefCell needed
    }
}

/// Breadth-first search: visited flags are a Vec<bool> indexed by the same ids.
pub fn reachable<T>(g: &Graph<T>, start: NodeId) -> Vec<NodeId> {
    let mut seen = vec![false; g.nodes.len()];
    let mut queue = std::collections::VecDeque::from([start]);
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    seen[start.0 as usize] = true;
    while let Some(n) = queue.pop_front() {
        out.push(n);
        for m in g.neighbors(n) {
            if !std::mem::replace(&mut seen[m.0 as usize], true) {
                queue.push_back(m);
            }
        }
    }
    out
}
```

Benefits over `Rc<RefCell<_>>`:

| Aspect | `Rc<RefCell<Node>>` | Indices into a `Vec` |
| ------ | ------------------- | -------------------- |
| Cycles | Need `Weak` to avoid leaks | No issue |
| Mutation | Runtime-checked `borrow_mut()`, can panic | Plain `&mut` through the graph |
| Memory layout | One allocation per node, scattered | Contiguous, cache-friendly |
| Edge size | 8-byte pointer plus refcount traffic | 4-byte `u32` |
| Side tables | `HashMap<*const Node, _>` or extra fields | `Vec<X>` indexed by the same id |
| Serialization | Hard (pointers) | Trivial (indices are data) |
| Risk | Panics on double borrow, leaks on cycles | Stale or wrong indices |

That last row is the price. The compiler no longer checks that an index refers
to a live node. If nodes can be **removed**, a slot may be reused, and an old
`NodeId` then silently points at a different node: the *ABA problem*.
**Generational indices** fix this by storing a generation counter in each slot
and in each key:

```text
slot 3: generation 1, node "D"       key (3, gen 1) -> "D"
remove slot 3          -> generation becomes 2
insert "E" into slot 3 -> slot 3: generation 2, node "E"
old key (3, gen 1)     -> generation mismatch -> None instead of "E"
```

The `slotmap` crate implements this, and `petgraph` provides full graph types
(with algorithms such as Dijkstra and topological sort) built on indices:

```rust
// Cargo.toml: slotmap = "1"
use slotmap::{new_key_type, SlotMap};

new_key_type! { struct EntityKey; }      // a distinct key type per map

fn main() {
    let mut entities: SlotMap<EntityKey, &str> = SlotMap::with_key();
    let d = entities.insert("D");
    entities.remove(d);
    let e = entities.insert("E");        // may reuse the same slot

    assert_eq!(entities.get(d), None);   // the stale key is detected
    assert_eq!(entities.get(e), Some(&"E"));
}
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Store nodes in a `Vec` and refer to them by index: no `Rc`, no `RefCell`,
>   no lifetimes in the node type, and a cache-friendly layout.
> - Wrap indices in a newtype (`NodeId(u32)`) so they cannot be mixed up with
>   other integers or other graphs' ids.
> - Side data (visited flags, distances) becomes a parallel `Vec` indexed by
>   the same id.
> - When nodes can be removed, use generational indices (`slotmap`) to detect
>   stale keys; use `petgraph` for ready-made graph algorithms.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `fn shortest_path(&self, from: NodeId, to: NodeId) -> Option<Vec<NodeId>>`
>    to the `Graph` above using BFS and a `Vec<Option<NodeId>>` of parents.
> 2. Implement a doubly linked list where nodes live in a `Vec` and `prev` and
>    `next` are `Option<u32>` indices, with `push_front`, `push_back` and
>    `remove`. Reuse freed slots with a free list.
> 3. Interview: Index-based graphs are sometimes described as "turning off the
>    borrow checker with integers". Is that fair? What can still go wrong, and
>    what does Rust still guarantee? (Hint: compare a stale index with a
>    dangling pointer: which one can cause undefined behaviour?)

<a id="153-embedded-and-no_std"></a>
### 15.3 Embedded and no_std

Rust can run without an operating system, on microcontrollers with a few
kilobytes of RAM, in bootloaders and kernels, and inside other runtimes; this
section covers how a crate opts out of the standard library, what remains
available, how to build for other targets, and the abstractions the embedded
ecosystem uses to talk to hardware safely.

#### The no_std Attribute

Much of the standard library assumes an operating system underneath: files,
threads, sockets, environment variables, a heap provided by `malloc`, a clock,
and a way to print panic messages. A microcontroller has none of these; it has
flash memory, some RAM, and hardware peripherals mapped to memory addresses.

The crate-level attribute `#![no_std]` tells the compiler: "do not link `std`
into this crate; link only `core`." It is like packing for a camping trip
instead of moving into a furnished flat: you bring only what works without
mains electricity, and you pack the rest yourself.

```rust
// src/lib.rs
#![no_std]                       // the prelude is now core's prelude

/// Computes a CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x07). Uses only core: slices,
/// integers, iterators and control flow are all available without an OS.
pub fn crc8(data: &[u8]) -> u8 {
    let mut crc = 0u8;
    for &byte in data {
        crc ^= byte;
        for _ in 0..8 {
            crc = if crc & 0x80 != 0 { (crc << 1) ^ 0x07 } else { crc << 1 };
        }
    }
    crc
}
```

What changes for a `no_std` **library**:

- Imports come from `core` (`core::fmt`, `core::mem`, `core::ops`) instead of
  `std`. Most `std` paths re-export `core` items, so the change is often just
  the path.
- No `Vec`, `String`, `Box` or `format!` unless you opt into `alloc` (next
  topic).
- No `println!`. Libraries usually return data and let the application decide
  how to output it.

A widely used pattern (Chapter 8) is to make `std` an optional, default-enabled
feature, so the same crate serves both desktop and embedded users:

```rust
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]

#[cfg(feature = "std")]
impl std::error::Error for MyError {}     // only when std is available
```

A `no_std` **binary** (firmware) has more to provide, because the standard
library normally supplies the program's start-up code and panic behaviour:

```rust
// src/main.rs: a minimal Cortex-M firmware
#![no_std]
#![no_main]                      // there is no OS to call a normal `main`

use cortex_m_rt::entry;          // runtime crate: vector table, RAM init, reset handler
use panic_halt as _;             // links a panic handler (see Panic Handlers)

#[entry]                         // the function the reset handler jumps to
fn main() -> ! {                 // `!`: firmware never returns, there is nowhere to go
    let mut ticks: u32 = 0;
    loop {
        ticks = ticks.wrapping_add(1);
        cortex_m::asm::nop();
    }
}
```

| | Normal binary | `no_std` binary |
| - | ------------- | --------------- |
| Entry point | `fn main()`, called by std's start-up code | `#![no_main]` + runtime attribute such as `#[entry]` |
| Return from main | Process exits | Not possible: `-> !` |
| Panic behaviour | Provided by std | You must provide a `#[panic_handler]` |
| Heap | Provided | Optional; you must provide a global allocator |
| Memory layout | Decided by the OS loader | Decided by a linker script (`memory.x`) |

Two practical tips:

- Testing a `no_std` library on your PC still works: `cargo test` compiles the
  test harness with `std`. Add `#[cfg(test)] extern crate std;` if the tests
  themselves need `std` items.
- Verify that the library really is `no_std` by building it for a target that
  has no `std` at all. On the host, a dependency that quietly uses `std` still
  compiles:

```bash
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf
cargo build --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf     # fails if anything pulls in std
```

> Key Takeaways
> - `#![no_std]` links only `core`, for environments without an operating
>   system.
> - Libraries mostly change import paths; a `std` feature lets one crate serve
>   both worlds.
> - Firmware also needs `#![no_main]`, a runtime-provided entry point that never
>   returns, a panic handler, and a linker script.
> - Check `no_std` compatibility by building for a bare-metal target, not just
>   the host.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `no_std` library with a fixed-point type `Q16_16` that implements
>    `Add`, `Mul` and `core::fmt::Display`, with tests that run on your PC.
> 2. Take a small existing library of yours and add a default `std` feature.
>    Make it build with `--no-default-features --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf`.
> 3. Interview: Your `no_std` crate builds for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, but
>    a user reports it fails on `thumbv6m-none-eabi`. How can that happen, and
>    how do you catch it in CI? (Hint: what does the host target always have
>    available, even when your crate does not ask for it?)

#### core vs alloc vs std

The standard library is really three layers stacked on each other. Each layer
adds what needs one more thing from the environment:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ std    needs an OS: files, threads, net, time, env,         │
│        process, HashMap (random seeds), println!, panics    │
│        with unwinding; re-exports everything below          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ alloc  needs a heap (a global allocator): Box, Vec, String, │
│        Rc, Arc, BTreeMap, VecDeque, format!, ToString       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ core   needs nothing: primitives, Option, Result, iterators,│
│        slices, str, traits (Clone, Iterator, Future, ...),  │
│        fmt, mem, ptr, cell, atomics, num, time::Duration,   │
│        net::IpAddr, ffi::CStr, error::Error                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Think of it as a house: `core` is the foundation and walls, `alloc` adds
plumbing (a water supply, the heap), and `std` connects the house to the city
grid (the OS). A cabin in the woods can have walls and plumbing without a grid
connection.

| Item | `core` | `alloc` | `std` only |
| ---- | :----: | :-----: | :--------: |
| `Option`, `Result`, iterators, slices, `&str` | Yes | | |
| `Cell`, `RefCell`, atomics, `Duration` | Yes | | |
| `fmt::Write`, `write!` into a buffer | Yes | | |
| `core::error::Error` (Rust 1.81+) | Yes | | |
| `Box`, `Vec`, `String`, `format!` | | Yes | |
| `Rc`, `Arc`, `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet`, `VecDeque` | | Yes | |
| `HashMap`, `HashSet` | | | Yes (use `hashbrown` in `no_std`) |
| `Mutex`, `thread`, `fs`, `net::TcpStream`, `Instant` | | | Yes |
| `println!`, `std::io` | | | Yes |

`HashMap` lives in `std` only because its default hasher needs random seeds
from the OS. The `hashbrown` crate, whose implementation `std` itself uses,
provides the same map for `no_std` + `alloc`.

To use `alloc`, declare it explicitly and, in a binary, register a global
allocator that manages a region of RAM:

```rust
// A no_std library that needs heap collections
#![no_std]
extern crate alloc;                       // alloc is not in the prelude: opt in

use alloc::{format, string::String, vec::Vec};

pub fn csv_line(fields: &[u32]) -> String {
    let parts: Vec<String> = fields.iter().map(|f| format!("{f}")).collect();
    parts.join(",")
}
```

```rust
// In the firmware binary: provide the heap
// Cargo.toml: embedded-alloc = "0.6"
use embedded_alloc::LlffHeap as Heap;

#[global_allocator]
static HEAP: Heap = Heap::empty();

fn init_heap() {
    use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
    const HEAP_SIZE: usize = 4096;                        // 4 KB of RAM for the heap
    static mut HEAP_MEM: [MaybeUninit<u8>; HEAP_SIZE] = [MaybeUninit::uninit(); HEAP_SIZE];
    // SAFETY: called exactly once at start-up, before any allocation, and
    // HEAP_MEM is never accessed anywhere else.
    unsafe { HEAP.init(&raw mut HEAP_MEM as usize, HEAP_SIZE) }
}
```

On a microcontroller, think carefully before adding a heap. Allocation can fail
at runtime (out of memory panics), fragmentation can make a long-running device
fail after days, and timing becomes less predictable. Many firmware projects
avoid `alloc` entirely and use fixed-capacity collections instead, such as
`heapless::Vec<T, N>` and `heapless::String<N>`, or `ArrayVec` (15.2), whose
capacity is part of the type.

When writing a library, depend on the lowest layer you can. A crate that needs
only `core` works everywhere; one that needs `alloc` excludes the smallest
devices; one that needs `std` excludes all bare-metal targets.

> Key Takeaways
> - `core` needs nothing, `alloc` needs a heap, `std` needs an OS; `std`
>   re-exports the other two.
> - Use `extern crate alloc;` to opt into heap types in a `no_std` crate; the
>   final binary must provide a `#[global_allocator]`.
> - `HashMap` is `std`-only because of random seeding; use `hashbrown` or
>   `BTreeMap` instead.
> - Embedded projects often avoid the heap and use fixed-capacity collections
>   such as `heapless`.
> - Libraries should depend on the lowest layer that is enough.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify each of these into `core`, `alloc` or `std`: `Arc`, `AtomicU32`,
>    `Instant`, `Duration`, `BTreeMap`, `HashSet`, `fmt::Write`, `Mutex`,
>    `RefCell`, `VecDeque`. Check your answers in the documentation.
> 2. Port a function that builds a `HashMap<String, u32>` word count to
>    `no_std` + `alloc` using `BTreeMap`, and then to `no_std` without `alloc`
>    using `heapless::FnvIndexMap`.
> 3. Interview: Why is `HashMap` not available in `alloc`, even though
>    `BTreeMap` is? (Hint: think about what the default hasher needs from the
>    environment in order to resist denial-of-service attacks.)

#### Cross-Compilation Targets

Embedded development is almost always **cross-compilation**: you build on a
laptop (the *host*) for a different CPU (the *target*). rustc is a cross
compiler out of the box, because LLVM supports many architectures. What you
need per target is a precompiled `core`/`alloc`/`std` for it, and a way to
link.

Targets are named by a **target triple** (which today often has four parts):

```text
  thumbv7em - none - eabihf
  │           │      └── ABI: embedded ABI with hardware floating point
  │           └── OS / vendor: none = bare metal
  └── architecture: ARM Thumb-2, ARMv7E-M (Cortex-M4/M7)

  x86_64 - unknown - linux - gnu
  │        │         │       └── C library / ABI (gnu, musl)
  │        │         └── operating system
  │        └── vendor
  └── architecture
```

| Target | Typical hardware | `std`? |
| ------ | ---------------- | ------ |
| `thumbv6m-none-eabi` | Cortex-M0/M0+ (RP2040, STM32G0) | No |
| `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` | Cortex-M4F/M7F (STM32F4, nRF52) | No |
| `thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf` | Cortex-M33 (nRF5340, RP2350) | No |
| `riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf` | RISC-V microcontrollers (ESP32-C6) | No |
| `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` | Raspberry Pi 4/5, ARM servers | Yes |
| `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` | Fully static Linux binaries | Yes |
| `wasm32-unknown-unknown` | WebAssembly in browsers | Partial (no OS APIs) |

Rust supports targets in three **tiers**: tier 1 targets are guaranteed to
build and pass tests, tier 2 targets are guaranteed to build (most embedded
targets are here, with precompiled `core`), and tier 3 targets have no
precompiled standard library and need the nightly `-Z build-std` option.

The workflow for a bare-metal target:

```bash
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf          # precompiled core + alloc
rustc --print target-list | grep thumb           # all known targets
rustc --print cfg --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf # cfg values: target_arch, features, ...
cargo build --release --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf
```

Typing `--target` every time is tedious, so firmware projects set it in
`.cargo/config.toml`, together with the linker script and the command that
flashes and runs the program:

```toml
# .cargo/config.toml
[build]
target = "thumbv7em-none-eabihf"         # default target for this project

[target.thumbv7em-none-eabihf]
runner = "probe-rs run --chip STM32F411RETx"   # `cargo run` flashes the board
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-Tlink.x"]        # cortex-m-rt's linker script
```

The runtime's `link.x` includes a `memory.x` file that you write for your
chip, describing where flash and RAM live (values from the datasheet):

```text
/* memory.x at the project root */
MEMORY
{
  FLASH : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 512K
  RAM   : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 128K
}
```

For targets with an OS (for example, building an `aarch64` Linux binary on an
`x86_64` laptop), rustc compiles fine but needs a **linker and C libraries for
the target**. The options, from manual to automatic:

| Approach | How |
| -------- | --- |
| System cross toolchain | Install `gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu`; set `linker = "aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc"` under `[target.aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu]` |
| `cross` | `cross build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`: runs the build in a container that has the toolchain |
| `cargo-zigbuild` | Uses Zig as a cross linker; also lets you pick the glibc version to target |
| `musl` targets | Static binaries with no glibc dependency on the target system |

Code can adapt to the target with `cfg` (Chapter 8):

```rust
#[cfg(target_arch = "arm")]
fn wait_for_interrupt() { cortex_m::asm::wfi(); }     // sleep until an interrupt

#[cfg(not(target_arch = "arm"))]
fn wait_for_interrupt() { std::thread::yield_now(); } // host simulation
```

> Key Takeaways
> - rustc cross-compiles natively; per target you need its standard library
>   (`rustup target add`) and a linker.
> - Target triples encode architecture, vendor, OS and ABI; `none` means bare
>   metal.
> - Embedded projects set the target, linker script and `probe-rs` runner in
>   `.cargo/config.toml`, and describe flash and RAM in `memory.x`.
> - For Linux targets, use a cross linker, `cross` or `cargo-zigbuild`; tier 3
>   targets need nightly `-Z build-std`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a "hello world" for `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` and
>    `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` using `cross` or `cargo-zigbuild`, and inspect
>    the results with `file` and `ldd`.
> 2. Run `rustc --print cfg` for `thumbv6m-none-eabi` and `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`
>    and compare the output. Which differences matter for atomics and floating
>    point?
> 3. Interview: A firmware build links fine but the board does nothing after
>    flashing. Your colleague copied `memory.x` from another project. What
>    would you check first? (Hint: compare the addresses and sizes in the file
>    with the chip's datasheet.)

#### Panic Handlers

In normal Rust, a panic prints a message to stderr, unwinds the stack running
destructors, and ends the thread. All of that is implemented in `std`. On bare
metal there is no stderr, no threads, and usually no unwinding support, so
`core` leaves one decision open: **what happens on panic?** Every `no_std`
binary must answer it by defining exactly one function marked
`#[panic_handler]`.

It is like the emergency procedure for a building. The fire alarm (the panic)
is built in, but each building has to post its own evacuation plan: stop the
machines, call for help, or restart.

The required signature:

```rust
use core::panic::PanicInfo;

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(info: &PanicInfo) -> ! {        // `!`: the handler must never return
    let _ = info;                        // location() and message() describe the panic
    loop {}                              // simplest possible policy: halt forever
}
```

Rules:

- Exactly one `#[panic_handler]` per final binary. Zero gives the error
  "`#[panic_handler]` function required, but not found"; two give "found
  duplicate lang item `panic_impl`".
- **Libraries never define one.** The application chooses the policy.
- Bare-metal targets use `panic = "abort"` behaviour by default (no unwinding).
  If you build a `no_std` binary for a hosted target, also set
  `panic = "abort"` in both the `dev` and `release` profiles.

Usually you pick a ready-made handler crate and link it with
`use crate_name as _;`:

| Crate | Behaviour | Use case |
| ----- | --------- | -------- |
| `panic-halt` | Infinite loop | Simplest; attach a debugger to inspect |
| `panic-reset` | Resets the microcontroller | Production devices that should recover |
| `panic-probe` | Prints the message over the debug probe (with `defmt`), then triggers a breakpoint | Development with `probe-rs` |
| `panic-semihosting` | Prints through the debugger's semihosting channel | Debugging (very slow; requires a debugger) |

A custom handler can combine policies, for example logging the location to a
serial port and then resetting. It runs in a broken program state, so it must
be simple and must not panic itself:

```rust
use core::fmt::Write;
use core::panic::PanicInfo;

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(info: &PanicInfo) -> ! {
    cortex_m::interrupt::disable();                  // nothing may preempt us now

    // SAFETY: interrupts are disabled and we never return, so no other code
    // can be using the UART concurrently. (debug_uart is board-specific.)
    let uart = unsafe { debug_uart::steal() };
    let mut w = uart.writer();
    if let Some(loc) = info.location() {
        let _ = writeln!(w, "PANIC at {}:{}", loc.file(), loc.line());
    }
    let _ = writeln!(w, "{}", info.message());       // PanicMessage implements Display

    cortex_m::peripheral::SCB::sys_reset();          // reset the chip; returns `!`
}
```

Panics also cost **flash space**: the formatting machinery and the message and
file name strings of every possible panic end up in the binary. On small chips
this matters, so firmware developers reduce panic sites (use `get()` instead
of indexing, handle `Result`s instead of `unwrap()`), use `defmt`, which sends
compact indices instead of formatted strings, and check what takes space with
`cargo bloat` or `cargo size` from `cargo-binutils`.

> Key Takeaways
> - `no_std` binaries must define exactly one `#[panic_handler]` with
>   signature `fn(&PanicInfo) -> !`; libraries must not define one.
> - `PanicInfo` provides `location()` and `message()` for logging.
> - Choose a policy: halt (`panic-halt`), reset (`panic-reset`), or report via
>   the debug probe (`panic-probe`).
> - Keep custom handlers minimal and non-panicking; reduce panic sites to save
>   flash.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a firmware with `panic-halt`, then switch to `panic-probe` and
>    `defmt`, trigger a panic with an out-of-bounds index, and read the message
>    with `probe-rs run`.
> 2. Write a panic handler that stores the panic line number in a
>    `#[unsafe(link_section = ".uninit")]` static (memory that survives a reset),
>    resets the chip, and reports the stored value on the next boot.
> 3. Interview: Why does Rust require the application, not the library, to
>    provide the panic handler, and what would go wrong if two dependencies
>    each defined one? (Hint: think about policy decisions and the linker's
>    view of a single global function.)

#### Interrupt-Safe Abstractions

A microcontroller usually has a single core and no threads, so it may seem that
data races cannot happen. They can, through **interrupts**. When a timer
expires or a byte arrives on the UART, the CPU pauses the main program at any
instruction, runs an interrupt handler, and then resumes. If both touch the
same variable, the result is the same as a race between two threads:

```text
main loop                         interrupt handler (TIMER)
---------                         -------------------------
load  COUNTER -> r0  (r0 = 5)
                     ◄── interrupt fires here
                                  load  COUNTER -> r1 (5)
                                  add   r1, 1          (6)
                                  store r1 -> COUNTER  (6)
                     ──► return to main
add   r0, 10        (r0 = 15)
store r0 -> COUNTER (15)          the interrupt's increment is lost
```

This is why accessing `static mut` requires `unsafe`: the compiler cannot know
whether an interrupt handler touches the same static. Rust's answer in embedded
code is the same as for threads (Chapter 10): make shared state `Sync`, and use
a primitive that makes each access safe. Interrupt handlers are like a phone
that can ring while you are writing in a shared notebook; you either use an
indivisible action (atomics) or briefly turn the phone off (a critical
section).

**1. Atomics** for single values, when the target supports them:

```rust
use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};

static TICKS: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0);    // no unsafe, no static mut

// #[interrupt] comes from the chip's PAC/HAL crate, e.g. stm32f4xx_hal::pac::interrupt
#[interrupt]
fn TIM2() {
    TICKS.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);      // one indivisible read-modify-write
    // ... clear the timer's interrupt flag here
}

fn uptime_ms() -> u32 {
    TICKS.load(Ordering::Relaxed)
}
```

Cortex-M0/M0+ (`thumbv6m`) have atomic loads and stores but no
compare-and-swap, so `fetch_add` does not exist there. The `portable-atomic`
crate provides the same API and emulates the missing operations with critical
sections.

**2. Critical sections** for anything larger than one word. A critical section
temporarily disables interrupts so that a block of code runs without being
preempted. The `critical-section` crate gives a portable API, and its `Mutex`
can only be accessed by presenting a `CriticalSection` token, a value that
proves interrupts are currently disabled:

```rust
use core::cell::RefCell;
use critical_section::Mutex;

struct Uart { /* the peripheral's registers */ }
impl Uart {
    fn write_byte(&mut self, _b: u8) { /* ... */ }
}

// Initialized to None: the peripheral is created in main and moved in later.
static UART: Mutex<RefCell<Option<Uart>>> = Mutex::new(RefCell::new(None));

fn init(uart: Uart) {
    critical_section::with(|cs| {
        UART.borrow_ref_mut(cs).replace(uart);  // move ownership into the global
    });
}

#[interrupt]
fn USART2() {
    critical_section::with(|cs| {               // interrupts disabled inside
        if let Some(uart) = UART.borrow_ref_mut(cs).as_mut() {
            uart.write_byte(b'!');
        }
    });                                          // interrupts restored here
}
```

The type does the enforcement work:

| Piece | Role |
| ----- | ---- |
| `critical_section::Mutex<T>` | `Sync` wrapper; its contents are reachable only with a `CriticalSection` token |
| `CriticalSection<'cs>` token | Only obtainable inside `critical_section::with`, so holding one proves interrupts are off |
| `RefCell<T>` | Interior mutability, so the `static` can be mutated without `static mut` |
| `Option<T>` | The peripheral does not exist at compile time; it is moved in after start-up |

Keep critical sections short: while interrupts are disabled, the system cannot
react to events, and real-time deadlines can be missed.

**3. Frameworks** remove most of this boilerplate:

- **RTIC** (Real-Time Interrupt-driven Concurrency) lets you declare shared
  resources and task priorities; it checks at compile time which tasks share
  what, and implements locking with the hardware's interrupt priorities, often
  with zero runtime cost.
- **Embassy** is an async runtime for microcontrollers: tasks are `async fn`s,
  interrupts wake futures (Chapter 11), and sharing uses async mutexes and
  channels from `embassy-sync`.

Finally, keep **volatile** and **atomic** apart. Hardware registers are read
and written with `read_volatile` and `write_volatile` (usually wrapped by the
PAC), which stops the compiler from removing or merging accesses. Volatile
does *not* make an access indivisible or synchronize anything; for sharing
data between the main loop and interrupts, use atomics or critical sections.

> Key Takeaways
> - Interrupts preempt the main program at any instruction, so shared data
>   needs synchronization even on a single core.
> - Use atomics for single values (`portable-atomic` on cores without
>   compare-and-swap) and critical sections for larger state.
> - `critical_section::Mutex<RefCell<Option<T>>>` is the standard pattern for
>   moving a peripheral into a global that interrupts can use.
> - RTIC and Embassy enforce safe sharing with compile-time analysis or async
>   primitives.
> - Volatile is for memory-mapped I/O, not for synchronization.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a button-press counter: a GPIO interrupt increments an
>    `AtomicU32`, and the main loop prints the count when it changes. Then make
>    it build for `thumbv6m-none-eabi` with `portable-atomic`.
> 2. Move an LED pin into a `Mutex<RefCell<Option<Led>>>` and toggle it from a
>    timer interrupt. What happens if `init` is called after the interrupt is
>    enabled?
> 3. Interview: A colleague replaced a `critical_section::Mutex` around a
