>    16-byte struct with `read_volatile`/`write_volatile` "because it is
>    faster". Why is the new code wrong? (Hint: what can happen between two
>    volatile writes of the same struct?)

#### Embedded HAL Ecosystem

Every microcontroller family has different registers for the same jobs: set a
pin high, send bytes over SPI, read from I2C. If a temperature sensor driver
were written directly against one chip's registers, it would have to be
rewritten for every other chip. The Rust embedded ecosystem solves this with
layers and shared traits, the same idea as the `Read` and `Write` traits that
let any code work with files, sockets or memory buffers.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Application / firmware          your logic                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Board support crate (BSP)       "LED is pin PA5, sensor on I2C1" │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Device drivers                  generic over embedded-hal traits │
│ (sensors, displays, radios)     work on ANY chip                 │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ HAL crate                       implements the embedded-hal      │
│ (stm32f4xx-hal, nrf-hal, ...)   traits for one chip family       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PAC (peripheral access crate)   typed register access, generated │
│                                 from the vendor's SVD file       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Core crates                     cortex-m (CPU instructions),     │
│                                 cortex-m-rt (start-up, vectors)  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Layer | Example crates | What it gives you |
| ----- | -------------- | ----------------- |
| Core support | `cortex-m`, `cortex-m-rt`, `riscv`, `riscv-rt` | Entry point, interrupt vector table, CPU instructions (`wfi`, `nop`) |
| PAC | `stm32f4`, `nrf52840-pac`, `rp2040-pac` | One typed struct per peripheral; generated by `svd2rust` |
| HAL | `stm32f4xx-hal`, `nrf52840-hal`, `rp2040-hal`, `esp-hal` | Pins, buses and timers as safe types implementing `embedded-hal` |
| Trait crates | `embedded-hal` 1.0, `embedded-hal-async`, `embedded-io` | The shared vocabulary: `OutputPin`, `I2c`, `SpiDevice`, `DelayNs` |
| Drivers | `ssd1306`, `bme280`, `lis3dh` | Hardware support, written once for every chip |
| Frameworks and tools | `embassy`, `rtic`, `probe-rs`, `defmt` | Concurrency, flashing, debugging, logging |

The HAL layer uses Rust's type system to prevent hardware mistakes at compile
time. Peripherals are **singletons**: `take()` returns them once, so two parts
of the program cannot both own the same UART. Pin modes are encoded as types
(the typestate pattern, Chapter 16), so calling `set_high` on a pin configured
as an input is a compile error, not a silent bug:

```rust
// Shape of typical HAL code (stm32f4xx-hal style)
let dp = pac::Peripherals::take().unwrap();     // Some only the first time
let gpioa = dp.GPIOA.split();                   // one struct per pin
let mut led = gpioa.pa5.into_push_pull_output(); // type changes: Pin<Input> -> Pin<Output>
led.set_high();                                  // only exists for output pins
```

The key benefit is in drivers. A driver written against `embedded-hal` traits
works with every HAL:

```rust
// A driver for the TMP102 temperature sensor, usable on any chip
#![no_std]
use embedded_hal::i2c::I2c;

pub struct Tmp102<I2C> {
    i2c: I2C,                       // owns the bus (or a shared-bus handle)
    addr: u8,
}

impl<I2C: I2c> Tmp102<I2C> {
    pub fn new(i2c: I2C, addr: u8) -> Self {
        Self { i2c, addr }
    }

    /// Temperature in thousandths of a degree Celsius.
    pub fn read_millicelsius(&mut self) -> Result<i32, I2C::Error> {
        let mut buf = [0u8; 2];
        self.i2c.write_read(self.addr, &[0x00], &mut buf)?; // register 0x00: temperature
        let raw = i16::from_be_bytes(buf) >> 4;             // 12-bit signed value
        Ok(raw as i32 * 625 / 10)                           // 0.0625 °C per step
    }

    /// Gives the bus back, e.g. to use it for another device.
    pub fn release(self) -> I2C {
        self.i2c
    }
}
```

Because the driver only depends on a trait, it can be tested on your PC with a
mock bus that checks the expected transactions, with no hardware attached:

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use embedded_hal_mock::eh1::i2c::{Mock, Transaction};

    #[test]
    fn converts_25_degrees() {
        // 25 °C = 400 steps of 0.0625 °C = 0x190, left-aligned: 0x1900
        let expected = [Transaction::write_read(0x48, vec![0x00], vec![0x19, 0x00])];
        let mut bus = Mock::new(&expected);
        let mut sensor = Tmp102::new(bus.clone(), 0x48);
        assert_eq!(sensor.read_millicelsius().unwrap(), 25_000);
        bus.done();                                // all expected transactions happened
    }
}
```

The day-to-day tooling:

| Tool | Purpose |
| ---- | ------- |
| `probe-rs` | Flash and debug through SWD/JTAG probes; `cargo run` via the runner setting |
| `defmt` + `defmt-rtt` | Efficient logging: strings stay on the host, the device sends indices |
| `flip-link` | Linker wrapper that turns stack overflows into a clean fault instead of memory corruption |
| `cargo-binutils` | `cargo size`, `cargo objdump` for flash usage and disassembly |
| `svd2rust` | Generates a PAC from a vendor SVD file |

Most projects start from a template (`cargo generate` with the
`cortex-m-quickstart`, `embassy` or `esp-generate` templates), which comes
with `memory.x`, `.cargo/config.toml` and a working panic handler.

> Key Takeaways
> - The ecosystem is layered: core runtime, PAC (registers), HAL (safe
>   peripherals), drivers, board support, application.
> - `embedded-hal` 1.0 defines the shared traits (`OutputPin`, `I2c`,
>   `SpiDevice`, `DelayNs`), with async and I/O variants in companion crates.
> - HALs use singletons and typestate to turn hardware misuse into compile
>   errors.
> - Drivers generic over `embedded-hal` traits run on any chip and can be
>   unit-tested on the host with `embedded-hal-mock`.
> - `probe-rs`, `defmt` and `flip-link` form the standard development toolkit.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a driver generic over `embedded_hal::digital::OutputPin` and
>    `embedded_hal::delay::DelayNs` that blinks a Morse code message, and test
>    it with `embedded-hal-mock` pin and delay mocks.
> 2. Extend the `Tmp102` driver with a method that sets the conversion rate
>    (configuration register 0x01), and test negative temperatures with the
>    mock.
> 3. Interview: Why do embedded HALs make `Peripherals::take()` return an
>    `Option`, and how does that relate to Rust's ownership rules? (Hint:
>    consider two parts of a program that each believe they control the same
>    UART.)

---

## 16. Applied Rust and Ecosystem

The previous chapters taught the language; this one is about using it to build
real software. It covers the design patterns that experienced Rust programmers
reach for, the standard library and crates for command-line and systems tools,
serialization and database access with `serde`, `sqlx` and Diesel, networked
services built on Tokio, and compiling Rust to WebAssembly for browsers, edge
platforms and plugin hosts. The aim is to know which crate to pick for a job,
why the ecosystem converged on it, and the idioms that make it work well.

<a id="161-idiomatic-design-patterns"></a>
### 16.1 Idiomatic Design Patterns

Rust has no classes, no inheritance, no default arguments and no null, so many
classic patterns look different in Rust; this section covers the ones that
come up in nearly every codebase and the guidelines that make a public API
feel idiomatic.

#### Builder Pattern

Rust functions have no named arguments, no default parameter values and no
overloading. That is a deliberate choice (a call site always shows exactly
which function runs), but it makes one situation awkward: constructing a value
that has many settings, most of them optional. A constructor with nine
parameters is unreadable (`Server::new(8080, None, None, true, 30, ...)`), and
a struct literal forces callers to spell out every field and to depend on all
of them being public.

A **builder** solves this with a separate type whose methods each set one
option, followed by a final `build()` call that produces the real value. Think
of ordering a sandwich: you do not hand over a form with twenty boxes; you say
"wholegrain, add cheese, no onions" and then "that's it". Every unspecified
choice gets the shop's default.

```text
ServerBuilder::new("0.0.0.0")      required input goes into new()
    .port(8080)                    each call sets one optional field
    .workers(4)
    .timeout(Duration::from_secs(30))
    .build()?                      validates and produces Server
```

There are two styles, depending on what each method takes:

| Style | Method signature | Pros | Cons | std example |
| ----- | ---------------- | ---- | ---- | ----------- |
| Non-consuming | `fn port(&mut self, p: u16) -> &mut Self` | Builder can be reused and configured in steps (`if` branches) | `build(&self)` must clone owned fields | `std::process::Command` |
| Consuming | `fn port(mut self, p: u16) -> Self` | `build(self)` moves fields out, no clones; one-liner chains | Conditional configuration needs `b = b.port(..)` reassignment | `std::thread::Builder` |

```rust
use std::time::Duration;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Server {
    host: String,
    port: u16,
    workers: usize,
    timeout: Duration,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ServerBuilder {
    host: String,                 // required: taken by new()
    port: u16,                    // optional fields hold their defaults
    workers: usize,
    timeout: Option<Duration>,    // None = "not set", decided in build()
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum BuildError {
    ZeroWorkers,
}

impl Server {
    // Convention: the target type offers a `builder()` entry point.
    pub fn builder(host: impl Into<String>) -> ServerBuilder {
        ServerBuilder {
            host: host.into(),
            port: 80,
            workers: 1,
            timeout: None,
        }
    }
}

impl ServerBuilder {
    // Consuming style: take `self` by value, return it for chaining.
    pub fn port(mut self, port: u16) -> Self {
        self.port = port;
        self
    }

    pub fn workers(mut self, n: usize) -> Self {
        self.workers = n;
        self
    }

    pub fn timeout(mut self, t: Duration) -> Self {
        self.timeout = Some(t);
        self
    }

    // Validation happens once, at the end, so the setters stay infallible.
    pub fn build(self) -> Result<Server, BuildError> {
        if self.workers == 0 {
            return Err(BuildError::ZeroWorkers);
        }
        Ok(Server {
            host: self.host,                                       // moved, not cloned
            port: self.port,
            workers: self.workers,
            timeout: self.timeout.unwrap_or(Duration::from_secs(60)),
        })
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), BuildError> {
    let server = Server::builder("0.0.0.0").port(8080).workers(4).build()?;
    println!("{server:?}");

    // Conditional configuration with a consuming builder: reassign.
    let mut b = Server::builder("localhost");
    if std::env::var("SLOW_CLIENTS").is_ok() {
        b = b.timeout(Duration::from_secs(300));
    }
    let _dev = b.build()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Design decisions worth making explicitly:

- **Required versus optional.** Put required inputs in `builder(..)`/`new(..)`
  so they cannot be forgotten. If there are many required fields, a typestate
  builder (next topic) enforces them at compile time.
- **Where validation lives.** If no combination of options can be invalid,
  `build()` can return `Server` directly. Otherwise return `Result` and check
  everything in one place.
- **Defaults.** If the target type implements `Default`, a builder may not be
  needed at all: `Config { verbose: true, ..Default::default() }` is often
  enough for plain-data structs with public fields.
- **Generating builders.** For large structs, the `bon` and `derive_builder`
  crates generate builders from attributes; `bon` can also produce typestate
  builders that check required fields at compile time.

> Key Takeaways
> - Builders replace named and default arguments: one method per option, then
>   `build()`.
> - Consuming builders (`self -> Self`) avoid clones; non-consuming builders
>   (`&mut self -> &mut Self`) are easier to configure conditionally.
> - Put required inputs in the entry function and validate everything in
>   `build()`.
> - For plain data with sensible defaults, struct update syntax with
>   `..Default::default()` is often simpler than a builder.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a non-consuming `EmailBuilder` (`to`, `cc`, `subject`, `body`) in
>    the style of `std::process::Command`, where `cc` can be called several
>    times and `build(&self)` returns a `Result`.
> 2. Rewrite `ServerBuilder` using the `bon` crate's `#[derive(Builder)]` and
>    compare the generated API with the hand-written one.
> 3. Interview: When would you not use a builder and instead accept a config
>    struct with public fields that implements `Default`? (Hint: think about
>    invariants between fields and about adding fields in a later release.)

#### Typestate Pattern

Chapter 13 introduced type-state programming as a compile-time technique and
showed how phantom type parameters and sealed traits implement it. This topic
looks at it as a design decision: which problems it fits, how it combines with
builders, and what it costs.

The core idea is to move a runtime check into the type system. Instead of a
`state` field that every method inspects, each state is a separate type, and a
transition consumes the old value and returns a new one. An operation that is
invalid in some state simply does not exist on that type. Consider a locked
door: a runtime design lets you call `open()` and returns an error if the door
is locked; a typestate design gives you a `LockedDoor` that has no `open()`
method at all, only `unlock(key) -> UnlockedDoor`.

A common application is a builder with **required fields**. The builder starts
in a "missing" state for each required field, and `build()` exists only once
all of them have been set:

```text
RequestBuilder<NoUrl, NoMethod>
   │ .url(..)                         │ .method(..)
   ▼                                  ▼
RequestBuilder<Url, NoMethod>     RequestBuilder<NoUrl, Method>
   │ .method(..)                      │ .url(..)
   └──────────────► RequestBuilder<Url, Method> ──► .build()  (only here)
```

```rust
// Marker types for "set" and "not set". They hold the data once it exists.
pub struct NoUrl;
pub struct Url(String);
pub struct NoMethod;
pub struct Method(&'static str);

pub struct RequestBuilder<U, M> {
    url: U,
    method: M,
    headers: Vec<(String, String)>,   // optional data lives outside the states
}

pub struct Request {
    pub url: String,
    pub method: &'static str,
    pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
}

impl RequestBuilder<NoUrl, NoMethod> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        RequestBuilder { url: NoUrl, method: NoMethod, headers: Vec::new() }
    }
}

// Available in every state: generic over both parameters.
impl<U, M> RequestBuilder<U, M> {
    pub fn header(mut self, k: &str, v: &str) -> Self {
        self.headers.push((k.into(), v.into()));
        self
    }
}

// Setting the URL is possible only while it is still missing.
impl<M> RequestBuilder<NoUrl, M> {
    pub fn url(self, url: &str) -> RequestBuilder<Url, M> {
        RequestBuilder { url: Url(url.into()), method: self.method, headers: self.headers }
    }
}

impl<U> RequestBuilder<U, NoMethod> {
    pub fn method(self, m: &'static str) -> RequestBuilder<U, Method> {
        RequestBuilder { url: self.url, method: Method(m), headers: self.headers }
    }
}

// build() exists only when both required fields are present.
impl RequestBuilder<Url, Method> {
    pub fn build(self) -> Request {
        Request { url: self.url.0, method: self.method.0, headers: self.headers }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let req = RequestBuilder::new()
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .method("GET")                      // order does not matter
        .url("https://example.com")
        .build();                           // no Result: nothing can be missing
    println!("{} {}", req.method, req.url);

    // RequestBuilder::new().url("x").build();
    // error[E0599]: no method named `build` found for struct
    //               `RequestBuilder<Url, NoMethod>`
}
```

When to use typestate versus a runtime state enum:

| Question | Typestate | Runtime enum (`enum State { .. }`) |
| -------- | --------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Is the state known statically at each call site? | Required | Not required |
| Must values in different states share one collection? | Awkward (needs an enum wrapper or `dyn`) | Natural |
| Is the state driven by external input (network, files)? | Poor fit | Good fit |
| Cost of misuse | Compile error | `Err` or panic at runtime |
| API surface | Many types, harder docs and error messages | One type |

Typestate works best for protocols that a single piece of code drives from
start to finish: builders, connection handshakes, file formats written in a
fixed order, hardware initialization (Chapter 15's HAL pins). It is a poor fit
when the state changes in response to data, such as a TCP connection whose
peer can close at any time, because the program cannot know the state at
compile time. A common compromise is to use typestate for the setup phase and
a runtime enum once the object is live.

> Key Takeaways
> - Typestate turns "called in the wrong state" into a compile error by giving
>   each state its own type; transitions consume `self`.
> - Typestate builders guarantee that required fields are set, so `build()`
>   needs no `Result`.
> - It fits protocols driven by one caller in a known order; it fits poorly
>   when the state depends on runtime data.
> - The costs are more types, more complex docs and harder error messages;
>   keep the number of states small.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Extend `RequestBuilder` with a third required field, `timeout`, and note
>    how the number of `impl` blocks grows. Then consider how a crate like
>    `bon` avoids writing them by hand.
> 2. Model a `Connection` with the states `Disconnected`, `Connected` and
>    `Authenticated`, where `query()` exists only after authentication and
>    `close()` is available in every connected state.
> 3. Interview: A colleague wants to model an HTTP/1.1 connection that may be
>    closed by the server at any moment using typestate. What is your advice?
>    (Hint: who decides when the state changes, and when is that known?)

#### Newtype and Wrapper Types

Chapter 5 introduced the newtype pattern as a way around the orphan rule:
wrapping a foreign type in a local tuple struct lets you implement foreign
traits on it. This topic covers its wider use as a design tool: giving
distinct meanings to values that share a representation, and making invalid
values impossible to construct.

Primitive types carry no meaning. A function `fn transfer(from: u64, to: u64,
amount: u64)` happily accepts arguments in the wrong order, and a `String`
says nothing about whether it contains a valid email address. Programmers end
up re-validating the same data in many places, or forgetting to. A newtype is
a single-field struct that wraps a value and gives it a name of its own:

```rust
pub struct AccountId(u64);
pub struct Cents(u64);
```

At run time, `AccountId` is exactly a `u64`: same size, same layout, no
indirection. At compile time it is a completely separate type, so passing a
`Cents` where an `AccountId` is expected is an error. The idea is like colour
coding cables: all of them carry electricity, but the colour stops you from
plugging the speaker into the power socket.

The second, more powerful use is **"parse, don't validate"**: check the data
once, at the boundary, and return a type that proves the check was done. Code
that receives an `Email` never needs to check it again, because the only way
to obtain one is through the validating constructor.

```rust
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct Email(String);               // private field: no direct construction

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct InvalidEmail;

impl Email {
    pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Email, InvalidEmail> {
        let s = s.trim();
        // Deliberately simple check; real validation would be stricter.
        match s.split_once('@') {
            Some((user, domain)) if !user.is_empty() && domain.contains('.') => {
                Ok(Email(s.to_lowercase()))   // normalize once, here
            }
            _ => Err(InvalidEmail),
        }
    }

    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        &self.0
    }

    pub fn domain(&self) -> &str {
        // unwrap is fine: the constructor guarantees an '@' is present
        self.0.split_once('@').unwrap().1
    }
}

impl fmt::Display for Email {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.write_str(&self.0)
    }
}

// TryFrom lets the type plug into generic conversion code (and serde, see 16.3).
impl TryFrom<String> for Email {
    type Error = InvalidEmail;
    fn try_from(s: String) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        Email::parse(&s)
    }
}

/// Units in the type: adding metres to seconds will not compile.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
pub struct Metres(pub f64);

impl std::ops::Add for Metres {
    type Output = Metres;
    fn add(self, rhs: Metres) -> Metres {
        Metres(self.0 + rhs.0)
    }
}

fn send_welcome(to: &Email) {
    // No validation needed here: an &Email is always valid.
    println!("sending to {to} (domain {})", to.domain());
}

fn main() {
    let email = Email::parse("  Ada@Example.com ").expect("valid");
    send_welcome(&email);
    let total = Metres(1.5) + Metres(2.0);
    println!("{total:?}");
}
```

How much of the inner type to expose is the main design choice:

| Approach | Effect | Use when |
| -------- | ------ | -------- |
| Private field, explicit methods | Full control over invariants and API | Validated types (`Email`, `NonEmptyVec`) |
| `pub` field (`pub struct Metres(pub f64)`) | Pure labelling, no invariant | Units, IDs without rules |
| `impl Deref<Target = Inner>` | All of the inner type's `&self` methods become callable | Smart-pointer-like wrappers; avoid it for domain types, since it leaks the whole inner API |
| `AsRef<Inner>` / `as_str()` | Read-only access on request | Most validated types |
| `#[repr(transparent)]` | Guaranteed same ABI as the inner type | FFI, and casting `&[Inner]` to `&[Wrapper]` in unsafe code |

Writing forwarding impls (`Add`, `Display`, `From`) by hand gets repetitive.
The `derive_more` crate derives them, and `nutype` generates validated
newtypes from declarative rules such as `#[nutype(validate(len_char_max =
50))]`.

> Key Takeaways
> - A newtype gives a value a distinct type with zero runtime cost, so mixing
>   up IDs, units or amounts becomes a compile error.
> - With a private field and a validating constructor, holding the type
>   proves the data is valid ("parse, don't validate").
> - Expose the inner value deliberately; avoid `Deref` on domain types because
>   it re-exposes the entire inner API.
> - `#[repr(transparent)]` guarantees layout compatibility when it matters.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Create `UserId(u32)` and `OrderId(u32)` and write a function that takes
>    both. Confirm the compiler rejects swapped arguments.
> 2. Write `NonEmptyVec<T>` whose constructor returns `None` for an empty
>    `Vec`, and give it a `first(&self) -> &T` method that cannot fail.
> 3. Interview: Why do many Rust style guides advise against implementing
>    `Deref` for a newtype like `Email(String)`? (Hint: list which `String`
>    methods become available, and which invariants they could bypass if
>    `DerefMut` followed.)

#### Interpreter and Visitor with Enums

Many programs process tree-shaped data: a calculator evaluates expressions, a
compiler walks a syntax tree, a query engine transforms a plan, a linter
inspects a configuration file. In object-oriented languages, each node kind is
typically a subclass, and operations are added with the **Visitor** pattern,
a double-dispatch technique that is notoriously verbose.

Rust has a better starting point: an `enum` describes a closed set of node
kinds, and `match` with exhaustiveness checking performs the dispatch. An
**interpreter** is then just a recursive function with one match arm per
variant. Adding a new operation means writing one new function; if you later
add a variant, the compiler lists every `match` that needs updating.

```text
       Mul                     (2 + x) * 3
      /   \
    Add    Num(3)
   /   \
Num(2)  Var("x")
```

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
enum Expr {
    Num(f64),
    Var(String),
    Neg(Box<Expr>),                       // Box: a recursive enum needs indirection
    Bin(Box<Expr>, Op, Box<Expr>),
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Op { Add, Sub, Mul, Div }

// Operation 1: evaluation. One arm per variant; the compiler checks coverage.
fn eval(e: &Expr, env: &HashMap<String, f64>) -> Result<f64, String> {
    Ok(match e {
        Expr::Num(n) => *n,
        Expr::Var(name) => *env.get(name).ok_or(format!("unbound: {name}"))?,
        Expr::Neg(inner) => -eval(inner, env)?,
        Expr::Bin(l, op, r) => {
            let (a, b) = (eval(l, env)?, eval(r, env)?);
            match op {
                Op::Add => a + b,
                Op::Sub => a - b,
                Op::Mul => a * b,
                Op::Div if b == 0.0 => return Err("division by zero".into()),
                Op::Div => a / b,
            }
        }
    })
}

// Operation 2: pretty-printing. Adding it touched nothing else.
fn show(e: &Expr) -> String {
    match e {
        Expr::Num(n) => n.to_string(),
        Expr::Var(v) => v.clone(),
        Expr::Neg(inner) => format!("-{}", show(inner)),
        Expr::Bin(l, op, r) => {
            let sym = match op { Op::Add => "+", Op::Sub => "-", Op::Mul => "*", Op::Div => "/" };
            format!("({} {sym} {})", show(l), show(r))
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    use Expr::*;
    let e = Bin(
        Box::new(Bin(Box::new(Num(2.0)), Op::Add, Box::new(Var("x".into())))),
        Op::Mul,
        Box::new(Num(3.0)),
    );
    let env = HashMap::from([("x".to_string(), 4.0)]);
    println!("{} = {:?}", show(&e), eval(&e, &env));   // ((2 + x) * 3) = Ok(18.0)
}
```

When a tree has many variants and you write many passes over it, each pass
repeats the same traversal logic: recurse into children for every variant you
do not care about. A Rust-style **visitor** factors that out. The trait has
one method per node kind with a default implementation that simply walks into
the children; a concrete visitor overrides only the methods it cares about.
This is how `syn::visit::Visit` (Chapter 13) works.

```rust
trait Visitor {
    // Default behaviour for every hook: keep walking.
    fn visit_expr(&mut self, e: &Expr) {
        walk_expr(self, e);
    }
    fn visit_var(&mut self, _name: &str) {}
}

// The traversal lives in one free function, shared by all visitors.
fn walk_expr<V: Visitor + ?Sized>(v: &mut V, e: &Expr) {
    match e {
        Expr::Num(_) => {}
        Expr::Var(name) => v.visit_var(name),
        Expr::Neg(inner) => v.visit_expr(inner),
        Expr::Bin(l, _, r) => {
            v.visit_expr(l);
            v.visit_expr(r);
        }
    }
}

// A pass that collects free variables: it overrides a single hook.
#[derive(Default)]
struct FreeVars(Vec<String>);

impl Visitor for FreeVars {
    fn visit_var(&mut self, name: &str) {
        if !self.0.iter().any(|n| n == name) {
            self.0.push(name.to_string());
        }
    }
}

fn free_vars(e: &Expr) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut v = FreeVars::default();
    v.visit_expr(e);
    v.0
}
```

The choice between enums and traits for a tree is the classic **expression
problem**:

| Design | Adding a new operation | Adding a new node kind | Rust example |
| ------ | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------ |
| Enum + `match` | Easy: one new function | Every `match` must change (compiler finds them) | ASTs, IRs, state machines |
| Trait objects (one type per node) | Every node type must change | Easy: one new type | Plugin systems, UI widgets |
| Enum + visitor trait | Easy, and new passes override only what they need | Update the walker and the trait | `syn`, compiler passes |

Two practical notes: recursive evaluation on very deep trees can overflow the
stack (convert to an explicit work stack, or use the `stacker` crate), and
for large ASTs an arena with index-based nodes (Chapter 15) avoids one heap
allocation per `Box`.

> Key Takeaways
> - An enum is a closed set of node kinds; an interpreter is a recursive
>   `match`, and exhaustiveness checking finds every place to update.
> - Enums make new operations cheap; trait objects make new node kinds cheap.
> - A visitor trait with default methods plus a shared `walk_*` function lets
>   each pass override only the nodes it cares about.
> - For deep or large trees, watch stack depth and consider arena storage.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Let(String, Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>)` variant (`let x = a in b`) and
>    update `eval` and `show`. Note which errors the compiler reports first.
> 2. Write a `constant_fold(e: Expr) -> Expr` pass that replaces `Bin` nodes
>    whose children are both `Num` with their computed value.
> 3. Interview: You are designing a configuration-language interpreter that
>    third-party crates should be able to extend with new built-in functions.
>    Enum or trait objects for built-ins, and why? (Hint: decide which axis of
>    the expression problem third parties need to extend.)

#### Composition over Inheritance

Inheritance bundles two different things: **code reuse** (a subclass gets the
parent's fields and methods) and **subtyping** (a subclass can be used where
the parent is expected). Bundling them causes well-known problems: deep
hierarchies that are hard to change, the fragile base class problem, and
classes that inherit methods that make no sense for them (a `Square`
inheriting `set_width` from `Rectangle`).

Rust has no struct inheritance at all and provides the two halves separately:

- **Reuse** comes from composition: a struct contains other structs as fields
  and delegates to them. Shared method bodies can also live in trait default
  methods.
- **Substitutability** comes from traits: any type that implements a trait can
  be used through generics (`impl Trait`, static dispatch) or trait objects
  (`dyn Trait`, dynamic dispatch). Supertraits express "an X is also a Y"
  between interfaces, not between data.

Think of building with Lego instead of carving from one block of wood: you
assemble a car from a chassis, wheels and an engine, and you can swap the
engine without touching the rest.

| OOP concept | Rust equivalent |
| ----------- | --------------- |
| Base class with shared fields | A struct embedded as a field |
| Calling `super.method()` | Calling `self.inner.method()` |
| Abstract method | Required trait method |
| Shared method implementation | Trait default method or a free function |
| Interface | Trait |
| Polymorphic collection `List<Shape>` | `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`, or `Vec<Shape>` with an enum |
| Decorator / proxy | Generic wrapper struct implementing the same trait |
| Template method | Trait with a provided method that calls required ones |

The **decorator** pattern shows composition at its best. Each layer wraps an
inner value that implements the same trait and adds one behaviour:

```rust
use std::time::Instant;

trait Fetch {
    fn fetch(&mut self, key: &str) -> Result<String, String>;
}

// The core component.
struct Database;
impl Fetch for Database {
    fn fetch(&mut self, key: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
        Ok(format!("value-of-{key}"))
    }
}

// Decorator 1: timing. Generic over any inner Fetch: static dispatch, no Box.
struct Timed<F> {
    inner: F,
}
impl<F: Fetch> Fetch for Timed<F> {
    fn fetch(&mut self, key: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
        let start = Instant::now();
        let r = self.inner.fetch(key);                     // delegate
        eprintln!("fetch({key}) took {:?}", start.elapsed());
        r
    }
}

// Decorator 2: caching. Adds state of its own next to the wrapped value.
struct Cached<F> {
    inner: F,
    cache: std::collections::HashMap<String, String>,
}
impl<F: Fetch> Fetch for Cached<F> {
    fn fetch(&mut self, key: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
        if let Some(v) = self.cache.get(key) {
            return Ok(v.clone());
        }
        let v = self.inner.fetch(key)?;
        self.cache.insert(key.to_string(), v.clone());
        Ok(v)
    }
}

// Template method: `fetch_many` is written once in terms of `fetch`.
trait FetchExt: Fetch {
    fn fetch_many(&mut self, keys: &[&str]) -> Vec<Result<String, String>> {
        keys.iter().map(|k| self.fetch(k)).collect()
    }
}
impl<T: Fetch + ?Sized> FetchExt for T {}                 // blanket impl: every Fetch gets it

fn main() {
    // Layers are assembled at the call site; the order is a visible choice.
    let mut svc = Cached { inner: Timed { inner: Database }, cache: Default::default() };
    let _ = svc.fetch_many(&["a", "b", "a"]);             // second "a" is served from cache
}
```

This is the same structure as `tower::Service` layers in web frameworks
(16.4) and `BufReader<File>` in `std::io`: behaviour is stacked from small,
independent wrappers rather than inherited from a common base.

Delegation boilerplate is the main cost. When a wrapper needs to forward many
methods unchanged, either implement only the trait (not every inherent
method), or use a crate such as `delegate` or `ambassador` to generate the
forwarding code. Resist the temptation to implement `Deref` to simulate
inheritance: it works for method calls but not for trait impls or generics,
and it surprises readers.

> Key Takeaways
> - Rust separates reuse (composition, default methods) from substitutability
>   (traits); there is no struct inheritance.
> - Wrappers generic over a trait (`Timed<F: Fetch>`) give decorators with
>   static dispatch and no allocation.
> - Use trait objects for open sets of types and enums for closed ones.
> - Do not emulate inheritance with `Deref`; forward explicitly or with a
>   delegation macro.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Retry<F>` decorator that retries a failed fetch up to three times,
>    and compose it with `Cached` and `Timed`. Does the order of the layers
>    change behaviour?
> 2. Model a game with entities that can be `Movable`, `Renderable` and
>    `Damageable` in any combination, first with traits and then with
>    components stored in separate `Vec`s (ECS style). Compare them.
> 3. Interview: A Java developer asks how to share fields between `Admin` and
>    `Customer` in Rust without inheritance. Sketch two designs. (Hint: one
>    embeds a common struct; the other uses an enum for the role.)

#### API Design Guidelines

A library's public API is the hardest part to change: once published, every
rename or signature change breaks users (Chapter 8's semver rules). The Rust
community maintains the **Rust API Guidelines**
(<https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/>), a checklist distilled from the
standard library and popular crates. Following them makes your crate feel
familiar: users can guess method names, conversions and trait support without
reading the docs.

**Naming conventions** carry meaning about cost and ownership:

| Prefix / name | Meaning | Example |
| ------------- | ------- | ------- |
| `as_` | Free, borrowed view (`&self -> &T`) | `str::as_bytes`, `Path::as_os_str` |
| `to_` | Expensive or allocating conversion, borrows `self` | `str::to_lowercase`, `Path::to_path_buf` |
| `into_` | Consumes `self`, usually cheap | `String::into_bytes`, `Vec::into_boxed_slice` |
| No `get_` prefix | Plain getters are named after the field | `len()`, `name()`, not `get_name()` |
| `iter` / `iter_mut` / `into_iter` | Iterators over `&T`, `&mut T`, `T` | All std collections |
| `try_` | Fallible version of an operation | `try_reserve`, `try_from` |
| `_mut` suffix | Mutable variant of an accessor | `get_mut`, `first_mut` |
| `with_` | Constructor with one specific argument | `Vec::with_capacity` |

**Flexible inputs, concrete outputs.** Accept the most general type that works
and return the most specific one:

```rust
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

pub struct Project {
    name: String,
    root: PathBuf,
}

impl Project {
    // impl Into<String>: callers pass &str or String without .to_string().
    // impl AsRef<Path>: callers pass &str, String, &Path or PathBuf.
    pub fn new(name: impl Into<String>, root: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Self {
        Project { name: name.into(), root: root.as_ref().to_path_buf() }
    }

    // Return borrowed views; let the caller decide whether to clone.
    pub fn name(&self) -> &str {
        &self.name
    }

    pub fn root(&self) -> &Path {
        &self.root
    }

    // Return iterators, not Vec, when the caller may not need everything.
    pub fn src_dirs(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = PathBuf> + '_ {
        ["src", "tests", "benches"].into_iter().map(|d| self.root.join(d))
    }
}
```

**Implement the common traits eagerly.** Because of the orphan rule, users
cannot add std traits to your types later. A public type should implement
whatever applies among `Debug` (always), `Clone`, `PartialEq`/`Eq`, `Hash`,
`PartialOrd`/`Ord`, `Default`, `Display` (for user-facing types),
`From`/`TryFrom` conversions, and, behind an optional `serde` feature,
`Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Check that types are `Send` and `Sync` when users
would expect them to be.

**Design for evolution.** These tools let you add things later without a
major version bump:

```rust
// Users cannot construct this with a struct literal or match it exhaustively,
// so adding a field in 1.1 is not a breaking change.
#[non_exhaustive]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default)]
pub struct Options {
    pub verbose: bool,
    pub retries: u32,
}

// Users must keep a `_ =>` arm, so adding a variant is not breaking.
#[non_exhaustive]
#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum Error {
    NotFound,
    PermissionDenied,
}

// Sealed trait: users can call it but not implement it, so new methods
// can be added without breaking downstream impls.
mod sealed {
    pub trait Sealed {}
}
pub trait Backend: sealed::Sealed {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
}

// #[must_use] warns when a caller ignores an important return value.
#[must_use = "the builder does nothing until .build() is called"]
pub struct Builder {/* ... */}
```

A short checklist for public APIs:

- Errors: return a meaningful error type implementing `std::error::Error`
  (Chapter 7); never panic on bad input in a library unless the function's
  docs say so.
- Do not expose dependency types in your public API casually: a public
  `reqwest::Client` parameter ties your major version to theirs.
- Keep `pub` minimal: everything public is a promise. `pub(crate)` is free.
- Document panics, errors and safety (`# Panics`, `# Errors`, `# Safety`), and
  give every public item an example (Chapter 12).
- Run `cargo semver-checks` before each release to catch accidental breaking
  changes.

> Key Takeaways
> - Follow naming conventions: `as_` is cheap and borrowed, `to_` is
>   expensive, `into_` consumes; getters have no `get_` prefix.
> - Accept generic inputs (`impl AsRef<Path>`, `impl Into<String>`) and return
>   concrete or borrowed types.
> - Implement `Debug` and the other applicable std traits on every public type.
> - `#[non_exhaustive]`, sealed traits and minimal `pub` keep future changes
>   non-breaking; `cargo semver-checks` verifies it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Review a small struct you have written and rename its methods to follow
>    the `as_`/`to_`/`into_` and no-`get_` conventions.
> 2. Add `#[non_exhaustive]` to a public struct, then try to construct it with
>    a struct literal from another crate in the same workspace. What do you
>    have to add to the original crate to make construction possible again?
> 3. Interview: Your crate's public function takes a `chrono::DateTime`.
>    `chrono` releases a new major version. What happens to your crate's users,
>    and how could the API have been designed to avoid it? (Hint: think about
>    whose semver your signature depends on.)

<a id="162-systems-and-cli-development"></a>
### 16.2 Systems and CLI Development

Command-line tools are one of Rust's strongest niches (ripgrep, fd, bat,
uv and the Rust toolchain itself are examples); this section covers the
standard library's file, I/O and process APIs and the crates that complete
the picture: `clap` for arguments, `tracing` for diagnostics, and layered
configuration.

#### File and Path APIs

File paths look like strings, but they are not. On Unix a path is an arbitrary
sequence of bytes except `\0`, and it does not have to be valid UTF-8. On
Windows it is a sequence of 16-bit units that may contain unpaired
surrogates. A program that stores paths in `String` will either reject real
files or corrupt their names. Rust therefore has dedicated types:

| Owned | Borrowed | Analogous to | Holds |
| ----- | -------- | ------------ | ----- |
| `PathBuf` | `&Path` | `String` / `&str` | A platform path, with path-aware methods |
| `OsString` | `&OsStr` | `String` / `&str` | Platform string data, possibly not UTF-8 |

`Path` is a thin wrapper around `OsStr` that understands separators and
components. Converting to `&str` is fallible (`path.to_str() -> Option<&str>`),
and for display there is `path.display()`, which replaces invalid sequences
with the replacement character.

```rust
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

fn main() {
    let p = Path::new("/var/log/app/server.log.gz");
    println!("{:?}", p.parent());          // Some("/var/log/app")
    println!("{:?}", p.file_name());       // Some("server.log.gz")
    println!("{:?}", p.file_stem());       // Some("server.log")
    println!("{:?}", p.extension());       // Some("gz")

    // join() uses the right separator; an absolute argument replaces the base!
    let mut out = PathBuf::from("target");
    out.push("reports");                   // target/reports
    out.set_extension("json");             // target/reports.json
    println!("{}", out.display());
    println!("{}", Path::new("a").join("/etc").display());   // "/etc", not "a/etc"

    for c in Path::new("./src/../lib/mod.rs").components() {
        println!("{c:?}");                 // CurDir, Normal("src"), ParentDir, ...
    }
}
```

`std::fs` provides convenience functions for whole-file operations and
`File`/`OpenOptions` for finer control:

| Task | API |
| ---- | --- |
| Read a whole file | `fs::read_to_string(p)`, `fs::read(p)` (bytes) |
| Write a whole file (create or truncate) | `fs::write(p, data)` |
| Open for reading / create for writing | `File::open(p)`, `File::create(p)` |
| Append, create only if missing, etc. | `OpenOptions::new().append(true).create(true).open(p)` |
| Directories | `fs::create_dir_all`, `fs::read_dir`, `fs::remove_dir_all` |
| Metadata | `fs::metadata(p)` (follows symlinks), `fs::symlink_metadata(p)` |
| Move, copy, delete | `fs::rename`, `fs::copy`, `fs::remove_file` |
| Resolve to an absolute path | `fs::canonicalize(p)` (the path must exist) |

Two patterns matter in real tools. First, `io::Error` does not include the
path, so "No such file or directory" with no file name is a classic bad error
message; add context at the call site. Second, writing a file in place is not
crash-safe: if the program dies midway, the file is half-written. Write to a
temporary file in the same directory and `rename` it over the target, which is
atomic on the same filesystem.

```rust
use std::fs::{self, File};
use std::io::{self, Write};
use std::path::Path;

/// Write `data` so that readers see either the old or the new file, never half.
fn write_atomic(path: &Path, data: &[u8]) -> io::Result<()> {
    let tmp = path.with_extension("tmp");          // same directory => same filesystem
    let mut f = File::create(&tmp)?;
    f.write_all(data)?;
    f.sync_all()?;                                 // flush OS buffers to disk
    fs::rename(&tmp, path)                         // atomic replace
}

/// Recursively total the size of all files below `dir`.
fn dir_size(dir: &Path) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let mut total = 0;
    for entry in fs::read_dir(dir)? {
        let entry = entry?;                        // each entry can fail too
        let ft = entry.file_type()?;               // does not follow symlinks
        if ft.is_dir() {
            total += dir_size(&entry.path())?;
        } else if ft.is_file() {
            total += entry.metadata()?.len();
        }
    }
    Ok(total)
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let cfg = Path::new("settings.json");
    write_atomic(cfg, br#"{"theme":"dark"}"#)
        .map_err(|e| format!("writing {}: {e}", cfg.display()))?;   // add the path
    println!("{} bytes under .", dir_size(Path::new("."))?);
    Ok(())
}
```

For real recursive traversal, prefer the `walkdir` crate (symlink loop
detection, depth limits, sorting) or `ignore` (which also respects
`.gitignore`, as ripgrep does). For temporary files, `tempfile` creates them
securely and deletes them on drop, and its `NamedTempFile::persist` implements
the atomic-rename pattern above.

> Key Takeaways
> - Store paths as `PathBuf`/`&Path`, not `String`: paths need not be UTF-8.
> - Use `display()` for printing and `to_str()` only when UTF-8 is required.
> - `join` with an absolute path replaces the base; validate untrusted path
>   components.
> - Add the path to I/O errors yourself; write important files via temp file
>   plus `rename`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a function `find_by_extension(dir: &Path, ext: &str) ->
>    io::Result<Vec<PathBuf>>` using `fs::read_dir` recursively, then rewrite
>    it with `walkdir`.
> 2. Create a file whose name is not valid UTF-8 on Linux (for example with
>    `OsStr::from_bytes(b"bad\xff.txt")` from `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt`)
>    and check how `display()`, `to_str()` and `to_string_lossy()` behave.
> 3. Interview: A web server joins a user-supplied file name onto its static
>    directory with `base.join(name)`. What attacks does this allow, and how
>    would you prevent them? (Hint: consider `..` components and absolute
>    paths.)

#### Standard I/O and Buffering

Every I/O operation in `std` goes through two traits: `Read` (pull bytes into
a buffer) and `Write` (push bytes out). Files, sockets, pipes, `stdin`,
`stdout`, in-memory `Vec<u8>` and `&[u8]` all implement them, so a function
generic over `impl Read` works on all of them, which also makes it easy to
test.

The performance trap is that **`File` and `TcpStream` are unbuffered**: every
`write` call is a system call, and system calls cost hundreds of nanoseconds
to microseconds. Writing a million short lines one call at a time can be ten
or more times slower than necessary. A buffer collects small writes in memory
and hands them to the OS in large chunks, like a delivery driver who waits
until the van is full instead of driving each parcel separately.

```text
Unbuffered:   write("a\n") -> syscall   write("b\n") -> syscall   ... (1 per line)
BufWriter:    write("a\n") -> memory    write("b\n") -> memory    ...
              buffer full (8 KiB) -> one syscall for hundreds of lines
```

| Type | Purpose |
| ---- | ------- |
| `BufReader<R>` | Reads in large chunks; adds `BufRead` (`read_line`, `lines`, `split`) |
| `BufWriter<W>` | Collects writes; flushes when full, on `flush()`, or on drop |
| `LineWriter<W>` | Flushes at each newline (interactive output) |
| `io::stdin().lock()` | `StdinLock`, already buffered and implements `BufRead` |
| `io::stdout().lock()` | `StdoutLock`, line-buffered; wrap it in `BufWriter` for bulk output |
| `io::copy(&mut r, &mut w)` | Moves all bytes from a reader to a writer efficiently |

`println!` locks `stdout` on every call and the output is line-buffered, so a
loop of `println!` performs one lock and one system call per line. For bulk
output, lock once and wrap the lock in a `BufWriter`:

```rust
use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufWriter, Write};

/// A tiny `grep`: copy lines containing `needle` from input to output.
/// Generic over BufRead/Write, so tests can use byte slices and Vec<u8>.
fn filter(input: impl BufRead, mut out: impl Write, needle: &str) -> io::Result<u64> {
    let mut matches = 0;
    for line in input.lines() {
        let line = line?;                          // fails on invalid UTF-8
        if line.contains(needle) {
            writeln!(out, "{line}")?;
            matches += 1;
        }
    }
    out.flush()?;                                  // surface write errors explicitly
    Ok(matches)
}

fn main() {
    let needle = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap_or_default();
    let stdin = io::stdin().lock();                // lock once
    let stdout = BufWriter::new(io::stdout().lock());

    match filter(stdin, stdout, &needle) {
        Ok(n) => eprintln!("{n} matching lines"),  // diagnostics go to stderr
        // `mytool | head` closes the pipe early: exit quietly, not with an error
        Err(e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe => {}
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("error: {e}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}

#[test]
fn filters_lines() {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let n = filter(&b"apple\nbanana\napricot\n"[..], &mut out, "ap").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(n, 2);
    assert_eq!(out, b"apple\napricot\n");
}
```

Points that trip people up:

- **Flush errors are lost on drop.** `BufWriter` flushes in its destructor, but
  `Drop` cannot return an error. Call `flush()` yourself when write failures
  matter (a full disk, a closed pipe).
- **`lines()` allocates a `String` per line and requires UTF-8.** For speed,
  reuse one buffer with `read_line` (Chapter 15); for arbitrary bytes, use
  `read_until(b'\n', &mut vec)` or the `bstr` crate.
- **stdout versus stderr.** Results go to stdout so they can be piped;
  progress, warnings and errors go to stderr. `eprintln!` writes unbuffered
  to stderr.
- **Interactive prompts.** Text printed with `print!` (no newline) stays in
  the buffer; call `io::stdout().flush()` before reading the user's answer.

> Key Takeaways
> - Write I/O code against `Read`/`BufRead`/`Write` so it works on files,
>   pipes and in-memory buffers alike.
> - `File` and sockets are unbuffered; wrap them in `BufReader`/`BufWriter`.
> - For bulk output, lock stdout once and wrap it in a `BufWriter`; flush
>   explicitly to see errors.
> - Handle `BrokenPipe` gracefully, and keep stdout for data and stderr for
>   diagnostics.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a program that prints the numbers 1 to 5,000,000, once with
>    `println!` and once through a locked `BufWriter`. Time both with output
>    redirected to `/dev/null`.
> 2. Implement `wc -l` that counts newline bytes with a reusable buffer and
>    `read_until`, so it also works on non-UTF-8 input.
> 3. Interview: A program writes its output with `BufWriter` and exits with
>    `std::process::exit(0)`. Some users report that the last part of the
>    output is missing. Why? (Hint: what does `process::exit` skip?)

#### Process and Environment Handling

A command-line program interacts with its environment through a small set of
channels: arguments, environment variables, the working directory, standard
streams, and the exit code. It may also start other programs. `std::env` and
`std::process` cover all of them.

```rust
use std::env;
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    // args() panics on non-UTF-8 arguments; args_os() never does.
    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().skip(1).collect();   // skip program name

    // var() returns Err if unset *or* not valid UTF-8.
    let home = env::var("HOME").unwrap_or_else(|_| "/".into());
    let verbose = env::var_os("VERBOSE").is_some();           // presence check only
    let cwd = env::current_dir().expect("cwd");

    if args.is_empty() {
        eprintln!("usage: tool <file>...");
        return ExitCode::from(2);                              // conventional "usage error"
    }
    if verbose {
        println!("home={home} cwd={} args={args:?}", cwd.display());
    }
    ExitCode::SUCCESS                                          // destructors run, buffers flush
}
```

Returning `ExitCode` (or `Result<(), E>`, which exits with 1 on `Err`) from
`main` is better than `std::process::exit`, because `exit` terminates
immediately without running destructors, so pending `BufWriter` output is
lost. Common exit code conventions are 0 for success, 1 for general failure,
2 for usage errors, and 128 + N for termination by signal N.

Modifying the environment is unsafe in edition 2024: `env::set_var` and
`env::remove_var` are `unsafe fn`, because on most platforms another thread
reading the environment at the same time (C libraries do this, for example
`getaddrinfo`) is undefined behaviour. Set variables for **child processes**
through `Command` instead, which is always safe.

**Running other programs** goes through `std::process::Command`, a builder
(16.1) with three ways to run:

| Method | Waits? | Captures output? | Use when |
| ------ | ------ | ---------------- | -------- |
| `.status()` | Yes | No, inherits the parent's stdio | Run a tool and check that it succeeded |
| `.output()` | Yes | Yes, stdout and stderr into `Vec<u8>` | Use the program's output as data |
| `.spawn()` | No, returns a `Child` | Configurable via `Stdio::piped()` | Streaming, feeding stdin, running in parallel |

```rust
use std::io::{self, Write};
use std::process::{Command, Stdio};

fn git_branch() -> io::Result<String> {
    let out = Command::new("git")
        .args(["rev-parse", "--abbrev-ref", "HEAD"])   // no shell: no quoting issues
        .output()?;                                    // Err only if git could not start
    if !out.status.success() {
        let err = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stderr);
        return Err(io::Error::other(format!("git failed: {}", err.trim())));
    }
    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).trim().to_string())
}

/// Pipe data through `sort` and collect the result: spawn + piped stdio.
fn sort_lines(text: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut child = Command::new("sort")
        .env("LC_ALL", "C")                            // safe: affects only the child
        .stdin(Stdio::piped())
        .stdout(Stdio::piped())
        .spawn()?;

    // Write stdin, then drop it so `sort` sees end of input.
    // (For large inputs write from another thread, or both pipes may fill up and deadlock.)
    child.stdin.take().expect("piped").write_all(text.as_bytes())?;

    let out = child.wait_with_output()?;              // reads stdout, waits for exit
    Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).into_owned())
}

fn main() -> io::Result<()> {
    println!("branch: {:?}", git_branch());
    print!("{}", sort_lines("pear\napple\nfig\n")?);
    Ok(())
}
```

Two cautions. `Command` does not use a shell, so wildcards, pipes and `&&`
are not interpreted; this is a security feature (no shell injection from
arguments). Running `sh -c` with user input reintroduces that risk. And a
child process that is never waited on stays a zombie on Unix until the parent
exits; always call `wait`, `wait_with_output` or `output`.

For Ctrl-C handling, the `ctrlc` crate installs a portable handler (often
setting an `AtomicBool` that the main loop checks); `signal-hook` gives access
to the full set of Unix signals, and in async programs
`tokio::signal::ctrl_c()` is a future.

> Key Takeaways
> - Use `args_os`/`var_os` when input may not be UTF-8; `args`/`var` are
>   convenient but stricter.
> - Return `ExitCode` or `Result` from `main` rather than calling
>   `process::exit`, so destructors run.
> - `env::set_var` is `unsafe` in edition 2024; configure children through
>   `Command::env` instead.
> - `Command` runs programs without a shell; choose `status`, `output` or
>   `spawn` by whether you need output or concurrency, and always wait.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `time`-like tool: run the command given as arguments with
>    `Command::status`, print the elapsed time to stderr, and exit with the
>    child's exit code.
> 2. Spawn two `ping -c 3` processes concurrently with `spawn()` and stream
>    each child's stdout line by line, prefixed with the host name.
> 3. Interview: Your program spawns a child with both stdin and stdout piped,
>    writes 10 MB to its stdin, then reads its stdout. It hangs. Why? (Hint:
>    pipe buffers are only tens of kilobytes.)

#### Argument Parsing with clap

Parsing `env::args()` by hand works for one or two arguments, but real tools
need flags, options with values, defaults, subcommands, validation, `--help`,
`--version`, environment variable fallbacks and helpful error messages.
Writing all that by hand is tedious and inconsistent. `clap` is the standard
crate for it. Its **derive API** lets you describe the arguments as a struct,
and the struct is also the parsed, type-checked result: the definition, the
parser and the help text cannot drift apart.

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive", "env"] }
```

```rust
use clap::{Args, Parser, Subcommand, ValueEnum};
use std::path::PathBuf;

// Doc comments (///) become the help text shown by --help.
/// Fast backup tool.
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)] // version/about read from Cargo.toml
struct Cli {
    /// Increase output verbosity (-v, -vv, -vvv)
    #[arg(short, long, action = clap::ArgAction::Count, global = true)]
    verbose: u8,

    /// Configuration file
    #[arg(long, env = "BACKUP_CONFIG", default_value = "backup.toml")]
    config: PathBuf,

    #[command(subcommand)]
    command: Command,
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Debug)]
enum Command {
    /// Create a new backup
    Create(CreateArgs),
    /// List existing backups
    List {
        /// Show at most N entries
        #[arg(short = 'n', long, default_value_t = 10)]
        limit: usize,
    },
}

#[derive(Args, Debug)]
struct CreateArgs {
    /// Directories to back up (at least one)
    #[arg(required = true)]
    paths: Vec<PathBuf>,

    /// Compression algorithm
    #[arg(short, long, value_enum, default_value_t = Compression::Zstd)]
    compression: Compression,

    /// Compression level 1-19
    #[arg(long, value_parser = clap::value_parser!(u8).range(1..=19), default_value_t = 3)]
    level: u8,

    /// Show what would be done without writing anything
    #[arg(long)]
    dry_run: bool,                               // bool => flag, no value
}

#[derive(ValueEnum, Clone, Debug)]
enum Compression {
    None,
    Gzip,
    Zstd,
}

fn main() {
    let cli = Cli::parse();                      // on error: prints message, exits 2
    match cli.command {
        Command::Create(args) => {
            println!("backing up {:?} with {:?} level {}", args.paths, args.compression, args.level);
        }
        Command::List { limit } => println!("listing {limit} backups"),
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use clap::CommandFactory;

    #[test]
    fn cli_definition_is_valid() {
        Cli::command().debug_assert();           // catches conflicting definitions
    }

    #[test]
    fn parses_create() {
        let cli = Cli::try_parse_from(["backup", "-vv", "create", "src", "-c", "gzip"]).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(cli.verbose, 2);
        assert!(matches!(cli.command, Command::Create(ref a) if a.paths.len() == 1));
    }
}
```

Running `backup create --help` produces a generated help page:

```text
Create a new backup

Usage: backup create [OPTIONS] <PATHS>...

Arguments:
  <PATHS>...  Directories to back up (at least one)

Options:
  -c, --compression <COMPRESSION>  Compression algorithm [default: zstd] [possible values: none, gzip, zstd]
  -v, --verbose...                 Increase output verbosity (-v, -vv, -vvv)
      --level <LEVEL>              Compression level 1-19 [default: 3]
      --dry-run                    Show what would be done without writing anything
  -h, --help                       Print help
```

How field types map to argument kinds:

| Field type | Argument behaviour |
| ---------- | ------------------ |
| `T` (no default) | Required |
| `Option<T>` | Optional |
| `bool` | Flag (`--dry-run`) |
| `Vec<T>` | Can repeat or take several values |
| `u8` with `ArgAction::Count` | Counted flag (`-vvv`) |
| Field with `#[arg(short, long)]` | Option (`-c x`, `--compression x`) |
| Field without `short`/`long` | Positional argument |
| Any `T: FromStr`, or a `value_parser` | Parsed and validated automatically |

Related crates: `clap_complete` generates shell completion scripts and
`clap_mangen` generates man pages from the same definition. For very small
binaries where `clap`'s size and compile time matter, `lexopt` and `argh` are
lighter alternatives.

> Key Takeaways
> - `clap`'s derive API makes one struct serve as definition, parser, help
>   text and typed result.
> - Field types determine argument kinds: `Option` is optional, `bool` is a
>   flag, `Vec` repeats, enums with `ValueEnum` restrict the allowed values.
> - Doc comments become help text; `env = ".."` and defaults give fallbacks.
> - Test with `try_parse_from` and validate the definition with
>   `Command::debug_assert`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `restore` subcommand with a required `--id` and an optional
>    `--target` directory that conflicts with a `--in-place` flag (look up
>    `conflicts_with`).
> 2. Generate Bash and Zsh completions with `clap_complete` from a hidden
>    `completions <SHELL>` subcommand.
> 3. Interview: Why does `Cli::parse()` exit the process on error, and when
>    would you call `try_parse()` instead? (Hint: think about `--help`, which
>    is reported as an "error", and about programs that are not the main
>    binary.)

#### Logging and Tracing

`println!` debugging does not scale: you cannot switch messages on and off per
module, they mix with real output, and they carry no timestamps or context. A
logging system adds **levels** (error, warn, info, debug, trace), **targets**
(usually the module path) and runtime filtering, so a production binary can
run quietly and still be made verbose with an environment variable.

Rust separates the API from the implementation. Libraries call a lightweight
**facade** and never decide where output goes; the final binary installs one
**backend** that formats and filters it. This way a library does not force a
logging framework on its users.

```text
 your_lib ──┐                     ┌─► stderr (formatted)
 reqwest  ──┼─► facade (macros) ──┤
 sqlx     ──┘   log / tracing     └─► JSON file / OpenTelemetry
                                      (backend chosen by the binary)
```

Two facades exist:

| | `log` | `tracing` |
| - | ----- | --------- |
| Model | Individual messages | Events plus **spans** (time intervals with context) |
| Structured fields | Limited (`kv` feature) | Built in: `info!(user_id = 42, "login")` |
| Async-aware | No: interleaved tasks produce interleaved lines | Yes: spans follow a task across `.await` points |
| Typical backend | `env_logger` | `tracing-subscriber` |
| Use for | Small, synchronous tools | Servers, async code, anything with Tokio |

`tracing` is the default choice for new applications, and it can receive
`log` records from libraries that still use `log` (through the `tracing-log`
bridge, which `tracing-subscriber` enables by default).

A **span** represents a unit of work, such as handling one HTTP request. Every
event recorded while the span is active inherits its fields, so each log line
from deep inside a request handler automatically carries the request ID:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter", "json"] }
```

```rust
use tracing::{debug, error, info, info_span, instrument, warn};
use tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Order {
    id: u64,
    amount_cents: u64,
}

// #[instrument] creates a span per call, recording the arguments as fields.
// skip(order) avoids logging the whole struct; we record one field instead.
#[instrument(skip(order), fields(order_id = order.id))]
fn process(order: &Order) -> Result<(), String> {
    debug!("validating");                         // carries order_id automatically
    if order.amount_cents == 0 {
        warn!("zero-amount order");
        return Err("empty order".into());
    }
    charge(order.amount_cents)?;
    info!(amount = order.amount_cents, "order processed");   // structured field
    Ok(())
}

#[instrument]
fn charge(amount: u64) -> Result<(), String> {
    debug!("contacting payment provider");        // nested span: process > charge
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    // The binary decides: human-readable to stderr, filtered by RUST_LOG.
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(
            EnvFilter::try_from_default_env().unwrap_or_else(|_| EnvFilter::new("info")),
        )
        .with_writer(std::io::stderr)
        .init();

    let _batch = info_span!("batch", size = 2).entered();   // manual span
    for order in [Order { id: 1, amount_cents: 500 }, Order { id: 2, amount_cents: 0 }] {
        if let Err(e) = process(&order) {
            error!(error = %e, "order failed");    // %: record with Display
        }
    }
}
```

```text
$ RUST_LOG=info cargo run            # timestamps omitted
 INFO batch{size=2}:process{order_id=1}: my_app: order processed amount=500
 WARN batch{size=2}:process{order_id=2}: my_app: zero-amount order
ERROR batch{size=2}: my_app: order failed error=empty order
```

With `RUST_LOG=info,my_app=debug`, the `debug!` events appear as well, nested
as `batch{size=2}:process{order_id=1}:charge{amount=500}`. `RUST_LOG` uses
`EnvFilter` directives: `warn` (global level),
`my_app=debug` (per crate or module), `info,sqlx=warn` (a combination), and
even span-based filters such as `[process{order_id=2}]=trace`. In production,
switch the formatter to `.json()` for log aggregation systems, or add the
`tracing-opentelemetry` layer to export spans as distributed traces.

Rules of thumb:

- Libraries only use the macros and never install a subscriber.
- Never hold an `entered()` span guard across an `.await`: the span would be
  attached to whatever task runs next on that thread. Use `#[instrument]` on
  the `async fn` or `future.instrument(span)` instead.
- Do not log secrets: use `skip(password)` in `#[instrument]`, and consider
  wrapper types whose `Debug` output is redacted.

> Key Takeaways
> - Libraries log through a facade (`log` or `tracing`); only the binary picks
>   and configures a backend.
> - `tracing` adds spans and structured fields; spans give every event its
>   context, even across `.await`.
> - `#[instrument]` creates a span per function call; use `skip` and `fields`
>   to control what is recorded.
> - Filter at runtime with `RUST_LOG` directives, and log to stderr or a
>   structured sink rather than stdout.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add `tracing` to a small CLI. Use `-v`/`-vv` from `clap` (previous topic)
>    to select the default level when `RUST_LOG` is not set.
> 2. Switch the subscriber to JSON output and pipe it through `jq` to select
>    only events with `level == "WARN"`.
> 3. Interview: In an async web server, log lines from concurrent requests are
>    interleaved and impossible to attribute. How does `tracing` solve this,
>    and what mistake would break it? (Hint: span guards and `.await`.)

#### Configuration Management

Most applications need settings that change between environments: a database
URL, a port, feature switches, timeouts. Hard-coding them requires a rebuild
for each change; reading them in an ad-hoc way from several places scatters
parsing and validation across the codebase. The established approach is
**layered configuration**: define every setting once in a typed struct, then
fill it from several sources in increasing order of priority.

```text
priority    source                        typical content
  low       built-in defaults              port = 8080, log = "info"
   │        config file (app.toml)         per-environment settings, checked in
   │        environment (APP_*)            containers, CI, secrets
  high      command-line flags             one-off overrides
                    │
                    ▼
        merged and deserialized into  struct Config  (validated once)
```

Each layer overrides only what it specifies. The pattern follows the
"twelve-factor app" guideline of keeping deployment-specific configuration
in the environment, while still allowing readable files for local
development.

The `figment` crate implements this merging on top of `serde` (16.3); the
`config` crate offers a similar model. Both only need the target struct to
implement `Deserialize`:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
figment = { version = "0.10", features = ["toml", "env"] }
clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
```

```rust
use clap::Parser;
use figment::{
    providers::{Env, Format, Serialized, Toml},
    Figment,
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Config {
    port: u16,
    log_level: String,
    database: Database,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Database {
    url: String,
    max_connections: u32,
}

impl Default for Config {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Config {
            port: 8080,
            log_level: "info".into(),
            database: Database { url: "postgres://localhost/app".into(), max_connections: 10 },
        }
    }
}

/// CLI overrides: every field is optional and omitted when not given,
/// so it only overrides what the user actually typed.
#[derive(Parser, Serialize)]
struct Cli {
    #[arg(long)]
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    port: Option<u16>,

    #[arg(long, default_value = "app.toml")]
    #[serde(skip)]                                 // not a setting itself
    config: String,
}

fn load() -> Result<Config, figment::Error> {
    let cli = Cli::parse();
    let config: Config = Figment::from(Serialized::defaults(Config::default()))
        .merge(Toml::file(&cli.config))            // a missing file is silently skipped
        .merge(Env::prefixed("APP_").split("__"))  // APP_DATABASE__URL -> database.url
        .merge(Serialized::defaults(&cli))         // highest priority
        .extract()?;                               // deserialize + type-check everything

    // Cross-field validation that types alone cannot express.
    if config.database.max_connections == 0 {
        return Err("database.max_connections must be > 0".into());
    }
    Ok(config)
}

fn main() {
    match load() {
        Ok(cfg) => println!("{cfg:#?}"),
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("configuration error: {e}");   // names the key and the source
            std::process::exit(2);
        }
    }
}
```

```toml
# app.toml
port = 9000

[database]
url = "postgres://db.internal/app"
```

With this file, `APP_DATABASE__MAX_CONNECTIONS=50 app --port 7000` produces
`port = 7000` (CLI), the file's database URL, and 50 connections (env).

Practical advice:

- **Fail fast.** Load and validate the whole configuration at start-up and
  exit with a clear message; do not discover a malformed setting on the
  first request an hour later.
- **Pass the typed struct around** (or the relevant sub-struct) instead of
  reading environment variables deep in the code. This keeps functions
  testable.
- **Locate files per platform.** The `directories` crate returns the right
  config directory (`~/.config/app` on Linux, `~/Library/Application
  Support/...` on macOS, `%APPDATA%` on Windows).
- **Keep secrets out of files and logs.** Read them from the environment or a
  secrets manager, and wrap them in `secrecy::SecretString`, whose `Debug`
  output is redacted.
- **Reject typos.** `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` turns a misspelled key
  (`max_conections`) into an error instead of a silently ignored setting.

> Key Takeaways
> - Define configuration once as a typed, `Deserialize` struct and fill it
>   from layered sources: defaults, file, environment, CLI.
> - `figment` and `config` implement the merging; each layer overrides only
>   the keys it provides.
> - Validate everything at start-up and fail with a message that names the
>   key and its source.
> - Keep secrets out of config files and logs; use `deny_unknown_fields` to
>   catch typos.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add a `Profile` setting (`dev`/`prod`) and load `app.toml` plus an
>    optional `app.<profile>.toml` that overrides it.
> 2. Write a test that sets up a `Figment` from an inline TOML string and a
>    fake environment (see `figment::Jail`) and asserts the merged result.
> 3. Interview: Why is reading `std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")` directly inside
>    a repository function considered a design smell? (Hint: think about
>    testing, about start-up validation, and about where the full list of
>    settings is documented.)

<a id="163-serialization-and-data"></a>
### 16.3 Serialization and Data

Almost every program reads or writes structured data, whether configuration
files, API payloads, caches or database rows; this section covers `serde`, the
framework nearly the whole ecosystem uses for this, the main data formats, and
the two dominant approaches to SQL databases.

#### Serde Derive and Attributes

Without a framework, every pair of (type, format) needs its own code: a JSON
encoder for `User`, a TOML parser for `Config`, a binary writer for `Event`.
With N types and M formats that is N × M pieces of code. `serde` reduces it
to N + M by putting a common **data model** in the middle:

```text
 your types                serde data model                 formats
 ----------                ----------------                 -------
 struct User   ─Serialize─►  struct, seq, map,  ─Serializer──► JSON
 enum Event                  string, i64, f64,               TOML
 Vec<Order>  ◄Deserialize─   option, enum, ...  ◄Deserializer─ YAML, CBOR,
                                                               postcard, ...
```

A type implements `Serialize` and `Deserialize` once (almost always via
`#[derive]`), describing itself in terms of the data model. A format crate
implements `Serializer`/`Deserializer` once and works with every type. The
generated code is specialized at compile time (monomorphization), so there is
no reflection or runtime type inspection: serde is typically as fast as
hand-written code.

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
```

```rust
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]           // created_at <-> "createdAt"
struct User {
    id: u64,
    display_name: String,
    #[serde(default)]                         // missing in input -> Default (false)
    is_admin: bool,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    email: Option<String>,                    // omitted from output when None
    #[serde(rename = "tags", default)]
    labels: Vec<String>,
    #[serde(skip)]                            // never (de)serialized; uses Default
    session_cache: Option<String>,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), serde_json::Error> {
    let json = r#"{ "id": 7, "displayName": "Ada", "tags": ["math"] }"#;
    let user: User = serde_json::from_str(json)?;          // type drives parsing
    println!("{user:?}");

    let out = serde_json::to_string(&user)?;
    println!("{out}");   // {"id":7,"displayName":"Ada","isAdmin":false,"tags":["math"]}
    Ok(())
}
```

The most useful attributes:

| Attribute | Level | Effect |
| --------- | ----- | ------ |
| `rename_all = "camelCase"` | container | Rename all fields/variants (`snake_case`, `kebab-case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`, ...) |
| `rename = "x"` | field / variant | Use a different external name |
| `alias = "old"` | field | Also accept another name when deserializing (migrations) |
| `default` / `default = "path"` | field / container | Fill missing fields from `Default` or a function |
| `skip_serializing_if = "path"` | field | Omit a field based on a predicate |
| `skip` | field | Ignore the field entirely |
| `flatten` | field | Inline a nested struct's fields, or collect unknown keys into a `HashMap` |
| `deny_unknown_fields` | container | Reject input with unexpected keys |
| `transparent` | container | Serialize a newtype as its inner value |
| `try_from = "T"` / `into = "T"` | container | Convert through another type (validation, 16.1 newtypes) |
| `with` / `serialize_with` / `deserialize_with` | field | Custom logic for one field (next topics) |

**Enum representations** are the attribute choice that matters most, because
they must match whatever the other side of an API expects:

```rust
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]      // internally tagged
enum Event {
    Click { x: i32, y: i32 },
    KeyPress { key: char },
}
// Event::Click { x: 1, y: 2 }  ->  {"type":"click","x":1,"y":2}
```

| Representation | Attribute | `Click { x: 1, y: 2 }` becomes |
| -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------ |
| Externally tagged (default) | none | `{"Click":{"x":1,"y":2}}` |
| Internally tagged | `tag = "type"` | `{"type":"Click","x":1,"y":2}` |
| Adjacently tagged | `tag = "t", content = "c"` | `{"t":"Click","c":{"x":1,"y":2}}` |
| Untagged | `untagged` | `{"x":1,"y":2}` (tries each variant in order) |

Untagged enums are convenient for loosely typed input, but error messages
become unhelpful ("data did not match any variant") and every failed attempt
costs time. Prefer a tagged form when you control the format.

Libraries should not force serde on their users: put it behind an optional
feature (`serde = { version = "1", optional = true, features = ["derive"] }`)
and use `#[cfg_attr(feature = "serde", derive(Serialize, Deserialize))]`.

> Key Takeaways
> - serde separates types from formats through a shared data model, so each
>   type and each format is implemented only once.
> - `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` generates specialized code with no
>   runtime reflection.
> - Attributes adapt the external shape: `rename_all`, `default`,
>   `skip_serializing_if`, `flatten`, `deny_unknown_fields`.
> - Choose the enum representation deliberately; internally tagged is a common
>   match for JSON APIs.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Model this JSON with a struct and derive attributes only:
>    `{"order-id": 5, "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}], "note": null}`,
>    making `note` optional and rejecting unknown fields.
> 2. Write an internally tagged `Shape` enum (`circle` with `radius`, `rect`
>    with `w` and `h`) and print each representation from the table by
>    changing only the attribute.
> 3. Interview: Your service added a field to a response struct, and an older
>    client using `deny_unknown_fields` started failing. What are the
